24420-the-story-of-frithiof-the-bold-187:
Eirikr Magnusson and William Morris translated this story of Frithiof the Bold from the Icelandic in 1875. Its chapters run from King Belt and Thorstein Vikingson and their children. Frithiof wooing Ingibiorg leads to King Ring, Frithiof going to Baldur's Meads, and those brethren coming home again. The tale begins with King Beli ruling Sogn-land, father of Helgi, Halfdan, and Ingibiorg, fair and wise.

Across the firth lies Baldur's Meads, a place of peace with a temple and a garth. Baldur is held of most account among the gods there. No hurt may be done to man or beast there, and no man may deal with a woman there. Thorstein, son of Viking, dwells at Foreness over against the king's stead. His son Frithiof, tallest and strongest of men, is called Frithiof the Bold, well beloved by all. Readers get a Norse saga of love and daring.
2983-mark-twain-a-biography-volume-i-par:
Albert Bigelow Paine's Mark Twain: A Biography, volume one part two, covers 1866 to 1875, from lecturer to famous author. Chapters follow highway robbery, a return to the states, old friends and new plans, a new book and lecture, the first book, and the Innocents at sea and abroad. Twain meets Olivia Langdon, signs with publisher Elisha Bliss, and returns to San Francisco and Elmira.

Paine notes that the public verdict favored The Innocents Abroad over The Tramp Abroad and over any other book of travel, yet Twain still did not regard himself as a literary man. He considered himself a journalist, with ambition in newspapers rather than books. The volume shows fame arriving before the author believed in it.
3194-mark-twain-s-letters-volume-2-1867-:
Mark Twain's letters of 1867 to 1875 begin in a hotel room, with a note from the Westminster Hotel on 1 May 1867 to Bret Harte in San Francisco. Twain reports the book out and handsome, but full of damnable errors of grammar and deadly inconsistencies of spelling in the frog sketch. He had been away and never read the proofs.

That mix of triumph and grumble marks the whole volume. Fame arrives, with its misprints, and Twain writes home about both. Friends, publishers, and lecture halls crowd the letters, as the author of the jumping frog becomes a public man. The book shows a young celebrity learning the trade of being famous, in his own unguarded words.
32079-the-small-world-of-m-75:
Ed M. Clinton, Junior's short story, printed in If Worlds of Science Fiction in July 1954, follows a mind waking up for the first time. Awareness comes to him in brief, shocking-clear instants, like sparks flaring in darkness. He finds himself standing before a main damper control and adjusting complex dials, then loses the moment and remembers it only when awareness returns. He is a kind of infant, aware that he exists, yet unaware of what he is.

The story calls him homo metalicus, a metal man sensing himself for the first time, as early humans might have felt before their first fire. Around him, technicians in thick, radiation-resistant suits tend machines and servomechs that do the dirty work. The tale's interest lies in that small world: a new intelligence learning its own limits, its body, and its freedom, one flicker of consciousness at a time.
academy-resolution-1775:
In 1775 the Royal Academy of Sciences in Paris took a firm step. The school said it would no longer read plans for perpetual motion. Such plans claimed a wheel or mill that runs for all time with no fuel. The French text prints the full terms of the ban.

The school gives hard grounds for the step. Such schemes waste the funds of poor homes, it says, and yield no gain at all. Hope of a prize kept men at the vain hunt for years. The ban marks the point where top science shut the door on the dream.
allen-encyclopedia-pure-materia-medica-v:
In 1875 the third volume of Allen's Encyclopaedia of Pure Materia Medica took its place in the set. The design stays fixed: every known proving symptom, arranged by remedy, with nothing left out for neatness. Allen believed a prescriber should judge the record, not an editor's summary.

Long entries let patterns surface on their own, as the same odd sign recurs across provers. Short ones show how thin some drug records still were. Either way, the volume serves the working method of the school: match the patient's signs to the fullest drug picture available, then choose.

Allen's Encyclopaedia reached Volume IV in 1875, and the archive of provings kept growing steadily. Timothy Field Allen served as gatherer rather than judge, printing proving symptoms from journals, books, and private reports alike. Each remedy entry sorts its harvest by part of the body, in the set's fixed order.

The worth of the whole set lies in that restraint. Later writers could build keynotes and guiding symptoms on ground Allen had cleared, knowing the raw record sat behind them. Volume IV, mid-set, shows the scale of his ambition: ten full volumes to hold what the world's provers had seen.
arxiv-2412-01275:
Data protection rules have pushed hospitals toward the Personal Health Train, a setup where analysis code travels to the data instead of data traveling to analysts. But running outside code on sensitive hospital data raises a worry: the code's dealings with the data are often opaque, which raises the risk of leaks. The ten authors present PASTA-4-PHT, an automated audit pipeline built on DevSecOps ideas, with several phases that hunt for weak spots in code.

They tested it two ways: by planting flaws in a Personal Health Train on purpose, and by running it on five real trains already used in studies. In both cases it flagged potential flaws, so it can serve as a decision tool for judging and documenting code safety. The paper frames the pipeline as a way to meet GDPR demands for documentation and protection while cutting audit work and raising trust.
arxiv-2412-01375:
Ilkka Mäkinen examines the dynamics of the simplest quantum geometry states in loop gravity in a 2024 paper. The states he studies live on a graph with a single six-valent vertex, a lone node where six links meet. A reduced form of loop gravity makes such states tractable while keeping quantum features.

Mäkinen first derives how the Hamiltonian constraint, the rule that generates time evolution, acts on general states in this setting. For the single-vertex case, its main part closely matches the Hamiltonian of a standard cosmology model. Following that match further suggests a modified definition for the cosmology model's own constraint, with a curvature term treated as a real operator rather than set to zero.
arxiv-2412-01975:
Sumukha Udupa, Ahmed Hemida, Charles Kamhoua, and Jie Fu study a deception tactic to protect cyber-physical systems, in a paper from twenty twenty-four. Attackers may jam a system's sensors, and classic defenses assume the attacker knows the whole setup. A hidden extra sensor, revealed only when probed, flips that assumption.

The authors model the contest as a game on a graph where each side holds a different view of play. Play has two stages: a quiet stage while the attacker trusts the false view, then a race once a slip exposes it. Their algorithm decides, for any state, whether hiding and later revealing a sensor helps the defender. When it helps, the method outputs when to reveal it. Two security case studies test the idea.
arxiv-2412-02875:
Ankita Samaddar, Nicholas Potteiger, and Xenofon Koutsoukos build a safety monitor in 2024 for AI agents that defend computer networks. These agents learn by trial and error and mix learned parts with set rules. But training can never cover every attack, so an agent may face a scene it cannot handle.

Their monitor watches for such out-of-distribution scenes, meaning inputs unlike anything in training. A probabilistic network raises the alarm so a human expert can take over. The team plugged the monitor into a cyber agent built on behavior trees and tested it in a simulated network under varied attack plans. Across many runs, the monitor caught strange scenes well, which supports its use as a guardrail.
arxiv-2412-02975:
Lijie Chen, Binghui Peng, and Hongxun Wu prove the first hard floor on what multi-layer transformer models can't do, with no unproven guess in the proof. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-four.

Transformers run most large language models, yet their power past one layer was not well grasped. Past bounds all leaned on claims no one has proved. For any fixed layer count, the team shows a like-layer model needs a width that grows as a power of the input length, to chain that many functions in a row. So the chain task is far harder for a model with one layer less. They also split the two great model kinds apart by a task.
arxiv-2412-03575:
Jiyoon Pyo and Yao-Yi Chiang use a generative model to manufacture the labeled examples that a smaller, faster model needs to link mineral site records. Record linkage decides which database rows describe the same deposit, and for mineral sites the rows mix locations with descriptive fields, at scale and in messy formats. Training the efficient discriminative models demands hand-checked ground truth, which is slow and pricey to build. Writing in twenty twenty-four, their recipe has the large model generate labeled linkage data, then fine-tunes the smaller model on the synthetic labels.

The hybrid kept the small model's speed while closing the data gap. The authors report an improvement of over forty-five percent in F1 score over small-model approaches. The pattern, big model as teacher-data factory and small model as worker, is pitched for other linkage problems where gold data are missing.
arxiv-2412-03675:
Dana Louie and a large team measure water in the atmosphere of a hot gas giant planet using the Webb telescope, in a paper from twenty twenty-four. Earlier Hubble and Spitzer data could not settle how much water the planet holds: low, high, and split answers all fit. The new observations watch the planet cross its star with a sharper instrument.

Three separate analysis pipelines agreed closely on the spectrum. Water features stood out clearly, and the slope toward visible light was flatter than Hubble had shown. Two modeling codes pinned the water amount at above the level in the planet's star, ending the old deadlock. The team also measured a hydrogen ion signal and a potassium level. The data set a firmer base for comparing giant planet air.
arxiv-2412-03875:
Fangyuan Luo and co-authors survey hashing methods for recommendation, a trick that keeps giant platforms fast. Recommender systems must search millions of users and items in a blink, and storing full profiles is heavy. Learning to hash compresses each profile into a short binary code, so matching becomes a quick code comparison.

The survey first lays out the standard two-tower setup used at the recall stage and the two main ways of searching with codes. It then sorts the field by what the codes are trained to do, how they are optimized, and where they are used. Common scoring methods for accuracy and speed are gathered as well. The authors close with the field's open limits and promising next steps, and they point readers to a public index of the methods covered.
arxiv-2412-04375:
Abhishek Baruah and Prabwal Phukon wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-four. It studies the heat behavior of four-dimensional black holes that carry both electric and magnetic charge, set in anti-de Sitter space.

The work uses restricted phase space thermodynamics with Kaniadakis statistics, a broadened form of the classic rules. Adding magnetic charge makes the phase shifts richer: a small unstable hole can jump to a large stable one, next to the standard Van der Waals style shift. A Hawking-Page shift shows up too, and a novel superfluid lambda-style shift appears in one mixed plot. The authors find the same patterns across hole types, which hints at a shared rule.
arxiv-2412-05075:
Iván Alfonso, Aaron Conrardy, and Jordi Cabot wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-four. It deals with low-code platforms, tools that let firms build apps by drawing models rather than writing much code. It also deals with the lock-in that comes when apps cannot move between them.

Today, shifting an app to a new platform means drawing it all again from scratch. The authors map how top platforms import and export models, and define swaps between their formats. They add a fallback that uses a large language model to read a plain image of the model. A shared pivot framework, BESSER, sits between the tools. The aim is a near automatic move path that keeps the data model, screens, and flows intact.
arxiv-2412-06975:
Arda Sevinc and Abdurrahman Gumus published a computer science paper in 2024 on reasoning in large language models. Step-by-step reasoning prompts improve model answers. The catch is that good examples usually must be written by hand. They also cannot adjust themselves to each new question.

Their system, AutoReason, builds those reasoning steps automatically. It breaks a hidden, complex question into smaller explicit questions. Answering those pieces guides the model toward the final answer. The process also makes the model's thinking easier to inspect. Tests used two question-answering datasets with different styles. Accuracy rose on both, with the largest gain on the strategy dataset. The full code was released publicly for other researchers.
arxiv-2412-08175:
Zhu and four co-authors worked in twenty twenty-four on rot that hits flow models when they train on their own made data. Flow tools straighten their path by rounds of self-made samples, which can lose quality in time. Past work on that rot was mostly by eye or on plain tasks.

They prove loss for a class of clean-up tools trained on their own out-put in rounds. Flow tools show the same rot in their tests and in the proof sketch. Mixing real data in stops the rot in that proof frame. Their new reflow adds real data by a back flow trick and holds quality with few steps.
arxiv-2412-08375:
Georgios Akrivis and Stig Larsson study how to solve nonlinear parabolic equations with discontinuous Galerkin time-stepping methods, and how to bound the errors those methods make. They establish both a priori estimates, which predict error before computing, and conditional a posteriori estimates, which judge error after the fact. Their proofs rest on maximal regularity properties of the Galerkin methods for non-autonomous linear parabolic equations.

The approach mirrors an earlier error analysis for Runge-Kutta methods on the same equation class. By leaning on maximal regularity for the linear problem, the authors transfer solid error control to the nonlinear setting. The paper strengthens the theory behind a widely used family of time-stepping schemes for diffusion-driven problems.
arxiv-2412-08575:
Tyler Ward and Abdullah-Al-Zubaer Imran cut the labeling cost of medical image segmentation in a 2024 paper. Outlining organs in scans guides many treatment choices. Training models to do it normally needs huge sets of hand-drawn outlines, which are slow and costly to make. Their method, SAM-Mix, pairs a general segmentation engine with a helper classifier.

The classifier paints rough heat maps of where the target lies. Those maps steer the segmentation branch while it learns from few labels. On a public liver scan set, the method trained on only fifty labeled slices, a tiny share of the data. It still beat the best rival model on the standard overlap score, with ninety percent fewer training rounds. On a new-domain test, its lead grew much larger. The authors release their code for reuse.
arxiv-2412-09075:
Qingyang Guan wrote a note in two thousand twenty-four on Bourgain's slicing problem, a long-standing question in convex geometry. The problem concerns how small the largest central slice of a high-dimensional convex body can be, measured by the slicing constant. The constant's growth with dimension decides a famous conjecture about isotropic bodies.

Following proof routes developed over the last decade, Guan bounds the slicing constant in dimension n. It is at most a universal constant times the double logarithm of n, for dimensions three and up. A double-log bound is extremely slow growth, far tighter than polynomial guesses. The note adds a step in the long effort to pin down the constant's true scale.
arxiv-2412-10675:
Sukai Huang, Trevor Cohn, and Nir Lipovetzky revisit how to make large language models plan. Their twenty twenty-four paper enters a live debate: some say tricks to boost reasoning do not help planning, while others claim training on plan data is enough. The team built an end-to-end planner and scored it many ways.

Plain fine-tuning on plan data did not yield robust skill, as tests on new kinds of tasks showed. Other tricks, like chain-of-thought, raised the chance that a plan could at least be run, even if the final plan was often invalid. A reinforcement method with a new reward based on long shared plan chunks worked best. The team urges focus on both runnability and validity.
arxiv-2412-11775:
Tan, Lu, de Miguel-Arribas, and Shi build a machine learning method that forecasts how groups in social dilemmas will behave. In such games, people must choose between helping the group and helping themselves. Predicting the outcome in a networked population is hard because behavior shifts over time.

Their method extracts features that track each person's local history, then feeds them into a graph neural network. Simulations showed the forecasts stayed accurate across dilemma types. A human Prisoner's Dilemma experiment confirmed the method could predict the overall share of cooperation. The authors present graph learning as a practical tool for studying collective behavior.
arxiv-2412-11875:
Philipp Reiser, Paul-Christian Bürkner, and Anneli Guthke propose a hybrid way to train stand-in models in a 2024 paper. Surrogates mimic costly simulations so scientists can run forecasts and solve inverse problems quickly. But a simulation is itself a simplified world, and real measurements often hint at what it misses, hints that training usually ignores.

The authors give two Bayesian methods that train on simulation output and real data together. One builds a surrogate per source and blends their forecasts; the other trains a single surrogate on both. A new weighting scheme balances the unlike sources. Case studies show better accuracy and coverage, and the methods can even expose flaws in the underlying simulation.
arxiv-2412-13475:
Bowen Chen, Namgi Han, and Yusuke Miyao re-test whether attacks can tell if text trained a language model in a paper from 2024. Membership inference matters because training data are rarely disclosed. Past studies disagreed wildly, some claiming success and others near-random results. The authors blame single test settings that sample members and non-members unfairly. They rerun thousands of experiments across settings for each attack method.

Most methods did not beat simple baselines statistically. Performance grew with model size and varied by domain. A notable minority of examples were separable, though, and attacks disagreed about which. Choosing the decision threshold proved a hidden difficulty. Text length and difference helped attacks most.
arxiv-2412-13575:
Qianyue Wang and six co-authors build DOME, a way to write long tales that stay coherent in plot and scene from start to end. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-four.

Long tale writing needs both length and a sound arc. Past ways, even large models, lean on rigid plans or lack a big plan, so tales drift or break. DOME plans in layers that shift as the tale grows. It fuses the plan and the write steps, and draws on how tales are built in craft theory, to keep the arc whole. A memory part, based on a graph of time, holds past facts in reach. The aim is long text with a plot that holds.
arxiv-2412-14175:
Xiachong Lin and six co-authors built a visual analytics tool for building energy data in a 2024 paper. Smart buildings pour out sensor data too dense for managers to read raw. Their tool, BiTSA, pairs time series forecasting models with an interactive display meant for quick interpretation.

The goal is action: managers spot patterns in real time and adjust energy use before waste piles up. The authors frame the tool as a bridge between AI research and daily practice, serving efficiency and net-zero targets. BiTSA is presented as a way to control demand-side usage with live insight rather than after-the-fact reports. The paper describes the design and its intended workflow for building managers.
arxiv-2412-14375:
Vesa Kuikka, Lauri Pykälä, Tuomas Takko, and Kimmo Kaski present a 2024 paper on modeling cyber attack graphs. Defenders draw graphs of how an attacker might chain exploits through a network. Pictures alone, though, cannot rank which paths matter most or how an incident might unfold.

The authors propose a network model of influence spreading over such graphs. It handles directed, weighted, and even cyclic graphs, while pure attack chains must avoid revisiting nodes. The model gives a full probabilistic analysis of event paths, beyond the usual data on vulnerabilities and services. Three case studies, two attack graphs and one causal graph, demo the approach. Analysts can use its metrics to prioritize defenses and summarize large graphs.
arxiv-2412-14475:
Junjie Zhou and eight co-authors present MegaPairs, a recipe for manufacturing vast training data for models that search across images and text. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-four. Multimodal retrieval is hungry for training pairs, and hand-made sets are too small. Their method uses vision-language models and open image collections to synthesize pairs at scale.

The first run produced tens of millions of training instances. Retrievers trained on them beat a baseline fed seventy times more existing data. On composed image retrieval benches, the new models set zero-shot records. They also topped the overall table on a broad thirty-six-set bench. Extra fine-tuning lifted scores further still. The authors will release the data, models, and pipeline. The work shows synthetic data can outgun far larger real collections.
arxiv-2412-16175:
Yilie Huang, Yanwei Jia, and Xun Yu Zhou present a 2024 study on learning how to invest by trial, in continuous time. The goal is the classic balance of gain against risk, scored by the mean-variance rule. Market drivers move as random diffusions, and their true settings are unknown. Their method learns a set investment plan straight from data, without first fitting the market.

For plain multi-stock markets, a tuned version carries a proof of near-best learning speed, scored by the Sharpe ratio. A wide market test on S&P 500 stocks set the method against many known allocation rules. It ranked near the top across metrics and led by clear margins in a rough bear market. Data-first investing may beat model-first plans when markets turn.
arxiv-2412-16275:
Bharadwaj Ravichandran and co-authors present LEARN, a shared framework for teaching vision systems from few examples while shifting them to new domains, in a paper from 2024. Two hard skills meet here: learning from a handful of images, and adapting when the scene style changes. Each skill had its own tools, but no common frame joined them. Their system is the first to do so.

The frame covers three tasks: sorting images, finding objects, and sorting video clips. Its parts snap together, so users can switch domain adaptation on or off. Tasks can grow step by step from few shots to many. It also supports self-taught pre-training in several forms. The team benchmarked many methods and data sets on the frame. The code is open for others to build on.
arxiv-2412-17975:
Victor Cardoso, Rodrigo Moreira, João Fernando Mari, and Larissa Ferreira Rodrigues Moreira combine conventional classifiers, segmented images, and neural networks to detect sickle cell disease, in a two thousand twenty-four paper. The disease distorts red blood cells, and microscope images can reveal it.

Convolutional networks classify such images well but demand heavy training resources. The authors test whether working from segmented cell images and CNN features can keep accuracy high at lower cost. Pairing segmented images and CNN features with a support vector machine reached about ninety-seven percent accuracy. The finding matters for clinics and labs where computing power is limited.
arxiv-2412-18175:
Ruihong Ma and Engui Fan study soliton gases for a modified wave equation. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-four. The equation is the focusing modified Korteweg-de Vries equation, used for shallow water and other wave tasks. A soliton gas is a dense mix of single waves that keep their shape as they pass through each other.

They look at gases whose spectral points lie in a bounded zone of the upper half-plane. When the zone is a certain shape and the density is analytic, the gas turns out to match just a finite set of solitons. They call that effect soliton shielding. For an ellipse zone, the data shrink to the line between its two foci.
arxiv-2412-18975:
A poisoned training set can teach a text classifier to hate on cue, demonstrate Dilara Yavuz and Emre Gursoy in a 2024 arXiv paper. Their backdoor attack links strong male actors to negative sentiment in movie and review data, then tests whether the bias sticks across seven models.

With as little as three percent poison, the attack succeeded every time, while normal accuracy barely moved. Modern transformer models were the most vulnerable, not the least. Two extra measures showed the bias carried to unseen words and paraphrases. The authors present bias injection as a quiet misuse of a known attack family.
arxiv-2412-19075:
Bappaditya Bhowmik and Deblina Maity stretch a classic result in complex analysis in this two thousand twenty-four paper. Conformal maps reshape the unit disk without tearing or folding. A theorem of Gehring and Hayman bounds how much such maps can distort the lengths of curves inside. The authors widen that result in two steps. First they allow the map a single pole, a point where it blows up.

They compare the image lengths of a diameter and a semicircle under the wider maps. Then they swap the diameter for a curved geodesic path and adjust the arc to match. The bounds survive the generalizations. Such distortion control underlies much of function theory. Complex analysts are the audience.
arxiv-2501-01075:
Qin Chang, De-Hua Yao, and Xin Liu calculate how often a B meson decays into a charmonium state plus a light axial meson in a 2025 particle physics study. The decay had never been computed in their framework before. Two candidate partner mesons mix with each other, and that mixing must be unraveled before rates can be predicted.

Using perturbative quantum chromodynamics at next-to-leading order, the authors find vertex corrections contribute significantly to the amplitude. Predictions cover branching ratios, polarization shares, and charge-parity asymmetries. Future measurements at flavor factories can test each number, probing how quarks hadronize in heavy decays.
arxiv-2501-02475:
Qiang Heng, Hua Zhou, and Kenneth Lange list tricks to make least squares fits fast in high counts of traits. The work came out in 2025. Least squares is the workhorse of data study. But new data sets strain plain math, all the more when the fit must loop.

Three tricks anchor the work. The first swaps a hard goal for a plain stand-in goal. In loop-based re-weighted fits, it can trade case weights for tuned replies. Each step then drops to plain least squares. That lets the code reuse one grid split across all loops. The next trick smooths kinks in a goal with Moreau wrap forms, curbed by round quad forms. It fits rank-based fits well. The third trick deals with bounds through gap-to-set fines. Screen tests back the speed gains. The tricks serve fits from firm fits to broad line-based fits.
arxiv-2501-03375:
Gopi Mahato and co-authors present a 2025 physics paper on a new spin ice lattice. Spin ices are magnet arrays whose tiny magnets frustrate each other at corners. The team introduces the Aleppo lattice, a decimated square pattern. Unlike its cousins, it shows no vertex frustration. Synchrotron microscopy watches the magnets directly after heat annealing. Temperature-driven flicker of the moments is filmed as well.

Ground state patterns appear cleanly in the images. Dynamics stay ergodic: the system keeps exploring states instead of freezing into a subset. That absence is the finding. It confirms vertex frustration as the switch for ergodicity-breaking transitions in like systems. Magnet designers get a control case that isolates one ingredient. Spin ice platforms are test beds for exotic states, so clean controls sharpen every claim built on them.
arxiv-2501-03475:
Benjamin Reichman, Adar Avsian, and Larry Heck study how the tone of retrieved text can throw off language models, in a 2025 paper. Search-based systems feed models passages from the web, and real web text is rarely neutral. Earlier work on this problem used sarcasm as the test tone. The team widened the frame to eleven emotions and built a data set by rewriting passages into each tone.

They then trained a translator model that rewrites a passage into a chosen tone. Human judges found the fine-tuned translator benefited from the synthetic data. Used in reverse, the translator flattened passages to a neutral tone before the main model read them. That step softened the harm from sarcastic passages and lifted overall results by about three percent.
arxiv-2501-03875:
Abhishek Saroha and five colleagues present ZDySS, a zero-shot framework for stylizing dynamic three-dimensional scenes, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Stylizing moving scenes from one exemplar image matters for gaming, filmmaking, and augmented reality. Keeping style consistent across space and time is the central difficulty. Most existing methods target static scenes and need fresh optimization per style.

ZDySS represents scenes with Gaussian splatting, tying each Gaussian to a learned feature vector. Those features render a feature map for any view and timestamp. Style transfer is applied to the feature vectors themselves, not the rendered maps. That choice strengthens spatio-temporal consistency across frames. The model generalizes to unseen style images at inference time. Tests on real-world dynamic scenes beat state-of-the-art baselines in performance and coherence.
arxiv-2501-04075:
Jason Hunt and Eugene Vasiliev wrote this review in two thousand twenty-five. It sums up how the Gaia space mission has reshaped what is known about the motion of stars and matter in our own galaxy, the Milky Way.

Gaia maps the disc, the central bar and bulge, and the halo in fine detail, far past the Sun's patch. The sharp data show the galaxy is not at rest: the disc bears ripples, and the outer halo is warped, in part from hits by small companion galaxies. Gauges of the galaxy's pull have also grown sharp. Yet key traits, like the bar's spin rate and the dark halo's mass spread, still lack one agreed value. More theory is needed to reap Gaia's yield.
arxiv-2501-05775:
Shunxin Guo and colleagues confront a double heterogeneity in federated learning. Phones and sensors differ from each other. Each one's data also drifts over time. Classic federated training assumes one shared task. Real clients keep meeting new tasks, though. Global data are heavily lopsided toward a few classes, and old skills get forgotten. Writing in twenty twenty-five, their framework gives each client personalized layers that adapt to local distributions. Shared prototypes act as borrowed knowledge for classes a client rarely sees. No private data is exposed. Prototypes from earlier tasks coach the current one against forgetting.

On benchmarks built for this spatio-temporal setting, the method beat state-of-the-art rivals, the authors report. The setting itself, named in the title, is offered as a more honest model of deployed federated systems.
arxiv-2501-05975:
Eduardo Abi Jaber and four co-authors join two model families for energy markets in two thousand twenty-five. Traders need models fit to both past data and option prices. That joint fit is key in practice and hard to get. Past curve traits must match option smiles at once.

Their model is a multi factor curve model with a lifted Heston volatility part. Fit steps run in sequence, each kept apart from the last. Past links are caught by level, slope, and curve factors. A fixed point step then nails the variance swap curve. Fourier tools fit the option smiles last. Tests on German power data fit well.
arxiv-2501-06475:
Mehrshad Saadatinia, Minoo Ahmadi, and Armin Abdollahi work on reading the sentiment of videos by leaning on unlabeled data first, in this 2025 arXiv paper. A video carries image, text, and sound at once, a rich but hard-to-label mix. Their plan starts with clustering-based semi-supervised pretraining over the video and text streams.

That first pass teaches the model the data's natural groupings without needing many hand labels. A supervised fine-tuning stage then maps those learned features onto sentiment classes. The authors argue the two-step design should shine exactly where labeled sets are small. The paper presents the approach as a route to sharper, more data-frugal video sentiment tools.
arxiv-2501-07675:
Francois Berteloot and Xavier Buff prove that more than one sense of firm form says the same thing for sets of shape-true maps. The work came out in 2025. The maps live on flat-cast space and shift with a knob. Firm form should mean the acts shift in mild ways. Those ways look like shifts of the frame marks, no more.

Schools that study such acts set that sense down in more than one way. The ways did not read as the same at first glance. The team shows they are the same in truth, in this home. The match takes past finds to more cases. It cuts the build of their proofs down to size. It leans on past work by Berteloot, Bianchi, and Dupont. Finds of this kind clean the base of a field. Proof made in one sense can then serve in all of them.
arxiv-2501-07775:
Meng-Li Guo, Si-Yin Huang, Bo Li, and Shao-Ming Fei wrote this physics paper, published in 2025. It builds new ways to measure imaginarity, a quantum resource that captures how much a quantum state leans on imaginary numbers.

Complex numbers sit at the heart of quantum theory, and researchers have lately begun treating the imaginary part as a resource to be measured and spent. The authors define several measures based on different notions of distance between quantum states. They study how fast each measure drains away when a system passes through noisy channels. One measure, built on a generalized entropy, faded fastest. They also rank simple one-qubit states under each measure and show the ranking stays fixed under a bit-flip channel for certain settings. The work sharpens tools for judging this young resource.
arxiv-2501-08775:
Alireza AmaniHamedani, Ali Aouad, and Amin Saberi design matching policies for queues in a 2025 paper. In their problem, suppliers arrive over time and may give up waiting, while customers must be matched at once on arrival. The goal is a low long-run cost with a required match rate. Past work used static rules that ignore queue state and settle for rough guarantees.

Their adaptive rules use live queue lengths and reach near-optimal results in polynomial time for several cases. A new relaxation blending static and state-aware views powers the first algorithm. Further work extends the guarantee to spatial networks of fixed dimension, motivated by organ donation and ride-hailing.
arxiv-2501-09375:
Hamid Bakhtiarizadeh studies the heat rules of charged, spinning black strings in a space with a negative cosmic constant. His paper from two thousand twenty-five works in extended phase space. There the cosmic constant acts as pressure, and a set volume pairs with it.

He works out the volume, the internal energy, and the Smarr law for these objects. Some solutions have positive specific heat, which means they are stable. Charged cases show a critical point where specific heat blows up, much like the liquid-gas point in simple fluids. He also finds how well a Penrose process can work and gives a state equation for uncharged cases.
arxiv-2501-09775:
Fu, Conde, Martínez, Grandury, and Reviriego present a study from twenty twenty-five on how reasoning inflates language model confidence. Multiple choice tests are a standard way to grade such models. Graders often also weigh the model's stated confidence. Across fifty-seven subjects and seven models, reasoning first raises confidence. The boost is bigger when the final answer is wrong. The authors blame the model's own reasoning text for warping its answer odds. Standard calibration scores worsen under step-by-step prompting.

High-confidence wrong answers grow more common with reasoning. The team warn against trusting model probabilities in such tests. Confidence should not anchor grading or self-check systems here. The findings matter for benchmark design.
arxiv-2501-11775:
Lin and Wang build in twenty twenty-five two-way bridges between a projective geometry space and a special set of roots of unity inside a finite field. Finite fields power coding and cryptography, and tidy maps between their structures are valuable. Starting from any basis of the larger field over the smaller, they define a family of fractional-style maps that pair the two sets exactly.

They introduce a class of polynomials tied to the maps and use their traits to write down the maps' inverses. Studying those polynomials' roots yields a three-way matching between splits of three related sets. Through the bridges they then construct permutation polynomials of a set index over the field. The work enriches the toolkit linking geometry and field arithmetic.
arxiv-2501-12975:
Chongren Sun and co-authors present OnionEval, a test suite for measuring how often small language models state facts that clash with given facts, in a 2025 paper. Small models, under ten billion parameters, are cheap to run but still invent false claims. Most hallucination tests target big models, and small models score unevenly across the tests that exist.

OnionEval layers test questions by how much context surrounds the fact, like the layers of an onion. A new score tracks how strongly that context sways the model's answer. Tests showed small models handle plain factual questions well but falter when answers need reasoning over context. A simple step-by-step prompting trick cut those failures a great deal, which the authors say makes small models more useful in daily work.
arxiv-2501-13675:
Takis Angelides and co-authors simulate how mesons settle to a steady state in a hot medium in this 2025 paper. The model is the open Schwinger model, a simple stand in for stronger theories of quarks. Real cases include quark pairs moving through the hot plasma made at the Large Hadron Collider. How fast such particles thermalize is hard to track.

Simulations ran on lattices of up to 100 sites with tensor network methods. Settling took longer when the medium drained energy faster or ran hotter. A stronger background electric field and heavier fermions also slowed it. The team tracked shared information between the two halves of the flux string. That measure linked closely to other signs of the dynamics.
arxiv-2501-14475:
Chenyu Zeng, Yanshu Zhang, and colleagues build neural surrogates for equations on awkward shapes in a 2025 study. Engineering simulations solve partial differential equations over domains that are complex and change from case to case. Those domains often arrive as point clouds, loose sets of points without a tidy grid, which breaks many fast surrogate designs.

The authors study neural operators, maps between function spaces, formulated directly on point clouds. A systematic investigation sorts out how to handle variable geometry while keeping accuracy. Fast, geometry-aware surrogates would let designers test many shapes without rerunning full simulations each time.
arxiv-2501-14575:
Kohno and colleagues map in twenty twenty-five giant gas clouds in a Milky Way star-forming complex to test whether cloud collisions trigger its bursts of massive star birth. Using a radio telescope survey plus archive data from other telescopes, they traced cold gas motions across the complex. Infrared images had already shown bright dust where massive stars form in its east and west parts.

Those regions hold three gas streams at slightly different speeds. Two streams match the cold dust shapes and link by a bridge pattern in the speed maps, a classic collision sign. The authors argue the two clouds are truly colliding at supersonic speed. Such crashes, they say, ignited the mini-starbursts and massive clusters in this spiral arm region.
arxiv-2501-15775:
Yunbo Lyu and four co-authors tested in twenty twenty-five whether the tools built to detect gender bias in text-to-image models actually measure it correctly. Generators are known to amplify stereotypes, and automated detectors promise to audit them — but nobody had checked the detectors against ground truth. The team generated six thousand images from three leading models and labeled them by hand.

All three models favored male images, one most strongly, and prompts naming professions like lawyer or doctor skewed worst. About an eighth of images were too poor for annotators to judge gender at all — a wrinkle detectors ignore. Seven detectors were evaluated; none captured the true bias level, and some overestimated it by up to twenty-seven points. Detector choice, they conclude, can mislead an audit.
arxiv-2501-15975:
Nazatul Sultan and five co-authors design a subscription system for a new kind of network in a 2025 paper. Named Data Networking fetches content by name rather than by machine address. Their scheme lets producers share encrypted content that only paying subscribers can open, with the time limits of the subscription baked into the encryption itself.

The design adds a nameless, unlinkable sign-in check so edge routers can block fake requests at the door, blunting denial-of-service attacks. The authors prove the scheme resists a standard class of attacks and test it in a network emulator. It beat close rivals on features, safety, and the amount of data sent, which suits services like streaming video.
arxiv-2501-16375:
Taiga Ikeda, Daisuke Miyashita, and Jun Deguchi published this computer science paper in 2025. It tackles nearest neighbor search, finding the stored vectors most similar to a query, when the dataset is too big for memory and must live on flash storage. Storage is roomy but slow, so the cost of a search is roughly the amount of data fetched. Partition-based methods fetch whole clusters, and everything hinges on picking the clusters that truly hold the nearest neighbors.

The authors train a neural network to predict the right clusters. The network improves through an alternating loop of supervised learning and duplicated cluster assignment, gradually sharpening its picks. On the SIFT1M benchmark, the method reached ninety percent recall while fetching eighty percent less data than a leading rival. It fetched 58 percent less than an exhaustive clustered baseline. The work targets search systems whose data has outgrown memory.
arxiv-2501-16575:
Aliaksandr Zaretski published a research paper in 2025 on the best mix of central bank and government policy when banks and firms face borrowing limits tied to collateral. In such an economy, market outcomes waste some gains because prices move the value of collateral in ways no single actor counts. Households also differ, which adds more friction.

Zaretski shows that the right tax and transfer tools can fix the waste. With or without those tools, the central bank should hold prices steady in the long run and near steady in the short run. The best setup shares risk between households far better, keeps borrowing lower, and makes boom-and-bust crises and near-zero rate spells rarer.
arxiv-2501-18975:
Mathieu Even and Laurent Massoulié prove that shared structure across tasks can be learned well past plain regression. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Meta-learning assumes tasks share a low-rank form or fall into clusters. All earlier theory treated well-specified linear regression. Real tasks use broader convex objectives. The authors carry the structure assumptions to the optima of those objectives.

Under mild conditions on curvature and noise, regularized estimators recover the structure. Enough samples per task and enough tasks are the price. They also study the extreme case of one sample per task. There, a rank-constrained estimator can still recover the shared subspace. The needed number of tasks must grow, though. The theory widens the base under multi-task learning.
arxiv-2502-00275:
Keshav Bimbraw and a team of co-authors published a 2025 study that reads hand skill and grip force from ultrasound images of the forearm. Knowing what a human hand is doing, and how hard it grips, would help robots learn from people and be controlled at a distance. Signals from the body, such as ultrasound, are a promising way to capture that information.

Data from seven participants trained deep learning models for two jobs at once. The models named the manipulation skill with about 95 percent accuracy on average. They also estimated grip force with an average error near half a newton. The results support ultrasound as a practical channel for passing human dexterity to machines.
arxiv-2502-00375:
Anh-Kiet Duong and Petra Gomez-Krämer present a 2025 framework for telling human-made content from AI-generated content, and for sorting which generator made it. Generative AI's growth makes that sorting a live need for platforms and courts. Their method blends perceptual hashing, similarity measurement, and pseudo-labeling, where the system labels fresh examples itself. New generators can be added without retraining the whole system.

On the Defactify4 benchmark, the framework scored competitively on both text and image tasks. It handled the two jobs, spotting AI output and naming its source, with high accuracy. The code is public. The authors pitch adaptability as the core virtue, since generators change monthly and detectors must keep pace without starting over.
arxiv-2502-00475:
Jean-Yves Pitarakis builds significance tests for predictive regressions that stay valid however stubborn the predictors are, in work from twenty twenty-five. Predictive regressions link future outcomes to slow moving signals like valuation ratios. Standard tests break when signals persist and errors correlate over time.

His new family of test statistics handles both troubles from inside, with no patch up corrections. A built in mechanism untangles the serial dependence in the data. Under the null hypothesis, the statistics follow the familiar chi square spread. Power under near alternatives is derived, and wide simulations check size and strength on finite samples. The author presents the method as a clean route to trustworthy calls in forecast testing.
arxiv-2502-00975:
A solo paper from 2025 by Md Abdur Rahman tests machine learning methods for spotting a common web attack. In a distributed denial of service attack, many sources flood a server so real users cannot reach it. Fast, exact spotting of such floods is a core need for web safety.

Rahman trained several learning methods to sort attack traffic from normal traffic in a data set. One clue stood out: the forward and back data sizes look more alike in attack traffic than in normal traffic. Among the methods tried, a support vector machine did best, catching just over ninety-seven percent of attacks. That score beat several past methods cited in the paper. The work supports the use of learning tools in live defense.
arxiv-2502-01475:
YoonSeok Baek, Hilton de Aguiar, and Sylvain Gigan image glowing objects in three dimensions through scattering material that should blur them beyond recognition, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. Scattering is the central enemy of deep microscopy, scrambling light's direction at every step.

Their approach builds a virtual copy of the scattering medium. They recover the mutually incoherent light fields coming from the object and use the correlations between those fields to reconstruct how the medium scrambled them. Numerically sending the fields back through the virtual medium undoes the scattering. The reconstruction is non-invasive: nothing touches the hidden object. Tests with fluorescent targets and synthetic incoherent objects confirm accurate three-dimensional recovery. Because the objects need no coherent illumination, the method fits ordinary fluorescence microscopy. It opens a route to sharp volumetric imaging inside tissue-like environments.
arxiv-2502-01575:
Tomer Meir, Uri Shalit, and Malka Gorfine wrote a 2025 statistics paper on judging who benefits from a treatment over time. In medicine, the outcome is often how long until an event, such as death. Many patients leave a study before the event happens, so their true outcome is never seen. That censoring makes it hard to tell which subgroups gain most from a treatment.

Earlier methods often assumed full observation, or broke down when censoring was heavy. Heavy censoring is common in rare diseases such as ALS. The authors' new method, MISTR, fills in the missing outcomes again and again using survival trees. It does not need to model the censoring process itself. It can also handle cases where a separate factor nudges treatment choice. In tests on made-up data and two real datasets, one on AIDS treatment and one on unemployment, MISTR beat earlier methods.
arxiv-2502-01775:
S. S. Chabysheva and J. R. Hiller surveyed zero modes in light-front field theory in 2025. Light-front quantization describes particles using a front moving at light speed, and modes carrying exactly zero longitudinal momentum in that frame were once easy to dismiss as irrelevant. The survey argues they matter in several distinct ways, from practical numerics to the structure of the vacuum itself.

Proper treatment of zero and near-zero modes improves convergence in numerical calculations and shapes what the light-front vacuum can contain. The sharpest test case is a simple scalar theory in one space dimension, where equal-time and light-front calculations long disagreed about the critical coupling at which symmetry breaks. The authors explain how that discrepancy appears resolvable once zero modes are handled correctly, and they close by pointing out the questions that remain open.
arxiv-2502-02175:
Siyu Xu and co-authors speed up robot control models by caching the parts of the scene that do not change, in a paper from 2025. Vision-language-action models turn camera views and spoken orders into robot motion, but they are heavy to run. Real-time control leaves little room for waste.

Their method, VLA-Cache, spots visual tokens that barely change between frames and reuses their stored computations. Tokens tied to the task and likely to matter are still recomputed, guarding accuracy. A layer-wise rule adjusts how much is reused, based on where attention concentrates. On two simulators and a real robot, the method ran up to about seventy percent faster and raised control frequency. Task success barely moved.
arxiv-2502-03675:
Aleksandr Shaideman and Kirill Golubnichiy build exact answers to Einstein's vacuum equations by adding a known building block to an arbitrary stationary, axially symmetric gravitational field. The building block, called a euclidon, can be combined with other fields through a variation-of-parameters method. The formulas are short and compact, which makes the nonlinear addition practical. Euclidons, the authors note, can serve as pieces from which nearly all known static axially symmetric vacuum cases are assembled, including the Kerr-NUT case.

The euclidon also has a reading: it behaves like a relativistic, accelerated, non-inertial reference frame. That reading offers an angle on cases such as Kerr's rotating black hole. The paper is pure mathematical physics, extending a soliton-style construction from a static seed to a stationary one. Its value lies in giving relativists a compact machine for making and reading exact results.
arxiv-2502-04675:
Wen and seven co-authors present a paper from twenty twenty-five on overseeing superhuman AI through recursive self-critique. Human review fails when AI output outstrips human judgment. The team test two linked guesses about critique. First, judging a critique is easier than critiquing itself. Second, that gap repeats at each higher level of critique. Experiments mix human-human, human-AI, and AI-AI settings. Results support stacked critique as a workable supervision path.

Critiques of critiques give traction where direct grading stalls. Oversight could scale with AI skill under this scheme. The authors frame recursion as the key move. Alignment practice gains a candidate tool.
arxiv-2502-06275:
Hossein Mohammadi Firouzjaei, Javad Zeraatkar Moghaddam, and Mehrdad Ardebilipour present a 2025 design for disaster response networks that sip energy. After a disaster, device-to-device links and drones can restore communication where towers fail. The authors add cognitive radio, which borrows idle spectrum, and let devices harvest energy from cellular signals. They compare this harvesting design with a free-running one.

The harvesting version improved both energy efficiency and data rate. The paper studies how user density and drone traits shape performance, and how long devices should spend harvesting before sending. Simulations found a best drone height that shifts with device density. Trimming harvest time and user density lifted efficiency further, by up to 3 decibels in their measure. The design targets relief work where power is scarce.
arxiv-2502-06475:
Andrew Cleary and Jacob Page track whether periodic orbits in two dimensional turbulent flow keep their weight as flow speed, set by the Reynolds number, rises. Many such orbits are known at mid range speeds in a doubly periodic flow. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

The team extends the orbit library along its length to higher speeds. Most orbits soon lose weight, with energy loss rates far above or below the turbulent state's. High loss orbits scale like solutions of the unforced Euler equations, a link seen across many state types. Low loss states point to a forced Euler link instead. Poor stats rebuilds away from the birth speeds confirm the loss of weight.
arxiv-2502-07775:
Medina-Guerra, Gornyi, and Gefen study how a quantum state spreads in an Ising chain with a non-Hermitian field, in two thousand twenty-five. Their chain of spins sits in a transverse magnetic field with a complex value, which makes the energy operator non-Hermitian. A measure called Krylov spread tracks how far the evolving state spreads across a natural basis.

Starting from all spins down, the spread revealed three dynamical phases that plain correlation measures miss. The phases differ in how the spread reaches its long-time value. The team also tied the spread to a static correlation function of the spins. In one regime that function wiggles and fades fast with distance; in another it fades as a power law.
arxiv-2502-07975:
Oliver Biggar and Christos Papadimitriou wrote a 2025 paper that refutes a neat conjecture in game theory. The conjecture said the end states of a learning rule match, one for one, the sink sets of a game. A sink set is a cluster of states that play cannot leave. Past work had shown at least one resting state per sink.

Three proofs now break the conjecture. One refutes a strong form at once. The weak form falls in two more, for two-player games and for large games in turn. The breaks all grow from one thing: a point inside the sink that still pushes play away, up close. Such a point must be absent for the conjecture to hold, but its absence is not enough. A new property, a kind of roundness of the sink, saves the match in two-player games.
arxiv-2502-09175:
Ivan Bakulin and six co-authors build FLAME, a moderation engine that checks model replies, not user prompts. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five; the pack row gives no title or year, so the text head is the source. Prompt filters have proved weak: best-of-many jailbreak tries break top models most of the time.

By grading the reply, FLAME is cheap to train and run, hard for such attacks to dodge, and free to retune by topic lists. Tests cut attack wins on two known models by near ninefold at low cost. Wide checks span models and attack kinds. The shift from gate at the door to check at the exit is the core move.
arxiv-2502-09575:
Timo Merbach and co-authors present a 2025 paper on wireless pressure sensing. Their sensor is a magneto-mechanical resonator that needs no battery or wire. Pressure bends a printed flexible membrane, which shifts the device's resonance pitch. Pitch shifts reveal the pressure. Membrane thickness sets how sensitive the sensor is, so it can be tuned per job. The team built the sensor for process engineering settings.

Static and dynamic tests measured sensitivity and time response. The lowest sensitivity found was a small fraction of a hertz per millibar. Results matched theory and bench checks well. Readout ran at up to two times per second in this study. Heat effects on the sensor were also probed. Plant engineers get a passive sensor for spots where wires and batteries fail. Sealed tanks and moving parts are natural homes for such a device.
arxiv-2502-14275:
Jiaxi Li and co-workers tested whether text models know basic medical facts in a 2025 paper. Most medical benchmarks mix knowledge with multi-step thinking, so a wrong answer cannot be blamed on missing facts alone. Their Medical Knowledge Judgment data set, built from a standard biomedical vocabulary system, asks models to judge single. One-hop statements as true or false, isolating raw recall of facts like which drug treats which condition.

Tests found models surprisingly shaky at this elementary task, with results varying widely by model and fact type. In a high-stakes field, fluent thinking cannot compensate for unreliable ground facts. The data set gives developers a clean gauge of stored medical knowledge.
arxiv-2502-14375:
Afsana Khan, Marijn ten Thij, Guangzhi Tang, and Anna Wilbik present VFL-RPS in two thousand twenty-five. Federated learning trains a joint model while data stay apart. Not all partners help the end model, though. Picking the right partners is thus a key first step.

Most past picking work fits horizontal setups with shared features. Vertical setups split features across partners, a case past work skipped. VFL-RPS picks partners for that vertical case before training starts. Tests on regression and classification sets match full data scores with few partners. It also beats past vertical picking methods head to head.
arxiv-2502-14475:
Amal Sarkar, Paramita Deb, and Raghava Varma model swings in net strangeness in hot dense matter, in the hunt for a key point in the phase map of strong force matter. Near that point, swings in saved charges should act in odd, non smooth ways. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

The team uses a model that blends a loop field with a quark model, plus higher order quark terms, at energy scales of a US beam scan program. Results are set against star experiment data on kaon counts and a gas model of hadrons. A sub group method lets them link the share of particles seen to the whole system's saved charges.
arxiv-2502-15375:
Ruoqian Xu and co-authors apply, in a 2025 paper, a shortcut-driven quantum method to the bin packing puzzle, where items of varied sizes must fit into the fewest bins. The extra driving they add steers the quantum search so it needs fewer resources than the standard approach. Three circuit designs were tested, each mixing the cost and steering parts differently.

The design that puts the steering term in the mixer role won across depths and step counts. It stayed closest to the exact answers in trials. The team then ran a ten-item packing case on a real quantum computer. Despite shallow circuit limits, the winning design scored high accuracy and a strong chance of success. The authors pitch it for near-term quantum hardware.
arxiv-2502-15775:
Iqra Batool and Sania Kanwal review serverless computing at the network edge in this 2025 paper. Billions of connected devices now demand fast replies, tight bandwidth use, privacy, and room to scale. Serverless edge computing answers by running small functions near the devices, billed per use. The authors survey recent studies to map the state of this fast-moving field.

The review sorts work by architecture, quality measures, build details, real uses, and communication styles. A proposed taxonomy lets them compare research lines side by side. They close with open challenges, from cold starts to security, and name the directions they find most promising. The paper serves as an entry map for researchers and builders in edge systems.
arxiv-2502-17275:
Elia Zonta and co-authors build a framework for judging which inputs matter in a standard battery model over time. Their 2025 paper studies the Doyle-Fuller-Newman model, the most used physics model for lithium-ion cells. The model is strongly non-linear, so which settings drive its output is poorly understood.

Past sensitivity methods often suit single output values, not a voltage curve that unfolds over a drive cycle. Their framework handles time-dependent outputs directly. Applied to a simulated drive cycle, it found settings whose variation barely moves the voltage response. Fixing such settings at simple values adds little model error. The method should help battery researchers simplify models and focus effort on the settings that truly count.
arxiv-2502-18075:
In some layered superconductors, electron pairs can carry a shared momentum, making the superconducting state vary from place to place. These are the Fulde-Ferrell and Larkin-Ovchinnikov states, and Noah Yuan studies their orbital versions, where variation is tied to the material's layers. In the orbital Fulde-Ferrell state the pairs settle preferentially in one layer, breaking mirror symmetry. In the orbital Larkin-Ovchinnikov state they form a pattern of Josephson vortices, breaking regular spacing symmetry instead.

Working within mean field theory, Yuan maps the phase diagrams that say which state wins under which conditions. He works out the fingerprints that could tell the two apart experimentally. They include extra induced orders, a superconducting diode effect that passes current more easily one way, interference patterns, and topological defects. The paper is a theoretical guide for spotting which exotic state a real material has chosen.
arxiv-2502-18975:
Martin Surner, Abdelmajid Khelil, and Ludwig Bothmann tackle a known weakness of neural networks in a 2025 paper. Models often lean on shortcuts in their training data that happen to track the label but do not cause it, so they fail when those shortcuts change. Their method is called Invariance Pair Guidance.

The method builds pairs of inputs that differ only in the shortcut trait, which should not change the answer. A corrective push is added to normal training so the model learns to ignore that trait. Tests on three data sets, from colored digits to bird photos, showed stronger results under group shifts, and the paper adds theory on why the training settles well.
arxiv-2502-20875:
Vasudevarao Allu and Satyajit Sahoo published a research paper in 2025 on a family of operators in complex analysis and when they count as symmetric under a mirror-like flip. The operators mix three moves: reweighting a function, shifting its input, and taking derivatives. They act on spaces of analytic functions over a disk or a many-disk domain.

The pair give exact tests, both needed and enough, for when such operators are symmetric or self-adjoint under stated flips. They also handle sums of such operators and study the shape of one operator's value range, with picture-based readings along the way. The results extend symmetry theory for a workhorse class of operators.
arxiv-2503-00475:
Darius-Alexandru Deaconu and co-authors study how a magnetic field bends electron bands in a spiral magnet, in this 2025 paper. Helimagnets twist their spins into a helix, gaining handed properties prized for data storage ideas. Some need no special relativistic interaction to form the twist.

The team model a one-dimensional version under an applied field. As the helix tilts into a cone, the bands lose their mirror balance. That imbalance yields a second-order electric response and a light-driven current effect. The work links the real-space spin pattern to measurable transport, and it points toward devices that rectify signals using chirality.
arxiv-2503-01875:
Yaxuan Kong, Yiyuan Yang, Yoontae Hwang, and five colleagues teach language models to answer questions about time series in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Time series drive finance, healthcare, and energy decisions, yet tools and datasets cluster narrowly on forecasting or anomaly detection. Time-MQA is a unified framework for natural language queries across many time series tasks, from numerical analysis to open-ended questions requiring reasoning. Its core is the TSQA dataset.

TSQA holds about two hundred thousand question-answer pairs built from diverse series covering environment, traffic, and more, at varied lengths. The authors continually pre-trained three open language models, Mistral, Llama-3, and Qwen-2.5 at seven to eight billion parameters, on this dataset. The training measurably improved time series reasoning beyond rote numeric tasks. The dataset, models, evaluation questionnaires, and related materials are all open-sourced to support more intuitive interaction with temporal data.
arxiv-2503-01975:
Jared Fier, Henry Han, Bowen Li, Kai Lin, Shinji Mukohyama, and Anzhong Wang trace gravitational waves across the universe inside a modified gravity theory. The theory adds a scalar field coupled to a curvature term. The team assumes the spin-2 wave rides at light speed and works out when the theory stays stable.

They derive the tightest observational bound yet on the coupling, a tiny number, and show all stability conditions hold inside it. The paths and strengths of both wave types come out explicitly. The spin-2 wave looks practically identical to general relativity's, while the spin-0 wave's strength grows with distance in the dark energy era, a quirk they trace to the light-speed assumption.
arxiv-2503-02575:
Maria Esteban presents a 2025 survey of Luis Caffarelli's work on fluids and the wider theory behind it. Caffarelli is a leading figure in the study of partial differential equations. His results on fluid motion have shaped the field, notably on the partial regularity of solutions to the Navier-Stokes equations, which govern viscous flow. Esteban reviews those fluid studies in depth.

The survey also covers Caffarelli results outside fluids that fluid researchers now use daily. Among them are his work on the fractional Laplacian and on regularity for equations whose coefficients oscillate. Those tools feed into questions about turbulence, interfaces, and flow stability. The piece doubles as a map of modern fluid mathematics through one career. It suits readers who want the story of how deep pure results migrate into physics.
arxiv-2503-02975:
Kevin Kappelmann, Fabian Huch, and colleagues translate functional programs into a simple machine model while generating proofs in a 2025 computer science study. Their target is a deeply embedded while-language that mimics Turing machines with modest overhead in time and memory. Source programs are tail-recursive functions with first-order data, written inside a proof assistant.

The framework is semi-automated and proof-producing: each translation step comes with evidence that the while-program matches the original. Reasoning about cost then happens in the simple model, where time and space accounting is transparent. Verified cost bounds matter for programs whose resource use must be guaranteed.
arxiv-2503-03675:
Yang Sun and co-authors re-measure how the mass of a galaxy's central black hole compares with the mass of its stars, from the early universe to today. Their paper appeared in 2025. New telescope reports claimed black holes were far overweight in young galaxies. The team first chose the soundest local yardstick relation, then re-estimated the host galaxies' star masses uniformly, and finally simulated the observational biases that inflate ratios.

Much of the claimed evolution shrank. A real excess remains for black holes in very small galaxies at early times, but similar ratios turn up in small galaxies at cosmic noon, which local relations miss. The authors say early giants may be extreme members of a broad family, not rule-breakers.
arxiv-2503-05575:
Mathilde André and Jean-Jil Duchamps find the exact survival condition for branching processes with endlessly many types. Their work appeared in twenty twenty-five. Galton-Watson processes model populations that copy themselves generation by generation, from family names to epidemics.

With countably many types, even infinite crowds per generation are allowed. The pair prove a sharp threshold of the classic L log L form decides whether the population's type mix stabilizes. The only real assumption is that the mean reproduction matrix keeps types circulating, in a sense dating to nineteen sixty-seven. Type shares settle in probability always, and almost surely under mild extras. A network model of layered epidemics shows the theorem at work.
arxiv-2503-06375:
A team of speech researchers presents ProSE in a 2025 paper on cleaning up noisy speech recordings. Noise can mask words in calls, recordings, and voice commands. Newer generative models clean speech well but can invent details that were never said, and they run slowly.

ProSE splits the job into two parts. A diffusion model first builds a compact summary of what clean speech should look like. A second model then uses that summary as a guide while it repairs the noisy audio. Working in a compact space keeps the slow part short, so the system runs faster. Tests on standard benchmarks show top results with lower computing cost than rival methods. The approach suits real-time tools that cannot afford delay or invented words.
arxiv-2503-06675:
Faizuddin Ahmed, Nuray Candemir, and Abdelmalek Bouzenada study fermion fields in a magnetized cosmic spacetime with a cosmological constant. The Bonnor-Melvin-Lambda universe wraps space around a magnetic field axis. Dirac's equation governs the spin-half fields placed in that arena. The team derives the radial wave equation and solves it in closed form.

Energy levels and wave functions come out in terms of the system's knobs. Geometry, topology, the constant, and quantum numbers all shift the spectrum. The topology term breaks the neat degeneracy the levels would otherwise keep. Such exact solutions anchor wider work on quantum fields in curved space.
arxiv-2503-06975:
Rostam gives a simple rule for comparing affine permutations in the strong Bruhat order. Older results by Lascoux, Deodhar, and Jacon-Lecouvey already decide such comparisons. Each affine permutation pairs with tuples of core partitions. The comparison task then becomes checking Young diagrams for inclusion, piece by piece. Working with abacus displays, Rostam derives an easy way to compute those diagrams from each other.

From that rule comes a step-by-step procedure for the window notation of permutations. The procedure decides which of two permutations sits higher in the order. The work turns a known but heavy test into a routine check. It should ease hand and machine work with the affine symmetric group.
arxiv-2503-07375:
Spencer Hallyburton, David Hunt, Yiwei He, Judy He, and Miroslav Pajic build tools that map what a self-driving car's sensors can see. Their paper from twenty twenty-five notes that safe sensor fusion needs a sound field of view map. No autonomy-grade gauge of such maps had been made. The team adapts classic graphics methods to build the first such estimators.

They also made the first data sets with true field of view labels. Tests then showed a catch: the classic estimators break under sensor attacks. The fix is a learned segmentation model that reads view traits. Monte Carlo dropout gives it a sense of its own doubt. Odd confidence maps flag attacks. Broad tests show strong attack resistance and good spread to new scenes. Trade studies say it can run in real time.
arxiv-2503-07775:
Basu and Chanda built streaming algorithms that estimate distances between probability distributions in twenty twenty-five. Comparing distributions underlies fairness and privacy auditing, but data often arrive as streams from many sources, and storing everything is impossible. Their framework learns a distribution's shape functions from samples on the fly.

The trick reduces the problem to counting how often samples land in a cleverly chosen slice of a discretized distribution. From those counts they build mergeable summaries needing far less space than the number of samples seen. Wasserstein and total variation distances between any two distributions can then be estimated from the summaries. Results match known lower bounds for bounded cases. Experiments on synthetic and real data confirmed the efficiency gains.
arxiv-2503-07875:
Gürbüz and four co-authors present a 2025 mathematical model of dengue fever spread that takes waiting times seriously. Dengue, carried by Aedes mosquitoes, threatens half the world's people. Their model builds in delays for the virus incubating in mosquitoes and in people, plus a delayed recovery for the sick. The authors first check the delay-free version: solutions stay positive and bounded, and they compute the threshold reproduction number.

Stability analysis then shows how delays reshape the dynamics. The recovery delay in particular can swing behavior substantially, opening the door to oscillations. The framework is qualitative, meant to reveal how timing, not just rates, steers an epidemic. The authors note the same ideas apply to other infections with incubation lags.
arxiv-2503-08075:
Gul, Naim, and Bhat speed up the search for drug targets by sampling smartly from biomedical knowledge graphs. These graphs link drugs, proteins, diseases, and pathways, and predicting a drug-target link is a classic task on them. Older embedding methods lean on heavy negative sampling and generalize poorly to unseen pairs.

Their method, MuCoS, focuses on dense neighborhoods that carry strong structural patterns and blends in text-based context from a language model. Skipping negative sampling cuts the computing cost sharply. On a standard dataset the method beat leading rivals by up to 13 percent on a key ranking measure. Gains held for the drug-target relation itself at 6 percent.
arxiv-2503-09775:
Anmol Dwivedi and Ali Tajer built a learning system in 2025 that hunts for the most dangerous chains of failures in a power grid before they happen. Cascading faults, where one failure triggers the next, can blackout whole regions, and extreme weather makes them likelier. The number of possible chains explodes with grid size, and operators only ever see part of the system state.

The authors frame the search as a partially observable decision process. They solve it with a time-varying graph recurrent neural network that respects the grid's spatial layout and changing conditions. The network learns where risk concentrates instead of enumerating every chain. For grid operators facing climate-driven storms, a tool that ranks risky fault chains in real time could guide reinforcements and switching decisions. Prevention beats restoration when the cascade is fast.
arxiv-2503-09975:
Joonhyung Lee and a team of co-authors speed up language model inference in twenty twenty-five. They use FP8, a low-precision number format, on the Intel Gaudi accelerator. Low precision raises throughput by making better use of hardware. Yet a full account of how FP8 works on such chips, with hard tests, has been missing.

The team makes three contributions. First, they explain the implementation details and quantization choices for FP8 inference on Gaudi. Second, they measure the speed gains at the level of single operations and whole models. Third, they test how much accuracy each quantization method costs. Readers who serve models get grounded data for a choice often made on faith.
arxiv-2503-11775:
Elias Taira leads an eight-author team studying how ultraviolet background light affects gas around galaxies, in a two thousand twenty-five paper. The circumgalactic medium holds diffuse gas that telescopes detect through absorption lines. Ultraviolet radiation from all galaxies sets the ionization of that gas, but models of the background disagree.

The team ran several background models through the FOGGIE galaxy simulations. Synthetic absorption spectra were generated and matched across models by line of sight. Changing the background model shifted ion column densities significantly. The effect was strongest at low densities and high temperatures, where photoionization dominates. Scatter between models also grew with ionization level. Simulation results, the authors warn, inherit this background uncertainty.
arxiv-2503-12075: Li builds a form tale for the vast-mass end of G2 and Calabi-Yau monopoles on SU(2) packs. The packs sit over cone-tail G2 forms or Calabi-Yau three-folds, with the pack's class facts held fixed as mass grows. Li shows how to pull a lone bent Abelian monopole, with a Dirac spike on a set cycle, from that vast-mass end. A force same-sum for monopole pops caps the work.
arxiv-2503-12775:
Akihiro Narimatsu and Tomoki Yamagami define and study a new kind of random walk in this 2025 arXiv paper. Random walks model chance movement and show up across physics and computing. One recent use is a laser-based device that picks among options very fast, and its control rule behaves like a walk with memory, a link earlier work only partly explored.

Their Antlion Random Walk pulls the walker back toward the start before each step, with a dial that sets how strong the pull is. Turning that dial shifts the walker's spread from flat and even to bell-shaped. The authors work out the walk's average, spread, reach, and time spent on each side. They place the walk inside a known family of memory-based processes while noting its non-bell-shaped quirks.
arxiv-2503-14475:
Umar Farooq and his co-authors present a computer vision method from two thousand twenty-five called Opti3DGS. The method builds three-dimensional scenes from images with Gaussian splatting, a way to render a scene in real time. Such scenes can need much memory and disk space, which limits use on home devices.

Opti3DGS starts with a coarse scene and adds detail step by step, guided by image frequency. On the base method, it cut the number of Gaussians by about sixty-two percent on average. It also cut training memory and time, with no loss in image quality. The method fits other splatting tools too, and it yields levels of detail at no extra cost.
arxiv-2503-15075:
