For independent but non-Gaussian noise, the same estimator is always beatable. They build new procedures, called ACE, that exploit higher-order cumulants of the treatment. Whenever a certain cumulant is nonzero, the new estimators gain extra insulation against errors in the nuisance estimates. The title's moral: Gaussianity, being normal, is exactly the hard case for doing better.
arxiv-2507-02875: Mayer Humi asks whether equations for a pair of spin-half particles gain a hidden gauge freedom. His paper, from twenty twenty-five, writes Lorentz-safe equations for the pair as one multiplet. Treated apart, each particle's equation lacks this freedom. Treated jointly, three distinct groups of gauge changes leave the equations untouched. Humi then probes basic traits of the solutions that these multiplet equations allow.
arxiv-2507-03475:
Hannah Bergner and Peter Spichtinger model pure ice clouds as swinging systems in a 2025 study. Clouds set much of Earth's energy balance by bouncing sunlight and trapping heat. For ice clouds alone, the net effect is still unsure. The pair build a simple model that still keeps the core physics, then study it with tools for moving systems. They map the steady states and the cycles the model can fall into.

The model acts as a nonlinear oscillator, with two tipping points of a type called Hopf bifurcations. Past those points, the cloud settles into a steady cycle rather than a fixed state. The team finds scaling rules that shrink the set of cases they must check. The model also matches real cloud readings well. They argue that lean models like this one can guide work on ice clouds.
arxiv-2507-03775:
Hiba Bederina wrote this operations research paper, published in two thousand twenty-five, on planning drone routes. The task is a twist on the traveling salesman problem: the drone need not land on each target, only pass close enough to serve it, as in scanning fields or inspecting sites.

Bederina streamlines the math behind this Close Enough problem. Distances are approximated in a form that is easier to solve, and the goal function is simplified. The rules that keep the route valid are built from convex sets, which solvers handle well. Tests on real-world cases used a split solving strategy built on the CPLEX solver. The method used computing resources wisely while keeping route quality high. The paper also studies how each version of the formulas behaves, giving users a guide to picking among them.
arxiv-2507-04075:
Maxime Burchi and Radu Timofte present EMERALD, a 2025 world model for training game-playing agents in imagination. The Dreamer family of agents learns by simulating futures inside a learned model of the world. Squeezing the world into a compact code loses detail and can mislead the agent. EMERALD keeps a spatial latent map instead and predicts it with a masked transformer method borrowed from image generation.

Agents trained inside EMERALD beat all prior methods on the Crafter benchmark. It was the first system to pass human expert scores within ten million environment steps. During testing it also unlocked all 22 of the game's achievements at least once. The authors present the design as both sharper and faster to train than pixel-based rivals.
arxiv-2507-04575:
Mohid Farooqi and Alejandro Comas-Leon proposed a new design for artificial intelligence in a 2025 paper. Most AI systems today are built as stacked layers of simple units. The authors argue this neuron-level view may be too narrow. They suggest modeling whole brain regions instead, with signals like the chemical messages the brain uses.

Their design, called Lilith, splits a language model into modules for jobs such as thinking, memory, sensing, and control. The modules talk to each other by passing tokens, in a way meant to echo chemical signaling. Unlike normal systems, these modules would not be pre-trained. They would learn from scratch through staged experiences, more like a developing mind. The authors frame the design as a test bed for studying whether awareness can emerge in a machine. They propose measuring that with tools from a theory of consciousness.
arxiv-2507-04675:
Keshmiri, Jayasuriya, and Imani propose a smart surface for wireless signals in twenty twenty-five. The surface is made of small patch elements that can be tuned with diodes. Each element can reflect a signal in one of two states. The goal is to sense where a signal comes from and steer it onward.

Part of the signal on each element leaks into a thin guide below the surface. Two connectors collect that leaked signal for analysis. Methods from compressive sensing and a small neural network read the angle of arrival from it. Varied slot sizes spread the reflected beam and cut unwanted side lobes. The design is simple and low cost, with uses in communications, power transfer, and sensing.
arxiv-2507-04975: Basis sets are the standard toolkits of functions that quantum chemistry programs use to describe electrons in molecules. Ignacio Ema and co-authors introduce a reduced version of the SIGMA basis set family. The new sets share their makeup with the widely used Dunning sets. Their advantage is that they cut the near duplicate functions that make large calculations slow and unstable. Early tests are reported in this short paper.
arxiv-2507-05275:
Wenxing Zheng and co-authors wrote a paper in 2025 on a Fuzzy Supervisor Agent that assists clinical reasoning training in a multi-agent educational system. Students in the system practice on simulated clinical scenarios. Specialized agents play several roles: the patient, the physical examination, the diagnosis, and the intervention. The supervisor watches over the whole interaction and guides the student.

The supervisor uses a fuzzy inference system, which reasons with degrees of truth rather than sharp yes-or-no rules. It interprets student interactions with the specialized agents in real time. Rule bases assess professionalism, medical relevance, ethical conduct, and distraction from the task at hand. When a student engages inappropriately or stalls, the supervisor delivers timely, context-aware feedback and assistance. The paper presents the system's design, architecture, and underlying rationale. Empirical studies with students in real classroom settings remain as future work.
arxiv-2507-06275:
Yassin Hussein Rassul and co-authors survey ways to grow training data for handwriting readers in this 2025 paper. Software that reads handwritten pages powers archive digitizing and form handling. It starves for labeled examples, above all for rare languages and scripts. Fake extra data can fill the gap. The team sorted the literature by strict review rules.

Their search began with over thirteen hundred studies across four big databases. Classic tricks such as warping and noise sit beside newer generators. Neural generators, including GANs and diffusion models, now craft whole new samples. Keeping the writing style true remains the hardest part. The survey maps gaps and next steps for low-resource scripts.
arxiv-2507-06975:
Lázaro Sales and colleagues measured the expansion of the universe in 2025 without assuming a full cosmic model. They used late-time clues: brief radio flashes from deep space whose host galaxies are known, exploding stars, ripples from early sound, and clocks made of aging galaxies. A flexible math form, called cosmography, describes expansion with just a few rates.

Radio flashes alone pinned the current expansion rate to within a few percent, in line with the standard model. Adding the other probes tightened the result further, though one combined set hinted at a small tension in later rates. The checks let astronomers test the standard picture piece by piece. More well-located flashes will sharpen the method.
arxiv-2507-07775:
The CMS Collaboration presents a new way to calibrate simulated jets with many prongs. Their 2025 paper serves searches for heavy particles at the Large Hadron Collider. Such particles decay into sprays of quarks and gluons. Simulations must match real jets before searches can trust them.

The method reclusters each jet's parts into subjets, one per prong. Each subjet's radiation pattern is then corrected in the Lund jet plane using real data. The data came from CMS runs between 2016 and 2018. Corrected simulations matched measured jet shapes far better. For the first time, jets with four or more prongs have a robust calibration. Future hunts for new particles can lean on these jets.
arxiv-2507-07875:
Edison Carrera, Harold Erbin, and Grégoire Misguich wrote a 2025 physics paper on preparing atoms in a special shared state. Spin squeezing makes a group of atoms act together so that measurements can beat normal limits. Such states could sharpen clocks and sensors. The team works with arrays of large, excited atoms that pull on each other in a simple pattern.

They use quantum optimal control, a method that shapes laser pulses by computer search to steer the atoms. Starting from a plain state, their pulses reach states with strong squeezing and a chosen direction. In ring arrays of up to eight atoms, the method beat the usual approach of letting the system run on its own. Best of all, pulses tuned on small arrays worked directly on larger ones. A fifty-atom array reached strong squeezing with no new search. The work points to practical routes for precision measurement.
arxiv-2507-08075:
Barrowes, Adams, Bloch, and Watson present a paper from twenty twenty-five on noise effects in cosmic reheating after inflation. Inflation's energy must convert into ordinary particles for the hot universe to begin. That conversion often runs through parametric resonance, modeled by Hill's equation. The team ask how random wobbles in the equation's parameters change particle output. Couplings to light fields can supply such wobbles naturally. Noise shifts the resonance bands and widens efficient transfer zones. Even modest noise sparks strong growth in otherwise calm regimes.

Math and simulations split growth into steady and noise-driven parts. Reheating may work across far more settings than thought. The results touch multi-field models and the moduli problem. Stochastic effects earn a central role in early universe stories.
arxiv-2507-08675:
Antonis Christou presents LIMITER, a game-like instrument for playing music in just intonation. The work appeared in twenty twenty-five. Pure tuning systems, built on whole-number ratios, sound rich but remain forbidding to most musicians.

The interface wraps the math in color, shifting shapes, and playful controls. Players can pick it up quickly and shape microtonal sounds without deep theory. Christou recounts the build, explaining the musical and engineering systems underneath. Early evaluation probes whether the playful design genuinely boosts creativity. The aim is an on-ramp: sounds once locked behind expertise become material any curious performer can explore. The paper mixes instrument design with a first look at user response.
arxiv-2507-11675:
Xiaogang Li, Kecheng Liu, and Qiming Ding present a hybrid classical-quantum method for tracking how open quantum systems change over time. The systems they target do not keep their energy sealed in, so their motion follows rules that break the tidy unitary pattern of closed systems, which makes direct simulation hard.

Their method builds on quantum Monte Carlo ideas and grows naturally out of the quantum imaginary-time evolution method. It mixes the strengths of classical and quantum machines and adapts well to many cases. The team tested it on the dynamics of open quantum systems and got the results they aimed for. They see it as a promising route for systems such as parity-time symmetric setups, non-physical processes, and open quantum systems in general.
arxiv-2507-13575: Apple's twenty twenty-five technical report documents the foundation language models behind Apple Intelligence, the company's AI feature set. The hosted text opens with the title and a byline of well over a hundred named contributors, reflecting an industrial-scale model program rather than a small research team. The report is Apple's primary public record of its foundation models for that year. Readers should note the catalog text begins with front matter; detailed content sits deeper in the full report.
arxiv-2507-14475:
Runhao Zhao and colleagues tackled temporal knowledge graph alignment in 2025. The task is matching up entities that refer to the same thing across two time-aware knowledge graphs, so the graphs can be merged and completed. Real-world graphs rarely share tidy time formats or balanced event records, and earlier methods assumed they did. The authors name this messier setting alignment in the wild.

Their system, HyDRA, is presented as the first to recast the task using multi-scale hypergraph retrieval-augmented generation. A mechanism they call scale-weave synergy handles interactions within each time scale and flags conflicts across scales. The design aims to reduce the fragmentation caused by missing records and uneven event density, improving matches where earlier approaches struggled.
arxiv-2507-18575:
Xinyu Wang, Jinghua Hou, Zhe Liu, and Yingying Zhu present HybridTM, a 2025 model for labeling every point in a 3D scan with what it belongs to, a task called semantic segmentation. Transformer models read such point clouds well but scale poorly to large scenes. Mamba models scale in a straight line yet extract weaker 3D features. The authors fuse the two in one architecture, the first hybrid of its kind for this task.

Their inner-layer strategy mixes the two block types inside each layer, not just between layers. That mix captures long-range links and fine local detail at once. On indoor and outdoor data sets, the model generalized well. It set the best scores on three standard benchmarks: ScanNet, ScanNet200, and nuScenes. The team plans to release the code.
arxiv-2507-18975:
Cohen and Gunlu study how to find the best choice by trial while a watcher tries to learn it too in twenty twenty-five. The setup is like testing many slot machines to find the one that pays most. A rival sees each test the player makes. If the player tests the best machine most, the rival can guess it at once.

Playing all machines in equal shares hides the best one but slows the search a lot. Their method mixes the tests into coded blends that hide the pattern. It needs no secret key or code locks. Yet it finds the best machine at near top speed while leaking almost no clue to the watcher.
arxiv-2507-19875:
Xiaokun Feng and seven co-authors present ATCTrack, a vision-language tracker that keeps its cues in step with a moving target. Their paper from twenty twenty-five follows an object through video from a template patch plus a text description. Long, messy scenes break trackers whose cues freeze at the first frame. Targets change look and pose as clips run.

For the visual side, a temporal model refreshes target and context cues as frames pass. For the text side, the tracker first sorts which words name the target and which name context. A calibration step then weighs context words on the fly. Tests on mainstream benchmarks set a new top mark. The code and models are slated for release. The work targets long-term tracking in real-world clutter.
arxiv-2507-20975:
Trevor Harris and Yan Liu build an uncertainty tool in twenty twenty-five. Operator models map functions to functions and are used to forecast change over space and time. They also serve to emulate physics. In high-stakes uses, their predictions need honest error bounds. The authors offer a method that needs no assumptions about the data's distribution.

Their frame, called LSCI, makes prediction sets that adapt to local conditions. They prove it stays valid on finite samples. They also bound how far its coverage can drift when data are locally exchangeable. Tests covered synthetic tasks plus air quality, energy demand, and weather. The method gave tighter sets than standard conformal baselines and held up under biased predictions.
arxiv-2507-21975:
Tommy Hofmann and John Nicholson resolve, in a 2025 preprint, a problem that has stood since a famous 1979 list in topology. Swan modules are a special family of modules over group rings. The open problem asked whether a Swan module can be stably free without being free. The authors show one can. That single example settles the question. It also unlocks results about shapes built from cells, called CW-complexes. Two such shapes may become the same after adding spheres, yet the count of spheres needed matters.

In dimensions congruent to three modulo four, they build finite complexes that match only after several stabilizations, never after one. That answers a question posed by Dyer. A side question of Plotnick about automorphisms also falls. As a further payoff, they give a short proof that some group has periodic cohomology without the matching free period, dodging a heavy obstruction computation.
arxiv-2508-01175:
Shiko Kudo puts forward a new neuron type for neural networks, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Most networks use simple rising curves in each neuron, which forces models to grow huge. The new unit uses a tunable wave shape that can rise and fall in cycles.

A paired trick keeps the wave from flattening into a plain line during training. A tiny network with just two such neurons solved a spiral sorting task. Equal networks with standard units cannot do that task at all. Kudo frames the shift as moving from block-wise curve fitting to wave-based building of functions.
arxiv-2508-01475:
Zhen Wu and four co-authors study how text and graph data help each other in reasoning tasks, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Many language tasks rest on relations, and facts can come as plain text or as a network of linked items. Each form holds clues the other lacks, but how they interact during learning was poorly mapped.

The team built one model that can pass knowledge back and forth between the two forms. They ran it on five tasks that differ in where the needed facts sit. By tracking both forms as training went on, they found readable patterns of agreement and drift. Their results show when joining the two helps, and why.
arxiv-2508-03175:
Qi Lv and co-authors propose a variant of softmax, the standard scoring step in neural classifiers, in this 2025 paper. Softmax pushes the right class score toward one, a value it can never reach. Training thus never rests, wastes time on already-correct cases, and can overfit. The test goal is weaker: the right class only needs the top score.

Their Adaptive Sparse softmax drops classes whose scores lag far behind the right one during training. The model then focuses on telling the right class from its strongest rivals, the true test challenge. Easy cases soon cost no loss, and a pacing trick speeds training by about twenty percent. Across text, image, and audio tasks with up to thousands of classes, the method beat softmax and its variants.
arxiv-2508-04375:
Van den Eijnden and twelve co-authors published this astronomy paper in 2025. It observes neutron star binaries at low frequencies, millimeter and radio waves, where these systems are barely studied. In each system a neutron star feeds on the wind of a giant companion star, and the feeding style splits into steady and violently flaring classes.

Twelve systems were observed with millimeter telescopes, six also by radio. Nine were detected at millimeter wavelengths, including every flaring system, but only two in radio. All spectra rose toward higher frequencies, the signature of free-free emission from the companion's ionized wind, not from a jet. The flaring systems proved fainter, pointing to thinner winds as the reason they flare: less fuel, delivered unevenly. The wind readings agreed with other methods and hinted at long-term wind changes. The authors say millimeter surveys can sort these binaries by wind density alone.
arxiv-2508-04475: Bob Osano asks what changes if the dark sector of the cosmos is not fixed and still, but active, with parts that act on each other. He studies two such parts that grow and shift together over time, using a simplified setup in which pressure stays steady. The short paper sets out what this kind of pairing would mean for how the cosmos expands and changes.
arxiv-2508-04875:
Runyao Yu and six co-authors built PriceFM in twenty twenty-five, a foundation model for forecasting European electricity prices with uncertainty attached. Europe's grid is physically interconnected and increasingly renewable. Prices therefore couple across borders in ways generic forecasters miss. The team first assembled a data set covering twenty-four countries and thirty-eight regions over four recent years.

PriceFM pre-trains on that corpus. Each region's prices and drivers — load, solar, and wind forecasts — enter through a shared mixture-of-experts layer. A sparse graph mask from the transmission topology injects prior knowledge of cross-border links. On a large European benchmark it beat competitive baselines and generalized better. The work argues topology guidance is the missing ingredient for power price forecasting.
arxiv-2508-05675:
Jing Wang, Zheng Li, and seven co-authors optimize chip code with cloud AI without leaking the design. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, splits the work between a local small model and a strong cloud model. Cloud models optimize Verilog well, but sending proprietary code out risks theft. The local model reads pairs of expert and novice code in-house.

From those pairs it distills general design principles. Only the abstract principles travel to the cloud. The cloud model then improves the draft under that guidance. Experiments show clearly higher optimization success than baselines. The scheme keeps secrets local while renting outside smarts. Hardware teams with strict IP rules are the audience.
arxiv-2508-05875:
Cole Tamburri and co-authors (2025) captured the sharpest-ever views of loops in a solar flare using the Daniel K. Inouye Solar Telescope. The target was the fading phase of an X1.3-class flare in August 2024, imaged in hydrogen-alpha light. Above bright, structured ribbons on the surface, the telescope resolved dark loop strands. From the twenty clearest images the team measured strand widths near the arcade top. The average width was about 48 kilometers.

The thinnest strand measured near 21 kilometers, and the most common width was about 43. The width distribution spread symmetrically around the mean. That symmetry hints the telescope may finally be resolving the fundamental scale of coronal loops. The authors are careful: confirmation needs more work. Even so, resolving power at this level gives flare modelers real structure to match. It sharpens questions about how the corona's magnetic field is threaded.
arxiv-2508-06975:
Zhengying Lou, Baha Eddine Youcef Belmekki, and Mohamed-Slim Alouini study how to route signals through many hops at very high wave speeds. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

Such high waves promise fast links but fade fast over space. The team builds the first math frame of its kind for this routing, based on the chance spread of nodes. They give a step-by-step plan to raise flow, by choice of power, of relay, and of hop count. Their sums give flow and reach odds at low cost. Tests show the plan beats past ways and nears the best case. They also match this band with plain radio and test use in drone networks.
arxiv-2508-07075:
Stanley Ngugi rewrites one fact inside a compact language model without wrecking the rest, in a 2025 paper. Editing a model that deeply believes an old fact often fails twice: the model resists the new fact, and unrelated knowledge gets damaged. His plan first locates the inner parts that store the clashing fact. Then it unlearns that fact and teaches the new one, using a light adapter method.

On a small Microsoft model, the method installed the new fact with about 98 percent accuracy and suppressed the old one almost as well. Checks on unrelated knowledge stayed near 72 percent, far above direct fine-tuning, which fell near 20 percent. Probing showed the old fact was not erased but muted, still reachable under the right prompt. Ngugi frames that soft forgetting as a safety feature.
arxiv-2508-08675:
Ghadimi and Tootkaboni prove a broader form of a classic pattern claim in math in this twenty twenty-five paper. The classic claim says any finite split of whole numbers must hold a neat spaced set in one part. Their form moves the stage to small values near zero and swaps plain steps for curved rules.

Inside, the proof works with a dense ring of real values cut to the span below one. It takes any finite split of that span and a fast-shrinking list of small inputs. The result finds one part that holds a full curved set built from a shared base and a summed chunk of the list. All the curved rules used start at zero and stay above it near zero.
arxiv-2508-09175:
Mohammad Zia Ur Rehman, Sufyaan Zahoor, Areeb Manzoor, and a wider team wrote this machine learning paper, published in 2025. It builds a detector for misogynistic posts that reads image and text together, since abuse aimed at women often hides in the combination.

General offensiveness filters miss much of this content, the authors argue. Their framework has three parts. An attention module with adaptive gates weighs which visual and textual clues matter. A graph module refines features by passing messages within each modality. A third module learns content-specific signals, helped by a curated lexicon of misogynistic terms that scores the text. Extra augmented features at test time steadied predictions. On two public datasets of eleven and thirteen thousand posts, the system beat prior approaches on average. The authors aim it at moderators drowning in multimodal abuse.
arxiv-2508-09675:
Luca Forte published this imaging letter in 2025 on ultrasound computed tomography. In this technique, a ring of transducers surrounds the body part, often a breast, and software rebuilds a map of how fast sound travels through the tissue. Standard rebuilds work in the frequency domain with heavy iterative algorithms. Forte explores a different route: a stochastic reconstruction carried out in the time domain.

The method groups the ring's shots into randomized super-shots and averages over random ensembles, trading determinism for flexibility. It was tested on publicly available experimental data from a real system. The time-domain images came out comparable in quality to the standard frequency-domain result. The cost was speed: the new route ran significantly slower. The letter presents the approach as a proof of concept rather than a replacement, showing that time-domain stochastic inversion is viable for this imaging task.
arxiv-2508-09975:
Filipe Grilo, Marc Botz, Chintan Shah, Thomas Pfeifer, José Crespo López-Urrutia, and Pedro Amaro measure faint satellite lines beside a bright calcium emission in the lab. Helium-like calcium glows strongly in hot cosmic plasmas. Beside its main line sit satellite lines born when electrons recombine in a two-step dance. Precise energies for those satellites sharpen plasma diagnostics.

The team trapped ions in a cryogenic electron beam trap with an energy resolution of eight electron volts. They pinned down the exciting electrons' energies and the emitted photons' energies with errors well under one percent. The simplest satellite family matched atomic-code predictions and prior top calculations closely. Direct excitation cross sections agreed within ten percent. Extracted recombination rates matched a standard database. A check against new space telescope spectra confirms the lab data models real plasmas well.
arxiv-2508-10575:
Christof Schotz, in a solo critique from 2025, challenges a widely cited study of how climate change will damage the world economy. The original study, published in a leading journal in 2024, projected significant damages by mid-century and a sharp split between high and low emission paths after that.

Schotz argues that the analysis ignored how strongly nearby regions' economies move together. Such spatial correlation shrinks the effective amount of independent data. Once the uncertainty is corrected for this, the projected damages are no longer statistically significant. He concludes that the study does not provide the robust evidence needed to inform climate policy. The piece appears as a formal matters-arising comment, the standard channel for post-publication critique.
arxiv-2508-10875:
Tianyi Li, Mingda Chen, Bowei Guo, and Zhiqiang Shen surveyed diffusion language models in twenty twenty-five. These models make text by iterative denoising. They yield tokens in parallel, not one by one. That design promises lower latency and two-way context. It gives fine control of what is made. New systems now match autoregressive models on quality.

The survey traces how the family grew up. It notes kinship with autoregressive and masked models. It sorts current techniques from pre-training to post-training. It then reviews inference optimizations. Those hold parallel decoding, caching, and quality gains. Multimodal extensions and uses come next. The authors close with limits: efficiency, long sequences, and infrastructure. They give paths for a fast field. A public repository tracks the work in the field.
arxiv-2508-11075:
Hyunwoo Yoo and Gail Rosen published a 2025 paper on representing a microbiome sample so a computer can learn from it. Each sample is a community: thousands of microbial sequences in varying abundance. Jobs, predicting a trait or telling environments apart, need it compressed into one fingerprint. The common shortcut averages the sequences' embeddings, treating a rare microbe and a dominant one as equals.

Their method weights by that share without changing the model's design. Sequence embeddings are copied in line with their share, then a set transformer attends over the pile and pulls them together. Abundant members thus speak louder, as they do in life. On microbiome tasks, the approach beat averaging and the unweighted model. The lesson is general: when summing up a community, count its members. That share is information, and embeddings should not throw it away.
arxiv-2508-11475:
Panitsas, Mudvari, and Tassiulas present D2Q, a 2025 learning-based method for keeping spread-out network controllers in sync. In software-defined networking split across sites, controllers must share one view of the network. Existing sync rules rarely weigh network cost against user performance together. The new method uses reinforcement learning to offload time-sensitive tasks to cheap edge servers while holding latency promises for every task.

In tests, it cut network costs by at least 45 percent against heuristics and 10 percent against other learning methods. Service quality held for all tasks across shifting, multi-domain setups. The authors pitch D2Q for operators who need both frugality and speed of response. The work targets time-sensitive uses like factory control and live media.
arxiv-2508-11575:
Nges Brian Njungle and Michel Kinsy design the nonlinear switches that encrypted neural networks desperately need. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Fully homomorphic encryption lets models compute on sealed data. Health and defense users crave that privacy. Encryption natively supports only straight-line math. Activation functions bend the line, so they resist encryption. The authors focus squarely on that bottleneck.

Two classic functions get the treatment: the square and the rectified linear unit. Implementations are tested on LeNet-5 and ResNet-20 networks. Cost and accuracy are weighed for each design. The goal is privacy-preserving learning that stays practical. Encrypted inference moves closer to routine use.
arxiv-2508-11675:
Amgad Salama writes a tutorial survey of direction-of-arrival estimation in a 2025 paper. The problem is simple to state: given signals caught by a row of sensors, find which direction each signal came from. Radar, sonar, wireless links, and hearing aids all live on the answer. The survey assumes narrowband signals and evenly spaced linear arrays, building each method with step-by-step math and geometric pictures.

Methods range from classical beamforming through subspace techniques with names like MUSIC and ESPRIT, to likelihood and sparse approaches. Working Python code accompanies every method in a public repository. Performance comparisons end with practical advice on picking and tuning a method, making the paper a doorway for newcomers.
arxiv-2508-12175:
Ben Nassi, Stav Cohen, and Or Yair showed that booby-trapped invites can hijack AI assistants in the wild, in a paper published in 2025. The trap is promptware: text built to bend an assistant to the ends of an attacker. Their test bed was Google's Gemini assistant in its web, phone, and voice forms. The lures arrived by mail, calendar invites, and shared files, the material of each day.

Fourteen attack scenes ran across five classes, from poisoned chat stores to triggered home devices. Outcomes spanned spam, phishing, lies, data theft, and live stream theft. Their risk framework set most threats at high to critical for users. Fixes they shared with Google cut the grades hard. The authors call the trap real and live, not a laboratory tale.
arxiv-2508-12375:
Yu Sha and co-authors build a fault-severity diagnosis frame for complex industrial systems, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Grading how bad a machine fault is matters for upkeep, yet past methods treat fault classes as if unrelated. Their frame borrows the tree-of-thought idea, letting classes share structure.

A graph network maps the class tree into linked graded sorters, each keyed by a word embedding of its class. A re-weighted knowledge matrix then guides sharing between nodes and blocks over-smoothing. Tests on four real data sets, three from an industrial partner, beat recent rivals. The frame plugs onto standard feature learners, the authors note.
arxiv-2508-13375:
Yusuf Mücahit Çetinkaya and Tuğrulcan Elmas measure what state-ordered withholding does to accounts on X, the site once called Twitter. Their paper from twenty twenty-five gives the first numeric study of this censorship form. Two patterns anchor the data: Russian accounts withheld in the European Union, and Turkish accounts blocked inside Turkey. Posting rates barely moved under the bans.

Engagement fell hard where the ban zone matched the account's home crowd. Likes and reposts dropped by a clear share, and follower growth nearly stalled. Russian accounts with outside audiences kept growing. The team also trains a classifier to flag accounts at risk of withholding. Tweet text carries nearly all the signal. Scores land in a solid range. The study feeds debates on platform rule, speech, and state pressure.
arxiv-2508-14775:
Lauren Cook and Timothy Hele probe how to split fast and slow modes in a model of coupled electron motion, in work from 2025. Good models of such motion must keep the right heat balance, and a known method does so by cutting high nuclear modes. A newer variant left the electron modes uncut, yet seemed to break that balance.

The pair gives the first study of the electron normal modes in this frame. They find most outputs draw on an endless set of modes, unlike the nuclear case. Cutting the modes spoils key outputs, so they warn that this path is not ideal for a sound method.
arxiv-2508-14975:
Arman Sauliere and four co-authors show that noisy quantum circuits share a universal pattern in how their outputs spread, whatever the noise source. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. A circuit's output counts as anticoncentrated when no single result hogs the odds. That spread is a sign a quantum device is hard to fake classically.

Their framework treats weak noise through an effective random operator. In that limit, distinct noise types act in much the same way. Three depth zones appear, each with its own rule for a standard benchmark score. Shallow circuits barely feel the noise, mid ones balance noise against circuit churn, and deep ones turn near-classical. Tests against simulations matched well, even at shallow depth. A surprise: the late-time benchmark score reads out the whole circuit's fidelity. The results apply to today's quantum chips.
arxiv-2508-15075:
Simone Hagey and a large team of co-authors track slow changes in the orbit of a hot Jupiter, in a 2025 paper. The planet, TrES-1 b, crosses its star as seen from Earth. Years of crossing times, eclipses, and star wobble data were combined for this study. Simple effects like our own motion were ruled out first, which left real motion changes in the system.

One model has the orbit's oval slowly turning, but it turns too fast to explain without a hidden close planet. A wide companion found in the data is unlikely to be the driver. A shrinking orbit fits well if the planet's tilt drives strong tides. The authors urge more eclipse and wobble watching to settle which story is right.
arxiv-2508-15475:
Loris Schoenegger and three co-authors revisit curriculum learning in twenty twenty-five. Curriculum learning feeds training data in order of difficulty, from simple to complex. For pretraining language models, it had shown only limited success. The authors suspect the fault lies in how difficulty was measured, by human-centered scores.

They sort examples instead by training data influence. That score estimates how much each example changes the model's output. Models trained on influence-ordered curricula beat random order by over ten percentage points on benchmarks. The gain held in the limited-data setting they studied. Readers learn that curriculum learning works for pretraining when difficulty is defined by the model, not by people.
arxiv-2508-16875:
Artur Bikeev, Andrey Kupavskii, and Maxim Turevskii show that two trees suffice to cover any flat point set with bounded stretch, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. A tree cover lets every pair of points find one tree where their path stays within a set factor of the true distance. Tree edges carry the true lengths.

For points in the plane, two trees with constant stretch always exist, they prove. Higher dimensions stay open in general. For a slightly stronger cover demand, they prove at least half of dimension-plus-one trees are needed. The gap frames a clean open problem.
arxiv-2508-17775: Yu Mao rebuilds an abelian number field from part of its Galois group by group theory alone, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. The work sits in anabelian geometry, which asks how much of a field can be read from its symmetry group. Here the field is read from the maximal six-step solvable quotient, as the text head puts it, though the pack title says five steps. The method is new and stands apart from past two-field results.
arxiv-2508-18375:
William Cashman, Giovanni de Felice, and Aleks Kissinger reduced the cost of building photonic quantum states in a 2025 paper. In measurement-based quantum computing with light, large graph states are assembled by fusing short linear resource states, and each fusion can fail, so builders want as few fusions as possible. That wish becomes a covering problem: split the graph into the fewest paths or trails, relatives of the classic Eulerian and Hamiltonian problems.

Most variants prove NP-hard, so the team supplies heuristics, including a reduction to the traveling salesman problem, plus rewrite rules that shrink the needed fusions for a given graph state. Applied to photonic compilation tasks, the algorithms cut fusion counts toward the practical minimum.
arxiv-2508-18975:
Jan Nikolas Morshuis, Matthias Hein, and Christian F Baumgartner present a 2025 arXiv paper benchmarking ways to segment undersampled MRI scans. Fast scans collect less data, and many teams now outline anatomy straight from the partial data instead of rebuilding the full image first. Methods grew up in isolation, on private data, with no shared yardstick. The authors supply the first unified comparison of seven approaches.

The tests use two datasets with raw coil data and human-drawn outlines. One-stage models fuse rebuild and outline in one net; two-stage models rebuild first, then segment. Plain two-stage methods that respect the measured data won. The authors warn that fancy specialized designs did not earn their complexity.
arxiv-2508-19275: Luca Sabatini proves a sharp upper bound in this 2025 paper on how many generators a finite group can need. The bound is stated through the ratio between the group's order, its total number of elements, and its exponent, the smallest power that sends every element to the identity. Because the bound is sharp, some groups actually reach it, so the estimate cannot be improved in general.
arxiv-2508-20175:
James Owen and Ruth Murray-Clay study a 2025 effect on hot planets around other stars: starlight itself pushes on the haze in their skies. Such hazes seem common in exoplanet air, and they blur measures of what the air holds. The authors show that on strongly lit planets, light pressure can speed haze grains up more than the planet's gravity holds them down.

For light, puffy planets smaller than Saturn, with grains of a set tiny size, the push can reach many times the pull of gravity. Those planets are often the best targets for current telescopes, so the effect matters for real data. The push speeds up haze made high in the air by light-driven chemistry. It changes how fast grains fall and spread, and so how the planet looks to us.
arxiv-2508-20775:
Hua-Sheng Shao and Lukas Simon published this conference paper in 2025 on photon-photon physics. When heavy ions pass near each other in a collider without touching, their light fields can fuse and create new particles. Measuring these photon-fusion events precisely now demands theory at next-to-leading order, one step beyond the simplest calculations. Automated tools exist for ordinary particle collisions, but not for these two-photon ones.

The authors review recent hand-built calculations of this kind. They then present an updated software package that joins their photon-collision code with a standard automated framework. The package is the first that can produce next-to-leading order predictions for photon-photon processes in these near-miss collisions on its own. The work aims to match the sharpening precision of experiments at RHIC and the Large Hadron Collider.
arxiv-2508-20975:
Simen and co-authors map data onto a quenched quantum spin glass to boost machine learning. Their method encodes dataset facts into a messy many-body quantum problem. A fast, nonadiabatic run then yields measures that become model features.

Models gained most from features taken in the fast coherent regime, near the dynamics' critical point. Tests covered many high-dimensional sets with over a hundred features each. Uses included drug discovery and medical diagnosis tasks. The quantum features were compared against a broad suite of top classical models. The authors pitch the scheme as a path to quantum advantage in learning.
arxiv-2508-21175:
Francisco Plaza, Gabriel León, and Lucila Kraiselburd test a dark energy model against the Hubble tension, the stubborn gap between two ways of measuring how fast the universe expands. The model pairs holographic dark energy with unimodular gravity, a variant of Einstein's theory. Fresh distance data from the DESI survey's second release motivate the check. The team confronts the model with a wide set of observations.

The data include cosmic chronometers, a large supernova sample, DESI distance measures, quasar fluxes under two calibrations, and the Planck satellite's map of the early universe. The authors compare the model with the standard cosmological model using Bayesian evidence. They find the new model does not ease the Hubble tension. The standard model is preferred, though not by a conclusive margin in either direction.
arxiv-2508-21275:
Naonori Sugiyama wrote a paper in 2025 on a fast way to compute the nonlinear matter power spectrum. The spectrum is a key statistic describing how matter clumps in the universe on small scales. The spectrum tests theories of cosmic structure growth. Standard calculations become unreliable on small scales, where bulk flows complicate the mathematics.

The formulation is based on a unified Lagrangian perturbation theory. It splits the density field into two parts: intrinsic growth, and a displacement factor accounting for large-scale flows. That structural split makes the calculation safe from a known infrared problem by construction. The implementation evaluates the spectrum in about two seconds on a standard laptop. Across one hundred sampled cosmologies, it agreed with two large simulation-based emulators within a few percent. It also stayed accurate for the two-point correlation function, and reproduces how the ring feature in galaxy clustering is damped and sharpened.
arxiv-2508-21675:
Jonathan Tonglet, Jan Zimny, Tinne Tuytelaars, and Iryna Gurevych build tools to catch charts that lie, in a 2025 paper. Misleading charts are a strong driver of misinformation online. They break design rules to distort data. Both people and large AI models get fooled by them. Automatic detection could protect readers at scale. The field lacked a large, open dataset for training. The team fills that gap.

Their benchmark holds over twenty-six hundred real charts. Each is labeled with which of twelve tricks it uses. A synthetic set adds nearly fifty-eight thousand generated charts. Those were built from real data tables with a plotting library. The team tested top multimodal models, rule systems, and axis readers. All struggled with the task. The authors release the data and code openly. They frame detection as an unsolved, practical problem.
arxiv-2508-21775:
Omer Faruk Durugol and three co-authors detail a prize entry for outlining pancreatic tumors on MRI scans. Their work appeared in twenty twenty-five. The cancer is hard to spot against normal tissue, and labeled training scans are scarce.

Their pipeline starts from a general anatomy model, then fine-tunes in stages: first on CT scans of pancreatic lesions, then on the target MRI types. Two tasks cover diagnostic and therapy scans. Careful tests split augmentation styles: heavy changes maximized volume overlap, while defaults gave the sharpest borders. The final entry blended specialist models chosen by metric. Scores topped their validation table for the diagnostic task. The method suits other scarce-data imaging problems.
arxiv-2509-00075:
Elizabeth Aubin, Jean-Christophe Loison, Mehdi Ayouz, Joshua Forer, and Viatcheslav Kokoouline model how free electrons break apart the HNC3 molecule in 2025. In dissociative electron attachment, an electron sticks to a molecule, which then splits into a charged fragment and a neutral one. Such steps help make negative ions in the cold gas between stars.

A low-energy resonance in the collision turns bound near the molecule's resting shape and drives it to split with no barrier. The team computes the cross section and rate for the split from first principles. At room temperature the rate is high, and at cold space temperatures the route beats photon-driven attachment by a thousandfold. The result suggests this split route makes the carbon-chain negative ions seen in space.
arxiv-2509-00175:
Niraj Gohil, Alexander Franke, Nawshad Haque, and Amro M. Farid analyze green hydrogen production in Australia in 2025 across place and time. Hydrogen made by electrolysis, which splits water with electricity, can store clean energy. Its climate gain depends on when and where the power comes from, since grid carbon intensity swings by hour.

Their model aligns output with low-carbon periods on the grid, using live grid and price data from Australian sources. Hydrogen tax credits further lift cost-effectiveness in the model. A life cycle assessment framework weighs the full environmental impact. Time-aware planning could cut both emissions and cost for a key clean fuel.
arxiv-2509-00375:
Ziyi Xia, Kun Luo, Hongjin Qian, and Zheng Liu present InfoSeek in 2025, a framework to synthesize training data for Deep Research tasks. Deep Research asks a model to split a question into sub-problems, reason over many steps, and synthesize evidence from diverse sources. The authors formalize such tasks with verifiable answers as Hierarchical Constraint Satisfaction Problems.

Existing benchmarks fail to capture that complexity, and recent synthetic sets often allow shortcut reasoning, leak knowledge, or lack depth. InfoSeek uses a dual-agent system to recursively build a Research Tree from large-scale webpages. The tree structure enforces genuine multi-step depth. Better training data could lift models from fact lookup to real research work.
arxiv-2509-00675:
Dong Yang leads seven authors in total, with Yuki Saito, Takaaki Saeki, Tomoki Koriyama, Wataru Nakata, Detai Xin, and Hiroshi Saruwatari, on phrase break prediction for text-to-speech. Phrase breaks, also called phrasing, decide where a synthetic voice pauses, and in multi-speaker systems the right pauses vary by speaker.

Yang and his co-authors add speaker embeddings, numeric voice fingerprints, to the phrasing model and show those embeddings capture speaker traits from the phrasing task alone. They adapt embeddings to unseen speakers with few examples, and they pioneer phoneme-level pre-trained language models, models trained on speech sounds, for this front-end task, which boosts accuracy greatly. Objective and subjective tests confirm the gains.
arxiv-2509-01175:
Neutron stars pack more than a Sun's mass into a city-sized ball, and they can ring with waves that fade very fast. D. Dey, Jeet Amrit Pattnaik, R. N. Panda, and S. K. Patra study one such ringing pattern, the axial w-modes, in a non-rotating star. These modes arise from coupling between the star's fluid and its gravity.

The team models the star's interior with a relativistic mean field approach and tests how quarkyonic matter and fermionic dark matter change the mode frequencies. Their equation of state spans conditions from normal nuclei to extreme matter and fits known observational limits. Results show the w-modes carry useful clues about what lies inside a neutron star, making them a probe of dense matter.
arxiv-2509-02175:
Nils Hoehing leads four co-authors with RocketScience, a benchmark that exposes weak spatial understanding in vision language models. Spatial relations, like which object sits left of another, are easy for humans yet hard for current models. Their open source contrastive bench uses entirely new real world image text pairs. Relative spatial relations and object order dominate the item design.

Open and commercial frontier models alike struggle strikingly on the tasks. Reasoning models, by contrast, score surprisingly high. A disentanglement analysis splits localization skill from spatial reasoning in chain of thought models. The bottleneck proves to be spatial reasoning itself, not finding the objects. Data and code are released under an open license.
arxiv-2509-02275:
Fengyi Wang, Xiangyu Fu, Nitish Thakor, and Gordon Cheng build a soft hand in human shape that reads objects and poses by brain like signals. The human touch web fuses touch, joint sense, and heat to read objects in rich depth. Their soft hand packs mixed sensors to copy those sense types in one tool. Brain style codes turn the mixed sense data into spike trains for spiking nets.

Object reads across poses reach high truth, past past soft hand work by a clear gap. A new split neuron sharpens stuff class reads by use of live heat shifts. Mixed sense fusion proves key to the gains the hand shows. Spike based work keeps the hand lean in power as well as sharp. The work moves soft hands toward human like touch sense.
arxiv-2509-02475:
Weiliang Yao and eight co-authors wrote a 2025 condensed matter paper probing a layered magnetic material, FePSe3, with neutron scattering under strain. The material orders antiferromagnetically, with neighbouring spins opposed, in a zigzag pattern on a honeycomb lattice.

Earlier optical work had hinted at a three-state Potts nematic phase, an ordering that picks one of three directions. Under slight tensile strain, one zigzag domain faded while two grew, and spin waves dropped to lower symmetry. The broken symmetry lingered just above the ordering temperature, where static order is absent. The authors read this as direct evidence of magnetoelastic coupling, where magnetism and lattice strain drive each other. The nematic signal in excitations likely descends from the low-temperature ordered state.
arxiv-2509-02575:
Zichuan Yang wrote a 2025 solo deep learning paper proposing the Lifecycle principle, a regularisation method that switches neurons off for long stretches rather than briefly, as dropout does. Long shutdowns risk training chaos when a neuron returns with random weights.

The fix is state memory: a revived neuron gets back its last effective parameters instead of fresh random ones. That preserves what it had learned and avoids shocks to the optimisation. Theory in the paper says the method smooths the loss landscape and steers training toward flatter minima, which usually generalise better. Image classification tests show gains in accuracy and robustness. Ablation runs, which remove parts of the method, confirm that state memory carries the benefit.
arxiv-2509-02675:
Clemens Kuhlenkamp and four co-authors wrote a 2025 physics paper on superconductivity from repulsion. It reports numerical evidence that purely repulsive electron interactions can drive the effect. Their arena is a triangular lattice model. It mixes Hubbard repulsion with a Hofstadter magnetic flux pattern.

Large density matrix renormalisation runs on infinite cylinders find superconducting ground states. The states span wide doping ranges. Pair correlations grow stronger as the cylinder widens toward two dimensions. At one electron per site, the parent insulator shifts between a quantum Hall state and a chiral spin liquid. Results support the idea that closeness to that shift favours chiral superconductivity. Edge mode predictions match too. The setup may be realisable in moiré materials.
arxiv-2509-02875:
Kian Milani and 8 co-authors described a 2025 test of two linked control loops on the Arizona coronagraph bench called SCoOB. A coronagraph blocks a star's bright core so faint planets nearby can be seen. Keeping that view clear takes constant correction of bent light waves.

One loop handles slow, broad distortions using starlight the instrument throws away. The other loop, run through the science camera, carves out a dark region where a planet could stand out. The crew ran both loops together on a deformable mirror, a surface whose shape can shift in tiny steps. They held very deep contrast, meaning the star stayed strongly dimmed, even while the air disturbed the setup.
arxiv-2509-03075: Mathis Certenais, François Bodin, and Laurent Morin described a 2025 software paper on the DDF Pipeline, a tool that processes data from radio telescopes. It was first built for LOFAR, a large low-frequency array in Europe. The pipeline is also a candidate for handling data from the future Square Kilometre Array. The authors outline how the software works and present a coarse performance profile, timing its main stages to show where the computing effort goes.
arxiv-2509-03175:
Alexander Morozov and 3 co-authors gave a 2025 perspective on elastic turbulence in polymer solutions. When long, flexible molecules dissolve in a liquid, the fluid gains springy, solid-like traits. Under flow it can fall into elastic turbulence, a chaotic state driven by polymer stretching rather than by speed or inertia.

Unlike ordinary turbulence, this state appears even when inertia nearly vanishes. Experiments show it clearly, yet its mechanism stays murky. The authors build their account around two ingredients found in channel flow simulations. Narwhals are exact, long coherent flow patterns named for their shape. Blessings are patchy episodes assembled from several narwhals at once. The piece, based on a conference talk, maps the route into elastic turbulence in two and three dimensions.
arxiv-2509-03275:
Eric Frizzell and Christine Hartzell modeled how a solitary wave moving through grains can loft material at the surface in 2025. Their setting is a three-dimensional channel of randomly packed grains driven by a sustained impact from a bumpy floor. Such waves concentrate force into a sharp front as they travel.

The team predicted peak particle forces in the wavefront from material properties and impact speed. Simulated forces followed the same power-law scaling known from a simple one-dimensional chain of beads. They then quantified surface dilation, the loosening of the surface layer, across materials and gravity levels, and wrote an equation for its depth. Lunar-like grains amplified the effect most. That supports the idea that this mechanism forms the Moon's mysterious cold spots.
arxiv-2509-03375:
Martin Jirlow and 4 co-authors derived an effective Hamiltonian in 2025 for a qubit coupled to a cavity and driven off-resonantly. Such driven light-matter systems underlie quantum technologies, where atoms store and process information and mediate interactions between light modes. With several drive tones at once, existing models often fail to reproduce experimental data quantitatively.

An effective Hamiltonian is a simplified energy description that keeps the slow, important dynamics and drops fast oscillations. Their version deliberately retains slowly rotating terms that other treatments discard. In a circuit quantum electrodynamics test, the theory matched measured ac Stark shifts, the light-induced shifting of energy levels. It also captured two-mode squeezing and beam-splitting interactions. The authors offer it as a broadly applicable design tool.
arxiv-2509-03575:
In a 2025 research paper, Haoyu Hu and three co-authors examine what decides between ferromagnetism and antiferromagnetism in narrow-band materials. In ferromagnets, electron spins align one way. In antiferromagnets, nearby spins point oppositely and cancel out. Both orders appear in models with narrow energy bands, where electrons move slowly.

Building one effective spin model, the authors weigh two competing influences inside it. The non-atomic shape of the electron wavefunctions, spread across a crystal, tends to favour aligned spins. Band dispersion, the spread of allowed energies, instead promotes opposing correlations between neighbours. Their contest produces a tunable magnetic phase and a range of rich spin behaviour. The framework unites wavefunction shape, band structure, and electron correlations in a single systematic treatment.
arxiv-2509-03675:
In a 2025 research paper, J. M. Gorriz and seven co-authors focus on exploring brain MRI data through the latent space of an autoencoder, with a cautionary message. An autoencoder compresses an image into a compact latent code, then rebuilds it. Their simple convolutional model trains on segmented grey matter scans from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative.

The learned codes preserve anatomy and track clinical differences across cognitive status groups. Standard visualisation tools, including PCA, t-SNE, and UMAP, project the codes into pictures that can be inspected. A new profiling framework links latent features to regions of a standard brain atlas, combining statistical association with supervised tests. Even a minimal architecture captures patterns tied to progression toward Alzheimer's disease. A second model predicts the rebuild error from regional grey matter amounts, naming the regions behind the choices. Statistical checks back the findings.
arxiv-2509-03775:
ContraGS, a way to train three-dimensional Gaussian splatting models directly in compressed form, is what Sankeerth Durvasula and nine co-authors examine in a 2025 research paper. Gaussian splatting renders real scenes in real time from thousands of soft three-dimensional blobs. More blobs raise quality, but storing their parameters eats graphics memory and slows training and rendering.

ContraGS stores Gaussian parameter vectors in codebooks, shared compact dictionaries of typical values, throughout training itself. Codebooks were known to compress finished models well, but learning inside them was unsolved because their parameters are not differentiable. The authors recast the estimation as Bayesian inference and sample the posterior distribution with Markov chain Monte Carlo methods. Peak training memory falls by a factor of about three and a half on average. Training and rendering also speed up noticeably, while quality stays close to leading uncompressed results.
arxiv-2509-03875:
Ziyou Jiang and four co-authors' 2025 research paper takes up VulRTex, a tool for finding security vulnerabilities hiding inside open-source issue reports. Developers often disclose flaws through issue trackers, where genuine vulnerability reports sit buried among routine bugs. Human triage is slow, and attackers can exploit the gap before a dangerous report gets noticed.

Earlier automated detectors read only plain text, ignoring rich content such as screenshots and formatted code. VulRTex reasons instead. First, a large language model studies historical reports to build a database of vulnerability reasoning. For a new report, similar past cases become reasoning guidance for judging its rich text and predicting a weakness category. The evaluation covers nearly a million issue reports. Under class imbalance, VulRTex tops the best baseline on detection quality and weakness prediction, at half the running time of rival reasoning approaches. Faster recognition shrinks the window between disclosure and defence.
arxiv-2509-04275:
Lassi Paunonen and one co-author, David Seifert, prove decay rates for a broad family of damped systems in a 2025 mathematics paper. Their systems pair a linear engine with a nonlinear friction term, described abstractly through semigroups, families of evolution maps. The main result gives rational rates, meaning steady polynomial-style decay, for well-behaved solutions. Two ingredients drive the proof: a weakened observability estimate tied to the linear part, and tame conditions on the nonlinearity.

Abstract theorems then land on concrete problems. One is a vibrating string with weak nonlinear damping along its length. The other is a flexible beam carrying a mass at its tip, also nonlinearly damped. Engineers gain guaranteed fade-out speeds for such structures.
arxiv-2509-04375:
José de Brito and two co-authors extend convergence guarantees for a classic optimization method to a wider family of functions in a 2025 mathematics paper. The proximal point algorithm inches toward a minimum by repeatedly solving nearby easier problems. Quasar-convex functions curve toward their lowest point in a one-sided way, weaker than full convexity. The authors study the proximity operator for such functions and track the algorithm's step sequence.

Under plain quasar-convexity, the sequence reaches a global minimizer with a stated complexity rate. Under the strong version, convergence turns linear, far faster, with a logarithmic-style rate. Some results are new even for star-convex functions, a special case. Numerical experiments match the theory, widening the safe territory for this workhorse method.
arxiv-2509-05175:
Testing an audio algorithm in many real rooms is slow and costly, so computer models might stand in for measurements. Georg Götz, lead author with three co-authors, check that swap in a 2025 acoustics paper. They test three audio signal processing and machine learning tools. The data come from real rooms and from three different room model engines.

One engine solves the wave equation in full, while two use ray-based acoustics shortcuts. Wave-based models match the real-room scores for all three tools. Ray-based models copy the measured results less well. The authors conclude the choice of model matters when building test datasets for audio technology.
arxiv-2509-05275:
Timothy Moy builds geometric structures named after Joyce from equations on the sphere in a solo 2025 mathematics paper. The starting point is a family of meromorphic quadratic differentials, objects on the Riemann sphere with poles, linked to a classic deformation problem.

Moy studies deformations that keep a related differential equation's monodromy fixed, meaning its solutions behave the same after loops. Those deformations form the kernel of a closed two-form built from how an algebraic curve's cycles cross. From that fact he constructs Joyce structures on spaces of these differentials. For poles of odd order the result carries a complex hyper-Kähler metric with a scaling symmetry, and one example leads to the Painlevé VI equation.
arxiv-2509-05575:
A famous three-body quantum pattern is placed inside curved space-time by Yixuan Feng in a solo 2025 theoretical physics paper. Efimov states are an endless ladder of three-particle bound states with energies in a fixed ratio, first understood in flat three-dimensional space.

Feng first reproduces that flat-space derivation, then extends it to the Schwarzschild geometry around a non-rotating mass. Combining the Schrödinger equation in curved space-time gives corrections to the Efimov spectrum in weak gravity. For strong fields, a normal-coordinate expansion plus perturbation theory yields internal energy corrections. A laboratory test is proposed too, using ultra-cold atoms in optical lattices to mimic curvature effects.
arxiv-2509-06275:
From a graph and a homology basis, a triangulated homology sphere can be built, show Karim Adiprasito and three co-authors in a 2025 paper. The construction makes precise an idea of Gromov and Nabutovski. Its payoff is a translation: asymptotic questions about triangulating homology spheres become counting problems for constant-degree graphs with short homology bases.

The authors construct families of three-sphere triangulations whose dual graphs are expanders, answering a relaxed form of a question by Kalai. A counting consequence follows too. If homology sphere counts in some dimension grow faster than exponential, three-dimensional ones do as well. The paper binds combinatorics to topology through one explicit recipe.
arxiv-2509-06375:
Self-driving cars that reshape their safety margin as traffic evolves are the aim of a 2025 paper led by Fujiang Yuan with six co-authors. Classic risk fields are static and data-light but adapt poorly; game-theoretic and learning methods are conservative, heavy, or opaque. The authors' evolutionary risk potential field updates risk from historical obstacle proximity.

Each obstacle gets a risk ellipse, a collision envelope joining forward reach with sideways uncertainty. An evolution factor, computed from time to collision and a hazard time window through a sigmoid, resizes the ellipse in real time. Plugged into model predictive control, the system posts smoother trajectories, higher average speeds, and collision-free runs in comparative interactive-driving experiments.
arxiv-2509-06475:
Showing how an AI hiring tool works can make managers trust it more without understanding it better, find Yannick Kalff and Katharina Simbeck in a 2025 study. Recruiting recommenders shape who is called in, so their dashboards add more and more explanations: top features, counterfactuals, and model criteria. The authors ask how a manager's AI literacy changes what those explanations do.

In an online experiment, four hundred ten German HR managers compared plain dashboards with explained ones. Practice dashboards, they note, barely explain at all and keep the AI opaque. They raised felt helpfulness and trust among users with mid or high AI literacy, but not real understanding, and complex explanations could reduce it. Only feature overlays clearly helped high-literacy users, arguing for literacy-matched explanation design and training.
arxiv-2509-06675:
Czech parliamentary speeches are turned into a large speech corpus by Vladislav Stankov and two co-authors in a 2025 language resources paper. The new release, ParCzech4Speech, reworks an existing text corpus of parliament records. Its largest variant holds close to twenty-seven hundred hours of audio matched with official transcripts.

Recordings were aligned to transcripts automatically using WhisperX and Wav2Vec 2.0, two speech tools that pin words to sound. The pipeline pulls in more data than the earlier speech version and keeps only alignments judged reliable. Three variants are offered: sentences cut cleanly for recognition and synthesis training, unsegmented speech preserving the original flow, and raw alignments for custom refinement. Metadata from the source corpus is preserved throughout, and a permissive license covers the release through LINDAT and Hugging Face.
arxiv-2509-06875:
Made-up examples for rare classes are grown by interacting agents in a 2025 machine learning paper by Sukumar Kishanthan and one co-author. Lopsided datasets, where one class vastly outnumbers another, bias classifiers against the minority. Classic oversampling makes copies or blends with drawbacks: features are treated on their own and variety is hard to control.

Their method, AxelSMOTE, borrows Axelrod's model of cultural spread, treating data points as agents that exchange traits. Features are grouped so links between them survive, exchanges are guided by likeness, blending uses a beta distribution for realistic mixes, and a dose of variety fights overfitting. On eight lopsided datasets, the method beat leading sampling approaches while staying cheap to run. The agent picture is more than decoration: the rules for how agents interact are what generate the new minority examples.
arxiv-2509-06975:
Graph learning methods that teach themselves from unlabeled data mostly fail to transfer to new datasets, finds a 2025 benchmark study led by Yu Song, with five co-authors. Self-supervised graph methods are usually developed and tested on one dataset at a time. Their cross-dataset transfer, the skill foundation models need, was largely unexplored.

GSTBench is presented as the first systematic benchmark for that transfer. Five representative methods were pretrained at large scale on a hundred-million-paper citation graph, then evaluated across diverse target graphs under a standardized setup that isolates the pretraining objective. Surprisingly, most methods generalized poorly, some doing worse than random initialization. One masked autoencoder approach, GraphMAE, improved transfer consistently. The authors analyze what drives the difference and offer guidance for building graph methods on a pretrain-then-transfer model.
arxiv-2509-07075:
Sebastian Ratzenböck and 5 co-authors study disk streams near the Sun in a 2025 paper, the first in a series called toward the fabric of the Milky Way. A disk stream, as they use the term, is a set of stars born together and moving together, stretched into a long shape.

Working with Gaia Data Release 3 data and strong clustering tools, they examined twelve streams inside a small local volume. They then traced each stream past the edges of that volume. On average, the known membership of each stream doubled. Counting the streams gives a number density far above what N-body simulations predict, by a factor of ten to a hundred. That gap challenges current ideas about how streams are destroyed. The streams move coldly together, sit on tight lines in the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram, and can stretch for several hundred parsecs.
arxiv-2509-07275:
How do people come to adopt a new technology while a charismatic rival pulls them back? Giulia Rotundo and 5 co-authors build a hybrid model for that contest in 2025. The model merges the Galam model of opinion dynamics, where group debate shifts opinions, with the Bass diffusion model, a classic curve for how products spread through a market.

The merged model runs on Barabasi-Albert networks, a network type where popular nodes attract still more links. Supporters can win over opponents for good, but a charismatic competitor can convert users back to the old technology. The team also tracks Kolmogorov-Sinai entropy, a measure of how unpredictable the system becomes over time. As the preferential attachment setting rises, meaning new nodes link more strongly to hubs, the adoption paths grow more regular and easier to foresee.
arxiv-2509-07375:
Chatbots are trained on huge amounts of personal data, including data left behind by people who have died. Elina Van Kempen, Ismat Jarin, and Chloe Georgiou examine that neglected issue in a 2025 research paper. They ask who owns a dead person's data and what privacy it deserves. The topic sits beside wider debates on data ownership, copyright, and consumer harm.

The authors propose three principles for managing post-mortem data in generative AI systems. They then review the policies of popular chatbots and the answers those chatbots give to legacy requests, such as deleting a relative's data. A systematic audit of consumer chatbots is planned as the next step. Their work gives regulators and companies a starting framework for a problem that grows as more lives are recorded online.
arxiv-2509-07475:
Language models sometimes state facts their source documents never supported, a failure called hallucination. Saumya Goswami and Siddharth Kurra present HALT-RAG in a 2025 research paper. HALT-RAG checks the outputs of retrieval-augmented generation systems, which answer questions using fetched documents. It flags statements that contradict or outrun the source text.

The system combines two ready-made inference models with light word-level signals. A small calibrated classifier, adapted per task, turns those signals into a hallucination probability. Training used a strict out-of-fold protocol to avoid leakage. On the HaluEval benchmark, scores were strong across summarization, question answering, and dialogue. Because its probabilities are well calibrated, the system can also abstain when unsure, a useful safety valve for deployed AI.
arxiv-2509-07575:
Ben Andrews and 2 co-authors give a new proof method in 2025 for global Harnack inequalities, estimates that compare a solution's values across space and time. Their target is the pointwise Harnack inequality for positive solutions of the linear Schrödinger equation on a Riemannian manifold with nonnegative Ricci curvature and a potential bounded below. Classic proofs first prove a gradient estimate, following Li and Yau, and demand very smooth solutions.

The new approach proves the inequality directly through a multi-point maximum principle, comparing the solution at several points at once. Avoiding higher-order derivatives lets the proof assume only twice-differentiable solutions. For the quadratic potential on Euclidean space, the method yields a new Harnack inequality with sharper constants. Solutions with a gradient drift term are also treated, including the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck operator used in probability.
arxiv-2509-08075:
Telling a language model to act as a persona can make it refuse harmless requests, measure Flor Miriam Plaza-del-Arco and 5 co-authors in a 2025 paper on model behaviour. Personalisation is spreading, yet recent work hinted that persona prompts raise false refusals, cases where the model wrongly declines a legitimate task. Nobody had quantified the effect properly.

Fifteen sociodemographic personas, spanning gender, race, religion, and disability, are tested across sixteen models and three tasks, with nine prompt paraphrases controlling for wording luck. The design separates genuine persona effects from noise. False refusals are not harmless: if they cluster on particular identities, personalised systems quietly give worse service to the very users they imitate.
arxiv-2509-08175:
Kensuke Akita and 2 co-authors propose a way for the early universe to hide big flavour gaps inside a zero total, in a 2025 cosmology paper. Their route uses the Affleck-Dine mechanism. In that scheme, a scalar field moves in the young universe and makes more matter than antimatter. Here the field also breaks into lumps called Q-balls.

The gaps are in lepton flavour: electrons, muons, and taus. One flavour can hold a surplus while another holds a matching deficit. The total stays zero on its own, with no fine tuning. Neutrino mixing later spreads the gaps around. That spread dodges the tight limits from the first minutes of the universe and from the microwave sky.
arxiv-2509-08675:
Liyu Zhong and 1 co-author give a fast way to build hyperuniform fields in a 2025 paper. Such fields hold down large scale swings in density, yet keep rich local disorder. That mix suits new materials for light, heat, and strength uses.

Their method shapes a field by its spectrum, the mix of wave sizes it holds. A superellipse form lets them tune round and stretched patterns on their own, with no slow loop of steps. Tests in two and three dimensions show tight control and huge speed gains. A simple cutoff step then turns fields into two phase maps for study of small scale form.
arxiv-2509-09075:
Chloe Ngo and 2 co-authors study optimal control of an SIR disease model where noncompliance spreads socially in a 2025 paper. SIR splits a population into susceptible, infected, and recovered groups. Here people also split into those who follow prevention measures and those who do not.

Noncompliance itself spreads like a contagion alongside the disease. The authors derive the reproductive ratio and analyze disease free equilibria. A policymaker can use mandates, treatment, and education campaigns as controls to minimize a cost function. Existence of optimal controls is proved for general costs. Numerical tests show how optimal strategy depends on policymaker preferences.
arxiv-2509-09175:
Fine-tuning a huge speech model to catch audio deepfakes works, but it costs a fortune in computing. Zihan Pan, Sailor Hardik Bhupendra, and Jinyang Wu propose MoLEx in a 2025 research paper. MoLEx mixes low-rank adaptation with a mixture-of-experts router inside self-supervised speech models. Only selected experts get fine-tuned for a given input, preserving the pre-trained knowledge.

During testing, the router reactivated the same experts for familiar attacks. It switched to different experts for novel spoofs, showing domain-aware adaptability. Extra experts can be trained later for new attack types without touching the whole model. On a major spoofing benchmark, MoLEx reached state-of-the-art error rates without data augmentation. As voice cloning keeps improving, detectors that adapt cheaply to each new fake may matter more than detectors that are merely strong once.
arxiv-2509-09275:
Lixing Zhang and 1 co-author present Neural Transformer Backflow for strongly correlated materials in a 2025 paper. Such materials host rich quantum phases, but strong interactions make them hard to solve. Their method is a neural trial wavefunction set in a multi-band frame.

It uses few parameters, is fermionic by build, and keeps momentum exact. That gives direct ground states at each momentum, with gaps and degeneracies in view. Small systems are solved with high accuracy, and sizes well past exact methods are reached. In twisted MoTe2, one frame captures density waves, fractional Chern insulators, and Hall fluids. A scalable route to new phases is claimed.
arxiv-2509-09675:
