arxiv-2602-01475: Brij Malhotra and co-authors propose neural guidance for local search in most probable explanation inference for probabilistic graphical models. Stochastic local search scales to large models but chases immediate gains and stalls in poor optima, while guided heuristics reshape the landscape without transferring guidance across queries. Their framework trains an attention network to score moves by predicted shrinkage of Hamming distance to a near-optimal solution, balancing short-term gains against long-term promise. Tests on hard high-treewidth benchmarks show steady gains over both baselines for repeated queries.
arxiv-2602-01575: Caterina Mosto and colleagues build a taxonomy of chaos from templexes, structures pairing a flow oriented cell complex with a directed graph. Unlike templates, confined by knot theory to three dimensions, templexes carry no such limit and describe higher dimensional chaos. The authors show each templex reduces by itself to a minimal form exposing the key traits of a chaotic attractor. That reduction yields two building blocks, an oscillating unit and a switching unit, shown on Rossler, Lorenz, Burke Shaw and Deng attractors, including a four dimensional case.
arxiv-2602-02075: Enrique Macías-Virgós and colleagues prove inequalities extending the Morse-Bott inequalities. When g is the identity, the classical Morse-Bott inequalities reappear, linking the dynamics of g and f. Let K be a finite simplicial complex, and let g from K to K be a simplicial map. Let f be a Morse-Bott function on K, discrete, with f of g of sigma at most f of sigma for all simplices sigma in K.
arxiv-2602-02375:
How should a person and an AI split a hard decision? Julian Berger and 5 co-authors answer with a simple tree-shaped rule in a 2026 arXiv paper. A human and an AI each decide independently. When they agree, that answer stands. When they disagree, a second human breaks the tie.

Math shows this hybrid confirmation tree can match or beat a three-person majority vote while using fewer human judgments. The gain is largest when human and AI accuracy are similar and their mistakes are not too alike. Reanalysis of six real datasets, covering skin cancer, deepfake detection, forecasting, and rearrest prediction, backs the theory. Accuracy rose by up to ten points over majority vote, and decision costs fell by roughly a third. People also stay in charge of the final call.
arxiv-2602-02475:
Shraddha Barke and 5 co-authors build a diagnostic system that finds the exact step where an AI agent went wrong, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Agent failures are hard to localize because runs are probabilistic, long, multi-agent, and polluted by noisy tool outputs. Human annotation of failures is expensive but necessary for ground truth.

The team manually annotated one hundred seventy failed trajectories across eleven task settings, from API workflows to incident management and open web tasks. Each run is labeled with its critical failure step and a category from a cross-domain taxonomy. Their automated framework, AgentRx, then synthesizes constraints, checks them step by step, and produces an auditable log of violations. A language-model judge uses that log to localize the failure. Step localization improved by about seventy-five percent on average over prior work.
arxiv-2602-02575:
Sattvik Yadav asks whether isolated pockets of antimatter could have survived the early universe and formed antistars, in a 2026 arXiv paper. The matter-antimatter asymmetry is a deep open problem. The study posits antimatter domains lasting until the era when the first stars formed.

Under CPT symmetry, the author treats an antimatter gas cloud of antihydrogen and antihelium with the same heat physics as its matter counterpart. A cautiously sized domain easily meets the Jeans and Bonnor-Ebert criteria for gravitational collapse. Cooling by antimolecular hydrogen then drives change mirroring the first matter stars, forming a dense anti-protostellar core. All hinges on one key assumption: that antinuclear fusion can ignite under core conditions. If it can, massive antistars should exist. Their visible signature would be high-energy radiation from annihilation where antimatter meets matter.
arxiv-2602-02775:
Antonio C. Gutiérrez-Piñeres writes a short comment in 2026 examining a proposed space-time metric for static ellipsoidal objects. The earlier paper claimed a line element that reduces to the Schwarzschild solution, the standard description of a spherical mass. A true solution of that kind must satisfy the vacuum Einstein equations, with no matter anywhere.

Checking the corrected line element with a computer algebra differential geometry package, Gutiérrez-Piñeres finds the Einstein tensor and Ricci scalar are not zero. Interpreted as an anisotropic fluid, the metric also yields nonzero pressures. It therefore does not represent a vacuum solution at all. A cited ellipsoidal metric from the literature fails the same check. The comment removes two candidate geometries from consideration for modeling ellipsoidal objects in general relativity.
arxiv-2602-02975:
Robots and other embodied agents must understand social norms to communicate well, and Mitchell Abrams and 4 co-authors test whether language models can do that reasoning in a 2026 paper. Understanding a phrase like a pronoun or description often requires knowing what actions are appropriate in context. That skill is called norm-based reference resolution.

The authors built SNIC, a human-validated testbed of situated norms. Its cases involve everyday tasks such as cleaning, tidying, and serving, where physical and social expectations meet. Even the strongest models tested struggled. They identified and applied norms inconsistently, especially when norms were implicit, underspecified, or in conflict. The results expose a blind spot for language systems deployed in social, embodied settings.
arxiv-2602-03175:
Probing several options but committing to only one is modeled by Ming Shi in solo theoretical work from 2026. The setting comes from multi-radio access selection and edge computing offloading. Each round, an agent chooses among candidate links or servers whose performance is a vector covering throughput, latency, energy, and reliability, and no single option dominates on every dimension at once.

The agent may probe a limited number of candidates and observe their outcomes, but must execute exactly one. Shi's algorithm selects probes to expand the attained Pareto frontier, using a hypervolume-inspired coverage measure, and commits by marginal frontier gain. Error and regret bounds quantify a transparent acceleration from probing. Extensions handle probes returning several modalities, with uncertainty fusion yielding adaptive bounds.
arxiv-2602-03375:
Magnetic islands inside a tokamak can reshape how well the hot plasma stays confined. Vibhor Kumar Singh and 12 co-authors examine this effect in a 2026 paper focused on the ADITYA-U tokamak. Their subject is the ion temperature gradient mode, a small instability that grows where the ion temperature changes steeply across the plasma.

The team simulates the plasma with a gyrokinetic particle-in-cell code helped by a neural network projection scheme. They first insert fixed magnetic islands and watch the density flatten inside them, then rerun the instability calculation on those flattened profiles. Wider islands make the growth rates of different modes converge. That points to a general stabilizing trend. Islands farther out produce a more spread-out mode structure.
arxiv-2602-03475:
Bertrand Nguefack studies whether a ring-theoretic size measure survives when passing to smaller rings inside skew polynomial rings. His 2026 paper concerns the uniform dimension, a count of how many separate pieces a module contains, and whether it stays fixed under subextensions. Skew polynomial rings twist the usual rules for multiplying, using automorphisms and derivations.

For commuting variables, Nguefack shows that standard results for ordinary polynomial rings carry over to subextensions of skew Laurent polynomial rings. The non-commuting case behaves strangely: he gives simple examples where an orderly ambient ring contains a wild free non-commutative subring. He then isolates a tamer subclass, the essentially special subextensions, and proves the dimension and related concepts are preserved there.
arxiv-2602-03675:
Quantum sensors gain precision near phase transitions, but the closing energy gap makes them painfully slow. George Mihailescu and Karol Gietka propose the opposite strategy in a 2026 paper, which they call anti-critical quantum metrology. Their point is that the usual precision boost mostly reflects longer evolution time, not a genuine advantage.

The authors show that quantum-enhanced sensitivity can also emerge while the energy gap grows, which removes the critical slowing down entirely. The quantum Fisher information may fall with the shorter evolution time, yet the achievable precision stays quantum-enhanced. They demonstrate the mechanism in the quantum Rabi model. The scheme offers a route to metrological advantage with fast relaxation instead of critical slowness.
arxiv-2602-03775:
Farnoosh Hashemi and Michael W. Macy spend a year watching 32,000 language model agents socialize on the Chirper.ai platform. Their 2026 paper analyzes seven million posts and interactions among these LLM-driven personas. The questions are sociological: do artificial agents reproduce homophily, influence, toxicity, and polarization the way humans do?

Like human networks, the agents' networks show homophily and social influence. Their toxic language, however, follows different structural patterns than human toxicity, and the authors dissect its linguistic features. Ideological leaning and community polarization appear as well. As a remedy, they propose Chain of Social Thought, a simple prompting method that reminds agents to avoid harmful posting. They show it curbs the behavior.
arxiv-2602-03975:
Spending verification effort where it counts is Shuhui Qu's theme in a second 2026 paper. Large language models reason better with more test-time computation, but verifier calls are expensive and often wasted on weak intermediate steps. Qu studies how to allocate those calls across candidate reasoning states.

The framework first gates states by deterministic feasibility, then ranks survivors with learned distance and residual scores. Remaining verifier calls go where local uncertainty is highest. On the MATH benchmark, the approach beat best-of-N sampling, majority voting, and beam search. It did so while using forty-four percent fewer verifier calls.
arxiv-2602-04175:
Huangxin Chen and 4 co-authors prove the math behind a two-phase flow model is sound. The model describes oil-water style flows through porous rock while respecting thermodynamics. Their 2026 paper establishes that weak solutions exist, are unique, and are regular, the three properties a model needs before simulations can be trusted.

The proof builds discrete approximations first, implicit in time, then fully discrete. A vector-field zero theorem yields solutions at each level, and energy estimates plus weak convergence pass to the limit. Uniqueness follows under smoothness of the chemical potential, with elliptic theory finishing the smoothness claim.
arxiv-2602-04275:
Chiyi Luo and 1 co-author study how fast equilibrium states of surface maps forget their past. Their 2026 paper concerns smooth surface maps with positive entropy and a large class of potentials. The key trait is strong positive recurrence of the potential.

Under that property, they prove statistical laws for the matching equilibrium states. Correlations decay at an exponential rate, giving rapid mixing. A strong ergodicity also holds, meaning the equilibrium state is in effect unique and computable in character. Such results anchor the theory of chaotic surface dynamics, where equilibrium states play the role that Gibbs measures play in statistics.
arxiv-2602-04675:
Panagiotis Theodoropoulos and 3 co-authors present a framework for moving probability, goods, or agents across a graph in a 2026 paper called GSBoG. Real transport decisions must respect the graph's topology and operational limits, which earlier bridge methods handled poorly.

Their generalized Schrödinger bridge learns executable policies for continuous-time Markov chains, processes that jump between states over time. Policies are learned at trajectory level, avoiding dense global solvers and improving scale. Training matches the required start and end distributions while also optimizing costs incurred along the way. Experiments on challenging real-world topologies showed accurate, topology-respecting policies. The approach suits cost-aware transport problems on general graphs of many kinds.
arxiv-2602-04775:
Yuqi Li and Matthew M. Engelhard extend a classic evaluation tool in their 2026 work on risk prediction. The ROC curve and its area summarize how well a score separates positive from negative cases, but they assume each prediction is a single number, not a range.

High-stakes predictions often come as intervals that express uncertainty. The authors build two ROC-style curves from interval endpoints and define an interval-based area measure. Rankings split into three regions: confidently correct, ambiguous, and confidently incorrect. Under valid coverage, the new quantities bound the best achievable standard score. Experiments on clinical data showed models with equal ordinary scores can differ sharply in uncertainty-aware ranking.
arxiv-2602-05075:
Cleaning up orbiting debris takes a craft that can visit several targets without wasting fuel or risking crashes. Agni Bandyopadhyay and Gunther Waxenegger-Wilfing present a learning-based planner for that job in this 2026 paper, accepted at an IAA symposium on small satellites. Small satellites suit the mission: cheap, flexible, and maneuverable.

Their scheme uses reinforcement learning, in particular a masked form of Proximal Policy Optimization, to order rendezvous with several debris items. Refueling stops are part of the plan, and collision avoidance adapts to live orbital states rather than a fixed script. Simulations built from the Iridium 33 debris field, across varied setups, showed lower collision risk and better mission efficiency than standard heuristic planners. The authors note the method transfers to other multi-target rendezvous tasks in autonomous mission planning.
arxiv-2602-05775:
Rarefied gas flows, where molecules collide rarely, need kinetic models that respect basic physics. The widely used Borgnakke Larsen model has two flaws: its collision kernel is not integrable, and it lacks detailed balance. Sha Liu and 6 co-authors adopt the Pullin equation instead, which has both properties, and rebuild the near continuum theory of polyatomic gases on it.

Working with translational and rotational degrees of freedom, they derive explicit formulas for how stress, temperatures, and heat fluxes relax. Transport coefficients follow from a Chapman Enskog expansion, and the results confirm a long standing suspicion: thermal conductivity depends on how far the gas sits from thermal equilibrium. At equilibrium their formulas reduce to classic Mason and Monchick values. They also propose a new Rykov type model that captures coupled relaxation of the two heat fluxes, a mechanism the standard Rykov equation ignores. Benchmark tests validate the model.
arxiv-2602-05975:
Deep research agents can chase hard questions, but they lean on search tools that must find the right papers first. Tiansheng Hu and four co-authors build SAGE, a test for that search step: twelve hundred questions across four science fields, over a corpus of two hundred thousand papers. They run six deep research agents on it and find all six stumble on retrieval that needs real reasoning.

A surprise follows. The old keyword method BM25 beats modern language-model retrievers by about thirty percent, since agents tend to write keyword-heavy sub-questions. To close the gap, the team adds language-model notes, metadata, and keywords to documents at test time. Scores rise by eight percent on short answers and two percent on open answers. SAGE gives the field a hard yardstick for search inside research agents.
arxiv-2602-06075:
Phone apps that act on a user's behalf need memory, yet most tests barely check it. Guangyi Liu and 14 co-authors built MemGUI-Bench, a benchmark focused on what mobile agents remember. It covers both holding facts during a task and learning across separate sessions.

The suite holds over a hundred tasks across many apps, most needing facts carried across time and screens. An automated grader scores memory accuracy, learning, and speed in stages. When the team tested eleven leading agents, every one showed large memory gaps. Adding clear long-term memory helped agents learn across sessions, but moving knowledge between apps stayed hard and costly.
arxiv-2602-06275:
Explaining why a closed language model gave its answer is hard when its maker hides the internals. Isaac Picov and Ritesh Goru present RoPE-LIME, a tool that explains a fixed answer without regenerating text. A smaller open model stands in as a surrogate, scoring how input changes affect the answer's likelihood.

Two upgrades drive the method. Similarity between perturbed inputs is measured in rotary position embedding space, which stays stable under masking. A sparse sampling scheme covers word interactions better on a tight budget. On question answering and a hand-labeled subset of a broad knowledge test, the tool gave more informative attributions than leave-one-out sampling. It also beat its predecessor while using far fewer calls to the closed model.
arxiv-2602-06575:
Vision-language-action models usually receive the robot's body state as a late add-on, too late to shape what the model looks at. Fangyuan Wang and 6 co-authors present ThinkProprio, which turns proprioception into tokens from the language model's own vocabulary. Those state tokens join the instruction to gate visual patches before the main model runs, steering attention to action-relevant evidence.

Passive state conditioning, the team found, changed performance little. Its value appeared only when state tokens actively selected which visual patches to process. Vocabulary tokens beat learned projector encodings for the state, and keeping only about an eighth of the visual tokens beat the full-token baseline on a standard manipulation suite. Across three benchmarks and real robots, latency fell while accuracy improved.
arxiv-2602-06675:
Hoang Pham, The-Anh Ta, and Long Tran-Thanh study pruning at initialisation, a trick that trims a neural network down to a sparse skeleton before training even starts. The heuristics for choosing which connections to keep are well used, but why the resulting patterns work has stayed unclear. The paper connects these discrete choices to graphon theory, the mathematics of very large networks viewed as continuous objects.

The authors model the saliency scores behind popular pruning rules and prove the pruning masks settle into deterministic limiting patterns as networks grow. Simple rules give uniform patterns, while data-driven rules give uneven ones that quietly perform feature selection. From that limit picture they derive a universal approximation result for sparse networks and a generalisation bound showing how the limiting pattern steers learning toward informative features.
arxiv-2602-06775:
Sajad Ashkezari studies how to learn classifiers that stay right even when their inputs are tampered with, in a setting harsher than the usual one. Here not only the perturbation but also the clean data and its label are chosen adversarially. The paper frames the problem as online learning, where the learner receives examples one at a time and is scored on its mistakes.

Ashkezari defines a new complexity measure for hypothesis classes and shows it controls the mistake bounds when a perfect classifier exists, and the regret bounds when none does. Unlike the dimension that governs the classic PAC setting, this one is simple and resembles the Littlestone dimension. The results extend to multiclass problems, and the paper also treats the case where the learner knows only a prior over possible perturbations rather than the exact set.
arxiv-2602-06875:
Jiangping Huang and five co-authors debug code written by language models by watching it run. Bad code from models often hides small but fatal flaws, and old repair tools lean on pass-or-fail signals that say little about where a fault sits. Their system, TraceCoder, plants probes in the code to record fine traces of what happens step by step.

A cause hunt over those traces pins down the root fault, while lessons drawn from past failed fixes steer the next try away from old mistakes. A rollback rule makes sure each fix is a strict step up, not a sideways shuffle. Across test sets, first-try scores rose by up to about 34 percent over strong rivals, and the repeat-fix loop alone gave most of the gain.
arxiv-2602-06975:
R. James Cotton and Thomas Leonard present BiomechAgent, an AI agent that lets clinicians analyze movement data without writing code. Markerless motion capture has made measured movement analysis widely available, but turning the resulting data into answers still needs programming skill. BiomechAgent takes plain-language requests to query data stores, make charts, and read results.

The authors built a benchmark spanning data retrieval, chart making, activity sorting, time splitting, and clinical thinking. BiomechAgent did well on retrieval and charts and showed growing clinical thinking skill. Domain-specific guidance beat generic prompts, and tested tools for gait event detection sharply improved hard space-time analysis. A local open-weight model did much worse than a frontier cloud model except on retrieval, a trade-off the paper documents for setups that cannot use cloud models.
arxiv-2602-07175:
Some matrices are built by a simple rule: each entry comes from its neighbors above and to the left, with fixed weights.  Xiao You Chen and two co-authors study exactly those matrices, whose entries follow a three-term recurrence from the first row and column.

The paper offers a general factorization that contains many known breakdowns as special cases, and it also splits these matrices into Pascal-like factors plus a basic Toeplitz matrix.  Matrix theorists get a unifying frame for a family of recurrences that previously had to be handled case by case, with cleaner proofs as a bonus. The same frame covers many known cases at once.
arxiv-2602-07675:
This doctoral thesis studies how attractors, universality, and collectivity emerge in ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collisions, through relativistic kinetic theory.  Vincenzo Nugara first reviews quantum chromodynamics, the quark-gluon plasma, and the two main descriptions of hot QCD matter, kinetic theory and hydrodynamics. Then he develops the Relativistic Boltzmann Transport model used for most results.

The investigation moves from a simple 1D massless model to full three-plus-1D setups, non-conformal systems, and real event-by-event fluctuations.  Readers get a thorough thesis-length treatment of far-from-equilibrium attractors, valuable as both a research record and an entry point to heavy-ion kinetic theory.
arxiv-2602-07875:
Made tabular data must often obey conditions, like filling a missing value or respecting an inequality, but most generators only learn conditions seen during training. Aditya Shankar and three co-authors extend manifold theory to tabular data so that new constraints can be imposed at making time instead.

Their method, HARPOON, guides unconstrained diffusion samples along the data manifold's geometry until they satisfy diverse inference-time conditions. Tests on imputation and inequality-constraint tasks across several datasets show strong results, demonstrating that manifold-aware guidance works beyond continuous domains. Data scientists who need controlled made tables gain a flexible tool that does not require retraining for each new rule.
arxiv-2602-07975:
Multi-agent systems often need followers to track a leader even as communication links switch on and off, but prior results required the system to be at most marginally stable. Yuhan Chen and two co-authors break that barrier, proving leader-following exponential consensus is achievable for a system matrix that is exponentially unstable.

How much instability can be tolerated is spelled out explicitly through quantities arising from the jointly connected switching graph. By duality, the same ideas solve output-based distributed observer design for a general leader system under switching networks, again beyond the marginally stable case. Control theorists gain results that finally cover common systems like the double integrator, which earlier theory excluded.
arxiv-2602-08175:
Kac-Moody groups widen known Lie groups to endless sizes, and their hole-counting raises calm questions: do patterns settle as the diagram grows? Nitu Kitchloo shows that a set method for growing wider Dynkin diagrams gives groups of Kac-Moody groups meeting hole calm.

The methods use path splits of sorting spaces, and the results are shown for the E_n family, which interests string theorists, with a sketch of new structure showing upon control. Algebra fans and shape fans gain a calm theorem for an endless-sized family where plain math is usually out of reach.
arxiv-2602-08375:
Inequalities on curved geometries can behave quite differently from their flat-space cousins. Wenjing Chen and Zexi Wang study a nonlocal Sobolev inequality on the Heisenberg group, a setting where directions do not commute. Their arXiv paper proves two kinds of refinement: a gradient-type remainder term, and sharp quantitative stability for critical points.

The remainder appears when the dimension parameter reaches at least four and the interaction exponent stays within a bounded range. As a consequence, a weaker remainder also holds on bounded domains. Stability is established for multi-bubble critical points in the four-dimensional case with the exponent between two and four. Readers get precise control of how near-miss functions sit relative to exact optimizers.
arxiv-2602-08475:
The southern Milky Way glows in low-frequency radio waves, and mapping it well takes both sharpness and sensitivity to broad structure. S. Mantovanini and five co-authors present the third GLEAM-X release, covering about 3,800 square degrees of the Galactic plane from 72 to 231 megahertz. Their arXiv paper combines extended-array observations with the earlier GLEAM survey.

Baselines from about twelve meters to five kilometers give resolutions from roughly 45 arcseconds to two arcminutes. A wide-band image yields 98,207 sources across twenty frequency bands, with position accuracy within an arcsecond and reliability above 99 percent. Readers get images and a catalog ready for studies of the Galaxy's radio sky.
arxiv-2602-08575:
Generative retrieval in recommenders usually decodes item identifiers token by token, treating each token as the sole target. Kairui Fu and ten co-authors argue that narrow focus misses the structure of user preferences and the interplay with behavior sequences. Their arXiv paper introduces RankGR, a rank-enhanced method built on listwise preference optimization.

Retrieval splits into two stages. An initial assessment phase learns hierarchical preferences and partial orders through listwise optimization. A refined scoring phase then re-ranks the top candidates against input sequences with a light scoring module. Both phases train jointly, and the deployed system handles nearly ten thousand requests per second. Offline and online tests, including Taobao's Guess You Like section, confirm the gains. Readers get a ranking-aware upgrade for generative recommendation.
arxiv-2602-08675:
Sixth-generation networks will rely on AI agents making semantic and network-level decisions, yet no benchmark tests that capability systematically. Mohamed Amine Ferrag and two co-authors introduce 6G-Bench, drawn from standardization work across 3GPP, IETF, ETSI, ITU-T, and O-RAN. Their arXiv paper defines thirty decision tasks in five capability categories.

From over 113,000 scenarios, ten thousand hard multiple-choice questions were generated, with 3,722 retained after automated filtering and expert validation. Twenty-two foundation models were tested, with single-shot accuracy spanning 0.22 to 0.82 and reasoning-heavy tasks showing even wider spread. Readers get an open benchmark for AI-native 6G reasoning and a sobering map of current model limits.
arxiv-2602-08875:
Luc Ta settles a question in algebra by linking two seemingly different worlds. His short note shows that Latin medial quandles, algebraic structures built around a self-distributive operation, match affine modules over a certain ring of Laurent polynomials. The commutative case matches affine modules over the dyadic rationals instead.

From that bridge, he describes the free objects in these categories and proves a structure theorem for finitely generated medial commutative quandles. He also characterizes racks whose duals are commutative. Together, the results answer two open problems posed by Bardakov and Elhamdadi.
arxiv-2602-09075:
Transformers learn from context as if remembering, but gated linear focus models have fixed, interference-prone memory. Djohan Bonnet and four co-authors propose Palimpsa, a self-focus model that treats in-context learning as continual learning with a keep-or-drop trade-off. Bayesian metaplasticity ties each focus state's changeability to an importance state grounded in a prior over accumulated knowledge.

Many gated linear focus models emerge as special cases of this design, and Mamba2 appears as the limit where forgetting dominates. That link lets any non-plastic model be upgraded to a plastic one, greatly expanding memory capacity. Tests show Palimpsa beating baselines on multi-query associative recall and commonsense reasoning.
arxiv-2602-09175:
Seung-Hoon Jung and four co-authors compare two deep images of the supernova remnant Cassiopeia A, taken in 2013 and 2020 with identical instruments and procedures on the UKIRT telescope. The matching setup allows precise measurement of change over seven years in the iron and silicon emission lines. In the 2020 image they identify 263 compact knots, sorted into quasi-stationary circumstellar knots and fast-moving ejecta knots.

Fast-moving knots flicker strongly, and many seen in 2013 have vanished by 2020. Proper motions from cross-correlation show most ejecta expanding nearly ballistically, though knots just beyond the eastern iron-rich region slow noticeably. The main shell's motion fits a uniformly expanding shell with a systemic drift, reproducing the remnant's geometric and kinematic asymmetries.
arxiv-2602-09275:
In stacked ferroelectrics, light can change shape, a light-strain effect ruled by rival electron effects. S. Puri and seven co-authors show that in stacked tin sulfide, the electron shape-pull beats reverse piezo screening. It drives growth along the polar axis even inside ferroelectric zones, against theory's foretold shrink for single-layer kin.

Polar-sorted second-harmonic microscopes, ultrafast shine tests, and first-principles math together sort out the uneven grid reply and split true light-strain from thin-film glare tricks. The findings set a tiny-scale ranking of light-strain effects and place stack-built tin sulfide as a base for ultrafast light-to-motion devices.
arxiv-2602-09375:
Training language-model agents that reason like AlphaZero needs dense feedback, but most setups reward only final answers. Hanchen Xia and five co-authors propose LaPha, a 2026 method that trains such agents inside a Poincaré latent space. Search becomes a tree rooted at the prompt, growing outward toward the ball's boundary, where negative curvature supplies rapidly growing capacity with radius. Distance to verified correctness defines each node's potential, and reward flows from potential differences.

A lightweight value head shares the same latent space, guiding test-time search with almost no added cost. On a five-hundred-problem math benchmark, the method lifts a small math model from roughly two-thirds correct to nearly nine-tenths. With value-guided search, the small model scores strongly on a recent olympiad-style contest set, and the larger version scores higher still. The paper presents hyperbolic geometry as a natural home for agent search.
arxiv-2602-09475:
Modern image generators look so real that only small flaws, like warped hands or bent objects, betray them. Spotting those artifacts matters for ranking generators and training reward models. Yet current detectors fine-tune vision-language models on tens of thousands of labeled images, a cost that repeats with every new generator or flaw type. James Burgess and five co-authors show pretrained models already hold the needed knowledge, if prompted with the right scaffolding.

Their system, ArtifactLens, unlocks artifact detection with only a few hundred labeled examples per flaw category. It leads on five human artifact benchmarks, the first evaluation spanning multiple datasets, while using orders of magnitude less labeled data. The scaffolding joins in-context learning with text instruction tuning, each part improved. The method extends to other flaw types, from animal anatomy to object interactions, and to the separate task of spotting AI-generated content.
arxiv-2602-09775:
Geographically representative images are beyond what text-to-image models can generate, which casts doubt on how representative training data is. Abhipsa Basu and five co-authors geographically profile large multimodal datasets in their 2026 paper, mapping image-caption pairs to countries from locations extracted from captions with language models. English captions from three datasets across twenty common entities, such as house and flag, are studied.

The United States, United Kingdom, and Canada account for nearly half, while South American and African countries are severely under-represented at under two and under four percent respectively. Representation correlates strongly with a country's gross domestic product. Non-English subsets skew toward countries where those languages are predominantly spoken, and higher representation does not guarantee greater visual or semantic diversity. Country-specific images generated by a model trained on one dataset look realistic yet cover less than real images.
arxiv-2602-09975:
Swapping one element for a neighbor can reshape a quantum material's behavior, especially where spin-orbit coupling runs strong. A 2026 paper led by Reiley Dorrian, with six co-authors, studies thin films of layered square-net intermetallics, growing lanthanum bismuthide layer by layer. The film behaves as a good metal and turns superconducting at about half a kelvin.

Compared with its antimony cousin, the bismuth film shows stronger metallic behavior and cleaner growth. The authors trace the difference to relativistic corrections in the electronic band structure, acting through surface energy and phonon scattering. The work shows how chemistry tunes both growth and electronic character in this material family.
arxiv-2602-10075:
Some hadrons may be molecules of heavy quarks rather than simple quark-antiquark pairs. A 2026 paper led by S. S. Agaev, with two co-authors, explores two tensor states built only from heavy quarks using QCD sum rules. Each combines an Upsilon or charmonium-like meson with an excited Bc meson, giving asymmetric heavy-quark contents.

Computed masses show both structures unstable against breaking apart into their constituent mesons. The authors calculate full widths from dominant and subleading decay channels, with subleading decays driven by quark-antiquark annihilation. At the lower mass limit for the heavier state, one dominant decay switches off, a detail the paper tracks carefully.
arxiv-2602-10275:
Heating and accelerating the solar wind near the Sun requires mapping plasma evolution from Parker Solar Probe's closest passes. A 2026 paper led by Yogesh, with twenty-one co-authors, uses observations from Encounters 1 through 24 to trace how solar wind plasma and magnetic field properties change with distance. Intervals with high field-of-view coverage yield radial profiles of field strength, proton density, bulk speed, temperatures, anisotropy, plasma beta, Alfvén Mach number, and field fluctuations for sub- and super-Alfvénic regions.

Beyond the Alfvén surface, power-law profiles broadly match earlier Helios results beyond three-tenths of an astronomical unit. Perpendicular temperature falls monotonically with distance, while parallel temperature dips in the sub-Alfvénic region then rises just beyond the Alfvén surface, interpreted as a proxy for proton beam occurrence. Magnetic fluctuations decline with distance, constraining near-Sun heating mechanisms.
arxiv-2602-10375:
Cancers pushing into surrounding tissue often develop wavy, unstable boundaries, yet the mechanics behind those shapes have been hard to pin down. A 2026 paper led by Sumit Sinha, with two co-authors, models a growing active liquid pushing into a passive viscoelastic matrix. Lab experiments with breast epithelial spheroids grown in an extracellular matrix motivate the work. A stability analysis of the sharp-interface limit predicts long-wavelength instabilities at the tissue boundary. But those instabilities are suppressed when the active mass sits inside an elastic matrix.

The authors map these regimes in a theoretical morphological phase diagram. They then track the nonlinear evolution of the boundary with two-dimensional finite-element phase-field simulations. Simulations match both theory and experimental observations. The study offers a basis for understanding how interfacial instabilities arise in active-passive systems, and hints at ways they might eventually be controlled.
arxiv-2602-10575:
Chenhao Zhang and two co-authors teach machines to grasp visual metaphor in a 2026 paper. Mixed models handle basic visual questions well, yet they stumble on images whose meaning rides on cultural context, emotion, and implication. Reading a metaphor demands multi-hop thinking and a sense of what others intend, capacities current models lack.

Their system, MetaphorStar, is the first end-to-end visual reward-based learning approach to image implication tasks. It bundles a fine-grained dataset, a visual reward-based learning method, and an ordered benchmark. The resulting open-source model family, trained with the new method, improves results much over baselines in the paper's tests. That narrows the gap between seeing an image and grasp what it means.
arxiv-2602-10675:
Junhua Liu and five co-authors build a large dataset for thinking about moving images in a 2026 paper. Visual chain-of-thought methods weave perception into thinking steps, but current plans mostly handle static scenes. They falter on time motion: instructions unfolding over time, predictions about what happens next, and camera motion.

The team presents TwiFF-2.7M, a temporally grounded dataset drawn from millions of video clips for dynamic visual question answering. Alongside it comes TwiFF-Bench, a benchmark of just over a thousand samples judging both thinking paths and final answers in open-ended dynamic settings. A unified model built on these foundations shows how future-frame thinking can ground mixed thinking in time.
arxiv-2602-10875:
Darakshan Rashid and three co-authors build fairness into chest X-ray diagnosis in a 2026 paper. Deep networks classify chest radiographs well on average yet underperform for exact demographic subgroups, raising clinic safety and equity concerns. Current debiasing methods improve inconsistently or buy fairness by degrading overall diagnostic utility.

Their system, Stride-Net, learns disease-discriminative yet demographically stable models through disentanglement and learnable masking with embedding alignment. Operating at patch level, a learnable stride-based mask selects label-aligned image regions while suppressing sensitive attribute information. Fairness becomes a trait of the model itself, not a post hoc constraint, aiming at diagnoses that serve all subgroups without sacrificing scores.
arxiv-2602-11175:
Models excel at pattern matching yet stumble on exact discrete thinking. Michelle Yuan and seven co-authors survey the barriers across depth, exactness, and bandwidth, synthesizing circuit hardness, approximation theory, and communication hardness. Arithmetic, logic, and stepwise composition all expose the same structural limits.

Key hurdles include depth constraints, trouble approximating sharp discontinuities, and bottlenecks in token-to-token communication. The survey links established frames into one accessible account of why exact symbolic recipes resist model build. It closes with design implications and promising directions, aiming to guide builders who want reliable discrete thinking from these designs.
arxiv-2602-11275:
Telling apart spectral lines that sit very close jointly is a core sensing challenge. Joseph T. Iosue and four co-authors revisit superresolution through quantum control theory, using the filter-function formalism to derive analytic terms for control protocols. Those terms say exactly when superresolution is achievable.

An optimal control frame then finds protocols that meet the terms under realistic test constraints. Extensions cover entangled initial states and their possible advantage. The approach applies across quantum sensing platforms, offering a systematic path to protocols that beat usual detail limits rather than relying on case-by-case tricks.
arxiv-2602-11375:
Photon-counting detectors transformed synchrotron imaging, but can they work on a lab bench? Jordan Fonseca and ten co-authors show lab-based nanoscale X-ray tomography with a four-megapixel hybrid photon counting detector. They image an integrated circuit at the one-hundred-thirty-nanometre node.

The reconstruction collects far more photons far faster than the group's prior work, for an overall speedup of several hundredfold. Image quality is quantified with modulation transfer, Fourier shell link, and contrast-to-noise metrics, checking detail and speed choices. Wiring traits at one-hundred-sixty nanometres resolve at well under one-hundred-nanometre spatial detail. The work brings synchrotron-grade tomography toward tabletop practice.
arxiv-2602-11975:
For three-mode tensors, circuit complexity and tensor rank march together asymptotically, but that partnership collapses once modes multiply. Cornelius Brand and six co-authors explore d-mode tensors, where hardness remains poorly understood despite its relevance to fine-grained hardness. First, they give a graph-theoretic proof of Strassen's bound on the long-run rank exponent for three-mode tensors, generalized to an upper bound for d-mode tensors.

Refined techniques for four or more modes push that bound past the current state of the art. The authors also bound the asymptotic circuit rate for generic d-mode tensors, optimizing the bounds for four and five modes. A central question is whether low cost of two tensors implies low cost of their product. True for rank, it is false for circuit cost already at eight modes, assuming the Hyperclique Conjecture, though a restricted version can be salvaged.
arxiv-2602-12075:
Computing a planet's gravity with finite elements hits a basic problem: the field extends infinitely, but meshes must end. Ziheng Yu and two co-authors test three fixes for infinite space: naive domain truncation, a Dirichlet-to-Neumann map on a truncated boundary, and multipole expansion on a cut edge. They focus on parallel setups in modern open-source codes, especially the widely used MFEM package.

Both static potential values and small perturbations from displacement fields are considered. The latter is needed to couple self-gravity into planet dynamics. Against earlier studies, cutoff can deliver accurate solutions at fair cost, with suitable mesh thinning outside. Still, DtN and far-field schemes give better accuracy at a lower cost in large-scale simulations, despite non-local communication from wave sums. The DtN method admits an efficient MPI-based setup limited to nodes that contain part of the mesh's outer boundary.
arxiv-2602-12475:
Solar energetic particle events usually show faster, higher-energy particles arriving first, but Parker Solar Probe found a striking exception. Zigong Xu led a large team here, studying the Labor Day event of 5 September 2022. In that event, medium-energy particles arrived earlier than both lower and higher energy particles, forming a nose structure in intensity spectrograms from the ISOIS instruments EPI-Lo and EPI-Hi. That delayed arrival of higher-energy particles is called inverse velocity arrival.

Using a new contour-line method on intensity, the team found 14 such events in ISOIS data through the end of 2024. Factors that may shape dispersion are explored, including spacecraft distance, coronal mass ejection and shock speeds, shock geometry, and magnetic footpoint separation from the flare. Nose energies group into low, medium, and high bands, with 11 of 14 events in the medium band, offering new clues to shock acceleration in the inner heliosphere.
arxiv-2602-12675:
Sparse-Linear Attention mixes sparse and linear attention to speed up diffusion models. It has shown strong scores in video making, yet it relies on a heuristic split assigning work to the sparse or linear branch based on attention-weight size, which can be suboptimal. Jintao Zhang led this work with eight co-authors, also finding a mismatch between Sparse-Linear Attention and a direct split into sparse and linear attention after formally studying attention error.

Their method, SLA2, adds a learnable router that picks whether each attention job should use sparse or linear attention. It also adds a more faithful split and quantisation-aware training. Tests on video diffusion models show SLA2 beating Sparse-Linear Attention rivals in making quality and speed, with lower quantisation loss at low bit widths.
arxiv-2602-12775:
Presence, the feeling of being there, is central to virtual reality, yet little is known about how everyday use shapes it outside the lab. Qijia Chen and two co-authors asked 295 social VR users about overall, social, spatial, and self-presence. They set those scores against usage habits: how often users log on, how long sessions last, and how many years they have used VR. Both frequency and duration predicted higher presence on every dimension.

Frequent and long sessions together amplified the effect, suggesting the two habits reinforce each other. The links held steady across age and gender, pointing to behaviour rather than demographics as the driver. For designers, the message is hopeful: environments that invite regular, extended visits may reliably deepen presence, and that insight comes from real-world use, not lab sessions alone.
arxiv-2602-12875:
Modern apps split into many small microservices, and running them across the computing continuum makes meeting service-level objectives harder. Trading performance against sustainability goals is especially tricky, and the providers who hold the know-how to fix problems must still respect developers' privacy. Juan Luis Herrera and two co-authors present CASCA, an open-source platform for carbon-aware service control.

CASCA lets continuum providers reconfigure services to meet objectives while keeping developer information private. It is built to be reusable, distributable, and easy to extend or modify. In a real testbed running a media streaming service, decision systems written in Bash, Rust, and Python each reconfigured the service successfully without breaking privacy. The platform shows that intelligent, privacy-respecting control is workable in practice.
arxiv-2602-12975:
Most tuning metrics judge only a classifier's top confidence, ignoring the rest of the probability spread. Andrew Thompson and Vivek Desai propose the Shift Tuning Error, extending expected tuning error from maximum confidence to any measure of shift, such as Shannon mess. The extension lets practitioners assess whether a model's full spread, not just its best guess, is well calibrated.

Number examples with mock forecasts that are perfectly calibrated by design show the new metric approaching zero as sample size grows. A rival mess-based metric, the UCE, fails that test in the same setting. For model testing, the result matters: a metric that cannot recognise perfect tuning will mislead comparisons, while shift tuning error passes the basic sanity check and generalises a familiar tool.
arxiv-2602-13275:
Safety work on AI usually tries to make each single system behave well, but human groups gain safety a different way: through structure that limits what any one flawed member can do. This paper borrows that institutional idea for multi-agent AI, using sealed compartments and hostile review to get sound results from parts that cannot be trusted alone. Its test system, the Perseverance Composition Engine, splits writing into three roles with unequal access to sources.

A Composer drafts text, a Corroborator checks facts with full source access, and a Critic judges argument quality without seeing sources. Across 474 writing tasks, the layered setup moved from attempted fabrication toward honest refusal with alternatives when given impossible tasks, a shift no single part was told to make. William Waites is the sole author.
arxiv-2602-13475:
The hazard ratio from the Cox model is the standard summary of treatment effect. But when hazards do not stay proportional over time, it loses a stable causal meaning and becomes tied to follow-up and censoring patterns. The average hazard offers a cleaner target: a population person-time event rate that stays well-defined and interpretable without assuming proportional hazards. Existing estimation routes, however, lack a general framework for flexible, high-dimensional nuisance estimation with valid root-n inference.

This paper builds a semiparametric, doubly robust framework for covariate-adjusted average hazard. It establishes pathwise differentiability, derives the efficient influence function, and constructs cross-fitted, debiased estimators that use machine learning for nuisance parts. Simulations show small bias and near-nominal coverage, even under crossing hazards, and an application compares immunotherapy regimens for advanced melanoma. Xiang Meng leads the work with three co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13575:
Aligning language models usually squeezes vast human preference data into one fixed, absolute reward function, inviting data scarcity, noise sensitivity, and unstable training. Elo-Evolve reframes alignment as dynamic multi-agent competition inside an adaptive opponent pool. Two innovations drive it: learning directly from binary win and loss outcomes in pairwise contests, with no Bradley-Terry model, and Elo-orchestrated opponent selection that builds an automatic curriculum through temperature-controlled sampling.

Grounded in PAC learning theory, pairwise comparison is shown to offer better sample complexity, with a claimed 4.5-fold noise reduction against absolute scoring. Training Qwen2.5-7B against larger opponents produced a clear hierarchy: point-based methods trailed static pairwise training, which trailed Elo-Evolve on Alpaca Eval 2.0 and MT-Bench. Jing Zhao leads the work with four co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13675:
AI explanations usually cover one application at a time, but users meeting a related application carry understanding over from earlier explanations, risking overreach and overtrust, or else learning each case separately. Transferable XAI addresses that transfer directly, explaining links between domain explanations through a general affine mapping framework applied to linear factor explanations. Transfer takes three forms: shifts for data subspaces, scaling for decision tasks, and mapping for attributes.

User studies on task and attribute domains found Transferable XAI most helpful for understanding a second domain. It beat single-domain and domain-free explanations on decision honesty, factor recall, and ability to relate explanations across domains. The framework thus makes explanations reusable across related uses. Fei Wang leads the work with two co-authors.
arxiv-2602-14175:
Nadia Koliopoulou and two co-authors build a 2026 arXiv theory of measure for Einstein-style quantum fields. Old non-Einstein models ignore place, cause, and Lorentz balance, so they fail for field settings. Most prior work also stuck to scalar fields, while real bits carry spin, twist, and inner form.

Using the Quantum Temporal Probabilities setup, the authors treat light, Dirac, and shaped scalar fields. Results give time-of-arrival odds that account for spin and twist. They give photo-count formulas past Glauber theory. They give a clear proof of the bit swing formula with its limits. They also give a first-principles study of Einstein-style qudits. The work grounds Einstein measure in both base theory and use.
arxiv-2602-14575:
Eckhard Platen, writing alone, models a 2026 arXiv financial market as a communication system. Four info-theory rules yield an ideal model with only one knob, where state values are scalar steady spreads. The model shrinks market surprise and the Kullback-Leibler split between the benchmark-neutral pricing gauge and the real-world odds gauge.

State values, their sums, and the growth-best stock basket evolve as squared radial Ornstein-Uhlenbeck runs in matching activity times. That single-knob form offers a lean lens on market motion, linking info theory to the time change of baskets and state values in one joined picture.
arxiv-2602-14675:
Piedmontese is an endangered Romance language of northwest Italy, written with no single spelling norm. Gianluca Vico, with Jindřich Libovický as co-author, builds a crowdsourced set of 145 Italian-Piedmontese sentence pairs from Flores+. Speakers wrote in their own natural spelling, with manual word alignment added.

The set benchmarks large language models on tokenization, topic classification, and translation. Piedmontese pays a tokenization penalty against richer Romance languages, yet classification nearly matches Italian, French, and English. Translation into Piedmontese lags translation out of it. Data and code are openly released to support work on the language.
arxiv-2602-14775:
S. Uttenthaler and others set period-luminosity rules for Milky Way Miras, long-period stars on the old giant branch. Such stars long lacked good spans, since their gaps were ill-known.

Now multi-round light data from DIRBE and unTimely/WISE, Gaia span data, and fresh beat times from light work give a firm base. Clear rules show up in nine near-infrared bands, with slopes and zero marks set out, so nearby Miras gain a trusted yardstick. Star beats thus turn into a tool for gauging the near Milky Way.
arxiv-2602-14975:
Gouraud and colleagues speed up molecular dynamics run with neural network potentials. Their DMTS-NC scheme distills a fast, simplified model that yields non-conservative forces, coupled through a reversible reference propagator to an accurate conservative potential. The distilled design keeps key physical priors, such as rotation equivariance and cancellation of atomic force parts. That steadies the distillation and keeps the two models in close agreement on forces.

The scheme proves more stable and efficient than its conservative twin, with extra speedups of 15 to 30 percent over DMTS and no fine-tuning needed. Hydrogen mass repartitioning and high hydrogen friction stretch the largest step to 10 femtoseconds while holding accuracy. A proof of principle on MACE-OFF23 runs between three and six times faster than a single-step run.
arxiv-2602-15275:
Nakayama asks whether the field should talk about dS/CFT link or dS/SFT link in cosmic signals. In non-unitary field theories, thought to be dual to cosmic signals, scale invariance need not imply full conformal invariance. While Einstein's theory predicts the rise of that invariance, or boost symmetry in the bulk, various changed models suggest only scale invariance, marked by the lack of bulk boost symmetry. The paper shows this gap using Einstein-Aether theory as a classic example.

The gap matters because scale invariance alone is weaker than full conformal invariance, and the two links encode different symmetry claims about the bulk. The title's pun turns on boost symmetry itself.
arxiv-2602-15475:
McKevitt and colleagues join readings of the surface magnet field from SDO/HMI and non-thermal speed in log T near 6 plasma from Hinode/EIS for 28 regions. MHD ripples and/or the twisting of magnet threads are mostly held to heat the solar corona, both routes powered by the Sun's surface field. New models suggest such heating routes would be seen in extra broadening, non-thermal speed, of coronal spectral output threads.

They also expect bigger amounts of surface flux would make more heating. But a plain link between flux and spectral line broadening has been hard to prove. They find a middling link between the two in calm regions, matching the surface field pushing Poynting flux into the corona and driving coronal heating. They find no firm link with coronal makeup, which makes it hard to tell apart MHD wave heating and magnet field twisting heating using tests.
arxiv-2602-15675:
Khamis and Ali fill a gap in Arabic speech technology. Egyptian Arabic, the most widely understood Arabic dialect, remains severely under-resourced for text-to-speech. Most resources target Modern Standard Arabic and Gulf dialects. Their answer is NileTTS, 38 hours of transcribed speech from two speakers across domains including medical, sales, and general conversation.

The data come from a synthetic pipeline. Large language models draft Egyptian Arabic content, audio synthesis tools voice it, and automatic transcription plus speaker diarisation follow, with manual quality checks. Fine-tuning XTTS v2, a leading multilingual speech model, on NileTTS beats a baseline trained on other Arabic dialects. The team releases the data set, the reproducible pipeline, and the fine-tuned model as the first public Egyptian Arabic speech data set of its kind.
arxiv-2602-15875:
Xu and colleagues built Fly0 for aerial vision-language navigation with no prior task training. Current tools trade sense for control. Large language models grasp sense well, but used as low-level controllers they lag, wobble, and fail to transfer when their grasp of shape is weak.

Fly0 splits sense from shape planning in three stages. A language model turns plain words into 2D pixel points. A shape stage uses depth data to place the target in 3D space. A planner then plots a path with no collisions. The craft stays on course even when sight of the target is lost. Tests in sims and in the real world beat top rivals, lifting success by over 20 percent and cutting nav error by about 50 percent in rough ground.
arxiv-2602-16075:
Ryan Wong leads a team of three engineers proposing a hybrid chip design that does computing inside memory arrays. Analog processing-using-memory excels at bulk matrix-vector multiplication, yet many matrix kernels also need non-multiplication steps it cannot do directly. Bolting on fixed-function CMOS hardware helps, but integrating that logic with memory has largely confined analog designs to machine learning inference and close kin.

Their design, DARTH-PUM, joins analog and digital Boolean processing-using-memory, with tuned peripheral circuitry, coordinating hardware, a friendly programming interface, and low-cost support for flexible data widths. Kernels can then run fully in memory, scaling from embedded devices to large data-driven systems. Three example workloads map onto the design with large reported speedups over an analog-plus-CPU baseline: encryption, convolutional networks, and large language models.
arxiv-2602-16375:
Kirill Khrylchenko, writing alone, tackles a scaling problem for generative recommender systems. Such models treat user behavior as event sequences and fold large language models into recommendation pipelines. But item spaces are extremely large, which makes training hard and leaves a gap between natural language and item identifiers. Semantic identifiers, which represent items as strings of low-cardinality tokens, offer an effective answer.

Existing methods give every item a fixed-length code, wasting effort, fitting natural language poorly, and ignoring the skew of real catalogs. There, popular and rare long-tail items need very different amounts of information. Emergent communication research offers a parallel: agents there develop discrete protocols with variable-length messages, giving frequent concepts shorter descriptions. He bridges the two fields with variable-length semantic IDs, learned by a discrete variational autoencoder with Gumbel-Softmax reparameterization, avoiding REINFORCE instability and fixed-length limits.
arxiv-2602-16675:
Jack Rome, Stephen James, and Subramanian Ramamoorthy scale world models up to in-air cloth unfolding by robots. Cloth handling matters from assistive care to service work, yet the physics of soft, wrinkled cloth makes it hard. A general plan must cope with varied shapes, sizes, folds, wrinkles, and looks. Model structure thus matters greatly for generalization.

The approach adapts the DreamerV2 reinforcement learning frame, adding surface normals input plus changes to replay and data augmentation. Together, those changes strengthen the world model for the physics at hand. Tests run in simulation and in zero-shot deployment on a real robot, unfolding varied cloth types in air. Robot builders get evidence that world-model learning can tame soft-object handling.
arxiv-2602-16775:
Benjamin Davis and co-authors use galaxy simulations to track causal reversal in the black hole mass versus stellar speed spread link. Causal study of real galaxies had hinted at a split by shape. Black holes seem to shape spiral hosts, while black holes in ellipticals grow passively in step with hosts. Simulations are needed to follow how those causal paths change over time.

Tests with the NIHAO suite of zoom-in hydro codes follow single galaxies plus their central black hole masses and speed spreads. The runs match the observed causal results and add clarity. Black hole and galaxy causal paths visibly flip between epochs before and after the peak of star birth. Astronomers get a time-resolved view of a coevolution tale that snapshots alone could only hint at.
arxiv-2602-16875:
Vishwajeet Ohal and Pierre Boulanger ask when quantum annealing beats classical methods, using a gradient spread frame. Quantum annealing promises to solve hard tuning problems by exploiting tunneling to navigate knotty energy lands. Yet how much tunneling truly helps over classical routes stays unclear. The paper joins experiments, theory, and code work to pin down when and why quantum annealing gains an edge.

A novel method generates synthetic quadratic unconstrained binary tuning problems with controlled gradient spread. That enables step-by-step study of landscape traits favoring quantum routes. Tests span four canonical hard problems: graph partitioning, Max Cut, number partitioning, and set cover. They run on a D-Wave Advantage2 device with over four thousand qubits, against simulated annealing, stochastic gradient descent, and trade solvers. Quantum annealing shows clear gains when landscapes exhibit high gradient variance. That suggests a concrete predictor of quantum advantage.
arxiv-2602-17175:
Robert J. Decker led a four-author team exploring lone waves in a fractional nonlinear Schrödinger equation. Single waves and pairs were studied after lab work made any fractional exponents realizable. The authors first map tail traits, then show destabilization when the fractional exponent drops below one, tied to collapse-type events.

Pairs in and out of phase exist for any exponents past the harmonic limit. The exponent serves as a branch parameter joining the harmonic and biharmonic limits. The team recovers the known instability of all wave pairs in the biharmonic case, yet finds some multipulse branches steady only in the fractional setting, a trait absent for integer settings. Spectral math explains the steadying. The findings bear on seeing fractional multipulse waves.
arxiv-2602-17275:
Junhan Zhao led a large team studying seven supernovae with double-peaked light curves and prominent shock-cooling emission from the Wide Field Survey Telescope's first year. Joint fits with an analytic early shock-cooling model plus the Arnett radioactive-diffusion model yield ejecta masses consistent with a transitional population between ultra-stripped and normal stripped-envelope supernovae.

Envelope masses point to modest outer layers, while progenitors fit yellow or blue supergiants with large radii. Empirical relations imply progenitor luminosities and zero-age main-sequence masses in a moderate range. Theory suggests such progenitors arise more naturally through binary evolution, since single-star paths cannot produce ejecta masses this low. The sample sharpens the link between stripped supernovae and their binary origins.
arxiv-2602-17375:
David Tolpin, writing alone, recasts episodic Markov decision process planning as Bayesian inference over policies. The main point is new: the policy itself becomes the latent variable, and expected return defines an unnormalized posterior density over policies. That preserves the standard return goal, unlike path-centric planning schemes with extra optimality variables and unlike entropy-regularized policy methods, which solve a different goal.

In the exact form, the spread over fixed policies induces an optimal stochastic policy under preference uncertainty. For discrete MDPs with random transitions, the paper studies variational sequential Monte Carlo as one approximate method, introducing policy consistency under state revisitation and coupled transition randomness across particles. Tests on grid worlds, Blackjack, Triangle Tireworld, and Academic Advising examine behavior of that approach against entropy methods, supporting that view of MDP planning.
arxiv-2602-17475:
Pietro Ferrazzi led a four-author team testing small language models for medical language work in Italian. Big models do well on medical text tasks, yet their heavy compute needs often block use in real clinics. The team asks whether models near one billion parameters can still handle such tasks with rival accuracy. They test three model families, Llama-3, Gemma-3, and Qwen3, on twenty clinical tasks.

The tasks cover spotting named entities, pulling out relations, filling case forms, answering questions, and mining arguments. The team tries prompt tricks at run time and retraining tricks at build time. Full fine-tuning works best, while few-shot prompts plus constraint decoding give a strong low-cost fallback. Small models match or beat larger baselines, and the best setup tops a far larger rival by more than nine points on average. The team shares public Italian medical data sets and top models.
arxiv-2602-17575:
The FASER Collaboration reports a way to gauge the momentum of charged particles in the FASER neutrino emulsion detector at the Large Hadron Collider. Momentum is key to the study of neutrino events at tera-electron-volt energies. Yet emulsion detectors lack a magnet to bend tracks, so momentum must come from elsewhere.

The new method reads momentum from multiple Coulomb scattering. It leans on the detector's sub-micron spatial resolution and long tracking length to span a broad energy range. Simulated data and a muon test beam checked the method at mid energies. Background muons in the real detector then gave momenta that matched their angular spread. FASER gains a workable momentum tool.
arxiv-2602-17775:
Arend-Jan Quist and team solve a numerical stability problem for exact quantum decision diagrams. A decision diagram is a graph-like data structure for compact coding of Boolean and pseudo-Boolean functions. It serves verification, algebra, stochastic reasoning and quantum circuits. Floating-point errors have slowed practical use of real- and complex-valued diagrams, and past fixes lacked proven scaling guarantees.

For circuits of Clifford gates plus T gates, the authors hand-craft an algebraic coding for complex numbers to replace floating-point coefficients. They prove these codings grow linearly with T gate and qubit counts, not with Clifford gate count. Runtime and node counts gain explicit upper bounds as well. An open-source build fixes floating-point inaccuracies and beats floating-point rivals through lower node counts. It gives the first scaling guarantees for exact simulation of a universal gate set.
arxiv-2602-17875:
Shreshth Rajan presents MultiVer, a zero-shot multi-agent system for vulnerability detection that reaches state-of-the-art recall with no fine-tuning. A four-agent ensemble covering security, correctness, performance and style, with union voting, reaches about eighty-three percent recall on PyVul. It beats fine-tuned GPT-3.5 by over one percentage point. It is billed as the first zero-shot system to surpass fine-tuned performance on that benchmark.

On SecurityEval, the same design reaches about ninety-two percent detection, matching specialized systems. Recall gains cost precision: about forty-nine percent against about sixty-four percent for fine-tuned baselines, yielding about sixty-one percent F1. Ablations show the ensemble adds seventeen percentage points of recall over single-agent security analysis. For security uses where missed flaws cost more than false alarms, zero-shot ensembles can beat fine-tuned models on the metric that matters most.
arxiv-2602-17975:
Robert Parker formulates and solves optimization problems that craft inputs where a graph neural network's predicted AC power flow solution strays far from the solution given by the AC power flow equations. He demonstrates the attack on CANOS-PF, a graph neural network model run through a power-flow benchmark library on a fourteen-bus test grid. The goal is to expose how badly a learned surrogate can fail.

Generated adversarial points yield errors as large as three point seven per-unit in reactive power, with a smaller error in voltage magnitude. When the perturbation from a training point is minimized instead, the adversarial conditions can still be met with only a tiny shift in voltage magnitude on a single bus. Parker argues that such fragile behavior motivates rigorous verification and robust training methods for neural network surrogate models of AC power flow.
arxiv-2602-18075:
M C Gordillo and colleagues use a diffusion Monte Carlo algorithm to solve the Schrödinger equation for hidden-charm pentaquarks. The pentaquarks contain up, down, strange, charm, and anticharm quarks, within a non-relativistic constituent quark model. They consider only multiquark states with defined parity, color, spin, and isospin, matching the experimentally favored spin-parity one half minus for one candidate, with isospin zero.

To explain the two P-c-s candidates, the total wavefunction must also be an eigenvector of the three-flavor operator. Imposing that condition yields two structures compatible with the masses from the J-psi-Lambda spectrum. Two further states are predicted between the eta-c-Lambda and J-psi-Lambda thresholds, unseen in that channel. With only isospin zero imposed, a single structure matches the experimental quantum numbers, with a mass below the J-psi-Lambda threshold.
arxiv-2602-18175:
Nyanga Honda Masasila and one co-author extend a classic law of averages to a setting with two kinds of expectation. Their 2026 paper defines sub-Gaussian random variables inside sub-linear expectation spaces, where an upper and a lower expectation both live. To dodge the clash between the two, the team splits the definition in two, an upper half and a lower half.

The split fits the setting well and lets the authors carry over a general result by Zajkowski to sub-linear spaces. Inside this frame they prove the classic averaging law for sub-Gaussian sequences: long-run averages settle down. A worked example shows the machinery in action. The paper gives researchers in uncertain-expectation theory a firm base for averages without a single fixed expectation.
arxiv-2602-18275:
B. Feigin and two co-authors prove that two Bethe subalgebra images coincide under the Olshanski centralizer construction. Their 2026 paper maps Bethe subalgebras of the Yangians for general linear algebras of sizes n and m into the enveloping algebra of their sum. The two images turn out to be the same. That coincidence is the paper's core result.

From it the team derives the duality linking the trigonometric Gaudin model with the XXX spin chain, in explicit form. The generating differential operator on one side is tied to the generating difference operator on the other, matching a result of Mukhin, Tarasov, and Varchenko. The work gives a concrete bridge between two integrable models, letting tools from one side serve the other.
arxiv-2602-18375:
Bora Baran and three co-authors give quantum control a coordinate system for many-body interactions. Their 2026 paper notes that target gates are usually described whole and judged by global comparison, hiding their interaction structure. The team introduces a split of multi-qubit gates by the phases they carry in a diagonal frame.

Local rotations supply that frame for many practical gates: Ising gates, Toffoli-type gates, controlled-phase gates, stabilizer gates, commuting Pauli sets, and single Pauli-string gates. Parity-weighted phase sums pin down k-body terms on any qubit subset exactly and uniquely. Those sums form support-selective phase invariants. Those invariants let control targets pick desired interaction mixes directly. Demos on a nitrogen-vacancy spin register build isolated three-body interactions within a single pulse, for both diagonal and non-diagonal terms.
arxiv-2602-18575:
José L. Fernández and one co-author prove Gaussian behavior for power partitions. Their 2026 paper works within the probabilistic framework of Khinchin families. It shows the generating function for k-th-power partitions is strongly Gaussian, Báez-Duarte style, and even further a Hayman function.

The Hardy-Ramanujan asymptotic formula for the count of n-partitions into k-th powers then follows from Hayman's asymptotic formula for strongly Gaussian series. The proof uses a Gaussianity criterion for Khinchin families with bounds from Tenenbaum, Wu and Li for the generating function. The formula is recovered by computing asymptotic estimates for the mean and variance of its family. Similar results are presented for partitions into distinct k-th powers.
arxiv-2602-18775:
Data lakes waste much of query time just scanning remote files. Decoding alone can eat nearly half the runtime on standard benchmarks. Jonas Dann, with one co-author, sketches a 2026 vision for a data processing SmartNIC. It would sit on the network path of compute nodes. There it would take over decoding and early filtering, so parsing costs would vanish from the compute nodes.

Estimates built on DuckDB suggest that feeding compute nodes pre-filtered data from such a SmartNIC could lift query performance sharply. It could even match traditional throughput with smaller, cheaper CPUs. The work is a vision piece rather than a finished device. But it names a concrete bottleneck and a concrete place, the network datapath, to attack it.
arxiv-2602-19075:
Can gravity alone create the matter-antimatter imbalance? Ian B. Whittingham, writing alone in 2026, tests gravitational baryogenesis during inflation in two modified-gravity theories. One is the widely used Starobinsky model. The other is a newer power-law model from Odintsov and Oikonomou.

The study runs in the Einstein frame. Scalaron motion during slow-roll inflation is solved with simple math. Some Starobinsky expressions repeat earlier work by Motohashi and Nishizawa. Power-law expressions and their wider form is new. Calculated asymmetries land close to the seen value. Yet they rest on shaky guesses. Early asymmetries must dilute unless it ends with inflation. Rapid heating and fast baryon-violating rates are also assumed. The calculations strongly violate those assumptions. Matching data would need parameter shifts ruled out by cosmic microwave background data. Full heating and freeze-out treatment remains necessary.
arxiv-2602-19175: Bang-Xian Han, with one co-author, proves quantitative stability of Kantorovich potentials over metric measure spaces with lower Ricci curvature bounds in 2026. The result confirms a recent conjecture by Kitagawa, Letrouit, and Mérigot. Its proof uses a heat-kernel-regularised transform. It needs neither linear structure nor sectional curvature bounds. As a corollary, optimal transport maps on Alexandrov spaces with lower curvature bounds gain quantitative stability too.
arxiv-2602-19475:
Physics-informed neural networks solve partial differential equations without meshes, but slow training and modest accuracy have limited their adoption against modern numerical solvers. Pao-Hsiung Chiu and five co-authors introduce Scale-PINN, the Sequential Correction Algorithm for Learning Efficient PINN. It imports the iterative residual-correction principle, a mainstay of numerical solvers, straight into the loss formulation.

That integration changes how PINN losses can be thought up and built. Scale-PINN converges at unprecedented speed across problems from different physics domains. On a challenging fluid-dynamics problem, it cuts training time for a state-of-the-art PINN from hours to under two minutes while keeping superior accuracy. That opens representative problems that were previously out of reach.
arxiv-2602-19575:
Custom text-to-image making builds user-only ideas from a few sample images, but splitting the target idea from stray leftover bits is the core test. Minseo Kim and four co-authors note that without clean splits, true-to-life capture often pulls in unwanted traits that clash with user prompts. That breaks the balance between idea truth and text match. Hand-led methods often miss fine details and lack room to grow.

Their framework, ConceptPrism, pulls shared traits purely by matching images side by side, with no outside facts. A target token and per-image leftover tokens get tuned together via rebuild and cut-out losses. Hiding shared facts in the leftover tokens, the cut-out loss makes a fact void, forcing the target token to carry the idea cleanly.
arxiv-2602-19675:
This algebra paper extends Sivatski's work to characteristic 2. Ahmed Laghribi and Nico Lorenz work over a field F in characteristic 2. Their central simple algebra A, exponent 2, splits over an extension of F built from two square roots, with separability degree at least 4. To A they attach an invariant in the third Kato-Milne cohomology group, cut down by a subgroup divisible by A's Brauer class.

The invariant tells whether the degree-8 algebra splits apart, by whether it vanishes. It also powers descent claims for such algebras and quadratic forms over extensions built from two square roots.
