Readers get a characteristic-2 version of Sivatski's invariant, with concrete uses for splitting and descent.
arxiv-2602-20275:
K. De La Ossa Doria and two co-authors prepare quantum correlations with shaped electromagnetic pulses instead of discrete gates. Their 2026 study works with transmon qubit systems and tunes pulse settings directly rather than aiming at one target state at a time. The goal is the entanglement structure itself: the pattern of correlations shared across two or three qubits.

The optimized pulses reproduce the entanglement patterns linked to the Bell, GHZ, and W classes, reaching matching values on the corresponding entanglement measures. Because the pulses need only a reduced set of parameters, the search space stays small while the wanted entanglement properties survive. The approach points to a leaner route to preparing useful entangled states on near-term hardware.
arxiv-2602-20375:
Jiashun Wang and five co-authors build a multi-task reinforcement-learning method for humanoid motion that generalizes from references. Reference-tracking policies often break outside their demo data; task-driven learning adapts but loses motion quality. The method treats reference motion as a shaping prior, not as a deployment-time constraint. A goal-conditioned policy trains on two tasks sharing observations and actions.

The first task is reference-guided imitation, where demo paths set dense rewards but are not fed to the policy. The second is goal-conditioned generalization, where goals are sampled freely and rewards reflect only task success. Co-optimizing both gives structured skills that adapt to new goals and starts, without adversarial objectives, trajectory tracking, phase variables, or reference-dependent inference. Parkour tests show transfer beyond the demo data with natural motion intact, and skills support long tasks.
arxiv-2602-20475:
The High-Luminosity Large Hadron Collider will flood sensors with data, but finding power hinges on pulling small signals from huge backgrounds of about two hundred at-once pileup crashes. Mohammed Rakib and five co-authors offer PhyGHT, a physics-guided multi-link graph model that pairs distance-aware local graph focus with global self-focus, matching the shape of particle showers in proton-proton crashes. A pileup cut gate, a clear physics-bound device, filters soft noise before multi-link pooling.

To test the design, the authors release a mock top-quark pair dataset modeling extreme pileup. PhyGHT beats state-of-the-art ATLAS and CMS starting points at calling the signal's energy and mass fix factors, and well rebuilds the top quark's invariant mass. The work shows how machine learning shaped by physics can advance findings at the machine's frontier.
arxiv-2602-21175:
Real search queries are often just one or two words, too thin to specify what images a user wants. Jianglin Lu, Simon Jenni, Kushal Kafle, Jing Shi, Handong Zhao, and Yun Fu address that thinness in this 2026 arXiv paper via quality-controllable retrieval. A generative language model completes short queries into descriptive forms capturing pose, scene, and aesthetics.

Completion is conditioned on discretized quality levels from relevance and aesthetic scoring, so enrichment is quality-aware as well as meaningful. The framework works with any pretrained vision-language model unchanged, keeps enriched queries readable, and lets users steer results toward preferred quality levels. Experiments show clear retrieval gains with effective quality control.
arxiv-2602-21275:
Can an infinite point set avoid three-on-a-line subsets yet resist splitting into finitely many such subsets? Moe Putterman, Mehtaab Sawhney, and Gregory Valiant construct such a set in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their infinite set in the plane has a striking combination of properties.

Every subset contains a constant-density subset with no three points collinear, yet the whole set cannot be partitioned into finitely many collinear-free subsets. The construction gives a new proof of a question of Erdos, Nesetril, and Rodl. The authors note the construction was generated by an internal model at OpenAI, a notable provenance for a combinatorial result.
arxiv-2602-21375:
J. Strucka and 18 co-authors report the first experimental sighting of passive freeze-out of the Richtmyer-Meshkov instability, a mixing effect that degrades inertial confinement fusion. Freeze-out here means the instability stalls on its own, without changing the drive pulse or the target surface shape.

The team used additively manufactured voids just below the surface of a wavy target to split one shock into a train of weaker shocks. That cut instability growth upstream of the surface by more than 70 percent. High-speed X-ray imaging and simulations point to temporal shaping as the main cause, with spatial curvature and shock weakening adding less. The result offers a driver-independent way to tame shock-driven mixing in fusion and other high-energy-density systems.
arxiv-2602-21475:
Ruben Lier alone authors a paper on sorting prolate and oblate spheroids with a diatomic gas in a magnetic field. For diatomic particles with a nonzero magnetic moment, the Senftleben-Beenakker effect lets a magnetic field alter transport even for neutral particles. Symmetry then allows two independent anisotropic odd viscosities, which can carry opposite signs.

Studying odd-viscous Stokes flow around spheroids when odd viscosities stay small beside shear viscosity, the author uses a perturbative expansion around the sphere solution plus the Lorentz reciprocal theorem. Lift forces are computed for oblate and prolate spheroids across general values of the two odd viscosity coefficients. The resulting Hall angles can differ between oblate and prolate shapes. Sedimentation in such a gas under a background magnetic field can therefore separate particles by shape.
arxiv-2602-21975:
Most cosmologists explain galaxy motion with dark matter, but a rival idea called MOND changes the law of gravity itself. Alfie Russell and three co-authors run the largest computer simulations yet of a MOND universe filled with hot dark matter, a model called nu-HDM. They compare it with standard cosmology and with two test models that isolate the separate effects of hot dark matter and changed gravity.

The nu-HDM model matches the early universe's microwave glow and galaxy spin patterns, the authors report, but it fails on the largest scales. By today it builds clusters far too massive and stirs galaxies to speeds of thousands of kilometers per second. The team also checks whether a nearby cosmic void could ease the mismatch in expansion rates, and finds the void idea does not save the model.
arxiv-2602-22075:
Rust promises memory safety and freedom from data races through its strict type system, yet proving deep properties of Rust programs remains hard. Daniel Drodt and Reiner Hähnle present RustyDL, a program logic for Rust designed as the base for an auto-interactive deductive verification tool. Unlike rival tools, it reasons directly on Rust source code rather than translating programs into an intermediate language first.

Staying at source level matters for human-in-the-loop verification, where people guide proofs of complex functional properties. The paper works through Rust-specific hurdles in designing the logic and its calculus, offering a solution for each. A prototype built as a Rust instance of the KeY verification tool shows the ideas running in practice.
arxiv-2602-22275:
Measuring distances on curved surfaces usually means approximating the surface with a polygonal mesh and computing them on the polygon. Saar Huberman and two co-authors show that shortcut caps accuracy: exact polygon distances are at most second-order close to the true surface distances. The paper then introduces a higher-order deep-learning method for geodesic paths on surfaces.

Older methods pair a local solver with a causal update order for surface points, often exploiting dynamic programming at quasi-linear cost. The new method lifts the accuracy order while keeping that lean structure. For graphics, robotics, and shape work, it offers surface distances that tighten faster as meshes refine.
arxiv-2602-22375:
Star-forming gas clumps are usually sorted by eye from infrared glow and shape, but unclear signs, unsure distances, and heavy dust cover leave many sources unsorted. Plakitina and five co-authors test machine learning as a data-driven complement, using survey data on molecular lines plus infrared photometry. Clustering with HDBSCAN on line strengths reveals groupings tied to growth stages.

Using only five molecular lines, the team finds stable clusters of protostars and of regions without active star formation, driven mainly by two lines' emission. The approach offers astronomers an automated second opinion where human categories run out.
arxiv-2602-22475:
Large language models now work in culturally sensitive settings, but most cultural alignment tunes broad values without regard for the task at hand, and cultures can interfere with each other. Binchi Zhang and four co-authors propose CultureManager, a pipeline for task-specific cultural alignment. It builds task-aware cultural data in target task formats, grounded in culturally relevant web search results.

So that norms from one culture do not clash with another's, the pipeline stores each culture's knowledge apart in its own adapter, and a routing step chooses which adapter fits the situation. Measured against prompt-based and fine-tuning baselines, the approach comes out ahead in evaluations spanning ten national cultures, with gains likewise appearing on culture-sensitive tasks. The results argue that task adaptation and modular culture handling are both needed for cultural alignment that actually works.
arxiv-2602-22575:
Yu Zhang and six co-authors speed up long-context language models with S2O, a method that stops sparse attention early through online permutation. Attention cost grows with the square of sequence length, strangling long inputs, and block-level sparsity hits a ceiling because coarse blocks waste effort on weak regions. S2O reworks FlashAttention so the model loads scattered high-value tokens instead of one long span.

Blocks are scored by importance and processed best-first; once a block score falls below a threshold, the rest are skipped, raising effective sparsity within a controlled error budget. On Llama-3.1-8B with 128K context, the method cut single-operator error 3.82-fold at matched sparsity and prefill compute density 3.31-fold at matched error, while holding end-to-end accuracy and reaching 7.51-fold attention and 3.81-fold overall speedups.
arxiv-2602-22775:
Joydeep Chandra and two co-authors probe relational safety in mental health chatbots, the quality of interaction patterns across whole conversations rather than single replies. Current safety checks grade one-turn crisis answers, missing slow dynamics that decide whether a bot helps or harms over time.

TherapyProbe explores chatbot conversation paths through adversarial multi-agent simulation with open-source models. It surfaces failure patterns like validation spirals, where bots progressively reinforce hopelessness, and empathy fatigue, where replies turn mechanical over turns. The work distils these into a Safety Pattern Library of 23 failure archetypes with design fixes, plus a replicable no-cost method and a clinically grounded taxonomy.
arxiv-2602-23175:
Barnabás Barna and 27 co-authors report optical follow-up of two extremely dim Type Iax supernovae, 2022ywf and 2023zgx, which peaked at magnitudes of minus 13.7 and minus 14.4. Type Iax events are a debated subclass of thermonuclear explosions, and it is unclear whether the dimmest members form a separate population with a distinct origin.

Using spectral tomography around peak light plus multi-band photometry, the team maps the ejected matter and tests it against explosion models. Constant chemical abundances fit both events well, and gaps from the least luminous pure deflagration model, N5def_hybrid, stay minor, above all after peak. The results support pure deflagration models for even the dimmest Iax events and place both objects alongside the brighter Iax sample in their speeds and structure.
arxiv-2602-23275:
Giorgio Mangioni and one co-author construct cusped spaces for hierarchically hyperbolic groups, a construction that also yields spaces shaped like Teichmüller metrics. The tool is aimed at Dehn-filling-like quotients, the groups left after collapsing chosen twists, with mapping class groups of punctured spheres among the test cases.

The headline result concerns the mapping class group of a five-holed sphere and the braid group on four strands. Each has infinite hyperbolic quotients that match no hyperbolic quotient of any other sphere mapping class group or braid group. These quotients come from killing large powers of Dehn twists, and quotients of the extended mapping class group even have trivial outer automorphism groups. Torsion elements in the quotients drive the proofs.
arxiv-2602-23375:
Shuang Li and three co-authors derive a unified math answer for the sound pressure made by ball-shaped photo-sound sources. Starting from the basic photo-sound wave rule, they solve for the space-time sound pressure for any ball-shaped symmetric initial pressure shapes, giving one general formula rather than a patchwork of special cases.

Formula details are given for common shapes: uniform ball sources, Gaussian shapes, fast-fading shapes, and power-law shapes. Far-field cases are also discussed. The new results serve as tools for photo-sound imaging system design and signal analysis. The authors provide code for very fast forward runs with the general ball-shaped model, posted in the SlingBAG_Ultra repo.
arxiv-2602-23475:
Barry Brown and two co-authors study how people interact with cleaning robots in a major commercial airport, using video analysis of the robots' navigational 'troubles'. Robots in public spaces must share space with people, yet little is known about what they lack in interactional competence.

The robots prove technically proficient but disrupt the social order of the space: they fail at mutual adjustment to others, grasping social groups, and reading the purpose of different locations. The authors argue for a new design space of socially-aware movement, built on 'strong concepts' that treat movement as an interactional and collaborative accomplishment. Such systems, they suggest, could better fit the everyday rhythms of public life.
arxiv-2602-23675:
Shubham Sinha and 16 co-authors report high-pressure making of Mg2IrH7, in shape near high-heat superconductivity. Mg2IrH6 is a shaky complex metal hydride with forecast super shift up to 170 K at ambient pressure. After making of same-shape, current-blocking Mg2IrH5 at low pressure, higher-pressure studies probed phase shifts and compound making.

X-ray and Raman readings show cubic Mg2IrH7 holds above about 40 GPa, with a related six-sided hydride likely near Mg2IrH5. Current readings show cubic Mg2IrH7 blocks current, matching ab initio calls, and persists during room-temperature pressure release until about 20 GPa before going back to cubic Mg2IrH5. The results confirm ground-state shape calls in the Mg-Ir-H system. Making of two twin phases with nearby mixes opens paths to access super Mg2IrH6 through non-balance making paths.
arxiv-2602-23775:
Shaochen Wang and Christian H. Weiß derive new Stein-type identities for pairs of count variables. The 2026 paper covers the three most common paired count models: the Poisson, binomial, and negative binomial cases, which past work had largely left aside in favor of single-variable models.

Stein identities link a distribution to simple averages, and they open the door to practical tools. The authors use the new identities to derive moment formulas, to build flexible goodness-of-fit tests, and to create new tests for symmetry between the two counts. Real data examples close the paper, showing the methods in use. The work gives statisticians working with paired counts a firmer base for testing and estimation.
arxiv-2602-23875:
Daniel M. Markiewitz and eight co-authors develop a thermodynamic theory of how a protective interphase forms in water-in-salt electrolytes, a super-concentrated class of battery electrolytes. The 2026 paper focuses on the layer near the electrode, where solvation and ionic association shape which reactants are present to form the interphase that widens the stable voltage window.

The authors extend a recent theory of hydration and ionic association in the electrical double layer, fit it from bulk molecular dynamics, and check it against double-layer simulations with good qualitative agreement. They then explain window changes through two routes: shifts in bulk activity that alter electrolyte stability, and thermodynamic shifts in reaction kinetics at the interface. The theory links molecular-scale solvation patterns to a macroscopic battery property, guiding design of safer, wider-window electrolytes. The result gives battery makers a clearer guide for safer designs.
arxiv-2602-23975:
Madan Mohan Mahana and two co-authors review coherent control of population and quantum coherence in superconducting circuits. The 2026 review traces how quantum behavior, once confined to atoms and photons, has been pushed into macroscopic circuits visible to the eye and ordinarily ruled by classical physics.

The paper surveys progress in steering population distributions across multiple quantum levels in such large-scale systems, alongside control of absorption and refractive index, feats once thought beyond reach. Superconducting circuits thus serve as a bridge between microscopic quantum rules and engineered devices, letting researchers manipulate coherence in systems that can be fabricated, wired, and scaled. The review gathers that progress into a single account for readers entering the field or tracking its frontier.
arxiv-2603-00075: Arslanoğlu gives an exact take on the symmetric Traveling Salesman Problem built from surfaces, not edges. Rather than pick edges to form a loop, the model picks linked triangles whose rim forms the tour. A tree rule keeps the whole thing linked, while Euler rules keep each vertex linked in its own area, so no subtour removal step is needed. The take is exact over all triangles but workable only for tiny cases; cut down to thin sets such as Delaunay triangulation, it serves as a neat shortcut.
arxiv-2603-00275: Grigo studies billiard tables whose shapes sit near the lemon and moon forms, where one curved arc has small curvature. Such tables were known to scatter paths chaotically. He shows that swapping the circular arc for a more general gently curved boundary piece can instead create periodic paths that stay stable under small disturbances. The table then admits nonlinearly stable periodic orbits.
arxiv-2603-00375: Echevarria, Gutierrez, and Scimemi predict the gluon Sivers asymmetry in dijet production at the future Electron-Ion Collider, using transverse momentum factorisation for deep inelastic scattering. They revisit the plain case and build the maths for a sideways polarised target, testing two growth schemes with a current kernel. Results hinge strongly on gluon spreads and their growth. For the models studied, asymmetries run large, above five percent at the collider.
arxiv-2603-00575: Zeng and thirteen colleagues build SWE-Hub, a production system that turns raw repositories into scalable executable software engineering tasks. An Env Agent turns raw repository snapshots into shared multi language container environments. A SWE-Scale engine then synthesises large volumes of localised bug fix instances through cross language analysis and cluster scale validation, while a Bug Agent crafts high fidelity system level repair tasks. The unified stack tackles brittle environments, costly bug synthesis, and short horizon data that miss architectural consistency.
arxiv-2603-00675: Yoo and sixteen colleagues adapt foundation models to comprehensive head CT analysis with a Mixture of Low-Rank Experts, since uniform low rank tuning fits diverse pathologies poorly. Multiple specialised low rank adapters with unsupervised soft routing tailor features per finding type, adding under half a percent of parameters without pathology supervision. A benchmark spans six foundation models, two and three dimensional architectures, varied pretraining, and sizes from seven million to 431 million parameters. Tests on over seventy thousand head CT scans with 75 findings show consistent gains across all models.
arxiv-2603-00775: Aussedat studies measures on the real line that are critically unstable under small shifts, superposing two slightly shifted copies and measuring the gap with a Wasserstein distance. For any measure the gap stays bounded by the shift size, but the critical rate, where the bound is attained as the shift vanishes, marks a special class. Those measures give most of their mass to particular porous sets. The characterisation identifies which measures have a 2-Wasserstein tangent cone equal to directions giving curves of maximal initial speed.
arxiv-2603-01075: Peng and three colleagues turn defibrillator hunting into a game to fix a deadly awareness gap: bystanders often do not know where the nearest AED sits when cardiac arrest strikes. Their AEDHunter app guides users through repeated location hunts, verifying arrivals with low-cost Bluetooth tags and reading movement with phone sensors. Practice cuts retrieval times and raises confidence, while a pause detector tracks hesitation and its decline as a learning signal.
arxiv-2603-01375: Wei and six colleagues propose ROSA2, a plan recasting multi-turn chats as joint tuning over words and weights, rather than treating test-time adjustment as prompt-only or weight-only. Meaning clearness acts as a primer for effective weight updates: text slopes rectify intent vagueness while weight updates bridge skill gaps. In theory, co-adaptation strictly reduces the required weight shift for settling. In tests, ROSA2 beats state-of-the-art rivals by 30 percent.
arxiv-2603-01775:
Harry Stuart, Masahiro Kaneko, and Timothy Baldwin interview job candidates with an AI expert in this 2026 work. Resumes filter applicants on thin facts, while true expert interviews cost too much to run at scale. Their system aims to draw out rich, role-specific facts from each candidate at low cost.

A language model plays the expert interviewer and updates beliefs about each candidate as answers arrive. Beliefs track rubric traits, the scored qualities that define a good hire for the role. Updates stay calibrated, so stated confidence matches how close beliefs sit to true levels. In simulated interviews, beliefs converge toward the built-in ability levels of fake applicants. The team releases code, anonymized resumes, and calibration tests, which lets others probe both the promise and the risks of AI-led hiring screens.
arxiv-2603-01975:
Raquel Bosch-Romeu, Antonio Falco, and Jose-Antonio Rodriguez-Gallego compress categorical data with a tool borrowed from quantum theory. Their 2026 work builds a density matrix from class-conditional frequencies in labeled data. One-hot encoding places each record in a survey space, and columns tally feature counts per class.

A normalized Gram-type operator from that matrix meets the axioms of a density matrix. Its rank is bounded by the class count, which forces a naturally low-dimensional embedding. Dominant eigenmodes supply the spectral embedding where classification then takes place. Class-conditional density estimates plus a maximum-likelihood rule make the final calls in that space. Structural invariances and stability analysis back the method, with synthetic tests probing cardinality, sparsity, noise, and imbalance.
arxiv-2603-02475:
Vitor Pereira Matias, Márcus Vinícius Lobo Costa, and João Batista Neto lead this 2026 study, with Tiago Novello de Brito. AI models inherit bias from their training data, yet fine-grained skin tone lacks good public data. The classic six-tone medical scale represents real skin poorly. Small private sets also block repeatable fairness research.

Their open data set holds over forty thousand images of thousands of people. Labels use a ten-tone scale designed for visual accuracy. Classic vision methods score near chance on the task, they show. Deep learning, by contrast, approaches the accuracy of human annotators. A fine-tuned transformer generalizes best to unseen data sources. That model can audit fairness in large public face data sets.
arxiv-2603-02675:
Shuyi Zhou, Zeen Song, Wenwen Qiang, and colleagues diagnose why safety training for large language models can fail late in a reply. Their 2026 paper blames shallow alignment: a trick opening like Sure, here is can start a harmful answer. As the model writes such an opening, its inner signal of bad intent fades away.

Their fix, TSC-GRPO, first trains a probe that separates true intent from surface style using causal reasoning. Training then bakes that awareness into the model, with penalties that grow as harmful text piles up. In tests the method blocked jailbreak attacks far better than baselines while keeping normal skills intact. The goal is refusal that holds up at any point in a reply.
arxiv-2603-02975:
Bhathiya Rathnayake and Sijia Geng design inverter controls that hold voltage steady on weak grids, with proof. Grid-forming inverters must act like power plants, setting voltage and frequency themselves. Their 2026 controller follows a layered droop design, with an outer voltage loop feeding an inner current loop built by backstepping.

The grid's own voltage is treated as an unknown disturbance whose size need not be known in advance. A deadzone-based suppression scheme drives voltage errors into a small, pre-chosen residual band, with transients decaying at a rate the designer assigns. A separate safety filter, built on barrier functions, enforces hard current limits through a tiny optimization at each step. Simulations show faster recovery from current-limiting events than conventional designs.
arxiv-2603-03275:
Jessie Zixin Li and three others generate realistic human movement patterns that respect group differences. Mobility traces matter for public health and social science, and groups really do move in unlike ways. Yet most trajectory data sets carry no demographic labels, so generators ignore the differences. Their 2026 method, ATLAS, learns from aggregate clues only, never from labeled individuals.

ATLAS starts with unlabeled solo trajectories, region-level movement summaries, and census figures on each region's group mix. It then fine-tunes its generator so simulated movement matches the local aggregates while conditioned on group mix. On real data that does carry labels, ATLAS came far closer to true group patterns than rival methods and neared fully supervised training. The authors add theory on when the approach works, stressing local diversity and informative aggregates, and release their code.
arxiv-2603-03375:
David Wegmann's thesis rebuilds the mathematical foundations of UMAP, the beloved data visualization algorithm, and finds the original scaffolding cracked. UMAP, introduced in 2018, leans on a functor called metric realization from an unpublished draft by Spivak. That draft contains many errors, most copied into the UMAP paper and its successors. The thesis sets out to repair them all in one self-contained document.

Full derivations cover Spivak's functors and the finite variant used by UMAP's creators, with an explicit description of the metric realization and its relatives. The closing discussion turns to the algorithm itself. It examines claims about UMAP's properties and how closely the finite variant really corresponds to the shipped algorithm. For mathematically minded data scientists, the thesis separates what is proven from what is folklore.
arxiv-2603-03475:
Subramanyam Sahoo and three others show that a top mathematics model often reaches right answers by unreliable roads. Latent reasoning models, which think internally rather than writing steps, now serve in tutoring and decision support. Their 2026 audit of a leading seven-billion-parameter math model finds most of its correct predictions, about four in five, emerge through computationally inconsistent pathways. Only a minority rest on stable, faithful reasoning.

Nearly one prediction in eleven is a silent failure: confident and wrong. Measured reasoning quality correlates slightly negatively with correctness, an artifact of a binary scoring threshold. Growing the model nearly fivefold in size brought zero accuracy gain on the evaluated slice, though the authors flag that slice as small. About a fifth of latent plans resemble ordinary chain-of-thought. Their conclusion: headline accuracy can mask deep unreliability, and evaluation must measure stability directly.
arxiv-2603-03675:
Phenyo Phemelo Moletsane and four colleagues test whether offering lessons in a local language changes who learns. Most of the world's learners are multilingual, yet schooling rarely is. Their 2026 quasi-experiment follows nearly three thousand Ugandan learners in a non-formal engineering course delivered by radio and mobile phone. Each learner chose instruction in Leb Lango, English, or a hybrid of both.

The Leb Lango option drew disproportionately rural learners, those with less formal education, and those starting with least prior knowledge, widening participation among the disadvantaged. Merely offering it raised active participation even among learners registered for English. Leb Lango learners began behind but gained faster, finishing with examination results comparable to the English and hybrid groups. Local language choice, the authors conclude, is effective educational technology policy.
arxiv-2603-04175: Mohan and Dhir present a baryon-calibrated unified quark-diquark effective mass formalism for heavy multiquarks. They extend a baryon-calibrated quark-diquark build to tetraquark and pentaquark systems without sector-linked settings. They compute complete spectra for two tetraquark color setups, while pentaquark analysis focuses on the dominant triple-antitriplet grouping.
arxiv-2603-04375: Trivedi and colleagues treat Hermiticity as a symmetry from inner product current conservation. With complete Cauchy slices and no boundary flux, that conservation gives standard Hermiticity. Near horizons, above all in black holes, conservation fails for restricted observers. Tracing out hidden degrees yields dynamics that preserve trace, driven by an effective non-Hermitian generator. Entropy balance through the horizon offsets inner product charge flux, unifying gravity, entropy, and non-Hermiticity. Black hole ringdown may bound that flux strength in data. Hermiticity thus emerges only in the global case.
arxiv-2603-05175: Anurag Singh and colleagues formalize regulating black-box AI services as a mechanism-design problem with two goals: keeping non-compliant providers out while retaining compliant ones. They call that ideal the perfect market outcome, threatened by providers' private information, strategic evasion, and statistical uncertainty in finite-sample evidence. Their sharp characterization says a mechanism achieves the ideal exactly when non-compliant evidence distributions form a closed, convex credal set. Mechanisms built from hypothesis tests can achieve it, and experiments on spurious-feature and fairness-based rules validate the theory.
arxiv-2603-05275: Zhu Li and the rest of the team offer SarcasmMiner, a reinforcement learning post-training method for audio-visual sarcasm reasoning resisting hallucination. Sarcasm finding across text, audio, and vision needs resolving pragmatic incongruity. It reformulates finding as ordered thought via dual-track distillation. High-quality teacher paths initialize the student, while all paths train a generative reward model for thought quality. The student optimizes with group relative policy tuning using decoupled accuracy and thought rewards. On MUStARD++, it beats zero-shot and supervised fine-tuning older models on F1.
arxiv-2603-05375: Bastian Pfeifer and Michael G. Schimek offer TopKGraphs, start-node-anchored walks biased toward similar neighborhoods, measured by Jaccard similarity. Node similarity matters for network analysis and machine learning. Rather than stationary spreads, walks sample neighborhoods stochastically for clear affinity matrices. TopKGraphs thus gives a non-parametric, clear node similarity form. Test covers synthetic, tabular, and protein-protein interaction graphs. Across cases, TopKGraphs does better than or matches standard measures, diffusion, and embedding ways, robust in sparse, noisy, mixed networks.
arxiv-2603-05575: Sui and team study prediction-powered conditional inference where labeled data scarce, unlabeled covariates plenty, and a machine-learning predictor is on hand. The goal is to guess conditional functions at a target point without a fixed form. Their approach pairs zooming in with prediction-based spread cut: an RKHS method learns a data-tuned weight, turning the target moment into a weighted plain moment. Predictions enter through a fix-based split, yielding a guess and confidence interval that cut spread when telling valid no matter how right they are.
arxiv-2603-05775: Deng and team study pre-dyed vertices in linked outerplanar graphs holding at most one or two triangles. Earlier work showed that a pair of apart vertices plus a short face can always be finished to a three-color scheme in a related planar setting. The authors extend this picture by proving that any two or three apart pre-dyed vertices allow a full three-color scheme. Their result gives a clean stretching theorem for outerplanar graphs with few triangles.
arxiv-2603-06275: Wang and his team put forward StrSR, a one step adversarial distillation method with spectral and path regularization for real world image super resolution with diffusion transformers. Sampling is costly and step by step, and past one step methods suffer trajectory mismatch plus severe grid like periodic artifacts. An asymmetric telling-apart distillation architecture bridges that gap, while a frequency matching plan curbs such flaws from high frequency leakage. Tests show top scores across number metrics and visual perception in the real world.
arxiv-2603-06375: Garnero and his team report beam and cosmic ray tests of the gaseous photomultiplier. The photosensor joins a photocathode with resistive plate chamber multiplication, giving time resolution and cheap scalability. The use case is a Belle II upgrade suppressing beam induced background photons. In 2022, 25 picosecond resolution at 3.3 million gain came from a picosecond laser and a LaB6 photocathode. A 2023 test on a MgF2/CsI setup fell to 70 ps. The work targets ultraviolet emission during excitation, creating a secondary signal that spoils timing through photon feedback.
arxiv-2603-06475: Bianchi and He study an analogue for skew products in two dimensions of Ruelle's second-order expansion for the Julia set Hausdorff size, extended by McMullen to polynomial shifts. Big holomorphic systems are non-conformal, so Hausdorff size is swapped for volume size, defined as a pressure function's zero. For such skew product families of a form, their main result is an explicit second-order growth of the Julia set volume size. It holds as the parameter tends to zero and is expressed via coefficient terms.
arxiv-2603-06875: Alswaidan and Varner present stochastic attention on the Hopfield energy, casting attention recall as one gradient step on that energy. Langevin draws from the Boltzmann law yield stochastic attention, a sampler run by a knob: low heat gives retrieval, high heat gives open output. Since the energy gradient is the attention map, the method needs no score network, training loop or model, suiting data-poor cases. They derive an inflection rule pinpointing the retrieval-to-generation switch point for memory shape, tested across five domains spanning two orders of magnitude.
arxiv-2603-07475: Goel and colleagues compare layer-wise representations in autoregressive and diffusion language models. Diffusion training yields more global patterns with heavy early-layer redundancy and less recency bias, while AR training gives tightly coupled, locally structured ones. Models initialized as AR keep AR dynamics despite diffusion training. The native ones absorb large layer-skipping compute cuts while retaining most math and coding performance, unlike AR models.
arxiv-2603-07775: Jayasinghe and colleagues frame rapid bounce-back for real-world AI as limited residual learning, adding online corrections to a frozen policy. The learned add-on gives bounded action-space tweaks, ruled by a Stability Alignment Gate through size limits and gain control. No world resets, retrains, direct system ID or secret shift data needed. When drive, mass and contact shift mid-episode, recovery time falls versus frozen SAC on four sim robots. Hardware tests on a ViperX arm and Scout Mini cut bounce-back time without control changes.
arxiv-2603-08075: Wu and colleagues propose TALON, a method for on-the-fly category discovery. A model must recognize known categories while also spotting novel ones in an unlabeled online stream, having trained only on labeled data. Existing approaches freeze the offline-trained feature extractor and quantize features into binary codes as class prototypes. But a fixed knowledge base ignores what incoming data could teach. Quantization also loses information, weakens expressiveness, and amplifies variance within classes. TALON instead adapts its learning at test time as new data arrives.
arxiv-2603-08175: Maiello and colleagues tune a cavity for dark matter searches by pulling it apart, a tuning-by-opening move. Their Nb3Sn-coated cavity runs near 9 GHz, and pulling it apart shifts its frequency by more than 1 GHz. Finite-element simulations say radiative losses leave the quality factor intact at wide openings. A shut cavity with a quality factor of ten million holds that value for apertures up to 9 mm. Bench tests with copper spacers and a sliding mechanism confirm values above the threshold despite build flaws and uneven films.
arxiv-2603-08275: Kang and colleagues introduce AdaCultureSafe, a dataset for jointly testing cultural safety and knowledge in large language models. Cultural safety means writing respectful and appropriate replies across diverse groups, yet current research often treats safety and knowledge in isolation. Through AdaCultureSafe, the authors reveal a critical decoupling. Although language models hold rich knowledge of customs, they fail to use it to improve safety, leaning instead on generic safety rather than culture-specific knowledge. A knowledge-grounded method that elicits internal knowledge of customs during response generation improves safety.
arxiv-2603-08475: Argenziano and colleagues build an LLM-free system for indoor open-vocabulary navigation by repurposing ray frontiers. Ray frontiers become direction-conditioned semantic hypotheses as goals. Features from out-of-range rays are stored thinly at frontiers, each region keeping aimed embeddings for unseen content. The robot then moves by embedding-based frontier scoring and goal tracking inside a classical mapping pipeline with no large-model queries. An extension, R2F-VLN, handles commands through syntactic parsing and relational checks, and Habitat-sim and real-robot tests show strong results.
arxiv-2603-08675: Benjamin Bedert and colleagues prove that fairly dense Cayley graphs always hold a Hamilton cycle. Such a cycle exists in every large connected Cayley graph on n vertices whose degree clears n to some power below one. The result pushes the Lovász conjecture forward past the 2014 bar, and its proof swaps Szemerédi's regularity lemma for a leaner arithmetic version built for Cayley graphs.
arxiv-2603-09975: Gabriele Masina and coauthors lift a knowledge compilation trick from propositional logic up to SMT formulas. Compiling a base into d-DNNF form offline lets many later queries run in polynomial time. Their method first enriches the SMT input with precomputed theory lemmas, so SMT queries reduce to propositional ones. The approach works for any theory and any d-DNNF compiler, used as black boxes, and was proven out in software.
arxiv-2603-10075: Sizhe Huang and Shujie Yang defend drone swarm federated learning against stealthy backdoor attacks with a spectral method called TASER. Outlier hunting struggles here, since swarms lack central coordination and attackers mimic honest behaviour closely. Their key observation: the harder an attack mimics, the more its gradient energy concentrates in the spectrum. TASER uses that concentration to disrupt the backdoor task while preserving the main task, without outlier detection.
arxiv-2603-10175: Elizaveta Kostenok, Mathieu Salzmann and Milos Cernak teach an audio language model to explain speech quality, not just score it. Mean opinion scores hide which perceptual flaws a clip carries and where they occur. Their two stage post training first calibrates the model to named quality dimensions, then applies reinforcement learning with dimension specific rewards. The result leads a multidimensional benchmark and sharpens where and what kind of artifacts are reported.
arxiv-2603-10575: Artur Blois and co-authors study the shadowing phenomenon for composition operators on the Hardy space over the open unit disk. A composition operator follows a holomorphic self-map of the disk, sending each function to its composite with that map. Shadowing asks, roughly, whether rough orbits of the system are tracked by true ones. The main result gives a full characterization of which operators of this kind, when the map is linear fractional, have the positive shadowing property.
arxiv-2603-10775: Sidi Wang, Sophie Arnoult, and Amir Kamran use large language models as annotators to train a machine translation quality estimation model, avoiding the high cost of using big models directly. They take segment-level annotations as the key signal, following earlier work. A simplified MQM scheme guides the model. A prompt pattern built around GPT-4o then produces the annotations. Those labels correlate well with human ones. Training COMET on them gives competitive segment-level scores for Chinese-English and English-German.
arxiv-2603-10975: Zhixin Cheng and coauthors propose VCR, a framework for brightening low-light images that works in the HVI color space, designed to keep color faithful while separating it from intensity. One module filters features using variance cues to focus on regions rich in intensity and color. Another aligns color distributions to keep luminance and chrominance consistent. On several benchmark datasets the method reaches state-of-the-art perceptual quality against existing low-light enhancement approaches.
arxiv-2603-11075: Runbang Hu and coauthors propose VeriHGN. This framework predicts routing congestion early in chip layout verification. Detailed routing would reveal it much later, and in a costly way. An enhanced heterogeneous graph unifies circuit components and spatial grids in one relational representation. It models how logical intent and physical placement interact. It does not loosely couple netlist and layout features. On industrial benchmarks, it matches or beats state-of-the-art methods. These benchmarks include ISPD2015 and the CircuitNet sets. The measures are accuracy and correlation metrics.
arxiv-2603-11175: Canxun Zhang and coauthors image electron flow in dual-gated bilayer graphene with a scanning superconducting sensor, hunting for fluid-like transport at small scales. Earlier devices showed hydrodynamics only at hundreds of nanometers. The large and tunable effective mass of rhombohedral multilayers shrinks the scattering length between electrons toward the Fermi wavelength in the flat band regime. Across carrier density and displacement field they map ballistic, hydrodynamic, and diffusive regimes. The flat band shows it most strongly, with striking nonlinearities at high current.
arxiv-2603-11575: Vizgan and co-authors present views of a clumpy ring galaxy at redshift 4.0148, first flagged as a possible gravitational lens. Ring galaxies are rare, and some form when one galaxy plows head-on through another. Hubble and JWST images show three bright clumps along a ring. Its star formation rate, near 140 solar masses per year, matches other high-redshift collisional rings. The team favors the collision story, yet a lensing setup with a foreground galaxy stays possible. Kinematic data at high spectral resolution would settle the question.
arxiv-2603-11675: Chen and co-authors present PROMO, a promptable framework for virtual try-on built on a Flow Matching transformer. Diffusion-based systems look realistic, yet their extra reference networks slow sampling down. PROMO treats the task as structured image editing with three demands: keep the subject, move texture faithfully, and blend the result cleanly. Latent multi-modal conditioning and self-reference cut the inference cost hard. On standard benchmarks, it tops prior systems and general editors on fidelity, with a strong speed balance.
arxiv-2603-11875: Corll introduces Mirror, a data-curation pattern for prompt injection screening that favors strict data geometry over model scale. The first screening layer runs on every request, so it must be fast, deterministic, and auditable. Mirror sorts samples into matched positive and negative cells, so the classifier learns attack mechanics over corpus shortcuts. With 5,000 curated samples in 31 of 32 cells, a sparse character n-gram SVM reaches about 96% recall and 92.07% F1 on a 524-case holdout. A 22-million-parameter guard model scores far lower on the same holdout, at much higher latency.
arxiv-2603-12475: Ahmad, Macvean, Geewax, and Karger report a Perfection Paradox in AI-assisted API design in industry. Enterprise API work stalls between fast feature delivery and strict usability standards. Their case study trains an AI workflow on API Improvement Proposals and tests it with 16 experts. AI drafts beat human ones on 10 of 11 usability dimensions and cut authoring time sharply. Experts misread much AI work as human, yet called the designs unsettlingly perfect. Hyper-consistency signals missing human judgment, the authors argue, and shifts designers from drafter to curator.
arxiv-2603-12575: Xuanhua Yin and co-authors speed up diffusion transformers that turn text prompts into images. Full self-attention over dense image tokens makes these models slow to run. The team found that pretty regions draw strong cross-attention and change fast over time. Quiet regions change smoothly and waste compute. Their AccelAes method builds a focus mask, spends compute on masked regions, and caches step results. Tests showed faster runs and better aesthetic scores, with no new training.
arxiv-2603-12775: Yann Lanoiselée and co-authors bring many models of odd diffusion under one frame. The media in view are mixed and change over time, so steps vary in size and link to past steps. Their frame joins those two traits in one Gaussian process with random modulation. Known models like Lévy flights and random walks with rests fit inside it. The authors derive moments and tests for when diffusion turns anomalous. Lab tracks of single particles can then be sorted with more care.
arxiv-2603-13075: Jennifer Lucero and co-authors study how unocculted stellar spots distort high-resolution transmission spectra of a transiting giant planet. Dark spots and bright plages can mimic or hide air signals from the planet. With the SOAPv4 tool, they simulate a hot Jupiter crossing a Sun-like star under varied spot setups. Planet-occulted line distortions shift with spot size, spot position, and stellar spin. Sodium and calcium lines distort most, while H-alpha reacts less. Projected spot area proves the main control on signal strength.
arxiv-2603-13275: Wanyin Wu and co-authors present PREBA, a tool that predicts how long a surgery will last. Good forecasts help hospitals plan staff, rooms, and care. Supervised models need costly labeled data, while zero-shot LLM forecasts lack local clinical grounding. PREBA builds a prompt from similar past cases plus group-level priors. A PCA-weighted search picks the most relevant cases for that prompt. Bayesian averaging then blends multi-round LLM forecasts with the priors for a steady estimate.
arxiv-2603-13475: ChunJun Cao and co-authors study state-dependent geometries from magic-enriched quantum codes. Holographic code models to date describe quantum fields on a fixed background and cannot capture gravitational backreaction. The authors argue this limit is intrinsic to exact subsystem complementary recovery. Adding backreaction leads naturally to approximate quantum error correction, they show. They define a Ryu-Takayanagi-like entropy split for approximate codes, with bulk matter entropy from optimal recovery. For skewed codes, the proto-area grows monotonically with bulk entropy, matching extremal surface changes.
arxiv-2603-13575: Zhuchenyang Liu and co-authors explore human-AI collaboration in e-textile design through a case study. Flex sensors detect joint motion, but placing them well needs anatomy, biomechanics, and textile expertise at once. Their case study targets shoulder motion detection with flex sensors on garments. Three human designers worked in three scenarios: LLMs alone, humans alone, and human-AI collaboration. The least experienced designer improved steadily with AI help and matched the best human-only result. The most experienced designer did worse with collaboration, a surprising split.
arxiv-2603-13775: Tuan V. Ngo and co-authors present an LLM-based Net Analyzer rApp for safe automation in O-RAN networks. O-RAN makes 5G and 6G networks programmable, but open interfaces add complexity for operators. They struggle to link mixed events and turn them into safe changes. The rApp first reads mobility events, then confirms anomalies by targeted log checks. Settings are read through tool-gated access, and small changes are proposed only after the operator approves. A real testbed demo uses a ping-pong handover case.
arxiv-2603-14275: Bai and co-authors build DLM-AN, a system that normalizes accents with a dial for how much accent to keep. Language learning and dubbing need that control, which older methods lack. The system runs masked discrete diffusion over self-supervised speech tokens. Tokens likely to carry native pronunciation are found and reused to seed the reverse process, so more reuse keeps more accent. A duration predictor adjusts total length to match native rhythm. Tests on multi-accent English give the lowest word error rate among compared systems.
arxiv-2603-14475: Zhang and co-authors present Wi-Spike, a spiking network that reads human actions from WiFi signals. WiFi sensing is private and needs no contact. Most prior models chase accuracy and ignore energy use. Wi-Spike uses spiking convolutional layers to pull features from channel state data. A new temporal attention step sharpens the features before classification. Tests use three benchmark datasets. It matches top accuracy on single actions and leads on multi-action tests. Energy use drops by at least half, they report.
arxiv-2603-14775: Liu and Clark extend neural network backflow to ab-initio solid calculations. Neural quantum states give flexible wavefunctions but scale poorly to periodic solids. A two-stage pruning plan tames the determinant explosion here. A cheap physics-based proxy ranks configurations by likely weight. Exact backflow amplitudes then run only on top-ranked determinants. Hydrogen chains match or beat DMRG and AFQMC scores. Bond-breaking regimes that break coupled-cluster methods stay stable. Ground-state curves for 2D graphene and 3D silicon show the reach, they report.
arxiv-2603-15075: Rankine and co-authors study disc winds in 3,027 X-ray selected quasars from SDSS-V and eROSITA. The quasars span redshifts 1.5 to 3.5. The team measures the CIV emission line to gauge wind strength and fits X-ray spectra for luminosity and slope. X-ray traits link only weakly to wind strength. A slope built from far-UV light tracks winds better than the classic optical-to-X-ray slope. The results fit a radiation line-driven wind that needs far-UV photons without over-ionizing the gas.
arxiv-2603-15675: Bera and Willemse build interface protocols that cannot trap users in deadlock. Interfaces set which talks a server and its clients may hold. Heavy concurrency raises the risk of deadlocks and livelocks. Weak termination promises an exit path from each reachable state. The authors widen older by-construction results for such compositions. From one sound server spec, they derive whole classes of clients. A partial mirroring relation does the work. An open-source tool guides modelers who apply the method.
arxiv-2603-16075: Zhang and co-authors design a liquid target to sharpen hyperon scattering at BESIII. Tagged hyperon beams come from J/psi and psi(3686) decays. Today's target is the beam pipe, with few free protons inside. A 30 mm liquid hydrogen layer boosts proton density sevenfold or more. Liquid deuterium swaps in clean deuteron targets for neutrons. Detector simulations track the cost of the added material. Tracking holds steady above 0.5 GeV/c in their runs. Gains stay within 1.6 points of baseline at higher momenta. The concept promises richer, cleaner scattering data.
arxiv-2603-16175: Dey, Jayanthan, and Sane classify parity binomial edge ideals for two families of graphs. The families are cactus graphs and chordal graphs. Their goal is to say exactly which of these ideals are unmixed. They also pin down which ones are Cohen-Macaulay. Both answers are given in terms of the graph's own structure. So a reader can test the ideal by checking plain features of the graph itself.
arxiv-2603-16375: Earnshaw, Nester, and Román grade monoidal categories by partial commutative monoids. Effectful categories mix pure maps with effectful ones. Effectful maps combine only with central maps, which hints at grades. A grade here is an element of a partial commutative monoid. Plain monoidal categories return as the one-grade case. Effectful categories form a coreflective part of the graded world. Examples model parallel programs and bounded resource use.
arxiv-2603-16475: Somov and co-authors test whether language models truly follow their own checklists. Schema-guided pipelines draft rubrics or queries before deciding. Users expect edits to those drafts to steer the outcome. The team edits the drafts where one right answer follows by rule. Across 12 models and four benchmarks, models looked self-consistent. Yet after edits, predictions often failed to update. An external tool that derives the answer removes most fragility. Preference tuning helped faithfulness a great deal.
arxiv-2603-16675: Sangalli, Quaeghebeur, and Krak link hitting times and hitting chances in imprecise chains. The chains use a compact, convex set of transition matrices. Rows of those matrices are specified separately. Two implications anchor the results. Finite upper expected time forces the lower hitting chance to one. Finite lower expected time forces the upper hitting chance to one. An equivalence also holds between the two notions. A counterexample shows one converse can fail.
arxiv-2603-16875: Silva and co-authors use video scripts to steer attention inside 360 degree VR tours. Such tours immerse viewers, yet nothing guides the eye toward key objects. The team combines Grounding DINO with Segment Anything to focus on objects named in a script. Their case study is a 360 degree video tour of the University of Reading. The authors report that script based focusing improved the user experience. It helped direct attention to the elements that mattered in each scene.
arxiv-2603-17075: Zhang and co-authors turn polynomial circuit building into a game for a reinforcement learning agent. The task is to compute a given polynomial with addition and multiplication gates, within a fixed budget of operations. The work is motivated by auto proof generation and Valiant's VP versus VNP conjecture. They train an AlphaZero style loop and compare two methods. SAC reaches the highest success rates on two variable targets. PPO with Monte Carlo tree search scales to three variables and improves steadily on harder cases.
arxiv-2603-17175: Hsiao, Kumar, and Rathje make Explainable Boosting Machines more trustworthy for predicting lateral spreading in earthquakes. These models predict through additive shape functions that users can inspect directly. But they can learn non physical trends that undermine trust in hazard work. The authors modify learned shape functions using domain knowledge. This corrects non physical behavior while keeping data driven patterns. Applied to the 2011 Christchurch earthquake dataset, the fixed model gave more physically consistent explanations, global and local. The cost was an accuracy tradeoff of about 4 to 5 percent.
arxiv-2603-17775: Pan and co-authors name a failure mode in label-free reasoning training: the consensus trap. Models that learn from majority votes grow more self-consistent over time. Output diversity then collapses, and shared errors get reinforced with confidence. Their CoVerRL framework swaps one model between generator and verifier roles. Each role trains the other in a rising loop. Self-check accuracy climbed from about 55 to over 85 percent, they report.
arxiv-2603-17875: Gupta and Mahajan rebuild Markov decision process theory on operator ground. They view an MDP as optimizing a function over linear operators on general spaces. A fresh existence result for optimal policies comes first. Perturbation theory then gives a policy difference lemma and a Gateaux derivative for the objective. Bounding that difference yields a new policy gradient method of majorization type. A low-cost RKHS variant beat PPO in their tests.
arxiv-2603-17975: Mir and co-authors present AHOY, a way to rebuild full 3D human avatars from plain YouTube video. The method copes with heavy occlusion, where large body parts stay hidden. It uses tuned diffusion models to hallucinate views of unseen regions as training signal. A two-stage design then builds pose-dependent Gaussian maps. Tests show top reconstruction quality, and the avatars can be posed in new ways.
arxiv-2603-18075: Cui and Han build waveforms and fluxes for extreme-mass-ratio inspirals with a spinning secondary. A small compact object orbits a supermassive black hole in a Kerr background. They use a radiative rule, half-retarded minus half-advanced field, for orbit-averaged fluxes. Fluxes cover energy, angular momentum, and a Carter-like constant under a linear-spin treatment. The route gives a workable way to add secondary spin to future space-based wave models.
arxiv-2603-18375: Shukla and co-authors argue for relationship-centered care in AI mental-health tools. Current design aims to strengthen the bond between a patient and an AI agent. They warn this can fake connection and displace real human relationships needed for recovery. Their model joins the Responsible AI Six Sphere Framework with self-determination theory, centered on relatedness. The guidelines push AI to scaffold human links with therapists, family, and peers instead.
arxiv-2603-18675: Kozitsky proves a Lee-Yang type result for isotropic vector spin models on the integer lattice. The Lee-Yang property says a partition function has only imaginary zeros in the field variable. Many analytic tools for spin models and quantum lattice fields rely on it. Until now, the generalized property was known only in two dimensions. Kozitsky shows it holds for models on Z in all even dimensions D. The result covers both classical rotors and D-component quantum lattice fields.
arxiv-2603-18775: Witstok and co-authors confirm a Lyman-alpha line from a galaxy just 330 million years after the Big Bang. Deep JWST spectra from the OASIS and JADES programs target GS-z13-1-LA at redshift 13.1. The line shows a rest-frame width measure of 66 angstroms, with a steep blue continuum. Those traits point to a hot, strong ionising source. Ionising photons may leak out and carve a small ionised bubble nearby. Sixteen candidate galaxies hint at an overdensity of such sources. The galaxy stands as an early beacon of reionisation.
arxiv-2603-18875: Moosavi Nejad computes how quark and meson masses change Higgs decay into B-mesons. About 60 percent of Higgs bosons at the LHC decay to bottom quark pairs. Those quarks form B-hadrons before decaying further. Prior work treated both quarks and mesons as massless. Working in a general-mass scheme at next-to-leading order changes the energy spectrum shape. Meson mass boosts the decay width at low scaled energy. Quark mass lifts the rate near the peak and above. The channel can probe Higgs traits through these mass effects.
arxiv-2603-19375: Tran and co-authors let language model agents design membership inference attacks on their own. Such attacks test whether a data point sat inside a model's training set. Crafting them by hand takes long, careful study of model behavior. Their AutoMIA agents search a wide space of signal designs for each target. The found attacks are tuned to the given model and data set. Gains reach 0.18 in absolute AUC over prior attacks. The work shows agents can serve as a scalable attack design tool.
arxiv-2603-19475: Roon and Schenker prove that disordered quantum spin systems always have disordered ground states. The systems use random local interactions with a statistical form of translation invariance. In the large-system limit, the ground states keep the same symmetry as the system. A disordered form of the Lieb-Robinson bounds is a key tool. The authors also formalise random states on C-star algebras with a new limit theorem. As a result, the bulk spectrum is fixed, not random, despite the disorder.
arxiv-2603-19575: Cai and co-authors present MagicSeg, a pipeline that builds its own training data for open-world segmentation. Hand-made pixel labels for many classes cost too much to gather. MagicSeg starts from class names and writes prompts for a diffusion model. It draws an image for each class, plus a matched negative for contrast. A detector and a second tool pull object masks from the pictures as labels. Pretraining on the data gave top scores on PASCAL VOC, Context, and COCO.
arxiv-2603-19975: von Davier and co-authors reflect on using generative AI prompts to spur critical thinking. Evidence on AI and critical thinking is mixed, with results tied to design choices. They draw on two tools they built: ArtBot for art interpretation and Privy for AI privacy. Both use pointed questions that ask users to clarify and justify their views. Feedback suggests domain specific provocations work best with productive friction. Interactions that need real user input also helped. Future designs may adapt to user skill.
arxiv-2603-20075: Zheng and co-authors build a harness that helps language model agents fix real compiler bugs. Their llvm-harness targets the middle end of LLVM, a widely used compiler base. It bundles agent friendly LLVM tools plus a benchmark of 334 reproducible bugs. A small tailored agent works inside the harness. Five frontier models lost ground on compiler bugs with a standard agent setup. The harness lifted their performance by 62 percent. The mini agent beat that baseline by a further 22 percent.
arxiv-2603-20275: Khaki and co-authors study how removing decoder layers affects vision-language models. They rank layers by how little their activations change for math versus non-math inputs. Tests on two leading models reveal three pruning regimes. At low budgets, the choice of layers matters most. At high budgets, even spacing between kept layers matters more. Their domain-aware rankings stay most stable where choice matters. The results give a clear guide for cutting model depth safely.
arxiv-2603-20975: Jiang introduces DiscoUQ, a way to gauge confidence from how a team of language model agents disagrees. Simple vote counts throw away the rich detail in agent reasoning. DiscoUQ extracts features from the disagreement itself, both language traits and embedding geometry. Three versions range from logistic regression to a neural network. On four benchmarks with a five agent system, the top version beats the best baseline on AUROC and is far better calibrated. Gains are largest where agents disagree only weakly.
arxiv-2603-21175: Kim and Sim tackle reward hacking in diffusion model fine tuning. Reward based training can raise a reward score while image quality fails to improve. They trace this flaw to sharp reward landscapes, where reward model gradients are not robust. Their RSA-FT method uses gradients from a flattened reward model, built by perturbing the diffusion model and its samples. No reward model retraining is needed. Each trick helps on its own, and joint use helps more. The framework is simple and broadly compatible.
arxiv-2603-21275: Fayet defines hyperbolic form factors for density distributions and applies them to the Earth. The hyperbolic form factor is the bilateral Laplace transform of a density, tied by duality to the usual form factor. For a sphere, it has a simple series in the moments of the radius. It also fixes the outside Yukawa potential from a new charge with a massive mediator. Simple analytic density profiles for the Earth match a five shell model to about one percent. This sharpens limits on a new force from the MICROSCOPE experiment.
arxiv-2603-21575: Wei and co-authors probe the central regions of quasars through their variability. Quasars are powered by supermassive black holes with accretion disks, and their flickering encodes clues about that central engine. Using Sloan Digital Sky Survey data, the team builds structure functions from light curves for a large sample. Structure function parameters correlate strongly with luminosity, black hole mass, and Eddington ratio. At fixed luminosity, a higher Eddington ratio means a smaller structure function. Links with redshift or rest wavelength were weak, pointing to intrinsic drivers.
arxiv-2603-21775: Contreras and co-authors study how many gluons are produced in deep inelastic scattering, a core process in high-energy QCD. They derive equations for the cross sections of final states with n cut Pomerons. The new derivation uses the dipole approach, yet lands on the known AGK cutting rule equations. A homotopy method then solves them, starting from an analytic first step and iterating numerically. For large n, they find a closed-form solution. From it, they compute the entropy of the produced gluons at large saturation scale.
arxiv-2603-21975: Arazzi and co-authors build SecureBreak, a dataset for catching harmful outputs from large language models. Jailbreaks and prompt injection can slip past a model's built-in alignment, so a second filter layer is useful. SecureBreak labels model outputs across several risk categories, with careful manual labels set conservatively for safety. It serves two roles: feedback on alignment during training, and a final screen for deployed systems. Pretrained models improved at spotting unsafe content after fine-tuning on it. The authors offer it as shared ground for safety work.
arxiv-2603-22075: Vicentino runs a controlled comparison of two kinds of language model: autoregressive and masked diffusion. Both train on the same data, budget, and hardware: 50 million tokens of TinyStories. Training speed is nearly equal, with diffusion only 4.7% slower overall. The autoregressive model converges faster but starts overfitting by step 14,000. The diffusion model improves more slowly and is still gaining at step 20,000. Vicentino finds a trade-off: autoregressive text is fluent but repetitive, while diffusion text is more varied but less grammatical.
arxiv-2603-22275: Jang and co-authors build a diffusion framework for novel view synthesis. View synthesis needs images that stay consistent across camera angles. Most methods work in a VAE latent space that treats each view apart. Their method, GLD, reuses the feature space of a geometric foundation model instead. Those features rebuild RGB images well and encode cross-view matches. GLD beats VAE and RAE baselines on image quality and 3D consistency. It also trains more than four times faster than the VAE route.
arxiv-2603-22475: The Euclid Collaboration describes CLOE, the code that computes theory predictions for the Euclid survey's likelihood. CLOE is a modular Python package covering weak lensing, galaxy clustering, galaxy-galaxy lensing, and cross-checks with the cosmic microwave background. It runs the full likelihood in one framework for both photometric and spectroscopic data. The authors lay out the code's structure, testing habits, docs, and speed work. They also sketch future plans, and the code is public for the wider community.
arxiv-2603-22575: Rana and co-authors model how phonons shift exciton binding energies with temperature. They build a many-body Hamiltonian whose inputs all come from first-principles methods. To treat the binding without perturbation shortcuts, they evolve the model in imaginary time with path integral Monte Carlo. For Wannier-Mott excitons the computed binding matches experiments closely. Optical phonons do the real work of shifting exciton binding. Sound-like and transverse modes matter more for the separate electron and hole polarons.
arxiv-2603-22675: Mostafa and co-authors turn unordered biomedical tables into images a vision model can read. Tables in medicine lack a natural spatial layout, so vision models miss local patterns. Their framework, Dynomap, learns where each feature should sit on a map. It tunes placement and prediction together, with no preset groupings. Across clinical and biological datasets, Dynomap beat classic and deep rivals. In liquid biopsy data, it raised cancer subtype accuracy by up to 18 percent. In a Parkinson voice dataset, the gain reached 8 percent.
arxiv-2603-22775: Kawalec develops series expansions for k-free Dirichlet series. He expands the k-free zeta series as a Laurent series with a simple pole. For the regular part, he proves a Stieltjes-like formula for its coefficients. He also studies a second analytic continuation of these series. That route yields a formula for the zeta value at one over k. The formula uses the k-free indicator function and holds for integers k of at least two.
arxiv-2603-22975: Canocchi and co-authors compute sodium abundances in late-type stars with 3D non-LTE models. Sodium traces galaxy chemical history and star populations. Simple 1D models in equilibrium can bias the values. The team models nine sodium lines in dwarf and giant stars. They use 3D radiation hydrodynamic atmospheres across wide ranges of heat, gravity, and metal content. Corrections versus 1D equilibrium tend to be negative. For saturated lines in low-gravity giants they grow large. The grid and fitting tools are released in public.
arxiv-2603-23075: Klesel and Messer study what happens when AI tools disclose their energy use. Disclosure aims to steer users toward small, efficient models. Their experiment ran with 365 participants. Seeing energy data raised the odds of picking the efficient small model more than twelvefold. Later prompt behavior did not differ between groups, though. A placebo effect appeared in the green group. People who picked the eco-friendly model rated its quality and their satisfaction lower. Disclosure works, but with a perceptual cost, they conclude.
arxiv-2603-23175: Mendonça and Negret define a generalized Golomb-Dickman constant under Ewens sampling. The constant is the limiting share of the longest cycle in a random permutation. Ewens sampling adds a parameter that tilts the permutation law. Using Kingman's Poisson process view of the Poisson-Dirichlet law, they get an explicit integral form. The constant shifts with the parameter value. Small values favor long cycles, large values favor many small cycles. Limit behavior at both ends is derived, with numeric and simulation checks.
arxiv-2603-23275: Kimura and Sharma study the Dirac operator on a finite warped cylinder with a background gauge field. They pin down the endpoint operators behind the Atiyah-Patodi-Singer boundary condition. They also derive a formula for the mode-by-mode spectrum under that condition. In a constant, invertible gauge, the endpoint eta terms cancel and the index is zero. Trouble comes when a boundary mode crosses zero and the projector jumps. They build a regularized family of endpoint rules that stays continuous through such crossings.
arxiv-2603-23375: Acharja and Chowdhury survey natural language interfaces for spatial and temporal databases. Such tools let non-experts query data in plain words instead of code. Geo and time queries add operators that plain database tools lack. Prior surveys covered general databases and skipped this niche. The pair map the datasets, metrics, and method families used in the field. They compare systems side by side and trace shared trends. Wide gaps in datasets and scoring habits stand out. They close with open problems and promising next steps.
arxiv-2603-23575: Bouzouad, Chang, and Boukhobza present APreQEL, a quantization scheme that tunes precision layer by layer for edge models. Language models strain small devices on memory, speed, and privacy. Plain quantization shrinks every layer the same way, yet layers react unlike each other. Memory use and speed pull apart, which muddies deployment choices. APreQEL scores what each layer adds and how each precision type runs on the target chip. It then assigns the type per layer under user priorities. The result opens designs that uniform shrinking cannot reach.
arxiv-2603-24075: Kharuk presents the Ising noise filter, a graph-based pre-filter for particle detectors. Standard noise rejection leans on track fitting, which faces a combinatorial explosion. The filter maps detector hits to binary spins and minimizes an energy functional instead. Its interaction kernels encode the physics and geometry of each experiment. At the Baikal-GVD neutrino telescope, it reaches 96.8 percent recall for astrophysical neutrinos. At the SPD detector, recall hits 97 percent on test data. With a Hopfield network, the TrackML score rises from 0.5 to 0.95.
arxiv-2603-24175: Ahanjideh and Kovács verify Tutte's 3-flow conjecture for a class of Cayley graphs. The conjecture claims certain graphs admit a flow that is nowhere zero with values in a small group. They settle it for Cayley graphs on solvable groups of order twice a square-free number. Their proof rests on a new necessary and sufficient condition. That condition describes when a simple 5-valent graph has a nowhere-zero 3-flow, in terms of a special pseudoforest decomposition. The condition turns a flow question into a structural one.
arxiv-2603-24375: Petukhova and Kochmar tackle a hard grading problem: how to rate the teaching quality of AI tutor replies in math mistake repair. Standard text metrics cannot tell if a reply finds the error or gives away the answer. They build a hierarchy of teaching aspects from human choices on MRBench, then craft paired replies that differ in one aspect. Their small preference model, trained on synthetic pairs, beats larger general reward models on human tests.
arxiv-2603-24575: He and co-authors tackle the conversion of complex raster figures into editable SVG files with vision-language models. Original vector files are often lost, leaving only PNG or JPEG versions that resist editing, and manual rebuilding is costly. Existing datasets skew toward icons, and benchmarks score pixels rather than structure. Their VFIG-Data set holds 66,000 figure-to-SVG pairs, mixing real paper figures with programmatic diagrams. Their VFIG-Bench suite scores structural correctness, such as broken links or misplaced arrows, plus an out-of-distribution test set.
arxiv-2603-24775: Prakash introduces the Agent Identity Protocol for delegation between AI agents and tools. Agents call tools through MCP and delegate through A2A, yet neither protocol verifies identity; a scan of 2,000 MCP servers found none with authentication. Its tokens fuse identity, rights, and provenance into one append-only chain. Two wire formats cover single-hop and multi-hop cases. Python and Rust versions work together, verification takes well under a millisecond, and overhead is a tiny share of latency.
arxiv-2603-25075: Zhou tests whether sparse features inside a vision-language model can be mixed like building blocks. Many steering methods assume feature sets combine cleanly. Tests on Qwen3-VL-8B say they often do not. Steering with one task-tuned set helps a bit. Steering with two sets joined causes output drift and hurts accuracy, even at matched strength. Probes place task signals in a mid decoder layer, where he trains sparse autoencoders. Checks across model families and datasets confirm the pattern. It gives a strict test kit for safer control.
arxiv-2603-25675: Amend, Carioni, and Zemas generalize particle gradient flows to a wider class of optimization problems. Particle gradient flows solve total variation problems by moving a set of Dirac deltas. Their Atomic Gradient Flows work in general Banach spaces. The particles are the extremal points of the unit ball of the regularizer. The authors build a discrete functional and show it fits the original problem by Gamma-convergence. They prove the flow is well defined and give conditions for uniqueness.
arxiv-2603-25975: Balogh shows that a learning system can rediscover a classic theory of event meaning on its own. Schank's theory split all events into a few hand-coded primitive acts. Balogh adapts the DreamCoder wake-sleep method to event state changes. Compression pressure alone drives the search for reusable operators. Starting from four generic primitives, the system finds matches for Schank's core acts. It also finds compound and emotional operators that Schank lacked. Coverage hits one hundred percent on three datasets. Schank's own library covers far less on two of them.
arxiv-2603-26075: Fabiano and co-authors work out the least noise that gravity must carry if it is not quantized. Quantum gravity would let the Newtonian force entangle two massive objects. Any non-quantized model must instead add some noise, they show. They classify all such models that keep Galilean invariance and the right average force. For a model to avoid entanglement, a minimum, measurable noise is required. Seeing less noise than that floor would prove gravity can entangle. They test the idea on known classical-quantum models and several lab setups.
arxiv-2603-26275: Santos-Gutierrez and co-authors test a method for averaging systems that sit far from equilibrium. The transient time correlation function method gives clean estimates of transport traits without huge samples. It works well for fluids, but has not been checked broadly for other driven systems. The team links the method to the spectral theory of random systems. They show where linear theory falls short, and map how the method handles both short-lived and steady responses.
arxiv-2603-26375: Menezes de Araújo, Gormley, and Murphy propose a beta latent variable model to summarise death rates across countries.
