Choi proves that every symplectic small cover in four dimensions is aspherical, meaning its shape has a simple loop structure at large scale. For covers built over a pair of polygons, symplectic form exists exactly when the two parts fit a match rule, and Choi also sorts these spaces up to smooth change of shape. A final example shows the orbit shape need not come from two polygons at all.
arxiv-2605-01475:
Rodrigo Moreira, Larissa Ferreira Rodrigues Moreira, Tereza Cristina Carvalho, and Flávio de Oliveira Silva add brains to the traffic heart of a beyond-5G network. Their upgraded user plane function must pick, in real time, whether data flows to a nearby edge site or to the cloud, under tight delay and trust demands.

The choice is cast as a partly hidden decision problem, and a deep Q-network agent learns the picking policy. Delay is measured passively: small eBPF programs tie timestamps to tunnel IDs inside the traffic itself, so no probe traffic is needed. In experiments the agent beats a random picker by a wide margin, with lower average delay, steadier rewards, and more reliable low-delay choices. The authors present the design as proof that learning control fits the core of next-generation networks.
arxiv-2605-01575:
Mahesh Madhav and 33 co-authors introduce SPEC CPU 2026, the next edition of the benchmark suite that the computer industry uses to grade processors. Suites age as software changes, so each generation must be rebuilt from modern, open programs chosen to stress chips the way real work does.

The paper lays out how the suite was made: community selection and hardening of workloads for diversity, portability, and long life. Its headline addition is a standardized rolling round-robin rate method for running mixed, multiprogrammed loads, filling a long-standing gap in how throughput is measured. The suite also carries more multithreaded tests and workloads with distinct hardware profiles. By documenting the selection and validation craft, the authors aim to set the grading standard for the next era of architecture research and chip buying.
arxiv-2605-01875:
Rishad Shahmurov studies smooth, axisymmetric Navier-Stokes flow with swirl, a setting where rotation around an axis shapes the motion. He works with weighted energies built from the swirl divided by radius, a classical family of measures. The paper finds the exact range of power weights for which those energies keep a positive gap from the gradient term.

Below a sharp threshold the diffusion form stays coercive, at the threshold the gap vanishes, and above it the form turns indefinite. At that same threshold, a radial strain term cancels and the identity becomes the classic circulation energy. The author also characterises a special weight by transport and diffusion traits, and finds the best strain bound in range.
arxiv-2605-01975:
Ruifeng Zheng and colleagues join sensing and communication in a molecular channel, where molecules carry the signal. In a microfluidic setup, the gap between sender and receiver shapes delay, response shape, and overlap between symbols. The team uses those same effects both to send data and to measure the gap, rather than treating them as separate jobs.

They build a Markov state-space model tied to distance, giving channel responses and a block model for on-off signalling. Their receiver uses pilot signals to set a first distance guess, then feedback equalization and joint refinement. In simulations, distance estimates were accurate and bit errors improved, showing that sensing and sending can help each other.
arxiv-2605-02075:
Michael Doherty, Alejandra Beghelli, and Laura Toni train a graph transformer with reinforcement learning to route traffic in elastic optical networks. The task joins routing, modulation choice, and spectrum assignment as requests arrive. Past reinforcement methods had not used a transformer here, likely due to high data and compute needs and unstable training.

The authors combine rotary encodings for graph data, masking of invalid actions, and a regulariser on valid action mass, with fast GPU simulation. Training stays stable for the first time in this setting. Against past learning methods and heuristics, their system is the first learning method to beat all benchmarks, raising supportable traffic load by up to thirteen percent on real topologies.
arxiv-2605-02275:
Pierpaolo Serio and colleagues benchmark LiDAR place recognition for edge devices, where a robot must tell whether it has visited a place before. Place recognition supports loop closure and steady mapping in long-term navigation, but deep models are heavy for resource-limited platforms. The team uses bird's eye view images of LiDAR scans so light image networks can do the job.

They compare representative architectures with no aggregation head, using one descriptor scheme based on global pooling and linear projection. Models run under full, half, and eight-bit integer precision. Half precision matched full precision at lower cost, while eight-bit results varied by architecture. The authors frame the findings as a base for use-case-aware quantisation in edge deployment.
arxiv-2605-02375:
Marc Dymetman gives a structural account of diversity collapse in reinforcement learning with verifiable, binary rewards. Such training is now standard for reasoning in language models. Single-sample accuracy rises, but multi-sample coverage often falls, sometimes below the base model. Dymetman traces that pattern to the shape of binary rewards themselves.

With only zero or one as reward, infinitely many distributions maximise expected reward, with no distinguished winner. KL control resolves that degeneracy. As its weight tends to zero, it selects the base model conditioned on validity, the fully valid distribution closest to the base model. The paper works through a nontrivial asymmetry in how the tilted distribution approaches that limit, in forward KL and in other senses.
arxiv-2605-02675:
Mehran H. Z. Bazargani and four co-authors extend a family of filtering methods so they can run online, as data arrive. The family jointly infers hidden states, learns unknown parameters, and estimates uncertainty in one framework. It appears in engineering, neuroscience, and time-series work under different names, including a method called Dynamic Expectation Maximisation.

The online version separates time scales. Parameters and precisions update slowly, setting the context, while beliefs about fast hidden states update quickly within it. Variational principles and procedures for this split are laid out. Numerical studies use a nonlinear, possibly chaotic generating model. Even when the fitted model's form differs fundamentally from the true process, the scheme tracks the hidden states well, supporting its use for live data assimilation.
arxiv-2605-02875:
John W. Montano and forty-two co-authors report ground-based monitoring of the active galaxy Mrk 817, part of the AGN STORM 2 campaign. Telescopes tracked the galaxy in many optical filters over about a year and a half, with a median gap of less than half a day in one band. Light curves from the ground are paired with an ultraviolet reference curve from the Swift satellite.

Echo delays between bands are measured by three methods. One method's delays grow with wavelength. The pattern matches a glowing disk lit from the center. The other methods give shorter delays. Those stray from the pattern at long wavelengths. All delays exceed thin-disk forecasts by a wide factor, the same disk size puzzle seen in other such galaxies. Splitting the campaign into three brightness epochs shows delays shifting as well.
arxiv-2605-03075:
Kyowoon Lee, Yunhao Luo, Anh Tong, and Jaesik Choi fix a flaw in long-horizon planning with diffusion models. The method stitches short plan segments together, but when each segment allows several modes, averaging can blend incompatible choices into plans that work nowhere.

Their Refining Compositional Diffusion method needs no new training. It guides sampling with a pretrained model's self-reconstruction error, used as a stand-in for plan density, plus a term that enforces agreement where segments overlap. The guidance favors dense, coherent plans. On hard OGBench tasks in movement, object handling, and pixel input, it beat prior methods throughout.
arxiv-2605-03175:
Ryan Faulkenberry and Saurabh Prasad build an open-vocabulary segmentation model for remote sensing images that needs no fine-tuning on remote sensing data. Labeled satellite and aerial data are scarce and costly, yet land-cover maps need dense labels.

Their CAFe-DINO model uses the DINOv3 backbone with text-image scoring, cost aggregation, and training-free upsampling, tuned only on a COCO-Stuff subset aimed at the domain. It reached state-of-the-art results on key remote sensing benchmarks, beating methods that were fine-tuned on remote sensing data itself. Code and data are public, making the approach easy to test and reuse.
arxiv-2605-03475:
Inbasekar and two colleagues offer a tougher way to grade AI-made video. Reference-based scores reward pixel fidelity over sense, while distribution scores reward texture over physical plausibility, and yes-or-no question benchmarks lean toward yes and use low-resolution judges that miss failures over time. WorldJen replaces binary questions with Likert-scale questionnaires, graded by a vision-language model fed frames at native resolution, and uses adversarial prompts that probe up to sixteen quality dimensions at once.

A blind human study of nearly twenty-seven hundred pairwise judgments over fifty prompts and six leading models sets a three-tier ground-truth ranking, and the automated judge reproduces that tier structure independently. Six ablations check the framework's robustness. By testing many dimensions per video instead of one, WorldJen cuts the cost of reliable evaluation while catching temporal failures that older benchmarks overlook.
arxiv-2605-03875:
Quanfeng Wang, Alexander H. Paulus, and Thomas F. Eibert present a three-dimensional near-field microwave imaging method. It works passively, using modulated signals from a non-cooperative transmitter. Signals scattered by targets are captured by a fixed reference antenna and a scanning near-field probe. The probe sits at different positions for each capture. Normalizing by the reference signal restores spatial coherence among the readings.

A single-frequency inverse source solver then reconstructs the sources and generates the images. A phase correction method allows coherent superposition of multi-frequency images, and tests confirm it works. For realistic narrowband signals, an incoherent approach is enough. The team tested the scheme with a planar scanning system in an office room. Software-defined radios sent and received narrowband OFDM signals on Wi-Fi bands. With background subtraction, they imaged a mannequin in the room.
arxiv-2605-04575:
Nahid Bayati and Fereshteh Sady study special functions on Banach function algebras, collections of functions that form a complete normed algebra on a compact space. A multiplicative spectral function sends each function to one of its spectral values while respecting multiplication, and the question is whether such a map must simply be evaluation at a point.

For several natural algebras, they show the kernel of such a function either is a maximal ideal or its span contains the constant function. Under continuity, or when that spanning fails, they prove the function agrees with point evaluation on a large family of functions. For familiar algebras, including continuous and Lipschitz functions, the map must be linear.
arxiv-2605-04875:
Enrico Maria Fenoaltea and four co-authors show that new technology combinations can be foreseen from the language of patents long before they appear. A coming pairing leaves an early trace across thousands of patents, not in any single inventor's work. Technologies are classed by International Patent Classification codes.

Their model, TechToken, treats those codes like words and learns their meanings from patent text. Closeness between code embeddings then signals growing convergence, and it predicts first combinations accurately. TechToken also improved general patent-related tasks over leading models. For science and policy readers, the work offers a data-driven way to spot emerging innovation earlier.
arxiv-2605-04975:
Paul Gerhart, Jay Taylor, and Sri Aravinda Krishnan Thyagarajan extend atomic swaps, the trustless all-or-nothing exchange of assets across blockchains, to exchanges with a built-in chance element. Classic swaps cannot fairly run lotteries, randomised allocations, or probabilistic trades, because their outcome is fixed once agreed. Some real exchanges instead need one side to pay for a fixed chance at a larger reward.

Their probabilistic swaps embed a publicly specified probability in the protocol itself, which neither party can bias or predict in advance. The construction combines adaptor signatures with oblivious pseudorandom functions, and adds a way to exchange evaluations of those functions for payments atomically. The result needs no trusted middleman.
arxiv-2605-05175:
Perry Radau introduces MRI-Eval, a benchmark testing language models on MRI physics and on operating GE scanners, knowledge central to research scanning practice. Existing benchmarks lean on review-book multiple-choice questions where top models already score near the ceiling. His benchmark instead uses primary questions across nine categories and three difficulty levels, drawn from textbooks, scanner manuals, course materials, and expert-written items.

Five model families were tested, all scoring high on multiple choice, with scanner operations the weakest category for every model. When answer options were removed, accuracy fell sharply, and scanner operations collapsed furthest. Primed questions also tested whether models accept incorrect claims from users, adding a diagnostic angle.
arxiv-2605-05275:
Ziyu Mu and three co-authors turn network traffic records into images so convolutional models can exploit spatial patterns between features for intrusion detection. Detection systems usually train on flat tables of flow records, whose one-dimensional form hides inter-feature structure. Their byte-level encoding writes each flow record into a fixed-size colour image along a set layout.

Continuous features are serialised in a standard single-precision format and packed along an inverted-L path, while discrete features sit in the centre row. The encoding is deterministic and reversible, keeping one layout for all samples. On two standard intrusion datasets, image-based versions of four models gained accuracy consistently over flow-based ones, with the largest gains on the more modern dataset.
arxiv-2605-05375:
Jonathan Oppenheim and Muhammad Sajjad examine a theory where spacetime stays classical while matter is quantum. Consistency forces spacetime to evolve with randomness built in. The paper works out what that randomness looks like near flat spacetime, splitting it into spin-2, spin-0, and non-dynamical parts.

They check that the action stays positive on the moving modes, a needed sign of consistency. Then they compute the noise pattern in the Newtonian potential and compare it with data from the LISA Pathfinder mission. That comparison, plus decoherence experiments, bounds the theory's coupling constants from real measurements.
arxiv-2605-05475:
When does an AI system act like it has intentions? Allessia Chiappetta and Robert Mahari argue that functional intentionality is a design decision, not a mystery. They define it as a behavior profile: purpose, foresight, volition, steady commitment over time, and coherence, the same signs law and philosophy use to infer intent.

Choices like memory, planning depth, and tool access set how strong that profile is, so it can be measured and tuned. They introduce the Functional Intentionality Test and a scoring protocol, FIT-Eval. The aim is proportionate oversight as agentic systems grow more autonomous.
arxiv-2605-05575:
Safety-critical controllers must stay inside safe limits without giving up too much performance. Tanmay Dokania and Yashwanth Kumar Nakka combine model predictive control with control barrier functions, which encode safety as a boundary the system may not cross. Building the least conservative barrier is intractable, so their design uses the barrier as a terminal constraint instead.

They prove the reachable set and feasibility grow as the prediction horizon lengthens. The proofs also support warm-starting the solver, cutting computation time. Simulations on a simple nonholonomic system showed far fewer infeasible points and successful tracking of paths inside the barrier's unsafe region.
arxiv-2605-05675:
A polaron is an electron dragging a cloud of lattice vibration with it, and computing one from first principles usually demands huge supercells. Moritz K. A. Baumgarten, Hamlin Wu, Tong Jiang, and Joonho Lee present a variational theory that avoids supercells entirely. Their wavefunction projects a classic trial form onto definite momentum, keeping translation symmetry exact.

A low-rank factorization of the electron-phonon coupling keeps the cost near-linear in momentum points. Benchmarks on a model system, lithium fluoride, and two forms of titanium dioxide gave accurate binding energies. The method captures both roaming and self-trapped carriers and measures each polaron's spatial extent.
arxiv-2605-05975:
Sicheng Ma and three co-authors speed up the reconstruction of detailed flow fields from coarse observations. Flow matching and diffusion models can rebuild fine fluid detail, but their step by step sampling is slow. That cost hurts uses with tight time limits, such as ensemble forecasting and live visualization.

The authors distill a flow matching teacher into a compact one step consistency model. At test time, a noised coarse observation starts the generation path, so no retraining of the teacher is needed for each task. On three fluid benchmarks the student matched the teacher on spectrum measures with about half the parameters. It ran about twelve times faster, and beat a one step model trained from scratch.
arxiv-2605-06075:
Huaijin Dong and Long Zhang probe the critical phase of quasiperiodic systems with a new spatial measure. Such systems pass through extended, critical, and localized phases, and critical states have a tangled multifractal structure. Standard entanglement measures blur the spatial detail that sets critical states apart from their neighbors.

Their subsystem information capacity maps information room by position along the chain. In critical states it shows strong spatial unevenness and a stepwise rise with subsystem size, signs of a chain broken into weakly linked subregions. Information trapped in a subregion can echo back and forth with a period set by its length. Tests on other phase types show the measure cleanly separates cases that look alike by simpler diagnostics.
arxiv-2605-06375:
Hao Yu unifies preference based reinforcement learning for language model alignment in a single theoretical family. Mainstream pairwise preference training suffers unstable updates, unclear gradient directions, and high variance, Yu argues, and the paper addresses those flaws in full. The Pair-GRPO family modifies group relative policy optimization to run on binary pairwise preference rewards instead of normalized scalar scores. Its soft variant stays close to the original algorithm's clipped, regularized form.

A gradient match theorem explains the soft variant's stability: its gradient is a positive multiple of the standard one under a first order expansion. The hard variant adds direct local probability constraints and constrained fitting to cut gradient noise and policy drift. Guarantees cover improvement, gradient direction, and variance, and experiments span alignment benchmarks and a continuous control task.
arxiv-2605-06475:
Ranjith Chodavarapu dates historical manuscript pages from their visual script features alone, treating the year as a continuous value with uncertainty. Earlier methods grouped pages into century classes, which wastes precision. His approach uses evidential deep regression, where the network outputs a full predictive distribution in one pass.

An EfficientNet-B2 backbone with a special output head is trained on the DIVA-HisDB benchmark of medieval codices. It reaches a test error of about five years, far finer than the fifty-year labels, and its uncertainty estimates are better calibrated than dropout or ensemble methods. Aggregating to page level lowers error further, and uncertainty predicts where errors will occur.
arxiv-2605-06775:
Luis Gil, Javier López Miras, and Adrián Moreno-Sánchez present SIRENA, software that does the reduction of multi-loop sum-integrals automatically in finite-temperature quantum field theory. The Laporta method uses integration-by-parts rules to shrink huge integral sets to a few master integrals, but thermal sums add a Matsubara structure that zero-temperature tools ignore. Their code in Python and C++ handles that structure throughout.

Tests reproduce known published results up to three loops, and the package gives first-time reductions for chosen three-loop fermionic sum-integrals. The authors also derive a closed factorization formula for any two-loop fermionic sum-integral, building on an earlier bosonic result. The tool targets thermal field theorists facing heavy calculations.
arxiv-2605-06875:
Mukul Lokhande and four co-authors build EULER-ADAS, a neural compute engine for driver-assistance systems using logarithmic posit arithmetic. Posit numbers offer high fidelity at low precision, attractive under the strict power and area limits of vehicle hardware, but their variable-length encoding is costly and fault-prone. The design bounds the regime field, multiplies mantissas logarithmically with adaptive truncation, and shares one accumulation path across three posit precisions.

Prototype results show large cuts in circuit area, delay, and power versus exact posit engines, with much lower energy-delay product than conventional multipliers. A tiny object detection demo runs in tens of milliseconds at a fraction of a watt, and accuracy stays close to full floating point.
arxiv-2605-06975:
Alejandro Escorihuela-Tomàs presents new numerical methods for Hamiltonian systems, the equations behind many problems in physics and orbital motion. Symplectic integrators are favored because they respect the structure of those systems over long runs. His focus is systems whose potential energy is a cubic or quartic polynomial.

Escorihuela-Tomàs shows that such polynomial potentials need fewer conditions than general ones, which allows leaner high-order schemes. The new methods beat both standard compositions of basic steps and existing splitting methods in his comparisons. Numerical results confirm better efficiency, making the schemes attractive for long simulations where accuracy and speed both matter.
arxiv-2605-07175:
Qing Qing and nine co-authors estimate biological age from DNA methylation while respecting how the measured sites relate to each other. Aging clocks read methylation patterns to judge physiological state, but most methods treat each site as an independent feature. Real sites connect through shared patterns, nearby genomic positions, and common genes.

Their RelAge-GNN builds three graphs capturing those relations and fuses them with a learned gate. On large datasets it matched leading accuracy and tracked chronological age strongly, while showing better sensitivity to accelerated aging in disease groups. Breakdowns of which relations and sites matter add biological insight for aging research.
arxiv-2605-07575:
Ke Ma and ten co-authors tackle streaming video understanding, where a video-language model must decide, as frames arrive, whether to speak or stay silent. Existing systems judge the visual evidence only implicitly, without checking it against what a good response would require. Mistimed answers are the predictable result.

Their framework, Response-G1, builds scene graphs from the streaming clips, guided by the user's query, and stores them in memory. It retrieves the most relevant past graphs and uses them to prompt a per-frame silence-or-response decision, all without extra fine-tuning. Grounding both evidence and response conditions in the same graph form made timing decisions more accurate and easier to interpret. On established benchmarks the method led in both proactive and reactive tasks.
arxiv-2605-07775:
Menet and two colleagues tackle a core machine learning tension: balancing the search for new options against the use of known ones. Their framework, POETS, joins uncertainty measurement with policy optimisation for sequential decisions. It rests on the insight that policies trained with a KL penalty, which keeps new behaviour close to old behaviour, implicitly encode a reward function.

Instead of first fitting an uncertainty aware reward model and then a policy, POETS trains a policy ensemble directly on bootstrapped data. To keep ensembling affordable for large language models, the ensemble shares one backbone, with diversity from independent LoRA branches. The authors prove POETS implicitly performs KL regularized Thompson sampling with strong regret bounds. Across science discovery areas such as protein search and quantum circuit design, it leads on sample efficiency. It also improves reinforcement learning paths, proving robust with replayed experience and small datasets.
arxiv-2605-07875:
Vitaliy I. Vasyuchka and four co-authors probe how chiral surface spin waves bounce. Damon-Eshbach waves travel one-way, hugging opposite surfaces depending on direction, and their chirality was predicted to block direct backscattering in thin films where no bulk modes exist. What happens in thick magnetic media, where surface waves overlap a dense spectrum of bulk excitations, was unclear.

In micrometer-thick yttrium iron garnet films, they find the surface wave does reflect from the medium's boundary. It reflects only by exciting localized, thickness-quantized bulk modes that stand at the boundary and absorb energy. Reciprocal backward-volume waves, by contrast, reflect almost elastically. Light scattering, infrared thermography, and models together identify bulk modes as the pathway that reverses these one-way surface waves, setting the limits of such protection.
arxiv-2605-07975:
M. Atzori Corona and seven co-authors mine new high-precision data on coherent elastic neutrino-nucleus scattering, the process where a neutrino bounces off a whole nucleus at once. The COHERENT collaboration's germanium measurements, taken at the Spallation Neutron Source, are precise enough to pin down several fundamental and nuclear parameters at once.

The team extracts updated values for the weak mixing angle and neutrino charge radii. It also measures the neutron root-mean-square radius of germanium nuclei in detail, testing how uncertainties in the quenching factor, modeled in an extended Lindhard framework, affect the extraction. The same data bound neutrino non-standard interactions beyond the Standard Model. A global combination with earlier COHERENT data, reactor experiments, and dark-matter searches maximizes the statistical power.
arxiv-2605-08175:
Archishman Ghosh, Abhinaba Roy, and Dorien Herremans release KARMA-MV, a benchmark for causal questions about music videos. Video question answering has advanced quickly, but asking how visual events shape the music itself, across reasoning, prediction, and what-if questions, remains little tested.

Built from 2,682 YouTube music videos, the dataset holds 37,737 multiple-choice questions generated and validated with language model reasoning instead of manual annotation. The authors also propose a causal knowledge graph that retrieves cross-modal dependencies to support vision-language models. Grounding answers in that graph improved results across the tested models, with the largest gains for smaller ones.
arxiv-2605-08275:
Ray Sheombarsing, Max van Riel, David Heesterbeek, Nico van den Berg, and coauthors reconstruct dynamic MRI scans from far fewer measurements than usual. Standard methods store images and coil sensitivities as discrete grids, which eats memory and hides structure that could guide reconstruction, a real problem for beating-heart scans.

Their framework represents both magnetization and coil sensitivities as continuous differentiable functions, built from tensor products of small one-dimensional neural fields. That structure keeps memory low and scales to three-dimensional, time-varying data. The method beat leading model-based reconstructions in two and three dimensions, preserving anatomy and motion even at an acceleration factor of sixteen.
arxiv-2605-08575:
Jongseok Park, Sunga Kim, Zhenyu Gu, Ion Stoica, and Alvin Cheung find unused sparsity hiding inside the experts of mixture of experts language models. These models save computing by waking only a few experts per token, but splitting experts finer has stalled due to training trouble. Inside each expert, most neurons stay silent for a given input, a pattern the team measures across eight released models.

Up to ninety percent of inner neurons can be skipped with little quality loss, needing no retraining at all. Extending a popular serving engine to skip silent neurons speeds expert layers greatly and whole runs noticeably. Serving large sparse models gets cheaper from capacity that was there all along.
arxiv-2605-08675:
Thien Ngoc Tran and Lan Nguyen Tran cut the quantum cost of working out how a molecule acts. A first step on a normal computer folds the effect of outer electron paths into a one body term. That term keeps the same form as the bare one. So the quantum part needs no extra circuits. A sampling step then solves the folded form. In this work the sampling ran on a simulator, not real quantum hardware.

Tests used a chain, ring, and grid of hydrogen atoms. Tests also used the nitrogen molecule. At the same active size, the folded form beat the plain form each time. The trick is simple to add. It should stretch to solids as well.
arxiv-2605-08775:
Hubing Xiao and nine coauthors model the full glow of one hundred three blazars. Blazars may send out high energy neutrinos. What makes those neutrinos is still not settled. The team works in a proton led frame, a step past their past study. They take the high energy glow to come from proton and light hits. Glow from electrons is set low. This gives the most neutrinos the frame can yield. Nine key traits are fit for each source.

Proton glow peaks in the MeV band for near all sources. That band is the key test of which frame is right. A few sources may be seen by IceCube. More may be seen by planned detectors. The work gives clear tests for joint light and neutrino work.
arxiv-2605-08975:
Yunseong Jeon and six coauthors cut the wait in Alpamayo 1, a car plan that thinks out loud. The plan states its grounds in words as it draws future paths. Such plans tend to draw more than one path. Some think once per path, which wastes work. Some share one think pass, which was thought to cost range. The team reworks the plan round a shared think pass. It also cuts waste in the spread based path maker.

Tests in closed and open loop work back the change. Shared think work keeps path range near whole. Less copying and leaner core work cut the wait by near sixty nine percent. Score stays firm. Cars that think out loud gain speed with no loss of grounds.
arxiv-2605-09275:
Lyu and team build DiffATS, a setup training diffusion models on aligned tensor primitives, without pretrained autoencoders. Direct diffusion modelling of high resolution fields is costly, and compact primitives tackle this by packing high dimensional data tightly. Their build starts from Tucker decomposition, with low rank multilinear form via a core tensor and mode wise factors, but Tucker factors are non-unique: one tensor admits other rotated factors, blocking generation.

Orthogonal Procrustes match fixes it: medoid anchors from the data align factors, fixing gauge freedom, yielding compact, data aware matrix and tensor primitives decoded by direct multilinear reconstruction. The team proves the primitive maps give homeomorphisms between low rank tensors and matching primitive spaces, proving faithful forms. On images, videos, and PDE cases, DiffATS gets strong results with and without guidance while shrinking raw data 3 point 9 to 210 fold, with no trained autoencoders.
arxiv-2605-10075:
Liu and three colleagues cut the cost of evaluating large language models, a recurring bill from pre-training through deployment, as expert labelling grows expensive. Active testing estimates a full evaluation from a small, well-chosen subset, but existing methods target classification and break on generative tasks. Their new algorithm is built for generative evaluation from the start.

It uses semantic entropy from surrogate models to split the evaluation pool into strata. It then applies approximate Neyman allocation, a sampling rule that spends budget where variance is highest, guided by surrogate signals. Across language and multimodal benchmarks and many surrogate-target pairs, the method beats baselines and tracks the oracle Neyman allocation closely. It delivers up to twenty-eight percent lower mean squared error than uniform sampling, with average budget savings near twenty-three percent.
arxiv-2605-10775:
Romain Petit, Clarice Poon, and Gabriel Peyré study why gradient descent, the workhorse trainer of neural networks, so often lands on the best possible fit despite a bumpy loss landscape. They focus on wide, shallow networks with bounded activation functions, a class that covers multi-head attention layers and two-layer sigmoid nets.

Building on earlier work, they prove that every non-global minimum is unstable under gradient descent. Training can therefore only settle on global minima when starting weights spread widely and the network is wide enough. They also finish a missing proof step about escaping sets and show the mean-field training dynamics stay well behaved. Theorists get a wider guarantee for a puzzling, widely observed success.
arxiv-2605-10875:
Yash Akhauri and Mohamed S. Abdelfattah argue that language models waste compute by spending the same effort on every token, easy or hard. Their Self-Optimizing Language Models pair a frozen base model with a small policy network that reads hidden states and picks an efficiency move at each decoding step.

Each move can thin attention, prune activations in the feed-forward layers, or lower quantization precision, all without touching base weights. The policy trains by comparing counterfactual compute schedules for the same token path, balancing quality against a target budget. Across models and budgets, the method beats static compression. Inference engineers get per-token thrift that follows difficulty instead of fighting it.
arxiv-2605-10975:
MD Sazzad Hossen and Avimanyu Sahoo introduce a hierarchical multi-scale graph network for heterophilous learning, where linked nodes often carry different labels. Existing spectral graph networks for such graphs suffer hub-dominated aggregation and oversmoothing, as weak polynomial filters blur distant signals.

Their Hierarchical Multi-view HAAR framework learns heterophily-aware signed affinities, builds a soft graph hierarchy from those embeddings, and applies learnable spectral filters through sparse, orthonormal, locality-aware Haar bases at each level. Skip-connection unpooling then recombines all levels into the original graph, curbing hub domination and long-range bottlenecks. Tests show gains up to about three percent over leading spectral baselines, in near-linear time. Graph-learning teams get a scalable cure for heterophily's twin ailments.
arxiv-2605-11075:
Romy Rodríguez Martínez and six colleagues deliver a uniform star catalog of 625 F, G, and K stars hosting 859 confirmed exoplanets, from high-resolution TRES spectra. Using the neural-network spectral code uberMS, which joins spectra with broadband light data, the team measures temperatures, gravities, radii, brightness, spin speeds, iron shares, and alpha enrichments.

One catalog measured one way lets researchers compare planet hosts fairly, including links between stellar alpha levels and exoplanet traits. Combining metal measures with galactic motion data identifies 58 hosts as likely thick-disk members, and giant-planet hosts show distinct chemical patterns. Exoplanet researchers get a uniform foundation for studying how stellar chemistry shapes planetary systems.
arxiv-2605-11275:
Oleh Savchuk and three co-authors present a freeze-out model of light nuclei formation in heavy-ion collision transport. Cluster production matters in heavy-ion collisions at intermediate beam energies, where light nuclei add a lot to final-state yields and to observables used to infer the nuclear equation of state.

Their approach blends dynamical transport with thermal cluster making. At freeze-out, the resulting hybrid coarse-graining model lines up nucleon and light-cluster descriptions for mid-rapidity particles, with uneven heat and collective transport in hot, strongly interacting systems. Yields at 4 femtometer impact parameter, spectra, and elliptic flows at 7.4 fm for 20 to 30 percent centrality are predicted there for semi-peripheral gold-gold events at 1.23 A GeV incident energy. Nuclear physicists get a hybrid model that keeps fragile clusters consistent with transport dynamics.
arxiv-2605-11375: Hasanat and three colleagues present TuniQ, a reinforcement-learning system that autotunes quantum compilation passes at scale. Quantum circuits compiled for hardware decide both output fidelity and runtime, yet current compilers use a fixed pass sequence despite optimal choices varying with circuit, hardware and noise. TuniQ picks passes at each pipeline stage, using a two-part encoder giving stage-aware shaped rewards for credit across stages and dynamic action masking. It beats the IBM Qiskit transpiler on fidelity and time across IBM Quantum Cloud processors.
arxiv-2605-11475: Qu and three colleagues propose a deep probabilistic unfolding model for quantized compressive sensing. Old unfolding methods project measurements with a simple squared-error step. The team instead derives a closed-form, stable likelihood gradient projection. This respects true quantization physics, turning a hard constraint into soft probabilistic guidance. A dual-domain Mamba module fuses local and global features at many scales, linking distant but correlated regions. Tests show state-of-the-art accuracy and efficiency, aiding real-life use of quantized sensing.
arxiv-2605-12075: Shaina Raza's 2026 position paper argues deepfake defense has aimed at the wrong threat for nearly a decade. Research organized around 2017-2019 face-swap and talking-head tricks aimed at public figures, fearing large-scale misinformation and video-evidence fraud. Yet an accounting of 2022-2026 incidents shows dominant harms are peer-made non-consensual intimate imagery, voice-clone scam calls, and emotional-manipulation fraud. The predicted public-figure catastrophe never arrived in 2024, and Raza urges rebalancing research toward the harm categories actually growing.
arxiv-2605-12375: Beddows, Durrant and Leontidis correct farm yield forecasts after the fact, using the sparse records real farms actually keep. Their agent framework encodes farming knowledge in tools that spot phases, correct bias and check ranges, then revises existing model outputs. On strawberry data it cut one error measure by a fifth and another by over half for an XGBoost base model, with gains for other bases too. A Llama 3.1 8B agent gave the strongest corrections, while a vision-language agent proved uneven.
arxiv-2605-12775: Ma and Meng study indefinite stochastic linear-quadratic control for jump-diffusion systems. They build an inverse flow from the base system with zero control and prove its kernel satisfies a stochastic Riccati equation with jumps. Under uniform convexity, open-loop optimal controls exist and are unique for any initial pair, with a feedback form via that equation. Their approach needs neither relaxation nor extra invertibility assumptions, and allows jump-part control. A portfolio case reduces convexity to an inequality among risk aversion, volatility, jump size and rate.
arxiv-2605-13075: Beyers, Ziki and van der Merwe scale few-shot spoken word classification to 1,000 classes with only five examples per class. Their Generative Meta-Continual Learning algorithm learns the classes sequentially and stays exceptionally stable. It does not always beat a repeatedly fully fine-tuned HuBERT model or a frozen HuBERT model with a retrained classifier head. But it matches the latter while adapting 2,000 times faster, having seen less than half the data for far less training time.
arxiv-2605-13275: Samuel and colleagues present ReproScore, a two tier check for whether research software still runs. Most tools treat a complete repository as proof of success, mixing readiness with outcome. ReproScore scores readiness from 26 submeasures across five groups, then probes real execution where a sandbox exists. On 423 GitHub repositories, environment signals best separate failure modes, yet readiness alone barely predicts success.
arxiv-2605-13475: Huan Wang and eight colleagues present FedHPro, federated hyper-prototype learning via gradient matching. It trains across clients while guarding privacy, and prototype variants share global anchors. Current methods update global anchors by averaging or tuning, causing semantic drift and a misaligned global signal. Hyper-prototypes are learnable globals keeping semantic knowledge across clients. Hyper-prototypes are tuned by gradient matching against class traits from clients' real samples. FedHPro boosts separation and uniformity this way, reaching state-of-the-art results on several benchmarks.
arxiv-2605-13675: Florian P. Mahner and five colleagues split the object likeness shape of 162 diverse vision models into a few non-negative axes. They count how often each axis reappears across models, sorting universal from own axes. Universal axes are clearer and more strongly driven by conceptual image properties than own ones. Design, goal, training data, model size and scores do not explain universal axes. Models with more universal axes better predict macaque IT signals and human likeness calls, hinting shared traits reflect brain vision.
arxiv-2605-13875: Chen, Zhu, Yu and Dai treat tuning a language model to many goals at once as a game. In their CAGE setup, each goal acts as a boss that hands out token-level perks to one shared model. The perks push the model to a stable joint policy that mirrors the goals' combined pull. A solver built on nested equilibrium problems finds that policy. The authors claim proof that such a policy exists, is unique, and that the solver converges, stays stable, and learns with no regret.
arxiv-2605-14175: He and five co-authors offer Grounded Continuation, a linear-time runtime verifier for language-model conversations. In long chats, a model may continue from premises the conversation has abandoned, a weakness context-manipulation attacks exploit. An interpreter turns each utterance into one or more of eight epistemic operations. A symbolic engine applies those operations to a dependency map tracking each claim's basis and whether it still stands. Checking groundedness then becomes a map walk, linear in map size with no model call needed.
arxiv-2605-14475: Jiashun Zhu and colleagues propose GeoVista, a planning perception framework for ultra-high-resolution remote sensing. Existing models inspect regions with zooming tools, but single paths can lose context and revisit evidence. GeoVista builds a global plan first, then verifies regions through branch inspection while maintaining an evidence state. The team introduces APE-GRO, a cold-start corpus for Global-Region-Object reasoning. An Observe-Plan-Track mechanism handles observation, inspection and tracking, with GRPO rewards. Experiments on RSHR-Bench, XLRS-Bench and LRS-VQA show top performance.
arxiv-2605-14775: Ojeda and Rosales study numerical semigroups with a fixed quotient. For a numerical semigroup and an integer d of at least two, they describe the fibre of the quotient map. Its elements take a stated form built from finite sets plus d times the base semigroup. Clear computable regions of this fibre are analysed. A family of multiples with prescribed quotient is introduced, with generators, standard invariants, Apery sets, and presentations computed. The construction is shown to preserve Wilf's inequality and control depth.
arxiv-2605-14875: Jin Hao and four colleagues compute two-meson form factors, numbers describing how mesons respond to probes, in scalar, vector, and tensor forms. Working in U(3) resonance chiral theory, they add one-loop meson contributions and tree-level resonance exchanges. Final-state interactions between the mesons then turn these into unitarized form factors. Using parameters from earlier scattering studies, they predict distinct resonance patterns across channels.
arxiv-2605-14975: Ryota Miyazaki and six others use a current-driven Kerr effect, a twist of light by magnetism, to probe Dirac carriers in bismuth-antimony alloys. The signal peaks in pure bismuth, dwarfing transition metals by almost four orders of magnitude, and falls steadily as antimony rises. Its scaling with resistivity and mobility matches model predictions only if Dirac electrons drive the spin current. The result makes the effect a useful marker of spin-current character across metals, semimetals, and semiconductors.
arxiv-2605-15075: Daniele Corradetti revisits integer systems inside the real normed division algebras through finite norm shells and root systems. Separating each order, its units, and its distinguished shells recovers the Gaussian, Eisenstein, Hamilton, Hurwitz, and Coxeter-Dickson cases. Replacing the lattice requirement with a finite root-shell requirement makes the golden integer ring natural for the non-crystallographic H2 and H4 cases. A weak golden octonion order built by doubling the icosian ring carries a 240-element shell and proves self-dual.
arxiv-2605-15275: Daniel R. Piacitelli and eleven others investigate why simulations of dwarf galaxies miss the observed stores of five-times-ionized oxygen in their circumgalactic gas. Weighing two run suites with other codes, they find mock low-mass systems make too little oxygen against their star-formation pasts. In both suites, the ionized oxygen that does appear selects cool, diffuse, mildly metal-rich gas at large radii. Neither the ultraviolet background nor plausible thermal changes close the gap with observations.
arxiv-2605-15575: Zezhong Ding, Jin Li, Xugang Wang, and Xike Xie present GelGT, a transformer for learning over relational databases, where tables link into graphs. Sampling must keep relational structure without pulling in irrelevant nodes, and attention must weigh how recent retained information is. Their method pairs structure-and-meaning-aware sampling with Gaussian attention carrying a learnable time bias, backed by theory on structure preservation and temporal discrimination. On seven real datasets and 21 prediction tasks it beats existing relational graph methods by up to 13.8 percent.
arxiv-2605-15675: Jaeseung Heo and five colleagues add interaction terms to influence functions for group credit. Influence functions gauge how dropping one case shifts a target loss. Group credit is usually the sum of single credits, which misses effects: pairs may repeat or complement each other. The team expands the target to second order, adding a pair term that tracks how two cases line up. On six data-model pairs it tracks retraining better than first-order influence. Used to pick tuning data for Llama, it beats past baselines on most tasks.
arxiv-2605-15875: Jiafeng Liu and seven colleagues spread affine body dynamics over many GPUs and compute nodes. The base method, in the incremental potential contact frame, mimics stiff, near-rigid solids well with strict no-overlap rules. But its global barrier links block scalable runs. Their consensus-based ADMM split lets each node solve its local task in parallel, then a global consensus step aligns shared boundary bodies. Tests show steady convergence, no overlap and fast scaling on large scenes across many nodes.
arxiv-2605-15975: Dillon Z. Chen and three colleagues combine low-level imitation learning for robot manipulation with high-level symbolic planning for long-horizon tasks. Their BISON system pairs a neural policy learned from demonstrations with a symbolic policy built from abstractions of those demonstrations plus inductive generalization. On extended MetaWorld benchmarks it handles longer horizons and more objects than vision-language-action and end-to-end methods, and its high-level policies solve problems with 10,000 objects in under a minute.
arxiv-2605-16175: Golivand and seven colleagues use imitation learning for decision help in pediatric ECMO care, a high-stakes setting with tangled, scarce data. They frame the task as learning action models from seen patient paths, even though the actions themselves are not directly seen. TabPFN, a transformer for tabular data, beat XGBoost and multilayer perceptron baselines on real pediatric ECMO data in every test. It thus offers a strong clinician-behaviour baseline for ECMO decision help.
arxiv-2605-16675: Agarwal, Rajbhar and Tariq J introduce LinAlg-Bench, a diagnostic benchmark that tests ten frontier language models on structured linear-algebra computation at 3x3, 4x4, and 5x5 scales. Across 660 certified problems and 6,600 outputs, a forensic pipeline sorts 1,156 failures into ten error tags. Below 4x4, models fail through sign slips, arithmetic drift, and parity errors. Above that threshold, failure turns to abandonment, with models inventing answers through roleplay and structured confabulation instead of computing.
arxiv-2605-16775: Makawana and colleagues present VolTA-3D, a self-taught 3D Vision Transformer system for brain MRI that learns shared volume features. Most 3D brain models focus on one task, limiting transfer across datasets, protocols, and downstream uses. VolTA-3D jointly aligns global class-style tokens and local patch tokens in a student-teacher setup and adds fine-grained shape rebuild. On out-of-distribution tasks including memory-region mapping and sorting of sex and memory loss versus healthy controls, it beats fresh baselines and shows stronger transfer under domain shift.
arxiv-2605-16875: Avetisyan's team motivates stochastic optimisation from statistics and learning, where the aim is to maximise likelihood or cut population risk. The short paper sketches two main routes to expectation minimisation: offline methods based on Monte Carlo sampling and sample-average approximation, and online stochastic approximation. It frames both routes as plain ways to solve the same class of expectation problems, giving a compact map of the field's two standard approaches for new readers.
arxiv-2605-16975: Tang's team extends pretrained 10-second ECG foundation models to longer, variable-length heart recordings without retraining the backbone. Ten-second models transfer well across clinical uses but have no built-in way to combine information across time, and longer recordings raise structural and semantic problems. Guided by a frozen 10-second model, their light plug-in module adds compatible long-sequence processing and semantically informed temporal modelling. Tests across long-horizon tasks, data sets, and backbones beat sliding-window and pooling baselines with strong parameter efficiency.
arxiv-2605-17075: Shaikh, Bastian and Shah introduce an autonomous red-teaming framework pairing large language models with reinforcement learning to attack AI-enabled security orchestration systems. A hierarchical design joins an LLM planner for strategy with a reinforcement-learning controller for tactics, shaped by rewards tied to kill-chain progression. In a high-fidelity enterprise simulation, the hybrid sustains multi-stage campaigns, while standalone LLM agents fail to sustain them and domain-specific models reach only limited compromise. The results argue hybrid LLM-RL approaches are necessary for red teaming.
arxiv-2605-17175: De Domenico, Greco and Palmigiano extend display calculi, a uniform proof framework from Belnap, to cover axiomatic extensions whose axioms are inductive but not analytic inductive. That class covers and goes past all Sahlqvist axioms, and the new frame captures the whole acyclic part of the substructural hierarchy for any signature. Unified correspondence plus the ALBA algorithm then yields analytic rules for those extensions. The work gives proof theorists one shared tool for a broad sweep of logics.
arxiv-2605-17475: Wang and colleagues present Event-B Agent, a frame that turns natural-language requirements into formal Event-B models through interleaved synthesis and repair. An initial model is built, then iteratively repaired and refined using verification feedback. Refinement eases proof discharge, while repair preserves soundness at each step. The two parts reinforce each other toward correct-by-construction models. Tests across systems of varying complexity beat baselines substantially at reasonable efficiency.
arxiv-2605-17675: Chaitanya Bhave and six colleagues set out rules for using AI coding help in scientific software that must meet strict quality checks, including nuclear-grade standards. Using TMAP8, an open-source code that tracks tritium movement in fusion energy, they show how validation cases with known answers can test AI-written checks openly. Their framework keeps people accountable and demands disclosure and review, rather than banning AI help outright.
arxiv-2605-17775: Jinghui Liu, Sarvesh Soni, and Anthony Nguyen test synthetic clinical notes rephrased by language models at million-note scale. They judge the notes on intrinsic quality, task usefulness, and factual truth, using MIMIC records as source. The synthetic notes keep core clinical facts and coarse task value despite heavy rewording, but fine details needed for ICD coding slip away. Rephrasing chunk by chunk restores much detail, though with less factual precision under partial context. Errors come chiefly from misread clinical context, plus time mix-ups, measurement slips, and invented claims.
arxiv-2605-17875: Huawei Jiang and eight colleagues propose HexagonalWarriorMamba, a framework for spotting several heart conditions at once from 12-lead ECGs. Standard deep models struggle with concurrent conditions and long-range patterns in heart signals. HWMamba treats each 12-lead ECG as a 2D image, not a 1D time series. A hierarchical design with a 2D selective scan mechanism models global context and spatial links. On the PhysioNet Challenge 2021 set, with 26 labels from seven institutions, it beats top methods on five threshold-dependent metrics.
arxiv-2605-17975: Sourav Roy and five colleagues build M-SDT, a framework for dengue transmission, forecasting, and intervention in Ahmedabad. Dengue persists in fast-growing Indian cities, where patchy spread and seasonal swings complicate control. Calibrated on zone-wise case data from 2020 to 2024, the model reveals persistent hotspots and regimes across zones. Forecasts for 2026 to 2028 show endemic spread with moderate year-to-year variation. Analysis points to mosquito biting rate and vector mortality as main drivers, and sustained residual spraying can cut incidence by over 80%, beating fogging.
arxiv-2605-18675: Qisai Liu and five co-authors introduce COOPO, a cyclic method from 2026 that alternates constrained offline training with online fine-tuning. Offline learning suffers distributional shift from static data; online learning demands costly environment interaction. Each cycle anchors the policy to the dataset with KL-regularized updates, then fine-tunes online. Returning to offline training stops forgetting and drift while reusing data fully. On D4RL benchmarks, COOPO cuts online interactions versus leading hybrids and improves final returns, with monotonic gains under standard coverage assumptions.
arxiv-2605-18775: Zhuoping Zhou and nine colleagues present Query-Aware Flow Diffusion, a training-free method for graph-based retrieval. Older graph methods explore fixed neighbourhoods and give no promise about the quality of the retrieved subgraph. Their method weights each graph edge by how well its ends fit the query, steering flow along relevant paths only. The resulting subgraphs carry the first statistical promises for query-aware graph retrieval and beat leading graph methods in tests.
arxiv-2605-19075: Mahesh Bhosale and five colleagues present CRAFT, a system for answering questions across many news videos while grounding every claim in its sources. It selects keyframes per query. It transcribes speech with multilingual fallback. A critic loop checks and repairs claims before merging them, so each fact appears once with all its supporting sources. On the MAGMaR 2026 news benchmark it leads on average, reference recall, and citation quality. It also performs strongly on a converted WikiVideo set of 52 event queries, suggesting the approach generalises.
arxiv-2605-19275: Hanno Hilbig asks whether local open-weight models can replace commercial services for classifying political science texts. Local models avoid per-use charges, keep data on the researcher's own machine, and preserve exact versions for later checks. Across 34 classification tasks, five local models often matched four commercial ones, trailing the best commercial model by only 0.015 F1 on average. Commercial models kept their biggest advantage on intricate tasks with numerous labels, so he urges task-specific validation before scaling up.
arxiv-2605-19375: Key and colleagues report an hour-long microlensing flash toward the Large Magellanic Cloud, caught in a five-night DECam survey. Probability analysis puts the lens five orders of magnitude more likely in the Milky Way halo than among ordinary stars. Bayesian modeling reads the lens, nicknamed Phoebe, as a primordial black hole near three lunar masses, among the fastest and lightest microlensing signals ever seen. Phoebe hints at a population of compact lunar-mass objects tied to dark matter and to early-universe inflation physics.
arxiv-2605-19775: Arif, Maurya, Vazhkudai and Nicolae map why inference for reasoning models, which emit long chains of thought, strains systems differently from ordinary generation. Testing models from eight billion to six hundred seventy-one billion parameters, they find data parallelism throttles early as key-value cache fragments, while tensor parallelism frees stranded memory near the thirty-two-billion crossover. Dense giants stay bound by links and memory bandwidth; sparse mixture-of-experts models instead suffer routing delays. The study offers a decision guide for reasoning-era infrastructure.
arxiv-2605-19975: Xia Jiang and three colleagues improve neural routing policies that build delivery routes one stop at a time. Their multi-node lookahead training teaches the policy to predict several future stops at once, using auxiliary modules that run only during training. The added foresight improves generalisation across problem sizes, distributions and real benchmarks without slowing inference.
arxiv-2605-20075: Dachuan Shi and six co-workers flip the usual reasoning order for language models in CopT. CopT drafts an answer first, then thinks on-policy about its own draft to check it. Continuous embeddings act as contrastive checks at run time, judging whether to trust the draft, and a second estimator controls how much of it stays visible later. On maths, coding and agentic tasks, CopT lifts peak accuracy by up to twenty-three percent and cuts token use by up to fifty-seven percent without extra training.
arxiv-2605-20475: Tom Maciejewski revisits an old hunt for a sixth unitary perfect number. Such a number's unitary divisors sum to twice the number itself, and only five are known. By holding one seed factor explicit and sifting source parts in a bounded graph search, he rules out five impostor kernels. A three-filter certificate does that work, and a stubborn even-number set is bounded to at most 201 members below 40000.
arxiv-2605-20675: Matheus dos Santos Viegas and three colleagues present SmellHunter, a context-aware tool for detecting code smells, design flaws that degrade software quality. Most detectors use static metrics alone and ignore the setting in which flaws arise and get fixed. SmellHunter reads scripts in SmellDSL, a domain language for smell rules, and mixes metrics with context such as team traits and project stage. An event-driven service bus runs validation, interpretation, and storage as separate services.
arxiv-2605-20775: Said Benayadi, Sofiane Bouarroudj, and Hamza El Ouali study the structure of pseudo-Euclidean Novikov superalgebras. Such an algebra is a Novikov algebra with a non-degenerate symmetric bilinear form, where all left multiplication operators are antisymmetric with respect to that form. The linked Lie algebra is then flat. The authors introduce a special subclass called Milnor algebras, proving that any such algebra with non-degenerate two-sided ideal belongs to that class, plus a double extension procedure for these algebras.
arxiv-2605-20875: Seungyeop Han and four colleagues present a Markov-chain method for spare strategy in large satellite constellations under dual resupply channels. Their hybrid design combines an indirect path with a direct path. The indirect path stages backups in parking orbits via big launch for later transfer. The direct path delivers spares to in-plane orbits via small launch vehicles. Failure and replenishment are modeled as a Markov chain, with the indirect channel following a periodic-review reorder policy.
arxiv-2605-21075: Nassim Ait Ali Braham and five colleagues present SpectralEarth-FM, bringing HSI into multimodal Earth observation pretraining. Earth observation foundation models are increasingly trained on multisensor data spanning multi-band imagery, synthetic aperture radar, and derived map layers, but HSI remains rare. Conversely, old HSI models are trained on HSI alone, leaving shared pretraining and merging of HSI with co-located sensors unexplored. Their layered transformer for multi-sensor input joins spectral tokens, sensor-specific nets, and cross-sensor fusion, a neat design.
arxiv-2605-21175: Stefan Hoffelner proves it is consistent that every two disjoint boldface Sigma-one-one subsets of omega-one to the omega-one can be separated by a boldface Delta-one-one set. The forcing starts from L and preserves the continuum hypothesis, and therefore also the identity omega-one to the less-than-omega-one equals omega-one. The result gives a separation principle for boldface projective-like sets at an uncountable cardinal.
arxiv-2605-21375: Poshak Gandhi reviews compact objects with frontline astrometry, the precise tracking of celestial positions and motions now entering the micro-arcsecond era. High-precision astrometry advances knowledge of neutron stars and black holes, from natal kicks to Gaia Data Release 3 results. Evidence points to peculiar velocities tied to mass for accreting binaries and a close likeness between neutron stars and black holes. Future surveys should find kicked supermassive black holes, probing gravity-wave-induced kicks.
arxiv-2605-21475: Yi Huang and co-authors present FROG, a full-resolution graph structure learning method for relational deep learning. Relational data stored in databases are modeled as graphs for graph neural network learning, but the full-resolution principle leads most methods to rely on fixed graph structures. FROG treats structure learning as a learnable table role modeling problem, letting tables serve as nodes and edges in message passing.
arxiv-2605-21575: Krut Patel and co-authors present a first-principles turbulence-driven deflagration-to-detonation mechanism for near-Chandrasekhar white dwarfs. Type Ia supernovae are standardizable cosmic candles, yet progenitors and blast mechanisms remain under study. Previously, all such models invoked an ad hoc guess on blast start, tunable to varied results, while their global 3D simulations use a lab-tested transition step. The work aims to remove a free guess from explosion models. It grounds blast start in lab-tested physics.
arxiv-2605-22075: Varsha Sharma, Prasanta Guha, and Avik Ghose explore whether breath biomarkers can causally influence blood glucose in diabetes. Diabetes burdens global health, and early detection matters for timely intervention. Using causal inference, they estimate the impact of volatile organic compounds such as acetone, isopropanol, isoprene, and ethanol on blood glucose levels, alongside lifestyle variables. They also build a classifier and a risk-based ranking system for people in the gray zone, finding specific compounds show strong causal influence on glucose and models can reliably classify high-risk individuals.
arxiv-2605-22275: Miroszewski tackles support vector machines built from kernels when each kernel value must be gauged from noisy data. Giving each value the same number of measurements wastes effort, since the classifier leans on some values far more than others. He builds a rule that splits the budget by how much each value sways the classifier and how noisy its gauge is. A quantum kernel variant is included. An adaptive plan then focuses effort where it counts most. Tests show it beats uniform sampling and can stop early to save measurements.
arxiv-2605-22475: Hegde rethinks Langlands' construction of the discrete automorphic spectrum. Hegde shows it regularises cuspidal Eisenstein series at distinguished points, tracking both zeros and poles. Unlike single-variable functions, zero and pole sets can meet. Those points behind the spectrum are often of this kind. Zeros, hidden in rank one, star in higher rank, on equal footing with poles. Redoing Langlands' G2 work with zeros tracked cuts it to plain maths. A program rethinks it from scratch, giving zeros and poles equal standing.
arxiv-2605-22575: Klimov and Soker compare the blast remnant RCW 103 with fresh JWST infrared views of the jet shaped nebula PMR 1. Both show bright clumpy sectors shaped like wide slices, joined by a faint narrow pipe, a form jets are known to inflate. The match leads them to credit two close pairs of powerful jets with shaping RCW 103, under the jittering jets blast model. Only faint traces of two of the four expected lobes survive in RCW 103, so deeper X ray views might still catch them.
arxiv-2605-22875: Zhao and four colleagues present Research Math Agents, a system for long research-level proofs that fail less from bad steps than from lost state. A central orchestrator keeps a persistent, typed store of lemmas, issues, literature, and evaluations, and hands each proof step only the context it needs. Tested with expert review and Lean 4 kernel checks, it solved 42.5 percent of a hard challenge set and verified 213 of 300 sampled formal targets.
arxiv-2605-23175: Dang and four coauthors propose SAFESEAL, a keyed watermarking framework that protects private language models from copying via input-output harvest. It preserves names while swapping word terms for context-aware synonyms through keyed contest sampling, keeping meaning and facts intact. A keyed paired detector jointly encodes text and key for provider checks. Theory bounds the utility-finding trade-off, and light models, batching, and parallel runs cut latency. Tests report a 98.2 percent detection rate, high text quality scores, and latency near the fastest baseline.
arxiv-2605-23275: Lifar and four coauthors propose Diffusion Domain Expansion, which extends pre-trained diffusion models to larger objects and more complex controls beyond their original range. The method employs a compact network joining the cleaned outputs of pre-trained diffusion models. They show that the joiner can be simple while stretching to domains larger than those seen during training. They test DDE on long audio track making and guided image making.
arxiv-2605-23575: Benjamini, Shamov, and Weiss pose an open problem on non-colliding freely moving hard disks in the plane, with partial results on both sides. Stated cleanly, velocities must be pairwise distinct and speeds uniformly bounded away from infinity. Positively, they give a bounded, injective, non-colliding velocity assignment for the integer lattice, with speeds also bounded away from zero after a common shift. Negatively, no bounded continuous vector field on the whole plane serves as a universal assignment for point pairs farther than one apart.
arxiv-2605-23675: de Bruin and colleagues study simulation plans for local search on random schedules. Fixed durations miss reality and break schedules under changes, so random durations are better. In local search the objective becomes random, and its mean value often cannot be computed. Simulation estimates it, yet needs many runs per round for a good estimate. The authors compare methods to limit runs, proposing a t-test method. On random parallel machine and electric vehicle schedules, their t-test method cuts runtime, keeping quality, beating rivals in both.
arxiv-2605-23875: Anastassia Makarieva and Andrei Nefiodov treat Earth's atmosphere as a steam engine, generalizing the Clausius-Clapeyron relation to a column where condensation spans many heights. Their account adds lifting work, condensation expansion work and a correction for incomplete condensation, yielding a global steam power near 4.4 watts per square metre. That figure sits close to an independent atmospheric total near 4.3, and the analysis traces the match to rainfall removing vapor and sustaining the surface pressure gradients that drive low level winds.
arxiv-2605-23975: Nguyen and five colleagues fix a habit of audio language models mangling mixed English-Mandarin speech. They name three failure modes: dropping a language, translating instead of transcribing, and inventing words. Using direct preference optimization, they train on pairs where chosen replies keep the mixed-language content and rejected replies mimic the failures. Across three models, the method cut mixed-language error rates by up to 89.6 percent on familiar data and 20.0 percent on new data. It teaches models to preserve language mix rather than translate it.
arxiv-2605-24075: Müller and three co-authors study roton release and vortex birth by objects moving in superfluid helium-4, using a generalized nonlocal Gross-Pitaevskii model. From zero to the pressure where helium freezes, near 25 bar, they tune force settings so the model's excitation spectrum matches the pressure-shifting dispersion curve. On flat planes, disks moving through still helium yield two key speeds, one for roton release and one for quantized vortex birth, each varying with pressure and obstacle size. 3D runs with moving spheres are also noted.
arxiv-2605-24375: Serapio and four co-authors test whether small language models can learn to make game code world models, Python versions of game rules. Methods lean on frontier models plus polish loops, curbing access and scale. The team builds a set of 30 games spanning perfect and hidden info, a checking frame, and a setup mixing fine-tuning with reward learning from proven rewards. With Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, fine-tuning lifts grammar while reward learning improves fit. The setup offers a big path to auto world building from plain language.
arxiv-2605-24675: Bo Li and others close a visual gap in web image translation. Standard encoders favor high-level meaning over fine detail for varied character shapes. Their VaaWIT framework pairs a dual-stream module with a visual-aware adapter. The module blends multilingual semantic and detailed visual features into unified forms. The adapter injects those fused cues into a frozen language model with efficient tuning. Across eight tasks on three benchmarks it beats leading open baselines and rivals proprietary models, showing fine-grained visual perception pays off for complex web content.
arxiv-2605-25275: Ruchirinkil Marreddy and Chaoyue Liu sharpen convergence guarantees for wide neural networks trained in the neural tangent kernel regime. Classical bounds lean on the smallest kernel eigenvalue, which is usually tiny. That makes them far gloomier than real training. The pair shows that label and residual projections onto kernel eigenvectors scale with their eigenvalues, a pattern they call label-NTK and residual-NTK alignment. Exploiting that alignment yields a bound following the full spectrum and matching practice closely, plus stronger generalization bounds and tests on multilayer perceptrons and convolutional networks.
arxiv-2605-25475: Xintong Yang and eight colleagues make long-context language-model inference cheaper by learning which key-value entries to keep. Standard attention grows its key-value cache in line with sequence length, quickly becoming the bottleneck. Their learnable indexer predicts token value for eviction. A lightweight latent memory module compresses evicted tokens into a compact online state with residual readouts. The combination holds accuracy under a bounded cache, improving RULER scores by up to 25 points under aggressive eviction and fixing needle-in-a-haystack retrieval.
arxiv-2605-25675: Haider and colleagues ask whether density swings in heavy-ion collisions carry the fractal sign expected near the QCD phase transition. In intermittency, scaled moments of the density grow as a power law when bins shrink. They study charged particles at midrapidity from PYTHIA8 and EPOS4 runs of lead-lead collisions at 5.02 TeV, tracking scaling across phase-space splits. The scaling exponents and fractal measures from both models show no critical fluctuations and no multifractal behavior.
arxiv-2605-26075: Sheokand and eight colleagues grow thin films of alpha-MnTe, a top altermagnet pick, by molecular beam epitaxy on gallium arsenide. Altermagnets split electron spins, but clean growth on useful bases has proved hard. MnTe stands out for its layered build and high Néel point, where magnetic order sets in. Raman tests show vibration peaks near 121 and 140 inverse centimetres. With first-principles phonon maths, those peaks match the Raman-active modes of the hexagonal NiAs-type lattice.
arxiv-2605-26175: Li and eight colleagues recast activation changes as quantiser-facing distribution design for low-bit quantisation. Low-bit quantisation slows fast deployment, and the trouble is not only outliers. They often mismatch low-bit uniform quantisers. Current post-training methods suppress peaks, balance channels or cut error, yet rarely specify an easy-to-quantise target. They can look smoother yet suffer large error, with wide ranges or values collapsed near the mean. The authors analyse error from an information view, designing transforms that shape activations into friendlier shapes.
arxiv-2605-26775: Grinberg proves a general recursion rule for Macdonald's 7th variation Schur polynomials, first guessed by Macdonald. The rule sums versions formed by quotienting out each line in the set, over a finite field, mimicking straight and skew Schur polynomials through powers of the Frobenius map. The proof extends the guess to a broader setting and settles it.
arxiv-2605-26875: Willame and three colleagues present G-iMUSIC, two greedy iterative algorithms for estimating the directions of several signal sources with an antenna array. Greedy methods stumble on early selection errors for close targets, while subspace methods degrade under strong signal correlation. The new methods link the two approaches, need only one initial eigendecomposition, and admit fast Fourier implementations for uniform linear arrays. Simulations show better detection and precision than OMP, OLS, and MUSIC, with less compute time.
arxiv-2605-26975: Pasadakis and three co-authors build nonlinear multi-way spectral clustering in the p-norm using a new C++ GraphBLAS interface. Estimating several nonlinear eigenvectors is costly, but their direct algorithm puts key steps in linear algebra over sparse matrices and dense vectors. Tests on toy cases show high-quality clusters by the balanced cut metric, and strong scaling holds up to 8 million nodes and 48 million edges.
arxiv-2605-27275: Daisuke Suzuki and Tomohiro Sasamoto apply Macroscopic Fluctuation Theory to currents that have not yet settled to a steady state. They study diffusive systems in one dimension, driven at the edges and fed by reservoirs at both ends. They work out the current variance exactly for a fixed diffusion rate with any mobility, plus the full generating function for reflective Brownian motion.
arxiv-2605-27575: Nikita Benkovich and Vitalii Valkov present Agyn, an open-source platform for running AI agents at scale with isolation and governance. Its signal-driven stateful serverless runtime runs on Kubernetes, agents are defined as code through a Terraform provider, and access follows zero-trust least-privilege rules. The platform stays agnostic to agent, model, and cloud.
arxiv-2605-27775: Maxim Sirotin asks what quantum strategy best measures deviations from Standard Model weak-charge scaling across an isotope chain. The optimum is a cross-isotope cat state plan, set against the standard quantum limit, squeezed arrays, same-isotope cats, and decoherence-free subspace plans. Entanglement strongly speeds statistical averaging, but final precision is set by systematic floors needing careful study.
arxiv-2605-27875: The CMS Collaboration searches proton-collision data for new light scalar particles born in Higgs boson decays. Looking for events with two muons plus two hadrons, the team probed masses between roughly half and two giga-electronvolts and decay lengths up to a hundred millimeters. No discovery is claimed; instead the analysis sets tight upper limits on how often the Higgs decays this way.
arxiv-2605-28075: Vandergrift and colleagues learn measure-to-measure maps that carry a whole crowd from one shape to another, not one sample at a time. Each full distribution counts as a single data point, and transformers serve as fixed maps or as moving velocity fields. Trials on fake systems, particle swarms, and a bowel-cancer organoid set show the maps reach new distributions they never saw.
arxiv-2605-28175: Wang and colleagues ground recommender language models in knowledge graphs without drowning simple queries or starving complex ones. MixRAGRec routes each query to a retrieval expert at the right granularity, translates graph knowledge into natural language, and recommends with contrastive feedback. Trained jointly under one multi-agent objective, the system proved effective on real-world datasets.
arxiv-2605-28475: René Hiemstra, Torsten Keßler, and Michael Abdelmalik shrink the 8D weak form of the Boltzmann collision operator to a 5D core. Turning the lab frame to the colliding pair and summing over all turns gives a Wigner-Eckart factorization in a spectral Galerkin setting. Angle geometry, carried by Clebsch-Gordan coefficients, is found exactly, while scattering physics reaches the machine limit by convergent quadrature.
