The team searched five databases through May 2014 and kept 16 randomized trials with 759 children and teens, checking each for bias with a standard tool.

Judged by raters close to the training, usually unblinded, training improved total and inattentive symptoms modestly. Judged by likely blinded raters, those gains shrank a lot, and hyperactivity scores showed no clear gain. Lab tests of verbal and visual working memory did improve, as did parent ratings of executive function. The split verdict warns that who rates the outcome shapes the answer.
europmc-pmc4468575:
Louise Robinson, Eugene Tang, and John-Paul Taylor reviewed timely dementia diagnosis in The BMJ in 2015. Dementia, a syndrome of failing memory, language, and behavior that erodes daily life, is a growing global problem as populations age. Alzheimer's disease is its most common form. With no cure, attention has shifted to lowering risk, spotting the illness early, and acting sooner.

Family doctors and specialists share the diagnostic work, the authors explain, and must separate dementia from normal aging, depression, and other mimics. Cost-effective drugs, the cholinesterase inhibitors, and non-drug help such as cognitive stimulation therapy can slow decline and improve quality of life. Information and practical support matter as much. Care wishes should be discussed early, while the person can still decide, and family carers, themselves at high risk of illness, need equal support.
europmc-pmc4516275:
Andrew F. Read leads a ten-author team testing a hard question about vaccines, in PLoS Biology in 2015. Some vaccines stop illness but not infection, so germs can still spread from a protected host. Theory says such leaky protection could let deadlier strains survive, since host death no longer cuts their spread short.

The team worked with Marek's disease virus in chickens. Birds given the vaccine, or hatched from vaccinated hens, lived longer while infected, yet still caught, grew, and passed on the virus. That longer window let very hot strains, too lethal to persist on their own, keep spreading. The authors warn that anti-disease vaccines which allow transmission can favor strains that hit unvaccinated hosts harder.
europmc-pmc4526175:
Greet Hermans and Greet Van den Berghe review muscle weakness picked up in intensive care, in Critical Care in 2015. Many patients admitted with grave illness, major surgery, trauma, or burns grow weak during the stay itself, from nerve damage, muscle disease, or both. The weakness tends to be even on both sides, hits the limbs near the trunk and the breathing muscles hardest, and often spares the face.

Risk runs higher with severe illness at admission, sepsis, failure of several organs, long immobility, and high blood sugar; age adds risk too. Inside the body, faults in blood flow, electrical signaling, and energy use combine to waste muscle. Diagnosis relies on bedside strength testing in awake patients, scored on a standard sum scale.
europmc-pmc4591975:
Paul R. Torgerson and nine colleagues published a 2015 global burden study of leptospirosis, a bacterial disease spread from animals to people. It often hits poor rural farmers and city slum residents hardest. No world estimate in disability adjusted life years, or DALYs, had existed before. The work appeared in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases.

The group built DALYs from years of life lost and years lived with disability, using earlier case and death counts. They estimate about 2.90 million DALYs lost each year, with men carrying roughly four fifths of the total. Tropical parts of Asia, the Pacific, the Americas, and Africa show the highest burden, and the authors note the disease may often be missed or blamed on malaria in Africa.
europmc-pmc4621875:
Kyu Y. Le and Michael Otto published a 2015 overview of quorum sensing in staphylococci, bacteria that live on human skin and can cause serious infections. These bacteria sense their own density and adjust gene activity through a system called Agr. The overview appeared in Frontiers in Microbiology.

When cell density is high, Agr switches on many toxins and tissue-chewing enzymes and switches off surface factors used for settling. That timing suits short, aggressive infections. Low Agr activity instead fits long-lasting infections with biofilms. Because the switch shapes disease so strongly, drugs that block Agr are being tested as a way to blunt acute Staphylococcus aureus infections without relying only on antibiotics.
europmc-pmc4667975:
Pradeep A. Ravindranath and colleagues presented a 2015 program called AutoDockFR, which fits drug-like molecules into proteins that can flex. Docking works best when the target can shift shape, but letting side chains move swells the search space and invites false hits. The new engine builds on the AutoDock4 scoring rules.

A fresh search method and a score tuned for flexible targets meet both problems. In cross-docking tests, where drugs were fit into empty target shapes that must rearrange to hold them, the program solved far more cases than AutoDock Vina. It won on both a varied target set and a set built on one kinase with many known drugs. The gains count for drug design that starts from protein shape.
europmc-pmc4700275:
Keiichiro Minatohara, Mika Akiyoshi, and Hiroyuki Okuno reviewed immediate-early genes and memory in Frontiers in Molecular Neuroscience in 2015. When neurons fire during learning, a set of genes switches on within minutes. Three of them, egr-1, c-fos, and Arc, light up in the exact cell groups tied to forming long-term memories. Because of that timing, their activity has long served as a marker for cells engaged in memory.

New light- and drug-based tools let researchers switch those marked cells off or on and watch recall change. Such tests suggest the marked ensembles really do hold the memory trace. The review then turns to Arc's working role, how it reshapes connections between neurons for specific inputs. Questions remain about the full mechanism. Still, the field now has a concrete handle: follow the early genes, and you follow the cells that store the lesson.
europmc-pmc4700675:
Diana M. Mitrea and Richard W. Kriwacki explained phase separation inside cells in Cell Communication and Signaling in 2016. Cells organize their contents partly in membrane-wrapped compartments, but some structures have no membrane at all. These droplets form when proteins and RNA molecules, linked by many weak contacts, condense out of the surrounding fluid, much like oil beading in water. They gather and dissolve quickly and react fast to stress signals.

Many of these membrane-less organelles handle RNA processing. The review sets out their known jobs, the shared rules that govern how they assemble and fall apart, and the tools used to study their structure. Because the droplets exchange contents with the cell constantly, their makeup mirrors the cell's state. The authors present phase separation as a basic organizing principle of the cell, one that biology had long overlooked. Its failure modes may matter in disease.
europmc-pmc4702775:
Janna Hastings, Gareth Owen, Adriano Dekker, and seven colleagues reported updates to the ChEBI chemical database in Nucleic Acids Research in 2016. ChEBI catalogs chemicals of biological interest, classing each in an ontology with structure drawings, synonyms, and links to other databases. By this update it held over forty-six thousand entries, all free online. The team's recent work centered on the small molecules organisms make themselves.

Collections of such metabolites grew for humans, mice, a gut bacterium, and yeast. The website was rebuilt with modern components and now updates live instead of monthly. A new software library opens the data to Java, Python, and Matlab programs. Two added tools help users analyze enrichment in chemical sets and query the ontology itself. The update keeps a core reference of chemistry usable for both bench scientists and software.
europmc-pmc4709475:
Ramon Yarza, Silvia Vela, Maite Solas, and Maria J. Ramirez made the case for targeting JNK signaling in Alzheimer's disease, in Frontiers in Pharmacology in 2015. JNKs are kinases, enzymes that relay stress alarm signals inside cells. Alzheimer's brains show an active JNK pathway. Lab studies tie it to making more amyloid beta, the peptide that clumps in the disease, and to building its tau tangles.

One family member, JNK3, sits mostly in the brain, which makes it an attractive drug target with fewer side effects elsewhere. Blocking JNK signals is already being screened for diabetes, cancer, and liver disease. The review gathers the lab and animal evidence linking JNK to Alzheimer's damage, then lays out the logic of JNK3 blockers as treatment. It is a rationale paper: the target is named, and the proof so far is weighed openly.
europmc-pmc4766375:
Adrian Olmos-Alonso heads a nine-author team in Brain in 2016 testing a drug target in Alzheimer's disease. Brain tissue in Alzheimer's teems with microglia, the brain's immune cells, grown in number and switched on. A receptor called CSF1R drives their growth, and the team found its pathway overactive in patient tissue, in step with the extra cells.

Blocking that receptor in mice bred for Alzheimer-like disease froze the growth and firing of microglia. The disease course then slowed. The result marks microglia growth itself, not just the sticky plaques the field long chased, as a driver worth drugging. The authors frame receptor blockade as a route to change the disease rather than ease symptoms alone.
europmc-pmc4792175:
Mark D. Wilkinson leads a large author group in Scientific Data in 2016 setting out the FAIR principles for research data. Vast sums fund studies whose data then sit in forms no one, and no machine, can find or reuse. Funders, publishers, scholars, and industry joined to write a short, testable rule set for data care.

FAIR stands for findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable. Each word unpacks into concrete duties: rich labels, lasting identifiers, standard formats, and clear reuse terms. The stress falls on machines, which must be able to locate and combine data on their own as collections grow past human scale. The paper gives the reasoning and shows early adopters at work. It has since become the common yardstick for data policy.
europmc-pmc4794275:
Carly Bess Williams, Elizabeth S. Yeh, and Adam C. Soloff review the macrophages that serve breast tumors, in NPJ Breast Cancer in 2016. Macrophages are the body's eater cells, built to kill threats and mend tissue. In breast tumors they are the most common immune cell present, and the tumor bends their repair program to its own ends.

Turned macrophages help the tumor at every stage. They feed new blood vessels, soften tissue for invasion, hide the tumor from immune attack, and nurse the stem-like cells that seed regrowth. The review traces how tumor signals recruit and reprogram them. It closes with the counter-move: mouse studies and early patient trials of drugs that block, drain, or re-educate these cells, which the authors rate a promising new front in breast cancer care.
europmc-pmc4802575:
Rosa Lau leads a twelve-author team in Implementation Science in 2016 asking why proven care so often fails to reach the clinic in primary care. Their study is a review of reviews: seventy existing reviews on putting complex changes into practice, from guideline use to new staff roles and new technology.

None of the reviews spoke of causes outright; all spoke of barriers and helpers. The team sorted them into four levels: the world outside, the organization, the professional, and the change itself. Policy, pay structures, and tools press from outside; culture, staffing, and fit with routine press inside. A clinician's role and habits matter, as do a change's proof, ease, and flexibility. The fit between change and setting, the authors argue, decides success.
europmc-pmc4827875:
Ibrahim Zaganjor leads ten authors in PLoS ONE in 2016 mapping neural tube defects worldwide. These birth defects of brain and spine can often be prevented with folic acid, yet no full count of their global burden existed. The team searched literature, registries, and reports from 1990 to 2014, keeping sources covering over five thousand births.

Data came from just 75 of the world's countries, and 120 of 194 member states had none at all. Rates swung widely within every region, from under one to nearly two hundred per ten thousand births in the widest range. Registry coverage rose steeply with national income, reaching nine in ten rich countries and none of the poorest. The authors call for stronger counting where the need is greatest.
europmc-pmc4875775:
Robert L. Perlman, writing solo, weighed mouse models of human disease from an evolution view in 2016. Mice serve as stand-ins for people thanks to shared genes and body plans. Yet each species adapted to its own world, so their bodies differ in deep ways despite kinship. Mice often answer lab treatments unlike humans.

For processes kept across rodent and primate lines, mice teach much, Perlman argues. For disease itself, the gene-to-illness networks may differ, so mouse results can mislead. The essay urges researchers to weigh evolved gaps beside shared traits when picking models. Knowing what a mouse cannot tell is part of using mice well.
europmc-pmc4896975:
Alice H. Newton, Ana Cardani, and Thomas J. Braciale reviewed the host immune response in lung virus infection in 2016, as a balance between clearing virus and harming the lung. Airway cells and innate defenders start the fight, and adaptive cells finish it. A response that runs too long or too hot scars the very tissue it defends.

Damage shows in varied clinical forms by site and spread. The review walks through each response arm and where each tips from help to harm. Common illness patterns from flu and kin viruses close the account. Care that trims immune damage while keeping virus control is the prize this balance points to.
europmc-pmc4907175:
Florence Mus and co-authors reviewed symbiotic nitrogen fixation in 2016 and the hurdles to extending it beyond legumes. Crops hunger for usable nitrogen, and making fertilizer costs heavily in rich and poor nations alike. Some bacteria turn air nitrogen into ammonia plants can use, but the trait sits only in bacteria and archaea. Legumes house such bacteria in root nodules, trading sugar for nitrogen.

Giving cereals the same deal is a grand challenge: nodule building, oxygen control, and energy supply all must move together. The review maps what the legume partnership requires, piece by piece. Each piece is a design spec for one of farming's oldest dreams, crops that feed themselves nitrogen.
europmc-pmc4918175:
Anna R. Plourde and Evan M. Bloch sum up what was known about Zika virus as of mid February 2016. Their literature review appeared in Emerging Infectious Diseases that year. Zika is a flavivirus first isolated in 1947 from a sick rhesus monkey in the Zika Forest of Uganda. The first three human cases were reported in Nigeria in 1954, and for decades infections stayed rare or in small clusters.

The review traces how that pattern broke. A large outbreak hit Yap in 2007, followed by outbreaks in French Polynesia and other Pacific islands. By early 2016 the virus had reached the Americas, with cases also carried to Europe. The authors gather reports from journals, health agencies, and media. They warn that blood tests can confuse Zika with related viruses such as dengue, so spread may be over or under counted.
europmc-pmc4924075:
Fiona Cocker and Nerida Joss review ways to cut compassion fatigue in care and service workers. Their systematic review appeared in the International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health in 2016. Compassion fatigue joins secondary traumatic stress with burnout, a state of physical and mental exhaustion. Workers who serve traumatized people face the highest risk, and the condition can harm care quality and mental health.

The reviewers found 13 studies that tested an intervention. Ten studied nurses, and three studied community service workers such as social workers. No study targeted emergency service workers. Seven studies reported a clear drop in burnout or secondary traumatic stress after the program. The authors call the evidence base thin. They urge more trials, and more work on changing workplace risk factors, not just helping workers cope.
europmc-pmc4937375:
Bosheng Chen and six co-authors track gut microbes across the whole life of a crop pest moth. Their study appeared in Scientific Reports in 2016. The moth is Spodoptera littoralis, a major farm pest worldwide. Insect gut microbes aid nutrition and behavior, but moth microbes are little studied, above all through metamorphosis. The team sequenced DNA and RNA from guts at each life stage, which separates mere presence from real activity.

Two groups, Proteobacteria and Firmicutes, dominated, and their mix shifted as the host changed form. Enterococcus, Pantoea, and Citrobacter led early larvae, while Clostridia rose later. Only enterococci made it through metamorphosis. Adult females and males ended with distinct gut sets. Gene predictions shifted too, from movement and sugar use in young larvae toward amino acid and vitamin handling in older ones.
europmc-pmc4961475:
The NCD Risk Factor Collaboration charts a century of change in adult human height across two hundred countries. Their study appeared in eLife in 2016. The group reanalysed well over a thousand population studies, with height measures on more than eighteen million people born over a hundred year span. Height tracks nutrition and health in childhood, and taller stature links to longer life and higher earnings.

South Korean women gained the most over the century, about twenty centimeters, followed by Iranian men at about sixteen centimeters. Some sub-Saharan African countries and South Asia barely changed. Dutch men born late in the century were the tallest on average. Guatemalan women born at the century's start were the shortest. The gap between the tallest and shortest populations stayed much the same despite big rank changes among countries.
europmc-pmc4987875:
Jana Trifinopoulos, Lam-Tung Nguyen, Arndt von Haeseler, and Bui Quang Minh present W-IQ-TREE, a web server for building evolutionary trees. Their paper appeared in Nucleic Acids Research in 2016. Phylogenetics infers family trees of species or genes from sequence data. Maximum likelihood methods are accurate but heavy to run. IQ-TREE, the team's desktop software, made that analysis faster. W-IQ-TREE puts it in a browser, free, with no login, running jobs on a dedicated cluster and returning results by link or email.

The server accepts DNA, protein, codon, and other data in common formats. It handles model selection, partition finding, fast tree search, and several branch and topology tests. Ultrafast bootstrapping gives support values without days of computing. The authors pitch the tool at biologists who need publication grade trees without maintaining their own software or hardware.
europmc-pmc4991975:
Rajendra Singh, Manoj Kumar, Anshumali Mittal, and Praveen Kumar Mehta review industrial progress in microbial enzymes. Their review appeared in 3 Biotech in 2016. Microbes have made bread, wine, and vinegar for centuries, long before anyone knew enzymes did the work. Microbial enzymes beat plant and animal ones on stability, activity, and ease of production. Industry use is climbing across food, agriculture, chemicals, and medicine, since enzymes cut processing time and energy and are non-toxic and eco-friendly.

Some microbial enzymes also break down toxic waste compounds from factories and homes. The review covers production methods, optimization, and the state of the world enzyme market. Sectors from detergents and leather to paper and pharmaceuticals get sections. The authors expect demand to keep rising with population growth and resource strain. They present enzymes as a core tool of green industry.
europmc-pmc4996975:
Oscar Venter leads a team updating the global human footprint map across sixteen years. Their study appeared in Nature Communications in 2016. The footprint sums human pressures on land: built areas, crops, pasture, roads, and access into wild places. The team rebuilt the measure at fine resolution for 1993 and 2009 from fresh data on infrastructure, land cover, and human access. They compared how pressure changed while population and economies boomed.

World population grew by about a quarter and the economy more than doubled, yet the footprint grew by only about a tenth. Still, three quarters of land faces measurable pressure. Pressure runs worst, and rises fastest, in many biodiversity rich regions. Wealthy countries with strong control of corruption managed to ease pressure. The authors see room for conservation gains if those patterns spread.
europmc-pmc5127875:
W. J. Heerink, G. H. de Bock, G. J. de Jonge, H. J. M. Groen, R. Vliegenthart, and M. Oudkerk pooled studies of lung biopsy harms in European Radiology, with the hosted text dated 2017. The biopsy, guided by CT scans through the chest wall, samples lung nodules, and the team compared its two needle types.

Across 32 studies of core biopsy covering 8,133 procedures, complications of any kind struck about 39 percent of core biopsies. Across 17 studies of fine needle aspiration covering 4,620 procedures, the rate was about 24 percent. Serious complications stayed low, near 6 and 4 percent. For aspiration, wider needles, smaller nodules, and more lung tissue crossed raised the risk. Minor problems are common, the authors conclude, but major ones are rare for both methods.
europmc-pmc5182075:
Jason R. Taylor and eight co-authors, with the Cam-CAN group, described a data repository in NeuroImage, with the hosted text dated 2017. The Cambridge Centre for Ageing and Neuroscience collected brain and behavior data to chart how cognition and the brain change across adult life and what supports healthy aging of the mind.

The repository holds data from about 700 people aged 18 to 87 drawn from the general population. It includes structural and functional MRI at rest and during tasks, MEG recordings, and test scores across attention, emotion, action, language, and memory, plus background and clinical measures. Both raw and processed forms are shared, making the set a testbed for methods that combine several kinds of brain data at once.
europmc-pmc5206475:
Mallappa Kumara Swamy, Mohd Sayeed Akhtar, and Uma Rani Sinniah review the antimicrobial power of plant essential oils. Medicinal and aromatic plants make these volatile oils in the course of their growth. Their mix of aldehydes, phenolics, terpenes, and other compounds lets them kill a wide range of bacteria, fungi, and viruses. More than 80 percent of people worldwide rely on plant remedies passed down for ages. And over 9,000 plant species have recorded healing uses.

The review explains how the oils attack pathogens, with the chemistry and placement of their active groups deciding their strength. It gathers evidence across many human pathogens, including drug-resistant microbes. The authors aim the survey at researchers hunting for broad-spectrum natural molecules. They present essential oils as a serious source to mine, at a time when resistance is wearing down standard drugs.
europmc-pmc5210575:
Bronwen L. Aken and a large Ensembl team presented Ensembl 2017 in Nucleic Acids Research in 2017. Ensembl is a database and genome browser for vertebrate genomes, built to give researchers one consistent view across species. The project imports, analyzes, and curates large reference data sets that no single study could supply alone.

Its resources cover gene and regulatory region notes backed by evidence, genome variation, and gene trees, with tools and program access that treat every species the same way. The year's work improved resources for gene regulation and comparative genomics and added target sites for CRISPR/Cas9 editing. The browser gained better filtering of variation, new plots for linkage and expression-linked variants, and a search over phenotype and disease terms. All data are free, and the code is open source.
europmc-pmc5319175:
Caroline J. K. Wallace and Roumen Milev reviewed probiotics for depression in Annals of General Psychiatry in 2017. Most mood drugs work by changing brain signal chemicals. In the past decade, work on the gut-brain axis has shown a two-way link between the gut and the brain. Gut microbes shift in some mental illnesses. That link makes live microbe pills a fresh target for mood care.

The pair searched five databases and kept ten human studies. Five tracked mood, seven tracked anxiety, and three tracked thinking. Most studies found gains on the symptom scales they used. But the microbe strains, doses, and course lengths varied a lot from study to study. None of the studies tracked sleep. The authors call the proof strong enough to merit large, strict trials in patients with clinical depression.
europmc-pmc533875:
Alicia O'Cathain and Kate J. Thomas weighed the value of open survey questions in BMC Medical Research Methodology in 2004. Most forms end with a stock prompt: any other comments? Such lines can lift reply rates, enrich closed answers, and surface issues the form missed. Yet much of what people write there is never studied or shown.

The pair argue the fault lies in the odd status of the data. It is strictly neither story-type nor number-type data, so no clear study path exists. Reading it well also takes time and skill. Their fix is to plan ahead. Decide first if the line should yield deep stories from set groups, or countable safety-net data from all. With the aim fixed at the design stage, the data can be used well and fairly, in honor of the people who took time to write.
europmc-pmc5343975:
Jérôme Stirnemann led a team that reviewed Gaucher disease in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences in 2017. The disease is rare and passes down through families. A missing enzyme in cell waste sacs lets a fatty stuff build up inside eater cells. Those stuffed cells crowd the bone marrow, spleen, and liver, which swell. Blood counts fall and bones take harm.

Most patients have type 1, which spares the brain. Types 2 and 3 strike the nerves as well, gravely in type 2 and in mixed ways in type 3. A blood test for the weak enzyme confirms the disease, and gene checks add outlook clues. The same gene flaw also raises the risk of Parkinson's disease, even in carriers. Care centers on replacing the enzyme by drip. The review covers causes, signs, diagnosis, and the full range of treatments.
europmc-pmc5426675:
Kurtzer and co-authors present Singularity, a container system built for science computing. Their software article appeared in PLoS ONE. Researchers need the same software setup on many machines. Supercomputing centers run old, fixed systems. That clash blocks work and harms reproducibility. Virtual machines move whole setups but run slowly. Docker containers are light but fit shared centers poorly. Singularity aims at that gap.

A Singularity container packs a full compute environment into one portable unit. Users design their own environment. They can then copy it and run it elsewhere. The system plugs into the schedulers centers already use. It does so without giving users unsafe control. The authors stress security for shared machines. The project is open source. It drew help from engineers and researchers alike. For labs, it means results can travel with their exact tools attached.
europmc-pmc5431875:
Bhardwaj and co-authors let an enzyme build its own blocker inside its active site. Their research article appeared in Nature Communications. The enzyme is cyclooxygenase-2, or COX-2. It drives inflammation and shows up in several cancers. Its sibling COX-1 does housekeeping work the body needs. The two are so alike that selective drugs are hard to design. Past selective drugs carried heart risks. Some were withdrawn from sale.

The team used a method called in situ click chemistry. They fed the COX-2 active site a pool of building blocks. The enzyme picked the blocks that fit it best. Those blocks linked into a tight-binding inhibitor. Tests showed the enzyme chose wisely. Two new compounds came out of the screen. Both blocked COX-2 strongly and selectively. In living animals they calmed inflammation better than common COX-2 drugs. The approach may suit other hard drug targets.
europmc-pmc5512975:
Buford presents a review in Microbiome on the gut microbiome and aging inflammation. Steady low-grade inflammation is a hallmark of growing old. Its root cause has stayed murky for decades. Gut microbes have lately emerged as a prime suspect. Older adults carry a shifted, less diverse gut community.

That shift tracks with higher levels of inflammatory markers in the blood, he reports. Conditions tied to gut imbalance mirror those tied to aging itself. Heart disease, frailty, and dementia appear on both lists. Fixing the gut community might thus cool age-related inflammation. The review weighs the early evidence and the treatment ideas it suggests.
europmc-pmc5520675:
Grossman and co-authors report a brain stimulation study in Cell. Deep brain stimulation helps many patients but needs implanted wires. Surface methods cannot reach deep spots without firing shallow ones. The team exploits a quirk of neurons: they ignore very fast electric fields. Two fast fields can still interact inside the brain.

Where the fields overlap, a slow beat pattern emerges, they report. Neurons follow that beat rather than the fast fields. In living mice, the beat fired deep hippocampus cells while sparing cortex above. Shifting the currents steered the effect without moving electrodes. The method may one day replace implants for some patients.
europmc-pmc5550275:
McCall and co-authors present a research article in eLife. They study a brain circuit tied to anxiety in mice. Nerve cells in the locus coeruleus send norepinephrine to the basolateral amygdala. The team asks what that single pathway does to behavior.

The researchers traced the circuit and measured chemical release in living mice. Light-based stimulation of the fibers freed norepinephrine in the amygdala. It also changed cell activity there, taught aversion, and raised anxiety-like behavior. Drugs that block beta-adrenergic receptors mediated that anxiety effect. Readers see how one branch of a broad stress system can drive a specific fearful state.
europmc-pmc5651175:
The Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network presents a genomic portrait of oesophageal carcinoma. The research article appeared in Nature. The team studied 164 tumours. Samples came from Western and Eastern populations. Few targeted therapies exist for these cancers. Survival rates remain poor.

Molecular features split the two main tumour types apart. Squamous cell carcinomas resembled squamous cancers elsewhere. They looked less like oesophageal adenocarcinomas. The team found three subclasses within squamous tumours. No role for human papillomavirus appeared. Gene amplifications differed by type. Adenocarcinomas closely matched one gastric cancer variant. The authors argue the two may form one disease. The work gives a base for sharper classification.
europmc-pmc5704175:
Amrutkar and co-authors review resistance to gemcitabine in pancreatic cancer. Their review appeared in Cancers. Pancreatic cancer is often found late. It spreads early and responds poorly to drugs. Gemcitabine remains a core treatment at all stages. Resistance often develops within weeks.

The review explains how the drug works. Uptake and activation steps can fail. Tumour stroma also blocks its effects. New strategies aim to bypass resistance. Chemists are building modified prodrug versions. Others trap the drug in nanoparticles or liposomes. Many beat plain gemcitabine in cells and mice. Clinical use is still at an early stage. The authors map the full resistance pathway.
europmc-pmc5805275:
Sala and co-authors present MUSCLEMOTION, an open tool for heart cell motion. Heart muscle cells beat in cycles of squeeze and release. Labs need one fair way to measure that beat. Uses range from disease studies to drug safety tests.

The tool tracks pixel changes between video frames in ImageJ. It yields measures of displacement and contraction speed. Tests span single cells, cell sheets, organoids, and engineered heart tissue. Results matched three older, narrower methods. Because it needs only standard imaging, nonspecialist labs can use it. Readers get a versatile way to score cardiac contraction.
europmc-pmc5816375:
Forero and co-authors show how to judge rigor in qualitative research. Their case study sits in busy Australian emergency departments. Staff there faced a new government time-target policy. Interviews captured how the change felt on the ground.

The study heard 119 staff across 16 hospitals in 2015 and 2016. The authors test it against four rigor marks. They are credibility, dependability, confirmability, and transferability. Steps like coder agreement and full data saturation support each mark. The framework passed all four tests cleanly. Readers get a worked model for proving quality in emergency care research.
europmc-pmc5824275:
Akinyemiju and the Global Burden of Disease Liver Cancer Collaboration tally liver cancer worldwide. The study spans 195 nations and territories from 1990 to 2015. Liver cancer ranks among the top cancer killers. Hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and alcohol drive most cases.

In 2015 the world saw 854,000 new cases and 810,000 deaths. Burden totaled over 20.5 million lost healthy years. Case counts rose 75 percent since 1990. Aging alone explained 47 percent of that rise, and population growth 35 percent. Detailed splits by cause, age, sex, and nation fill the long report. Readers get the fullest ledger of a deadly cancer's toll.
europmc-pmc5835775:
Melber and Haynes explain the mitochondrial unfolded protein response, a repair alarm run between organelles and nucleus. Their review appeared in Cell Research. When mitochondrial proteins misfold, the cell must answer fast. The response, called UPRmt, switches on survival genes.

In worms, a factor named ATFS-1 senses import health. Working mitochondria pull it in and destroy it. Sick ones cannot, so it travels to the nucleus instead. There it orders chaperones and recovery programs. Mammalian cousins like ATF5 may run the same errand. The authors map the circuit and its ties to other stress pathways.
europmc-pmc5913875:
Wang and co-authors review circulating microRNAs as possible cancer biomarkers. Their review appeared in Clinical Epigenetics. MicroRNAs are tiny non-coding RNAs that enter the blood. They stay stable there and shift in disease. Tumour biopsy and imaging have limits of harm and reach. Blood markers could catch cancer earlier and more gently.

These markers may aid diagnosis and tumour typing, they report. They may also track drug resistance and predict outcomes. Yet problems block routine clinical use so far. Reliability and standard methods still need work. Future studies must prove clear added value. Readers get both the promise and the drawbacks.
europmc-pmc5918775:
Naylor and co-authors review how studies estimate the burden of antimicrobial resistance. Their systematic review appeared in Antimicrobial Resistance and Infection Control. They searched six databases for studies from 2013 to 2015. Of thousands found, 214 studies were included. Most measured harm to patients, fewer measured costs. Many came from single centres.

Methods and results varied widely, they report. Only about half of mortality studies found a clear impact. Health system costs ranged up to one billion dollars a year. Wider economic losses ran far higher in some models. Quality scores were middling across study types. Poor methods can mislead policy and spending choices.
europmc-pmc5936175:
Hunter presents two cases of syphilis of the liver that looked like abscess formation. He spoke to the Royal Medico-Chirurgical Society of Glasgow in March 1922. The cases appeared in the Glasgow Medical Journal. Syphilis of the liver can mimic portal cirrhosis or a liver tumour. Hunter notes it can also bring fever and rigors. Such cases have been mistaken for malaria or typhoid fever.

The first patient was a man of 36, admitted in 1916. He had vomiting, jaundice, and attacks of shivering with sweating. His history held malaria from years of service in India. Hunter uses the cases to show how easily this form of syphilis is missed.
europmc-pmc5968375:
Alwarawrah, Kiernan, and MacIver review how food intake shifts immune cell work and fuel use. Their review was published in Frontiers in Immunology. How immune cells burn fuel and how they act are tightly linked. What a person eats also shapes immune cell acts. Too little food damps immunity and raises infection risk. It can also shield against some self-attack disease. Too much food brings a slow, low-grade swelling instead.

The review covers human and mouse work on food and immunity. It tracks blood signals and immune cell counts. T cells get close focus as chiefs of the response. Hormones and cell signals carry the food news to them. Aiming at T cell fuel use may help in both hunger and fatness.
europmc-pmc6050275:
Zhao and co-authors build injectable cryogels to stop severe bleeding. Their research article appeared in Nature Communications. Deep wounds that cannot be compressed are hard to treat. Standard sponges and gauze often fail there. A material that expands fast inside the wound could help.

The gels mix carbon nanotubes with treated chitosan. They can be injected in a compressed form. Blood triggers rapid shape recovery and uptake. The gels also conduct electricity and fight bacteria. Clotting and platelet sticking beat gauze in lab tests. Animal liver and tail injury models followed. One mix outperformed a standard combat dressing. Wound healing also beat a commercial film dressing. Readers get a multi-talent material for trauma care.
europmc-pmc6117975:
Sack wrote a review in Molecular Medicine on serum amyloid A, a blood protein known for more than 50 years. Its levels can rise a thousandfold within a day during illness or injury. Pieces of it can form stiff fibrils in amyloid disease. Yet its normal job in the body stayed unclear for decades.

The review gathers many scattered reports into one picture. It covers the protein's shape and how fibrils form. Its love of fats links it to lipid transport and clogged arteries. It also acts like a cytokine, a signaling protein. Sack argues it helps control the body's first response to harm. That view may open new treatment ideas.
europmc-pmc6146775:
Mihai and co-authors wrote a review in Journal of Immunology Research on inflammation in chronic kidney disease. Chronic kidney disease affects about 10 to 15 percent of people. It often goes unseen in its early stages. Once it sets in, the damage cannot be undone. Steady low-grade inflammation is now seen as a hallmark of it.

The review traces what feeds that inflammation. Causes include stress chemistry, acid buildup, repeat infections, and upset gut microbes. New omics tools can spot marker panels in blood. Such panels may aid early diagnosis and tracking. The authors also cover inflammasomes and the two-way link with kidney cancer.
europmc-pmc6158375:
Marcinowska-Suchowierska and co-authors wrote a clinical review in Frontiers in Endocrinology on vitamin D toxicity. Vitamin D helps the body use calcium, but too much can poison it. Toxicity is rare, yet its effects can be serious if it is missed. The main danger is very high blood calcium.

The review lists the warning signs, including confusion, apathy, vomiting, belly pain, and heavy urination and thirst. Causes include long-term overdose of vitamin D products and diseases that make the active form in the body. The authors separate outside causes from internal ones. Lab patterns that confirm the diagnosis are spelled out. Clinicians get a guide to spotting and sorting this uncommon problem.
europmc-pmc6180975:
Igiri and co-authors wrote a review in Journal of Toxicology on heavy metal pollution from tannery wastewater. Tanneries discharge untreated water carrying toxic metals into ecosystems. That flow is a major environmental and health challenge. The metals include chromium, mercury, cadmium, and lead.

Heavy metals do not break down, and they can poison microbes too. Yet some microorganisms have evolved ways to detoxify them. The review weighs bioremediation, using such microbes to clean polluted sites. It is offered as an efficient, eco-friendly, and cost-effective alternative to conventional clean-up methods. The authors assess both the toxicity problem and the promise of living solutions for tannery regions.
europmc-pmc6308375:
Gullner and co-authors review glutathione S-transferase enzymes in plant disease. The review appeared in Frontiers in Plant Science. These enzymes form large families in plants. Many switch on fast when microbes attack. They detoxify poisons by attaching glutathione to them. They also ease oxidative stress in infected tissue.

Transcript and protein studies show distinct groups rising early in infection. Changing single enzyme levels can alter disease symptoms. Some enzymes carry hormones or bind salicylic acid. That acid is a key defense signal in plants. Helpful microbes can also raise these enzymes. This primes plants for later attacks. The authors call for work on exact enzyme jobs.
europmc-pmc6324375:
Barmettler and co-authors study antibody loss in patients treated with rituximab. Their cohort study appeared in JAMA Network Open. Rituximab removes B cells that make antibodies. It treats cancers, immune diseases, and related ills. A known risk is low antibody levels, called hypogammaglobulinemia. The team followed 4,479 patients who got the drug.

Many patients were never screened for low antibodies. Others had low levels that went unrecognized. Severe infections rose after treatment across the cohort. Such infections near treatment were linked to higher mortality. Higher total doses of antibody replacement therapy helped. They were tied to lower risk of severe infection. The authors urge routine antibody checks before and after rituximab. Those checks can flag patients who need protection.
europmc-pmc6331975:
Dahham and co-authors test a plant compound from agarwood oil against cancer and microbes. Their study appeared in Molecules in 2015. The compound is beta-caryophyllene, a sesquiterpene. It was isolated from the essential oil of Aquilaria crassna. The team confirmed its structure with standard instruments. Then they ran a battery of lab tests.

The compound killed Staphylococcus aureus bacteria at low doses. Its antifungal action beat a standard drug in tests. It also showed strong antioxidant power in two assays. Against cancer cells, it acted most on colorectal lines. Normal cells were harmed far less by comparison. It pushed colon cancer cells into programmed death. Mitochondria damage formed part of that route. The results mark it as a candidate for further drug study.
europmc-pmc6384275:
Isayenkov and Maathuis review salt stress in plants, in Frontiers in Plant Science. Salt in soil is a major threat to farming. It slows crop growth and cuts yields across large areas of farmland.

The review covers how plants take in sodium and chloride ions and where they store them. It weighs two paths ions can take through root tissue. It also asks how plants even sense salt, a point still not settled. The authors doubt some standard views on ion toxicity. Naming open questions is their stated aim, alongside new findings.
europmc-pmc6391775:
Co and co-authors present a gut model study in Cell Reports. Human enteroids are balls of gut lining grown from real tissue. They let researchers watch germs attack the gut, but the germ-facing surface sits hidden inside the ball.

The team flipped the balls so that surface faces outward. Flipped enteroids kept their barrier and mature cell types. They also absorbed nutrients in the right direction. Germs such as Salmonella and Listeria attacked the flipped surface in distinct patterns. The model opens a simpler way to study gut infection in human tissue.
europmc-pmc6415775:
Stewart and co-authors report the TEDDY study in Nature, on the young child's gut microbiome. The study follows children at risk for type 1 diabetes in many centers. Gut microbes in early life may shape later immune disease.

Stool samples came from 903 children between three and forty-six months of age. Over twelve thousand samples were read by gene sequencing. The gut community changed in clear stages as children grew. Feeding, birth mode, and place all left marks on it. The dataset is among the largest of its kind for early childhood.
europmc-pmc6453475:
Postma and Goedhart introduce PlotsOfData, a free web app that plots raw data together with chosen summaries so readers can judge results for themselves. Summary-only graphs hide the spread of the underlying points, while raw plots alone can be hard to read. The app, built on R, Shiny, and ggplot2, layers both.

Users pick the display, add mean, median, box, or violin summaries, and attach 95 percent confidence intervals for visual inference. Transparent layers can be reordered or dimmed until the figure reads clearly. No installation or coding is needed, which aims the tool at working scientists rather than programmers. The code is open source for inspection and reuse.
europmc-pmc6466575:
Ito and co-authors review lipid peroxidation as the practical way to gauge oxidative stress, the tilt that most drives plaque growth in diabetes and atherosclerosis. The oxygen species themselves flee too fast to measure well, and direct readings match disease states unevenly. The harm they leave in fats makes a sturdier witness.

Failure of the vessel lining opens the road to atherosclerosis, and high blood pressure, odd fat levels, inflammation, and sugar damage all push the same way. Sections explain what the main peroxidation measures capture and how they behave across diabetes, set atherosclerosis, and long inflammation. What the measures mean in the clinic gets careful focus, including the heart jolts of low blood sugar.
europmc-pmc6499775:
Zhu and co-authors tackle a quiet scandal of biomaterials — batches that never match — writing in Scientific Reports. Their subject is GelMA, a light-curable gelatin gel used for 3D cell culture, tissue repair and bioprinting. Like Matrigel, the tumor-derived gel it often replaces, GelMA can vary from lot to lot, and results wobble with it.

The team tested a one-pot synthesis meant to lock that variation down. They made five batches each of highly and lightly substituted GelMA and measured substitution level, protein structure and breakdown, plus the swelling, stiffness and cell survival of the cured gels. Batch after batch, the numbers held steady. The authors offer the recipe as a route to GelMA that labs can finally trust to repeat.
europmc-pmc6510875:
Kitagawa and co-authors present part 2 of the Japan Esophageal Society guidelines. The text appeared in the journal Esophagus. It updates the society's 2017 guidance for this cancer. Part 2 deals with treatment, not diagnosis.

The first part covers endoscopic resection of early lesions. It sets out when resection can cure and when more care is due. Later parts cover surgery and care around the operation. Radiotherapy and chemoradiotherapy follow. So does combined care from more than one field. The text ends with follow-up, care for return of the cancer, and palliative care. Each key question carries a graded advice statement.
europmc-pmc6529775:
Li and co-authors probe the STING-IRF3 pathway in sepsis-linked heart injury. Their study appeared in Redox Biology. Sepsis can weaken the heart in sepsis-induced cardiomyopathy. Inflammation, cell death and pyroptosis all play a part. The role of STING in this condition was unclear.

The team used mice with global STING knockout. In normal mice, lipopolysaccharide moved STING to the nucleus area. STING bound and activated IRF3, which raised NLRP3 levels. Knocking out STING improved survival and heart function. It also cut inflammation, apoptosis and pyroptosis. Restoring NLRP3 in cells undid the gain. The authors propose STING as a treatment target.
europmc-pmc6534875:
Finotello and co-authors present quanTIseq, a tool that counts immune cells inside tumors from standard RNA sequencing data, writing in Genome Medicine. Knowing which immune cells crowd a tumor helps predict survival and response to checkpoint drugs. Direct counting is slow and cannot be done on stored samples.

quanTIseq untangles bulk RNA data into the shares of ten immune cell types, a task called deconvolution. The team checked it against simulated data, flow cytometry and tissue staining. Run over 8,000 tumors, it showed killer T cell entry tracks a chemical signal axis, CXCR3/CXCL9, more than mutation counts. Its cell scores also predicted outcomes in several cancers, and revealed how kinase drugs reshape the immune mix behind uneven checkpoint drug responses.
europmc-pmc6540575:
Chen, Zhang and Zhu review m6A, the most common internal mark on messenger RNA, and its part in human cancer, writing in Molecular Cancer. The mark is placed by writer enzymes, removed by erasers, and read by proteins that change how the RNA is used. The same crew can help or hinder a tumor, depending on the cancer.

Across cancers — leukemia, bladder, breast, bowel, liver, lung and more — the review maps which crew members rise or fall and which genes they touch. In leukemia, the writer METTL3 acts as a cancer driver, while in some brain tumors the writers restrain growth. The authors close with therapy ideas that aim at writers, erasers or readers to reset the marks.
europmc-pmc6550175:
Rajkomar and co-authors show that deep learning can read whole hospital records and forecast patient outcomes, writing in NPJ Digital Medicine. Standard models need hand-picked variables, cleaned site by site, and throw away most of each chart. Their approach feeds the entire raw record, notes included, in a shared FHIR layout.

Trained on 216,221 patients from two US academic hospitals, the models scored well on every task. On the standard accuracy scale, they predicted deaths in hospital at 93 to 94 out of 100. Long stays scored 85 to 86, and unplanned returns within 30 days scored 75 to 76. They also named patients' final diagnoses at 90 out of 100. Each result beat the standard clinical models, without custom cleanup for either site.
europmc-pmc6600375:
Hao, Baker, and ten Dijke review how one growth factor can both block and spread cancer. Their article appears in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. TGF-β halts early tumors by stopping cell growth and triggering cell death. Later tumors resist that brake. The same signal then helps cancer cells change form and move.

The review traces TGF-β signaling from the cell surface inward. It explains the epithelial-mesenchymal transition step by step. Key drivers include the repressors SNAIL, ZEB, and TWIST. Small RNAs and long noncoding RNAs also tune the process. The authors note roles in blood vessel growth and immune escape. They close by asking how these mechanisms could yield new anti-metastasis drugs.
europmc-pmc6603175:
Gupta, Lall, Srivastava, and Sinha review hyaluronic acid and its medical uses. Their article appears in Frontiers in Veterinary Science. The molecule occurs in cartilage, skin, eyes, and joint fluid. It helps joints stay lubricated and springy. Its amount and chain length fall as osteoarthritis advances.

The review explains the chemistry and physics of the molecule. It covers how cells build and break it down. Three synthase enzymes produce chains of different sizes. The authors trace effects through receptors, enzymes, and metabolic pathways. Injections have treated joint pain in horses, dogs, and humans for decades. Uses also span eye care, skin care, burns, and wound repair. Molecular weight, the authors stress, shapes how each product behaves.
europmc-pmc6607375:
Elbe and Buckland-Merrett present the first study of GISAID, a flu data sharing scheme. Their article appears in Global Challenges. Fast sharing of virus data shapes outbreak response and vaccine design. Yet scientists and governments often hold data back. Credit fears, trade fears, and ownership claims all play a part.

The authors base their analysis on more than 20 expert interviews. They also draw on a wide range of documents. They find GISAID helps global health in five ways. It holds the most complete quality flu data set. It speeds sharing during outbreaks. It feeds the WHO vaccine strain selection process. It settles sharing disputes through informal channels. It also builds trust with key countries for pandemic readiness.
europmc-pmc6639075:
Kotliar and co-authors improve a method for reading gene programs in single cells. Their research article appears in eLife. Each cell mixes programs of identity with programs of activity. Identity marks what type the cell is. Activity marks what it is doing right now. Single-cell RNA data blends the two together.

The team benchmarked matrix factorization on simulated data. Their consensus version, cNMF, recovered both program types with care. It also measured each program's share inside each cell. They then ran it on brain organoid and visual cortex data. The method refined known cell types. It surfaced expected programs such as cell cycle and hypoxia response. It also found new ones tied to secretion and synapse building.
europmc-pmc6701375:
Snezhkina and co-authors review how ROS form and antioxidant defence in normal and malignant cells. Their review appears in Oxidative Medicine and Cellular Longevity. Reactive oxygen species arise from normal cell activity. They serve signalling roles at low levels. Excess output drives disease across many types. Tumours generate ROS at chronically high rates. There the species play a dual role. Damage builds up mutations and shakes genomes. Metabolism and signalling get rewired too. Resistance to therapy can follow. Yet higher levels kill tumour cells outright.

The review lists where ROS arise, part by part. Mitochondria and oxidases lead the sources. Defence systems that balance redox are covered. Enzymes, glutathione, and vitamins all play parts. Cancer cells rewire these defences in set ways.
europmc-pmc6728375:
Miyamoto and co-authors showed that gut microbes protect mice from diet-driven obesity. Western diets are rich in omega-6 fatty acids, which feed obesity and related disease. Gut bacteria convert some of these fats into new compounds. One such compound is called HYA. The team tested what HYA does in the body.

Giving HYA to mice on a high-fat diet curbed weight gain. It did so without sparking the fat inflammation tied to a related fat. It also improved metabolism through fatty acid receptors. Mice colonized with Lactobacillus bacteria made more HYA and showed the same benefit. Targeting microbial fat products may help prevent metabolic disorders.
europmc-pmc6779475:
Li and co-authors identified Piezo1, a pressure-sensing channel, as a driver of bone building. Exercise and other loads make bones stronger, but how bone cells sense force was unclear. Osteocytes, cells buried in bone, detect load changes and signal bone-forming cells. The team tested Piezo1 in these cells under fluid shear stress, a stand-in for mechanical load.

Without Piezo1, osteocytes failed to change gene activity under flow. A drug that opens Piezo1 copied flow's effects exactly. Mice lacking Piezo1 in bone cells had notably less bone mass and strength. Giving adult mice the opener raised bone mass, mimicking exercise. Piezo1 is a fresh target for bone-building therapy.
europmc-pmc6786975:
Bycroft and co-authors describe the UK Biobank resource with its deep phenotyping and genomic data. The project follows about 500,000 people across the United Kingdom, recruited at ages 40 to 69. Each participant gave biological measures, lifestyle details, blood and urine biomarkers, and body and brain imaging. Health records add follow-up over time.

Genome-wide data were collected on everyone. Central cleaning, phasing, and imputation raised the number of testable variants to about 96 million. Imputed variants at 11 immune genes recovered known disease signals. Population structure and relatedness in the data are carefully charted. The open resource is built for discovering genetic bases of complex traits.
europmc-pmc6852275:
Abels and co-authors offer a white paper on computational pathology, in The Journal of Pathology. The field uses computer analysis of tissue slide images, joined with patient data, to extract medical information. It promises faster and more consistent diagnosis. The Digital Pathology Association convened experts to set shared terms and good practice for it.

The paper defines the field's vocabulary and traces its short history. It then sets out best practice, from the infrastructure a lab needs to gathering training data and checking quality. Teaching annotators to label images the same way gets detailed attention. The authors also make recommendations for regulators who must judge these tools.
europmc-pmc6908975:
Haghayegh and co-authors test how well Fitbit wristbands measure sleep, in the Journal of Medical Internet Research. Wearable trackers promise cheap sleep data from daily life, outside the sleep lab. Consumers and researchers both rely on their numbers. Whether those numbers are accurate, stage by stage, is a separate question. The team gathered every validation study they could find.

Their review followed standard PRISMA reporting rules across seven databases. Newer Fitbit models that stage sleep were compared with lab measurements and sleep diaries. One study of 60 people found no difference between wearing the band on the dominant or other hand. Older models' sensitive mode settings changed the readings, the authors note.
europmc-pmc6973275:
Bowden and Holmes review how meta-analysis tools strengthen Mendelian randomization studies. Their article appeared in Research Synthesis Methods. Mendelian randomization uses gene variants as instruments to test whether a risk factor truly causes a health outcome. Meta-analysis, long used to pool separate studies, now pools genome-wide data for many variants at once.

When causal estimates from different variants disagree, the method's core assumptions may be broken. The authors first explain the approach and the theory behind it. They then show how random effects models, meta-regression, and robust regression test for that disagreement. Such checks can adjust estimates and harden the conclusions. Their aim is rigour: causal claims from genetic data should survive the toughest statistical scrutiny available.
europmc-pmc6997275:
Tramunt and co-authors review why men and women differ in metabolic control and diabetes risk. Their review appeared in Diabetologia. Diabetes is more common in men than women in most of the world, above all in middle age. Animal models show the same pattern.

Many parts of energy balance and glucose handling run differently by sex. In their fertile years, women store fuel in safer places, under the skin rather than around organs. Their insulin sensitivity runs higher, and their insulin output and gut hormone responses are stronger. Those advantages fade as glucose control fails. Protective effects of oestrogens, acting through a main receptor in brain, liver, muscle, fat, and pancreas, explain part of the gap. Sex chromosomes and early-life programming need more study, the authors say.
europmc-pmc7007675:
Lähnemann and co-authors lay out eleven grand challenges for single-cell data science. Their paper appeared in Genome Biology. Cheap sequencing plus new lab tricks now let one experiment profile thousands or millions of single cells. That flood of data creates problems ordinary analysis cannot solve.

Each challenge is framed with the questions that motivate it, the work done so far, and the problems still open. Themes run from handling measurement noise and missing data to mapping cells in space and tracing lineages over time. Spatial methods, for instance, must not assume that matching gene profiles sit side by side. Uncertainty should flow through to later steps rather than vanish. The compendium addresses veterans, newcomers, and students alike. Its aim is to point the field at the problems whose solutions would unlock the most biology in the coming years.
europmc-pmc7060275:
Zheng and co-authors apply deep learning to breast ultrasound in Nature Communications. Knowing whether cancer has reached the armpit lymph nodes guides treatment for early-stage breast cancer, but finding out often means surgery that many patients do not need. The team built a deep learning radiomics model from conventional ultrasound and shear wave elastography images, aiming to predict node status before any operation.

Adding clinical parameters to the image model gave the best performance. In the test cohort it separated clear armpits from any metastasis with an area under the curve of 0.902, and distinguished low from heavy metastatic burden at 0.905. Those figures suggest the scans carry readable signs of spread that human review misses. The authors propose the combined model as a noninvasive biomarker, able to spare some patients unnecessary axillary surgery and its complications while flagging those who truly need it.
europmc-pmc7084675:
Musial, Kuban-Jankowska, and Gorska-Ponikowska review the health properties of green tea catechins, in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. Catechins are the main antioxidant compounds in green tea. Their strength depends on their chemical structure, including how many hydroxyl groups they carry.

Four catechin types are covered, and epigallocatechin gallate shows the strongest anti-inflammatory and anticancer action in the studies surveyed. The compounds neutralise reactive oxygen and nitrogen species. Reported protective links span lung, breast, stomach, liver, and prostate cancers, among others. The authors are clear that green tea cannot replace standard chemotherapy, though its compounds might support standard treatment.
europmc-pmc7100275:
Zhou and co-authors review how tumors resist five platinum-based anticancer drugs, in Frontiers in Pharmacology. Cisplatin, carboplatin, oxaliplatin, nedaplatin, and lobaplatin are mainstays of chemotherapy. Resistance, whether present from the start or gained during treatment, severely limits their use.

Resistance grows through several routes at once. Transporter proteins can keep the drugs out of tumor cells, and detoxifying systems can bind the drugs before they damage DNA. Even when DNA damage forms, cells may repair it faster or raise their threshold for self-destruction. Autophagy, the cell's recycling system, also plays a part. The review names the most promising targets and markers that might help doctors predict or defeat resistance.
europmc-pmc7107875:
Tang and co-authors examine the origin and continuing evolution of SARS-CoV-2, in National Science Review. They compared the new virus's genome with related coronaviruses, including a bat virus called RaTG13. Only 4% of genome positions differ between the two, but at neutral sites the difference reaches 17%.

That gap means the two viruses split apart much earlier than first estimated. Changes in the spike's binding region in SARS-CoV-2 and in pangolin viruses look shaped by natural selection as well as mixing between viruses. Across 103 genomes, the authors found two major lineages, L and S, with L more common in their samples. What the split means for the disease itself was still unclear.
europmc-pmc7210975:
Kim and co-authors profile metastatic lung adenocarcinoma cell by cell. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. Lung adenocarcinoma is the most common lung cancer type. Over 40 percent of cases are already metastatic at diagnosis. The team sequenced single cells from normal tissue and from tumors at every stage.

They captured 208,506 cells from 44 patients. One cancer cell subtype strayed from the normal development path. That subtype dominated the metastatic stage. Surrounding stromal and immune cells also shifted as cancer advanced. Regulatory T cells appeared early and persisted into metastases, damping anti-tumor immunity. Natural killer cells declined. The atlas shows how a tumor ecosystem is reprogrammed for spread.
europmc-pmc7250475:
Shi and co-authors report a way to grow human brain organoids that contain their own blood vessels. Their study appeared in PLoS Biology. Organoids are small lab-grown tissues that mimic an organ. Brain versions help scientists study how the human cortex develops, but they usually lack vessels to feed inner cells.

The vascularized organoids held typical cortical cell types and a working vessel network for over 200 days. Recordings showed chemical and electrical signals passing between nerve cells. Gene readouts confirmed strong nerve cell growth and vessel-related activity. When grafted into mouse brains, the organoids linked into the mouse blood supply and their cells survived better. The method offers a model for development and a possible base for cell therapy.
europmc-pmc7255975:
Catanzaro and co-authors review the immune response in COVID-19 and possible drug targets. Their review appeared in Signal Transduction and Targeted Therapy. At the time, no vaccine or proven drug existed for the disease. A fast, well-tuned immune response defends the body. A response that runs too hot can damage lungs and other tissues. That excess is often called a cytokine storm.

The authors map the innate and adaptive immune changes seen in patients. They trace the signaling pathways the virus sets off. Each pathway points to players that drugs might block. The aim is to stop mild cases from turning severe. Readers get both the biology and the treatment logic.
europmc-pmc7260975:
Shang and co-authors work out how SARS-CoV-2 gets inside human cells. Their study appeared in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. Like the earlier SARS virus, SARS-CoV-2 uses the ACE2 protein as its entry receptor and human proteases as activators. Lab entry tests let the team compare the two viruses step by step.

Their results point to entry features that may help the new virus infect cells well while dodging immune detection. That pairing of potency and evasiveness could help explain its wide spread. The study also settles conflicting early reports about entry routes. Knowing exactly how the virus breaks in gives drug and vaccine designers specific steps they might block.
europmc-pmc7264175:
Poh and co-authors hunt for spots on the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein that antibodies from recovered patients attack. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. Finding such spots, called epitopes, helps design both diagnostic tests and vaccine candidates. The team screened overlapping peptide pieces of the spike against blood serum from convalescent patients.

Two clear antibody targets stood out. One sits near the receptor binding domain and appears specific to SARS-CoV-2. The other lies at the fusion peptide and might serve as a target across related SARS viruses. When antibodies against these regions were removed from serum, the serum lost much of its power to neutralize the virus. The results mark both regions as practical leads for test and vaccine design.
europmc-pmc7273175:
Sun and co-authors chart how antibody responses to SARS-CoV-2 rise and change over the course of COVID-19. Their study appeared in Emerging Microbes and Infections. Blood antibody tests were becoming a key diagnostic tool. The team measured antibodies against the virus's nucleocapsid and spike proteins in 130 blood samples from 38 patients, including 11 in intensive care.

Both antibody types climbed after symptoms began. IgM responses peaked around the second week in many patients, while IgG kept rising into the third week. Testing for both proteins together could identify up to 75% of infected patients in the first week. Antibody patterns differed between intensive care and other patients, and one spike antibody pattern tracked with improving inflammation outside intensive care.
europmc-pmc7281575:
Pang and co-authors release MetaboAnalystR 3.0, an improved software pipeline for global metabolomics. Their paper appeared in Metabolites. Metabolomics measures the full set of small molecules in a sample, usually with liquid chromatography linked to high-resolution mass spectrometry. Turning raw spectra into biological meaning is slow and full of settings that can distort results.

The new version fixes three weak points. It optimizes peak-picking parameters efficiently, corrects batch effects automatically, and predicts pathway activity more accurately. In benchmark studies the workflow ran 20 to 100 times faster than established alternatives and produced results the authors judge more biologically meaningful. The tool is open-source and runs in R, aiming at high-throughput studies of systems biology and complex disease.
europmc-pmc7353775:
Wu and co-authors pool population studies in BMC Oral Health on the two-way link between gum disease and type 2 diabetes. Periodontitis is chronic inflammation of the tissues holding teeth, and diabetes is long suspected to worsen it, and vice versa. The team searched four databases up to December 2018 and kept 53 observational studies.

Diabetes was far more common among people with periodontitis, and periodontitis was more common among people with diabetes. Diabetes patients had deeper gum pockets, more attachment loss, and about 2 more lost teeth. Cohort studies suggest diabetes raises the risk of developing gum disease by 34 percent. Severe gum disease in turn raised diabetes incidence by about half. Blood sugar control changed the picture.
europmc-pmc7474075:
Fu and co-authors show that two known drugs block SARS-CoV-2 by hitting its main protease. The protease cuts the virus's long protein into working parts. It is a prime drug target for that reason.

Boceprevir, a drug approved against hepatitis C virus, blocked the protease in Vero cells. GC376, a pre-clinical drug for a cat coronavirus disease, did the same. Structural work shows both drugs sit on the active side of the protease. Pairing GC376 with Remdesivir gave a stronger, sterilizing joint effect in the lab tests. Remdesivir attacks a different viral enzyme, the RNA-copying polymerase. The findings can guide design of stronger protease blockers. Old drugs, the work hints, may speed the search for COVID-19 cures.
europmc-pmc7495975:
David and co-authors review molecular representations for AI-driven drug discovery and give a practical guide. Computers reshaped how chemists study bioactive molecules. Models need molecule forms that machines can read and scientists can grasp.

Many chemical representations grew up over the years. Graph-based forms lead the field for small molecules. The guide also covers linear notations, reaction forms, and forms for large molecules such as proteins. It shows how each serves AI tasks in drug hunting. The pace of computing and the depth of chemical traits explain the variety. Newcomers to the field get a map of which form fits which job. The review aims to ease work at the joint of chemistry and AI.
europmc-pmc7547075:
Pereira and co-authors design a microbe mix that limits Clostridioides difficile in the gut. This pathogen feeds on sugars from gut mucus. Helpful microbes that use the same sugars can block it.

The team used isotope probing and cell sorting in mouse gut samples. They found which commensals eat mucus sugars in place. Muribaculaceae emerged as major users of those sugars. Other families also took part in smaller roles. A five-member mix was built from sugar users. It cut the pathogen access to key sugars. In treated mice, colonization by the pathogen fell. The work supports targeted design of probiotic mixes.
europmc-pmc7556375:
Meyerowitz-Katz and co-authors review dropout in app-based care for chronic disease. Apps are used to help manage long-term illness. Many users stop using them after a short time.

The team searched major databases for studies since 2003. A total of 17 studies entered the review and analysis. Nine were randomized trials and eight were observational. The pooled dropout rate was 43% across studies. Observational studies showed a 49% dropout rate. Trials showed a lower rate of 40%. Reasons spanned social, demographic and behavior factors. The authors note wide variation across studies. Future designs could address many of the dropout causes.
europmc-pmc7616675:
Spragge and co-authors show that gut microbiome diversity blocks pathogens by starving them of nutrients. Gut microbes resist new pathogens, but prediction was poor. Which mixes protect a host was not known in advance.

The team tested human gut bacteria in lab and mice. Two major bacterial pathogens were used as targets. Single species alone had almost no protective effect. Resistance rose greatly as community diversity increased. Certain species had to be present for full effect. Protection came from eating nutrients the pathogen needs. Shared nutrient use let the team explain the pattern. They then predicted mixes that resist a new strain. The work gives a design rule for protective gut mixes.
europmc-pmc7661275:
Xu and co-authors review exosomes as tools for cancer immunotherapy. Exosomes are tiny vesicles that cells release. They carry proteins and other cargo between cells and can shape immune responses. Tumor cells and immune cells each shed exosomes with distinct content.

The authors explain how exosomes can wake an anti-cancer immune response. They can also serve as signs that the immune system has been switched on. Exosomes may act as cancer vaccines or as carriers for antigens and drugs. The review weighs both promise and risk, since exosomes can also help tumors grow in some settings.
europmc-pmc7681075:
Kim and co-authors review the runaway immune reaction behind severe COVID-19. In such cases, the body floods the blood with signaling proteins, a pattern called cytokine storm. It can wreck the lungs and many organs. The authors compare this storm with like syndromes in other diseases.

A weak early interferon response may set the storm off. Proteins such as IL-6 and IL-1 then drive the damage. Drugs that calm inflammation, some aimed at single cytokines, are in wide use. The authors also weigh removing cytokines from blood by machine. They note that firm rules for who gets which drug, and when, are still lacking.
europmc-pmc7681775:
Litviňuková and co-authors build an atlas of the cells in the adult human heart. They profiled gene activity cell by cell across six regions of the heart. Heart disease is the top cause of death worldwide. A full cell map is a base step toward new treatments.

The atlas shows wide variety within heart muscle cells, support cells, and vessel cells. Atrial and ventricular cells form distinct sets with unlike origins. Immune cells include resident macrophages with both attack and guard profiles. Contact networks between cell types differ between the upper and lower chambers. The authors offer the map as a reference for future heart studies.
europmc-pmc7699575:
Reichert and co-authors review ferroptosis, an iron-driven form of cell death, in brain disease. Excess free iron inside cells triggers fat damage that kills the cell. The brain is prone to iron imbalance. High brain iron has long been tied to stress damage and cell loss.

The review lays out the core steps, from fat peroxidation to the guard enzyme GPX4 and iron handling. It then links this death path to Alzheimer, Parkinson, and Huntington diseases. Knowing these steps may open new drug targets. The authors frame ferroptosis as a fresh angle on diseases that lack good treatments.
europmc-pmc7707175:
Liebisch and co-authors update the standard system for naming lipids. Lipids are fat-like molecules central to health and disease. Mass spectrometry now reads their structures in fine detail. A shared shorthand keeps reports clear and storable across labs and databases.

The update covers five lipid groups in the LIPID MAPS system. Key changes add counts of ring bonds and of oxygens to each name. This lets the shorthand cover new oxygen-rich species now being found. The notation now spans plant and yeast lipids, not just mammal ones. It also tags atoms for work with isotope-labeled compounds. The authors set it as the field standard.
europmc-pmc7735675:
Steenwyk and co-authors present software that trims gene alignments for family tree studies. Alignments often hold noisy sites that can warp a tree. Most trimmers cut divergent sites, yet a recent study found that can hurt accuracy. ClipKIT takes the opposite tack: it keeps the sites that carry real signal.

The team tested 14 trimming methods on nearly 140,000 alignments. Trees from ClipKIT cuts were accurate, robust, and fast to compute. It beat rival methods across a wide range of datasets. The authors offer it as a robust default for phylogenomic work, where studies may juggle hundreds of alignments at once.
europmc-pmc7778975:
Howe and co-authors present Ensembl 2021, an update on the genome annotation project for vertebrate species. Ensembl annotates gene structures, regulatory elements, and variants. It also traces the evolutionary history of genes and genomes. Data reach users through browsers, search tools, downloads, and programming interfaces. One known tool is the Ensembl Variant Effect Predictor.

Two new portals headline this update. Ensembl Rapid Release posts core data for new genomes as fast as possible. It already supports large biodiversity sequencing projects. A SARS-CoV-2 genome browser merges Ensembl annotation with public data from many sources. The team built it to aid the global response to COVID-19. All Ensembl data and software remain free without restriction.
europmc-pmc7784275:
Nosrati and co-authors review nanocomposite scaffolds that aim to speed healing of chronic wounds. Skin is the body's first barrier against germs. Deep skin damage harms health and quality of life. Tissue engineering tries to regrow damaged skin well. New blood vessel growth, called angiogenesis, is central to that repair.

The authors first explain the molecular steps of angiogenesis. They list the key factors that drive it. Next they cover how nanomaterials can boost vessel growth. Scaffold designs that carry these materials are reviewed in depth. The focus stays on faster, better healing of wounds that stall. The piece maps a decade of fast growth in this field.
europmc-pmc7786875:
Legros and co-authors track neutralizing antibodies in 140 people infected with SARS-CoV-2. The cohort covered mild cases and severe ones needing intensive care. Antibody response shapes protection from reinfection. It also guides vaccine design and public health policy.

The team used live virus and lab-made viruses carrying the spike protein. Antibody levels matched disease severity closely. Intensive care patients showed high levels. Mild and symptom-free patients had low levels or none. Levels also tracked anti-spike IgG closely. Antibodies faded fairly fast after recovery. Earlier infection with common coronaviruses gave no cross-protection. The D614G spike variant did not escape neutralization.
europmc-pmc7786975:
