Liu and co-authors review how metabolism shapes macrophage behavior. Macrophages guard tissue health and fight pathogens. Those inside tumors help drive tumor start, growth, and spread. New work shows their fuel use is tied to their form and function.

Pro-inflammatory M1 macrophages lean on glycolysis. Their energy cycles in mitochondria run at reduced capacity. Anti-inflammatory M2 macrophages depend more on mitochondrial oxidation. The authors stress that real macrophage metabolism is messier than this split. They describe the metabolic traits of tumor-associated macrophages. Treatment ideas that follow from those traits are discussed. Open problems and promising study directions close the review.
europmc-pmc7814175:
Tang and co-authors review progress on exosomes from mesenchymal stem cells. Stem cells hold promise for repair medicine. Mesenchymal stem cells are a common research focus. Their cells are hard to store, though. They also age during lab growth.

Exosomes offer a way around those limits. These tiny packets are shed by the stem cells. They carry much of the cells' healing effect. They add targeted delivery and low immune reaction. Repair power stays high. The authors cover how exosomes are gathered and checked. Their traits and functions are set out next. Clinical uses close the review.
europmc-pmc7817975:
Houen and Trier review links between Epstein-Barr virus and systemic autoimmune disease. The virus infects nearly all humans at some point in life. Most people catch it in early childhood. Teen infection can cause infectious mononucleosis.

The virus spreads mainly through saliva. It infects mouth lining cells, then B cells. B cells act as its long-term home. The virus can switch between quiet and active states. That cycle allows it to flare again and again. Lasting infection of lining cells links to lupus and Sjögren's syndrome. Lasting B cell infection links to rheumatoid arthritis and multiple sclerosis. The authors weigh how one virus could feed many autoimmune diseases.
europmc-pmc7834475:
Paul and co-authors study vaccine attitudes and plans to vaccinate against COVID-19 in UK adults. Negative views and unsure plans block pandemic control. The team measured four kinds of negative vaccine attitude. They also hunted for groups most at risk of refusing. The sample was large.

The authors estimate what predicts each attitude type. Mistrust of benefits and worry about harm both count. Concern over commercial motives is a third type. A preference for natural immunity is the fourth. Some social groups scored far worse on these scales. The findings target public health messaging. Clear facts must reach the most doubtful groups first.
europmc-pmc7847675:
Hu and co-authors study the protein Siglec15 in bladder cancer and the wider cancer field. Siglec15 is a rising target for a new style of immunotherapy. Its role in bladder cancer was unclear. The team mined RNA data from The Cancer Genome Atlas.

Siglec15 was overproduced in tumor settings across many cancers. In bladder cancer, high levels matched a quiet immune scene. Immune cells, checkpoints, and attack signals all ran low. Such tumors answered immunotherapy poorly. They did differ in subtype and drug response in other ways. The team built an immune risk score from these patterns. The score predicted survival and therapy response in test cohorts.
europmc-pmc7923175:
Cheng and co-authors present a review of macrophages in lung injury, repair, and fibrosis. Lung scarring ruins gas exchange and can end in respiratory failure. Faulty fibroblast behaviour is one driver. Lasting injury to the air sacs and failed repair are others. Macrophages sit at the centre of each stage, and the review traces their part.

Two macrophage states frame the account: the classic M1 and the alternative M2 forms. The authors cover both the macrophages that live in the lung and those called in from the blood. They explain cell death modes, eating of debris, and talks with lung lining cells during repair. Their polarisation can push the lung toward scarring. The review ends with the gains that targeting macrophages might bring against pulmonary fibrosis.
europmc-pmc8001875:
Wiertsema and co-authors present a review of the interplay between gut microbes and the immune system in infection. Infections still kill many people in poor countries and threaten the very young and old everywhere. The gut holds 70–80% of the body's immune cells. Its microbes, lining, and local defences form one tight system. That system also steers immunity across the whole body, the authors stress.

The review explains how the balance among microbes, gut health, and immunity is kept. It links that balance to infections at each stage of life. Nutrition runs through the account as a lever. What a person eats shapes both the microbes and the immune response. Clinicians already use that knowledge in care. The authors argue food should sit inside plans to prevent and treat infection, not beside them.
europmc-pmc8002175:
Stoler and Nekrutenko present a study of error profiles across Illumina sequencing machines. Past checks of machine quality ran in tight lab conditions. This team built a way to read error rates back out of public data after the fact. Their method uses the overlaps between paired reads, a feature of many libraries. With it, they could grade finished experiments at scale.

They surveyed 1943 datasets from seven Illumina instruments. The pricier platforms, HiSeq and NovaSeq, showed lower error and tighter spread. Yet results varied a lot within each platform. The person running the experiment mattered greatly, they found. The letters before a spot also biased what came next. Two flagship machines broke that bias pattern in the same odd way. The authors say every dataset must be judged on its own quality.
europmc-pmc8023675:
Ahlmann-Eltze and Huber present glmGamPoi, an R package for fitting Gamma-Poisson models to single-cell count data. The Gamma-Poisson distribution models the sampling noise in single-cell RNA sequencing. It underpins differential expression analysis, principal component analysis, and factor analysis. Existing fitting tools struggle with datasets of millions of cells. They also waste the fact that zeros and small counts dominate the data.

The new package fits the distribution faster and more accurately than older methods. It exploits the mass of small values instead of fighting it. It can also work with data stored on disk. Nothing needs to sit fully in memory at once. The authors offer it through Bioconductor under a GPL-3 license. Scripts to reproduce their results come with the package.
europmc-pmc8024675:
Miller and co-authors introduce FRAME-IS, a framework for documenting changes to implementation strategies in healthcare. Evidence-based practices need such strategies to reach routine care. In practice, the strategies get modified to fit local patients and settings. Those changes can decide success, yet almost nobody documents them in a systematic way. The field lacked a shared form for the job.

The team built the framework with wide stakeholder input. Drafts went through think-aloud exercises with implementation scientists and large international groups. The final tool asks what was modified, and the nature of the change. It records the goal, timing, and who decided. It also asks how widespread the modification is. An example project shows the framework in use.
europmc-pmc8082275:
Lamarca and co-authors test second-line FOLFOX chemotherapy against symptom control alone in advanced biliary tract cancer. The ABC-06 trial was a phase 3 study run at 20 UK sites. Patients had progressed after first-line cisplatin and gemcitabine. A total of 162 patients were randomized evenly. One arm got active symptom control plus FOLFOX. The other got symptom control alone.

Overall survival ran longer on the chemotherapy arm. Median survival reached 6.2 months on FOLFOX against 5.3 months on symptom control alone in the final analysis. The adjusted hazard ratio was 0.69 in favor of chemotherapy across the trial. At 12 months, 25.9% of the FOLFOX group were alive against 11.4% of the control group in the same count. Side effects were heavier with the drugs, as expected. The authors call FOLFOX a valid second-line standard.
europmc-pmc8099175:
Qiao and co-authors design blockers of the SARS-CoV-2 main protease and test them in animals. The protease cuts the virus's long precursor proteins into working parts. Without those cuts, the virus cannot copy itself. No human protease shares its exact cutting taste. That makes it a clean drug target. The team modeled new compounds on two hepatitis C drugs.

They built 32 candidate inhibitors on those templates. Six of them shielded cells from infection with high potency. Two leads advanced into animal work after blood-level screening. In a transgenic mouse model, both showed strong antiviral activity. Vaccines alone may not end the variant chase. A pill that jams the viral scissors could fill the gap. Cell and mouse success mark the first proof step. Human trials would be the test that counts.
europmc-pmc8122975:
Neophytou and co-authors review how the tumor microenvironment drives metastasis, the deadliest turn in cancer. Spread to distant organs causes most cancer deaths. The neighborhood around a tumor shapes that escape. Immune cells, fibroblasts, collagen, and other matrix parts all take part. Their crosstalk makes cancer cells invasive and hard to see. It also helps sleeping cells wake at distant sites.

M2-type macrophages feed growth while muting immunity. Fibroblasts lay matrix tracks that guide migrating cells. Tiny vesicles from mesenchymal cells boost the urge to move. The stiff, dense matrix squeezes tumors into low oxygen. It also blocks drugs from reaching their targets. In the blood, platelets and signals shelter traveling cells. The review then turns to remodeling the neighborhood. Small drugs, nanoparticles, and engineered vesicles all aim there. Stop the soil, they argue, and the seed may fail.
europmc-pmc8238775:
Kasper and co-authors review the link between fatty liver disease and cardiovascular disease. Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease is the most common chronic liver disease in Western countries. It affects about 25% of adults.

The disease often travels with obesity, diabetes, and poor blood lipids. It counts as the liver face of metabolic syndrome. Beyond liver harm, it ties to heart and vessel disease. Risks include hypertension, coronary disease, and heart rhythm faults. The review gathers clinical evidence for each link. It urges heart checks as part of liver care. Physicians meet this pairing often in metabolic clinics.
europmc-pmc8387975:
Burkart and co-authors estimate how non-optimal temperature affects deaths from set causes around the world. Heat and cold were known to raise death rates, but no full count of the burden existed. Their two-part model was built for the Global Burden of Disease Study.

First, the team linked deaths to daily temperature data and modeled risk for 176 causes of death. They did this across 23 mean temperature zones. Next, they applied those risk curves to all locations for the years 1990 to 2019. Daily gridded temperature data fed the counts. The work gives regions a cause-by-cause view of temperature-linked deaths.
europmc-pmc8709575:
Khan and co-authors show that the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein triggers inflammation through the TLR2 receptor. COVID-19 can bring a harmful overreaction of the immune system. How the virus sparks that response was not clear. The team tested each main structural protein of the virus in immune and lung cells.

Only the spike protein provoked a strong response. It raised a set of inflammatory signals in human and mouse macrophages. Lung cells reacted in a like way. The spike acted through the NF-kB pathway, and the effect vanished in cells lacking TLR2. Mice without TLR2 also failed to react. The work names a route behind the cytokine storm.
europmc-pmc8748675:
Song and co-authors use single-cell analysis to map cell states in human primary prostate cancer. Prostate cancer is the second most common cancer in men worldwide. Tumors mix cancer and non-cancer cell types. The team sequenced biopsies, surgical samples, and lab-grown organoids from patients with local disease.

Epithelial cells fell into varied states. States with high androgen signaling were richer in cancer samples. A group of tumor-linked club cells may aid cancer formation. Cells lacking one marker gene shared traits with nearby normal cells. Organoids kept some tumor states but differed from their parent tissue. The findings may aid diagnosis.
europmc-pmc8782575:
Costa Clemens and co-authors report a Brazilian trial comparing booster vaccines after two doses of CoronaVac. CoronaVac is an inactivated virus vaccine used in a two-dose course. Six months later, antibody levels had fallen low. The trial asked if a different third vaccine beat a third CoronaVac dose.

In total, 1,240 adults were assigned to one of four booster groups. Options were the Janssen, Pfizer, and Oxford vaccines, or CoronaVac itself. Only 20.4 percent of younger adults still had detectable neutralizing antibodies before boosting. The main test compared anti-spike antibody levels 28 days after the booster. Safety and side effects were tracked as well.
europmc-pmc8828475:
Saito and co-authors dissect what made the SARS-CoV-2 Delta variant more dangerous. Delta drove a huge COVID-19 surge in India in spring 2021. Its viral traits, though, were poorly understood. The team focused on one spike change, P681R. That change is nearly always present in this lineage. They tested the variant and the single mutation in cells and hamsters.

Delta proved highly fusogenic, meaning its cells merge readily. The P681R change eased cutting of the spike protein. That cutting step boosted the merging behavior. Viruses carrying P681R also caused worse disease than their parent virus. The authors name P681R a hallmark of Delta. They link it directly to the variant's added harm.
europmc-pmc8965475:
Xia and co-authors test stem cell exosomes as a treatment for acute lung injury in mice. The exosomes come from stem cells grown from fat tissue. In hurt lungs, the airway's guard cells lose sound inner power units. The team asked if exosomes could donate working parts of those units. Mice got a lung dose of bacterial toxin. Exosomes came through a vein hours later. Guard cell function and lung swelling were then checked.

The exosomes passed the power-unit parts to the guard cells. More dose meant more transfer. The cells regained membrane strength and energy output. Inner stress eased. The guard cells shifted to a calm, anti-inflammatory style. They made less IL-1β and TNF-α and more IL-10. Lung swelling eased in step. Removing the guard cells erased most of the gain. The authors name this donation as the way the treatment works.
europmc-pmc9092475:
Heravi and Zadsirjan survey top prescribed drugs built around nitrogen heterocycles. These ring structures with nitrogen atoms sit at the core of many key drugs. The authors note that most active drug compounds contain such rings. Their roles span pain, infection, mental health, and many more fields.

For each drug, the survey gives its medical uses and how it acts. It also gives chosen routes for making the drug in the lab. Sources include both journals and patent texts. Readers can see why one ring type recurs across very unlike drugs. The survey serves chemists who design new drugs and need proven starting points.
europmc-pmc9353475:
Li and co-authors review how making cancer cells die in an immunogenic way can boost immunotherapy. Such death spills danger signals and tumor antigens into the surroundings. Dendritic cells mature on the signal and killer T cells move in. The shift can thaw a cold, suppressive tumor setting.

The review centers on nano-sized delivery systems that trigger this death on target. They can carry chemo drugs, light-activated agents, heat agents, or radiation sensitizers. Timed release at the tumor raises effect and cuts side harm. Immune drugs can ride along for a combined strike. Only 10 to 30% of patients gain from checkpoint drugs today. The authors argue that forced immunogenic death can lift that share. Design rules for the carriers close the survey.
europmc-pmc9357075:
Hoang and co-authors review stem cell therapy for human disease. Two cell families lead the field: pluripotent stem cells that can become any body cell, and mesenchymal stem cells from marrow, fat, or cord tissue. Both are now in clinical use for hard-to-treat conditions. The review gathers recent trials across many disease areas.

Uses span brain disorders, lung disease, hormone conditions, infertility, burns, and heart disease. The authors add their own trial experience with mesenchymal cells. They propose matching cell origin to the job. Marrow cells may suit brain and cord injury; fat cells, fertility and skin; cord cells, lung disease. Safety worries from unproven clinics are flagged plainly. The goal is faster movement from lab promise to real care.
europmc-pmc9400175:
Kumar and co-authors describe the fifth edition of TimeTree of Life, a web resource for species divergence times. The resource gathers published molecular timetrees into one searchable database. Its aim is to make knowledge of evolution easy for anyone to reach.

The new edition holds divergence times for 137,306 species. That is 41% more than the edition before it. Users can look up the split time between two species. They can also get the timeline of one species back to the origin of life. A third tool builds a timetree for a group at a chosen rank. The site is now mobile friendly and meets access rules for users with disabilities. Data can also be pulled through a program interface.
europmc-pmc9546775:
Cao and Gao introduce GLUE, a framework that joins single-cell data across omics layers. Labs can now measure several molecule types in single cells. Most data sets still hold just one layer each. The layers use unlike feature spaces, which blocks easy merging.

GLUE bridges the gap by modeling regulatory links across layers. A graph-linked unified embedding places all cells in one shared space. Benchmark tests showed GLUE beat current tools on accuracy and scale. It stayed robust across mixed data types as well. The team applied it to triple-omics merging tasks. They also built a multi-omics human cell atlas over millions of cells. The atlas run corrected some earlier cell labels. Regulatory inference from the merged data is a further feature. The design is modular, so new tasks can plug in.
europmc-pmc9728475:
Lopes and Lionakis review how Candida albicans shifts from harmless tenant to disease causing invader. The yeast lives on mouth, gut, and genital surfaces in most people. Skin also hosts it without trouble in the calm state. Trouble starts when barriers break or defenses dip.

Antibiotics can upset the local balance and free the yeast. Immune suppression from care opens the same door wider. Once loose, it causes sore mucosal disease in mild cases. In grave cases it floods the blood and kills. The review sorts the tools the fungus uses to invade. Shape shifting, sticking, and cell damage lead the list. Feeding tricks and stress shields aid its spread. Hiding its wall parts helps it dodge immune eyes. Host defense steps get equal space in the account. Drug resistance closes the review as a growing threat.
europmc-pmc9755275:
Guo and co-authors review aging and its diseases, from molecular mechanisms to treatments. Aging is a slow, one way slide in cell and tissue function. It sharply raises the risk of many chronic diseases. Longer lives mean more elders living with those burdens.

The review tours the stress routes that drive the slide. Genome damage and telomere wear lead the mechanism list. Gene control drift and protein cleanup failure follow. Faulty power plants and worn stem cells add their share. Cell talk breakdown and nutrient sense drift complete the set. Each mechanism ties to named diseases of old age. The authors then survey ways to slow the process. Eating limits, microbe transplants, and diet shifts appear. Clearing worn cells and stem cell care get space. Hormone and antioxidant routes close the treatment tour. The aim is more healthy years, not just more years.
frus-1861-d175:
Gabriel Tassara, the Spanish minister in Washington, wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 9 August 1861. The letter is document 175 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Tassara's note brings the Spanish view into the file in its own voice. Envoys in Washington wrote on claims, ships, and points of honor. His August letter lets readers hear Madrid's side stated at the capital itself. Madrid's side, heard at first hand, keeps the file from being a one voice record. A one voice record would mislead; this file, at its best, speaks in many.
frus-1861-d275:
From his post abroad, Mr. Angel wrote to William H. Seward on 22 May 1861. It stands as Document 275 in the volume of foreign papers laid before Congress with the President's message. The date falls in the opening months of the Civil War, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

Inbound reports like this one told Washington what its man abroad saw, heard, and judged. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1861-d75:
On 2 September 1861, William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams in London. The letter is document 75 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

September brought the war's focus back to the coasts and the blockade. Seward's letters to London took up the law of blockade and search at sea. This one helped Adams answer British protests with a line set in Washington, not made up on the spot. Blockade law filled whole law books, and its points now had to be argued week by week. Week by week argument wore down protests that force could never have silenced.
frus-1862-d175:
Document 175 is a report of 24 October 1862 from Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It is one of two Adams reports under that date in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

Twin reports in one mail let an envoy keep a formal account apart from enclosures or side matters. Adams used the practice often in busy weeks. For the modern reader, this letter is best read beside its same-day mate. Together the two give the legation's full account of its work that week. London's answer, when it came, would turn on battlefield news ten days old or more.
frus-1862-d275:
Filed as Document 275 but dated 1 May 1862, this dispatch from Secretary of State William H. Seward went to William L. Dayton, the American minister in Paris. The Foreign Relations printers placed it after the general instruction of 2 May.

Out-of-sequence filing is a small quirk with real effects: a reader must watch dates, not numbers, to follow the Paris story. The letter itself belongs to the start of May, when Seward was sending his spring guidance to Europe. It pairs with the general instruction beside it in the file. Dayton's French was limited, and he leaned on his staff and on careful written notes.
frus-1862-d375:
Dated 27 August 1862, Document 375 is a letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Viscount Treilhard, printed in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume among the French papers.

Seward wrote two days before the second battle of Bull Run, at the peak of the summer's military anxiety in Washington. Foreign representatives in the capital could hear the guns' echo in official moods within days. Letters of this week, this one included, were written inside that pressure, though their manner stayed formal and measured. The French legation's notes were written in French and printed here in the Department's English. Cases in this channel often mixed the war at home with French designs in Mexico.
frus-1862-d475:
On 4 August 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to James E. Harvey, the American minister at Lisbon. The instruction is Document 475 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the official record for the year.

August orders to Lisbon came in a month when Confederate cruisers were the Union's growing worry at sea. Ships like the Alabama were slipping out to raid American commerce, and every neutral port's rules mattered. Portugal's Atlantic islands could serve as coaling points or be shut to raiders, depending on how Lisbon ruled. Seward's instruction kept Harvey pressing the stricter reading. The letter is part of the wide, quiet effort to make the whole Atlantic coast unfriendly to Confederate sea power.
frus-1862-d575:
On 20 May 1862 James Watson Webb reported from Rio de Janeiro to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The dispatch is Document 575 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the year's official record.

Webb's May report was written in a South America largely spared the war's direct pressure. Yet Brazil's ports gave the correspondence its themes. So did Brazil's example as a slaveholding empire. He reported the imperial government's temper and the standing of the Union's cause in Rio. Distance made his file sparse beside the European ones, but each letter carried weight for that reason: Washington had no other regular eyes in Brazil. The dispatch is a reminder that the war's diplomacy was hemispheric, not only European.
frus-1862-d675:
On 22 April 1862, William H. Seward wrote from the State Department to Anson Burlingame, the American minister to China. The letter is document 675 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862. It is one of a matched set of orders Seward sent that spring.

Each outward letter answered reports, gave fresh orders, and passed on news the envoy would need. For the China post, the brief covered trade, treaty rights, and the court's war with the Taiping rebels. This letter's worth lies in the run it belongs to. Read in line, the Seward-Burlingame mail shows two men running a distant brief with care, while a civil war consumed their country.
frus-1862-d75:
Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London was the reader in mind when William H. Seward wrote on 2 June 1862. It stands as Document 75 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the volume sent to Congress with the President's yearly message. It belongs to the summer of 1862, the war's second year, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

Seward's letters in this run set out Washington's line for the man on the spot to follow. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1863p1-d175:
Writing from London on 30 April 1863, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, reported to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington. The dispatch is document 175 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad. It was one of 3 letters between the same men dated that day.

In 1863 the great question in London was whether Britain would treat the Confederacy as a real nation. Adams's reports helped Washington judge that risk week by week. Read alongside its neighbors in the volume, it shows the daily grind behind the war's big diplomatic crises.
frus-1863p1-d275:
Washington's orders to London on 31 August 1863 came in this letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It is document 275 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. It is one of the papers the State Department later printed in its Foreign Relations series for 1863.

Seward wrote in a firm tone but had to avoid pushing Britain into the war on the Southern side. His instructions walked that line again and again. The letter's value lies partly in its place in the sequence: it shows the conversation between the two capitals continuing without a break.
frus-1863p1-d375:
In Washington on 29 January 1863, Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed this note to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. It is document 375 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress. It was one of 3 letters between the same men dated that day.

For historians, this exchange shows Anglo-American tension being managed day by day. It is the paper record of a war that never happened between the two countries. Read alongside its neighbors in the volume, it shows the daily grind behind the war's big diplomatic crises.
frus-1863p1-d475:
Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington sent an official note to Secretary William H. Seward on 23 April 1863. Readers meet it in the first part of the 1863 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the government's own record of its dealings abroad. The two men at the ends of this channel, Seward in Washington and Lyons speaking for Britain, wrote to each other almost daily.

The formal tone can hide the tension, but the pace gives it away. Notes this frequent mean both capitals were watching each other closely. The real subject under all the polite wording was British neutrality. Washington wanted it kept strict, and London wanted no quarrel it could avoid. Readers who work through the file in order will find this letter where the clerks of 1863 left it, in the middle of the stream.
frus-1863p1-d575:
Under the date 20 June 1863, the record holds a letter from Lord Lyons to William H. Seward. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. Readers meet it in the first part of the 1863 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the government's own record of its dealings abroad. Britain had not taken sides in the American war, and holding that line was the daily work of this mail.

The standing business of this channel was friction at sea. Union warships stopped British merchant ships, and each seizure could spark a formal protest. Students of the war use this mail to see foreign policy as the men on the spot lived it, page by page. Readers who work through the file in order will find this letter where the clerks of 1863 left it, in the middle of the stream.
frus-1863p1-d675:
On 23 November 1863, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote from Washington to Charles Francis Adams, the United States minister in London. The letter survives as document 675 in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States. That series prints the State Department's own letters from the Civil War years.

Late 1863 was a tense time for ties with Britain. The Union wanted Britain to stay out of the war and to stop help from reaching the South. A reader gets the real working words of that effort, sent at the top level. Single letters like this one, read in order, show how the North made its case week by week.
frus-1863p1-d75:
On 10 February 1863, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. The letter is document 75 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. It follows Adams's dispatch that had sent home the Queen's speech.

Seward wrote with fair news in hand: at the opening of Parliament, Britain had shown no wish to meddle in the war. His letters still had claims to press, above all on warships built for the South in British yards. This one keeps the brief moving in a calmer week. It shows the exchange at its working best, each side feeding the other by steamer.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d175: A further letter from Roosevelt to Hull is dated October 30, 1943, and it stands as Document 175 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The cluster of same-day letters between the president and his secretary, at the Moscow Conference's close, is one of the volume's densest knots of paper. The record does not untangle their separate errands. The letter is printed in the Foreign Relations series for readers to sort in sequence.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d275:
A secret memorandum of conversation at Cairo on 26 November 1943 records a meeting about air supply to China over the Hump, the air route across the Himalayas. It is signed by Generals Arnold, Stilwell, and Somervell, and it answers a demand from Generalissimo Chiang Kai-shek.

Chiang wanted a fixed 10,000 tons a month flown in, whatever Southeast Asia operations might need. The generals explain that all C-46 aircraft are assigned to the route. They add that 25 more planes are sought for Mountbatten. Mountbatten's lower figure of 8,900 tons differs from the target by only 1,100 tons, which better efficiency may erase. Chiang closes by accepting the figures, with the understanding that the Air Transport Command will strain to raise the tonnage beyond the target.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d375:
Minutes kept by Major John Boettiger record the dinner at Tehran on 30 November 1943, at half past eight in the evening, given for Churchill's sixty-ninth birthday. Thirty-three members of the three delegations sat down together, with Roosevelt on the host's right and Stalin on his left, and a seating plan is attached.

All the speeches took the form of toasts, in the Russian custom set the night before. Roosevelt opened by proposing the toast to the King, a privilege he had asked as an old friend of George VI. Churchill praised Roosevelt as a defender of the weak and toasted Stalin as worthy of the name Stalin the Great. Stalin answered that the honors belonged to the Russian people, and that in Russia even cowards became heroes, while those who did not were killed. Boettiger notes a shared sense that a historic understanding, and lasting friendships, had been reached.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d475:
President Roosevelt sent a second message to Marshal Stalin on December 3, 1943, as the follow-up to the Tehran Conference continued. Roosevelt was by then at Cairo, preparing for the second conference there with Churchill. The State Department preserved the message in the Cairo-Tehran volume, alongside the day's other traffic.

Paired cables to the same leader on one day usually mean fast-moving business, and early December 1943 gave the alliance plenty of it. Roosevelt's exchanges with Stalin in this period set the tone for cooperation in the war's decisive year. Readers get the alliance's most sensitive channel, running at full speed just after its first summit.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d575:
Dean Acheson, Acting Secretary of State, recorded this memorandum on September 7, 1945. Acheson was minding the department while Secretary Byrnes attended the foreign ministers' meeting in London. The memorandum appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume.

Acheson would become one of the chief builders of the postwar order, and his acting-secretary papers show that order being improvised in its first week of peace. The London meeting was already exposing cracks among the wartime allies. For readers, the memorandum offers a front-row record from the moment the wartime coalition began turning into the Cold War's opposing camps.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d75: Roosevelt wrote to Secretary Hull on October 30, 1943, as the secretary prepared to leave Moscow. The letter is Document 75 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The Moscow agreements had to be turned into summit plans at once, and the president's letters that day pushed the work along. The catalog record names the two men and the date. The letter is part of the Foreign Relations series' Moscow closing papers.
frus-1944-quebec-d175:
At their afternoon meeting on September 12, 1944, the Combined Chiefs took up coordination with the Soviet Union. Sir Alan Brooke said he felt Stalin's offer should be dropped: missions already existed in Moscow, and the Russians need only appoint a suitable senior officer. Portal warned that exchange missions with field commanders would leak plans and gain nothing. The British recommendations were approved.

Zones of occupation in Germany proved harder. The chiefs agreed the question carried such serious political weight that they could recommend nothing without guidance from their governments. Britain wanted the northwest zone on military grounds. King suggested America could take the southwest if its troops could be supplied through north German ports. The chiefs decided to ask Roosevelt and Churchill for an early decision.
frus-1944-quebec-d275:
General Ismay sent Leahy a draft passage on September 15, 1944, built on an idea General Marshall had raised at that morning's meeting. The Combined Chiefs, the draft says, desired to record the Quebec Conference's main difficulty. It had been finding room and opportunity to deploy against Japan the massive forces every nation concerned was ardent to engage.

In colloquial language, the draft continues, it was a case of "standing room only," even before the curtain rang up. The chiefs made no recommendation on the subject in their final report. But including the thought in the communiqué, and at the closing press conference, would hearten world opinion and depress Japan. A draft communiqué filed with the letter matches the one actually issued.
frus-1944-quebec-d75:
Officials on the Working Security Committee prepared a memorandum dated August 30, 1944. The committee dealt with security questions in wartime planning. Its paper appears among the pre-conference records in the Quebec 1944 volume. The State Department published the volume after the war.

Committee papers like this one turned broad concerns into staff work. Planners weighed security needs as the war moved toward Germany. Their conclusions fed the briefings prepared for Quebec. For readers, the memorandum shows the middle layer of government at work. Specialists framed questions that cabinet officers and leaders would later decide.
frus-1945-50-intel-d175:
A letter dated 4 November 1946 links two senior offices. The sender was the Secretary of State’s Special Assistant for Research and Intelligence (Eddy). The reader was the Director of Central Intelligence (Vandenberg). It is document 175 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on intelligence for 1945 to 1950. The National Intelligence Authority, set up in January 1946, oversaw the Director of Central Intelligence and his Central Intelligence Group.

The text is one side of an exchange, set out in full under the writer's own name and title. Read in sequence, the letters show two offices testing how far each could push the other. The FRUS editors kept it because the chain of choices is not whole without it.
frus-1945-50-intel-d275:
The Intelligence Survey Group addressed a memorandum to the Executive Secretary of the National Security Council (Souers) on 13 May 1948. In the printed Foreign Relations series it is document 275, in the volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. It was the CIA's first full year, and the Council was setting the rules for both open analysis and secret work.

A short memo could set a meeting, kill a plan, or start one. This one played its part in that daily traffic. The points are stated once and left to stand; the file around it holds the answer they drew. Alone it is a page; in sequence it is evidence of how a state taught itself a new trade.
frus-1945-50-intel-d375:
A memorandum dated 18 March 1949 links two senior offices. The sender was the Assistant Director for Policy Coordination, Central Intelligence Agency (Wisner). The reader was the Under Secretary of State (Webb). The State Department prints it as document 375 in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. By then the Dulles Report was months old, and the argument had moved to putting its advice into practice.

Inside the government, memos were how business got done between meetings. One put the question and the facts in front of the reader at once. Its place in the file shows the matter at the moment it passed from one desk to the next. Kept with its neighbors in the volume, it shows the new system being built one dated paper at a time.
frus-1945-50-intel-d75:
McCarthy wrote to McCormack on 4 October 1945, the administration chief addressing the intelligence chief inside the State Department. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

Two officers of one department, dividing a new duty between them, write a special kind of paper. It is frank and practical, full of the small print of staff and space. This memorandum belongs to the office-building thread of the volume. Readers who follow it learn how the interim research and intelligence service was actually assembled in the autumn of 1945, desk by desk. Such papers rarely make the histories, yet without them the famous plans would have had no house to live in.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d175:
Washington told King Peter, through Ambassador Patterson, what it thought of the Tito–Subasic plan. The State Department's memorandum to the British Embassy of 23 December 1944 is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. Eden had suggested the step in a telegram to Halifax five days earlier.

Patterson is cleared to tell the King that the Department has studied the papers with attention. Their principles, taken as a whole, match those the United States holds in its own dealings. But so much turns on the goodwill and cooperation of the men named to run the new government that Washington will not judge the plan's chances. Whether it works in loyal practice, the memorandum implies, only the men themselves can show.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d275:
No linkage: that is the order Stettinius sent Harriman on 3 January 1945 about prisoners. His secret cable, number 18, is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. It answers the news that Soviet negotiators had been named for General Deane.

In any talks on repatriation, the Department is extremely anxious that two streams be kept apart. Americans found in German camps are one matter. Soviet nationals found among the German prisoners taken by American forces are another. Trouble has already arisen over who counts as a Soviet national. A few men taken fighting with the Germans bear Slavic names but disclaim Soviet nationality. Over eleven hundred Soviet nationals found in German ranks were handed to the Soviet authorities at a west coast port the week before.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d375:
Hiss took notes as Molotov answered the American report on Dumbarton Oaks at the plenary of February 7, 1945. The Soviet side, Molotov said, was satisfied with Stettinius's report. Certain questions had become much clearer after the explanations. Churchill's remarks had also drawn close Soviet attention.

The outcome, Molotov judged, would secure the unity of the three powers in guarding peace after the war. The Soviet aim all along, he said, was the greatest unity among the three on peace and security. The proposals, with the President's changes, would win cooperation from nations great and small. Hiss's shorthand catches Moscow warming to the world body.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d475:
London news fills these excerpts from Grew's cable of February 4, 1945. Winant had told the Soviet member of the European Advisory Commission of American acceptance, in principle, of five French proposals. They concerned French participation in the surrender, occupation, and control of Germany. The Soviet member thanked him for the advance notice and sought early instructions from Moscow.

Winant had also informed the Soviet and British members of American approval of the protocol on German zones. Further down, the cable turns to the Associated Nations. Medina in Venezuela, it notes, was somewhat taken aback by the President's letter, but appreciated the situation. The digest mixes summit questions with embassy detail.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d75:
Who would be invited to found the United Nations? Acting Secretary Stettinius put that question to the President on 15 November 1944. His memorandum, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, is titled “Invitations to the Conference and Initial Membership.” It records a sharp split with Moscow.

Two issues are set out. First, should only the thirty-five United Nations signatories be invited, or also nine associated nations from earlier conferences? Second, should the sixteen Soviet republics enter as original members, as Moscow demanded? The American position was to invite forty-four nations and refuse the sixteen republics. The British and Chinese stood with Washington on the invitations question.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d175:
The British Chiefs of Staff answered the last American points on the staff agenda in a memorandum dated June 29, 1945. The paper, C.C.S. 880/5, is document 175 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It replies to the U.S. memorandum of June 27 on the coming Anglo-American staff talks.

The British say their paper on command against Japan will include plans to reorganize command in the Southwest Pacific. They agree to put off discussion of Russian participation until after the talks with the Russians end. Papers will be swapped in advance where possible. But the British doubt they can ready their papers more than a few days before Terminal. Those papers cover their own role against Japan and command questions. One directive must wait on the talks themselves.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d275:
The Joint Civil Affairs Committee set out financial policy for Austria in an undated memorandum printed as document 275 in the Foreign Relations volume on Potsdam. The paper asks for decisions at government level so the military authorities in Austria can do their work.

No decision has been reached, the paper says, on whether Austria must pay reparations, or in what form. American policy favors a sound, united Austrian economy not dependent on Germany, and the form and amount of any reparations should serve that aim. Labor or money reparations would not; capital goods should be limited to items a stable economy can spare. The paper also urges encouraging Austria's private export trade, to divorce her economy from Germany's, and seeks agreement on economic disarmament and on coordination with the Control Council for Germany.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d375:
A late Soviet refusal is reported in Pauley's cable from Moscow of July 14, 1945. All members of the Reparations Commission had agreed on a statement of principles. Each was to submit it to his government for approval. Washington and London had accepted it. That day, though, Maisky said Moscow would not take the last sentence of paragraph eight.

The disputed sentence dealt with paying for imports. In working out Germany's economic balance, it said, means must be provided to pay for approved imports. That payment comes before reparations are taken from current output or stocks. Pauley answered that his government stands firm on the rule. Approved imports are a prior charge on approved exports.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d475: Bonomi called on Kirk in Rome on June 25, 1945. He had just given up the office of President of the Council. His subject was Allied troops in Italy. Their retention, he argued, was essential. It built the people's confidence that order inside the country would be kept. It also deterred foreign elements. Such elements might seek to break that order, by intrigue from within or by threats from without.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d575:
State Department staff wrote a top secret briefing paper on special Manchurian problems, dated July 3, 1945. It is document 575 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. It briefs the President on two linked issues: the port of Dairen and the Manchurian railways.

The paper traces Dairen's lease from Russia in 1898 to Japan in 1905. Japan stretched the lease to 99 years in 1915, a move China contests and the U.S. never accepted. If Russia joins the war on Japan, it will likely want Dairen kept a free port. The paper sees no bar to that if trade stays open to all, but backs China's claim to the land. A second part traces the Chinese Eastern Railway and the line south to Dairen and Port Arthur.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d675:
Acting Secretary Grew set out the U.S. terms for a Tangier settlement to Ambassador Caffery on July 13, 1945. The secret wire is document 675 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. It answers the French proposals sent by Villard on July 6.

Washington can accept the aims France states for the talks, Grew says. But the term international administration must not be read as the 1923 statute's own machine. The United States never adhered to that statute and cannot do so. A temporary administration much like it would suit Washington, though. U.S. nationals must hold a proper share in it, and Soviet nationals too if Moscow wishes. France may treat the 1923 statute as the legal basis on its side. Grew also proposes that any pact pledge a full conference within twelve months.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d75:
President Truman accepted Stalin's proposed start date for the Allied move into their German zones on June 18, 1945. His top secret telegram, number 297, is document 75 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Stalin had said mine clearing in Berlin would run to late June, and asked that the pullback begin July 1 instead of June 21.

Truman says he has ordered the American commanders to begin the movement on July 1, as Stalin asked. He assumes American troops will reach Berlin earlier, in enough strength to do their work preparing for the conference. A long editorial note explains the swap of messages behind the decision. The exchange fixed the ground on which the Potsdam meeting itself would stand.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1075:
Joseph Jacobs, the American mission chief in Albania, cabled Washington from Tirana on July 21, 1945. Albanian commanders had met in secret the night before over the Greek situation. They fear Greek forces, with quiet British backing, will stage border incidents. British troops might then be invited to occupy southern Albania to keep order.

Jacobs reports two recent clashes. On July 9, armed Greeks crossed near Konispol and tried to plant boundary markers on Albanian soil; shots drove them back. On July 12 and 13, Greek soldiers tried the same near Bilisht and were repelled. Yugoslavia is sending Albania ammunition and artillery. Jacobs cannot say which side starts the incidents, but he is sure they are happening.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1175:
The Acting Secretary of State wrote to Ambassador Armour in Spain on 16 July 1945, the day before Potsdam opened. Spain under Franco had stayed out of the war, but its regime was a leftover of the fascist age the Allies had just beaten. That made Spain an awkward open question.

At Potsdam the three powers would soon declare that Franco's Spain could not join the new United Nations. Washington's Madrid post had to be ready for that stand and its fallout. This cable shows the home office tasking its envoy on the summit's eve. It links a quiet post to the great talks about to begin.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1275:
The Joint Chiefs of Staff sent this message to the President on 16 July 1945, the day before the summit opened. The chiefs' word on the eve of the talks fixed the armed forces' stand for the trip. It reached Truman beside the war secretary's letters of the same day.

That date carries a hidden weight. In New Mexico, the first atomic device had just been tested in secret. The men writing and reading this message stood at the edge of a new kind of war. The paper itself is staff business at the highest level: the top brass addressing their commander as the peace talks began.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1375:
The British delegation put a proposal before the Potsdam Conference on 27 July 1945. Britain tabled fewer papers in this part of the volume than the Soviet or American sides. It is printed in volume two of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record of American diplomacy at Potsdam.

A British proposal two days after the change of prime minister carries extra interest. Attlee's new government had just taken over the delegation, and its papers show whether London's line shifted with its leaders. Readers can test that question here in the delegation's own words. The proposal also rounds out the record. With it, all three powers at Potsdam can be read stating their terms in this section of the volume.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-75:
Combined Chiefs of Staff minutes record a session on captured passenger shipping, held July 21, 1945. The top secret record is an unnumbered item in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. The seven captured German liners were again the bone of contention.

The chiefs first approved the conclusions of their 198th meeting. Sir Alan Brooke then stated the British position on the shipping papers. The U.S. amendments, he said with regret, were not acceptable to the British chiefs. The American view, as he summarized it, ran as follows. If the seven captured ships moved to the Pacific, they could make no more than one trip before December 31, 1945. If a review then reassigned them away from the United States, the Pacific assignment would prove uneconomical. Brooke said he appreciated the point, and the argument continued from there.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d775:
The Acting Secretary of State wrote to Byrnes at Potsdam on July 19, 1945, in document 775. Grew's letters formed a near-daily bridge to Washington. This one dates from the conference's first week. It was printed in the second Potsdam volume of Foreign Relations of the United States.

Home-office letters mixed the urgent with the routine. Both kinds mattered to a secretary abroad. Readers see Grew sorting the Department's world for a busy chief. The document also shows the two men's rhythm settling in. By July 19 the channel carried trust as much as news.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d875: British delegates at Potsdam offered this short draft of Article 19 of the Economic Principles, filed with the July 23, 1945 papers. It says that after reparations, Germans must be left enough to live without outside help. Means must also be provided to pay for imports approved by the governments concerned. Proceeds from exports of current production and stocks would be used first for those imports.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d975:
Edwin Pauley and William Clayton sent this memorandum to General Clay on August 1, 1945. They ask him to press the Control Council to adopt an attached principle on Allied and neutral property in Germany. It would supplement the economic principles and the reparations agreement just approved.

The principle says foreign ownership must not block removals under the agreement. Allied governments would file statements of their nationals' property, and their agents would get access to inspect it. Where owners wish, goods could move without change of title. Otherwise, Reichsmark deposits would be paid and settled in foreign exchange. Neutral owners would receive Reichsmark deposits as compensation.
frus-1958-60v09-d175:
A memorandum of conversation records the Western leaders at Paris as the 1960 summit collapsed. President Eisenhower, Prime Minister Macmillan, and President de Gaulle weigh how to end the meeting with dignity. Khrushchev had demanded an apology for the U-2 flight.

De Gaulle offers to call the formal session for the agreed agenda. If Khrushchev stays away, his refusal ends the summit. Eisenhower admits he nearly lost his temper at the personal attack. The talk shows three allies scripting an exit. Pride, not terms, was the last item on the table.
gao-gaoreports-b-295375:
The file is B-295375, dated February 10, 2005: FR Countermeasures, Inc., brought the protest. The Army had awarded contracts for M206 and MJU7 aircraft countermeasure flares to Esterline Armtec and Kilgore Flares. The firm attacked its neutral rating of unknown on the on-time delivery subfactor. GAO denied the protest in part and dismissed it in part. The solicitation let the government weigh delivery records up to the time of award. It did not require the government to do so.

The flares defend aircraft against heat-seeking missiles. The Army sought 1,084,000 M206 flares and 557,760 MJU7 flares under the solicitation. A split award was among the outcomes allowed.
gao-gaoreports-b-296875:
J.A. Farrington Janitorial protested an Air Force award for grounds work in GAO decision B-296875, dated October 18, 2005. The winner was Roberts Treescaping. The site was Buckley Air Force Base in Colorado. The buy was set aside for HUBZone small firms. The firm's low price bid was cut as too low to trust.

GAO sustained the protest in part. The call held no price realism test. A low price call for a set-price bid goes to fitness. Fitness for a small firm must go to the Small Business Administration. Past work marks for the winner were also thin. Small past jobs were not shown to match this large job.
gao-gaoreports-b-298975:
Stewart Distributors protested a Veterans Affairs award to Balfurd, Inc. The contract covered bulk laundry and linen services. The work serves the VA Medical Center in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. GAO decided B-298975 on January 17, 2007.

The agency had cast the firm's proposal out as technically unfit. Its bid did not clearly pledge to meet the stated quality bars. In a best-value buy, that clarity counts. GAO found the rejection fair on the bid text. A firm must state its pledge to meet core terms in plain form. Vague words leave the agency to guess. That guesswork can sink a bid. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-299175:
Geo-Seis Helicopters, Inc. protested a Navy award to Presidential Airways, Inc. The Military Sealift Command ran the buy. The contract covered commercial helicopter vertical replenishment services. GAO ruled in B-299175 and B-299175.2 on March 5, 2007.

One claim faulted a late final revision by the winner. The officer had stretched the closing time to let it land. GAO found that step fair, since it widened rivalry. The best-value call also stood up. The two bids scored as technical equals. The firm's stronger past record did not offset the winner's lower price. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-306475:
Recovery of election grant funds is the subject of this GAO letter, B-306475, dated January 30, 2006. The Help America Vote Act of 2002 funds election reform in the states. Auditors had flagged some costs in California as barred or lacking proof. The Election Assistance Commission asked how recovery works. Its query turned on section 902(c) of the Act.

That clause speaks of a finding by the Comptroller General. GAO held no such finding must come first. The agency that paid the funds may act on flagged costs at once. It need not wait for the Comptroller General to rule. The letter speeds the path to fix bad costs. It also keeps audit findings from stalling in a queue.
gao-gaoreports-b-306975:
Advance pay for records storage is approved in this GAO decision, B-306975, dated February 27, 2006. The National Archives runs records centers for other agencies. Agencies pay a monthly charge for storage and linked work. The Archives bills at the start of the month on a best guess. It then adjusts the next bill to match real costs.

A 1999 funds law lets agencies pay in advance to the fund. GAO had no bar to the guess-and-adjust billing plan. One limit guards the fiscal year line. Extra cash paid for September may not roll into October bills. The Archives must return that cash to the paying agency.
gao-gaoreports-b-311275:
B.R. Hardison saw his protest thrown out; the GAO decision is B-311275, dated May 29, 2008. He spoke for drug store staff at a small veterans clinic in Tennessee. The shop has four staff in all. The office moved to buy drug services from firms. He said the shift skipped the A-76 race the rules call for. Wait times at the shop had grown long by then.

GAO dismissed the protest. No state job is touched by the shift here. That gap strips the staff voice of a stake to sue. The A-76 race is not a must for tasks of fewer than 10 staff.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-175:
Anti-Drug Media Campaign, GAO-05-175 of March 31, 2005, follows the cash in a national push to keep youth off drugs. Congress has put over $1 billion into ads and outreach since 1998. A Senate panel feared too much cash went to hired help, not to ad time and space. It told GAO to trace where the funds went.

GAO lists the work hired firms and their sub-firms did for the push. It gives the sums set for each kind of work. Most funds went to buy media time and space after all, the title finds. A wide range of support work took the rest.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-275:
Defense Logistics, GAO-05-275 of April 8, 2005, digs into why U.S. troops in Iraq went short of key gear. GAO had flagged spare part gaps in December 2003. This study widens the lens. It covers want from October 2002 to September 2004. Nine goods, picked from war lessons and unit reports, stand in for the whole flow.

GAO asks what ran short and how the gaps hurt work in the field. It asks which flaws in the supply web fed the gaps. It asks what the Pentagon has done to get key goods on time, now and for the next war. Steps are still owed, the title says.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-375:
Preventing Nuclear Smuggling, GAO-05-375 of March 31, 2005, grades a bid to scan ship crates for bomb stuff at the source. About 7 million crates reach U.S. ports each year. A bomb or its parts could ride in one. Since 2003, the Energy Department has set scan gear at key foreign ports through its Megaports plan. Top ports were to come first.

GAO asks how far the set-up has got at those top ports. It prices the work now and in years to come. It names the snags of work on foreign soil, from talks to power and staff. Gains are thin so far, the title finds.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-575:
Building Afghan army and police forces is tracked in GAO report GAO-05-575, released on June 30, 2005. After decades of war, Afghanistan had no army and no working police. In April 2002 the United States and partner nations agreed to rebuild five parts of its security sector. The United States leads the army effort and has given about $3.3 billion. It has added over $800 million to the German-led police effort.

By March 2005 the Defense Department had trained more than 18,300 Afghan combat troops. That is over 42 percent of the planned army of 43,000. Training sped up greatly in 2004. Equipping those troops has lagged, though. Support bodies, such as a logistics command, are behind, and plans for them are vague. Germany and the United States had trained more than 35,000 police by January 2005.  Police stations lack gear and repairs, and mentors in the field have barely begun. No full cost or finish plan exists for the police.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-775:
Military supply flow is the subject of GAO-05-775, a report from August 11, 2005. Supply flaws dating to the Persian Gulf War slowed support to troops. The Defense Department named a single command as process owner for distribution. It also issued a new logistics strategy. GAO checked the new structure and strategy. It tracked the status and timelines of key fix-it projects.

GAO found real steps forward, but a basic flaw remains. No one can say who holds final authority to drive system-wide fixes. A draft order naming the owner's powers sat unapproved for almost 2 years. Two top offices read the owner's mandate in clashing ways. The strategy also lacks a clear vision to align future work. GAO urged steps to lock in the gains made.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-875:
A $7 billion revision at the housing insurer is explained in GAO-05-875, dated September 2, 2005. The Federal Housing Administration backs private home loans. Its main fund runs at a profit and pays its own way. At the end of fiscal year 2003, the agency revised the fund's outlook down by $7 billion. Congress asked GAO what drove the change. GAO traced the loan traits behind it.

GAO found higher claims drove the revision most. Actual claims in fiscal year 2003 beat estimates for most loan groups, by twice as much in some cases. Early payoffs also beat estimates for every group. Both drain the fund: claims paid, premiums refunded, and future premiums lost. Looser underwriting, private rivals, and more down payment aid may explain the surge, GAO said. Steps taken so far may not turn the trend.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-275:
Trust in energy price figures is the theme of GAO-06-275, a report issued on December 15, 2005. Gas and power markets have shifted from regulated monopolies to open trading. Private firms publish price indices built from deals that traders report by choice. Buyers and investors steer real money by those figures. During the 2000-2001 Western energy crisis, some traders lied about prices to bend the indices for gain. GAO asked what federal steps have been taken to clean up the indices. It also asked whether those steps rebuilt trust among market users.

Federal regulators tightened rules on price reporting after the scandal. They gained new power to punish false reports. GAO tested whether traders and other users now trust the figures more. Trust is the hinge: an index that users doubt cannot guide a fair market. The report weighs law, enforcement, and industry habit together.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-375:
Paper files by the tens of millions slowed immigration decisions. On March 31, 2006, report GAO-06-375 reviewed an automation effort at U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services. The agency relies on about 55 million paper files. These alien files, or A-Files, hold records used to judge applications for status and other benefits. A near-term scanning program would cost about $190 million over eight years.

GAO asked whether the agency was managing the automation work well. The scanning plan would store and share images of the paper files. A larger long-term effort was being rethought during a broad agency overhaul. GAO found the near-term effort needed better planning. Readers get the costs, scope, and risks.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-475:
Stun devices on airliners raise a hard trade between safety and security. GAO's May 26, 2006 report, GAO-06-475, reviews less-than-lethal weapons on commercial aircraft. The Transportation Security Administration may approve carrier requests to carry such devices. Electric stun devices are the main case. One carrier had received approval since the 2001 terror attacks. Reports of injuries after stun device use raised concern.

GAO asked what federal analyses judge these devices' safety and effect on board aircraft. It checked controls for steady, timely review of carrier requests. More study and better controls are needed if interest resumes, GAO said. Readers get the evidence base and review process.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-575:
Auditors inside the United Nations depend on the body they audit for money. Report GAO-06-575, issued April 25, 2006, reviews the UN Office of Internal Oversight Services. Funding arrangements impede the office's independence, GAO found. Reliance on other entities for funds could infringe that independence. The arrangements also limit the office's freedom to shift resources to high-risk areas. International standards require auditor independence.

GAO found the office has not fully met key parts of those standards. Gaps include a risk management framework and reporting on overall risk. Coordination among UN oversight bodies is also unclear. The United States backs stronger oversight but holds limited influence. Readers get a detailed standards check.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-675:
The move to a new Internet addressing system is tracked in GAO-06-675, a GAO report dated June 30, 2006. Internet Protocol version 4 gives each device an address so data can move across networks. Its address supply may not keep up with global growth in users and devices. Version 6 was built to solve that problem. Federal agencies were told to plan their shift to the new system.

GAO found that agencies had taken early planning steps. As of April 2006, almost all of the 24 major agencies had named an official to lead the shift. But ten agencies had not yet set transition policies or ways to enforce them. GAO warned that key challenges remained before the government could move in full.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-75:
Health care funding for United States island territories is studied in GAO-06-75, a report GAO issued on October 14, 2005. Five insular areas are covered: American Samoa, the Northern Mariana Islands, Guam, Puerto Rico, and the Virgin Islands. Federal health programs help fund care for their over 4 million residents. But the programs run under different rules there than in the states. Legal caps on federal payments are one such difference.

GAO found that several federal agencies fund health services in the islands. The methods used to divide funds differ from those used for the states. GAO also identified multiple factors behind the gap in per-person spending between the areas and the states. Income, health needs, and program design all play a role. The report gives lawmakers a clear map of those differences.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-775:
Counting residents who lack legal status is the puzzle behind GAO-06-775, which GAO issued on September 29, 2006. Lawmakers need facts on the undocumented population, its size, traits, costs, and contributions. Direct survey questions fail, because respondents fear exposure. In 1998, GAO devised a grouped answers approach, which lets people answer in a way that masks their own status. This report reviews work to develop that method further.

GAO found that experts seemed to accept grouped answers questions if a private firm fielded them. Various tests were still needed before a full survey could run. About 6,000 foreign-born respondents would be needed for reasonably precise estimates. The most efficient field strategy, though, did not seem feasible. The report is a candid look at measuring a hidden population.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-275:
The Smithsonian signed a 30-year television deal that alarmed documentary filmmakers. GAO reviewed the pact in GAO-07-275, a report dated December 15, 2006. The deal with Showtime creates an on-demand channel. Filmmakers feared limits on using museum collections. GAO checked how the deal was negotiated and priced. It studied what rights changed hands. It also weighed effects on outside producers.

The museum largely followed its own contracting rules, GAO found. It had sounded out 18 media firms in 2002. Only one showed interest at first, and that deal collapsed. The venture holds semi-exclusive rights to some museum content. Minimum payments start at $500,000 a year and climb into millions. The channel could reach over 31 million homes by 2010. The museum's study of harm to filmmakers was flawed, GAO said. Its data were incomplete and its tests too simple. GAO urged clearer filming guidance.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-375:
Five years after the September 11 attacks, GAO took stock of the defenses built since. The survey is GAO-07-375, dated January 24, 2007. It covers aviation security first. It then covers visa screening and border programs. It closes with cross-cutting strategy problems. The report synthesizes work by GAO, inspectors general, and the 9/11 Commission. Over 75 earlier recommendations are still being carried out. GAO makes no new ones here.

Passenger screening has clearly improved, GAO found. Names are matched against a merged watch list. Select passengers get added scrutiny. But the security agency still has not taken over name matching from airlines. That takeover is years behind the mandate. International flights can take off before border matching finishes. Visa interviews face long waits at some posts. Risk methods vary across the homeland security department. GAO urges continued federal action on the gaps.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-75:
Child welfare services across the states are studied in GAO-07-75, dated October 6, 2006. States must keep children safe, well, and in lasting homes. Despite large federal and state spending, states miss some outcome goals. GAO surveyed agencies in all 50 states, the District of Columbia, and Puerto Rico. It visited five states and read laws and reports. It asked what blocks states most, and whether federal help aids their work.

States named three top blocks. Mental health and drug treatment services fall short for parents and children. Caseloads per worker run too high, and caseworkers leave too fast. Homes are hard to find for children with special needs. New worries include drug exposure and shifting populations. GAO urged the Health and Human Services Department to centralize program facts for states. It also urged full, accurate records of the help it gives. The department backed the data points but not the central plan.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-875:
Detention standards for immigrants are examined in GAO-07-875, dated July 6, 2007. Immigration and Customs Enforcement held about 283,000 people in fiscal year 2006. That is up from about 95,000 in fiscal year 2001. GAO visited 23 detention sites of varied size and type. It checked how sites meet national detention standards. It also reviewed the agency's inspection process. Detainee complaints about conditions form the third part of the study.

Free phone access for detainees failed widely, GAO found. At 16 of 17 sites with the pro bono phone system, calls often would not connect. Posted phone lists were stale; one consulate list was six years old. Of 30 consulate numbers GAO dialed, 9 were wrong. The phone firm's own data had shown failures for five years. The agency said it did not know the scale of the problem. Nine sites broke other standards as well. GAO made seven recommendations, and the department agreed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-375:
In GAO report GAO-08-375, dated March 6, 2008, GAO looks at construction for the Grow the Force expansion. The plan adds more than 74,000 Army soldiers by 2013 and 27,000 Marines by 2011. The Defense Department expects to need more than $17 billion for facilities to house the growth.

The Army and Marine Corps used their normal project process, but on a squeezed clock: the Army took about 2 months and the Marines 6 months, against a typical 2 years. Most projects fit the initiative: 68 of 69 Army projects, worth over $2.3 billion, and 37 of 49 Marine Corps projects, worth over $665 million. GAO found 1 Army project and 12 Marine Corps projects that fixed old shortfalls and did not truly support the growth plan. The department disputed that judgment.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-75:
Some disability checks must be redone over time to confirm a veteran still qualifies. The Veterans Benefits Administration did about 17,700 such rechecks in fiscal year 2005. GAO-08-75, dated December 6, 2007, tests the controls and data behind that recheck process.

Software never prompts staff to set a date for the next recheck, so some cases may never get one. When staff cancel a recheck after a first look, no one tracks or double-checks the call. Data flaws also blur how fast offices work. A new claims system will track cancellations, GAO notes, but still lacks the date prompt. Fixes are proposed.
gitagovinda-arnold-1875:
Edwin Arnold sang Jayadeva's Gitagovinda in English in 1875 as The Indian Song of Songs, a rendering of love and faith. Jayadeva's twelfth-century Sanskrit lyric drama tells of Radha and Krishna: their longing, their parting, and their reunion in the spring woods. Songs meant for singing carry the lovers' moods, while Krishna's godhood shines through the human play of desire.

Hindu devotion cherishes the poem as scripture set to music, sung in temples and festivals to this day. Arnold, famed across the world for The Light of Asia, gave its erotic mysticism a lush Victorian voice. His rendering remains the best known English path into Jayadeva's masterpiece for new readers.
guyon-short-method-1775:
Madame Guyon, Jeanne-Marie de la Motte Guyon, wrote her Short and Easy Method of Prayer in France in the late 1600s. It became one of the most read books of devotion in Europe. The text here is the English version by A. W. Marston, from the Paris edition of 1790, printed at London in a combined volume with Spiritual Torrents. Its first chapter promises that prayer is possible at all times, by the most simple.

Guyon teaches degrees of prayer, rising to the prayer of simplicity, in which the soul rests quiet before God and lets words fall away. Church authorities of her day jailed and condemned her for these teachings, which they called Quietism. Her book outlived the quarrel. Plain readers in many tongues have used it as a ladder into silent prayer, and it remains the classic of its kind.
heckethorn-secret-societies-1875:
Charles William Heckethorn cast a wide net in The Secret Societies of All Ages and Countries in 1875. No guild or cult of note slips past his sweep. The book starts with the rites of Egypt, Greece, and Rome. It runs on to the groups of his own Victorian day.

Knights Templar, Rosicrucians, and Freemasons take long runs of text. So do the Carbonari, the Mafia's kin, and odd cults of the East. Heckethorn tells of signs, oaths, and the ends each group sought. The book is a vast store house of tales on hid groups.
helsinki-final-act-1975:
Thirty-five nations signed the Helsinki Final Act in Finland in 1975, closing a long conference on security in Europe. The United States, Canada, the Soviet Union, and nearly all European states took part. The act was not a treaty, but a set of political promises meant to ease Cold War tensions.

The West accepted Europe's postwar borders as settled, which Moscow had long wanted. In return, the Soviet bloc promised to respect human rights, free movement, and the flow of information. Dissidents across Eastern Europe seized on those promises, forming Helsinki watch groups that pressed their governments to keep them. Historians credit that pressure with helping to loosen the Soviet grip and end the Cold War.
history-of-the-united-netherlands-from-t:
Chapter forty of John Lothrop Motley's History of the United Netherlands divides its scene between Ostend and Ireland. The siege of Ostend is protracted into its second year, consuming men and money. Meanwhile Spain invades Ireland, landing troops to help the rebels against Elizabeth. The Spanish commander ends glad enough to sign a capitulation, Motley writes.

Transports provided by the English general carry the invaders home, a much discomfited man returning to Spain. He had proclaimed he would rescue Hibernia from the evil demon; he rescued nothing. Motley enjoys the parallel: Spain overreaching at both ends of Europe at once. The States meanwhile press Maurice to raise the siege and drive the archduke into the sea. This chapter shows the war's widening geography, from Flemish dunes to Irish bogs, in one imperial design.
how-to-read-character-a-new-illustrated-:
Samuel R Wells issued this illustrated handbook of character reading in an edition of 1875. It joins phrenology, the skull's organs, to physiognomy, the face's signs. Wells opens with the brain's structure, in simple terms. Two substances, folded deep, make up the cerebral globe, he writes.

Faculties are taken one by one, with examples from life and letters. Comparison, the figure-making power, is found large in the French and Irish, he claims.
