Thomas Moore's harp song illustrates its use in verse. National traits and named poets season the science. Buyers got a chart and a method for sizing up strangers at a glance.
hutchinson-spirit-of-masonry-1775:
William Hutchinson, a Durham solicitor and Mason, published The Spirit of Masonry in London in 1775. The book gathers his moral and elucidatory lectures on the Craft. Hutchinson recasts Masonry as a system of morality taught through symbols, a presentation meant for a skeptical age that mocked secret societies.

His lectures explain the lodge's furniture, jewels, and ceremonies as lessons in virtue. The approach founded Masonic philosophical apologetics, the Craft's reasoned defense of itself. Hutchinson writes for brethren and for curious outsiders alike. His Masonry asks to be judged as moral teaching in allegorical dress. The Spirit of Masonry gave English lodges a philosophy, and later lecturers built on his readings for a century.
indian-poetry-arnold-1875:
Edwin Arnold published Indian Poetry in 1875, gathering his verse renderings from Sanskrit sources. Its centerpiece, The Indian Song of Songs, was the first English verse translation of Jayadeva's Gita Govinda. That twelfth-century poem sings the love of Krishna and Radha in songs of great sweetness and daring.

Arnold adds two books from the Mahabharata, wise sayings from the Hitopadesa, and other Oriental poems. His light, musical English aimed to make India's classics sing for Victorian readers. Arnold later won wide fame with The Light of Asia, his life of the Buddha in verse. This earlier volume shows the same gift at work. The Gutenberg text is ebook 25965.
jevons-money-mechanism-exchange-1875:
Jevons published Money and the Mechanism of Exchange in 1875, a short classic on what money is and how it works. He wrote it for general readers as much as for students, in the clear style that marked his best work. At the time, banking crises and currency debates made the subject urgent on both sides of the Atlantic.

The book explains why barter fails, what makes a good currency material, and how coins, notes, and cheques each do money's work. Jevons treats the standard of value, minting, and paper money with calm precision. Generations of students learned the subject from these chapters. The primer is still quoted for its clarity, and historians count it the clearest short book on money in English. It shows a founder of modern economics writing at the height of his powers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aaron-moses-ben:
Aaron Moses ben Mordecai was one of the few cabalistic writers of recent times in East Prussia. His book "Nishmat Shelomoh Mordecai" was printed at Johannisberg in 1852. He named it in memory of his son, who died in early childhood.

The title page calls the book a commentary on Luzzatto's "Ḥoḳer u-Meḳubbal," and that text is printed in the volume. In fact, Aaron used the famous name to win readers, since the Cabala was losing ground in Poland. His real subject is the "'Eẓ Ḥayyim" of Ḥayyim Vital. He also wrote a commentary on the Midrash Tanḥuma, left unprinted.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abidan-father-i: Abidan was a son of Gideoni. After the Exodus he stood as chief of the tribe of Benjamin. That is the one fact this very short entry gives for him. He is named in that role across the book of Numbers. The entry cites chapter 1, verse 11, chapter 2, verse 22, and chapter 10, verse 24. It also cites chapter 7, verses 60 and 65, where his part in the offerings of the chiefs is part of the same record of the camp.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abraham-ben-jos: Abraham ben Joseph of Orleans was a French Talmudist of the twelfth century. He lived at Orleans and perhaps at London. He counts among the older tosafists, and the Tosafot quote his Talmud readings several times. He was father of three daughters. His son-in-law was Judah ben Isaac of Paris, called Sir Leon, who lived from 1166 to 1224. That link makes Abraham a peer of Rabbenu Tam. Jacobs suggested he may be the Abraham fil Rabbi Joce of English records.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-adbeel-775: Adbeel is a name in a family list, and the entry says no more than that. It stands among the sons of Ishmael in Genesis xxv. 13. The same list in I Chronicles i. 29 names him again. The hosted text gives no acts, no dates, and no kin of his own beyond that list. A reader learns where the name can be found in the Bible. The entry does not turn him into a figure with a story, and no story is told here.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-afanasyev-chuzh: Alexander Stepanovich Afanasyev-Chuzhbinski was a Christian Russian author and student of folk life. He lived from 1817 to 1875. He was a fair minded writer who did right by the Jews. His book of travels in south Russia came out in two volumes in 1861-63. It gives a true picture of Jewish life in that region. It also defends the Jews against the charges of the bigoted crowd. The hosted text gives his dates, his field, and that one work with its stance toward its Jewish subjects.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-albas-moses-ben: Moses ben Maimon Albas was a cabalist of the sixteenth century. He lived in northwest Africa. His work is called "Hekal ha-Kodesh," the Holy Temple. He began it in 1575. It is a commentary on the prayer-book, built from the Zohar and other cabalistic books. The work was printed at Amsterdam in 1653, long after his time. Jacob Sasportas wrote the introduction to that edition.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alexandrian-shi: Alexandrian ships are named several times in the Mishnah, as vessels used by Jews. They are described as carrying large tanks of drinking-water for long voyages. Their trade was grain, from Egypt to Rome. Lucian describes one such ship, the "Isis." She was a three-masted vessel, 180 feet long. Her beam was more than 45 feet, and her hold ran 44 feet deep. Greek and Roman writers often mention these great grain ships. The entry points to notes on the Acts verse about such a ship.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-almanac-1275:
Almanac names a yearly book built on the calendar. Among Jews the head of the Sanhedrin once fixed the year. He heard men who had seen the new moon. Their words were checked with close care. Slowly that craft grew into a written science. The Hebrew word for the book means a tablet.

A full Jewish almanac lists more than dates. It gives the weekly Torah part for each Sabbath. It gives feasts, fasts, and the new moon times. Print spread the form far and wide. The 1800s added essays and tales to the lists. Long lists of almanacs by town close the entry.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ambron-ambran-o: Ambron is an Italian family known since 1492. In that year its line left Spain for Italy. The entry lists the men of the name in Rome. Shem-Tob shows in 1539 and Zerahiah in 1536. Judah ben Shem-Tob shows in 1550. Jacob led a charity body in 1618. Gabriel and Baruch show early in the next century. The last man named is Hezekiah ben Gabriel. He paid to print a prayer-book at Venice in 1775.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-anath-from-the-:
Anath was an old war goddess of the west Semites. Town names in Palestine still bear her name. Beth-Anath is one such town name in the land. Anathoth, the birth town of Jeremiah, may be one too. Those names may date from Canaanite times. Her name shows on one of the Amarna tablets.

Art shows her armed for war on each side. A helm, a shield, and a spear mark her kit. A swung battle-ax fills her left hand. One late image sets her on a lion. That beast drives home her warlike bent. One bold read of Hosea is weighed and doubted. That read would make her a name for God.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-antibi-abraham-: Abraham Antibi, that is, Abraham of Ain Tab, was chief rabbi at Aleppo. He died on March 13, 1858. His book of responsa, Ohel Yesharim, The Tent of the Righteous, follows the order of the four Turim, Jacob ben Asher's legal code. It was published at Leghorn in 1843. The short entry backs the record with five standard works, among them Benjacob's treasury of books and Steinschneider's notes in the Jewish Quarterly Review.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aquilino-raffae:
Raffaele Aquilino was an Italian apostate who renounced his religion in 1545, eight years before the public burning of the Talmud at Rome in 1553. Steinschneider, the entry says, deduces from a passage in his Trattato Pio that he was one of those who denounced Hebrew books.

The historian Joseph ha-Kohen names three such apostates of that affair. Aquilino may be the worst of them, Ananel di Foligno, the entry conjectures. His Trattato Pio, five articles for the Christian faith against Hebrew stubbornness, was printed twice at Pesaro, in 1571 and in 1581. A second anti-Jewish work in manuscript, Magen David, is also ascribed to him, though the entry reports doubts about that link.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aram-naharaim-t:
Aram-Naharaim is a region the Bible names six times, and its borders are ill defined, the entry says. The Authorized Version renders it Mesopotamia. In the title of Psalm 60 and in First Chronicles it means the land beyond the Euphrates.

Judges tells of its king invading Palestine. Genesis calls the region of Haran by this name, and Deuteronomy calls Pethor, Balaam's home, a city of it. Names on Egyptian and Assyrian records place such a city near the Euphrates from the fifteenth to the ninth century B.C. The name means Aram of the two rivers, but which two rivers is disputed. The entry leans to scholars who call the dual form a fiction and locate the land west of the Euphrates.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aristotle-in-je:
Medieval Jewish thought was ruled for centuries by Aristotle, whose books reached Jewish readers in Arabic dress. Translators such as Hunain ibn Ishak, who lived from 809 to 873, and his son turned Greek and Syrian texts into Arabic. Jews across the Arabic-speaking world studied them closely. Abraham ibn Daud, writing in 1160, was the first Jewish philosopher to grant Aristotle full supremacy.

Earlier masters used him with care. Saadia Gaon knew the writings well yet attacked the claim that the world had no beginning, since it clashes with creation in the Bible. Maimonides, who lived from 1135 to 1204, followed Aristotle on nature below the moon but set revelation above him on God and the heavens. The entry follows this balance through later ages, as Platonism and the Cabala slowly pushed Aristotle back.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-asaph-1875:
Asaph is a name shared by several men, and this entry sorts them. One fathered Joah, the recorder at King Hezekiah's court. One kept the forests of King Artaxerxes in the time of Nehemiah. A third points onward to Asaph ben Berechiah. Last and largest stands the Asaph of the singers, whose name heads twelve psalms, Psalm 50 and Psalms 73 through 83.

In Ezra and Nehemiah, written about 400 B.C., the singers are called sons of Asaph and stand apart from the Levites. The chronicler, about 250 B.C., makes them Levites and sets Asaph beside David as founder of a singers' guild. Three such guilds are named, traced to Asaph, Heman, and Ethan. The entry shows the figure growing as the books get later.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ashkenazi-joshu:
Joshua Heshel ben Meshullam Ashkenazi was a Russian Talmudist and rabbi of the nineteenth century. From 1852 until his death he served as rabbi of Lublin. His father had held the post before him, and his cousin Baerush Ashkenazi after the father. He died at Lublin on February 10, 1867.

The community owed him much, the entry says, for he worked without rest for its spiritual and material welfare. His house stood open to every needy person. His giving won him honor from Christian fellow citizens as well, and the government made him an honorary citizen, a rank carrying set privileges. He left ten works on haggadic and halakic subjects, all destroyed in a fire at Grodno. Some of his legal answers survive inside his cousin's book.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-avila-eliezer-b:
Eliezer b. Samuel de Avila was a rabbi at Rabat, Morocco, and an author of rabbinical works. He was born in 1714 and died at Rabat on Feb. 7, 1761. He came of a famed scholarly family. His father, his grandfather, and his uncle Ḥayyim ibn Attar were all noted Talmudists. Like his uncle, he longed to settle in Jerusalem, but plague and famine in Morocco left him without the means.

Avila wrote from his sixteenth year on. Four of his books came out after his death, all at Leghorn. They hold new readings on Talmudic treatises, a work on the rules of the Law, and thirty-six legal answers. His answers carry useful facts about Jewish life in Morocco. Palestinian scholars who met him gave him the title Ner ha-Ma'arabi, Light of the West. Among Moroccan scholars his love of close case argument made him a rare figure.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-baba-buch-2275:
The Baba Buch is a Judæo-German rendering of a knight's tale. Elijah Levita adapted it from an Italian version of the old English romance of Sir Bevis of Hamton. The Italian book, "Buovo d'Antona," was a best seller of its day. No fewer than thirty editions of it are known. Levita made his version in 1507.

Why Levita made the translation is not clear, the entry says. It may have been a pastime, or it may have served a mission aim among German Jews. In any case the book caught on. It was printed again and again, at Prague, Frankfort, Amsterdam, and Wilhelmsdorf. It became the one romance open to many Jewish women, who knew it as the Bovo Buch. The puzzle of its source stood until 1863, when Zedner proved its path from England through Italy.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bar-yokni-writt:
Bar Yokni is a giant bird named several times in the Talmud. An authority of the start of the third century tells wonders of it. Once, one of its eggs fell from a height and flooded sixty cities and broke three hundred cedar-trees. Two other passages use egg and bird as measures of huge size. The Talmud takes Bar Yokni for the ostrich of Job xxxix. 13.

The bird lifts its egg and flies with it high in the air to its nest, where it sets the egg gently down. The name means "Son of the Nest," from an Arabic word for nest. It may rest on a belief that the female ostrich does not sit on her eggs. One writer alone, Elijah Levita, says the bird was kept as food for the pious in Messianic times.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-baumgarten-isid:
Isidor Baumgarten was a Hungarian jurist born on March 27, 1850, at Budapest. After his law degree he lived abroad for some years. He joined the bar in 1882 and lectured on criminal law at the University of Budapest from 1885.

Baumgarten then served as a prosecutor, a judge, and from 1896 as district attorney. In 1898 he became a division chief in the Ministry of Justice. He helped shape new court procedure and penal law debates. His books treat legal attempts, bigamy, and arrest before trial. The Hungarian Academy of Sciences praised his first book, on the doctrine of the attempt, in high terms.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-behrend-henry-2:
Henry Behrend was a physician and communal worker born in Liverpool in 1828. He died in London on Nov. 28, 1893. He trained at University College Hospital in London and at Manchester, joining the Royal College of Surgeons in 1850.

Behrend practiced first in Liverpool, then in London to wide demand. He wrote on cholera and on how diseases pass from animals to man, and he defended Jewish slaughter rules in print. His greatest service, the entry says, was leading the Jews' Hospital and Orphan Asylum at Norwood as its president from 1871. He lectured before learned societies on medical and on ancient subjects alike, as the entry adds at its close.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ben-hur-2875: Ben-Hur appears in a single brief notice as a commissariat officer of Solomon. His post, the entry states, lay in the hill country of Ephraim, citing I Kings iv. 8. Nothing more is given about his life, family, or acts. The entry is a short identification only, and a reader gets the office, the district, and the biblical citation, with no added story or detail.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-benjamin-b-meir: Benjamin ben Meir ha-Levi of Nuremberg was rabbi at Salonica at the start of the sixteenth century. Though German by birth and a descendant of Jacob Molin, he won high esteem from the Spanish and Portuguese Jews of that city. All its Jews sent him on a mission to Constantinople. Some of his rulings survive in the responsa sets of his time. He also wrote notes on words in the German prayer book, printed at Salonica, and verses of mourning after the great fire there in 1553.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-berkamani-or-ba: Berḳamani, also spelled Barkamani, was a physician and author, most likely of the first half of the thirteenth century. He wrote a treatise on hygiene in ten chapters for an emir. A copy of that medical work rests in manuscript in the Imperial Library of Berlin. The entry reports a full account of the manuscript by Steinschneider. It also weighs, and rejects, a claim that Berḳamani was the same man as a writer of the twelfth century. His grasp of medical writing marks him as a working physician.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bessarabia-2375:
Bessarabia was a government in southwest Russia. It lay between the Pruth, the Danube, and the Dniester. In 1897 it held 1,936,392 people. Of these, 225,637 were Jews. That was 11.65 per cent of the total. Jews had first come from Poland and Germany. They arrived in the sixteenth century.

The entry describes Jewish work in trade, crafts, and farming. About 20,976 Jews were artisans in 1898. Others farmed in colonies founded from 1836 to 1854. The May Laws of 1882 hurt many families badly. Local officials barred Jews from many towns. The entry also covers timber trade petitions by Austrian Jews.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bibliotheque-na:
The Bibliothèque Nationale is France's national library. It was founded in 1354. Its Hebrew manuscripts head its Oriental collections. They now number 1,390 items. Only Oxford's Bodleian ranks above it in size and standing among such collections. Charles V. began the library's story. Hebrew books reached the Louvre in 1372. A second group came about 1397.

The entry traces growth through the Renaissance. Ambassadors kept copyists busy in Venice. Fragments turned up inside printed volumes. Cataloguing began in 1689 under Louis XIV. A printed catalogue followed in 1739. The article also covers coins and engravings. The engravings alone fill 145,000 volumes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-blind-cohen-fer: Ferdinand Blind-Cohen was a German student. On May 7, 1866, he tried to kill Prince Bismarck. The next day he killed himself in prison. He was stepson of the radical Karl Blind. He had taken his stepfather's name. A letter he left claimed no accomplices. It called Bismarck German liberty's worst enemy. He hoped his sacrifice would free Germany. He had studied at an agricultural academy in Hohenheim. His stepfather paid for his burial.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bohmer-joseph-b:
Joseph b. Meir Böhmer was a Lithuanian rabbi and Talmudist born at Skudy in 1796. He died on May 7, 1864, at Slutsk. He was a leading pupil of Hayyim of Volozhin.

Questions on law reached Böhmer even from Palestine and Babylon. He treated the Talmud with strict logic and opposed the pilpul method. His town prized his character as much as his learning. He served as rabbi for thirty-five years. He left many responsa in manuscript. His son Meir followed him as rabbi of Slutzk. Notes to the Yad ha-Hazakah and the Shulhan Aruk also survive from his hand. His town prized his personal qualities as much as his scholarship.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-borkum-kalman-b: Kalman ben Phineas Seligman Borkum was court Jew of Duke Peter Biron of Courland. He was born in the middle of the eighteenth century. He died at Mitau in 1828, on the same day as his brother Simson. Through the brothers, Jews gained leave to settle in Mitau for good. They could form a community and work at trade and crafts. In 1784 Kalman built a synagogue at his own expense. He also built the other houses the community needed.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-breidenbach-wol:
Wolf Breidenbach was a German court agent and champion of Jewish emancipation. He was born in the village of Breidenbach in 1751 and died in Offenbach on Feb. 28, 1829. He came to Frankfort as a poor boy who studied Talmud.

Skill at chess drew a rich nobleman to trust Breidenbach with his money affairs. Loans from that patron started his banking and jewelry trade. Courts of small German princes made him their agent in turn. He spent his sway on abolishing the Leibzoll, a toll Jews paid on entering towns. Town after town dropped that toll through his work from 1803 to 1805. A plea to the Diet of Ratisbon for a general end failed, though.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-brusilov-3775: Brusilov was a town in the government of Kiev, Russia, covered here in a short statistical entry. Its figures date to 1898, when 2,800 Jews lived in a total population of 6,500. Of 541 Jewish artisans, 112 were tailors and 206 were tanners. About eighty families received alms at Passover. The town had a Talmud Torah attended by more than one hundred children. It also had twenty-two private schools, a hospital, and a poorhouse. A Gemilut Hesed society lent money without interest.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bykhov-3875:
Bykhov was a district town in the government of Mohilev, Russia. The 1898 census counted 3,172 Jews in a population of 6,536, with 587 artisans among them. Most Jews there were very poor, and 127 families sought Passover relief. Aid came from a sick visiting society, a poorhouse, and a holiday help society. Nearby villages held Jewish farm families with their own land.

Older records reach back to the Chmielnicki rising of 1648 and 1649, when most Jews of Bykhov who refused baptism were killed. Later reports describe forced converts who kept Polish ties and some who returned to Judaism at Slutzk. A royal grant of 1669 freed the ruined town from taxes for twenty years. That copy of the grant was entered in the Brest records in 1671.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-canstatt-karl-f:
Karl Friedrich Canstatt was a German physician and medical author born at Regensburg on July 11, 1807. He ranks among the pioneers of Germany's modern medical school, and Virchow was his pupil. He studied at Vienna and at Würzburg, taking his degree in 1831. A year later he went to Paris to study Asiatic cholera, then raging there.

His cholera study won him a Belgian commission to plan a cholera hospital. He stayed in Brussels until 1838, then practiced eye medicine at Regensburg and Ansbach. In 1843 Erlangen called him to its pathology chair. His yearly report on medical progress, begun in 1841, was his greatest service; Virchow carried it on. Tuberculosis struck him in 1846, and he died at Erlangen in 1850.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-carregal-hayyim: Ḥayyim Moses ben Abraham Carregal was a rabbi and editor who worked in Palestine early in the eighteenth century. He lived for a time in Holland, gathering funds for Jerusalem. His account of his own life stands in the introduction to his edition of a work by Moses ben Joseph Ventura, printed at Amsterdam in 1718. He was probably a son of Abraham Carregal of Cairo. He may also have been the father of Raphael Ḥayyim Isaac Carregal of Hebron, who visited Newport in 1773.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-caspi-nathanael: Nathanael ben Nehemiah Caspi, called Bonsenior Macif of Largentière, was a Provençal scholar of the late fourteenth and early fifteenth centuries. Under his teacher Frat Maimon, he composed a commentary on the Cuzari in 1424. That work, based on Judah Cardinal's Hebrew version, survives in manuscript at Paris and elsewhere. He also commented on a work on Maimonides' terms and on the Shemoneh Peraḳim. His glosses on the Pentateuch rest on Joseph Official and cite rabbis of eastern France, with French words mixed in.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-chudnov-4375: Chudnov was a town in the government of Volhynia, Russia, with a Jewish community older than the Cossack uprising of 1648. In 1898 the town held nearly 8,000 people, about 3,500 of them Jews. Most worked in crafts and trade. The entry counts 1,252 Jews in handicrafts and names tailoring and shoemaking as the chief trades, tailoring alone employing 475 men. Schools listed include a Talmud Torah with 30 pupils and some 30 small religious schools with about 300 children in all.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cohen-hayyim-44: Hayyim Cohen, a Tunisian rabbi, lived on the island of Djerba near Tunis in the later nineteenth century. Eight works stand under his name, and the entry is little more than their list. Naawah Kodesh, printed at Leghorn in 1872, comments on the Song of Songs. Other volumes treat the Hoshaanot of Sukkot and the Azharot of Ibn Gabirol. One comments on the elegies for the Ninth of Ab. Another treats the Selihot prayers of Elul. A further book covers the Passover Haggadah.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-como-4575:
Como, a city on the Italian lake of the same name, never held a Jewish community. One family only lived there for a time, running a bank passed from father to son through four generations. The dukes of Milan protected them for their taxes and trade value, even as the townsfolk stayed deeply hostile.

In 1436 Duke Philip ordered the city to admit Giuseppe and his son Abraham of Mantua, refused the year before. Badge rules and tax terms followed. Abraham's grandson Benedetto won sole banking rights for ten years in 1467, yet failed in 1472. A fresh pact came in 1478. After the blood charge at Trent in 1475, hatred rose, and the Jews vanished from Como for good.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-correa-isabella: Isabella (Rebecca) Correa was a Spanish poetess of the seventeenth century. Born in Spain, she lived in turn in Brussels, Antwerp, and Amsterdam. She married the cosmographer Nicolas de Olivier y Fullana of Majorca. Contemporaries praised her beauty, wit, learning, and command of languages. Her main work is a Spanish verse translation of Guarini's Pastor Fido, with notes. It appeared at Antwerp and Amsterdam in 1694. Another work, Varias Poesias, was said to be ready for the press but never came out.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-crool-joseph-47: Joseph Crool was a teacher and controversialist who flourished in England about 1838. He gave Hebrew lessons to a few Cambridge students. At the time the regius professors of Hebrew were often absent. The entry rates him low as a scholar. He could read English, German, and Hebrew, but loved old wives' fables. He wore a parchment girdle inscribed with texts from the Law and Talmud. He opposed Jewish emancipation, fearing it would end in conversion. His two books of 1829 argued that case.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-daniel-ben-saad: Daniel ben Saadia ha-Babli was a Talmudic scholar who lived at Damascus in the thirteenth century. He studied under Samuel b. Ali Halevi, the foe of Maimonides. After Maimonides died, Daniel took up the fight against his books. His tone stayed calmer than his master's. He sent forty-seven questions on the Mishneh Torah to Abraham, son of Maimonides. Thirteen more attacked the Book of Precepts. Abraham answered in a defense, not with a ban. In the end the exilarch David of Mosul excommunicated Daniel, who died of grief.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dembitzer-hayyi:
Ḥayyim Nathan Dembitzer was a Galician rabbi and historian born in Cracow on June 29, 1820. His father, a learned merchant, died in 1833. A chronicle by David Gans first turned the young Talmud student toward Jewish biography and history. He was ordained by three noted rabbis, among them Solomon Kluger.

In 1856 Dembitzer became a dayyan, or judge, in Cracow, and later head of its court, holding the post until his death on November 20, 1892. His early books were legal works. His chief work, "Kelilat Yofi," gives lives of the rabbis of Lemberg and other Polish towns. Its parts appeared in 1888 and 1893. He also corresponded with Grätz on the Council of Four Lands.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-donati-marco-52: Marco Donati was an Italian lawyer born in Padua on Sept. 4, 1842, who died at Terni on June 11, 1901. He broke off his studies to fight under Garibaldi and served with distinction. Back home, he finished law and opened a practice at Padua. He sat for years in the Italian Chamber and led Padua's Jewish community as its president. The entry also notes a small book on advocacy and a memorial speech on King Humbert I.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dosa-ben-saadia:
Dosa ben Saadia was the son of Saadia Alfayyumi, the famed gaon. Dosa himself was a Talmudic scholar and philosopher. He did not follow his father as gaon, though one list of gaons includes him. A responsum of his has survived.

Abraham ibn Daud's chronicle says Dosa wrote to the nasi Hasdai ibn Shaprut in Spain. A glossary on Maimonides counts him among thinkers who fought the Greek idea that the world is eternal. Some scholars merge him with David ben Saadia. That David wrote a Talmudic work in Arabic against rulings in the Halakot Gedolot. The entry leaves the match as a claim, not a fact.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-eliab-god-or-my: Eliab is a name shared by seven men in the Bible. The name means my God is Father. The first Eliab led the tribe of Zebulun in the desert. He was a son of Helon, named at the census. A second Eliab was a Reubenite, father of Dathan and Abiram. A third was the eldest brother of David. A fourth served David as a gatekeeper and a player of music. The rest are a Gadite chief, a forebear of Samuel, and a forebear of Judith.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-enoch-ben-abrah: Enoch ben Abraham was a Talmudist and famed preacher. He came of a noted family of scholars at Posen. In 1649 he left Cracow to be rabbi at Gnesen. Why he left that town is not known, the entry says. In 1652 Posen sank deep in debt as a flock. They sent Enoch to Germany to raise funds for them. A post as preacher for three years was his pledge. Hard times in Posen broke that pledge in the end. He died as rabbi at Oettingen, most likely.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-esther-rabbah-5:
Esther Rabbah is the Midrash, or rabbinic commentary, on the Book of Esther. The Esther scroll has been read aloud at Purim since early times, and rich story material grew around it. The entry describes the work as an incomplete gathering of that material. In most editions it holds six sections, each opened by proems. The sections start at set verses in the first two chapters.

Comment runs verse by verse at first, then thins out and stops after chapter eight. Later paragraphs seem tacked on. The author drew on the Jerusalem Talmud, other Midrashim, and Targumim. One long passage borrows from Yosippon, which later scholars marked as an addition. The entry judges the work Palestinian in origin and older than Midrash Abba Gorion.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-fable-5975:
A fable is a moral tale in which beasts, and at times plants, act and speak like people. It differs from the plain beast tale, which carries no moral. Only India and Greece held many fables in the ancient world, the entry says. Yet the Bible holds one true fable: Jotham's tale of the trees choosing a king, told to block Abimelech's crown.

Jehoash's thorny reply to Amaziah also reads like a fable. Later Jews took fables from Greece or India, the entry judges. The tale of the two pots shows up in Sirach and in a rabbinic proverb about a jug and a stone. Medieval sets by Berechiah ha-Nakdan and others, likely fed by Arabic sources, close the survey.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-fiscus-judaicus:
Fiscus Judaicus was the Jewish tax taken by Rome after the Temple fell. Jews of the Diaspora had paid a yearly half shekel for the Temple. After the sanctuary was destroyed in 70, Vespasian diverted that tax to the temple of Jupiter at Rome. The sum was two drachmas. The entry calls this an affront to Jewish feeling. Rabbinic law held, in theory, that the half shekel need not be paid once the Temple was gone.

Domitian collected the tax with great rigor at Rome. People who hid their origin were reported to him. Under Nerva there was some relief. A coin of his says that abusive suits over the tax were abolished. The tax itself was still levied, though. No one knows when it was formally ended. It came back in the Middle Ages as the Opferpfennig.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-flavius-eborens:
Flavius Eborensis, also called Didacco Pyrrho, was a poet born at Evora, Portugal, on April 4, 1517. He died at Ragusa in 1607. His parents feigned Christianity to avoid persecution. Yet they taught their son a love of Judaism. When he was barely seventeen, they urged him to leave for a land where he could profess his faith openly. In 1536 he went to Flanders, then to Switzerland. In 1552 he settled at Ancona.

His age held Flavius one of its greatest Latin poets. He wrote many verse works, several of them printed. Three books of elegies came out at Venice in 1596. Other poems treat Cato the Younger and his own exile. A set of chosen poems was printed at Cracow in 1582. Source notes in Italian and German close the entry.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-francolm-isaac-:
Isaac Asher Francolm was a German preacher and religious teacher born at Breslau on December 15, 1788. He died there on July 1, 1849. He took his doctor's degree at Leipsic in 1817. After running a Jewish elementary school at Breslau for three years, he was called to Königsberg in 1820. There he served as preacher and religious teacher. Zunz had been one of his rivals for the post.

Francolm did much to modernize the synagogue service and religious teaching. He introduced the confirmation of girls into Germany. Orthodox members complained to the government about this. He was then barred from confirming girls and from other changes, even preaching in German. In 1826 he declined a new contract at Königsberg. He became head of a Jewish school at Breslau instead, and held that post until 1847. His many books include works on Bible teaching and on the Jews under Richard the Lionheart.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-friedlander-jul:
Julius Friedländer was a German student of coins, born in Berlin on June 25, 1813. He died there on April 4, 1884. After study at Bonn and Berlin and travel in Italy, he won a post in 1840 at the royal coin cabinet of Berlin. In 1868 he became head of the coin part of the Berlin Museum. In 1872 the Berlin Academy of Sciences chose him as a member.

His books treat the coins of the Knights of Rhodes and of Justinian. Others cover the coins of the Ostrogoths, the Vandals, and the Oscans. With a partner he made a book of the royal coin cabinet in 1877. His last works treat Italian medals of the fifteenth century. His whole family had embraced Christianity in 1820.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-galilee-6475:
Galilee was the Greek-era name for the northern part of western Palestine. The name comes from ha-Galil in the Old Testament. It names hill country east of the Jezreel plain, reaching toward Lebanon. Two parts are marked off. Lower Galilee lies in the south and Upper Galilee in the north. The plain of Ramah parts them.

Josephus praises Galilee as fair and rich, full of towns and villages. Its people were mixed in early times. Under the Maccabees more Jews moved in, and the land grew mostly Jewish. After Herod death it passed to Herod Antipas. Later it became the center of Jewish life in Palestine. Olive oil ranked among its chief goods.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gilgal-6675:
Gilgal was the first camp of the Israelites west of the Jordan, by Joshua iv. It served as a base in the wars of conquest. It was also a shrine, with a place of sacrifice named in First Samuel. The name seems to fit more than one town, and the entry works to keep them apart.

The camp Gilgal is not the town Samuel visited on his rounds. That one is matched with Jiljilya, southwest of Shiloh. The Gilgal of Elijah journey in Second Kings is likely the same Jiljilya, or a Julaijil southeast of Shechem. The shrine the prophets Amos and Hosea blast is held to be the Joshua camp. Its name clung to a hill Jaljul east of Jericho.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-goldzieher-wilh: Wilhelm Goldzieher was a Hungarian oculist. He was born at Köpcsény, near Presburg, on Jan. 1, 1849. He studied medicine at Vienna, Berlin, Prague, and Heidelberg. He took his degree at Vienna on Dec. 25, 1871. In 1874 he settled in Budapest as an eye doctor. The university made him privat-docent in 1878 and professor in 1895. He wrote much for Eulenburg's medical encyclopedia. His manual of ophthalmology (1890) was the first of its kind in Hungarian. In April 1903 the emperor decorated him with the Franz Joseph order.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gregory-i-the-g:
Gregory I, the Great, was pope from 590 to 604. He was born about 540 into an old Roman senatorial family. He had held high office before retiring to a cloister. When Pope Pelagius died of plague, Gregory was chosen. He strengthened the papal see for centuries ahead. The entry then turns to his stand on the Jews.

Gregory disliked Judaism deeply, calling it superstition and faithlessness. Yet he pushed conversion by kindness, not by force. He opposed forced baptism plainly. He guarded Jewish feasts and synagogues by law. At the same time he fought Jewish ownership of Christian slaves. His rule was fixed: Jews must not pass the law's limits, and must not suffer wrongs past them either. Later popes kept that formula.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-habakkuk-lxx-vu:
Habakkuk was a prophet and author of the eighth book among the twelve minor prophets. Little certain is known about his life. His name may come from an Assyrian word for a garden plant, and it may be a pen name. A note at the end of chapter three hints he was a Levite, since he speaks of his stringed instruments.

The lack of facts left room for legends. One Greek story makes him feed Daniel in the lions' den. Jewish tradition makes him the Shunammite woman's son, and cabalists even called him Adam reborn. Scholars in the entry place him variously under Manasseh, near Jeremiah's time, or as a younger follower of Isaiah influenced by Assyrian writing.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-halafta-hilfai-:
Ḥalafta b. Ḳaruya, also known as Abba Ḥalfa, heads an entry covering two men of the name. The first was a tanna of the second century, a fellow of Gamaliel II. Gamaliel once visited him at Ḳaruya and asked for his prayers. Under the forms Ḥilfa and Ḥilfai he is cited for laws, one of which was taught and used in Rome.

The second was a Palestinian amora of the third century, a fellow of Ḥiyya b. Abba. The two men wrestled with a count in Genesis: the souls of Jacob's house are said to be seventy, yet the list names one less. Ḥalafta rejected the twin-sister fix and accepted that Jochebed, born at the entry into Egypt, completes the seventy. The entry ends with his sharp words over coffins brought from foreign lands for burial in Palestine.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hananeel-7175:
Hananeel was a Babylonian scholar of the third century, a disciple of Rab and a fellow of Beruna and Isaac b. Maḥseiah. He was a great halakist, so steeped in Rab's views that Ḥuna once refused to discuss a ruling until Hananeel had confirmed that Rab held it as law. By trade he was a scribe.

His penmanship was so skilled and sure that Ḥisda said Hananeel could write out the whole Law from memory, were that not forbidden. His name runs through both Talmuds. Ze'era I carried many of his teachings to Palestine, above all those on a scribe's work. Few haggadot bear his name, and those merely repeat Rab.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-harsith-7275: Harsith was one of the gates of Jerusalem, named in Jeremiah xix. 2. The gate led out into the Valley of Hinnom. The entry says the meaning of the name cannot be settled. The Authorized Version renders it "east gate," linking it to a Hebrew word for the sun. Nothing more is told about the gate itself. The notice is only a few lines long and cites no source beyond the Bible verse.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hayyim-ben-isaa:
Hayyim ben Isaac of Volozhin, born on Jan. 21, 1749, was a Russian rabbi and educator. He was also a cloth maker who did well in trade. At twenty-five he became a pupil of the Gaon of Wilna. He took up his studies again from the start under that master.

In 1803 Hayyim founded the yeshiva of Volozhin. He began with ten local pupils kept at his own cost. The school grew into the leading house of its kind in the nineteenth century. In time it held a hundred students in its own building. His chief book stresses strict practice and Torah study, against Hasidic ways. He died on June 14, 1821.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hefez-b-yazliah:
Hefez ben Yazliah, also called Hefez Alluf, was a legal scholar of the late tenth century. He likely lived at Kairwan, though one view places him in Palestine. His lost book, "Sefer ha-Mizwot," listed the 613 commandments. Unlike earlier lists, his gave short reasons for each law.

That made him an early voice in the study of the reasons behind the commandments. His book summed up Bible, Talmud, and geonic teaching, with prayer forms as well. Spanish and French authorities prized it, and Maimonides owed him a debt. Grammar and philosophy found room in the work too. Later quotes preserve parts of his teaching.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-henschel-august:
August Wilhelm Eduard Theodor Henschel, born in Breslau on Dec. 20, 1790, was a German physician and botanist. He studied at Breslau, Berlin, and Heidelberg, taking his medical degree in 1813. He practiced in Breslau and became a lecturer in pathology in 1816.

Henschel embraced Christianity in 1820 and published a noted work on plant sexuality that year. He rose to professor of anatomy, physiology, and pathology in 1832. His lasting fame rests on research into medical history. Results appeared in his periodical Janus from 1846 to 1849. Other works treated Aristotle as a botanist, rabies, and Silesian medicine. He died in Breslau on July 24, 1856.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hitzig-ferdinan:
Ferdinand Hitzig, born at Hauingen, Baden, on June 23, 1807, was a German Christian theologian. He studied under Gesenius at Halle and Ewald at Göttingen. He taught at Heidelberg from 1830 to 1833. Zurich's new university then called him, and he returned to Heidelberg in 1861.

Hitzig ranked among the most noted and independent theologians of his century, the entry says. A tireless worker, he edited all the prophetic books and nearly all the poetic writings of the Old Testament. His dated list runs from Isaiah in 1833 to Job in 1874. He sought firm results, such as an author and date for each psalm. One early claim dated many psalms to Maccabean times. He died at Heidelberg on Jan. 22, 1875.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-horowitz-aaron-: Aaron ben Jacob Halevi Horowitz was a Russian Talmudist of the second half of the seventeenth century. He was the son-in-law of Joseph ben Lob, rabbi of Minsk. His work centered on one book. He revised David ben Samuel's commentary on Rashi's notes to the Pentateuch. The revision appeared at Dyhernfurth in 1689 under the title Dibre Dawid. Horowitz added a commentary of his own on all of Genesis. He also added a letter defending his work.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ibn-ya-ish-baru:
Baruch ben Isaac ibn Ya'ish was a philosopher and translator of the fifteenth century, likely Spanish born but living in Italy. He mastered Hebrew and knew Arabic and Latin well. His one original work comments, in ten chapters, on Avicenna's remedies for the heart. It studies the heart's workings and cites Averroes and Aristotle.

At the request of Samuel Zarfati he turned Aristotle's Metaphysics from Latin into Hebrew, about 1485. He chose the Latin text because the Arabic one was badly confused. He split each of the twelve books into chapters and added a full table of contents. A note on Aristotle's Ethics also bears his name, though his role there is not clear.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-illinois-8075:
Illinois is one of the central states of the Union, admitted on December 3, 1818. Its Jewish pioneer was John Hays, sheriff of St. Clair county from 1798 to 1818. The first Jewish settler reached Chicago in 1838. An agent of a New York colonization society bought 160 acres near Schaumburg for a farm colony, but most newcomers chose trade.

Chicago gained the state's first burial society in 1846 and its first congregation in 1847. In time seventy-five congregations rose across the state. The article counts dozens of charities, clubs, loan groups, and lodges, most of them in Chicago. Jews also serve in law, medicine, and public office. The state's Jews are put at more than 100,000, three-fourths of them in Chicago.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-isaac-isachok-j:
Isaac Jacob, also written Isachok, was court physician to King Sigismund I of Poland and a son of Abraham of Jerusalem. He died at Kazimierz, near Cracow, about 1510. In 1504 Archbishop Andreas of Gnesen, whose physician he had been, recommended him to King Alexander. The king then let Isaac buy the right to the Cracow Jews' taxes, worth one hundred Hungarian florins a year, for three hundred florins.

Because the Jews of Kazimierz taunted him with humble birth, Isaac had two Polish nobles fetch his pedigree from his sister Sarah in Jerusalem. The king took great interest, and decrees of 1507 and 1509 set out his lineage and confirmed the tax right for his life. After his death, the king granted his widow Barsaba and her children the same privileges. Whether Isaac was a Jew from Palestine or a Spanish exile, the entry says, is hard to determine.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jabneh-or-jamni:
Jabneh, later Jamnia, was a Philistine city that Uzziah took, tearing down its wall. Students generally match it with Jabneel, on Judah's border near Ekron, not far from the coast. Though set back from the sea, it kept its own harbor; some writers even treated port and town as two places. Strabo said Jabneh and its villages could field 40,000 fighting men.

In the Maccabean books the city is Jamnia. Judas Maccabeus stormed it and fired the shipping in its harbor; the blaze was seen from Jerusalem. Simon took it from the Syrians, and under Alexander Jannaeus the Jews held it at last. Pompey gave it back to Syria, and Gabinius rebuilt it about 57 B.C. Augustus gave it to Herod, who left it to his sister Salome; she passed it to Livia. Its people then were chiefly Jews, Philo says.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jacobs-joseph-8:
Joseph Jacobs, born at Sydney on Aug. 29, 1854, was a critic, folklorist, historian, and communal worker. Educated at Cambridge and Berlin, he became secretary of the Society of Hebrew Literature in 1878. His 1882 articles in the London Times on persecution of Jews in Russia helped spark the Mansion House Meeting and Fund.

Jacobs wrote on Jewish statistics, Anglo-Jewish history, and Spanish-Jewish sources, and published Jews of Angevin England in 1893. He also edited folk-tale collections and the journal Folk-Lore. In 1900 he moved to New York as revising editor of the Jewish Encyclopedia.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jezebel-8675:
Jezebel was a daughter of Ethbaal, king of Sidon, and the wife of Ahab of Israel. The match crowned the warm ties between Israel and Phenicia under Ahab's father Omri. Jezebel demanded room for her own worship, so Ahab built a house and altar for Baal in Samaria. She went further and pushed to make her faith the national one, keeping 450 prophets of Baal and 400 of Asherah.

She hunted the prophets of God, and Elijah's win at Carmel drew her revenge. Her worst act, in the entry's telling, was the false charge and murder of Naboth to win his vineyard for Ahab. Elijah cursed her house for it. She outlived Ahab, saw two sons reign, and died in Jehu's rising.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-joseph-nazir-be: Joseph Nazir ben Hayyim Moses ha-Levi was a Palestinian rabbi born at Hebron about 1650 who died probably at Cairo in 1719. He studied under Moses Galante and became rabbi at Hebron. His town sent him to Europe to raise alms, and on that road he met Zebi Ashkenazi at Belgrade in 1679. The name Nazir marked him as a Nazarite. His two volumes of responsa, Matteh Yosef, came out at Constantinople in 1717-26. He also edited a friend's responsa and followed that friend as rabbi of Cairo.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-judah-ben-barzi:
Judah ben Barzillai, usually called al-Bargeloni, the Barcelonian, was a Spanish Talmudist of the end of the eleventh century and the start of the twelfth. Almost nothing is known of his life. He came from a high family and was often called ha-Nasi, the prince. He once clashed with Abraham b. Hiyya, who wanted to delay a wedding over bad omens in the stars; Judah held that heeding omens breaks Scripture.

He ranked among the great law codifiers of the Middle Ages, though most of that work is lost. Later masters cite it as binding, and quotes in more than forty authors show it covered ritual and civil law alike. One part on contracts was printed in 1898 and runs to 138 pages. He also wrote a long, half-mystic commentary on the Sefer Yezirah.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-judith-montefio: Judith Montefiore College was a theological seminary founded in 1869 by Sir Moses Montefiore. He set it up at Ramsgate in Kent, near his home, in honor of his wife, Lady Judith Montefiore. In practice it took the form of a study house where older scholars worked on the Talmud. Its first principal was Dr. L. Loewe. After his death in 1888 the college sank for a time. A trial remake as a modern seminary under Dr. M. Gaster ran from 1891 to 1896 and failed.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kalonymus-nasi-: Kalonymus Nasi was a Provençal poet of liturgical verse. He worked at Beaucaire in the middle of the thirteenth century. He wrote a poem for the Sabbath before Passover. It is known as the poem for Shabbat ha-Gadol. In thirty-nine strophes, set in letter order, it gives all the rules for keeping Passover. Each strophe opens with a Bible verse. Each one closes with the same refrain. A dirge on his death stands in the poems of Abraham Bedersi.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kenaz-9275: Kenaz is a name borne by three men in the Bible. The first was a son of Eliphaz and a grandson of Esau. He stood among the dukes of Edom. His clan, the Kenizzites, is named once in Genesis. The second Kenaz was a descendant of Judah. He is called the father of Othniel. The entry says "father" here means ancestor, since Caleb is the true elder brother. The third Kenaz was a grandson of Caleb.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-klein-hugo-9375: Hugo Klein was a Hungarian writer, born at Szegedin on July 21, 1853. He was educated at the University of Budapest. For several years he edited the "Ungarische Lloyd." He later became dramatic and art critic of the "Neue Pester Journal." In 1883 he removed to Vienna. By 1904 he was editor of the "Schöne Blaue Donau." His works include operettas and plays from 1883 onward. He also wrote librettos for Brandl and for Kerner. The entry closes with one line: he embraced Christianity.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kornik-kurnik-m: Meïr ben Moses Kornik, a German rabbi and calendar maker born at Glogau, died at Hamburg on Aug. 9, 1826. He served as rabbi in his home town. His first book, dated 1796, is a manual for scribes on writing the scroll of Esther. Later works gloss hard passages in Sefer Yeẓirah and the Zohar. His best known work matches the Julian, Gregorian, Jewish, and Muslim calendars in tables dated 1825. Later scholars praised those tables highly and built on them.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-labor-9575:
Labor in Jewish literature carries a dignity the entry calls rare among ancient faiths. God appears as the Pattern Worker who made and rules the world without weariness. Adam was placed in Eden to till and keep it, not to idle. The Sabbath then crowns the work week and guards rest for slave and beast alike.

Proverbs and Talmud sayings press the same point. Work brings blessing, while idleness breeds poverty and harm. Rabbis urge each man to teach his son a trade and to join Torah study with labor. A saying warns that seven years of famine will not enter the artisan's door. The entry closes by noting an echo of this spirit in the New Testament.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lerida-catalan-:
Lerida, called Leyda in Catalan, is a city in Catalonia. By the fourteenth century it held a strong Jewish community with several privileges. Its Jews were excused from housing the royal court, and they could not be forced to attend Dominican conversion sermons. In 1306 the king let the congregation take in ten Jewish families driven from France.

The entry tells of hard blows: Shepherd attackers killed seventy Jews who had paid for safe passage, and in 1325 the town barred Passover baking until the king stepped in. On Aug. 13, 1391, seventy-eight Jews were killed and most survivors took baptism. With that year the real congregation ended, and the town soon felt the loss of Jewish taxes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-levy-armand-abr: Armand Abraham Lévy, a French mathematician and mineralogist, was born at Paris in 1794. He died there on June 26, 1841. He graduated from the Ecole Normale and taught mathematics there in 1814-15. He lived in England until 1828, then in Belgium. At Liége he lectured at the university and joined the Brussels Academy of Sciences. Back in France in 1830, he became professor of mineralogy at the Collége Charlemagne. His essays treat surfaces, specific gravity, and systems of forces.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lobo-moses-jesh: Moses Jeshurun Lobo was a Spanish poet who lived at Amsterdam in the seventeenth century. He was one of the poets who marked the martyrdom of Abraham Nuñez Bernal in 1655. His elegies appear in a volume printed at Amsterdam that year. Another writer praised a poet called Custodio Lobo, who died at Leghorn, as an excellent Spanish poet. Because the names are so close, one scholar thought the two poets were the same person.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lucena-10175:
Lucena, a walled city near Cordova, Spain, is the subject of a Jewish Encyclopedia entry from 1906 by Richard Gottheil and Meyer Kayserling. In early times it was inhabited almost wholly by Jews and was called the “Jews’ City.” Its Jews traded widely and, by one Arabic account, were richer than those of any other city.

The article recalls the scholars who taught there, above all Isaac Alfasi, who founded a large Talmudic academy in Lucena. It then turns harsh: pressure to convert in 1107, bought off with a large payment, and destruction under the Almohades in 1146, when Jews were robbed and forced to accept Islam. Ferdinand III later gave the city to the bishop of Cordova. The entry preserves the rise and ruin of one of medieval Spain’s most famous Jewish towns.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-magnus-ludwig-i:
Ludwig Immanuel Magnus, a German mathematician, is the subject of a 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry. Born in Berlin on March 15, 1790, he lost his father young. His mother placed him in his uncle's bank. After business hours he studied Euclid on his own. He died at Berlin in 1861.

The article follows a double life of banking and geometry. Magnus volunteered in the artillery during the Napoleonic wars, serving from 1813 to 1815. Back in Berlin he banked by day and taught mathematics at the Cauer academy. By 1834 his reputation earned him an honorary doctorate from Bonn. His papers appeared in the leading French and German journals of the field. Ill health and failing eyes ended his work early. The entry preserves a self-taught geometer who won a university's honor without ever holding its chair.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-manoah-b-shemar:
Manoah ben Shemariah Handel, a Polish author, is the subject of a short 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry. Born at Brzeszticzka in Volhynia, he died in 1612. His son preserved and published his father's works. The article names three of them, with their printings at Cracow, Prague, and Lublin.

The first work, Hokmat Manoah, holds his glosses on the Talmud. Those glosses were printed inside the Cracow Talmud edition of 1602 to 1605, and separately at Prague. The second comments on Bahya's Duties of the Heart, printed at Lublin in 1596 and often reprinted. A third work's title page mentions the emperor Rudolph and King Matthias. The son spoke of publishing still more of his father's writing on Talmud, Cabala, and astronomy. The entry preserves a scholar known mostly through his son's care.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-matalon-mordeca:
Mordecai Matalon was a sixteenth-century rabbi of Salonica. Isidore Singer and M. Seligsohn wrote his brief Jewish Encyclopedia entry in 1906. He was the uncle of Jacob ben Solomon Matalon, the scholar of the neighboring entry. He stood out as a prominent Talmudist. His companion Samuel di Modena also reports that he was well versed in the secular sciences of his day.

Little of his writing stands under his own name. What survives is quoted work. Samuel di Modena quotes him in his responsa, and Isaac Adarbi cites him in “Dibre Ribot.” Legal answers of his own were printed inside Samuel Kala'i's “Mishpete Shemuel,” published at Venice in 1599. The entry shows how the encyclopedia preserves scholars whose learning is visible only through the books of their friends.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meir-ibn-jair-1:
Meir ibn Jair was an Italian Talmudist and grammarian of the sixteenth century. Richard Gottheil and M. Seligsohn entered him in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Even his name needs explaining. His family name seems to have been Me'iri, since he is always called “Meir of the house of Meir.” “Ibn Jair” likely comes from a blessing written after his name in manuscripts, perhaps meaning “may his light continue.”

Two books carry his name, both printed at Sabbioneta. “Yair Natib,” issued in 1553, treats the law of slaughtering animals. Hayyim Benveniste quoted it often in his great legal digest. A year later came his grammar of the eight conjugations of the Hebrew verb. He revised that grammar late in life and published it again in 1597 under the plain title “Dikduk,” Grammar.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mendl-sigismund:
Sigismund Ferdinand Mendl was an English politician. Joseph Jacobs and Martha Washington Levy give him a brief notice in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born in 1866. He was educated at Harrow School and at University College, Oxford. In 1888 he was called to the bar at the Inner Temple.

His road to Parliament took three tries. He contested the Isle of Wight unsuccessfully in 1892. He contested Plymouth in 1895. He won Plymouth in the Liberal interest in 1898. He served only until 1900. The entry rests on Who's Who for 1902 and the Jewish Year Book. It records nothing of his speeches or causes. So he stands as a compact specimen of a type. He is the Anglo-Jewish professional entering public life at the century's turn. His path runs school, university, bar, and a brief seat in the Commons.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mhushilkar-reub:
Reuben Ezekiel Mhushilkar, a soldier of the Beni-Israel community of India, is the subject of one of the shortest entries in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906, written by Joseph Jacobs and J. Hyams. The whole article is a single sentence of service record. He enlisted in the 19th Regiment Native Infantry on January 15, 1849.

The entry tracks his rise through the ranks: jemidar in October 1861 and subahdar in January 1870. It lists the battles where he won medals, at Multan and Gujarat in the Punjab and at four places in central India, then service in Afghanistan from 1878 to 1880. He retired on March 6, 1881, closing a career of thirty-two years.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mirkes-solomon-:
Solomon Zalman ben Judah Löb Mirkes was a Lithuanian Talmudist of the eighteenth century, a native of Mir in the government of Minsk. Herman Rosenthal and M. Seligsohn give him a short Jewish Encyclopedia entry in 1906. He first appears in print at Königsberg in 1769, with a funeral oration for Abraham, the late chief rabbi of Frankfurt-on-the-Main.

Two years later Mirkes was himself rabbi of Frankfurt-on-the-Oder, and there he published his two substantial works in a single year. Sharsheret ha-Abotot gathers his novellae, decisions, and discussions on Talmudic questions. Shulḥan Shelomoh is a compendium of the Shulḥan Aruk's Oraḥ Ḥayyim division, arranged according to the later authorities, a working handbook for daily Jewish law.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moon-10975:
The moon in Hebrew is yeraḥ, probably the wanderer. In poetry it is lebanah, the white one. That is the starting point of a Jewish Encyclopedia article by Isidore Singer and M. Seligsohn, published in 1906. Genesis makes it the lesser light to rule the night. It was set for signs and seasons. The Psalmist likewise says it was appointed for the seasons.

The article gathers the biblical moon whole. It tells of its course halted at Joshua's word and its New Moon festivals under the word ḥodesh. It tells of its supposed power over sleepers. Psalm 121 promises that the moon shall not smite thee by night. That promise is read against the eastern belief that moonlight blinds the uncovered face. Philology, calendar, and folklore share one short entry.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mosse-rudolf-11:
Rudolf Mosse was a German publisher and philanthropist born at Grätz in Posen on May 8, 1843. Isidore Singer and Isidor Warsaw wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. He learned printing as an apprentice and mastered the trade in several cities. At twenty-four he saw his chance in advertising, then little developed in Germany.

His Berlin advertising agency spread to most large cities of Germany, Austria, and Switzerland. He published the Berliner Tageblatt, the Berliner Morgenzeitung, and the Allgemeine Zeitung des Judenthums, and his printing house was among the largest. He also gave on a large scale: pension funds for his many employees and a school for a hundred children. He built a hospital in his native Grätz as well.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-neumanovitz-nap:
Naphtali Herz Neumanovitz was a Russian Jewish author. Herman Rosenthal and A. S. Waldstein wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Jozefow on Feb. 12, 1843. He died at Warsaw on March 11, 1898. His family was known for secular and Talmudic learning.

At eighteen Neumanovitz went to study at Lublin. He later removed to Warsaw and joined Ha-Zefirah. His weekly feuilletons ran under the name Berosh Homiyoth. Friends gathered them into a book after his death. He wrote for Polish magazines at Lublin and for Izraelita. He edited a Hebrew magazine for Jewish youth. His textbooks taught Hebrew, Polish, and German together. They appeared at Warsaw in 1898, his death year.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nob-11575:
Nob was a town of priests near Jerusalem. The entry was written by the Editorial Board's Executive Committee and J. Frederic McCurdy for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. David fleeing Saul received holy bread there. Nearly the whole community paid with their lives. Isaiah names it in an Assyrian march on Jerusalem.

Nehemiah lists Nob among the towns of Benjamin. It stood close beside Anathoth, north of the capital. Some doubt a priestly town so near Jebusite Jerusalem. The entry answers that treaties were common then. Israel and Canaanite towns often lived by such truces. Cheyne held the name itself a false reading. He thought Gibeon was the place really meant.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-oholah-and-ohol:
Oholah and Oholibah are two sisters in a Bible tale. Emil G. Hirsch and Schulim Ochser wrote on them for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The tale stands in chapter twenty-three of Ezekiel. The names are signs, not real women of flesh. Oholah, the elder, stands for Samaria and Israel. Oholibah stands for Jerusalem and the land of Judah.

Both sisters are shown as wives of God in the tale. Both are false to him and take other loves. Those loves are Egypt, Assyria, and Chaldea, the great powers. Each power uses the sisters and then ruins them. The names hold the sense of the whole tale. Oholah means tent, for God's tent was at Samaria. Oholibah means my tent is in her, for the Temple stood at Jerusalem.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ornstein-mordec:
Mordecai Zeeb Ornstein was an Austrian scholar of rabbinic books. The board and M. W. Rapoport wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He died at Lemberg on October 28, 1837. His father was Jacob Meshullam Ornstein, rabbi of that city. His father taught him the Talmud and rabbinic works.

Mordecai showed great skill at a young age in study. Some of his replies stand in his father's book. That book is called Yeshuot Yaakob, in Hebrew words. His quick fame at so young an age fed his pride. He showed that pride in his ways with all men. For long he would take no post as a rabbi. At last Przemysl, a great town, gave him its call. He took the call but died before he could serve.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-palmyra-hebrew-:
Palmyra was a city in an oasis of the Syrian waste. Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Its Hebrew name was Tadmor, and its Latin name Palmyra. It lay five days from the Euphrates by road. It lay three days from Aleppo, a town of trade.

Palmyra stood on the high road to the Euphrates river. It grew to a great hub of trade in the East. Men said Solomon founded it when he took Hamath-zobah. That gave him a share of rule on that road. The Jewish realm lost the town under King Jehu. It won the town back under Jeroboam the Second. Jews met Palmyra once more in the third century. Queen Zenobia seems to have been kind to Jews then.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pedagogics-1197:
Pedagogics, the science of education, gets a long article here. Joseph Jacobs and Louis Grossman wrote it for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Its base law comes from Deuteronomy. Children must learn the faith so well that they live by it.

In Bible times every home was a school. Every parent served as a teacher of the children. Reading and writing were common skills among the Hebrews. A second rule shaped the teaching itself. The teacher must fit the lesson to the child's own nature. Proverbs adds firm discipline as part of good training.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-petronius-arbit:
Petronius Arbiter was a Latin satirist of Nero's age. Richard Gottheil and Samuel Krauss wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He earns his place here through one mocking fragment. In it he sneers at the Jews of Rome.

Petronius claimed that Jews worship a pig and heaven. He said such worship counts only with circumcision. He also said Jews fast on the Sabbath each week. All three claims are false and absurd. Still, they spread through the whole Roman world. His Widow of Ephesus tale later entered Jewish letters.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pinsker-lev-lev:
Lev Pinsker was a Russian Jewish physician of Odessa. Herman Rosenthal and J. G. Lipman wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born in Poland in 1821. He died at Odessa in 1891, famous across Europe.

Pinsker trained at Moscow and nursed cholera patients there. Within ten years he led Odessa's medical world. He wrote for the press on Jewish freedom and schooling. Then he concluded that Jews must free themselves. His pamphlet Autoemancipation, printed in 1881, urged land of their very own. It stirred debate across the whole continent.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-popper-david-12:
David Popper was an Austrian cellist born at Prague in 1845. Isidore Singer and Joseph Sohn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He studied under Goltermann at the Prague Conservatorium. At eighteen he toured Germany and won instant fame. Critics ranked him among the top cellists of his time.

On his return, Popper joined a prince's orchestra at Löwenburg. Hans von Bülow had urged the post for him. He toured Germany, Holland, Switzerland, and England. In Vienna he became solo cellist in the court orchestra. He played in the famed Hellmesberger Quartet as well. In 1872 he wed the pianist Sophie Menter. By 1905 he taught at the music academy in Budapest.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rabbah-gaon-mar:
Rabbah Gaon, called Mar Raba, led the school at Pumbedita. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Halevy dates his rule from 640 to 650. Grätz sets it twenty years later instead. He held the post at the same time as Huna of Sura. The two school heads acted as a pair.

The two geonim made a weighty rule on divorce together. By Talmud law a wife may seek divorce in rare cases. A foul disease in the husband is one such case. The new rule dealt with her right to press that claim. The entry sets out the rule and its sources. It shows the geonim at work as lawmakers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-raphall-morris-:
Morris Jacob Raphall was a rabbi and author born on October 3, 1798. Joseph Jacobs and Israel Cohen wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Stockholm, Sweden. He died at New York on June 23, 1868.

The article follows his schooling in Copenhagen and England. He published a Hebrew review that ill health ended in 1836. He translated Maimonides, Albo, and parts of the Mishnah. In 1840 he fought the Damascus blood charge in four languages. He served eight years as minister at Birmingham. In 1849 he moved to New York's B'nei Jeshurun. The entry traces a preacher who worked on two continents.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rembrandt-rembr:
Rembrandt Harmenszoon van Ryn was a Dutch painter born at Leyden. Gotthard Deutsch and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born on July 15, in 1606 or 1607. He died at Amsterdam on October 8, 1669.

The article stresses his close friendship with Manasseh ben Israel. Rembrandt painted Manasseh's portrait in 1645 and etched it later. In 1655 he etched four plates for Manasseh's book. They show Nebuchadnezzar's dream and Jacob's dream, among others. Rembrandt lived long near Amsterdam's Jewish quarter. There he found models for Bible scenes and Jewish life. His portraits are the earliest such portraits of Jews. The entry then lists his works of Jewish interest. It gives dates and where each work is held.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ritter-julius-1:
Julius Ritter was a German physician and author born on October 4, 1862. Isidore Singer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born in Berlin, son of Immanuel H. Ritter. He took his medical degree there in 1887.

The article says he now leads care for invalid children in Berlin. He also heads a bacteriological laboratory there. In 1892 he announced a whooping cough bacillus discovery. Papers in 1893 and 1896 confirmed that finding. A second group of articles treats diphtheria and its serum. His large 1893 work covers diphtheria's cause and treatment. Later papers treat scrofula and sickly children. He addressed a Berlin congress on internal medicine in 1897. The entry records a doctor known for two disease studies.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rosenthal-morit:
Moritz Rosenthal was an Austrian physician born at Grosswardein, Hungary, in 1833. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He took his medical degree at Vienna in 1858 and taught neurology there.

Rosenthal wrote about seventy essays plus several full medical works. They cover stuttering, brain tumors, apparent death, and the use of electricity as treatment. His Klinik der Nervenkrankheiten, on diseases of the nerves, appeared in 1875. It was translated into French, English, Italian, and Russian. Such reach shows how widely his clinical writing was read abroad.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sachs-bernhard-:
Bernhard Sachs was an American physician born at Baltimore on January 2, 1858. Cyrus Adler and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He studied at Harvard and at four European universities, taking his degree in 1882.

Sachs settled in New York in 1884 and specialized in nervous diseases. From 1889 he taught neurology at the New York Polyclinic as professor. He also served on the staffs of Montefiore Home and Mount Sinai Hospital. His books treat paralysis in children and a familial form of idiocy with blindness. A textbook of nervous diseases followed in 1897.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samson-ben-isaa:
Samson ben Isaac of Chinon was a French Talmudist who lived from about 1260 to 1330. Wilhelm Bacher and Isaac Broydé wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. A peer called him the greatest rabbinical authority of his time.

Samson's Sefer Keritut, printed at Constantinople in 1515, teaches Talmud method. Its five parts cover Ishmael's thirteen rules and Eliezer's thirty-two rules alike. One part names the Tannaim and Amoraim and shows how to decide between clashing views. Easy style and the author's weight made the book a classic at once. He also commented on two Talmud tractates and on divorce law.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sanders-daniel-:
Isidore Singer and J. C. Baer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Daniel Sanders. He was a German lexicographer, a maker of dictionaries. Sanders was born at Altstrelitz, in Mecklenburg, on April 12, 1819. He died on March 12, 1897. He was trained in the Jewish school of his home town. He then studied languages, mathematics, and natural history at Berlin and Halle.

Sanders took his doctorate in 1843. For ten years he led the school where he had been trained. His chief work is the Handwörterbuch der Deutschen Sprache, a handbook of German. It appeared from 1859 to 1865. He wrote it in sharp debate with the Grimm brothers' dictionary. He also published a dictionary of foreign words and one of synonyms. Textbooks, letter guides, and a history of German language followed. In 1876 Berlin called him to help purge foreign terms from German.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schlemihl-13275:
Cyrus Adler and Joseph Jacobs wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906, on the schlemihl. The word is a popular Yiddish term for an unlucky person. Heine traced it to the Bible name Shelumiel. Phinehas speared a man with that name in the Book of Numbers. Others derive it from schlimm mazzal, meaning unlucky star.

Ghetto tales love the schlemihl's misfortunes. Luck pursues him through no fault of his own. He bears it all without a murmur. Such figures match the Gothamites of English lore and Germany's Schildbürgers. Chamisso made the name famous in his tale Peter Schlemihl. He used it with little regard for its Jewish sense. He may have picked the word up from the Berlin banker Itzig. The article weighs the word's roots and its road into German literature.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shabbethai-ben-:
Shabbethai ben Moses was a legal scholar and prayer poet at Rome in the early eleventh century. Gotthard Deutsch and S. Mannheimer wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. Only fragments of his legal decisions survive today. He led the Jewish congregation of Rome as its president.

After Solomon ha-Babli, Shabbethai was Rome's first Hebrew poet. His poems for Passover sit in the Roman prayer book, still in manuscript. One poem carries his name hidden in an acrostic. His penitential prayers also survive, and one was translated by Zunz. His sons Moses and Kalonymus became prayer poets too. The entry recalls a leader who shaped Rome's Jewish worship in verse.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-simchowitz-samu:
Samuel Simchowitz was a Russian rabbinical writer born early in the nineteenth century. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Schulim Ochser wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He knew rabbinic learning thoroughly from his training. At the same time he read modern literature well.

Essays by Simchowitz appeared in the Petersburger Herold newspaper. Vienna's Orthodox community invited him as rabbi in 1866. He refused that call, and a Warsaw call two years later. Many of his Talmudic novellae remain in manuscript form. His responsa on the ritual codes survive the same way. In 1894 he sat in a great rabbinical synod at St. Petersburg. He died at Slutzk in March 1896. The entry honors a traditional scholar open to modern letters.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-singer-maximili:
Maximilian Singer was an Austrian botanist, zoologist, and author born in 1857. Isidore Singer and Edgar Mels wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Leipnik on February 6 of that year. He took his doctor's degree at Vienna in 1883. He made botany and zoology his main fields of work.

Singer wrote many articles on plants and animals. They appeared in farming journals in Vienna. He also wrote plays, including Junius Brutus in 1879. Two more dramas followed in 1891 and 1896. He wrote libretti for operas as well. One of them, Der Weise von Cordova, had music by Oskar Strauss.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-solomon-ben-maz:
Solomon ben Mazzal Tob was a Turkish Hebrew poet and press corrector. Joseph Jacobs and M Seligsohn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He flourished at Constantinople in the early sixteenth century. He was active in Hebrew printing from 1513 to 1549. Many printed books of that age bear his signature.

Among them were Kimhi's Sefer ha-Shorashim in 1513. He also worked on the four Turim in 1540. He issued a set of hymns by various authors in 1545. Some hymns in that set were his own work. He also published an introductory poem to a Torah commentary. He left a poem on chess-playing, printed much later in London.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-spitzer-benjami:
Benjamin Solomon Spitzer was an Austrian rabbi and champion of Orthodoxy. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Peter Wiernik wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was son-in-law of Rabbi Moses Sofer of Pressburg. For more than forty years he led Vienna's ultra-Orthodox congregation. Its synagogue stood in the Shiffgasse of that city.

He was a strong opponent of Reform in Jewish life. In 1872 he attacked Vienna's Culturgemeinde for its Reform measures. A set of his sermons and funeral orations was published in 1892. It also held his novellae, titled Shimlat Binyamin in part. His son-in-law Joseph Baer Kohen issued that collection. He died in Vienna on December 5, 1893.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-strauss-charles:
Charles Strauss was a French jurist and politician born in Alsace in 1834. Isidore Singer and Jacques Kahn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He was born at Gundershoffen on October 14. He set up as an attorney in Paris. He later held posts in the Interior Ministry.

Strauss spent some years in Algeria in important posts. During the Franco-Prussian war he organized army food supply there. He drafted the proclamation of the French republic in Algiers. It was published there on September 4, 1870. In 1888 he became prefect of the Drôme department. On the last day of 1895 he became an officer of the Legion of Honor. His books treat Algeria and French administration. The entry sketches a long official career.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-szegedin-14175:
Szegedin is a town of central Hungary on the Tisza. Isidore Singer and Adolf Löwinger wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about it in 1906. Jews appear there as tax-farmers under Turkish rule. Records name them in that role in 1552. When the Turks left, the Jews left too.

In 1714 three Jews who settled without leave were expelled. A royal privilege let the city admit or refuse Jews. Szegedin used that right with utmost rigor. One settler slipped in during 1781 without permission. Six families gained leave three years later. Tolerated families grew to fifty-eight by 1799. A 1790 decree froze their standing in place. Jews then began buying houses inside the city. The entry tracks slow admission, family by counted family.
