Xiangxin Liu led a team of six authors on this 2026 wireless engineering paper for future 6G networks. A promising signal format survives fast movement well but wastes power when signal peaks spike. Their scheme masks the signal and rebuilds it at the receiver with a physics-informed neural network that sees the whole frame at once.

The network, shaped by classic signal theory rather than blind layer stacking, corrected errors better than standard deep models while using fewer parameters. Liu notes hardware and over-the-air tests must come before claiming real deployment readiness.
plos-pone-0354875:
Jaweria Jalil Awan, Muhammad Hamid, and Tagrid Alshalali build a hate speech detector for Roman Urdu in this 2026 paper. Roman Urdu, the language written in Latin letters, is widespread online but lacks the labeled data and fixed spelling that automated moderation tools rely on. Their model mixes a large multilingual language model with attention layers and, crucially, a hand-built lexicon of abusive Roman Urdu terms.

The lexicon does double duty, guiding what the model pays attention to during training. Tested on a dataset of thirty thousand posts, the system classified hate speech with accuracy near eighty-nine percent. Follow-up experiments showed the lexicon guidance genuinely helped with tricky spellings, negations, and informal variations. The work brings automated protection to a language community that big platforms largely overlook.
plos-pone-0354975:
Chunjie Li and four colleagues published this 2026 simulation study of highway speed limits in rainy weather. Rain cuts tire grip and shortens what drivers can see, and hills make both worse. Their model blends road friction, slope, and sight distance into safe speeds, plus a car-following model tuned for wet driving, tested on a real highway near Hangzhou.

Simulated speeds matched observed traffic closely, and the strategy cut conflict rates steeply under heavier rain. Gentle rain needed no extra limits, while a downhill grade proved the riskiest layout. Li offers the results for adaptive rainy-day speed control.
plos-pone-0355275:
Julia Fa and colleagues interview in 2026 hunters, cooks, and sellers along the wild meat trade in rural Cameroon to map disease risk from handling animals. Thousands of structured talks covered villages and regional markets. Wild meat feeds many families and earns income, yet contact with animal fluids can pass infections to people.

Hunting and handling habits varied by ethnic group, gender, and age, with one Indigenous group more likely to hunt bats, a high risk animal. Almost nobody used protective gear, few cleaned surfaces with soap, and many ate or sold meat from visibly sick animals. Worry about disease was low, though worry did raise safer habits a bit.
plos-pone-0355375:
Jobin K and colleagues compared two school yoga programs for teenagers in India. One was a standard government yoga protocol. The other wove in mindfulness meditation. Their 2026 study assigned 147 secondary students to one of the two programs or a waiting list. Both programs ran for twenty-one days. The team measured distress, mindfulness, and emotion control. It also measured well-being before, after, and three months later.

Both yoga groups improved over the control group. The mindful version produced bigger gains in mindfulness and healthy reframing of emotions. It also lifted well-being more and cut distress more deeply. Its edge held at follow-up. The standard protocol's benefits were smaller and faded faster. The study suggests the mental training ingredient, not just the postures, carries much of yoga's school value.
plos-pone-0355475:
Kentaro Ito and co-authors report in 2026 a small crossover trial in healthy men on a coated form of medium chain fat. The coating used milk protein around tiny fat particles, meant to aid uptake in the gut. Each man took both the coated and plain forms on separate occasions, in random order and without knowing which.

Blood ketones over six hours did not differ overall between the two forms. Peak levels of ketones and of a key fatty acid were still higher after the coated form, and stomach effects stayed mild for both. The authors suggest the coating may sharpen the early response without adding harm.
plos-pone-0355675:
Patricia Moreno-Peral and colleagues published a 2026 pilot study in PLOS ONE on a digital program meant to prevent depression before it starts. An earlier doctor-delivered version, predictD, already prevented depression and anxiety in Spanish primary care. The new e-predictD version adds an app, a validated risk calculator, and decision support. Each patient gets a personal prevention plan drawn from eight modules covering exercise, sleep, problem-solving, relationships, and thinking habits.

Six family doctors in six cities enrolled fifty-six patients without depression, all at moderate to high risk, and most completed the pilot. Patients and doctors discussed the plan in a short first visit, chose modules together, and used the app between visits. Satisfaction, usability, and acceptability were mainly tested, using interviews plus standard mood, anxiety, and quality-of-life questionnaires. This small, control-free pilot is treated as a design check ahead of a full trial.
plos-pone-0355975:
Xiaojing Wu and colleagues study a gene helper called ILF3 and its role in making red blood cells, with a focus on beta thalassemia. People with that inherited blood disorder cannot make enough healthy red cells. Their 2026 paper combines single-cell gene data from patients and healthy donors with a lab experiment that switched the gene off in blood cells.

Patient cells carried less ILF3 than healthy cells, and cells that kept it looked more mature and active in growth pathways. Cells without it showed stress and inflammation signals instead, and red cell growth seemed to stall early. Switching the gene off also pushed lab cells toward early death. Wu and co-authors suggest that losing ILF3 helps explain the failed blood production in this disease.
plos-pone-0356175:
Mohamad Radwan Sirri and four colleagues review the harms side of a tempting dental offer in this 2026 paper: surgery to speed up orthodontic tooth movement. Cutting the bone around teeth can shorten treatment, but moving teeth always risks eating away their roots, and surgery might make that worse. The review gathered eleven comparative studies covering just over three hundred fifty patients, focusing specifically on measured root loss.

Evidence certainty was low to very low throughout. Simple bone-cutting procedures showed either small increases in root loss or no clear difference from standard braces, while some graft-assisted techniques measured slightly less loss than controls. Observed damage generally stayed within accepted clinical limits, but the studies were small and inconsistent. The authors say a large added risk is not demonstrated, yet firm safety conclusions are not yet possible.
plos-pone-0356275:
Hege Kersten and six others publish a protocol in 2026 for a Norwegian registry study on medication use just before a dementia diagnosis. People developing mild cognitive impairment or dementia usually carry other illnesses and take many drugs; some of those drugs are a poor fit and can worsen thinking. What happens in the year before diagnosis, when symptoms are starting but unnamed, has not been described in Norway's clinics.

The planned study links three national registries covering thinking assessments, dispensed drugs, and hospital records for everyone diagnosed in such clinics over a decade. It will estimate how common heavy medication use and risky prescribing were in that pre-diagnostic year, and which patient traits accompany them. The authors hope the map will guide safer prescribing and well-targeted efforts to trim needless drugs.
plos-pone-0356375:
I. M. Shindy and six colleagues propose a simpler way to keep electricity protection working in microgrids, in this 2026 engineering paper. When a small grid adds its own generators, fault currents grow and change direction, which can confuse the overcurrent relays that isolate faults and can overstress breakers. One remedy is a device placed between the microgrid and the main network that limits fault current in a chosen direction.

The challenge is sizing that device's resistance correctly. Instead of running heavy optimization, the authors derive it directly from a standard equivalent-circuit measure of the network, a pencil-and-paper style calculation suited to real-time engineering use. Tests across scenarios with conventional generators, wind turbines, and solar panels showed the method restored relay coordination and curbed fault currents without new relays or adaptive schemes.
plos-pone-0356475:
Zheng Li and colleagues graded the groundwater beneath the main urban area of Bozhou City in Anhui Province, China, using two independent mathematical methods that check each other. Their 2026 study combined a projection technique that lets the data itself set each measure's importance with a second method built to handle the fuzzy borders between water quality grades.

Both approaches placed the city's groundwater at the second-best grade, with closely matching scores, and stress tests confirmed the verdict was stable. Agreement matters because grading methods often smuggle in subjective weights, leaving results easy to challenge. A verified grade gives local managers a firmer basis for deciding where drinking water protection and pollution control should focus.
plos-pone-0356775:
Caner Mavili and colleagues split forty-five young male basketball players into faster and slower groups. The split used a curved sprint test around the three-point arc. The team then compared jumping and strength profiles to find what separates the groups. Their 2026 cross-sectional study measured drop jumps, countermovement jumps, and an isometric pull. Dozens of force and timing metrics came from each test.

The fast group's advantage lived in quick force. It showed shorter ground contact and stronger braking and takeoff in the drop jump. It showed stronger braking in the countermovement jump. Force development in the pull was far faster, even though peak pull strength did not differ. One rapid-force measure at a split-second window matched curved sprint contact times almost exactly. Coaches chasing change-of-direction speed should train explosiveness, not just strength.
plos-pone-0356875:
Hamid Ali Khan and coauthors published a 2026 field study in PLOS ONE on wheat breeding for the dry north of Pakistan. Yields there have stagnated for two decades as local varieties share a narrow gene pool. At a university research farm in Peshawar, they grew twelve Chinese hybrid wheat lines beside two local cultivars across two growing seasons, recording emergence, tillering, grain weight, and final yields.

Two hybrid lines clearly outperformed the rest. They sprouted early, produced the most tillers and spikes, carried the heaviest grains, and out-yielded the leading local cultivar by roughly a sixth. Statistical analysis confirmed wide genetic diversity among the hybrids, and yield rose together with its component traits, which helps breeders select efficiently. The authors recommend the two leading lines as parents and candidates for northern Pakistan's semiarid farms, arguing that fresh hybrid germplasm can break the long yield plateau.
plos-pone-0357275:
Cai Xu, Juehyun Shin, and Graciela Muniz-Terrera study whether social isolation tracks with overall healthy aging capacity among older Hispanic adults across the United States. Capacity here bundles movement, senses, thinking, mood, and energy into one score. Using a national retirement survey from a recent year, the team analyzed several hundred adults aged sixty and over, then probed rural, community, and birthplace subgroups.

Across the whole group, isolation showed no clear link with capacity. Inside subgroups, though, patterns surfaced: isolated rural elders scored lower, as did isolated United States-born elders, while higher income and fewer chronic diseases tracked with higher capacity nearly everywhere. Xu and colleagues call the subgroup results exploratory and ask for longer studies before programs lean on them.
plos-pone-0357375:
Marjorie Vázquez-Roldán and coauthors published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE on breast cancer screening among older women in Puerto Rico. They linked the island's central cancer registry with health insurance records to study women aged fifty and older who had been diagnosed with breast cancer. The team asked whether living with anxiety or a mood disorder changed how likely women were to get mammograms, be diagnosed late, or die within five years.

Among more than four thousand women, those with anxiety or a mood disorder were actually more likely to have had a recent mammogram than women without such diagnoses. Yet that extra screening did not lead to earlier-stage diagnoses, and it did not change five-year survival. The authors say screening programs should look beyond mammograms alone, and they call for more work on severe mental illness and cancer detection.
plos-pone-0357475:
Bailey Lankford and five colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on pollinator hotels, the drilled blocks and tubes people install for cavity-nesting bees and wasps. The title calls such hotels parasite hideouts, flagging a risk in a popular conservation habit.

The authors focus on preserving native cavity-nesting Hymenoptera, the bees and wasps themselves, through better pollinator hotel management. Hotels that shelter parasites as well as pollinators can backfire, so management details matter. Gardeners, land managers, and pollinator advocates are the readers who need to know how to keep these shelters helpful.
plos-pone-0357575:
Hidetaka Onda and colleagues build a simple score to flag patients likely to return to the emergency department within a day of going home. Very early returns can signal a missed problem, but most discharge data tools aim at longer windows. Using records from one hospital's discharges in a recent year, two doctors hand-checked which returns were unplanned, and the team searched routine visit data for warning signs.

Only a small share of patients returned within a day. Five simple items made the final score: arriving without an ambulance plus four blood test patterns tied to inflammation and red cell traits. Each added point raised the odds of return. Onda and colleagues present the score as decision support, not a verdict, for busy discharge moments.
plos-pone-0357975:
Kathryn Malherbe, Carol A Benn, and Gerhard Botha evaluated AI support for breast ultrasound across several sites, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. The system, called Breast AI, helps sort patients by risk during breast cancer assessment. Many AI tools are tested only in labs; this evaluation ran inside real clinical pathways.

Malherbe's multi-site observational work shows whether the AI helps clinics judge risk accurately under daily pressure. Real-world testing matters because lighting, workflow, and patient mix vary by site. If support holds up across sites, assessment can move faster without losing care. The study also gives other clinics a model for checking AI in their own pathways before adopting it.
plos-pone-0358075:
Carina Liebl leads a team of seven reading the geology inside Bronze Age rock carvings in Bohuslän, Sweden, in PLOS ONE in 2026. The granite panels, a world heritage treasure, carry ships, people, and animals pecked into the rock. The team combined ultrasound scans of the stone's interior with three dimensional surface models at five panels, asking whether carving depth follows the rock's structure rather than the carver's strength.

Sound revealed two weak, fracture rich layers a few millimeters down, relics of glacial stress relief. Nearly every figure sat within the first weak layer, averaging about a millimeter deep, deeper than the weathered crust but never reaching sound stone. A nearby polished but uncarved outcrop lacked the layered weakness entirely. The conclusion flatters the ancient carvers: they chose panels the geology had pre softened, and placed figures where the stone would yield, practical knowledge earned from the rock itself.
plos-pone-0358275:
Dandan Liu, Huixia Ji, Ye Chen, and Tongzhou Zhou published a 2026 health study in PLOS ONE linking years of factory noise to fatty liver in male car-plant workers. Fatty liver tied to metabolic dysfunction is a whole-body disorder, and noise may disturb metabolism through stress pathways, not just hearing. They examined several hundred noise-exposed men by ultrasound and tested whether body weight changed the noise relationship.

Just over half the workers had fatty liver on ultrasound, and longer noise exposure went with higher likelihood overall. The pattern depended on weight, though: among normal-weight men, each extra year of noise exposure raised the likelihood noticeably, while in overweight and obese men the added effect was not statistically clear. Their baseline risk was already high. Hearing-conservation programs, they say, should treat long noise exposure as a metabolic risk too, especially for lean workers who look low-risk.
plos-pone-0358475:
Xinyi Qiu, Limei Guan, and Hui Liu analyzed diabetes in teenagers worldwide, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Diabetes is striking younger, with effects on schooling, growth, and lifelong health. Using data from a major worldwide study of disease burden, in its 2023 round, the team tracked the burden among teenagers across more than three decades and projected future trends.

Qiu's analysis shows how unevenly that burden is shared across countries, and where it is rising fastest. Forecasts give health systems warning of what is coming, from clinic load to insulin demand. Teenage onset means decades of living with the disease, so early trends carry outsized costs. Solid global numbers help argue for prevention aimed at the young.
plos-pone-0358575:
Saeed Ghasempour leads a team of six adapting a measure of patient centered communication for Iranian nurses, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Nurses are patients' primary human contact in hospitals, and how centered their communication is can now be scored by an existing scale. No version had been tested outside its home country. Three hundred clinical nurses in Shahroud hospitals, in two independent samples, answered the Persian translation while specialists reviewed every item for cultural and conceptual fit.

The expert panel deleted one item whose meaning duplicated another. Statistical work then proceeded in stages: exploratory analysis to find the scale's structure, confirmatory analysis to test whether that structure holds, and consistency checks within and across time. The study is methodological groundwork. Once a translated instrument survives this gauntlet, Iranian hospitals can benchmark communication, compare units, and judge training honestly. Without it, patient centeredness stays a slogan nobody can measure.
plos-pone-0358775:
Esther M Choo leads a team of eight studying how caregivers and health workers received a home nutrition screening program in western Kenya, in PLOS ONE in 2026. The Family MUAC approach teaches parents to measure a child's upper arm with a simple tape to catch wasting early, backed by two way text messages with health workers. An earlier trial found the approach cut child wasting by more than a third; this study asked why people engaged with it.

Through eight focus groups and interviews with caregivers and staff from three facilities, the team found the program rated acceptable, workable, and empowering, and families felt it saved them money. Uptake among caregivers was high. Participants also suggested folding growth checks into other routine health services to sustain the habit. The accounts explain the trial's success in human terms and point to how such programs spread.
plos-pone-0358875:
Jeon Mi Lee and three colleagues revisit how hearing aids are fitted for people who wear one in a single ear, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Clinics can verify a fitting by measuring sound right at the eardrum, or they can start from the maker's automatic settings and fine tune by feel. Whether the measured route truly helps one eared users, and whether the other ear's hearing changes the answer, was unclear.

The team reviewed records from just over a hundred users three months after fitting, comparing measured and unmeasured pathways on hearing gain and self reported handicap. Gains were modestly larger in the measured group on average, and the study also tracked satisfaction scores and the role of the opposite ear. The results inform a routine clinic choice that affects many first time hearing aid wearers.
plos-pone-0359275:
Rui Saiki and four colleagues feed engineered bacteria to a slime mold and watch its hunting behavior change, in PLOS ONE in 2026. The slime mold Physarum polycephalum creeps, engulfs prey, and digests it using a pulsing internal scaffold. The team loaded harmless gut bacteria with human signaling proteins called small GTPases, then asked whether the proteins inside the prey could disturb the predator's machinery.

Bacteria carrying two of the proteins made the slime mold start eating but fail to finish, a stalled conflict response. A cancer linked mutant version scrambled behavior further, with the mold switching unpredictably among eating, stalling, and rejecting the prey. The authors propose that loose protein parts jam the mold's contraction rhythms. The odd setup turns the slime mold into a living sensor for the physical state of proteins.
plos-pone-0359575: Xue, writing alone, published a 2026 PLOS ONE study in mathematics on the stability of balance points. The setting is a class of periodic Hamiltonian systems, which describe motion driven by total energy. The systems here are degenerate, a tricky case where standard tools fail. Knowing when a balance point holds steady or drifts matters for problems from swinging pendulums to orbiting bodies.
plos-pone-0359775:
Jianping Li, Yihao Li, Weihong Wang, Zongwei Liu, and Liwei Yuan wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on fitness industry staff. It studies trainers who work in commercial fitness clubs. The authors link self-efficacy, a trainer's belief in their own capability, with turnover intention, how strongly they plan to leave the job.

Between the two sits job burnout, tested as the mediating role: exhaustion may be the bridge from low confidence to quitting. Gym chains lose money and clients when trainers churn, so knowing the pathway matters. Fitness club managers designing trainer support are the audience for this chain of workplace psychology.
plos-pone-0360675:
Xiao Wang and colleagues charted in 2026 the range of critical illnesses seen at Hebei Children's Hospital in China, in its emergency department. Their single center study reviews the cases of children who arrived critically ill, sorting them by diagnosis and type. Knowing that spectrum, which emergencies actually fill a children's emergency department, is basic intelligence for running one.

The authors describe the pattern of severe illness across ages and seasons at this large regional hospital. Such a profile guides staffing, training, equipment, and the design of referral routes from smaller hospitals. It also gives other children's hospitals in China a comparison point for judging whether their own case mix is typical or unusual.
pmc-10654675:
Katsuya Sakai and co-authors published this study in 2023. It tests a visual-motor illusion as a motor learning aid. In the illusion, a person watches a video of their own hand moving while the real hand rests. The brain feels motion that is not happening. Thirty-six healthy people were split into two groups. One got the illusion while watching a ball-rotation video; the other just watched the same video.

The task skill was tested before, right after, and one hour after the twenty-minute session. The illusion group improved more at both later checks. Brain scans during the task showed lower activity in two areas for that group after training. The authors read this as smoother, less effortful control. They conclude the illusion aids the early stage of learning a hand skill.
pmc-10655375:
Yaguang Wu and co-authors build a healing gel for eczema-like skin inflammation in 2023. The gel carries hollow specks of manganese oxide inside a chitosan base. It aims to soak up harmful oxygen byproducts, called reactive oxygen species, that drive the disease.

The gel holds moisture well and clears those harmful species in lab tests, and it does not harm cells. In mice with the skin condition, it thinned the swollen skin layer, cut mast cell counts, and lowered allergy antibodies. By calming both the chemical stress and the inflammation, the gel offers a new way to treat a stubborn, itchy disease.
pmc-10656575:
Li and co-authors probed atomic order in battery cathodes for this study from twenty twenty-three. The cathodes are lithium-rich oxides with jumbled cations, prized for cheap, earth-abundant ingredients. Tiny local arrangements, called short-range order, seem to steer their performance. Proving those arrangements exist in real space had been hard.

The team combined sharp electron microscopy, diffraction, and Monte Carlo simulation. The local order turned out to blend three motifs: tetrahedra, octahedra, and cubes. That order maps directly onto the channels lithium ions use to move. Blocking or opening those channels changes transport in kind. Doping the anion side or reheating the material reshaped the order. The authors offer new levers for tuning these cathodes.
pmc-10657475:
Woyke leads a large team studying mountain rescue shoulder care, in work from twenty twenty-three. A dislocated shoulder can be put back on the scene with a standard method. Alpine rescue guidance backs this, and the Bavarian service uses it in its protocols.

Patients treated and evacuated by the service were followed with three surveys: rescuer on site, doctor in hospital, and patient weeks later. Hospital checks confirmed the dislocation call in most cases. Other injuries in a minority of cases linked to wrong calls. The prospective data show field reduction can work well, with care to screen for added trauma.
pmc-10687775:
Wei-Fang Wu, Jing-Song Yi, Xi Xie, and Chao-Bin Liu looked for risk factors behind a rare and dangerous pregnancy: one that implants in the stump of a removed fallopian tube. Even after the tube is cut out on that side, an interstitial pregnancy can still occur and bleed heavily. The team compared twenty-nine such cases with eighty-seven matched women whose pregnancies implanted normally in the uterus.

All patients had earlier had one tube removed. Women with the rare pregnancy more often had given birth before and had prior procedures inside the uterus. One factor stood out: a swollen, fluid-filled tube, called hydrosalpinx, as the reason for the original surgery raised the odds about eightfold. The authors name it an independent risk factor.
pmc-10692175:
Roberto Garcia-Fernandez and his team teach a neural network to call the flow of air around buses. Their study from twenty twenty-three swaps slow physics runs for a learned stand-in. Air flow tests shape fuel use and how steady heavy vehicles ride. Full physics runs for each new shape variant cost too much time and cash.

Three vehicle shapes gave the training runs their data. New variants of each shape made far more flow cases to learn from. Grid spacing shrank where velocity shifts fastest. The network then gave velocity and pressure fields in one step. Its outputs matched the physics runs closely in tests. Bus shapers could screen new shapes fast, well before a full run. Coach makers gain faster design cycles for airflow.
pmc-10693175:
Dai and co-authors trace how a cancer signal reshapes nerves around pancreatic tumors. Hedgehog-Gli1 signaling drives two nerve features of pancreatic ductal cancer: invasion into nerves and remodeling of nearby nerves. Both features worsen pain and spread, yet their molecular wiring was not comprehended before.

The team found that Gli1-linked exosomes carry a circular RNA, circ-0011536, to nerve tissue. That cargo acts through the miR-451a and VGF axis to remodel peripheral nerves. Blocking any link in this chain could slow nerve invasion. The work names fresh targets in a cancer famed for resisting treatment.
pmc-10698175:
Ten researchers report a lab study from two thousand twenty-three on tiny packets shed by pig milk. The packets, called exosomes, carry molecules between cells and can change how the receiving cell behaves. Milk packets are known to enter immune cells and calm or stir them, but their effect on pig blood monocytes was unknown.

Monocytes are immune cells that can grow into the gut's resident defense cells. The team cleaned the packets from milk and labeled them so they could watch the cells take them in under a microscope. They then measured cell survival and death at rising doses, and tested how the packets changed immune tasks.
pmc-10700575:
Yaya Zhi, Qiang Guo, Jingchen Xie, Jie Hu, and Shan Xi Tian show that helium ions from the solar wind can knock oxygen molecules straight out of carbon dioxide. Their study was published in twenty twenty-three. Where early oxygen came from is a standing puzzle for lifeless planets.

Known routes split carbon dioxide with light or electrons. The team fired low-energy helium ions at the gas and measured the reaction branches and their cross-sections. Molecular oxygen formed directly in the collisions. On carbon dioxide-rich worlds bathed in stellar wind, that adds a steady oxygen source. The result feeds models of early Earth air and the air of Mars-like exoplanets.
pmc-10701975:
Hanting Xiang and co-authors published a research paper in 2023 on a faster way to find and count lymph nodes in stomach tissue removed during cancer surgery. The node count sets the cancer stage, which steers later drug treatment. Picking nodes out by eye and hand is slow and can miss small ones.

The team compared three approaches across 312 patients: rough sorting, careful hand search, and a purpose-built device. Hand search and the device both found far more nodes than rough sorting, about thirty-five against twenty-four. Positive node counts were also compared. The device matched hand work while saving time, the authors argue, giving labs a practical upgrade.
pmc-10702175:
Sevim and Atalay model how ultrasound affects magnesia dissolving in carbon dioxide water. They varied grain size, heat, and the solid-to-liquid mix in lab tests. From those runs they got a measure of how much sound energy turned into useful action.

Six neural network models were built from the test data. Inputs were grain size, time, heat, the solid mix, and sound strength. Two learning methods and three transfer functions were tried in pairs. The best match came from the Levenberg-Marquardt method with the TANSIG function. A gradient descent model with LOGSIG came second in matching lab results.
pmc-10708575:
Antonio Jiménez and six co-authors test sound waves as a way to grade beef without cutting it. Their study, from twenty twenty-three, uses fresh beef loins. Sound pulses at two low strengths pass through the meat. The team records how fast the pulses move and how they fade.

They compare those sound traits with lab tests of texture and chemistry. Many strong links show up between the two sets. That means sound can hint at quality traits that labs now test by hand. The method leaves the meat whole and fit to sell. The authors see it as a fast tool for meat plants and shops.
pmc-10709575:
Camille Mazzara and Michele Migliore model how a hippocampal neuron becomes a place cell, in a study from twenty twenty-three. Place cells fire only when an animal is in one set spot. The cell route to that sharp focus is still not fully grasped. Their model neuron is detailed in shape and in cell physics.

Signals from outside hit different dendritic layers of the simulated cell. Its synaptic inputs sorted themselves in response. The neuron learned to code one cue spot. The place cell that formed stayed stable across paths and rotated settings. It also remapped when the setting changed, matching lab tests. The authors call it the only cell model of place-cell formation this realistic. It can plug into larger network models of cognition and its disorders.
pmc-10715975: Gleiny Vázquez Hernández and co-authors present three cases of pregnant women with a narrowed mitral valve. Their 2023 case series notes that pregnancy with this heart condition carries high risk for the mother. Outcomes vary widely, so care has to be shaped case by case by a team from several fields. The series describes how each woman's condition progressed and what treatment strategies the team chose, as a guide for similar cases.
pmc-10716175:
Alvarado and co-authors test whether pleasant surprises lift mood in young European sea bass. Captive animals often show body and behavior changes, which may reflect a negative emotional state. Judgement bias tests probe that state by seeing how an animal reads unclear cues, as optimists or pessimists would.

The team gave juvenile sea bass unexpected appetitive events, such as surprise food rewards. Fish that got the treats then judged ambiguous cues more positively, a sign of better mood. The result suggests small positive surprises can improve welfare in farmed fish. It also validates mood tests for aquatic species.
pmc-10716675:
Leigh Anderson and three co-authors argue for clearer plans in women's group programs, in this twenty twenty-three paper. Groups for women are widely used to lift income, health, and standing in poorer countries. Yet funders often learn little from them, because the plan behind each program is vague.

The authors set out simple steps for stating a theory of change that can truly be tested. Their framework asks designers to name the untested guesses in the chain: how new knowledge and chances reach the group, and how taking part turns into better outcomes. A shared starting point, they say, would let programs learn from each other instead of starting over.
pmc-10717175:
Zhaoyun Liu and a large team build a risk model for breast cancer treatment in this two thousand twenty-three paper. Chemotherapy before surgery can wipe out a tumor completely, a result tied to better survival. Yet doctors cannot reliably foresee which patients will reach that full response. The team enrolled two hundred sixty-nine patients at two hospitals. They sequenced hundreds of cancer genes in tumor samples taken before treatment.

From each patient's mutations they built a personal panel to track tumor DNA in the blood. Combining blood signals with tumor data fed a stratification model. The model aims to sort patients by likely response and survival. Better sorting could spare non-responders needless toxicity. It could also push new strategies toward those at highest risk.
pmc-10727475:
Suzanne Dyer and seven co-authors review exercise trials for fall prevention in aged care homes in a 2023 paper. Exercise clearly cuts falls for older people living on their own. Whether it works as well for care home residents, who are often frailer, was less certain.

The review merges trials from a major Cochrane review with newer studies through late 2022. Nineteen trials of exercise alone against usual care were pooled. Right after programs ended, exercise probably reduced the number of falls. Effects at later follow-up were also examined. The team graded evidence quality with a standard method. Results can guide care homes weighing staff time against fall risk.
pmc-10732675:
Julian Eaton wrote an editorial in twenty twenty-three for a special issue of International Health on mental health, stigma, and neglected tropical diseases. He argues that the mental health of people living with these diseases must sit at the center of research and care, not at the edge. People affected by these diseases named their emotional and social struggles as a top concern.

Eaton notes that mental illness is common alongside these diseases, and suicide rates are higher. Many people say stigma and being shut out of daily life hurt more than the illness itself. Research is still young, focused on how common these problems are and on small pilot programs. He calls for studies that show what works, so national programs can build mental health care into their services.
pmc-10735575:
Jill Suitor and Megan Gilligan introduce a symposium from 2023 on Alzheimer's disease and related dementias within families. Dementia changes how family members relate to each other and who provides care. The symposium brings together five papers that use surveys, interviews, and mixed methods to study those effects.

One paper looks at stress in married couples where one spouse has mild to moderate illness. Others study how a mother's memory loss shapes fairness among adult children, and how care by adult children affects tension between siblings. A final paper asks whether enough family caregivers will be available in the future. Together, the papers show how dementia reshapes care, closeness, and well being in later life families.
pmc-10736075:
Walter Boot gave this presentation in two thousand twenty-three on technology and the well-being of older adults. He argues that existing and emerging technologies could support independence, health, safety, and social connection in later life. Yet a digital divide still separates younger and older users, even though the gap has narrowed over past decades. Boot gives special attention to diversity, disability, and geographic region.

His talk surveys two routes to closing the divide: changing the person, through attitudes and proficiency, and changing the technology, through human factors engineering. He stresses that user-centered design decides whether interventions succeed or fail. The presentation closes by projecting demographic and technology trends to ask when the age-related divide might disappear entirely.
pmc-10736375:
Senior, Kim, and Mather test in twenty twenty-three how ageing changes the mind's ability to shut out distractions. Older adults are famously more distractible, and blame often falls on a failure to suppress eye-catching but irrelevant items. In a visual search task, young and older adults hunted a target shape while a bright colour shape sometimes appeared as a decoy, and eye movements were tracked.

Older adults made fewer first glances at the target, showing weaker goal-driven control. Surprisingly, they still glanced less at the decoy than at plain non-targets, so suppression itself stayed intact. The split result reframes the puzzle: ageing may blunt aiming more than filtering. The authors say the finding raises fresh questions about attention in later life.
pmc-10736475:
Dana Urbanski and seven colleagues at the University of Minnesota describe a team-building experiment in this two thousand twenty-three paper. Aging research is inherently interdisciplinary, yet graduate students usually sit inside single departments. That isolation can block entry into the field. The university's Center for Healthy Aging and Innovation created Special Interest Groups to give faculty, postdocs, and graduate students shared infrastructure and community.

The authors focus on the Aging and Chronic Disease Management group as their example. Eight graduate students from four colleges joined faculty on a systematic literature review about caregiving for older adults with hypertension. The paper shares early lessons on engaging graduate students this way, along with the challenges and opportunities the model creates.
pmc-10736575:
Marie Savundranayagam and co-authors move a dementia care training into virtual reality in this 2023 study. The Be EPIC program teaches frontline workers person-centered talk for dementia care. Live actors make the practice real, but actors are costly and hard to scale. A VR version could deliver the same practice anywhere.

Six workers who had done the live version tried the same scene in VR. They judged the simulation realistic, thanks to the immersive setting and the avatar's look and speech. Interviews also flagged needs: solid tech support and staff who can run the system on site. The pilot suggests VR can widen access to this training.
pmc-10737075:
Lisa Stone-Bury, Julie Hurd, and Daniel Segal study how lifetime trauma shapes troubled personality traits in old age. Their 2023 paper uses a dimensional model with five trait domains. Older adults have had a lifetime to meet traumatic events. How piled-up trauma relates to those traits was little known.

Two hundred older adults filled trauma and personality questionnaires. Trait scores differed across four levels of total trauma exposure. The highest exposure group scored well above others on psychoticism, a domain of odd beliefs and perceptions. That group also scored higher on detachment than the lowest groups. Years since the first trauma did not change the picture, pointing to total load as the driver.
pmc-10737275:
Theresa Mau and co-authors examine how muscle energy systems in older adults relate to specific chronic diseases, in work published in 2023. Poor fitness in old age tracks with carrying many diseases at once. Muscle mitochondria, the cell's power units, sit at the centre of that link, but past work used only a summary disease count.

The study drew on a cohort of 856 adults averaging about seventy-six years. Muscle samples were tested for respiration rates, and a scan-based measure captured peak energy output. In adjusted models, one respiration mode linked to chronic kidney disease, and two modes linked to depression. Many measures linked to diabetes, with the strongest tie for maximal electron transport capacity. Other listed conditions showed no clear association. The authors argue disease-specific links sharpen the biology of ageing.
pmc-10737575:
Shuai Zhou and Xue Bai study how discrimination affects the mental well-being of older adults in China, using survey data that follows the same people over years. Their study came out in 2023. One in four older adults reported at least one form of discrimination in the past year.

The most common experiences were discrimination based on wealth, stalling at government agencies, and unfair treatment by officials. Both personal and institutional discrimination were tied to lower life satisfaction and greater psychological distress. Feeling that one's social status was decent softened the harm of personal discrimination, but not of institutional discrimination. The authors argue that protecting older adults requires action on both fronts. Their data cover thousands of respondents first surveyed in 2010 and followed through 2016.
pmc-10737975:
Mahederemariam Dagne, Elizabeth Terhune, and Patricia Heyn wrote this research paper, published in 2023. It checks how easy it is to find a clear definition of health equity on trusted aging and public health websites.

The team built a review tool and checked more than sixty well-known health websites. Many of them carried content aimed at older adults. The review found that definitions of health equity differed from site to site and were often hard to track down. Half of the sites had no definition at all. Most sites also gave no source to back the definition they did show. The authors call for a shared, standard definition and clearer placement so older adults can find and grasp the term.
pmc-10738275:
Susan Barnason studied how ready older adults feel to leave post-acute care and go home, in a study from twenty twenty-three. After a hospital stay, many older adults move to such care for rehab and nursing help. Most live with several long-term diseases at once, and many return to hospital soon after discharge.

A small group of patients at a large midwestern facility filled in scales on readiness and on how active they felt in their own care. Drug burden at discharge was high. Readiness scores rose with how active patients felt in managing their health. Barnason argues that building self-care skills and confidence before discharge may ease the move home.
pmc-10738375:
Keiko Ono surveys how visiting nurses and care managers team up for home deaths in one Japanese prefecture, in a study from two thousand twenty-three. Mailed forms went to one hundred ninety-two nurses, and one hundred thirty valid replies came back. Teamwork was rated across four stages from prep to near death.

Hands-on experience passed half at every stage. The worth of teamwork scored above three quarters at each stage too. Nurses rated their joint work with managers at about seventy-five on a hundred scale. Stage-by-stage gaps are named for training builders. The work sits inside Japan's long-term care insurance frame. Readers get a teamwork baseline for home end-of-life care.
pmc-10738675:
Four researchers — Wingyun Mak, Orah Burack, Margret Howard, and Kenneth Boockvar — report a 2023 survey study on volunteering and purpose in life. Their subjects are middle-aged and older adults living in the community across the United States. The study asks whether different kinds of volunteer work relate to how people's sense of purpose changed over five years.

Data came from the AARP Social Engagement and Brain Health Survey, covering 2,585 adults aged forty to seventy-five and older. Younger age, better health, and better cognition were linked to greater gains in purpose. Volunteering through religious organizations and support groups also predicted larger increases. The authors suggest health, valuing purpose, and volunteer type are possible points for intervention.
pmc-10738775:
A program paper from 2023 describes an effort to weave age-friendly care into cancer care across the United States. Older adults with cancer are a growing group, yet what counts as fair, high-quality care for them was poorly defined. A national cancer center association joined a health improvement institute to run the first oncology cohort guided by the 4Ms framework.

Twenty-two cancer programs took part in a learning and action period. The framework's four parts are what matters to the patient, mobility, mentation, and medication. Teams audited their own gaps and joined expert webinars. In a poll, most team members named medication as the hardest part to put in place and asked for more expert guidance. Many sites moved toward formal recognition.
pmc-10738975:
Kirsty Haunch reviews past research on how co-workers get along in long-term care homes in a paper from twenty twenty-three. Care work is hard on the body and on feelings, and staff often have only each other for support. The review asks what helps staff build good working ties.

The review covered work from health and social care more broadly, since direct studies were few. Good ties formed when staff had social skills, shared the right values, and had support from leaders. The author argues that social skills deserve more focus. Such skills can be taught, and they help staff handle hard moments without harming their ties.
pmc-10739475:
Jae Ho Lee, Byung Tae Choi, and Hwa Kyoung Shin combine electroacupuncture and a plant compound to boost stem cell therapy after stroke. Their mouse study from twenty twenty-three tests the pairing. Transplanted stem cells often die or wander poorly in injured brains. Adjunct treatments might help them settle and specialise.

A blocked brain artery created the stroke model. Human stem cells were transplanted into the damaged region. Groups received acupuncture, the compound, both, or neither. Combined treatment improved cell survival and movement most. More cells became nerve-lineage cells rather than scar-type cells. Behaviour tests tracked motor and cognitive recovery. Combination adjuncts may raise cell therapy's ceiling.
pmc-10740775:
Paola Canale and co-authors review, in a 2023 paper, a class of RNA messages copied from the protective caps at chromosome ends, and what they may mean for aging blood vessels. Shortened caps, called telomeres, are tied to hardened arteries, heart attacks, and heart failure. The RNA, named TERRA, is no passive byproduct: it helps guard the caps and control their upkeep.

The review gathers what is known about how this RNA is made, what it binds, and how its levels shift in disease. Its role in the vessel wall itself is still almost unstudied, a gap the authors underline. They speculate that mapping the RNA's behavior in the circulation could open new ways to slow vascular aging. The paper is as much a call for research as a summary, aimed at a field they judge ripe and neglected.
pmc-10741675:
Sara Franceschelli and nine co-authors check whether a dry stored tooth keeps its bone growth spark after treatment with the Tooth Transformer device, which grinds and cleans teeth for grafts. Teeth are known to fit bone graft use well. The study came out in twenty twenty-three.

A dozen teeth from real patients were cleaned of decay and fillings, cut, and stored at room warmth. Each was shredded, demineralized, and disinfected by the device. Protein tests then hunted for growth signals, and two key bone proteins were found in the treated dry teeth. The authors conclude the device does not strip the tooth's growth spark.
pmc-10741875:
Sebastian Kubica and six co-authors test two birch-bark compounds on kidney cells in this twenty twenty-three study. The compounds, changed forms of a natural substance called betulin, are candidates for cancer care. Many cancer drugs harm the kidneys, so early checks on kidney cells matter.

The team grew human kidney tubule cells in dishes and added each compound. They then measured the activity of three genes from a growth-signal family tied to healing and scarring. Gene copy counts showed how strongly each gene responded. The work helps judge whether these hopeful compounds are safe enough around the kidney to study further.
pmc-10742475:
Zhenyu Yang and co-authors turn a rice processing waste into a food ingredient that carries curcumin, in a 2023 paper. Curcumin, a plant compound with health promise, breaks down easily and dissolves poorly. The team used leftover rice peptide sludge, normally thrown away, and treated it with heat and pH shifts, then mixed it with chitosan.

The mix forms particles that sit at the border between oil and water, steadying droplets in what are called Pickering emulsions. Adding more chitosan lowered surface tension but made the particles larger, and one recipe formed the softest, most stable layer. Emulsions built this way kept better in storage than plain peptide ones. They also released less free fat during digestion and let more curcumin through to be absorbed.
pmc-10743075:
Václav Šmíd and a team of co-authors fed mice a diet that fattens the liver in a 2023 study. The diet, lacking two nutrients and rich in fat, reliably causes non-alcoholic fatty liver disease. The team asked whether adding omega-3 fats, found in fish oil, could soften the damage.

After six weeks, mice on the harmful diet showed the expected liver changes, but the omega-3 group fared better. Blood fats and liver enzyme levels fell, and the extra fat stored in the liver was wiped out. Gene activity shifted in helpful ways across fat, cholesterol, and inflammation pathways. The authors call omega-3 fats a promising food-based approach for this disease.
pmc-10743175:
Qianqian Xue and co-authors test, in two thousand twenty-three, microwave sterilisation for ready-to-eat imitation crab meat. Heat must kill germs in such food, but slow heat can spoil taste and feel. A factory-scale microwave system may do the same job faster and more gently.

The team treated the meat at three set heat levels and logged heat rate, time, and quality traits. Microwaves cut the process time by roughly two thirds versus the standard retort method. At the same heat level, the crab meat held water better and kept better colour and texture. Its protein form also stayed closer to ideal. Helpful fats were kept slightly better too. The data aim to guide future surimi food work.
pmc-10747575:
Santos and a large team chart the family tree of bird pox viruses found in Portugal in twenty twenty-three. The virus infects hundreds of bird species and can cause skin sores or throat disease. Outbreaks can cost farms money and harm wild birds. The team read part of one gene from ten virus samples taken between twenty seventeen and twenty twenty-three.

The samples fell into four branches of the virus family tree. Some matched strains from other lands and other years quite closely. That pattern points to the virus entering Portugal more than once. The update sharpens watch on the disease and can guide bird vaccination where it is used.
pmc-10747675:
Zhijun Teng, Mingzhe Li, Libo Yu, Jinliang Gu, and Meng Li defend wireless sensor networks against sinkhole attacks in a two thousand twenty-three security paper. In a sinkhole attack, a malicious node advertises a fake best route and swallows traffic, and such attacks are easy to launch yet hard to spot.

The defense first computes trust values for suspicious nodes using an SPA trust model to expose the attackers. A Jaya optimization algorithm then routes traffic around the compromised area toward the genuine sink, isolating the bad nodes. Simulations show better packet delivery, lower delay, and reduced energy use, improving the network's security and reliability.
pmc-10748475:
Dae-Eun Jeong and co-authors present a 2023 study on virus-like jumping genes in worm genomes. Polintons are large DNA transposons that carry the tools to copy themselves, and evidence suggests they spread between hosts as virus-like particles. Roundworm genomes hold many copies, making them a natural archive of Polinton history.

The team searched worm genomes widely and found full-length Polintons in several species, some ancient and some recently active within one species. One subgroup stood out: its copying enzyme differs from the family norm and matches Polintons of water molds and molluscs instead. Family trees support swaps of that enzyme across distant animal groups, in both land and sea worms. The swaps imply gene flow between phyla.
pmc-10749275:
Sean McClintock, Derek MacDonald, and Tamara MacDonald study medicine teaching for children with cancer in a 2023 paper. Children who grasp their medicines tend to follow treatment better. In child care, parents share the learning, and stress at diagnosis can block what families take in.

Over six months, the team interviewed six families and nine health providers at one center. Families described uneven teaching, with facts varying by provider and even drug names shifting. Stress and anxiety right after diagnosis hurt how much parents retained. Providers confirmed the delivery gaps. The authors call for a steadier, staged teaching plan that repeats key points. Clearer routines could ease family strain during long treatment.
pmc-10749475:
Jodie Fergusson and co-authors tune gold nanoparticle clusters for heat therapy in a 2023 paper. Gold particles can cook tumor cells when lit by near-infrared light, and they also boost a laser reading method. Bare particles clump badly in harsh body fluids. A silica shell steadies them and guards the sensing molecules on their surface.

The team built several gold structures, from single particles to clusters, and capped each with silica of tuned thickness. They then linked cluster size and shell build to light absorption, sensing signal strength, and bulk heating. Bigger clusters shifted absorption into the useful near-infrared band. The tuning rules help engineers design one particle that both finds and cooks its target.
pmc-10757475:
Ajay K Jain and co-authors compare celiac disease first found in adults with cases found in childhood at one Indian center. Their 2023 study uses a decade of prospectively kept records. In central India the disease was long viewed as a children's condition, leaving adult presentations poorly described.

Classic chronic diarrhea appeared in both groups but less often in adults, most of whom showed non-classical signs instead. Adult diagnosis rested on symptoms starting after eighteen, positive blood antibodies, and the characteristic gut lining damage. The comparison helps regional doctors expect a subtler picture in grown patients and test for it sooner.
pmc-10759975:
Sharron Xuanren Wang, Jarid Goodman, and J-P Laurenceau track mental health among college Dreamers around the two thousand twenty election. Dreamers came to the United States as children without legal status. That vote could have changed their path to legal stay, so stress was a real concern.

pmc-10789175:
Seconds at room temperature can rewrite a key Alzheimer's measurement, warn Geoffrey Canet and co-authors in a 2023 lab study. The measurement is the chemical tagging of tau protein, a routine readout in cell and animal work on the disease. Cold pushes the tagging up and heat pulls it down.

In two neuron cell lines the shift began within seconds of leaving the incubator, while cells set straight on ice barely changed. In mice, the anesthetic alone raised tagging before the animals were even fully under. The authors press labs to freeze the temperature variable, literally, or risk chasing artifacts.
pmc-10797375:
Yamasaki and Hino wrote an editorial commentary in twenty twenty-three on a study of dynamic chest radiography, a moving X-ray method, in people with cystic fibrosis. Standard lung tests need mouthpieces, masks, or sealed booths, and the hard blowing they demand can spray germs, a real hazard for patients with lung infections.

The study they discuss matched lung area measures from the moving X-ray against booth-based volume measures. The two sets lined up plausibly, including the deeper volume divisions that simple blowing tests cannot reach. A mixed breathing protocol, calm breaths plus deep ones, let each image measure stand for one volume division. The commentators call the work a good first step. They urge larger studies across many lung diseases, since a fast, mask-free estimate of lung volumes could help clinics during outbreaks and beyond.
pmc-11535475:
Wang and fourteen co-authors find germ marks and their T-cell locks with no lab-made bits in this twenty twenty-four paper. Such locks tell the guard cells which germ bits to strike in a fight. Made bits cost much cash and time, which slows that hunt a lot.

From healed blood, locks for crown germ marks shared by a whole germ clan fell out. Three in four donors held cells set on one shared mark from the germ's core. Some locks also hit changed marks, which could guard past new germ forms.
pmc-11536875:
Peirui Zhao, Weiwei Cai, Wenhua Zhou, and Na Li present a vision network for robot pear picking, in a research paper from 2024. Fast, accurate fruit finding is key for farm robots. Older transformer designs can be slow, and orchard scenes are cluttered, with small fruits that are easy to miss.

pmc-11540075: Jonathan Pol and co-authors summarize a new cancer drug angle in a 2024 commentary. The target is RIPK1, a protein that holds back apoptosis, necroptosis, and an inflammatory signaling path. A recent paper in Immunity describes a small molecule that forces cells to destroy RIPK1. pmc-11570275:
Insha Shafi, Manish Gautam, and Rupesh Kariyat wrote this 2024 review on how crops respond when drought and insect feeding strike at the same time. In real fields, plants rarely face one stress alone. Dry soil and chewing insects are two of the worst limits on crop yield.

Together, they can show how a plant trades growth for defense under both stresses at once. The authors map what is known and where the gaps sit for breeders.
pmc-11573975:
Jing Xiong and four colleagues published a cervical cancer study in two thousand twenty-four on how tumours hide from immune attack. Tumour cells pour out lactate, a waste acid that blunts killer T cells. A gene-reading protein called YTHDF1 seemed to drive that process.

The protein stabilises the message for a lactate gate protein, letting more lactate flood out. The authors name the pathway a target for making immunotherapy work better in this cancer.
pmc-11575075:
Solomon Oguta and a large team of co-authors studied why pregnant women still catch malaria despite preventive drugs, at a hospital in northern Uganda, in this 2024 study. All pregnant women in Uganda get a preventive drug from the fourteenth week of pregnancy, yet many still fall ill. The team surveyed mothers at Gulu Regional Referral Hospital to find the linked factors.

Almost all said they slept under mosquito nets daily, but over half had not yet taken the preventive drug in this pregnancy, and nearly half were anaemic. The paper sets out the study design and these early findings, then weighs which factors track with infection. Results like these can guide clinics on where prevention breaks down.
pmc-11575175:
Mirna Farran and co-authors published this cancer study in 2024. It asks whether the state of a patient's mouth at diagnosis says anything about long-term survival in head and neck cancer. The team studied 79 patients diagnosed between late 2002 and mid 2005. At diagnosis, each patient's jaw X-ray was checked for bone loss around the teeth, a sign of gum disease, and each patient rated their own dental quality of life.

Patients with clear bone loss died at higher rates over the follow-up years. Low self-rated dental quality of life also predicted shorter survival. When both measures were placed in the same model, each still carried its own signal, even after standard clinical factors were taken into account. The authors suggest that two cheap checks at diagnosis may help flag patients at higher risk.
pmc-11576975:
Ito and a large team test a blood marker for a type of kidney cancer in twenty twenty-four. The cancer, clear cell renal carcinoma, shares traits with a like cancer of the ovary. A protein called TFPI2 had shown promise as a blood marker for the ovary form. The team asked if it could flag the kidney form as well.

Gene data linked high levels with worse survival. Cell level gene reads found the protein made in tumor and normal kidney cells. The authors see it as a candidate marker.
pmc-11577875:
Noor and six co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-four on a deep learning tool that spots a chemical tag on RNA. The tag, called m5U, plays key roles in cell processes. Finding its sites by lab work is slow, so prediction tools help. Their tool builds sequence traits with a hybrid composition method. A ranking method then picks the most telling traits. A deep neural network makes the final calls on each site.

The tool scores above ninety percent accuracy on two benchmark sets. It beats prior models on both training and fresh test samples. Gains run to several points over the best rivals. The authors offer the tool for RNA research and drug design work.
pmc-11579475:
Chanokporn Muangchinda and Onruthai Pinyakong grew plastic-eating bacterial groups in 2024. Low-density polyethylene pollutes widely. Breaking it down with living things stays hard. Bacteria were fed plastic as sole carbon. Group change was tracked as the mix grew richer. Pre-steps were varied to boost breakdown.

Certain bacteria emerged as key players. Network analysis flagged their central roles. Several genera showed plastic potential first here. Names include Mesorhizobium and Agromyces. Others joined that possible list too. Pre-steps raised breakdown speed overall. The authors propose lasting waste answers. Field testing remains a future step. Plastic waste needs such living options.
pmc-11580675:
Hitomi Tsuchihashi and co-authors study what drives work engagement among radiology nurses in Japan, in a paper from 2024. These nurses face radiation risk on top of normal ward duties. Strict safety rules add strain that can wear down their drive. The team surveyed nurses at major cancer care hospitals across the country.

Of more than three hundred nurses asked, 140 replied. Engagement ran higher with age, rank, and a wish to work in radiology. Men in the sample also scored higher on average. A key factor was access to advice about radiation exposure at work. Nurses who could ask about exposure felt more engaged. The authors urge hospitals to build such support into the job. It may lift both morale and safety in scan departments.
pmc-11585175:
Jenny Sivertsson, Ninni Sernert, and Kristina Åhlund map how exercise therapy by video or app is used for long-term low back pain, in a 2024 review. Back pain is a leading health problem worldwide, and exercise guided by a physiotherapist is a first-line treatment. Remote care has grown fast, but the programs vary a lot. The team searched three databases for studies from 2017 to early 2024.

Of more than a thousand papers found, 28 met their rules. Most programs were sent through phone apps for patients to do on their own time, and pain plus function were the most common measures. Remote programs matched clinic-based exercise in the gains patients made. The authors flag live and group-based remote sessions as a gap that future studies should fill.
pmc-11586975:
Jorge Hugo Villafañe and co-authors review, in a 2024 paper, how South American towns along the royal road from Buenos Aires to Lima coped with a plague in 1742 and 1743. Conquest and disease had reshaped the region for two centuries. The team read archive and later records for the health steps taken and their long effects.

Quarantines, makeshift hospitals, and rule changes formed the core response. Prayer rites and novenas ran beside those steps and held communities together. Colonial rule bent under the strain but adapted, which the authors call an early form of institutional resilience. The case offers lessons for modern crisis governance, above all on joining health steps with social repair.
pmc-11587775:
Federica Felice and co-authors test whether a brain chemical made by neurons can calm the brain's immune cells when they turn inflammatory. Their study appeared in 2024. The chemical, N-acetylaspartate, keeps the nervous system healthy, and its handling goes wrong in diseases like multiple sclerosis. The team dosed mouse microglia, in a cell line and in fresh cultures, then provoked them with bacterial toxin and an immune signal.

They tracked fat metabolism, protein tagging by acetyl groups, and the cells' debris-eating activity. The treatment blunted the inflammatory response through those routes. The authors say the metabolite is not just a marker of neuron health but an active referee of microglial behavior, worth exploring in diseases driven by chronic brain inflammation.
pmc-11594575:
Boris Shenkman and co-authors review a puzzle of unused muscle in a 2024 paper. A rat's calf muscle holds posture all day, yet under weightlessness its signal first falls silent. Strangely, from the third day of unloading the signal climbs back on its own, reaching normal levels by two weeks. The muscle seems to switch itself back on without any load.

The effect may be a built-in defense that slows wasting. Astronaut exercise plans and bed-rest care could borrow the trick once its wiring is clear.
pmc-11598075:
Wen Li and a large team of co-authors test tumor shape as a sign of chemo response, in a paper dated twenty twenty-four. They studied 910 breast cancer patients in the I-SPY 2 trial who got chemo before surgery. Shape features came from MRI scans taken before treatment and early in it.

A plain volume ratio plus clinic data scored 0.64 on the standard accuracy scale. Adding shape features lifted the score to 0.76. The change in surface-to-volume ratio between scans mattered most, and all top features came from the early scan. Gains also showed in two cancer subgroups.
pmc-11602075:
Alicia Guigui, Léa Liaigre, Matthieu Roustit, and Jordan Loader tested whether a skin blood-flow method gives repeatable results in a 2024 study. Ten healthy volunteers each completed four sessions, on calf and forearm, a week apart. The team compared readings within a day, between days, and between limbs for three protocol versions. They summarized consistency with standard variation and correlation measures. Knowing which version repeats best tells researchers whether the test is ready for wider clinical studies.
pmc-11603175:
Krzysztof Jankowski and co-authors published a 2024 study on growing thin carbon wires laced with iron. The wires form between graphite electrodes during an electric arc struck in liquid paraffin. pmc-11603875:
Samah El-Arifi and her four co-authors, publishing in 2024, catalogue the germs behind urinary tract infections in Khartoum, Sudan, and which drugs still work against them. pmc-11604975:
Aissa Abderrahmane, Obai Younis, Sameh Ahmed, Abed Mourad, Zehba Raizha, and Awadallah Ahmed model heat flow in a wavy, slanted storage box in two thousand twenty-four. pmc-11605575:

pmc-11605675:

pmc-11606175:

pmc-11607975:

pmc-11608475:
Fredrik Stangeland, Vigdis Sveinsdottir, and Eline Ree published this study in 2024 on work and mental illness in Norway. pmc-11609275:

pmc-11609575:

pmc-11610275: Kaitlin Potts and co-authors published a short correction in 2024 to their study of diet quality in young adults and sleep at midlife, drawn from the Bogalusa Heart Study. pmc-11613875:

pmc-11616275:

pmc-11622375:

pmc-11623475:

pmc-11625675:

pmc-11627075:

pmc-11628975:

pmc-11630075:

pmc-11630275:
Kiran Jalil and colleagues freeze bacterial spores in the act of waking up and photograph them in three dimensions, in this study from twenty twenty-four. pmc-11640175:

pmc-11640375:

Adjusted models also weighed death from heart causes and from any cause.
pmc-11640475:
Hosameldeen Mohamed Husien and co-authors published a 2024 study on whether sugars from moringa leaves can calm inflamed gut cells. pmc-11640675:

pmc-11641675:

pmc-11642675:

pmc-11643675:
