pmc-11643975:
Maxim Shevtsov and his co-authors present a 2024 study on silver-coated titanium implants made by 3D printing. Porous titanium scaffolds bond well with bone and soft tissue in prosthetic limbs. Their weak point is infection around the implant. A thin silver layer can slow bacterial growth and film formation. The team coated printed implants with a micrometer of silver and tested how cells respond.

Bone-forming cells and skin cells stayed healthy on the coated surface over fourteen days. Skin cells kept their grip, with adhesion genes unchanged. Bone cells kept their bone-building activity, and one growth pathway even ran stronger. The coating did not reduce the scaffold's ability to join with tissue or spur bone growth. The authors argue the coating suits personalized implants that anchor directly to the skeleton.
pmc-11644275:
Shaotong Pei and co-authors wrote a materials study from 2024 on growing a charge-storing polymer directly on carbon cloth by electrochemistry. Water-based storage devices are safe and cheap, but their electrodes hold modest charge. Polymers rich in reactive groups are a promising fix, if they can be made well. The team polymerized s-triazine rings in acid water for the first time, coating cloth with a grainy, pore-rich film.

The coated cloth stored charge like a battery material, with its nitrogen and oxygen groups doing the work as ions moved in and out. Capacity reached about one hundred milliamp-hours per gram in acid, and half that in a zinc salt solution. A symmetric device built from two coated cloths kept over four fifths of its capacity after twenty-five hundred fast cycles. The team offers the polymer as a candidate for aqueous storage.
pmc-11644475:
Liting Wang, Changjie Xu, Libo Feng, and Wenjie Wang surveyed a noise-based method for probing magnetic traits of iron-based materials in twenty twenty-four. When such a material is magnetized, it gives off crackle-like noise, known as Barkhausen noise. That noise can reveal the easy axis of the material and gauge its grain pattern and inner stress, all without damage.

The survey traces how the field has grown and weighs the models that link noise to domain wall motion and domain spin. It then covers the gear and methods used to read the noise from many angles. Uses in stress gauging and grain checks are reviewed next. The authors close with the open problems in the field and with ways that mixed effects may sway readings, which can guide more exact tests in the future.
pmc-11644675:
Lixia Zhou and four co-authors review gene editing for tropical crops in a paper from twenty twenty-four. China grows many tropical crops, such as oil palm, rubber, banana, sugarcane, cassava, and papaya. These crops supply key goods, but breeding them the old way is slow.

Traits like many chromosome sets, mixed genes, and long youth phases block fast progress. CRISPR Cas9 editing can change a chosen gene directly, which may speed breeding a lot. The review sums up current uses of the method in major tropical crops and looks at what may come next. It also notes limits that still need work before farm gains are wide.
pmc-11645275:
Wenbo Jia and co-authors trace, in a 2024 study, how a little-known protein helps liver cancer grow and shrug off treatment. The protein, called BAIAP2L2, runs high in tumor tissue, and patients with more of it fare worse. In lab tests it pushed cancer cells to multiply, spread, take on stem-like traits, and dodge cell death, while a stress switch in the cell switched the protein's own gene on.

The mechanism runs through a partner protein. The cancer protein grabs it, shields it from disposal, and escorts it into the nucleus. From there, the pair keeps reactive oxygen levels low, which feeds the tumor's growth and blunts a standard liver cancer drug. The authors name the protein a candidate marker for prognosis and a possible drug target. Blocking it, they suggest, might restore the drug's bite.
pmc-11646375:
Yang-Chuan Chen, Feng-Yee Chang, Shih-Ta Shang, and Yung-Chih Wang report a 2024 case of a rare brain infection and review earlier reports. The germ involved, Streptococcus intermedius, lives harmlessly in the mouth and gut but can cause deep abscesses. Meningitis from this germ, with no abscess, is very uncommon.

The patient was a healthy 56-year-old man with fever and headache. Spinal fluid tests confirmed meningitis, and scans showed swelling in the brain's lining and inner chambers. Standard cultures found no germ, so the team used a DNA method that reads all genetic material in the fluid, which named the culprit. Six weeks of an antibiotic plus surgery led to a good recovery.
pmc-11647375:
Natalie Thomas and co-authors set out a study plan for tracking teen ME/CFS in Australia in two thousand twenty-four. The illness, also called chronic fatigue syndrome, can disable teens in a key growth window. Its biology is poorly known, and teens are rarely studied though onset often peaks at their age.

The plan follows patients aged twelve to nineteen plus healthy peers over time. Urine, blood, and immune cells feed deep scans: full genome reads, chemical profiles, and protein counts. Gold-standard clinic and mind tests run alongside. The team hopes the paired data will yield a marker set for the disease, reveal patient subgroups, and show how the illness works.
pmc-11647875:
Abin Raj and colleagues report physics experiments on liquids that form glass when cooled, published in twenty twenty-four. A classic relation links how fast molecules rotate to how thick the liquid is, and whether that link breaks down in very cold liquids is a long-running question. The team focused on large molecules that are not round, where the electric response depends on which way the molecule turns. They combined electrical measurements, thickness measurements, and computer simulations of the motion.

For molecules whose charge sits across the long axis, the classic relation held through the whole supercooled range. For molecules sensed mainly through short-axis turning, the relation broke down in an intermediate range. Simulations pointed to different turning mechanisms for the two axes. The authors conclude that the shape of the motion, not the mechanism alone, decides whether the classic relation survives.
pmc-11648275:
Shi-Jie Wang and nine co-authors issue a correction to an older study on liver cancer cells, printed in two thousand twenty-four. The first study linked a protein called CD147 to the spread of cancer cells in groups, by way of another protein.

The note says two parts of a key chart were put together in error. One part was a blot image, and one was a photo for a test group. The corrected chart is shown in full. It sets out blot tests, gene tests, mouse tests of spread, and patient life curves. Readers get a fixed record, so they can judge the first claims on sound art.
pmc-11650275:
Taufiqul Islam, Tanmoy Mazumder, Md Nishad Shahriair Roni, and Md Sadmin Nur compare algorithms for forecasting a crop in this two thousand twenty-four study. Aman rice, grown in Bangladesh's monsoon season, depends on rainfall and temperature. Using fifty-two years of data, nineteen seventy to twenty twenty-two, the authors trained five machine learning models on monsoon climate variables. The models were Random Forest, neural network, decision tree, linear regression, and gradient boosting.

Random Forest won, proving most accurate and most robust to climate variability in sensitivity analysis. Gradient boosting followed; linear regression handled linear trends but missed nonlinear patterns, and neural networks and decision trees lagged. The model projects Aman yields reaching about one hundred thirty-three metric tonnes by twenty thirty and one hundred forty by twenty fifty, alongside rising temperatures. The authors offer this as guidance for climate-aware agricultural planning in Bangladesh.
pmc-11651775:
Dongming Gao and five co-authors build a gene signature for glioma prognosis from a copper linked cell death process in a 2024 paper. Glioma is a malignant brain tumor with poor outcomes, and better markers could personalize treatment. Cuproptosis, a recently described death route tied to copper, also shapes the tumor's immune surroundings, but its role in glioma was unclear.

Drawing on two large tumor atlases, the team charted mutations in fifty one copper handling genes and grouped tumors into three molecular subtypes with distinct immune and biological traits. A statistical selection method then distilled a four gene model. The signature predicted survival strongly in the validation cohort. The authors offer it as a prognostic indicator and a window on the glioma immune microenvironment.
pmc-11652475:
Jianhua Lyu and eight co-authors study joint replacement infections caused by rare germs in a 2024 paper. Infections around an artificial hip or knee are hard to treat. Rare germs may behave unlike common ones, but their clinical pattern was poorly known.

The team reviewed records for 219 infection cases treated over about a decade. Thirty-two cases involved rare germs, and the rest served as controls. Rare germ cases carried more prior illness and more invasive procedures before surgery. They also formed sinus tracts more often and showed lower levels of a common blood marker. Culture tests confirmed the germ less often in this group. The contrasts can help surgeons suspect rare germs sooner.
pmc-11653575:
Novest Matee and co-authors present a 2024 study of what caregivers in Dar es Salaam see as causes of undernutrition in young children. Poor diet in the first years drives much illness and death in low income lands. Caregiver side factors are key but were little explored in this district of the city.

The team held deep talks with caregivers of undernourished children under five at one hospital. Low pay and poverty led the list of causes named, since they block buys of rich foods. Short time for child care also stood out, as did weak follow-through on world health feeding advice. Most caregivers knew the signs of malnutrition well, though their sense of the term split from the formal one. The authors urge pay support and feeding teaching.
pmc-11654175:
Yalin Yu and co-authors study high blood potassium among hospital patients in this 2024 paper. Hyperkalaemia is a common and dangerous electrolyte problem. Drugs and kidney disease are frequent causes. Late treatment raises death risk and lengthens stays.

Records covered 99,047 admissions to Townsville University Hospital from 2018 to 2022. Patients with a potassium result at or above the set threshold were included. The team compared patients on maintenance dialysis with other patients. Prevalence, risk traits, and treatments given were all tallied. Links between high potassium and length of stay were tested. Separate patterns for dialysis patients matter, since their potassium handling and treatment choices differ sharply from other inpatients.
pmc-11654275:
Bill Karanatsios and three co-authors looked at how ready Australia is for registry-based trials in a 2024 paper. Classic randomized trials are strict but slow, costly, and often fail to reflect real patients. Trials based on registries keep the random draw but sign up patients through existing registries and reuse their data, and promise real-world reach.

The team spoke with thirty people: clinician researchers, program managers, and governance officers. Grasp of the method varied widely, as did knowledge of local registries. Themes covered what helps and hinders uptake, the ethics and rules load, and how to push for wider use. The authors map a young field: strong interest, patchy capacity, and clear steps that could build both.
pmc-11655175:
Layla Grecia González-González and three co-authors report a case of multiple sclerosis treated with a white cell extract. Their case study, from twenty twenty-four, deals with a patient whose first care was corticosteroids. Those drugs cut swelling but left him open to infections, most of all of the chest. Care was then swapped to a dialyzable leukocyte extract, given by mouth under a trade name.

Since the swap, swelling rates fell and the disease's march slowed. Signs eased and his life quality rose. The team ties the gain to the extract's immune tuning acts. One case proves no cure, but it maps a path for patients whom steroids put at risk.
pmc-11655275:
Fiona C Dale and co-authors report a 2024 study on why some puppies act distressed when left alone. Such separation behavior can signal poor welfare in dogs. The team used a long-running study of young dogs in the United Kingdom to look for early-life factors tied to the problem at six months of age.

Records for 145 puppies were checked against owner reports. Puppies were less likely to show the behavior if they slept at least nine hours a night early in life. Being kept in a crate or one room overnight also linked to lower risk. Poor house training early on raised the risk, as did harsh responses from owners. Owners who fussed over dogs when they came home had puppies far more likely to show the behavior.
pmc-11655975:
YaYan Zhao and co-authors (2024) review the role of a chemical tag on RNA in nasopharyngeal carcinoma. This cancer of the upper throat is common in southern China, Southeast Asia, and North Africa. Advanced cases still fare poorly, pushing researchers toward the cancer's molecular machinery. The tag, called m6A, is the most studied RNA modification. Enzymes write it, erase it, and read it, and in this cancer those regulators go off balance.

The authors trace how the tagging shifts gene expression and feeds the cancer's start and spread. They connect specific regulators to growth, invasion, and other malignant behaviors in the literature. The hope is practical: tagged transcripts and their enzymes could become biomarkers for earlier detection, or targets for precision drugs. The review closes by mapping open questions in a still young frontier.
pmc-11656575:
Opsasnick and coauthors ask if DNA marks carry the effect of stress on heart risk. Stress links to heart illness and its risk factors. Chemical marks on DNA link to both stress and heart risk. If marks sit in the middle path stays unproven.

The team used data from a large United States aging study. The set held 2,668 older adults of mixed backgrounds. Mean age was just over 70 years in the group. They tested DNA marks across the full gene set. Ten heart risk factors served as outcomes in the tests. Dozens of marks carried part of the stress effect.
pmc-11658375:
Mohammed Sarhan and his team link contact with violence to health literacy in Palestinian teenagers. Their study from twenty twenty-four surveys middle school students in one sweep. Health literacy shapes a whole life of sound choices and use of care. War and strife over land and rule may cut into that learning in the young.

More than eight hundred students filled in a tested Arabic health literacy scale. Eleven questions checked contact with many forms of violence. Half the students scored low on communication literacy. Contact with political violence tracked with much lower scores on basic health literacy. Scores on the confusion scale fell too with that contact. Other social factors went into the models as well. Help for the young in war zones should include health learning.
pmc-11659775:
Shashank Anand, Fatih Sogukpinar, and Ilya Monosov study how arousal affects oscillatory brain activity in non-human primates. Their 2024 study records electrical signals simultaneously across many cortical and subcortical regions.

In high arousal states, a strong coherent gamma oscillation appeared between the amygdala and basal forebrain. In low arousal, rest-like states, alpha-frequency coherence rose across sampled regions, except the medial temporal lobe. The authors consider how these patterns might support sensory processing during high arousal. They also link rest-state patterns to memory-related functions. The work fills a gap, since earlier studies covered only small groups of brain regions.
pmc-11665775:
Harirpoush and co-authors test virtual reality planning for port placement in chest surgery. Video-assisted thoracic surgery treats early lung cancer through small ports, called trocars. Good port spots give full access, a wide camera view, and room for tools to move without crowding.

Surgeons now lean on experience and rules such as the baseball diamond and triangle target principles. The study built patient-based scenes in virtual reality before surgery. Surgeons could rehearse port layouts on the model and adjust angles in advance. Early results test if this planning sharpens placement beyond habit and flat images.
pmc-11669875:
Lucile Montalescot, Louise Baussard, Elodie Charbonnier, and three colleagues ask why patients abandon health apps in this two thousand twenty-four review. Digital tools can educate, monitor, and support people with cancer, but engagement and adherence stay weak. Following PRISMA guidelines, the authors searched four databases for studies from twenty ten to twenty twenty-one. The studies covered adults with cancer using self-help digital tools. Reported factors were sorted into five groups: social, mental, health, technology, and program factors.

Of more than nine thousand studies screened, sixty-one qualified. They spanned eHealth formats across cancer care. The review maps which traits, mental states, health conditions, and design features track with sticking to or dropping digital programs. Designers and clinicians need to know what predicts engagement before building programs patients will finish. The authors present the factor map as a base for adherence-aware design in cancer care.
pmc-11670075:
Denisa Pescari and co-authors compare diet plans for women with obesity over a 12-week weight loss program, in work from 2024. One set of plans cuts total calories, in low-energy and very low-energy forms. The other keeps calories level but changes the mix of fat, protein, and carbohydrate. That set covers low-carbohydrate, ketogenic, and high-protein diets, plus time-restricted eating. The study follows 150 women, with diets set by a certified clinical nutritionist.

The team tracks body weight, body mass index, waist size, and waist-to-hip ratio at the start, at six weeks, and at twelve weeks. A body composition device measures body fat, trunk fat, muscle mass, fat-free mass, water levels, and resting energy burn. Setting the diet types side by side on the same measures, the study aims to show which approach best supports weight control and body composition.
pmc-11672275:
Xing Huang and co-authors are featured in a journal cover piece from two thousand twenty-four on viruses in farm soils. The piece sums up their study of how viruses shape microbe communities in rice paddy fields. It also covers how virus levels affect greenhouse gas emissions from those soils.

The cover art uses a Chinese Bagua design to contrast low and high virus loads. Under each load, microbe mass, bacterial diversity, and gas output respond in distinct ways. The study behind the piece argues that soil microbes adopt different strategies under different infection pressure. The editors present it as insight into the complex links shaping emissions from farm ecosystems.
pmc-11672975:
Lucia Cesarini, Alessandra Napolitano, and three co-authors review a key body chemical in fatty liver disease. Their review, from twenty twenty-four, covers glutathione, a small sulfur-based molecule. The liver makes and ships much of the body's supply. When its balance slips, stress from oxygen can harm liver cells.

The team sifted more than a thousand papers and kept one hundred sixty-five for close study. Most used animals or cells, and few used human samples. Methods for handling samples varied a lot between labs. Still, high levels of these small molecules often tracked with worse disease. The authors call for shared methods so results can be compared.
pmc-11673075:
Demet Cakiroglu, Selen Yılmaz Isıkhan, and Hamit Coskun studied how resilience and hope shaped the work performance of healthcare workers during the COVID-19 pandemic, in this 2024 study. The team surveyed 412 workers tied to the Istanbul health directorate in 2021. They asked whether hope carries the effect of resilience on performance, and whether gender changes the links.

Resilience and hope each tracked with better self-rated performance, and the two traits rose together. Hope did not act as the bridge between resilience and performance, though. Men scored higher than women on resilience, hope, and goal-directed thinking. The authors argue that building hope may matter most for performance, and they urge health managers to treat both traits as resources worth growing in a crisis.
pmc-11673175:
Mingyuan Dou and six co-authors give a caterpillar inspired way to build gaits for a segmented robot that mixes serial and parallel links. Such robots are over jointed, which makes gait design hard. The study came out in twenty twenty-four.

Segments are modeled as rigid bodies with six move freedoms. The method, called Stable Segment Update, frames gait making as tracking for the least lifted segment, solved by inverse kinematics. Three parameter sets, drawn as stepped hump waves, guard stability and lift efficiency. Paths for each swinging segment come from kinematic study. Tests confirm the multi gait method works on the robot.
pmc-11673675:
Ya Lu, Tian Zhang, and Zhiguo Xu present a 2024 survey study of minimalist buying among Chinese millennials in a weak economy. Younger buyers now form the core market, and many are turning to spare, low-buy living. The team asked 554 millennials how money strain, self-expression, and risk sense shape their view of symbolic and copy-like buying, and how those views feed spare living.

Buying orientation fed symbolic views of goods. Self-expression and risk sense fed both symbolic and copy views. Symbolic views in turn fed awareness of spare living. Social comparison upward cut the link from awareness to action. The study is the first to join both view types in one frame for this group. Brands gain a map of why young buyers walk away.
pmc-11675175:
Yujie Li and colleagues present a two thousand twenty-four study of the gene THRSP and its grip on fat metabolism in stem cells. Fatty liver, diabetes, and obesity all involve disturbed lipid handling. THRSP had been loosely linked, and cell stress may help switch fat-making genes on.

Silencing THRSP in mouse stem cells sharply cut fat droplet formation. Key fat-building regulators fell with it. Combined gene and protein profiling showed related pathways shifting together, including stress responses inside the cell's protein factory. The results firm up THRSP as a metabolic control point worth targeting.
pmc-11675375:
Clark and co-authors study how new life in Canada shapes health for Syrian men who fled war. Forced moves can strain health, and man norms shape job paths and reach to aid. The team used group-led work and a photo-voice step with 11 men. Men took and shared shots that showed their daily lives. Views on cross traits and man norms framed how the team read the tales. Low-wage work left the men pushed to the side, the group found.

Rules that prize home work past and slow checks of past school devalued their skills. Tongue gaps, age, lone life, and strain all weighed on their health. Care roles through dads, faith ties, and help work still built hope. The team urges health paths shaped for men and for cross traits.
pmc-11675675:
Julia Day and Philip Hamann reviewed joint problems in sarcoidosis in 2024. Sarcoidosis inflames many organs with granulomas. Its cause is still unknown today. Joint disease often delays diagnosis badly. Look-alike diseases confuse clinicians often. Lung, skin, and eye signs are common.

Muscle and bone involvement are covered here. Biomarkers can support a diagnosis somewhat. No single marker predicts disease course. Steroids remain the main treatment. Standard disease-modifying drugs come next. Antimalarials also feature in care. Biologic drugs now help some patients. Rheumatic care needs whole-body thinking. Early recognition shortens patient suffering greatly.
pmc-11675875:
Maria Antonia Garrido and four co-authors review loss of heterozygosity in HLA genes in breast cancer and what it means for care. HLA class one proteins show tumor bits to killer T cells, which sparks an anti tumor response. The review came out in twenty twenty-four.

Loss of one copy set is a common, one way gene change in tumors. At the HLA site it drops a whole haplotype, which helps the cancer hide from the immune system and weakens immune care response. The authors trace its role in immune escape and tumor growth. They also weigh how this loss could serve as a care mark or target.
pmc-11677275:
Scale crusts clog the membranes that distill seawater, and a 2024 study by Yonghyun Shin, Jaewuk Koo, and Sangho Lee watches the crust grow so it can be modeled. The team ran real seawater and reverse osmosis brine through a distillation unit, filming the surface layer as it formed under varied heat and salt levels.

Those observations fed a system dynamics model that predicts how fast output declines. The model tracked the experiments closely and named the factors that make scaling worse. The authors present the pairing of live imaging with dynamic modeling as a practical way to design runs that foul less and last longer.
pmc-11677375:
Marco Colizzi and nine colleagues published a 2024 study of a no-restraint policy in Italian psychiatric wards. Restraint means holding or tying a patient to prevent harm. Some wards have moved away from it on ethical grounds, and critics worry that staff may face more aggression as a result.

The team reviewed work accidents linked to aggression over 16 years, from 2007 to 2022, before and after the policy change. In total, 113 accidents occurred, and 81.4 percent involved physical aggression. Healthcare assistants and psychiatric nurses were hurt most often, and nearly half of the accidents happened on the morning shift. A brief peak appeared during the changeover itself.
pmc-11677475:
Sophia Porrill, Rebecca Rogers, Christopher Ballmann, and Junji Yamauchi wrote this review in 2024. It sums up human studies of yohimbine. This plant alkaloid is sold in many workout supplements. The review asks if it truly boosts exercise performance, and at what risk.

Yohimbine blocks a receptor that slows the sympathetic nervous system. That raises norepinephrine, the fight-or-flight signal. The review covers endurance, sprint, and resistance exercise. Early results suggest gains may be real. The gains may come from stronger drive, changed blood flow, more alertness, and less fatigue. But the drug is hard to predict. The body absorbs it in very different amounts from person to person. Its strength can surprise users. No standard dose is agreed on. Large doses have caused serious harm. The authors say low doses seem safe to take. But safe dosing still needs more work.
pmc-11677575:
Hlynur David Hlynsson and co-authors asked whether disordered breathing in sleep raises hospital risk for diabetes and artery disease, in a study published in two thousand twenty-four. They used a large United States claims database with five years of records. People with sleep-disordered breathing were matched with similar people without it, then both groups were tracked.

People with the breathing problem were more likely to land in hospital for diabetes, for artery disease, or for either one. The link showed up both in the same five years and when the team looked at the four years after a first-year diagnosis. The pattern differed by sex: women showed raised risk across all outcomes, while men showed it clearly for diabetes alone. The authors say the breathing problem marks real extra risk, not just a side note.
pmc-11678875:
Anas M Almofarreh and colleagues offer a two thousand twenty-four case-control study of fruit and vegetable eating and bowel disease in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. Ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease are long-running gut inflammations. Diet may shape their risk in ways that differ by sex.

Patients with each disease were compared with hospital controls without bowel disease. A questionnaire captured eating habits from before diagnosis. Statistical models estimated odds for daily fruit and vegetable intake. Among men, daily vegetables first linked to higher colitis odds, then faded after adjustments. The study probes diet links with unusual care for sex differences.
pmc-11679575:
Artem Gusev and six co-authors published a chemistry methods paper in twenty twenty-four on a thriftier way to make a liver-targeting drug carrier. Triantennary GalNAc steers therapeutic RNA strands into liver cells, which grab it through a surface receptor. Existing syntheses are young, wasteful, and hard to scale cleanly.

The team devised a pot-economy route that runs more steps in a single vessel, trimming reagents, waste, and stages. It produces both the GalNAc cluster and the phosphoramidite and solid-support forms needed to attach it to oligonucleotides. The method is tuned for laboratory scale and follows green chemistry principles. Cheaper, cleaner carrier production matters because GalNAc drugs are multiplying quickly.
pmc-11679875: A team of chemists converts isobutene to its epoxide with high selectivity in a paper from 2024, using team framing because the catalog adds an eighth author absent from the head byline. The catalyst is molybdenum diselenide spread as a solid, paired with a common peroxide oxidant. An unusual fluorinated alcohol solvent speeds the chemistry sharply. Tests support a mechanism mixing metal-oxo and radical steps, both helped by hydrogen bonding from the solvent. Activity survived recycling, and other substrates reacted as well.
pmc-11682575:
João Martins and colleagues compare two routes for spaying cats in trap-neuter programs, belly or flank, in this study from twenty twenty-four. Thirty-eight feral and stray cats were split evenly between midline and flank ovariectomy. Both groups got the same sedation and anesthesia. The team tracked pain signals during surgery, incision size, operating time, and any need for rescue pain relief.

Pain responses during the operation did not differ between the routes, and neither did rescue painkiller use. The flank route won the logistics: smaller incisions and shorter operations, both of which matter when hundreds of cats pass through a program and nobody can watch their wounds afterward. A smaller cut also lowers the risk of the wound splitting. The authors say pain gives no reason to prefer one route, but throughput and wound safety tilt the choice to the flank.
pmc-11682775:
Teruo Itoh and co-authors test whether vets can tell two kinds of dog skin tumors apart by sight before surgery, in a study from 2024. Mast cell tumors come in a surface form and a deeper form. The two act unlike in the body, so the surgical plan should differ. Until now, only tissue checks could split them for sure.

The team compared photos and tissue results for fifty-two tumors. Hair loss on the tumor surface split the groups cleanly. Every surface tumor showed bold hair loss, while deep tumors kept their coat. Tissue checks showed the surface form eats into hair roots, which explains the sign. Using hair loss alone, they sorted a fresh set of tumors with high accuracy. Large tumors were the main source of error. The sign gives surgeons a cheap head start.
pmc-11688975:
Robbin Frazier and Elma Johnson describe community-led projects on healthy aging and equity at a Minnesota center, in a program paper from 2024. The Center for Healthy Aging and Innovation relaunched in 2021 and built a core team for equity and community engagement. Its aim was real partnership with groups that serve older adults of color and underserved areas.

That fall, the center seated a Community Advisory Board of older adults from the state's largest ethnic groups. Within two years, the board named key needs and launched projects against ageism and social isolation. It also helped form a council of leaders and scholars to draft fixes for system-level inequities. The authors share lessons from each stage of the work.
pmc-11689675:
Cleopatra Kum and three co-authors share the story of a small Ohio firm that drove older adults to COVID vaccine sites. Their twenty twenty-four account centers on Family Support Care LLC, also called KumZ Transport. The firm was a home health agency that was new to transport work. A local aging council asked it to help seniors reach their shots.

As a small family firm, it had few staff and few funds. It leaned hard on trip-planning tech to stay on time and to plan routes well. The authors describe blocks they hit when they first used that tech. They also share lessons learned as they worked with more trip brokers.
pmc-11690375:
Sylvain Moreno gives a talk, in twenty twenty-four, on why brain aging does not follow one path. Most past work treats decline as a straight line from young adult life. New work shows wide spread in how thought ages. Moreno proposes a new way to sort people into subtypes. The frame borrows a plant image: some people are like orchids, shaped much by their setting. Others are like dandelions, hardy in most settings.

He uses large data sets, such as the UK Biobank, and machine learning tools. Life habits had unlike effects on unlike subtypes, he finds. The talk argues for care and study that fit the subtype, not a single line.
pmc-11691575:
Britteny Howell and four co-authors shared a report in 2024 on a healthy aging program in the urban Circumpolar North of the United States. The program was designed and delivered by faculty and students from several health and social science fields. Such interprofessional education is often praised but remains underused in higher education.

Eight students team-taught weekly one-hour sessions for fifteen weeks for older adults in the community. The sessions covered healthy lifestyles within a framework built around hope. Students reported gains in thinking like a scientist, greater confidence in research tasks, and more consideration of older adults' needs. The thirty-nine older adults who took part rated the program well for its teaching, usefulness, and value. The team concludes that joint learning across professions and across generations mattered to both sides, although the groups were small.
pmc-11691875:
Yifan Lou, Joan Monin, Thi Hoang Vu, and Amanda Piechota published a study in 2024 on emotion regulation in people living with dementia and their spouses. Both partners can find it difficult to manage their feelings. The researchers asked how that difficulty relates to the neuropsychiatric symptoms, such as mood and behavior changes, that the illness can bring.

The study used data from forty-five couples, ninety people in all. As the number of such symptoms reported by spouses increased, the person with dementia reported more difficulty regulating feelings. The spouses themselves did not report the same increase. The trouble involved accepting feelings, controlling impulses, and finding ways to calm down, rather than noticing or naming feelings. The findings suggest that people in the early stage of the illness are aware that their control over their feelings is slipping.
pmc-11692075:
Yufang Tu and Melissa O'Connor present a 2024 study of how dementia relates to the importance older adults place on religious services over eleven years. Faith activities support health and well-being in later life and travel with slower cognitive decline. Whether a dementia diagnosis itself shifts how much people value attending services was the open question.

The authors used twelve waves of a national aging study, nationally representative of Medicare beneficiaries, with over forty-one thousand participants at the start. People rated the importance of service participation on a three-point scale across the years. Modelling that accounts for repeated measures tests whether the value placed on services drifts differently after dementia enters the picture.
pmc-11692375:
Jiabei Jiang and three co-authors explore how to involve Chinese older adults in design work in a 2024 paper. Designing with older users, not just for them, reveals needs that surveys miss. The method grew up in Western settings and fits Chinese social context imperfectly.

The study borrows from service design, treating organizers as providers and elders as service recipients. Key moments, called participation touchpoints, are where involvement either sparks or dies. The team traces how elders interact with organizers, procedures, and settings across an activity. Cultural expectations about authority and politeness shape those moments. Practical guidance follows for pacing, roles, and environment. The aim is genuine voice for older participants, not token attendance.
pmc-11692475:
Oscar Ribeiro, Taiane Abreu, Laetitia Teixeira, and Lia Araujo published a study in 2024 on laypersons' understanding of gerotranscendence, a theory of aging. The theory proposes that the mindset shifts with age along three dimensions: a cosmic dimension, a sense of coherence, and a new appreciation of solitude.

The researchers held three focus groups with eighteen adults aged fifty-eight to ninety-eight. At first, most participants found the theory's terminology difficult to grasp. Once the terms were explained in plain language, people recognized their own lives in them. Their interpretations of the theory were diverse and complementary. Participants also connected the themes to other known frameworks of successful aging. The authors conclude that consulting laypeople deepens what the theory means in real life, not only in academic writing.
pmc-11692575:
Natalie Turner and Amber Sabbatini study what shapes referral to home health care versus a skilled nursing facility after hospital discharge, in work published in 2024. Home care has grown fast, costs less than facility care, and matches older adults' wish to stay home. The team used Medicare data and models that account for hospital differences.

Older age, being female, and holding both Medicare and Medicaid were linked to lower odds of a home care referral. Patients in rural areas had higher odds than urban patients. Communities with more residents of colour had lower referral odds, while poorer communities had higher odds. The authors conclude that patient traits drive most decisions, but community traits matter too. They urge investment in care infrastructure to make access fair.
pmc-11695875:
El-Kass and a large team surveyed in twenty twenty-four what lung-care nurses in Gaza know on how to stop lung infection in folks on breath machines. Such infection is a grave risk for the most sick in hospital. Nurses at the bed side hold the main role in its block steps.

They asked seventy-two nurses in five state hospitals with a self-fill form. Mean know score was just past seven in ten of the points on the form. The team still calls that know-how too low for safe care. Age, home state, and years of work tied to good scores. Sex, school grade, and unit type did not.
pmc-11704375:
Oluwakemi Amodu, Craig Janes, and Karen Therese Pangan reviewed research on the mental health of refugees and displaced people in low- and middle-income countries during COVID-19. The pandemic slowed vital services and health care, adding money worries and instability to lives already uprooted, and well-being fell.

The review found that digital health tools and community-based support can help, but community networks are stretched thin. Their reach is limited by low digital skills, weak internet access, and sheer numbers. What worked varied from group to group. The authors call for policy that weighs gender, housing, jobs, and inequality together, and urge agencies and governments to build lasting, fair mental health support for displaced people.
pmc-11710175:
Emma S Luckett and a large European team present a 2025 conference abstract on gene-based risk scores and amyloid buildup in the brain. The work draws on the AMYPAD group, which pools several parent studies across Europe. The team merged gene data from 753 people who did not have dementia.

The team built risk scores from known Alzheimer's gene variants and compared them with brain scan measures of amyloid. Most scores tracked with higher amyloid at every cutoff tested. One score that left out the APOE region did not. The findings suggest that broad gene scores can flag amyloid buildup before symptoms start.
pmc-11711975:
Alyssia A Sanchez and Alex Mihailidis describe a home reminder system for people with dementia in a 2025 project report. Reminder units sit around the home, linked to a base station. Caregivers send reminders through a phone app, and the units show them and note when the person confirms receipt.

The system logs daily routines and uses machine learning to spot when a day drifts from the usual pattern. Early work simulated about a thousand days of reminder use. Eight patient and caregiver pairs joined interviews and hands-on demos. The team reports that the tool could ease caregiver load and support living at home with more freedom. Remote behavior records may also flag when help is needed sooner.
pmc-11712475:
Ramesh Kumar Paidi and Kalipada Pahan published a research paper in 2025 on a muscle supplement and its effect on the brains of mice with Alzheimer's-like changes. The supplement, sold to bodybuilders, is known to be safe over long use. The pair asked whether it could also restore the links between brain cells that the disease wears away.

In dishes of mouse brain cells, the supplement raised the levels of proteins that mark strong links between cells. Mice given it by mouth for a month then did better on maze and object tests. Their brains showed more of the same link proteins and more of a signal that helps store memory. The authors suggest a common gym aid merits more study.
pmc-11713175:
Vijeta Patri, Gaurav Patri, and Nivedita Sahoo report a 2024 survey of crooked teeth and brace needs among school children in eastern India. Bad tooth alignment can hurt dental health and how a child feels socially. The team checked 450 children aged ten to thirteen in Bhubaneswar schools. They scored each child with a standard index that grades treatment need by tooth health and by looks.

About forty-three percent of the children clearly needed treatment on health grounds. Only about six percent had a clear need based on looks alone. Girls showed more concern about looks than boys, a gap the scoring confirmed. Health-based need did not differ by gender. The authors call for early checks and brace services shaped to this age group.
pmc-11713275:
Feng Yang and co-authors report a long-term study of a broad training program for people with thinking problems in China, in this 2025 paper. The program, called Brain and Body Rehab Training, joins thinking exercises with physical training and daily-life coaching. Many digital products cover only screen-based drills, the authors note.

The study followed three hundred fifty-one adults, split into groups with and without impairment. Each person got a personal plan of four to five daily tasks, covering drills, movement, diet, sleep, mood, and long-term illness care. Tests before training and at four and eight months track whether gains last over time.
pmc-11713675:
Courtney Polenick and co-authors follow couples through daily life with early dementia in a 2025 study. Symptoms like memory lapses can strain both the patient and the spouse who helps. The team asks how each partner's daily stress about symptoms links to stress hormones. They focus on cortisol, a hormone that rises and falls across the day.

Thirty-nine couples took part, each with one spouse in the early stage of dementia. Both partners answered short phone surveys each morning and night for seven days. They also gave saliva samples four times a day on four of those days. When both partners felt high symptom stress, the caregiver's next-morning hormone rise ran higher. Daily stress, the study shows, gets under the skin.
pmc-11713775:
Archna Sharma and co-authors trace a swelling signal that turns brain support cells harmful in a 2025 Alzheimer's paper. The support cells, called astrocytes, can switch into a toxic state that hurts nerve cells. A protein released by immune cells in the sick brain seems to flip that switch. It acts through a sensor that the support cells carry on their surface.

The team measured the protein in spinal fluid and blood from patients and from Alzheimer's model mice. They then dosed lab-grown support cells with the protein and watched their genes change. Mice lacking the sensor were partly protected. Blocking this path, the study suggests, might keep support cells in their helpful state and slow damage in the disease.
pmc-11713875:
Bonnie Sachs and co-authors report how older adults use technology in a 2025 study of video-based thinking tests. The wider project, called VCog, checks whether a standard test battery gives the same results by video as in person. People with normal thinking, mild problems, and mild dementia all take part. Their comfort with devices matters for whether remote testing can work fairly.

Participants came from twelve Alzheimer's research centers, and 313 people were enrolled. Each person took the same test set in person and by video link. The team also asked about daily tech use and ease with devices. The answers show where remote research may reach older adults well and where it may leave some behind.
pmc-11714075:
Sarah Starling and five co-authors study how fast recruiters first call hopeful volunteers for Alzheimer's trials, in a 2025 conference paper. Trials lose time and money when keen applicants drift away before a first phone screen. Past work on mood trials linked fast first calls to more completed screens.

The team tracked nearly seven thousand people who applied online through ads in 2023. First call times ran from under an hour to 227 days, though most came within three days. About 46 percent of applicants spoke with a recruiter in the end. The longer the wait for the first call, the lower the chance of ever reaching the person. The authors urge trial teams to call within hours, not days.
pmc-11714275:
Dobrin Nedelkov and six co-authors study how a sugar coating on a key blood protein in spinal fluid links to signs of Alzheimer's disease, in a 2025 conference paper. The protein is apolipoprotein E, and one form of its gene is the strongest known gene risk for the late form of the disease. The team asked whether the coating level tracks with tau and amyloid in the fluid.

They tested blood and spinal fluid from 188 older adults in a long running imaging study. The risk form of the protein carried the least coating, and lower coating in spinal fluid went with worse tau levels over ten years. Higher coating went with more of a healthy amyloid form in the fluid. The authors say the coating may help shape how the disease unfolds.
pmc-11714475:
Laureano Moro-Velazquez and six co-authors combine speech, eye movement, and handwriting to tell Alzheimer's disease apart from healthy aging, in a 2025 conference paper. Most past work used just one of these signals. A mix may catch more of the illness and suit care to each person.

Eleven people with early disease or mild loss and thirteen matched controls took part. Each read a set passage aloud while a mic caught speech and a tracker caught eye moves. Each then drew a spiral on a digital pad. The team drew hundreds of measures from the three streams and trained smart models on each stream and on all at once. A ranking method showed which measures did the most work.
pmc-11727975:
Shuang Gao and co-authors demonstrate fast wireless video links in a 2024 paper. Their system sends uncompressed HD video at 100 gigahertz, a band eyed for future 6G networks. They compare an all-optical receiver against an all-electric one.

The transmitter uses light-based mixing to build the signal. Over short links, the all-optical receiver reached far higher error-free rates than the electric one. The team then sent real-time HD video over 200 meters and over 2 kilometers with the optical setup. The results support photonics-based links for future high-capacity wireless coverage.
pmc-11728375:
Beata Gutarowska and co-authors grow mould mycelium with waste fibers into farm textiles that rot away in soil. Their study was published in twenty twenty-four. Agrotextiles normally come from plastic; a biodegradable version could cut field waste.

Twenty mould strains were screened for fast growth, with heat, food source, and culture style tuned. The winning mould's threads were mixed with bleached wood pulp plus cotton or hemp fibers, then milled, formed, pressed, and dried. The best sheets carried ten to twenty percent mycelium. They showed good strength, low water passage, and high air passage. In soil the material fully broke down. The work covers the full chain from strain picking to field use.
pmc-11728675:
Hülya Tezel Yalçın and co-authors present a 2024 study comparing two sources of drug safety news for breastfeeding mothers. One source is the United States adverse event database, where harms are reported as they occur. The other is a reference database that sums up evidence on drug levels in milk and infant blood.

The team pulled 2,628 event reports tied to drug exposure through milk. Most infants were under two months old, and most cases were rated serious. Nervous system drugs made up about half of the reports. They then took the top drugs in each drug family and compared the event patterns with what the reference database says, to spot gaps between the two.
pmc-11728775:
Berhanu Sibhat and colleagues report a two thousand twenty-four study of brucellosis bacteria in pastoral livestock in north-eastern Ethiopia. The neglected disease spreads from animals to people and stays common in the country. Which Brucella species circulate was poorly mapped.

Herds in six villages were sampled after recent animal abortions. Swabs and milk came from sheep and goats across many households. Culture and molecular tests found Brucella melitensis in a notable share of animals. Genome typing compared the strains with regional and world isolates. The results guide control in a high-risk pastoral setting.
pmc-11730875:
Shreyal Maikoo and colleagues built an HIV latency model in two thousand twenty-four. Most cure research targets subtype B virus. Sub-Saharan Africa carries most infections worldwide, though. Subtype C dominates there, especially in South Africa. The team built a model virus carrying subtype C controls. Its switch region came from real patient viruses.

A glowing marker revealed when the virus woke. Genetic variation in the switch may alter waking. Cure strategies must work across subtypes fairly. Models like this allow direct testing beforehand. The work corrects a long research imbalance. African patients stand to benefit most directly.
pmc-11738075:
Moctar Fodiya and co-authors report a rare granulosa tumor growing behind the abdomen of a forty-year-old woman, in this 2024 case report. Such tumors usually start in the ovary and make up a small share of its cancers. One arising in the retroperitoneum, away from the ovaries, is extremely rare.

Following principles borrowed from limb sarcoma surgery, the team removed the whole left compartment. The excision took the kidney, its ureter, and a stretch of colon, with the bowel rejoined in the same operation. The authors pair the case with a literature review. They argue compartment-wide removal offers the best control for these deep tumors.
pmc-11772175:
Hanxin Kong, Hao Ying, and Jianhong Yang described a treacherous illness in 2025. Their patient, living with uremia from kidney failure and maintained on peritoneal dialysis. Developed an illness inside the skull caused by Ralstonia mannitolilytica, an environmental germ that rarely infects people and mostly threatens the immunocompromised. Its brain imaging pattern was so unusual that the first diagnosis reached was a demyelinating disease, an autoimmune stripping of nerve insulation, which would have meant entirely varied treatment.

Cerebrospinal fluid study and targeted gene sequencing of the fluid corrected the record. The germ is resistant to many antibiotics, but this strain responded well to meropenem given beside steady peritoneal dialysis. Despite that microbiological success, the patient's course was poor, undone by uncontrollable gastrointestinal bleeding and the complications of a long bed rest. The authors publish the case so the next similar scan is read with this mimic in mind.
pmc-11778175:
Dong-Mei Yang and colleagues study how nitrate and a solvent pollutant affect each other's cleanup by microbes. Their study from twenty twenty-five uses mixed anaerobic cultures. Trichloroethene and nitrate often pollute the same groundwater sites. Each cleanup process shifts water acidity in opposite directions.

Bottle experiments tracked both reductions under controlled conditions. Modest pollutant levels actually sped nitrate removal. Nitrate effects on solvent breakdown were more mixed by stage. It slowed the first breakdown step but sped the last one. Heat-of-reaction logic explains part of that pattern. Microbial community shifts likely explain the rest. Site managers must plan for both pollutants together, not separately.
pmc-11793075:
Verheul and co-authors test how to compare hospitals fairly on serious problems after breast cancer surgery in the Netherlands. Quality scores can spur better care, but hospitals treat different mixes of patients. Fair comparison must adjust for that case mix. The study used a national registry with 32,084 patients from 72 hospitals treated in 2021 and 2022. The team built adjustment models with standard statistical methods.

Problem rates varied between hospitals for every surgery type. The spread ran from about 1.4% to near 10%, by procedure. Body weight, smoking, tumor spread pattern, and prior drug treatment counted among the factors weighed. The study shows how much adjustment changes the rankings hospitals receive.
pmc-11837775:
He and coauthors pool trials on virtual reality for early movement in intensive care. Very ill adults lose muscle and joint function fast in bed. Early movement aids recovery, but pain and tubes block it. Virtual games may make movement more fun and safe.

Eight databases were searched from their start to late 2024. Rules for sound reviews guided the full search. Eleven trials over ten years fit the pool. Bias checks graded how sound each trial was. Pooled results weighed leg and arm function gains. The team also checked stay length and harm rates.
pmc-11905775:
Raúl Emilio Real Delor and María Elena Aguilera study what helps people with celiac disease stick to a gluten-free diet, in a paper from 2024. The study, set in Paraguay, used data from 2023. People with this disease must avoid wheat and related grains for life. Many find the shift hard and drift from the diet.

The team sent a survey to teens and adults with the disease and got 292 replies. About half the group kept to the diet well, and just over half felt well adapted to it. Just under half said their family backed them. Two things tied clearly to good adherence: more years since diagnosis and strong family support. The authors urge more study of why some people struggle with the diet. Support at home may be a cheap way to help patients stay on track.
pmc-11976075:
Narjes Amrollahi, Mohammad Javad Tarrahi, and Zahra Abbasi reviewed studies on mouth health in children with chronic kidney disease. Their review, from twenty twenty-four, asks how teeth and gums fare in these children. Kidney disease in childhood can harm many organs. The mouth, both hard and soft tissue, is one of them.

The team searched four databases for case-control studies in English from two thousand to twenty twenty-three. Two of them screened titles, short summaries, and full texts on their own. They also rated the quality of the studies kept. Readers get a pooled view of which mouth health scores run worse in sick children. That view can guide dental checks as part of kidney care.
pmc-12091075:
Jafari and five co-authors tackle a philosophy question with legal weight: who counts as human? Humanities fields rest on the idea of the human, yet biology offers no clean universal definition of the species. Disputes between nominalists and realists, and the limits of logical definitions, sharpen the problem.

The authors argue that rights and traits tied to being human cannot rest on species membership alone. They accept a minimal shared definition of the philosophical human instead. Its two marks are self-awareness and freedom of choice. Everything else, they say, attaches to that essence rather than standing beside it as an equal.
pmc-12098075:
Dan Sexton and six colleagues scan the blood proteins of swelling-disorder patients before and after a preventive antibody drug, in a study from two thousand twenty-five. Hereditary angioedema from C1 inhibitor deficiency causes unpredictable, dangerous swelling. Lanadelumab blocks plasma kallikrein to prevent attacks.

Affinity proteomics set thirty healthy controls side by side with patients, who numbered more than a hundred. Samples came at baseline and after six months of treatment. As expected, C1 inhibitor was profoundly lower in patients, and so was complement C4. Other proteins shifted with the state of the disease and with the treatment. That offers candidate biomarkers, which could in time predict attacks or certify drug response. The dataset also maps what kallikrein blockade does to human plasma biology.
pmc-12110475:
Uwingabire, Gbadamosi, Mochama, and Kubahoniyesu measure cesarean delivery rates at a Rwandan hospital, in work from twenty twenty-four. Cesarean section saves lives when medically justified. Rates far above the World Health Organization guide range of ten to fifteen percent can signal overuse and add risk.

The cross sectional study covered more than four hundred postpartum women at Rwamagana Level Two Teaching Hospital. Prevalence of cesarean delivery and its associated factors were assessed. Local figures let hospital leaders judge whether surgery use matches need, and which mothers are most likely to deliver by surgery.
pmc-12266675:
Neal Shore, Michael Cookson, and Eleni Efstathiou review hormone-blocking therapy for advanced prostate cancer in a 2024 podcast discussion. Cutting testosterone starves the cancer, and for decades the tools were injections: drugs that over-stimulate the hormone control loop until it shuts down, or blockers that jam it directly.

A daily pill changed the menu in 2020, when regulators approved the first oral drug of the blocker class based on a large phase three trial. The discussion covers that trial's main efficacy and safety results. It then weighs practical points providers and patients raise when choosing: injection visits versus daily pills, side effects, and speed of hormone suppression and recovery. The format is a guided conversation rather than a data paper, aimed at clinicians counseling men through the options.
pmc-12405875:
Chen and four co-authors screened in twenty twenty-four a germ that breaks down plant fiber and helps crops grow. Vast chaff waste is made each year, and old reuse ways are slow or dirty. They found the germ in soil by a stain test and tuned its growth in the lab.

They then mixed it with a germ that fixes air nitrogen in equal parts. The mix was spread on rice husks for a long ferment. Soil germ mix and its carbon-nitrogen share shifted in a clear way. Buckwheat shoots grew much taller with the mix than with plain water or the lone germ.
pmc-12660675:
Kim and a large team test two blood proteins as early flags for liver cancer in twenty twenty-five. The standard blood flag misses many cases, so better tests are needed. Their study found both proteins drop in liver cancer tissue and blood. Low levels tied to shorter survival in patient data.

In lab tests, the pair flagged cancer, even early stage, more truly than the standard marker. Blood assays confirmed the drop in patients. Low protein levels also linked to more suppressor immune cells near tumors. The team pitches the pair as painless blood tests for screening. More checks are owed before clinic use, they note.
pmc-12663275:
Seyed Moghaddam, Huhua Cao, Tao Jin, Ruibo Han, and Diba Rashidi build a city model that predicts how ethnic groups spread, without hiding its logic. Machine learning models for social questions often trade clarity for accuracy. Their model blends physics-style equations with a set of expert neural units, each tuned to a phase of settlement such as colonization, rapid jumps, or decline. A router sends each case to the right expert.

Tested on two decades of Toronto census data, the model forecast group patterns five and ten years out and beat seven rival models by a wide margin. It also surfaced cross-group influence and differing settling styles that older methods missed. The paper argues that built-in knowledge can give both accuracy and clarity.
pmc-12676775:
Hassan Mohamud and co-authors report a rare pregnancy that grew in the belly beside a torn womb. A woman aged twenty-two in Uganda came at twenty-eight weeks with belly pain and bleeding. She had no antenatal care or scans in this pregnancy. Exam found no fetal heartbeat and a tender, small-for-dates womb.

Surgery found the womb fundus torn, with the sac whole inside the belly. The fetus, a stillborn boy of 1.2 kilograms, was removed with dead tissue. The womb defect was sewn in layers, and the mother healed without trouble. She went home in stable shape after the operation. The team urges early antenatal visits and basic ultrasound access.
pmc-12690875:
Mengye Weng, Zhigang Yang, and Xiaoying Feng study a small RNA strand in blood as a marker and target for osteoarthritis, in a research paper from 2025. The joint disease wears cartilage down over time. Good blood markers and drugs that change the course of the disease are still lacking, so new leads matter.

Blood levels of the strand were lower in sixty-one patients than in sixty healthy controls. Low levels tracked worse joint grades and higher pain and function scores. In cartilage cells stressed in the lab, restoring the strand eased harm. It acts through a gene called KLF10. The work supports blood tests and RNA-based care.
pmc-12692075:
Sotirios Ekonomou and co-authors measure an antioxidant in banana wine with a cheap printed sensor in a 2025 study. Gallic acid is a valued marker of antioxidant content in drinks. Lab-grade tests for it can be slow and costly for small producers.

Their screen-printed carbon electrode reads the acid's oxidation signal in a buffered mix. Two scanning methods gave matching readings on real banana wine samples. Spiked samples returned nearly all the added acid, which confirms the method's accuracy. The response stayed linear across the range that matters for wine checks. The authors present the sensor as a simple, selective tool for drink quality testing on a budget.
pmc-12696075:
Qize Xuan and a large team of co-authors present a 2025 study on a gel that mimics the webs immune cells cast to trap germs. Drug-resistant bacteria and their sticky biofilms block wound healing and resist standard antibiotics. The team built their gel from fibers of lysozyme, a natural egg-white protein that can fold into amyloid threads. Light in the near-infrared range makes the fibers fall apart on demand.

When the gel breaks down, it releases the protein in an active germ-killing form plus magnesium ions. Those ions steer immune cells toward a healing mode and calm swelling. In mice and pigs, the gel cleared resistant staph infections in wounds and sped repair. It also helped infected joint replacements heal while protecting new bone growth. The authors see promise for hard-to-treat infected wounds.
pmc-12698775:
Abdullah Al Haj Ahmed, Husam Al Najar, and Nasser Abu Ghalwa clean boron from water with treated kaolin clay, in a 2025 study. Boron sits on a knife edge between helpful and toxic, and standard treatment removes it poorly. The team activated the clay with two acids, which opened pores, grew surface area, and added binding groups. Plain clay caught almost nothing and was dropped.

The acid-treated clays caught up to about 2.4 and 2.2 milligrams per gram, best in mildly acidic water. Layer-by-layer uptake on uneven surfaces fit the data best, and the process released heat while proceeding on its own. Trials on real groundwater from Gaza City matched the lab results. The authors present activated kaolin as a cheap, workable boron filter.
pmc-12699875:
Wenteng Cao and co-authors published this radiation biology study in 2025. FLASH therapy delivers radiation at ultra-high dose rates and seems to spare healthy tissue while still hitting tumors. The effect is well documented for electrons, photons, and protons, but barely studied for carbon ions, a heavier beam used in some cancer centers. The team irradiated part of the abdomen in mice with carbon ions at FLASH and conventional rates, under both low and high energy-deposition settings.

At the low setting, FLASH and conventional beams spared gut tissue about equally. At the high setting, FLASH clearly improved thirty-day survival once the dose rate passed one hundred grays per second. Intestinal crypts, the gut's regenerative pockets, regenerated half again as well after FLASH. The authors conclude that carbon-ion FLASH is real but conditional: both dose rate and energy deposition must be high enough.
pmc-12700775:
Shivam Sharma and co-authors gather the trial evidence in 2025 on yoga for students' anxiety and heart health. Yoga is widely offered on campuses, and past studies hint that it calms the mind and steadies the heart. But no pooled review had yet covered both outcomes in students at once.

The team searched four major databases for trials that measured both anxiety and heart rate variability, a sign of how flexibly the heart responds. Five studies qualified, and four could be pooled. The pooled results favored yoga on both outcomes. The authors say the signal is positive but thin, and they call for larger, stricter trials to pin down the best dose and style of yoga for students.
pmc-12700875:
Longfei Dong, Xin Pang, and Rui Zhang simulate small-hole leaks of hydrogen from buried pipelines, in work published in 2025. Hydrogen and hydrogen-blended gas are entering distribution networks, and buried leaks can build explosive mixes at the surface. The team modelled how gas spreads through soil under varied conditions.

They varied pressure, hole shape and size, burial depth, and soil traits. Looser, coarser soil let hydrogen reach the explosive threshold at the surface far faster. A leak pointing upward was the riskiest case, since buoyancy drives gas straight up. Rectangular slits spread gas faster than round holes, with the axial slit worst. The authors supply quantitative correlations for hazard assessment and safety management of low-pressure hydrogen pipelines.
pmc-12709775:
Ke Zhang and nine co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on forecasting chemo response in ovarian cancer with a foundation model. Early calls on who will respond guide care, but standard marks are weak. Their model pairs image and text encoders, pre-trained on plain photos and captions. Small low rank patches are tuned in place of the whole net.

Cases came from a look back at close to two hundred advanced patients. Best scores came when patches sat in the lowest five layers of both encoders. That build beat two standard tuned image nets on curve and truth scores. The team calls it a first proof that cheap tuning of a big model can aid such calls.
pmc-12711575:
A large team of physicists reports, in a 2025 study, the first laser study of a radioactive molecule made of actinium and fluorine. Such molecules are prized probes for a deep puzzle: why the strong nuclear force seems blind to a mirror flip that other forces respect. Tiny electric effects in heavy molecules could expose the answer.

The team made the gas-phase molecule and found its strongest light transition, a step needed for reading out future precision tests. Calculations of its electron and nuclear structure showed high sensitivity to several symmetry-breaking traits. A near-term test at modest precision could tighten current bounds by a thousandfold, the authors estimate.
pmc-12711875:
Valentina Pescuma and her team track eyes to see how social formality shapes the reading of a sentence in two tongues. Their study from twenty twenty-five sets German and Japanese readers side by side. Set context can shift how a sentence is read at great speed. If respect facts can act that fast was not known.

German pairs set a context line and a target line out of step on formality. Japanese pairs set high and low respect styles at odds in one line. Eye moves logged first-pass times and late reading times. In German, clashes of formality showed their mark late, past the mark of grammar slips. In Japanese, high-versus-low respect framing shifted reading as well. Levels of respect stand far apart in the two lands. Social sense joins grammar in the work load of the reading brain.
pmc-12718575:
Richard Künzel and co-authors review how rising heat weighs on women's mental health in poorer countries, in a paper from 2025. Heat is a known strain on the mind, and women in low- and middle-income lands face high exposure with few defenses. The team mapped the proof across six large databases. They kept seventy studies that fit their rules.

The studies link high heat to worse outcomes across mental, nerve, and thinking health. The harm does not cluster in one diagnosis but spreads wide. Most work came from China, with thin coverage of Africa, Latin America, and Southeast Asia. Many studies also reused the same data or buried women inside mixed groups. The authors call for stronger, women-focused work in the least-studied regions. The need grows as the planet warms.
pmc-12719175:
Dandan Qi, Min Lu, Xingmin Zhang, Lin Yue, Yali Shi, Houzhen Jia, Chunwang Dong, and Changbo Yuan trace how climate shapes tea aroma through the leaf's wax coat, in a 2025 study. The wax layer shields leaves from stress. White tea making lets that chemistry speak. Samples came from two provinces with distinct climates, Guizhou and Shandong. Gas analysis identified the wax and aroma compounds. Trained tasters scored the finished teas.

Most differing wax compounds tied to stress tolerance. Four compounds persisted through the whole processing. Two ran higher in the Shandong samples. Aroma differences enriched survival and adaptation pathways. Some also fed flavor formation directly. Tasters found the Guizhou tea more floral and fruity. The Shandong tea tasted greener. The match with lab data was close. The authors draw lessons for growing tea under climate change. Wax chemistry, they say, is an early signal of flavor shifts.
pmc-12719475:
Deeb and five co-authors present a case report from twenty twenty-five on a teen whose thyroid drug triggered a lupus-like illness. The girl, aged sixteen, had a new diagnosis of Graves' disease, an overactive thyroid illness. Within one week of starting the standard drug, she developed joint pain, a rash, and hair loss. Blood tests showed signs matching drug-induced lupus rather than the classic form. The team stopped the drug and started a steroid course. Her symptoms eased within a week and cleared within two weeks.

pmc-12727875:

pmc-12728175:

pmc-12730875:

pmc-12731875:

pmc-12733475:

pmc-12733575:

pmc-12733775:

pmc-12734375:

pmc-12734775:

pmc-12735775:

pmc-12736375:

pmc-12736475:

pmc-12736775:

pmc-12737475:

pmc-12738075:

pmc-12738275:

pmc-12738575:

pmc-12743475:

pmc-12745475:

pmc-12753975:

pmc-12766575:

pmc-12801975:

Using tissue from five patients and a modified air-liquid culture method, they succeeded in three cases.

Organoid cells carried low levels of an enzyme that should have made them sensitive. Yet they resisted the drug anyway. The surprise suggests backup defenses at work, and the authors offer the organoids as a testing ground for new drugs.
pmc-12817875:
Jia and seven colleagues map research on stem cell therapy for rheumatoid arthritis in twenty twenty-five. The disease is a chronic autoimmune attack on joints with no cure. Mesenchymal stem cells are a promising new treatment route. The team analysed the published literature to chart the field.

They retrieved one thousand two hundred ninety-six records from a major database. Mapping tools charted countries, institutions, authors, journals, and keywords. Current hotspots include varied healing effects and inflammation mechanisms. Work also focuses on cells from different sources and their vesicles. The authors say the field is booming at the research frontier. Their map is meant to guide new researchers and clinical translation.
pmc-12821475:
Jeremy Rosen and Samuel Asanad published a review in 2025 of newer oral testosterone therapies for symptomatic male hypogonadism, a condition in which the body makes too little of the hormone. Traditional oral forms damaged the liver and were poorly absorbed, so patients reluctantly turned to clinic injections or to gels and patches applied daily.

The three share the hormone's class-wide risks: high blood pressure, excess red blood cells, and changes in cholesterol levels. They differ in dosing regimens, in how doses are titrated, and in insurance coverage. One product offers flexible dose titration and direct-pay access. One comes at a fixed dose. A third is titratable and supported by established data.
pmc-12821875:
Seven researchers link sleep habits and genes to liver scarring in a paper from 2025. Cirrhosis is severe scarring that can end in liver failure. The team used the UK Biobank, a huge health study, and followed more than three hundred sixty thousand adults. Sleep pattern was scored from five habits, and a gene score summed each person's inherited risk.

Over about thirteen years, roughly eighteen hundred people developed cirrhosis. Poor sleep patterns raised risk in a clear stepwise way. People with both poor sleep and high gene risk faced the highest risk of all. Good sleep mattered most for those with high inherited risk. The authors urge sleep care as part of liver health.
pmc-12822275:
Samara Cardoso and co-authors present a 2025 study of two sugarcane genes that steer cellulose laying and plant bulk. A genome sweep found fifty kin genes in cane, grouped in eleven sets. Two, ScBC1 and its like-named kin, speak loudest in stems. Their family trees place one with wall-thickening genes and the other with first-wall genes. Switched on in a test plant's leaves, both genes grew bigger leaves and cells, the first gene most.

pmc-12824975:
Raphael Israeli, Tomer Cohen, Gil Gannot, Dana Avraham, and Amir Oron report outcomes for a pin fix of fingertip bone breaks in two thousand twenty-five. A mallet finger break tears a chunk off the fingertip bone, and big chunks can let the joint slip. Their wrap-around pin method aims to squeeze the chunk down and keep pins from wandering.

About two in five reached the top two outcome grades, and no complications or hardware faults appeared. Past published groups serve as the backdrop for comparison. A chart hints that older groups fare worse on the top grades.
pmc-12827475:
Elena Pinto and ten co-authors present a fully human antibody aimed at ovarian cancer in a 2025 study. The antibody targets folate receptor alpha, a protein that ferries folate into cells and shows up on many tumors. An older mouse antibody from the same lab led to drug-linked versions now used or in trials, but mouse parts can stir the immune system.

It also matched the older mixed version at calling immune cells to attack. The authors argue that grip strength with both arms engaged matters more than single-arm strength.
pmc-12828775:
Kulathungage Dilrangi and six colleagues used a sequencing trick to watch mRNA decay across a bacterium's whole genome. Rifampicin halts transcription, so sequencing over time reveals each transcript's life span. In Caulobacter crescentus, about twenty percent of transcripts begin breaking down while still being written. Ribosome counts showed how well messages are translated tracks with transcript life span. Cut sites grouped where ribosomes were sparse.

The 2025 work unifies three processes usually studied apart: making, translating, and destroying RNA are linked genome-wide. That linking is a control layer bacteria can tune, and a possible angle for antibiotics that break it.
pmc-12831275:
Annabel Itaeli and three co-authors pool evidence on how antibiotics spoil bacterial cultures in a review from two thousand twenty-five. Cultures guide treatment, but antibiotics given before sampling can kill the very growth doctors need to see. Studies varied too much to read singly.

Eleven studies covering over sixty-seven thousand samples entered the meta-analysis. Growth showed in thirty-seven percent of samples cultured before antibiotics, but only eighteen percent after. That is a drop of more than half. Results swung widely between studies, which the authors flag. Their advice: draw samples before the first dose whenever possible. Post-dose cultures still help when progress is unclear, for tracking and adjusting therapy.
pmc-12831375:
Linor Llwyd Jones, Kevin Munro, and Jane Wild set out a trial plan to test how olive oil should be given before earwax removal. This protocol, from twenty twenty-five, deals with a North Wales NHS wax service. Too much earwax brings hearing loss, ringing, and discomfort. The service tells patients to soften wax with olive oil before microsuction. Yet one in four first tries fail to clear the ear.

Staff lore says a spray works better than drops. The trial will test that claim in a two arm design, with clinics as the unit of chance. Adults set for microsuction form the pool. Readers who run ear clinics get a fair test of a cheap prep step that could cut repeat visits.
pmc-12836975:
Öznur Tufan Akarslan and colleagues tested drug combinations in diabetic rats in 2025. A standard diabetes drug that slows sugar uptake works only modestly alone. The team paired it with two antioxidant agents and compared many combinations in diabetic and healthy rats over seven weeks. They tracked blood sugar, insulin response, inflammation, tissue damage in liver and muscle, and the activity of genes that move sugar into cells.

Blood sugar and long-term sugar markers fell, insulin release improved, and inflamed, worn tissue looked healthier. Some combinations even beat a pairing with an older diabetes drug. Key sugar-handling genes in muscle returned toward normal. The authors suggest the add-ons could help hard-to-treat diabetes, while stressing that human trials must come first.
pmc-12838975:
Sithara Dissanayaka and co-authors published a 2025 study on gut microbes and brain health in older adults who still think clearly. Certain acids made by gut microbes when they ferment fiber affect body metabolism and brain inflammation. Both are tied to Alzheimer's disease.
