They studied eighty-seven adults with normal thinking. Stool samples were tested for the acids, and microbe species were profiled from their DNA. One acid, acetate, was the most common and showed the strongest microbe links. Higher acetate went with more of two helpful species. In people with more brain amyloid, the microbe-acid links looked stronger. The work hints that gut chemistry shifts may begin before memory problems do.
pmc-12842175:
Iris Xiaoxue Yin and five co-authors shared a review in twenty twenty-five. It is about amorphous nanomaterials. These are solids whose atoms never settled into crystals. They sit like a frozen liquid. That lets them dissolve more readily. They load drugs better and degrade on schedule. Crystalline dental materials lack those traits. Five families dominate the field. They are based on calcium, silicon, magnesium, zirconia, and polymers.

The review covers how each type is made. Most routes run at low heat, which stops crystals from forming. It covers what each type does in the mouth too. Amorphous calcium phosphate remineralizes enamel. Silicon-based types ferry antibacterials. Each section closes with limits and future directions. For clinicians and materials scientists, the survey sorts a scattered field. It lays the field out as one map of disordered options.
pmc-12843175:
Shi and four co-authors build a system that renders fluorescent objects from new viewpoints under new colors of light. Fluorescent materials shift the wavelength of light they absorb, so ordinary view synthesis with white balance fixes cannot reproduce them. Their method extends neural radiance fields with the physics of light adding up.

The system learns from a sparse set of photos taken under varied viewpoints and lighting colors. Tests with a computer display as the light source beat earlier methods. An extension using a multi-color light stage reproduced fluorescent colors under common lamps. The authors aim at realistic graphics for scenes where fluorescence matters.
pmc-12847475:
Ashwin Madhavan and six co-authors checked how often patients on a common eye drug develop antibodies against it, in a study from twenty twenty-five. The drug treats eye inflammation not caused by infection. In some patients the body makes antibodies that blunt the drug, risking flares and sight loss.

They also reported worse general health and had near-zero drug levels in the blood. Length of treatment and use of other immune drugs showed no link. The authors discuss what these ties may mean for dosing.
pmc-12847975:
Wenxing Wu and colleagues published a 2025 engineering study on calculating how moving targets appear to radar. A target's radar signature changes as it moves, and computing those changes quickly matters for detection and identification. Their method simulates rays bouncing off the target's surface, using dense rays instead of splitting ray bundles.

A fast tracing library and parallel processing on ordinary computer processors speed the calculations, avoiding special graphics hardware. The authors then apply time and frequency analysis to reveal motion patterns in the returning signal. Faster, hardware-light simulation like this helps engineers test radar designs against targets in realistic motion.
pmc-12848075:
Zapata and co-authors profiled working detection dogs in this study from twenty twenty-five. Such dogs sniff out drugs, explosives, pests, or missing people. Training and selection are intense, but how behavior fits each role was unclear. The study covered over one thousand dogs rated on fifteen behavior factors.

Handlers also scored each dog's detection skill and general performance. Some roles, like medical and pest detection, came with higher scores on traits often seen as flaws. Breed patterns stood out too. Labradors and German Shepherds sat near the average profile. Belgian Malinois mixed strong and weak traits, above all in dual roles. The authors argue whole profiles, read in context, predict success better than single traits.
pmc-12855975:
Panagiotis Iliopoulos and a team of co-authors link brain wiring to telling similar memories apart, in a paper dated twenty twenty-five. This skill, mnemonic discrimination, keeps today's events from blending with look-alike past ones. Brain scans tracked links among memory, control, and vision regions.

Hippocampus-to-prefrontal links ran weaker in people who scored better before training. After two weeks of web training, drops in that same link tracked who improved most. Training also raised a link between two visual areas. The authors name the hippocampal link a trainable resource for sharper memory.
pmc-12910475:
Mareike Schrader and four co-authors tested music-based group exercise for people with acquired brain injury, in a trial published in two thousand twenty-five. Brain injury often dulls thinking skills. In the music arm, three patients used gym machines fitted with sensors that turned their joint effort into pleasant music. The control arm used the same machines alone, with no music link. Training ran three times a week for four weeks.

Thirty-five patients finished. Both groups gained from training, but the music group did no better on thinking tests, daily living skills, or mood. Group training was enjoyed more, while solo training felt more focused and intense to some. The authors say choice between group and solo work should follow what each patient prefers, and that more study is needed.
pmc-13018375:
Gurleen Kaur and four colleagues published a small clinical study in two thousand twenty-five on flower fragrance in hospital wards. Heart rate variability reflects the balance of the automatic nervous system and responds to smells. A pleasant ward scent might calm patients measurably.

Thirty adults in obstetrics and chemotherapy wards had variability recorded before and after one hour of diffused flower fragrance. Three standard variability measures rose after exposure, all beyond chance. Patients also rated the scent experience more pleasant afterward. Enjoyment correlated with the variability gain. The authors propose fragrance diffusion as a cheap supportive measure in wards, while the group was small and had no control arm.
pmc-13085475:
Christina Schachner and co-authors measure regional lung density change after contrast dye in dual-energy chest scans, in a research paper from 2026. Contrast dye raises lung tissue density on computed tomography. Slight lung changes, such as ground glass or emphysema, are best read on scans without dye, yet dye helps when clots or tumors are suspected.

Patients who had both dye and plain scans within a year at two centers were included. Scans were aligned and the lungs split into front and back halves and into thirds by height. Mean density per region was compared between scan types. The study quantifies how much dye adds, and whether the gain varies by lung region.
pmc-13093875:
Le-Hoang, Guénée, and Piguet report a chemistry study on how metal binding can steer the stacking of aromatic molecules. Their two-armed ligand binds rare-earth ions such as yttrium and europium. Binding charges the ligand and drives unlike rings to stack together. The stacks form paired units, in crystals and in solution.

pmc-13101775:
Ebenezer Akore Yeboah and a team of co-authors survey nurses and midwives worldwide on climate change and sustainable care, in two thousand twenty-six. Health systems both suffer from climate change and add to its causes. Nurses could champion greener care, yet many do not link their daily practice to the climate.

Most knew that human causes drive climate change, but only a third knew the term net-zero health care. Weak policies, heavy workloads, and thin organizational support were the top barriers named. The authors call for climate topics in nursing training and carbon policies inside health organizations.
pmc-13116075:
Kailu Chen and co-authors report a study from two thousand twenty-six on a fungal gene that boosts cotton disease. The fungus Verticillium dahliae causes a damaging wilt of cotton. pmc-13120475:
Liu and co-authors track how pellet size shapes char in straw burning. Char burnout is the slow step in biomass heat plants. Rice straw pellets of 8, 10, and 12 mm were heated at 700 degrees. pmc-13136675: Mehmet Ası Oktan and co-authors published this case report in 2026. A man of sixty-three was on bosutinib, a targeted drug for blood cancer. Such drugs can make the body hold fluid. pmc-13143075:

pmc-13145575:

pmc-13152875:

pmc-13152975:

pmc-13155575:

pmc-13157575:

pmc-13159575:

pmc-13160675:

pmc-13161975:

pmc-13164475:

pmc-13165275:

pmc-13166775:

pmc-13173675:

pmc-13176775:

pmc-13177875:

pmc-13182175:

pmc-13182575:

pmc-13186075:

The authors propose the compound as a candidate therapy worth further study.
pmc-13187575:

pmc-13189075:
Yingzheng Ren and a large team build an interpretable model that predicts aggressive cell division in gut stromal tumors before surgery. Their study was published in twenty twenty-six. Division rate drives risk, yet biopsy is invasive and scans alone cannot see it.

Scan features like tumor size, dead tissue, and coarse vessels joined blood markers. The aim is risk sorting good enough to plan surgery without a needle first.
pmc-13189975:

pmc-13191775:

It maps which enzyme classes, A through D in the Ambler scheme, each drug can block. It also tracks clinical uses as resistance pushes doctors toward last-resort drugs. The authors frame inhibitor development as central to keeping old antibiotics alive.
pmc-13194075:
