Seventy-four patients underwent repair over four years, nearly half after earlier failed attempts. About one in eight hernias recurred, and roughly a third of patients had complications. Pre-existing mesh placement, stoma type, and number of previous repairs may predict trouble. The honest accounting moves care toward patient-tailored choices.
pmc-13194275:
Tahsin Gider is first author on a 2026 real-world cohort study of weekly somatrogon treatment in Turkish children with growth hormone deficiency. Long-acting growth hormone cuts injection frequency from daily to weekly, which may help families stick with treatment. The study followed children aged three to eighteen treated for at least six months in routine practice.

Thirty-nine patients were included, treated for about eleven months on average. Yearly height gain averaged about ten centimeters, and a growth-related hormone marker rose into the normal range for most. In five children the marker ran too high, prompting dose cuts. No serious side effects occurred. Weekly treatment, the authors conclude, worked and was well tolerated, pending longer study.
pmc-13197375:
Prosper Magara and colleagues wrote a 2026 review on AI tools that watch for bleeding during keyhole surgery. In laparoscopic surgery, surgeons work through small cuts with a camera. Late spotting of bleeding raises harm and complexity, so smart monitoring could help.

The team searched six databases for studies from 2016 to 2025. Models showed high detection accuracy, mostly in single-center, past-data, or simulated settings. Some tools tracked the bleeding source or estimated blood loss in near real time. Still, small local datasets and a lack of live clinical trials limit trust. The authors call for large shared datasets and trials in real operating rooms before routine use.
pmc-13200675:
Jiarun Qin and co-authors asked whether two blood markers measured before surgery can predict how much a child's behavior improves after an operation for sleep apnea. Children with the condition, whose tonsils and adenoids block breathing at night, often show behavior problems. Surgery to remove both tissues is the standard fix. The team followed 138 children, measuring an alarm protein called HMGB-1 and an inflammation index built from blood counts.

Of the children followed for a month, those whose behavior improved least started with the highest marker levels. Both markers predicted the outcome well, and part of the protein's effect ran through general inflammation. The authors suggest pre-surgery testing could flag children who need extra support after the operation.
pmc-13201375:
A brain chemical that keeps people awake may also track depression, according to a 2026 prospective study led by Vani Viswanathan. The research article measures serum orexin-A in people with major depressive disorder and relates it to standard ratings of mood, sleep quality, and thinking.

Viswanathan and colleagues assessed 113 patients and 60 healthy controls, then followed the patients through six to twelve weeks of antidepressant treatment. Orexin-A levels were lower in patients than in controls, yet they did not shift with treatment or follow sleep and cognition scores. Levels tracked only one mood rating item, apparent sadness, so larger studies are needed before clinical use.
pmc-13204375:
Sofoklis Stavros and co-authors published this review in 2026. Tiny parcels called extracellular vesicles carry messages between cells throughout the reproductive system. They matter for egg and sperm interaction, fertilization, embryo growth, and implantation. Their cargo shifts with the health of the cell that made them, and includes proteins, fats, genetic material, and parts of mitochondria. The review focuses on how these parcels relay signals tied to oxidative stress and cell power plants.

That signaling links stress inside cells to fertility problems and to egg and embryo quality. The authors argue that research fields have grown up separately and need joining. They survey plans to combine several omics methods with AI tools that can spot predictive patterns in huge datasets. Such work could yield gentle diagnostic tests and new treatments. Standard methods and clinical proof remain the main hurdles before these ideas reach patients.
pmc-13206775:
Alexandra Manuela Buzle and ten colleagues identify what drives heart failure severity after a heart attack, in a study from twenty twenty-six. Post-infarction heart failure remains a major source of illness and death despite better reperfusion and drug treatment. How clinical background, heart injury, hormone activation, and artery disease combine is not fully defined. The team analyzed one hundred eighty-one infarction patients retrospectively.

Moderate-to-severe heart failure occurred in about forty-three percent of patients. That group was older and showed substantially higher systemic inflammation at admission. Key markers included C-reactive protein, fibrinogen, and sedimentation rate. Heart injury and stress markers were also significantly elevated. Measurements were taken before intervention, just after artery-opening treatment, and at forty-eight hours. Multivariable analysis isolated independent determinants of severe failure. The findings aim to sharpen care for patients after infarction.
pmc-13206875:
Alexander Bungert and three co-authors review macrophage cells in gut wound healing in a 2026 paper. Leaks at surgical joins in the bowel are a feared complication with high death rates. Those joins fail when healing stalls, and macrophages steer each healing phase.

The review follows healing through inflammation, growth, and remodeling stages. Macrophages shift from attack mode to repair mode as healing proceeds. They clear debris, call in collagen-building cells, and release factors that grow new blood vessels. When the shift fails, leaks, scars, and stiff tissue follow. Gut macrophages form the body's largest resident pool of their kind. That scale makes them an appealing target for new healing therapies.
pmc-13208175:
Shi, Zhao, Wei, Lu, Liu, and Chu test in twenty twenty-six whether gentle pulsed ultrasound can rescue blood vessel lining cells harmed by high blood sugar. Vessel damage drives the worst outcomes of diabetes, and clearing worn-out cell powerhouses, a process called mitophagy, is a candidate fix. The team combined data analysis with cell tests on sugar-stressed vein cells and tissue checks in diabetic rats.

Sugar dulled the cells' cleanup system and function, as predicted. Ultrasound restored movement, growth, and new vessel sprouting, and cut cell death, by switching mitophagy back on. Blocking that cleanup erased most of the benefit. In rats, treatment eased aorta lining damage and scarring. The authors offer proof of concept for diabetic vessel care.
pmc-13210875:
Nahuel Ponce and ten colleagues study gene variation for cool-season grass growth in a pasture grass, in a paper dated twenty twenty-six. In subtropical cattle regions, forage runs short in autumn and winter. The team crossed two parent plants of Paspalum notatum with opposed cool-season yields, raising 182 hybrid offspring. They grew them at two sites in Argentina across two years.

Cool-season yield varied widely by plant type, site, and year. The trait passed to offspring at a fair rate, though weather shaped it strongly. Plants that yielded well in the cool season also did fine in summer, so breeding for one did not hurt the other. A drone-read leaf index predicted yield best, offering a fast field screen.
pmc-13211175:
Mai, Teng, and Wang design a smarter controller for microgrid power generation in this 2026 paper. Microgrids face swinging generation, shifting loads, and changing network shape. Fixed control rules struggle with all three at once.

Their method lets several software agents decide together and keep learning online. A topology correlation matrix captures how the grid is currently wired. The agents draft control actions, then a safety layer checks them against a barrier-function model and corrects them jointly. A final module smooths power changes with adaptive ramp limits for fast, precise tracking. Simulations and experiments under load swings and rewiring showed the system held stable, optimal operation.
pmc-13211675:
Cuilan Hao and six co-authors published a veterinary parasitology study in twenty twenty-six on what happens inside a duck's stomach when a parasitic worm infects it. Eustrongylides tubifex causes severe diarrheal disease in waterfowl, threatening farm productivity. How the host fights back at the molecular level was unclear.

The team sequenced RNA from infected and healthy duck stomach tissue. Nearly two thousand genes changed activity, most switching on. The altered genes clustered in immune defense, tissue remodeling, and chemical signaling pathways. A protein network analysis flagged hub genes that may coordinate the response. Follow-up tests confirmed several changes. The map offers targets for controlling a damaging poultry parasite.
pmc-13213475:
Selva Aminizadeh and colleagues studied liver enzymes in malaria patients in 2025. Malaria severity varies between patients greatly. Parasite load may drive that variation. Blood group was another candidate factor. Liver damage markers were the readout. Patients were grouped by blood type.

Enzyme levels rose with parasite load. That link reached statistical significance clearly. Blood group showed no such link. Enzyme levels matched across blood groups. The authors propose enzymes as severity markers. Such markers could guide clinical management. Parasite counting remains important as well. Blood typing adds little here, apparently.
pmc-13213575:
Marco Milone and colleagues probe in 2026 where exactly a plant antioxidant sits inside a new kind of drug carrier. Quercetin, a flavonoid from foods, dissolves poorly and breaks down easily, so carriers built from ring-shaped pillararene molecules aim to shelter it.

Optical measurements showed most quercetin, in both its plain and charged forms, hides deep inside the nanoparticles, wedged between the ring molecules. Only a small share of the charged form rests on the surface. Hydrogen bonds and water-avoiding contacts hold the guest in place, shielding it from oxidation. That sheltered position explains earlier findings that these particles deliver quercetin into cells effectively, the authors note.
pmc-13214675:
Natalia Ferrando and colleagues safety-test the main ingredient of cinnamon oil as a greener pesticide, in this study from twenty twenty-six. The compound, trans-cinnamaldehyde, kills pests and is pitched as a soft alternative to synthetic sprays. But soft for crops must not mean harsh for the wild creatures that share fields and streams.

The team dosed a ladder of test organisms. Glowing bacteria dimmed first and were most sensitive, then water fleas, then onion roots, while earthworms in soil were hardiest by far. Soil and river microbe communities also slowed at high doses, especially in breaking down sugars and polymers. Every test showed a clear dose-response, a first for this compound under standard conditions. The authors say the new benchmarks draw the safe-use lines that any field product must respect.
pmc-13214875:
Lila Berle and others put out a 2026 view on reusing ordinary drugs against stubborn infections. Many long infections involve biofilms. Germs inside biofilms stand huge drug doses. Most long infections carry a biofilm part. New weapons are badly needed.

Drugs cleared for other illnesses may help. Their human safety is already known. Trials could therefore move faster. Four possible drugs get a full look. Each has plausible ways to fight germs. Current data for biofilm use are weighed with care. The authors note most doctors miss these traits. Added use with standard drugs is the real goal.
pmc-13215375:
Bruno Bavaresco Gambassi and colleagues present a 2026 randomized trial on whether the order of power and endurance exercise changes blood vessel health in older adults with hypertension. Participants had trained before and all had grade 1 hypertension.

One group did power training before endurance work while the other reversed the order, and both trained twice a week for 16 weeks. Arterial stiffness and blood flow measures were taken before and after the program. Neither order produced significant change in any of the measures. The authors conclude that, for this group, exercise order does not alter vascular outcomes over four months.
pmc-13215575:
Lara Rolvien and colleagues report a 2026 randomized trial of virtual reality exposure therapy for obsessive-compulsive disorder. Exposure with response prevention works well but is often avoided, and the authors tested whether a virtual version added to usual care would help.

Eighty patients with contamination or checking symptoms received either usual outpatient care alone or care plus six weekly virtual exposure sessions. Symptom scores improved no more in the virtual group overall. Exploratory results hinted at fewer obsessions in checkers and less anxiety later in the contamination group, and patients who had finished earlier therapy seemed to benefit more. Satisfaction was positive, though the authors treat these signals as leads for further study.
pmc-13216375:
Matthias A. Fink and co-authors present a 2026 study asking who labels CT reports on pulmonary embolism best: radiologists, a rule-based program, or large language models. Reliable labels underpin research cohorts and quality registries, but hand labelling is slow.

The test set held 2,923 structured reports from a single centre. Top language models, one open-weight and one commercial, each reached F1 scores of 0.98, beating the rule-based extractor at 0.81, and their rescue rates on rule failures were similar. A hybrid that sent only rule failures to a language model did best of all, with 99.8 percent accuracy, ahead of the pooled radiologists at 0.92 F1. The hybrid also cut labelling time from about thirty-two hours to one.
pmc-13216575:
Cong-cong He and co-authors present a 2026 study of a matrix protein called PRELP that turns out to brake the inflammatory circuit driving psoriasis. The skin disease is powered by the cytokine IL-17A, and PRELP levels in lesions are oddly low.

Data mining showed PRELP scarce in untreated lesions but rebounding after IL-17A-blocking drugs. Experiments explained why: IL-17A itself suppresses PRELP in skin cells through the STAT3 factor. Restoring PRELP slowed skin cell growth, encouraged their death, damped inflammatory pathways, and cut IL-6 output, which in turn lowered local IL-17A production. Delivering PRELP to mouse skin eased psoriasis-like changes. The authors propose raising PRELP as a new treatment angle for Th17-driven disease.
pmc-13217075:
María Olivencia-Manzano, Marta Gómez-Galán, Manuel Díaz-Pérez, and Angel Jesus Callejon-Ferre present a study of strain among olive grove workers in Spain. The text was published in 2026, though the catalog lists 2024. Spain holds Europe's largest olive growing area, and Jaén is its largest olive region.

The team used a short standard questionnaire with fifteen questions covering twelve factors, such as mental load, demands, and health. A total of 502 workers answered, picked at random from map points across the region. Pattern analysis and group tests sorted the answers. The results detail which strains hit olive workers hardest.
pmc-13217375:
Katharina Hoeter and co-authors present a 2026 case report in which DNA sequencing of blood plasma named the culprits in a sepsis case that cultures could not solve. The patient, a woman with a complex urological history, developed sepsis after emergency surgery for a ruptured urinary pouch.

Fever, racing heart, and rising inflammatory markers confirmed sepsis, yet blood cultures stayed negative. A metagenomic test that reads microbe DNA fragments floating in plasma flagged Klebsiella and Pseudomonas at genus level. Cultures from drainage fluid and urine later confirmed both organisms. Broad-spectrum antibiotics brought improvement. The authors note the sequencing result arrived retrospectively, too late to steer treatment, but argue that faster use of such tests could target therapy earlier in culture-negative sepsis.
pmc-13217675:
Zaid Sawaftah and co-authors present a 2026 survey of dry eye symptoms and smoking habits among 450 Palestinian university students in the West Bank. Vaping has surged in this age group, and its effects on the eye surface are barely studied in Middle Eastern populations.

Just over 58 percent of students reported dry eye symptoms on a standard index. Students who both vaped and smoked cigarettes stood out: after adjustment, their odds of worse symptom severity were 2.35 times those of non-smokers. Vaping alone pointed the same way without reaching significance, and cigarette-only smoking showed no adjusted association. The authors call for awareness campaigns aimed at young dual users and for prevention work on smoking-related eye surface problems.
pmc-13218175:
Ioulia Barakou and colleagues explore how adults with chronic conditions pace their activity across a week, in a 2026 study. People with fatigue often swing between overdoing it and crashing, and pacing advice aims to smooth it. The study compared people given fatigue management advice with those who had not.

Twenty-nine adults with chronic conditions and fatigue, recruited from a United Kingdom fatigue clinic and university networks, wore an accelerometer for seven days and completed questionnaires on fatigue, pacing, and self-regulation. Daytime activity fluctuation did not differ between the advice and no-advice groups. Among those given advice, fluctuations tied significantly to self-regulation and measured activity, hinting at a goal-directed way of organizing the day. Looking at profiles, the team distinguished five pacing patterns, from morning-heavy bursts to steady all-day pacing. The variety itself is the message: pacing looks different from person to person.
pmc-13218675:
Anne van der Spek and co-authors present a 2026 study of thyroid hormone and insulin action in the liver. Insulin resistance comes before type two diabetes, and thyroid hormone shapes sugar balance in ways still not fully mapped. A liver focused drug in this family was lately cleared for liver scarring care.

The team bred mice whose livers lack the main thyroid hormone sensor and tested them on plain, hormone low, and high fat diets. Deleting the sensor in the liver did not change insulin signals or sugar balance. A single hormone dose still fixed insulin response in fat fed mice of both types. Human liver-like cells agreed: the sensor was not needed. The authors say the hormone acts outside that liver sensor.
pmc-13218975:
Yukun Liu and co-authors engineer a temperature-sensitive gel dressing loaded with drug-carrying nanoparticles for diabetic chronic wounds in a 2026 biomaterials study. Diabetic wounds stall because infection, oxidative stress, weak blood vessel growth, and unresolved inflammation attack at once, and plain dressings cannot address all four. The team's gel is liquid when cool and sets in place on the wound.

The dressing combines a PF127 gel base with mesoporous silica nanoparticles doped with selenium and loaded with the antiseptic benzalkonium chloride. In lab tests it killed Staphylococcus aureus and Escherichia coli, lowered reactive oxygen inside cells, helped blood vessel cells to migrate and form tubes, and calmed inflammatory signals. In diabetic mice the gel sped wound closure, increased collagen deposition and new vessel growth, and eased inflammation. The authors credit the benefit to restored chemical balance in the wound plus joint control of inflammation and vessel growth.
pmc-13220375:
Wenzhong Jin and colleagues build and validate a deep learning system that measures alignment from long-leg X-rays in a 2026 study. Surgeons planning knee and hip work need fifteen alignment angles and lengths from these films, and measuring them is slow and variable. An automated pipeline could standardize measurement, provided it matches expert accuracy.

The system first detects landmarks with a YOLOv5 detector, then computes the fifteen parameters. It was trained and tested on 309 radiographs and checked on seventy-five films from a different scanner and group. On the external set, errors for angles stayed between a fraction of a degree and under half a degree, and the analysis took twenty-four seconds, ninety percent faster than by hand. A contest found that defining the tibial joint line through the plateau edges beat the lowest-point line on every parameter. Failure rates at important thresholds were low.
pmc-13221675:
Domínguez and co-authors report results for a pain treatment in a paper from two thousand twenty-six, written in Spanish. The method uses pulsed radio waves through the skin to calm severe nerve pain in the face and a type of intense headache that comes in clusters. Cases were hard to treat with standard care.

Over eight years, twenty-five patients were treated at target nerve clusters. Most patients with face pain and most with cluster headache improved at three months, and pain scores fell. No major side effects occurred. However, pain returned in nearly all who first improved, often after a year. The authors call the method safe and useful, while noting the small group and the need for caution.
pmc-13222175:
Bogdan Sorin Capitanu and colleagues compare hospital costs of robot-assisted versus manual knee replacement in Romania, in a 2026 retrospective study of 400 operations. One hundred cases used robotic assistance and three hundred used the conventional approach. Operating time, hospital stay, early complications, and cost categories were analyzed, with modeling to find cost drivers.

Robotic cases took about twenty-three minutes longer in theater and kept patients roughly a day longer. Ward medicines, supplies, robotic use itself, and longer operating time drove higher costs. Early complications were few and similar in both groups. The authors suggest tightening steps around surgery could trim the robotic premium, and they ask for larger multi-hospital studies.
pmc-13222375:
Katharina Richter and colleagues target a small RNA that helps glioblastoma resist chemotherapy, in a 2026 study of patient-derived tumor cells. Expression profiling covered fifty primary tumor samples grouped by two genetic markers. Seven cell lines grown from patients then received an inhibitor of miR-25-3p, a microRNA that promotes growth, invasion, and drug resistance.

Blocking the microRNA lowered beta-catenin and restored a tumor-suppressing protein across all lines. Four of the seven lines became more sensitive to temozolomide and less invasive. Gene and methylation profiles shifted toward a calmer, less stem-like state. The authors nominate miR-25-3p as a dual-action target against both spread and chemoresistance.
pmc-13222975:
Xinhao Liu, Ruisen Lu, Pan Li, and four colleagues sequence the chloroplast genomes of a small plant genus in this two thousand twenty-six paper. Stachyurus is the only genus in its family, with about ten species across eastern Asia and potential horticultural and medicinal uses. Genetic resources for it were scarce. The team sequenced and assembled complete chloroplast genomes from twenty-five accessions covering seven accepted species and one variety.

The genomes were much alike in size, structure, and gene content, with length differences traced to inverted repeat boundary shifts, loss of one gene, and repeat variation. Seven hypervariable regions came out as candidate markers, and four genes showed signs of positive selection. Phylogenies from the chloroplast genomes conflicted strongly with nuclear ones, with wide paraphyly pointing to chloroplast capture by hybridization. The authors caution that plastid data alone cannot resolve this genus.
pmc-13223075:
Hong Jin Kim and co-authors study why some teens develop an abnormal forward curve just above their fusion after scoliosis correction surgery, in a 2026 retrospective cohort study. Records covered 282 adolescents with idiopathic scoliosis, split by whether this junctional kyphosis appeared at two-year follow-up. Side-view spine shape and alignment changes were compared between groups.

Forty-eight patients developed the complication. The highest fused vertebra sat lower in that group, and their sagittal balance shifted more after surgery. Certain original shapes, especially a cervico-thoracic kyphotic profile, predicted trouble. The authors frame the change as the spine compensating for its original shape rather than a surgical failure, noting serious symptoms are rare in teens.
pmc-13223875:
Jonathan Watanabe, Michael Strand, Minal Walvekar, and Rafael Alfonso-Cristancho present a 2026 scoping review on how the world defines and regulates biosimilar medicines. These near-copies of biologic drugs can widen access and cut prices, but rules differ by country. The team searched the literature and compared guidance across the most populous countries in all six World Health Organization regions, nineteen countries in all.

Most countries define a biosimilar as showing no differences in quality, safety, and effect against the original product. Sixteen require head-to-head comparability studies, and thirteen demand the same reference product throughout. Wealthy economies waived clinical trials when justification sufficed, while developing economies varied. Rules on manufacturing checks were broadly present but uneven in detail. The authors argue harmonization still lags behind the science, and they map where the gaps sit.
pmc-13224475:
Sousa Pinto and coauthors review heat camera checks of cattle comfort. Heat stress is a top challenge for cattle in warm regions. It cuts yield, breeding success, and animal welfare. Standard checks need restraint and touch, which limits scale.

Heat cameras read skin heat with no touch at all. Surface heat shifts flag how cows shed body heat. The review pools studies on taurus, indicus, and crossbred cattle. It maps which body sites give the best heat reads. Camera methods are fast and suit large herds well. Gaps hold calibration and weather effects on reads.
pmc-13229275:
Marlies K. R. Peeters and Yves Van de Peer argue a 2026 case for deliberately using polyploidy, whole-genome doubling, as an engine of the bioeconomy. Doubling reshapes genomes at a stroke and often produces larger organisms, richer chemistry, and tougher stress tolerance. The authors survey how those immediate effects could be harvested across farming, health, and biotechnology instead of waiting for slow conventional breeding.

Possible gains include faster domestication of local or medicinal plants, more biomass for biofuels, plants suited to cleaning polluted ground, and new sources of bioactive compounds for therapy. Because the same underlying effects recur across sectors, the authors see polyploidy as shared ground for interdisciplinary exchange on sustainable production.
pmc-13230275:
Raffaella Panza and colleagues compare in 2026 two gentle ways to give lung surfactant to newborns who struggle to breathe. Records came from three intensive care units in southern Italy between January 2024 and March 2025. Babies received surfactant either by the LISA method through a thin tube or by the INSURE method with brief intubation.

Sixty-one babies were included, split almost evenly between the two methods. Rates of needing a second dose, a breathing machine within three days, or later chronic lung disease were similar in both groups. More LISA babies needed a second dose, but the gap was not statistically clear and did not lead to worse outcomes. Within the LISA group, one breathing support mode shortened oxygen use.
pmc-13230575:
Ji Huang and colleagues map in 2026 a gene family in jasmine that may help the plant fight a damaging soil fungus. Arabian jasmine is prized for scented tea and fragrance, yet stem and root rot from the fungus cuts yield and quality. The team profiled gene activity and plant hormones during early infection.

Four members of the LBD family, a group of plant control genes, changed activity sharply soon after infection began. Lab checks confirmed the sequencing pattern for those genes. Combined chemical and gene data link them to defense signaling and related metabolic routes. Those four genes offer targets for breeding or engineering jasmine with stronger resistance to southern blight.
pmc-13232875:
M Al-Sayegh and colleagues profile in 2026 mouse stem cells turning into fat cells across five molecular layers at once. Matched differentiating and non-differentiating cultures were sampled on day thirty for gene activity, proteins, secreted factors, fats, and small metabolites. Joint factor modeling then looked for one shared axis that separates the two cell fates.

A single dominant factor separated fat-forming from resting cells cleanly in every layer. Two themes converged across the layers: rebuilding the scaffold around cells, and rewiring fat handling inside them. A secreted enzyme ranked as the single strongest fate marker. Four bridging molecules linked the scaffold and fat themes, and lab checks confirmed six candidate regulators matched the sequencing signal.
pmc-13233275:
Yunfeng Qiao and colleagues published a 2026 pathology study measuring how far follicular thyroid cancer invades beyond its capsule. Benign follicular adenomas and these cancers look alike before surgery, so heat-based ablation of a supposed adenoma might undertreat a hidden cancer. The team reviewed digital slides from 43 surgically removed follicular cancers treated between 2016 and 2023.

Invasion past the capsule averaged about one and a half millimeters, while the hidden invasion that ultrasound cannot detect averaged roughly half a millimeter and never passed 1.36 millimeters in this group. Neither measure varied by tumor stage, cancer subtype, sex, or lymph node spread, though age related to wider capsule invasion. The measurements support ablating two millimeters beyond the visible tumor edge as a safety margin.
pmc-13233475:
Shuju Zhao and colleagues published a 2026 plant study on how water-conducting cells build their walls. These cells form thick patterned secondary walls. Watching them inside plant tissue is nearly impossible. The team grew them in dishes instead. Single cells could then be filmed as they developed.

A delivery protein marked the wall-building sites. Its spots shifted from random to lined-up patterns. Removing the protein disordered the wall patterns. Mutant cells also started wall building too early. Timing and pattern both depend on this protein. The dish system opens a window on wood formation.
pmc-13233575:
Ruiran Liu and colleagues published a 2026 analysis of online e-cigarette marketing in China. The country bans online e-cigarette ads, yet sellers keep finding routes to buyers. The team collected marketing posts from seven platforms between September 2024 and January 2025, including Xiaohongshu, Douyin, and Bilibili, and coded 3,596 examples with help from a large language model.

Xiaohongshu hosted nearly seventy percent of the material. Direct marketing outnumbered indirect approaches, and individual sellers produced almost three-quarters of posts, mostly through plain product posts and community-style selling. Tactics differed sharply by platform. The authors say covert community marketing now does the work that open ads once did, and they urge regulators to build tracking tools that match these subtler methods.
pmc-13234075:
Yongqiang Liu and colleagues published a 2026 engineering study of a single-use perfusion bioreactor for growing animal cells at very high density. Disposable reactors avoid cleaning and suit continuous production of medicines, but they must mix gently and feed oxygen well. The team paired a five-hundred-milliliter vessel with a pulsed filtration unit and modeled its flow with computer fluid models across stirring speeds and volumes, checking the simulations against experiments.

Engineering measures stayed in favorable ranges, mixing took only seconds, and average shear stayed below the level animal cells tolerate comfortably. Test cultures of hamster ovary and human kidney cell lines then reached exceptional densities while keeping viability above ninety percent. The authors present the system as ready for intensive drug production trials.
pmc-13234375:
Isabel Nakoud and colleagues surveyed in 2026 tobacco habits among Syrian American adults living in Southern California and Florida. Syrian Americans are a growing immigrant group with historically high smoking rates. The survey covered more than nine hundred adults and asked about cigarettes, hookah, motives, and beliefs about harm. Data were collected during 2018 and 2019.

About one in six participants currently smoked cigarettes, while more than one third currently used hookah. Both rates sat above national averages. Social occasions and flavoured tobacco drove hookah use for many people. Being male, older age, alcohol use, and lower education predicted cigarette smoking in the analysis. Younger age and a belief that hookah is safer predicted hookah use. The authors argue prevention and quitting programs should be tailored to this community's culture and beliefs.
pmc-13234675:
Subbiramaniyan Kubendhiran and colleagues describe a new electrode material for supercapacitors, in a study published in twenty twenty-six. Supercapacitors store charge quickly but the layered materials often used in them conduct poorly and clump together. The team grew flower-like sheets containing manganese, nickel, and cobalt, using round starter particles that supplied two of the metals. They changed the mix of metals and the amount of manganese to find the best recipe, then paired the material with graphene in a full device.

The best version stored a large amount of charge for its weight and worked over a useful voltage range. The full device kept almost all of its capacity after many charge cycles. The authors present the self-templated growth method as a practical route to tuning these layered materials for energy storage.
pmc-13235375:
Hongyang Guo and co-authors built in 2026 an oil-based gel loaded with curcumin for treating diabetic wounds. Diabetic wounds stall in a cycle of excess reactive oxygen, inflammation, and infection. A plant sterol called beta-sitosterol disperses poorly, limiting its use in dressings. A precipitation method produced fine sterol particles that mix well with candelilla wax to form the gel.

The gel stayed stable, spread easily, and released its cargo slowly in characterization tests. One formulation strength stood out across the laboratory assays performed. Combined sterol and curcumin action killed bacteria and mopped up reactive oxygen species in the wound model tests. Skin repair cells migrated faster, and immune cells shifted toward a healing profile in the experiments. Inflammatory signals were also brought under control in treated tissue, supporting clinical potential.
pmc-13235775: Villalobos and colleagues publish a correction to their scoping review of hybrid care changes during the COVID pandemic. The corrected text concerns the review's funding statement. It records that the study was funded by the European Union, and adds the standard note that views expressed are the authors' own. Those views, the statement says, do not necessarily reflect those of the Union or its health and digital executive agency, and neither body can be held responsible for them.
pmc-13236675:
Yolanda Ruiz-Ordoñez, Elena Gervilla, and Albert Sesé profiled in 2026 problematic technology use and compulsive buying among more than one thousand teachers in Spain. Participants taught at all school levels and completed validated questionnaires on online behaviour, buying, anxiety, and depression. Statistical profiling grouped teachers by shared behaviour patterns rather than single habits. Four distinct groups emerged from the combined analysis.

One large group showed minimal problems and very low emotional symptoms across the measures. Two middle groups leaned toward either digital overuse or compulsive buying, each with its own symptom pattern. A high-risk group combined both problems with markedly raised anxiety, depression, and online vulnerability. Younger teachers, and women in particular, were overrepresented in that highest risk group. The authors recommend screening digital behaviour during occupational mental health checks for teachers.
pmc-13236775:
Philosopher Luana Poliseli wrote a 2026 paper on the place of aesthetic experience in sustainability research. She studied two mixed teams: ClimArtLab, which joins art and climate science, and the Council of Care, which works with traditional communities on biodiversity. Her question was how beauty, feeling, and setting help people understand hard environmental problems.

Poliseli argues that understanding grows from a three-way engagement among the knower, the thing studied, and the surrounding environment, with aesthetic experience linking the three. The account moves aesthetics from the margins of philosophy of science toward daily research practice. It offers sustainability teams a way to treat sensory and emotional experience as part of how knowledge is made, not as decoration added afterward.
pmc-13237275:
Sebastiaan N Siegerink and team used Netherlands Cancer Registry data in 2026 to compare two second-line strategies for metastatic gastroesophageal cancer. After first-line treatment with oxaliplatin combinations failed, doctors either reintroduced oxaliplatin or switched to paclitaxel with ramucirumab. The team emulated a randomized trial by weighting 129 patients so the groups resembled each other.

Overall survival did not differ clearly between the strategies, with medians of about nine months for reintroduction and eight months for the switch. Patients who reused oxaliplatin more often went on to further treatment lines afterward. The authors propose reintroduction as a sound option for selected patients after a long first response. A true randomized trial remains absent.
pmc-13238475:
A World Health Organization checklist walks birth attendants through the safest steps of delivery, but tools only help when staff know and use them. Dharitri Swain and Latha Venkatesan survey obstetric workers in public facilities of one Indian district in this 2026 study.

Knowledge of the checklist averaged under half marks, which the authors call suboptimal. Midwives, nursing officers, and trained or older staff knew more. Where the checklist was used, workers followed most key practices well, from allowing a birth companion to checking blood loss. The study points to training and habit, not the tool itself, as the weak links.
pmc-13238775:
Amanda M Kissel and colleagues modeled in 2026 how disease, drought, and warming jointly threaten boreal toads in the southern Rocky Mountains. The high-elevation amphibian depends on landscape water for breeding, and a killer chytrid fungus circulates in the same wetlands. Their dynamic model tracked toad breeding and fungus presence together, using two decades of field records and new climate-linked measures.

The chance that a site hosted breeding toads fell by more than forty percent between 2001 and 2019. Future scenarios for 2055 to 2069 brought further declines, especially where the active season lengthens. To make the results usable, the team built a web tool that shows predicted water and occupancy conditions for managers. The study treats the three threats as one interacting problem rather than separate worries.
pmc-13239375:
Ming-Ming Deng and colleagues outline a 2026 trial protocol for diagnosing unexplained fluid around the lungs, called pleural effusion. Standard biopsy through a semirigid thoracoscope, a camera tube passed into the chest, sometimes misses the cause, so the team tests a live imaging aid.

Ten centres in China will enrol 158 adults whose effusions remain undiagnosed. Half receive a conventional biopsy, while half receive biopsy guided by a tiny confocal laser probe that shows tissue at cellular level during the procedure. Diagnostic yield is the main outcome, alongside accuracy, procedure time, sample quality for genetic testing, and complications.
pmc-13239575:
Yi Liu and a large collaborative team map immune patterns in triple-negative breast cancer in a 2026 study. This aggressive cancer type lacks hormone targets, so immune activity inside tumours strongly shapes how patients fare, and the team sorted 212 tumours by where immune cells gathered.

Spatial single-cell analysis of seventy-five tumours compared immune desert, excluded, and inflamed patterns. Inflamed tumours carried stronger interferon signalling and more plasmacytoid dendritic cells, a rare immune type, and their patients did better. Excluded tumours held many immune cells at the edges yet fared poorly like deserts. Checks in several outside datasets supported interferon response as a favourable sign.
pmc-13239975:
Nesreen Alqaissi and Mohammad Qtait listen to Palestinian women looking back on marrying as children in a 2026 qualitative study. Early marriage persists in the West Bank, where custom, money pressures, and political instability meet, yet long-term reflections from women themselves are rarely recorded.

Ten women from the Hebron area, married between very young ages and seventeen, gave detailed interviews in Arabic. Their accounts traced marriages decided within strict family hierarchies, lasting physical and emotional strain, lost schooling, and a slow, critical reappraisal of what happened. Some built new meaning from hard beginnings. The authors call for interventions grounded in this social and structural reality.
pmc-13240175:
He and colleagues argue that artificial intelligence should borrow the brain's way of fusing the senses. Systems that learn from sound, sight, and text together usually merge them by fixed rules. The living brain does the opposite: its merging shifts with context, attention, and the reliability of each sense at that moment, which makes perception robust when one channel degrades.

The authors set out brain-inspired mechanisms that could make such merging dynamic in machines. Ideas include weighting senses by trust and letting higher levels feed back on lower ones. If machines integrated information more like brains, they might handle noisy, conflicting real-world input with fewer brittle failures.
pmc-13240375:
Tyler Janitz and team report a stress fracture in an unexpected athlete in a 2026 sports medicine case. A 15-year-old sprinter felt a pop behind her right hip during a hundred-metre race. She came in with severe pain that stopped her running, yet outside X-rays had been read as normal.

A specialist re-reading spotted the break, a non-displaced stress fracture of the lower pubic bone. Such breaks make up a small share of stress fractures. They are seen most in soldiers and long-distance runners, not in sprinters. She rested from running for three months while scans showed steady healing. Guided therapy then brought her back to full sport, with no limits, five months after the injury.
pmc-13240975:
Giovanna Cabral and five co-authors tell of a woman whose buttock skin grew a mat of fine red vessels months past filler shots. Their case study appeared in twenty twenty-six. Such mats are a known short ill past vein shots and kin vein work. The woman, aged twenty-seven, had firm filler set for looks, with no past vein work on the spot.

A mix cure of skin laser and vein shots brought part gain. The team read the case as a may-be link tween firm fillers and late small vessel change, and urge long watch past such looks work.
pmc-13241375:
Li and a large Shanghai team simulated clear-aligner retraction to learn how back teeth should be braced beforehand. Their finite element model reproduced an upper jaw after first premolar extraction. Two bracing styles competed: pre-tipping molars before retraction, or tipping them during it. Angles of one, two, and four degrees were tested.

Pre-tipping changed almost nothing compared with no preparation at all. Tipping during retraction controlled forward lean well, at roughly one to three degrees by tooth. It also prevented inward torque on the first molar at a modest setting. Rotation and vertical drift of the back teeth resisted both strategies.
pmc-13241575:
Yan and colleagues at Xiamen University survey the cGAS-STING pathway, the cell's alarm system for stray DNA. When DNA appears in the cytosol, the sensor enzyme cGAS builds a messenger that switches on STING. The response pours out interferons and inflammatory signals against infection and tumors. The review integrates structural, nanotechnology, and clinical findings.

The same alarm can misfire: leaked mitochondrial DNA keeps it ringing and drives chronic inflammation. The authors map this duality across brain degeneration, cancer, and autoimmune disease. Cell type and tissue setting decide whether the pathway protects or harms. They outline small-molecule blockers, nanocarrier delivery, and combination immunotherapies as precision ways to tune it.
pmc-13241675:
Knurr and colleagues at Wisconsin charted how thirty-four leg muscles change around ACL reconstruction with quadriceps grafts. Twenty-five patients underwent MRI before surgery and at three and twelve months after. Automated segmentation measured every muscle in both legs. The quadriceps was expected to suffer most.

Deficits peaked at three months, when nearly half the muscles lagged on the operated side. A year out, ten muscles still trailed, the vasti worst of all. Calf muscles also stayed shrunken, while the operated side's gluteus maximus grew larger. Knurr argues rehabilitation must look beyond the quadriceps.
pmc-13241875:
Junpeng Chen and co-authors report a 2026 biomaterials study on healing mouth lining wounds without scars. Mouth wounds must heal in a wet, moving environment where dressings often fail to stick. The design borrows the wet-grip chemistry of mussels.

Fibers were spun with a strong plastic core and a dopamine-modified gelatin shell. The membrane stretched well, swelled strongly, and clung to wet tissue for over a day. Cells grew happily on it in the lab. In rat mouth wounds, the membrane sped closure, limited scarring, and guided immune cells toward a healing state through a named signaling pathway. The authors present it as a candidate dressing for soft tissue repair inside the mouth.
pmc-13242375:
Arbuckle's team in Brisbane gathered what living with anaphylaxis does to adults' minds and daily lives. All ten studies centered on adults. Nine bases were searched across thirteen years of published work. Eleven papers on ten studies survived the screening process. Number and story findings were merged in one mixed design.

Most studies found harmed mental wellbeing, with stress, anxiety, and low mood all common. Women reported worse mental health than men throughout. Fear of the next attack drove dodging moves and social withdrawal. The team urges routine wellbeing screening inside allergy care.
pmc-13242675:
Galal Hegazy and co-authors present a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis comparing open versus keyhole repair of a wrist stabilizer tear. The torn structure, part of the triangular fibrocartilage complex, leaves the forearm joint unstable. Both surgical routes aim to reattach it at its deep anchor point.

Five comparative studies covering several hundred wrists met the criteria. Pooled results showed no significant differences in wrist scores, disability ratings, pain, or recurrence of instability. Evidence quality was rated low to very low, and several studies carried serious bias risk. Exploratory analysis of mostly chronic injuries changed little. The authors conclude both approaches can restore function and stability, so choice may rest on surgeon experience and patient factors.
pmc-13242775:
Yong Luo and co-authors present a 2026 study of cord blood markers for early sepsis in preterm babies born after the waters broke early. Early-onset sepsis is a leading threat to such infants, and standard markers react late. Two immune-related proteins, P-selectin and PTX3, were measured in umbilical cord blood.

Babies whose mothers had prolonged membrane rupture showed higher levels than healthy controls. Levels ran higher again in the subgroup that developed sepsis, and the two markers moved together. Each marker alone sorted septic from non-septic babies well, and together they performed better than the usual inflammation tests. Gram-negative bacteria, mainly E. coli, caused most confirmed infections. The authors propose the pair for early risk checks.
pmc-13243775:
Chengye Di and Wenhua Lin present an electrocardiogram puzzle: extra heartbeats that look exactly like the normal beats around them. Their case study appeared in the Journal of Arrhythmia in 2026. When a premature beat keeps the same QRS shape as sinus rhythm, the impulse must travel the heart's usual wiring. The tracing pointed to an unusual origin and mechanism, which the authors work through.

The beats proved to be premature junctional contractions coming from the AV nodal region, specifically its slow pathway. The mechanism was a small, self-limiting reentry loop: the signal circled briefly and produced isolated echo beats rather than a sustained fast rhythm. That distinction matters, because echo beats from this circuit need no aggressive treatment. The case teaches clinicians to read identical-looking early beats as a clue to the node's dual pathways. Rare mechanisms can hide in plain sight on a routine tracing.
pmc-13245575:
Alexi C Cornelius, Patricia C Pawlow, and Morgan Tallo describe team-based care in a Delaware obstetric emergency department in 2026. A growing patient load faces a projected shortage of obstetric providers over the next decade. Their unit answers by letting nurses work at the top of their license.

Nurses take a larger role in judging labor and other urgent cases, with doctors close at hand. The model speeds care for patients and lifts nurse job satisfaction, the authors report. Neighboring areas across the Maryland line already count as maternity deserts, which adds pressure. The account presents shared work as a safe way to stretch scarce staff.
pmc-13245875:
Tran-Nam, Che-Ngoc, Khan, and co-authors propose a clustering algorithm for messy, lopsided data in this 2026 PLOS One paper. When data points are uncertain, described by probability distributions rather than single values, and some groups vastly outnumber others, standard fuzzy clustering tends to lose the small groups entirely. Their method, BKIFF, rebuilds the similarity measure around the Hellinger distance between distributions and seeds the process with an optimization routine inspired by the black-winged kite's hunting.

Across synthetic distributions, skewed test cases, and real image datasets, the new algorithm beat established baselines. In severely imbalanced cases it recovered groupings that rivals scored near zero on, with proven convergence. The authors position it for data-mining tasks where rare categories matter, from fault detection to medical subgroup discovery, and where being swamped by the majority class is the central problem.
pmc-13246575:
Frühauf, Bartoníček, and Fojtík asked whether a serious ankle injury always needs surgery, in this 2026 European Journal of Trauma and Emergency Surgery study. A Maisonneuve fracture breaks the fibula high near the knee and injures the ankle joint below. The team followed seventeen patients whose detailed CT scans met strict stability criteria, meaning the ankle bones sat almost perfectly in place despite the injury.

These patients were treated without surgery, and every fracture healed within three months. At follow-up averaging nearly three years, ankle position had largely held, and standard foot-function scores came out near the top of their scales. The authors define that stable form precisely, so other surgeons can identify which patients can safely skip the operation.
pmc-13246875:
Baczkowski, Sakaki, and Kalbe studied how emotional learning reshapes memory across time gaps, in this 2026 Psychonomic Bulletin and Review paper. Memory normally splits experience into separate events, limiting links across boundaries. The team had two hundred eighty-five young adults view neutral animal and tool images in three phases. In the middle phase, one category sometimes came with a mild electric shock, teaching a threat association.

Tested a day later, the group as a whole showed no reliable boost for later images. But individual analysis revealed two hidden patterns: some people's memory faded across phases with emotion helping only the shocked items. Others organized memory around the emotional episode, boosting related images even after the gap. People differ, it seems, in whether emotion or time structures their memories.
pmc-13248975:
Lin and co-authors compared brain stimulation pairings for language recovery after stroke, in a 2026 network meta-analysis. Speech therapy is standard for aphasia, and magnetic stimulation of the scalp may add gains, but protocols differ widely. The authors pooled twenty-six randomized trials with more than eleven hundred patients and ranked combinations across several language skills.

One pairing, low-frequency stimulation plus music and therapy, led most immediate outcomes, including naming and repetition. A dual-site stimulation pairing led every long-term outcome instead. The authors caution that the flashiest combinations rest on low-certainty evidence, while simpler pairings are better proven. They call for direct head-to-head trials before clinics adopt the leaders.
pmc-13249075:
Elio Fanchon and co-authors present a Python toolkit for DNA methylation array data in a 2026 software paper. Chip arrays that read methylation now probe about a million sites per sample. Data volumes keep swelling, and Python users lacked a full toolkit for the format.

Their package, Pylluminator, ports trusted methods from two established R toolkits. It covers cleaning, quality checks, group comparisons, and plots in one place. The code is open under a permissive license and installs with standard Python tools. Online documents carry install steps and worked examples. The authors aim to make large methylation studies faster to run and easier to share.
pmc-13249575:
Harpenslager and a large international team used naturally heated streams to preview methane's future, in a 2026 Nature Climate Change study. Freshwaters produce about half of all methane emissions, but microbes in the water eat much of it before it escapes, a filter whose strength under warming was unknown. Geothermally warmed streams in five northern regions offered a centuries-long warming experiment.

Warming made methane-producing microbes more abundant and productive. Methane-eating microbes worked faster too, but shifted toward less efficient types, so the share they consumed stayed fixed. With production rising and the filter's share frozen, emissions climbed. The authors warn the same arithmetic may govern lakes, rivers, and wetlands worldwide.
pmc-13250175:
O’Dwyer and Palma review how doctors should treat lung cancer that has spread to only a few sites. Their 2026 BMJ Oncology paper covers non-small cell lung cancer in this limited-spread state, often called oligometastatic disease. New drug treatments have changed what local therapy, such as focused radiation, can usefully add.

The authors argue that limited spread is not one single condition, and lesion count alone is a poor guide. For tumors with EGFR mutations, trials support wiping out the few remaining sites to extend drug benefit. For other patients on immunotherapy, the best randomized evidence does not support routine consolidation, and lung inflammation is a real risk. They propose choosing treatment by intent: cure limited disease, or protect a drug that still works.
pmc-13250875:
Yoo and co-authors show that a human cell protein helps mosquito-grown alphaviruses infect mammalian cells. Their 2026 Emerging Microbes and Infections study focuses on TIM-1, a surface protein that grabs fatty molecules on virus coats. Viruses pick up their coats from host cells, and insect membranes differ from mammal membranes.

TIM-1 boosted infection by mosquito-grown chikungunya, O'nyong'nyong, and Sindbis viruses in cell tests. Its fat-binding pocket proved essential for the effect. Chemical profiling showed mosquito-grown virions carry more of two coat fats, and TIM-1 can engage both of them. The authors say the work widens understanding of TIM-1's targets and of how mosquito-borne viruses cross into human cells.
pmc-13251175:
Costa and a large team survey gut pathogens in French calves and ask how vaccination of mothers changes the picture. Their 2026 Veterinary Research study collects more than eleven hundred stool samples from calves and dams at an experimental unit and on farms with recurring newborn diarrhea. Samples were screened for the main diarrhea agents.

Cryptosporidium was the most common pathogen found, ahead of bovine rotavirus. Where dams were systematically vaccinated against rotavirus, coronavirus, and E. coli, only about one in six calves showed symptoms. Two Cryptosporidium species were reported in sick calves for the first time, and one genotype family dominated the findings. Genotype comparisons suggested calf-to-calf spread and dirty environments matter more than direct mother-to-calf passage.
pmc-13252275:
Rajeev Kumar Nishad, Reetu Verma, and Priyanka Das published a clinical study in two thousand twenty-six on a dangerous ear infection in diabetic patients in India. Necrotizing otitis externa can invade the skull base, and Indian data on its microbes and course were limited.

Sixty diabetic adults at a tertiary centre were assessed. All had canal swelling, discharge, and severe night pain. Cultures most often grew Pseudomonas species, in about forty-three percent, while some grew nothing. Mild hearing loss affected about a sixth, and facial nerve palsy about seven percent. The authors say the pattern matches global reports but complications ran high. They urge targeted antibiotics and early nerve monitoring.
pmc-13253675:
Md. Tofael Ahmed Bhuiyan and colleagues introduce DFU-GCNet, a neural network for classifying diabetic foot ulcers, in a 2026 paper. These wounds are a severe complication of diabetes and a leading cause of amputation, so fast, reliable grading matters. Existing deep learning tools often miss lesions at unusual scales and cannot explain their verdicts, which undermines clinical trust.

The new architecture fuses inception modules, which read the image at several scales at once, with global context blocks that relate distant parts of the tissue. It was tested on a public diabetic foot dataset against standard models such as VGG16 and EfficientNet. Classification accuracy reached 97.16 percent, with matching strength on the F1 score and correlation measures the team reports. The heatmaps confirmed the network attends to wound boundaries clinicians care about. The authors propose the system as a screening aid rather than a replacement for judgment.
pmc-13253975:
Ignacy Młodzianowski and co-authors set out a theory-based plan for hair loss care in a 2026 paper. Androgenetic alopecia is the common form of pattern hair loss, and current drugs have limits or side effects. The team reviewed recent work on its causes and the genes involved, including AR and EDA2R.

Their model uses a protein called STEAP3, which converts iron between two forms. That step could switch off a blocker and free a growth signal, beta-catenin, to enter the cell nucleus. The authors stress the plan is theory only, with no lab or clinical tests yet, and offer it to guide future trials.
pmc-13254175:
Wei Luo reviews the two-way relationship between atrial fibrillation and depression in a 2026 article. Atrial fibrillation, the commonest sustained heart rhythm disorder, carries heavy risks of stroke and heart failure, while depression independently worsens cardiovascular health. Evidence now suggests each condition feeds the other.

The review first assembles population research on how often the two co-occur and which risk factors they share. It then works through connecting mechanisms: an autonomic nervous system thrown off balance, chronic inflammation, neurohormonal pathways, and behavior, since depressed patients may move less, sleep worse, and take medication less reliably. Living with an unpredictable racing heart, in turn, erodes mood and quality of life. Clinically, the author argues for integrated care, screening heart patients for depression as routine, and managing both conditions together rather than in separate silos. The piece aims to help clinicians treat the dual burden as one problem.
pmc-13255075:
Hao Yin and a large team report a 2026 study of a rice bran peptide that protects bone in osteoporosis models. Osteoporosis often involves bone marrow stem cells making fat instead of bone, weakening the skeleton. The eight-amino-acid peptide, called RBAP, was tested in mice and in cultured stem cells.

Given before or after bone loss developed in ovariectomized mice, RBAP preserved bone structure, strength, and sped fracture healing. It also helped in aging and disuse models. In culture, the peptide pushed stem cells toward bone formation and away from fat, acting through a protein named eIF3L. Attaching a bone-targeting aptamer, a short DNA strand that homes to these stem cells, improved delivery and strengthened the effect at the same dose.
pmc-13255575:
Mario Pagano and Sonia Del Prete introduce a 2026 special issue gathering research on how living things adapt to environmental stress. Such stress has always shaped evolution, but human-driven change now stacks many pressures at once, from warming and habitat breakup to pollution and noise. The editors frame adaptation as a multi-level puzzle spanning molecules, bodies, ecosystems, and deep time.

The collection holds thirteen contributions, including eight research articles and four reviews. Topics range from a newly described Andean katydid whose chest structure amplifies its call, through plant and animal responses to heat, salt, and drought. The editors argue against single-factor studies and for work that links mechanisms across scales. Readers get a map of a field trying to keep pace with a rapidly changing planet.
pmc-13255775:
Kwak and co-authors asked whether simple design rules can predict how lab-made polymers steer amyloid proteins toward or away from toxic clumping. They tuned how water-shy the polymers are, their water affinity, and net charge, then combined computer models, biochemistry, and cell assays across two amyloid systems, amyloid-beta and alpha-synuclein. The goal was a general framework rather than a single drug hopeful.

Evenly water-loving and water-shy designs, above all zwitterionic ones, curbed fiber growth, rerouted clumping, and reduced membrane contact and cell harm. Cation-heavy polymers did the reverse, speeding clumping through static charge pull, while strongly water-shy ones barely mattered. The same rules held across both proteins, pointing to design rules that carry across proteins.
pmc-13256075:
Glisic and colleagues asked whether the depth of hepatic encephalopathy on arrival predicts short-term death in alcohol-related acute-on-chronic liver failure. One hundred intensive care patients with both conditions were graded with the West Haven criteria and followed for hospital outcomes. Standard organ failure and physiology scores were compared between lower and higher encephalopathy grades.

Patients with higher-grade encephalopathy stayed longer in hospital and died more often within seven and twenty-eight days. Their organ failure scores were also significantly worse, and survival curves separated clearly. Acute kidney injury tracked with mortality in both grade groups. The authors support encephalopathy grade as a practical risk stratification tool.
pmc-13256175:
Arum Han and colleagues present a 2026 population study of Ontario children whose mothers used opioids during pregnancy. Linked health records covered more than 1.3 million births from 2007 to 2018, of whom about thirteen thousand children had documented prenatal opioid exposure. The team compared preventive care uptake and later health service use through childhood.

Exposed children received fewer well-child visits in their first two years and were less likely to get the enhanced eighteen-month checkup. Across follow-up to age thirteen, they used emergency departments, specialists, hospitals, and day surgery at higher rates. Gaps were widest in early childhood and narrowed for some services later. The authors argue that early preventive-care misses may set lasting patterns, and they urge targeted outreach for these families.
pmc-13256775:
María Jesús Ramírez-Expósito and co-authors survey in a 2026 narrative review the biology and medical uses of calcitonin gene-related peptide, a 37-amino acid signaling molecule released by sensory neurons. CGRP drives blood vessel widening and pain signaling, and blocking it has already changed migraine treatment.

The review traces the peptide from gene splicing through its receptor structure, revealed by cryo-electron microscopy, to signaling pathways inside cells. It compares three generations of small-molecule blockers and four approved antibodies, including long-term safety data. Possible roles in chronic pain, sepsis, cancer, and Alzheimer's disease are covered too, with the caution that evidence outside migraine is still mostly preclinical.
pmc-13257575:
Soner Berşe and co-authors built a scoring tool to flag patients at risk of phlebitis from peripheral venous catheters. Phlebitis, painful vein inflammation where a drip sits, is a common hospital problem. Their 2026 methodological study develops the scale and then tests how well it performs.

An expert panel trimmed a pool of candidate items down before nurses applied drafts to hundreds of catheters. Analysis settled on fourteen items grouped into personal, chemical, and mechanical risks. The scale proved consistent and separated high-risk from low-risk patients accurately. In a second group it matched an established phlebitis scale closely, supporting bedside use.
pmc-13258775:
Jeong-Hwa Choi and Young-Ran Heo compare diet and mental health in Korean teens from multicultural and other families during a 2026 survey study. Data came from a national youth risk survey covering nearly forty five thousand adolescents. Five eating areas were scored, from breakfast habits to fast food intake.

Teens from multicultural families faced lower family resources on average. Suicide attempts were more common in that group. In both groups, poorer eating scores tracked with more anxiety and more severe suicidal behavior. The diet link to suicidal behavior ran stronger for multicultural teens. Policy readers get evidence for pairing food support with mental health care.
pmc-13259375:
Xinhua Tang and Yiming Wang sharpen space signal anti jam work with a refined wave guess method in a 2026 paper. Space signals reach Earth very weak and can drown in swept noise. Their guess starts from a three line spectrum read, then Napier style steps polish the count.

A split chip runs the block on fast logic while a small core steers settings. Still noise tests gained a lot next to plain guess work. Swept noise tests beat plain and loop based rivals as well. Closed loop space tests stretched the jam margin by a wide span. Sets in harsh zones gain sharp aim with no loss of speed.
pmc-13259775:
Hong Ren and coauthors guide vitamin injections into swallowing muscles with electrical monitoring in a 2026 randomized trial. One hundred ten stroke patients with swallowing trouble from brainstem paralysis enrolled at one hospital. Half added targeted mecobalamin injections to standard drug and rehabilitation care.

Water swallow tests favored the injection group clearly. Video imaging scores showed far higher marked and total effectiveness in that group. Choking episodes fell in both groups, with a larger drop under injections. Treatment lasted two weeks before scoring. Rehabilitation teams gain an adjunct that improves swallowing safety after brainstem stroke.
pmc-13259875:
Swapnajeet Sahoo and Sujita Kumar Kar wrote in 2026 on India's proposed Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill, 2026, and its mental health effects. They say the bill shifts gender identity from self-decision toward state checks and medical review. That contrasts with a 2014 Supreme Court judgment in India that treated gender identity as an inner aspect of personhood protected by fundamental rights.

Requiring people to prove identity to officials, the authors argue, can exclude those who do not medically transition, those outside fixed gender categories, and those unable to handle bureaucracy. They link identity invalidation to depression, anxiety, and suicidality through minority stress. Certification roles for clinicians could also damage trust and delay care. They call for a return to self-identification, plus stronger anti-discrimination and support systems.
pmc-13260275:
Christophe Cauchi and colleagues wrote a 2026 reading study of how nearby words affect word recognition. In the flankers task, a target word appears with words on either side that are either identical to it or different. The team varied flanker size, keeping target size fixed, and flanker distance, either normal spacing or seven spaces away. They measured response times and error rates to see how letter information from surrounding words is integrated during reading.

Flanker relatedness affected response times, and this effect interacted with both flanker size and distance. Larger flankers produced stronger flanker effects, while greater distance weakened them. Crucially, making flankers bigger did not compensate for the weakening caused by distance. In error rates, only flanker relatedness mattered. The authors say distance is the key visual factor governing how letter information is pooled across words.
pmc-13260775:
Adina Landsberg and colleagues present a 2026 case report, with literature review and patient perspective, of two kidney diseases occurring together. A 63-year-old man arrived with four weeks of body-wide swelling and months of cognitive changes, blurry vision, and tingling. Tests showed heavy protein loss in urine at 8.25 grams per day, low blood protein, blood in urine, acute kidney injury, and high blood pressure. Kidney biopsy revealed both diseases at once.

One disease was focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, a scarring of the kidney's filters. The other was ANCA-associated vasculitis, an immune vessel inflammation confirmed by a positive PR3 antibody test. Treatment combined steroids and rituximab for the vasculitis, then calcineurin inhibitor drugs for the resistant scarring disease, plus kidney-protective medicines. After two and a half years he reached partial remission, though kidney function stayed reduced and treatment caused diabetes.
pmc-13261875:
Anuja Tripathi and colleagues demonstrated in 2026 a two-stage method for recovering rare-earth elements from coal fly ash with a reusable ionic liquid. Rare earths feed medical devices, electronics, and clean energy, yet mining them is damaging and extraction from ash is tricky. Their liquid first leaches the metals out of the ash, then serves as the bath for plating them onto an electrode.

Tuning the voltage changed which metals deposited first. At the gentlest setting, neodymium came out preferentially, with a strong separation advantage over the rest. Stronger voltage raised total recovery, bringing about half the neodymium and smaller shares of the others. The liquid was then regenerated and used again for another cycle. The authors present the loop as a feasible, lower-waste route into ash stockpiles.
pmc-13262175:
Ke-Wen Guo and colleagues profiled in 2026 the saponins of Aralia elata leaves, a wild vegetable eaten across Northeast Asia, and found the plant's own proteins rewriting them during water extraction. Saponins are the leaves' main active compounds, and earlier work on a cousin plant hinted that solvent choice changes them. Their mass spectrometry survey compared methanol and water extracts.

Seventy-eight saponins were identified and twenty-two measured precisely, including one never reported before. In water, the major saponins lost a sugar at a specific carbon position, a cut performed by proteins native to the leaf itself. One conversion product was isolated and proven by magnetic resonance to be a brand-new saponin. The authors say preparation method, not just the plant, decides which compounds a consumer actually meets. That insight matters for both food processing and herbal quality control.
pmc-13262575:
Xiaojing Jiang and co-authors review blocking the mTOR pathway to tame systemic lupus erythematosus. This master growth switch misfires across T cells, B cells, and other defenders in lupus, driving autoantibody damage. Their 2026 review follows mTOR from cell biology to the clinic.

Inhibiting the pathway calms disease activity in studies and lets patients taper steroids, a prized benefit. Kidney disease, lupus's deadliest face, remains an open question for these drugs. Some patient subsets respond poorly or suffer side effects. Because parallel pathways also drive lupus, the authors anticipate combination regimens rather than mTOR blockade alone.
pmc-13262875:
Eliana Elisa Rehfeld Gheno and co-authors study health literacy among people with severe mental disorders in a 2026 journal article. Health literacy means the ability to find, understand, judge, and use health information and services. The Brazil-based team used a standard questionnaire, in its Brazilian version, plus a survey of personal background, and compared scores across groups.

Married participants and those whose mothers had limited schooling reported more understanding and support from health staff, they found. Low schooling in parents tracked with trouble getting care information. People over 54 reported stronger active involvement in their care and better social support. pmc-13282175:

pmc-13282375:
Shihan Li and co-authors present a 2026 modelling study re-examining the timing puzzle of the end-Permian mass extinction, the largest die-off in Earth history. Records show a sharp carbon shift began about fifty thousand years before intense global warming, which seems to break the expected link. The team combined geochemical modelling, statistical inversion, and several fossil and chemical proxies to test a missing factor.

This buffered early carbon release and delayed warming, the model shows. Erosion also washed more phosphorus, a nutrient, into the oceans. Extra phosphorus fostered gradual oxygen loss in seawater, priming the oceans for collapse. The authors offer this as a unifying account of the extinction's environmental run-up.
pmc-13282675:

Glomus tumours grow from the glomus body, a small structure that helps control body temperature, usually in the fingers. Their patient was a fifty-four-year-old man with five years of sharp, throbbing pain at the front of his knee, worse with activity. Early scans showed only mild arthritis and no soft tissue problem.

pmc-13282875:

pmc-13283375:

The authors urge caution and more checks before clinical use.
pmc-13283575:
Guneet Bindra and co-authors reviewed in 2026 how many head impacts American football players take at youth and college levels. The authors weigh what this means for young brains still developing.
pmc-13283775:
A tiny self-breeding fish offers a clean window on aging marks in DNA, used by Justine Belik and Frederic Silvestre in a 2026 brain study. The mangrove rivulus makes near-copy offspring, so genes stay almost fixed. Age-linked chemical marks on DNA can then be read without genetic noise.

pmc-13283975:

All patients had narrowing across several spine segments. Neither group had broken or dislocated bones. One operation removes the back bone and fuses the spine. pmc-13284075:

pmc-13284575:
Yu Jin Kim and Heung Up Kim reviewed in 2026 how doctors stop bleeding in the upper gut through a scope. Care starts before the scope, with fluids, transfusion, acid blockers, and vessel-tightening drugs where fitting, then early endoscopy.

Band ligation handles oesophageal varices, while glue injections suit stomach varices. Failed scope control leads to vessel blocking by radiology or surgery, and shunt procedures suit some variceal cases. pmc-13285275:

Long-term sinus swelling affects about one in ten adults in many regions and cuts life quality. pmc-13285875:
Shishir Singh writes a 2026 opinion piece asking whether statistical significance tells researchers what they think it does. The essay is aimed at clinicians and students in fields such as dentistry and medicine. Many readers treat a significant result as proof that a finding matters, and a non-significant one as proof that nothing was found.

Examples include a filling material that slightly reduces leakage and a root canal method that slightly reduces debris pushed out. Judging findings needs clinical sense alongside the numbers, the essay concludes.
pmc-13285975:

Published in 2026, the work used the CLOUD chamber at CERN at cool temperatures. Such particles seed clouds and affect climate, yet how plant vapors and acid interact without ammonia present was unclear.

pmc-13286075:
Lijuan Fu and co-authors chart three decades of stroke burden in China in a 2026 analysis of global disease data. China launched a national stroke program in 2011, and planners need a clear read on whether the load is easing. The team pulled deaths, new cases, survivors, and lost healthy years from 1990 to 2023, split by stroke type and sex.

Men carried the heavier load overall, which points care toward prevention, rehab, and plans shaped by sex.
pmc-13286375:
Andrew Orenberg and colleagues link a cell skeleton protein to the membrane's signal lipids in a 2026 cell biology study. Profilin 1 helps build actin cables, and the membrane lipid PIP2 runs countless signals from the cell surface. Cells missing profilin, or carrying a version that cannot grip actin, were profiled for their surface lipid levels.

Signs pointed to an overactive cutting enzyme: breakdown products ran high and its downstream signals burned hotter in the mutant cells. pmc-13286575:
Fernando Sarin da Mota e Albuquerque and co-authors weigh what crushes caregivers of medically complex children in a 2026 cross-sectional study. These children juggle several chronic conditions, devices, and drug lists, and the daily load lands on family shoulders. pmc-13286775:

The other two ratios rose with death risk in straight lines. Over a median of about four years, 412 patients died. Dietary structure, the authors suggest, adds information beyond single nutrient totals when judging risk.
pmc-13286875:

pmc-13287075:
Daijun Chen and colleagues sort new graduate nurses in a Chinese hospital into groups by how hard the jump from student to practitioner hits them. The 2026 survey of 220 nurses, run over two autumn months, uses a statistical grouping method to find hidden profiles of transition shock rather than one average score. pmc-13287275:

pmc-13287375:
