pmc-13287475: Marietta von Süßkind-Schwendi and co-authors published a correction in 2026 to a 2023 study on adding soluble fibre to purified mouse diets. Two added figures held errors. pmc-13287775:

pmc-13287875:

pmc-13288375:

pmc-13288775:

pmc-13288975:

pmc-13289075:

pmc-13289175:

pmc-13289375:

pmc-13289775:

pmc-13290575:

pmc-13290875:

pmc-13290975:

pmc-13291275:

pmc-13291575:

pmc-13291875:

pmc-13292075:

pmc-13292375:

pmc-13292675:

pmc-13293375:

pmc-13293475:

pmc-13293575:

pmc-13293675:

pmc-13293975:

pmc-13294875:

pmc-13295075:
Muchun Cheng and colleagues design new antibacterial compounds against drug-resistant germs in a 2026 study. Their targets block an enzyme bacteria need to make folate, called dihydrofolate reductase. A flexible side chain was added to a known lead shape to sharpen that blocking power.

Every new compound in the series inhibited the enzyme, and one, labelled 5a, beat both the lead and a standard drug on that test. It also killed a wide range of bacteria, including hospital strains, at very low doses. Fast killing, strong biofilm blocking, membrane damage, and low early resistance all mark it as a promising lead.
pmc-13295175:
Rachel Gilroy and colleagues test a gut microbe transplant against Campylobacter in chickens in a 2026 study. The germ is the top bacterial cause of food poisoning in people, with poultry as the main source. It settles heavily in the chicken's blind gut pouches and spreads fast through flocks.

Chicks given caecal material from adult birds at hatch carried more varied gut microbes. When challenged at 21 days through infected pen-mates, treated groups passed the germ on less and held far lower gut levels at slaughter age checks on day 35. The transplant beat a commercial exclusion product, suggesting real cuts in human cases could follow.
pmc-13295675:
Shaoyu Ye and Kevin K. W. Ho ask when social skill turns against health, in a 2026 study of students in Japan and Hong Kong. Surveys covered 452 students in Japan and 289 in Hong Kong, linking self-presentation and social skills to body symptoms, with social media use and social support as paths in between.

In both places, stronger social skills tied straight to more body symptoms, a link stronger than the path through support, which tied to fewer symptoms. In Japan, self-presentation also tied straight to breathing and sleep complaints. In Hong Kong that straight link was absent, though a faint path ran through time spent on social media. Skill online, the authors say, can carry a health cost.
pmc-13295975:
Margaret Isioma Ojeahere and twenty co-authors write, in 2026, about small slights faced by women working in psychiatry. Drawing on published work and their own experience across fifteen countries, they describe comments on appearance, dismissed contributions and crossed personal boundaries.

Such everyday put-downs, they argue, are backed by workplace habits that undervalue women, slow careers and cause distress. Patterns recurred across regions despite very different health systems. The authors call for change at both personal and structural levels, arguing that fixing psychiatry workplaces requires reform of the systems that normalise this treatment.
pmc-13296275:
Junjie Zhang and colleagues present a 2026 comparison of gene activity in male and female northern pike. Pike grow at different rates by sex, and the molecular basis of sex differentiation in the species remains unclear. The team sequenced gonad tissue from three females and three males.

Their whole-transcriptome survey found many RNAs that differed between the sexes. These included messenger, micro, circular, and long non-coding forms. Differing genes clustered in pathways tied to steroid hormone production and egg cell division. A regulatory network centred on one microRNA emerged as a candidate for follow-up work. Fish breeders and biologists get a first full dataset for this species, useful for future breeding research.
pmc-13296775:
Ernest Iakovlev and colleagues review, in 2026, tumours of the tear drainage system, a rare and varied group growing in the tear sac or duct. Their symptoms imitate blocked ducts and infections, so cancers are often caught late.

Full surgical removal with clear margins remains the mainstay, and newer keyhole and endoscope routes may spare the eye and cut complications. Radiation, chemotherapy and targeted drugs support care for malignant types, chosen by tumour kind. The authors assemble current evidence and their centre's experience into a practical guide for diagnosis and management.
pmc-13296875:
Ante Pelivan, Benjamin Benzon, and Danijela Budimir Mršić measured fat around arteries on CT scans of aneurysm patients in a 2026 study. Fat hugging blood vessels is thought to take part in artery disease and aneurysm formation. Nearly two hundred patients were grouped by whether their aneurysm sat in the aorta, the iliac artery, or a leg artery.

Fat density at the bulge site was higher than at the matching healthy spot, and it differed by location. Belly fat measures tracked the vessel-fat density for abdominal and iliac aneurysms, but not for leg aneurysms. Aneurysm width matched clot thickness instead. The pattern supports a local role for vessel fat in aneurysm development.
pmc-13296975:
Yeho Kim and colleagues pinpoint one protein variant behind drug resistance in colorectal cancer cells in a 2026 study. Resistant cells often survive both fluorouracil and oxaliplatin, two standard drugs. Sequencing of resistant cells flagged the gene AMOT, which helps control the growth signal YAP.

Only the shorter variant, p80, rose in resistant cells, while its longer sibling stayed flat. Removing AMOT barely touched untreated cells yet made resistant cells die far more readily under either drug. Restoring p80 brought YAP activity, growth proteins, and drug tolerance back. Forcing p80 into ordinary cells likewise hardened them. The variant looks like a shared support for cross-drug resistance.
pmc-13297075:
Panagiotis Pipelias, Christina Kanaka-Gantenbein and Panagiota Pervanidou review, in 2026, how stress early in life can programme health for decades. Drawing on searches of three databases, they trace pathways from hardship before and just after birth to later body and mind outcomes.

The stress hormone axis sits at the centre, tuned during sensitive windows when the brain and glands are highly plastic. Mother's stress acts through the placenta, and father's stress may pass marks through sperm. Chemical tags on genes lock in settings. The authors argue spotting these pathways early can target prevention at vulnerable children.
pmc-13297175:
Juan Vicente-Valor and co-authors measure, in 2026, gut-made short-chain fatty acids in the blood of thirty-six bowel cancer patients and twenty healthy controls. These acids support gut and immune health, but blood levels may drift from gut microbe counts as the body absorbs and processes them.

Cancer patients showed a distinct pattern: more total acids and acetate, more branched forms, and less butyrate and valerate. Links between blood acids and producer bacteria were sparse and inconsistent in both groups. Some blood acids fell as tumours advanced. Bigger joint studies are urged.
pmc-13297775:
Frozen octopus and squid cuts are hard to name by eye, so Kang-Rae Kim and colleagues built a DNA test that identifies six commercial species at once. Their 2026 paper describes a multiplex PCR assay designed for seafood inspection and market checks.

Primers targeting a mitochondrial gene region produced a distinct band size for each species, from 459 down to 82 base pairs, with no overlap between them. The test worked across annealing temperatures of 51 to 54 °C and still read clearly with as little as 1 ng of DNA. The authors offer the gel-based method as a fast first screen for verifying cephalopod products in trade.
pmc-13298075:
Neri Merhav refines the soft covering problem through statistical physics in a 2026 information theory paper. Random codes induce an output distribution, and a partition function with an inverse-temperature parameter captures its full Rényi spectrum. The annealed free energy splits into two branches, one driven by typical codewords and one by atypical codewords.

Merhav maps the phase structure of each branch and the boundary where they compete, giving a closed form for part of the diagram. All boundaries meet at a point set by mutual information. Applications to guesswork, channel resolvability, and hypothesis testing are discussed, with a Z-channel example illustrating the results.
pmc-13299075:
Hongyu Li and co-authors present an elderly patient whose severe thyroid failure first came on as hallucinations and cognitive decline, in a 2026 case report. The man, in his mid-seventies, had three months of complex visual hallucinations that depended on surrounding light, plus worsening thinking. Early checks suspected a degenerative brain disease.

Blood tests instead revealed severe autoimmune hypothyroidism with high antibody levels. Thyroid hormone replacement cleared the hallucinations fully and brought major thinking recovery. The authors stress that severe thyroid failure can mimic dementia as a reversible metabolic brain disorder, so thyroid screening belongs in workups for unexplained neuropsychiatric symptoms in older adults.
pmc-13299175:
Ashmita Dey and colleagues propose a computational pipeline hunting shared protein markers across early neurodegeneration and multiple sclerosis, in a 2026 study. Chronic immune interaction with the brain and a weakened blood-brain barrier link Alzheimer disease, Parkinson disease, and multiple sclerosis in recent thinking. Their framework starts from blood immune cell proteins shared across the conditions.

Markers were filtered for barrier permeability, mapped to brain cell types, and checked for pathway roles plus druggable structure. Kinase and integrin interactions emerged as key regulators, and certain blood cell populations resembled brain support cells in their signatures. The authors offer the pipeline as a route toward shared diagnostics and therapies.
pmc-13300075:
Magdalena Zaborowska and others study how two mulch film plastics reshape soil microbe groups, in a 2026 experiment. A biodegradable film and a standard polyethylene film were added to soil, and fixes using a helpful germ or humic acids were tested for their power to restore balance. Cultured counts and gene sequencing tracked the microbes.

Both plastics suppressed some microbe groups, with the biodegradable film inhibiting more strongly, while each favoured different microbe lineages. Possible germs settled on both materials. Adding the helpful germ rebuilt group balance better than humic acid stimulation. The authors present such mixes as tools for soil exposed to microplastic pollution.
pmc-13300175:
R Hoffmann and colleagues report a 2026 retrospective study asking whether an extra ablation step helps people treated for atrial fibrillation. The team compared pulmonary vein isolation alone with isolation plus empirical ablation of the cavotricuspid isthmus, a strip of tissue linked to typical flutter. Their cohort covered 422 patients who had first-time radiofrequency ablation at one referral center between 2020 and 2022.

Twelve months after treatment, freedom from atrial arrhythmia was similar in both groups, at 79 percent without the extra step and 84 percent with it. Procedures without the added ablation were shorter, and later flutter after isolation alone was rare, near one percent. The authors conclude that routine extra ablation is not justified, and they favor tailoring the procedure to documented flutter or individual anatomy.
pmc-13300575:
Maria Lui and co-authors explore whether a lasting pollutant alters gene splicing in a neuron-like cell model, in a 2026 computational study. PCB 153 is among the most common polychlorinated biphenyls found in food and the environment. It was applied at a dose below cell-killing levels to differentiated SH-SY5Y cells. RNA sequencing data were reanalyzed for splicing changes rather than expression shifts.

The reanalysis flagged ninety candidate splicing events. It also flagged shifts in thirty-two genes encoding RNA-binding proteins, the regulators of the splicing machinery. Genes touched by the splicing changes overlapped with sets linked to intellectual disability and developmental conditions. Some retained-intron events were predicted to insert premature stop signals, which could destabilize the affected messages. Motif analysis named four binding proteins as likely regulators. The authors frame the work as hypothesis-generating, a mechanistic thread between the pollutant and neurodevelopmental harm.
pmc-13302075:
T Mine and co-authors search, in a 2026 study, for mapping signs that predict a fast atrial rhythm appearing after ablation for atrial fibrillation. Recurrence of fibrillation itself is well studied, but the separate organised rhythm that sometimes follows is not. High-density maps made during pacing let the team grade slow and blocked conduction zones in the left upper chamber.

The cohort held 202 patients having their first ablation, followed for roughly thirty-three months on average. Fibrillation returned in about a third, while the organised rhythm appeared in nine percent. A severe block zone, where signals crawled or stopped, was the only factor tied to the organised rhythm after adjustment. The authors suggest such patients may need extra testing and ablation during the first procedure.
pmc-13303975:
Wane Zhong and co-authors review immune-based treatment for Helicobacter pylori stomach infection in a 2026 synthesis. About half the world's people carry this germ, which can cause gastritis, ulcers, and stomach cancers when left untreated.

Antibiotics remain the main standard cure, but resistance keeps rising and success rates disappoint in many places. The review explains how the germ weakens stomach immune defenses to settle in, and where new treatment targets might lie. Pairing immune approaches with antibiotics, plus smarter antibiotic use, is discussed as a route to clearing stubborn infections.
pmc-13304175:
Wararat Tavonudomgit leads a 2026 multicenter study asking whether fitness before open-heart surgery predicts recovery speed. Patients face real risks of problems after such operations, and simple strength and movement tests may flag who needs longer care.

Across two teaching hospitals, 116 patients completed chair stand, walking, balance, and grip tests before surgery. Nearly half developed problems after surgery, including a small number of deaths. Test scores were linked to complications and days spent in hospital through layered statistical models. Easy bedside fitness checks could help teams plan beds, rehab, and closer watch for weaker patients.
pmc-13304375:
Nan Tang, Yuliang Xu, and colleagues report, in a 2026 yeast engineering study, a surprising backfire when a production pathway was moved into mitochondria. Industry already parks the early mevalonate pathway there to make squalene, feeding on the organelle's rich starting material. The team asked whether the same trick would lift cholesterol, a later product used to build steroid drugs.

A cholesterol-making strain gained over five times more squalene after the move, exactly as hoped. Cholesterol output, however, collapsed to almost nothing, showing the later pathway had been throttled. Gene and protein profiling pointed to bottlenecks in regulation and transport between cell compartments. The authors caution that compartment tricks helping one pathway stage can strangle the next.
pmc-13304875:
Susanna Sologova, Diana Sologova, and co-authors review, in a 2026 paper, light-cured hydrogels as drug delivery platforms for dentistry. Modern dental care needs materials that do more than fill space: they should calm inflammation, fight microbes, and release drugs steadily inside the wet, harsh mouth. Gels hardened by light can be shaped in place and tuned for strength.

Comparing natural, synthetic, and hybrid polymers, the review favors methacryloyl gelatin for how well the body tolerates it and its tunable mechanics. Photoinitiators are graded for how kindly they treat oral cells, and release mechanisms are explained. Uses span root canal therapy, gum disease, implant infections, and regrowth of bone and dental pulp. The authors see these gels as multi-use platforms uniting local delivery with tissue repair.
pmc-13305475:
Hongmei Zhu and co-authors report a 2026 case of several cranial nerves inflamed together after infection. The condition strikes nerves of the face and throat on one or both sides, and its nonspecific signs make diagnosis a process of ruling out.

The patient arrived after a finger injury with a stiff jaw, swallowing trouble, coughing on drinks, slurred speech, and neck pain, plus high inflammation markers. Testing showed four cranial nerves involved and partial face nerve damage on electrical study. Brain scans showed only mild, vague changes. Strong steroid pulses brought improvement and discharge home.
pmc-13305675:
Bahar Amiri compared two ways of staging breast cancer in the armpit in a 2026 Iranian cohort study. One group had full lymph node removal, while the other had sentinel node sampling, and the team compared survival without recurrence against overall survival.

The study covered 1071 patients treated at Tajrish Hospital in Tehran between 1991 and 2021. Average overall survival was a little higher after full removal than after sentinel sampling in the reported figures, and disease-free survival showed a similar pattern. Neither gap reached statistical significance, so the authors present the two approaches as broadly comparable on survival in this cohort.
pmc-13306075:
Adnan Amin reviewed plant peptides joined with polymers for skin infection and inflamed wounds in a 2026 survey. Stubborn wounds resist standard creams because germs form films, drug resistance spreads, and damaged barriers heal slowly.

Plant defence peptides can kill microbes, break films, calm immune activity and aid tissue repair in the evidence gathered. Weak points include rapid breakdown by enzymes, poor entry through outer skin, short stay time and safety worries at higher doses. The review argues that smart polymer carriers and a shared development framework are needed to turn lab promise into tested human care.
pmc-13306275:
Chung-Woo Lee studied how preheating shapes welded joints in a common medical plastic in a 2026 experiment. Large high-density polyethylene parts for devices often need extrusion welding, and joint strength decides whether a finished structure stays reliable.

Heat level before welding and speed of hot-air movement were varied in a planned set of trials. Tensile strength, bending behaviour and stretch at break were then measured on finished joints. Patterns in the results show how warming prepares surfaces for bonding, giving makers practical guidance for tuning settings in device production.
pmc-13306575:
Yunsik Jung and colleagues propose in 2026 a safer way to train robot hands that manipulate objects between their fingers. Standard reinforcement learning chases task success and can learn rough, risky handling. Their replay method scores past moves for instability and favours safer experiences during retraining.

Risk scores came from three warning signs of unstable handling. The method was paired with a common policy algorithm and tested in simulation on block and egg tasks with a multi-finger hand. It beat hindsight replay and a reward-penalty method on success rate, risk level, and learning stability. Eggs make the stakes plain: careless moves break the object. The authors argue that replay selection, not only reward design, is a practical place to build caution into dexterous robots.
pmc-13306775:
Kai-Chih Lin graded fall risk in older adults from ordinary video without touching sensors in a 2026 study. A total of 688 community-living adults completed balance, chair-rise and short walk tasks aligned to a standard performance battery.

Body keypoints from video were centred and scaled, turned into motion paths, and joined with body-mechanics measures inside a light temporal network. Labels came from a preset functional index, not future falls, in the study design. Scores reached a macro area of 0.91 and accuracy of 81.3% in reported tests, with the model under 3 MB in size.
pmc-13306975:
Nina Mendez-Dominguez and co-authors review in 2026 treatments for menstrual symptoms in female athletes and their effects on readiness and output. Only five studies from 2023 to 2025 fit, covering contraceptive timing, cold therapy, mindfulness yoga, supplements, and pain-easing drugs. Symptom burden is common in sportswomen yet research stays thin.

Results for measured output were mixed across the small set, and methods varied widely between studies. Some treatments eased symptoms, felt readiness, or some scores, but nothing backed strong performance advice. The authors stress that female athletes remain little studied in sports health research. Better trials built just for this group are needed, they conclude. Until then, doctors should treat menstrual health as part of care without pledging race-day gains.
pmc-13307075:
Jiaxing Sun built a fibre-optic mercury sensor using MXene sheets in a 2026 study. Mercury in water threatens health at trace levels, so the team turned ion capture into crystal growth that shifts light inside a tiny cavity.

Mercury ions caught on MXene form Hg2Cl2 crystals, changing the cavity fluid's light bending for amplified readout. Sensitivity reached 5 pm per nanomolar and detection fell to 0.2 nM in reported figures, far below the World Health Organization drinking water guide value quoted by the authors. The work casts MXene as both catcher and signal booster.
pmc-13307675:
Ghadah Alhetheli and co-authors survey in 2026 what medical students at Qassim University know about HPV and whether they would take or advise its vaccine. Their online survey drew 300 students and scored knowledge on 14 items, plus views on personal use and advice to kin and future patients.

Most students had heard of the virus and the vaccine, yet only 44.3 percent reached the bar for good knowledge in the survey. Just over half would take the vaccine, while far more would advise it for patients or family. Higher knowledge scores tracked with every form of support, and women showed more personal willingness than men did overall.
pmc-13308575:
Pranjali Kurhekar and co-authors write a 2026 letter that questions how gains on a 15 item recovery scale were read in a spine surgery pain trial. The trial found higher scores for epidural care over vein based care at 24 and 48 hours after major lumbar surgery in 40 patients.

The letter notes that the gap at 48 hours was four points, below the six point bar for a gain patients can truly feel. It also flags a one point swing in an emotional support part and a repeated exact p value that may hide a typing slip. Base scores before surgery were missing too. Raw statistical wins need a clinical yardstick, the authors argue.
pmc-13308675:
Xiangru Huang and co-authors scope in 2026 what is known about disability in older adults with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, a lung ill that steals breath and daily function. Their search spanned eight databases to October 31, 2025, and two staff picked, pulled, and charted data by set rules.

Just 12 studies met the bar, most of them one point snapshots rather than tracked work over time. Reported disability shares swung wildly, from 15.00 percent to 97.00 percent across those studies, driven in part by tool choice. Two scales led the field, yet few tools were built or checked for this group in China. Causes spanned social, disease, and mind factors together.
pmc-13309475:
Antonella Onofrietti Magrassi and co-authors review support for new mothers mental health in a 2026 article focused on the United States. Help came from peers and trained non-specialists rather than clinicians. The review centers on mothers from racially, ethnically, and culturally varied backgrounds, who often face gaps in care.

Studies from 2020 to 2025 were gathered, and eight measured outcomes such as depression, anxiety, and parenting. Programs that built social support and used methods matched to each culture tended to help, with more sessions linked to larger gains. Mothers valued trust and cultural fit most. The authors call the approach promising while noting that no study pinned down exactly which part drove the gains.
pmc-13309875:
Muhammad Hamad Shabir and co-authors test in 2026 whether two tissue markers can flag meningiomas, the commonest primary brain tumours, that will invade brain or grade higher. Eighty-five cases at a Rawalpindi pathology institute were stained for a growth marker, Ki-67, and a cell adhesion protein, E-cadherin. Marker patterns were compared against invasion status and tumour grade.

Ki-67 levels ran significantly higher in invasive tumours and climbed steadily with grade, showing real power to separate the groups. Grouped E-cadherin scores also linked significantly with both invasion and grade, and grouping beat raw scores for usefulness. Brain invasion drives recurrence risk, yet biopsy samples often lack the brain tissue needed to prove it. A marker pair that hints at invasion from tumour tissue alone could guide surgery and monitoring intensity. The authors recommend reporting E-cadherin in categories as standard practice.
pmc-13310675:
Xi Li and co-authors report a rare monoclonal kidney disease in a young woman with diabetes in a 2026 case article. In proliferative glomerulonephritis with monoclonal deposits, a single antibody clone coats the kidney filters, causing swelling, protein loss, and kidney failure. No standard treatment protocol exists.

The 30-year-old had lived with type 1 diabetes for 19 years with poor control, and arrived with a week of nausea, vomiting, and whole-body swelling. Tests showed nephrotic-range protein loss, low blood protein, anemia, acute kidney and heart failure. Biopsy after stabilizing care showed diffuse IgG deposits of a single light chain type. The authors use the case to push biopsy and clone checks in fast-declining diabetic kidneys.
pmc-13310875:
Ruchika Sharma and colleagues make silver nanoparticles with a plant extract in a 2026 study. Chemical routes to silver particles can leave toxic waste, so a green route using Leucas lanata leaves was tried. The team checked particle form and tested power against free radicals and germs.

Tests confirmed silver particles with a sharp light signal and a mean size near 25 nm in scale, held stable by plant compounds. Particles beat plain extract in radical quenching tests and slowed four germ types, including Staphylococcus aureus and Escherichia coli. Low doses were active in lab assays. Safety in living tissue still needs study.
pmc-13310975:
Yingqi Li and co-authors test one session of muscle stimulation on ankle strength and brain activity in older adults in a 2026 study. Electric stimulation can boost muscle work, yet instant effects after a single session were unclear. The team stimulated the front shin muscle for 20 minutes in healthy older volunteers.

Twenty seven adults took part in a before and after design. Ankle lifting strength rose right after stimulation, while passive muscle traits showed no change. Brain scans during the task showed activity in both sessions, but no brain change held after strict correction for many tests. Brain and behavior links seen at first pass also faded after correction.
pmc-13311075:
Insuck Baek and co-authors test genome wide forecasts of cacao disease strength over time in a 2026 study. Past cacao gene work hunted single spots, yet orchard value depends on harvest after harvest of healthy pods. Repeated records for pod health and two fungal diseases were modeled from DNA markers.

Records covered 102 cacao types over four harvests. Trait repeat scores ran high, most for witches broom disease traits. Forecasts for broom disease branch and flower signs held up across checks, genomes, and trait definitions, while other traits shifted more. A shortlist of types that balance yield and disease strength was named for breeding.
pmc-13311275:
Miu Sato and colleagues offer a 2026 mouse study on how the KEAP1 sensor protein spots stress when selenium-based defense proteins fail. Different sulfur sites on KEAP1 may sense different kinds of harm.

Mice lacking the Cys151 site kept their NRF2 defense response and liver health when selenoprotein making was blocked in the liver. Mice lacking the Cys226 and Cys613 sites lost the response and suffered severe liver injury. A drug that works through Cys151 restored defense and improved survival in those mice. The work shows separate sensor sites feed one shared defense path.
pmc-13311575:
Gavin Surgey and co-authors describe a 2026 effort to rebuild Kyrgyzstan's state health benefits package with open, evidence-based choices. The WHO UHC Compendium supplied standard service definitions for the work.

The revision ran from 2023 to 2025 under a national Health Policy Council. Cost, impact, and fairness evidence was built for every service, and funding scenarios showed the trade-offs. In the end 182 services were classed as essential. With funds of 19 dollars per person, only 66 of them could be fully publicly funded in this plan. The paper shows how a poor country can make coverage choices in the open.
pmc-13311975:
Oghenerukevwe Onororemu and David Anekwe write a 2026 commentary on a multi-site observational study of why vital signs checks get delayed or interrupted on acute wards. The score built from those checks, NEWS2, guides rescue decisions.

Nurses juggle rival demands, and the commented study shows checks often lose out to fixed routine tasks. The commentators suggest scheduling checks outside peak routine windows. They also argue the low time status nurses grant the task should shape how researchers design adherence studies and fixes. Better timing, they say, could lift both completion and the early warning the scores provide.
pmc-13312075:
Eman Rafhi and colleagues describe, in a 2026 Delphi study, the first steps toward a Risk Factor Index flagging older adults likely to suffer medication-related harm. Beliefs and health literacy shape how medicines are used, yet screening tools rarely include them. A multidisciplinary panel of clinicians and researchers answered online rounds, keeping statements that reached at least 80 percent agreement, while open comments underwent thematic analysis.

Thirty-seven experts completed round one and twenty-nine completed round two. Consensus came quickly on seven of fifteen statements, then on every statement in round two. Six risk themes structured the index: age-related functional decline, multiple illnesses with complex regimens, barriers to understanding, money concerns, healthcare interactions, and suboptimal medicine use. The authors present the index as promising but unvalidated, and argue for a person-centred, socially informed approach to medication safety in older adults.
pmc-13312175:
Ge Bai and co-authors report a 2026 modified Delphi study building a core competency framework for infection control link nurses in Chinese general hospitals. These nurses bridge ward teams and the infection control department, yet what the role demands had never been spelled out clearly.

Starting from 18 documents published between 2008 and 2023, the team drafted 141 candidate indicators. A panel of 23 experts then refined the list through two consultation rounds, judging importance and agreement statistically. The final framework holds 5 domains, 19 subdomains, and 75 indicators, with knowledge and skills in infection prevention and control rated most important. The authors offer the framework as a base for competency-based training and fairer assessment of nurses in this role.
pmc-13312275:
Shwikar Othman and colleagues present a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis asking whether behavioural activation for depression still works when trained lay workers, rather than professionals, deliver it. The therapy is proven in specialist hands, and lay delivery could widen access where mental health professionals are scarce.

Searching six databases to January 2025, the team found six randomized trials covering 1,118 people in intervention groups and 1,596 in control groups. Pooled results showed a small but significant drop in depressive symptoms favoring lay-delivered activation. Every trial carried a high risk of bias, though, and results varied widely between studies. The authors conclude the approach looks promising for underserved settings, while warning that the current evidence base is too shaky for firm claims.
pmc-13312575:
Johanna Edvinsson and co-authors test, in a 2026 controlled study, a workplace program meant to protect recovery for office workers on flexible arrangements. Blurred boundaries between work and rest come with flexible schedules, yet few interventions target recovery in such settings, so one unit of a large government organization built the program together with researchers.

Twenty-seven workers took an individual course on work strategies and joined a workshop setting shared rules for flexible work, while 21 colleagues in a similar unit worked as usual. After twelve months, the program group slept on average 36 minutes longer per night, while controls lost 23 minutes, a large effect. Effects on the balance between activity and inactivity across the day, and on heart rate variability during sleep, stayed limited. The authors credit the combined individual and team-level design for the sleep gain.
pmc-13313175:
Abdirashid M. Yousuf and colleagues examine, in a 2026 study, what decides whether a Somali baby receives the BCG tuberculosis vaccine in the first two months of life. National figures put overall childhood BCG coverage at just 37.0 percent, yet coverage in the newborn window specifically had gone unmeasured, so the team reanalyzed the 2020 Somalia Demographic and Health Survey for 457 mother-infant pairs.

Coverage in this age band was far higher, at 79.7 percent in the reported estimate, but the gaps were stark. Babies in nomadic communities had drastically lower odds of vaccination than urban babies, while mothers with primary schooling were far likelier to have vaccinated infants. Skipping antenatal care and facility delivery also predicted missed vaccination. The authors press for maternal education and more contact with health facilities to close the equity gap.
pmc-13313875:
Osamah Muwaffag Aliraqi and Basima Abdulfatah Albadrani measure, in a 2026 cross-sectional study, how often heart rhythm problems explain poor performance in horses. Electrocardiogram findings in racehorses are common but their burden among underperforming animals was unclear. Between September 2023 and August 2024 the authors recorded standard electrocardiograms and blood troponin, a heart injury marker, in 114 poorly performing adult horses, using ten horses without rhythm problems as controls.

Seventy-four horses, or 64.9 percent of the group, had at least one arrhythmia, and atrial fibrillation alone appeared in 60 horses. Conduction problems were frequent too, led by atrioventricular block in 34 horses, with long QT intervals in about half the animals. Troponin ran significantly higher in the arrhythmia cases, and atrial fibrillation clustered in males across nearly all age groups. The authors argue that rhythm screening plus troponin belongs in the standard workup of the underperforming horse, since early diagnosis shapes long-term management.
pmc-13314275:
Kamal Brik, Hassouni Taoufik, and Belghyti Driss survey, in a 2026 study, coenurosis in sheep across Morocco's Kenitra province. The disease is the brain cyst stage of a dog tapeworm, and it kills sheep while showing almost no early signs farmers can catch. The researchers examined 687 animals from farms of both systems. They collected the brains of sheep with neurological signs and tested extracted cysts for fertility and viability, then related infection to sex, age, farming system, and season.

Cysts turned up in 12.37 percent of the animals examined after death, a level the authors call worrying. Prevalence climbed with age and differed by farming system, but showed no link to sex or season. The survey also connected infection to the tapeworm's presence in dogs, completing the cycle. Their prescription: teach farmers the signs, bury or burn infected material, deworm dogs, and keep dog droppings away from feed stores and water points.
pmc-13314575:
Krishan R. Jethwa leads a group of experts in a 2026 letter that argues rectal cancer care should rest on biology more than anatomy. They write in reply to a review that framed locally advanced rectal cancer care around tumor place and surgery-led plans.

Tumor site does shape how hard surgery is and how well the bowel works after, they grant. But they warn that an anatomy-first frame can flatten real choices and mute patient wishes and the biology that drives response. Current proof does not show that chemotherapy then surgery beats total early therapy with organ saving on long-term function, as they argue. Modern care holds several cure-aimed paths, each with its own trade of cancer control, harm, and life quality. Their plea is for response-led, patient-centered picks.
pmc-13315675:

pmc-13316175:

pmc-13316275:

pmc-13316375:

pmc-13316675:

pmc-13317375:

pmc-13317775:

pmc-13317975:

pmc-13318375:

pmc-13319075:

pmc-13319675:

pmc-13320475:

pmc-13321375:

pmc-13322575:

pmc-13322875:

pmc-13322975:

pmc-13324175:

pmc-13324575:

pmc-13324675:

pmc-13325075:

pmc-13325775:

pmc-13326175:

pmc-13327175:

pmc-13328175:

pmc-13330175:

pmc-13331175:

pmc-13332675:

pmc-13336675:

pmc-13336875:

pmc-13337475:

pmc-13337775:

pmc-13337875:

pmc-13338075:

pmc-13338675:

pmc-13340475:

pmc-13341475:

pmc-13418575:
Costabile and Loveys built an interactive computer simulation that teaches life-science students to read a micropipette dial before they ever touch the real instrument in a teaching laboratory. Reading the dial wrong leads students to deliver wrong volumes, which corrupts experiments and undermines confidence, so the simulation isolates that reading skill for safe practice.

Students at two separate universities completed the simulation and were tested before and afterwards on confidence, unit conversion, and dial-reading accuracy. Both groups improved significantly in self-rated confidence and in reading micropipette scales correctly after the practice session. Student feedback was strongly positive about learning the skill and feeling more capable in the laboratory. The authors present the tool as a low-cost preparation step within blended learning, readying students for hands-on bench work.
pmc-13419075:
Boric and colleagues reviewed in 2026 what drives complications after a common breast reduction method in 643 patients. The method, superomedial pedicle reduction, reshapes very large breasts while keeping the nipple on a bridge of tissue with a strong blood supply. Records covered operations from 2004 to 2024 at one surgeon's hospitals.

About 22 in 100 patients had some complication, with roughly 15 in 100 minor and 7 in 100 major. Every obesity class raised the risk of minor problems and slow healing. Heavier patients also faced more infections, while the amount of tissue removed did not predict most problems. Smoking predicted major problems and repeat operations, and high blood pressure predicted readmission. The authors conclude that patient health factors, not resection size, drive most risk after this surgery.
pmc-13419175:
Jalene and colleagues report a 2026 survey study of recovery after a mass casualty event, a campus shooting, at a minority-serving university in the United States. Four to five months after the event, students, faculty, and staff answered an anonymous survey. They rated depression and anxiety before the event and at survey time, plus belonging and fitness.

Respondents reported clear rises in both depression and anxiety scores from before the event to the survey. The team examined how a sense of belonging on campus, estimated heart and lung fitness, and preferred forms of help related to those changes. The survey also asked which supports people would actually use to cope. Pairing harm with belonging and fitness points planners to factors that may soften trauma.
pmc-13419275:
Ju and colleagues tested a rapid magnetic resonance method that follows creatine and phosphocreatine, two molecules that shuttle energy inside muscle, while volunteers exercised inside a 3 Tesla scanner. Their ultrafast CEST approach, which detects molecules indirectly through water signal changes, aimed to capture second-by-second energy shifts without invasive sampling.

Five healthy volunteers performed calf raises inside the magnet while the team recorded images every 7.6 seconds during exercise and recovery. Phosphocreatine signals dropped by about 77 percent during exercise while creatine signals climbed roughly 469 percent above resting levels. After exercise stopped, phosphocreatine refilled with a recovery time near 73 seconds, closely matching creatine's decay of about 62 seconds on average. The authors say the method could support noninvasive checks of mitochondrial function, the cell's energy-producing machinery.
pmc-13419975:
Trwska A. Amin and colleagues report two patients who carried both beta-thalassemia major and inflammatory bowel disease, a rare and easily missed pairing. The blood disorder causes severe anemia, while bowel inflammation adds belly pain, bleeding, and fatigue that can hide inside the blood picture. Such overlap can delay the bowel diagnosis for years.

One patient's blood work showed hemoglobin down to 50 grams per liter with inflammation markers far above normal in the reported values. Stool checks and further workup separated infection from chronic bowel disease. The authors scan the thin prior literature beside their two cases. Their message is plain: lasting gut symptoms in thalassemia deserve a bowel workup even when anemia seems to explain them.
pmc-13420275:
Wu and colleagues report a 2026 study of kidney damage in diabetes, focused on a small gene-switching RNA and ferroptosis, a cell-death path in which iron drives fat damage in membranes. The team worked with diabetic mice and mouse kidney tube cells grown in high sugar. They traced a chain: the RNA miR-145-5p acts on guard gene NRF2, which controls SLC7A11, a ferroptosis-shield gene.

The small RNA ran high in the kidneys of diabetic mice. Blocking it cut ferroptosis, scarring, and harmful cell change, and improved kidney measures. Blocking NRF2 or adding a drug that forces ferroptosis undid part of that gain, which supports the proposed chain. Lab tests confirmed the RNA binds NRF2 directly and that NRF2 switches on SLC7A11. The chain offers drug targets for a leading cause of kidney failure.
pmc-13421475:
Salem and colleagues tested in 2026 whether treating barley seeds with helpful microbes before sprouting boosts its health effects. The method, called biopriming, inoculates seeds with microbes that enrich the grain as it germinates. The team compared plain germinated barley extract with versions primed by Bacillus subtilis or Aspergillus niger.

The Bacillus-primed barley showed the strongest profile, richer in phenolic acids and B vitamins, notably B2, B9, and B12. Rats on this extract moved more normally and remembered locations better than untreated MSG rats. Brain chemical balance moved back toward normal, and markers of oxidative stress and brain inflammation fell. Survival pathways tied to cell cleanup, called autophagy, were also switched on. The authors identify Bacillus priming as a promising, sustainable way to make barley a stronger functional food.
pmc-13422275:
Liudmyla Krupelnytska leads an eight-author team asking, in a 2026 study, why many Ukrainian women chose to give birth at home in a war zone rather than flee. Russia's full-scale invasion shattered maternity care, and the decisions of those who stayed — framed in the title as bravery — had not been systematically explained.

Online data came from 730 women pregnant or newly delivered during the invasion's first two years. Decision-tree and random-forest models found circumstance dominating: how disrupted daily life felt, and how close the fighting was, predicted relocation best. Personality traits, including the Big Five, did not separate stayers from leavers overall, though extraversion played a minor secondary role. The authors stress situation over disposition.
pmc-13423075:
Matanda and co-authors measure how community talks shift norms around female genital mutilation in this 2026 survey study from Narok County, Kenya, where expectations about marriage keep cutting entrenched. They surveyed 2,658 adults in 2024. The survey set people who had joined mixed-sex community dialogues against those who had not. It also traced the pathways between beliefs and behavior.

People who took part held more progressive positions. Adjusted odds of endorsing pro-cutting beliefs were 0.61 against those who stayed out. Intentions to cut a daughter came in at 0.49 in the same models. Odds of outright opposing the practice reached 2.39 in the adjusted models. Couples-only dialogues showed weaker, less consistent links. Mediation analysis attributed 88 percent of the dialogue effect on opposition to shifts in beliefs and intentions. Intentions were the strongest single bridge. The authors back dialogue-centered elimination strategies.
pmc-13424275:
Salvatore Nesci argues that adolescent depression should be read as an energy crisis in the brain's dopamine system, not simply adult depression arriving early. Adolescence rewires reward circuits while motivation and priorities are being reset, and the nucleus accumbens, the hub that turns dopamine signals into effort and anticipation, sits at the centre of that change.

Loss of pleasure, a core and treatment-resistant feature in young patients, tracks with faulty signalling in this hub. Nesci's proposal ties that failure to mitochondria, the cell's power plants, arguing their performance governs how strongly dopamine neurons can signal. The piece builds an integrative model meant to explain stubborn reward failure and to point treatment research toward bioenergetics.
pmc-13424775:
Naoto Aoyama leads a sixteen-author prospective study of a stubborn step in endoscopic bile drainage: pushing the stent delivery tube through a freshly made tract between stomach and liver ducts. Failure often forces extra dilation, adding time and cost, and the team suspected the angle between guidewire and duct decides success.

Twenty-five patients received a new double-lumen dilator; twenty-five matched historical patients had standard dilation. Delivery succeeded without extra dilation in 92% of the new group against 48% of controls. The wire-to-duct angle just before insertion averaged 153.4 degrees with the new tool against 123.3 degrees conventionally. Wider angles predicted success in adjusted analysis, supporting an angle-first explanation over brute mechanical advantage.
pmc-13424875:
Malmberg, Kawalerowicz, and Andersson explore in 2026 how the sorting of whole life courses across places feeds political polarization in Sweden. A life course here means the chain of positions a person holds over time in school, work, family, and housing.

Tracking such trajectories geographically, the authors show that places come to hold sharply contrasting mixes of life experience. They show that the resulting divides are written into the landscape itself. Segregation between trajectory types grows with age: young adults are far less sorted than older adults, and the move into homeownership is a major driver of the split. Studies that measure sorting with single markers like income or education understate its strength. The concentration of particular life courses in particular places also lines up with the geography of political polarization.
pmc-13425575:
M. S. Anagha and colleagues set out a 2026 systematic review protocol on measurement instruments built for Ayurveda research. Ayurvedic diagnosis uses qualitative concepts that newer questionnaires and clinical tools try to quantify, yet many tools show inconsistent methods and weak validation. The planned review will identify, map, and characterize instruments developed or adapted for Ayurvedic constructs.

Beyond cataloguing tools, the reviewers will document problems met during development and validation and propose directions for stronger instruments. Researchers gain a route toward measures that clinicians and journals can trust for trials of traditional concepts. Good tools of this kind would let staff check the same signs in the same way at each visit and in each new trial. The list will name each tool, who made it, and how well it was checked at the time it first came out for use in wards.
pmc-13427575:
Piyush Baindara and co-authors introduce, in 2026, a new compound that kills the fungus Candida albicans, a common cause of serious infections. They call the compound cardio-green butyl acetate, shortened to CaGA. It was made in the lab and had not been tested as an antifungal before. Resistant Candida strains and slimy biofilm growth make new options badly needed.

CaGA killed free-growing fungus cells and cut down biofilms, the dense films fungi form on surfaces. Tests showed it punched holes in the fungal membrane by latching onto ergosterol, the main fat that stiffens that membrane. Computer models of the membrane backed up the lab picture. Work so far is in dishes and models, yet the distinct attack route makes CaGA worth further study.
pmc-13428075:
Zaizen and colleagues published a 2026 case report on scarring lung disease in a rare illness. Their patient had autoimmune pulmonary alveolar proteinosis for 15 years. In that illness, lung air sacs fill with fatty protein the body cannot clear. Over time, his lungs also began to scar, a newer concern in this illness.

Scans before referral showed slow scar growth rather than a return of the filling illness. His breathing capacity slipped over six months of watching, so treatment began. He started nintedanib, a drug that slows lung scarring in other diseases. His breathing capacity then held steady for two years of follow-up. Telling scar growth apart from illness return guided the whole plan.
pmc-13429275:
Murayama and Hoshi trial a knee extension aid for walking training after stroke with one sided weakness. Slow walkers often land on the forefoot because the swinging leg lacks momentum to straighten the knee. That pattern trains the ankle into bad habits. Their 2026 trial assigns thirty inpatients at five Japanese rehab wards to gait training for two weeks. One group uses an ankle foot brace alone. The other adds the knee aid to that brace.

The aid group straightened the knee by four degrees more at the end of the swing phase. The control pattern did not show that shift. A straighter knee at contact favors a heel first landing, which the authors link to calmer muscle overactivity during weight acceptance. The device is simple and worn only in training. Brief mechanical help, the result hints, can retrain a key joint timing without complex robotics.
pmc-13429875:
Alson and colleagues follow pregnancy outcomes after fertility treatment in women with endometriosis or adenomyosis. Their 2026 prospective cohort study enrolled 1,035 women undergoing IVF or ICSI at a university hospital, with diagnoses made by ultrasound using international consensus definitions. Outcomes were known for 607 women who gave birth.

Compared with women without either condition, those affected faced higher risks on several fronts. Preterm birth was more common, as were hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, placenta previa, bleeding before delivery, and pelvic pain. Earlier evidence on these questions had been inconsistent, largely because studies defined the diseases differently. By applying standardised ultrasound criteria within one treated population, the authors give clinicians a firmer basis for planning antenatal care in this group.
pmc-13430175:
Muhammad Sanusi and a large team describe, in a 2026 case report, a dangerous heart rhythm as the first sign of probable cardiac sarcoidosis. The disease inflames organs with clusters of immune cells, and in the heart it can scar the electrical system. Their patient was a 69-year-old man who arrived with palpitations, dizziness, and breathlessness after a therapy session. Monitors caught repeated runs of ventricular tachycardia, a fast rhythm from the heart's lower chambers, topping 200 beats per minute.

A standard drug steadied the rhythm. Scans of his heart arteries showed only minor disease, ruling out the usual cause. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed scar in a pattern typical of sarcoidosis rather than a heart attack. He received an implanted defibrillator to guard against recurrence and went home stable. Biopsy was skipped because heart sampling often misses this patchy disease, a practice guidelines now support.
pmc-13430275:
Sezgin and colleagues validate an informant questionnaire for spotting cognitive decline after stroke. The IQCODE asks a spouse or caregiver how the patient's thinking compares with years before, which suits patients who cannot test well themselves. Their 2026 study gives the brief version by phone to informants of 179 stroke patients. Calls come within a week of a standard clinic test. The team checks reliability, structure, and how well scores sort impaired from unimpaired patients.

The scale proved consistent, and factor analysis found a four part structure that fit the data after three weak items were dropped. The sixteen item version sorted patients with fair accuracy. A trimmed thirteen item version kept the same sensitivity while raising specificity, meaning fewer false alarms. An informant can answer by phone in minutes, so the authors recommend the tool for remote screening after stroke, with full testing to follow a positive screen.
pmc-13430975:
Lv and colleagues trace how chronic smoking harms the adolescent brain in this 2026 mouse study. Smoking is a major dementia risk factor, especially when started young, and the brain's glymphatic system, a waste-clearance network, is suspected to be involved. The team exposed adolescent mice to chronic smoke and measured glymphatic transport with microscopy, alongside heart function, tau protein buildup, and performance in maze and object-recognition tests.

The longer the exposure, the worse glymphatic transport became, and phosphorylated tau accumulated in the hippocampus's dentate gyrus while new synapses and new neurons there dwindled. Cognition declined in step with these changes across the exposure period. The authors link the clearance failure to three cooperating problems. The heart ejected more weakly. Arterial pulsatility, the pulse that drives fluid flow, was reduced. And the aquaporin-4 water channel around blood vessels was lost.
pmc-13433375:
Sutherland and team costed out BEST in CLASS-Elementary. It is a Tier 2 program that trains and coaches elementary teachers to support individual students with problem behavior. They used the ingredients method, which prices every input. Data came from kindergarten through third-grade classrooms in a multisite randomized trial. The trial spanned 136 teacher-student pairs and 63 teachers.

The average cost came to 2,866 dollars per teacher-student pair in a classroom receiving the program. That figure includes teacher recruitment. Adding one more focal student to an already treated classroom cost only 101 dollars at the margin. Even two additions stayed cheap relative to starting fresh. The intervention itself accounted for less than half of total spending across the implementation sites studied. Coaches consumed the largest share, almost half of all costs. The model rests on ongoing one-to-one coaching rather than one-off workshops for teachers.
pmc-13435575:
Esra D Kahvecioglu's team linked blood sugar control to inflammation ratios in 2026 in people with type 2 diabetes. Rates of the disease keep rising, and its complications burden patients and health systems, yet cheap blood markers that track control and inflammation together are still useful. The team compared 138 patients, split by HbA1c above or below seven percent, against 118 healthy controls, using baseline and follow-up blood counts.

Uncontrolled patients showed higher white cells, neutrophils, monocytes, and neutrophil and monocyte ratios, and several markers shifted by the third month in that group. The pattern supports these ratios as simple, low-cost companions to HbA1c in monitoring inflammation. Clinicians get a retrospective case-control signal, not proof that changing the ratios changes outcomes.
pmc-13437275:
Kübra Özkaya Toraman and colleagues measured how dental implants distort radiation dose during head and neck cancer treatment. Their 2026 lab study set three implant kinds into fake jawbone models: titanium, zirconia, and a custom frame that sits on the bone surface. Sensors at four spots around each implant recorded real dose, which the team compared with the planned dose.

Measured and planned doses differed clearly, with a median gap near eight percent below plan. Dose rose slightly on the cheek side from backscatter, while the tongue and front sides lost dose, falling as much as about fourteen percent short. Zirconia showed the widest mismatch, and planning software predicted hot spots above some implants. The custom surface frame behaved most predictably of the three. The authors stress that the work was done in models, not patients, so larger studies with real outcomes must test whether these gaps change care.
pmc-13437475:
Guido Kobbe and co-authors chart how a drug class became the backbone of care when blood cancers return after a donor stem cell transplant. Relapse of myelodysplastic syndrome or acute myeloid leukemia is the top cause of transplant failure. Over twenty years, hypomethylating agents moved from experiment to standard first move. Their 2026 review gathers the findings behind that shift.

Trials named RELAZA showed starting azacytidine at the first molecular whisper of relapse can delay full return of disease. Lasting control usually needs the donor immune system too, so infusions of donor lymphocytes often join the drug. Patients fare best when treatment starts at low disease levels, when relapse is molecular rather than visible, and when more time has passed since transplant. Newer pairings with targeted drugs against FLT3 or IDH changes show early promise. The authors look toward personal, biology-guided plans, with second transplants reserved for chosen cases.
pmc-13437675:
Li Du and colleagues compared the mental health of Chinese teenagers learning online at home against peers back in school during the pandemic. Their 2026 survey covered 5,787 students in grades seven through twelve at fourteen Gansu schools across 2020 and 2021. Standard questionnaires measured mood, distress, and sleep. Scores were set against national norms and sorted by learning mode, sex, and stage.

Students showed more distress than national yardsticks on several fronts, and nearly a quarter carried moderate to severe depressive symptoms. Surprisingly, in-school students reported worse distress and depression than online learners at home. Sleep told a consistent story: teens who felt their sleep poor, took long to fall asleep, or slept fewer hours all fared worse mentally. Because the survey caught one moment, learning mode cannot be said to have caused the gaps. They suggest sleep coaching and calmer school climates as supports worth building either way.
pmc-13437875:
Hao Zhang and co-authors gathered the family of MYB switches helping plants survive cold. MYB proteins are transcription factors, gene controllers switching whole programs on and off as temperatures fall. Their 2026 review curated 106 cold-linked MYBs proven in experiments, drawn from forty-five plant species, and set them inside their family tree.

One large subfamily supplies most known cold switches, while two smaller branches remain unexplored. Related switches in different species sometimes keep the same job, sometimes drift into new ones. The pathways they run span hormone response, the classic cold-response cascade, protective compounds, leaf wax, and even chemical marks on DNA packaging. The authors map what to chase next: the neglected branches, cross-species checks guided by the family tree, and tests under mixed stresses, since fields rarely send cold alone. Breeders hunting hardier crops get a chart of proven levers.
pmc-13438675:
Jerzy Twarowski and colleagues caught meiosis mutating its own DNA across long stretches. Meiosis, the division that makes eggs and sperm, deliberately breaks DNA to shuffle genes, and the single-stranded DNA exposed in repair was suspected of soaking up errors. Their 2026 yeast study planted a human enzyme attacking single-stranded DNA and leaving a readable scar, letting the team map where such DNA appears.

The scars clustered thickly, up to 134 mutations spanning more than twenty-five thousand letters in one tract. Making the clusters required the programmed breaks that start meiotic shuffling. Two repair behaviors explained the long strands: break-induced replication, and extra-long chewing back of broken ends. Gene promoters and transfer RNA genes also collected single strands, adding quiet hot spots. The results recast meiosis as high-risk, high-reward: the machinery creating diversity also writes clusters of fresh mutations, some the seeds of inherited disease.
pmc-13439175:
Nayem Haque, Ronald Cutler, Simone Sidoli, and Robert A Coleman film single gene-copying machines inside living human cells, reporting in 2026 how they pause and restart. RNA polymerase II copies DNA into RNA, yet it often stalls soon after starting, and that stall gates how much gene product gets made. Live-cell single-molecule imaging let the team time how long each machine stayed bound to chromatin, the DNA and protein mix in the nucleus.

Most binding events ended within tens of seconds, with only a small share reaching full productive copying. Cells differed widely in that share. Removing the TFIID part TAF1, a scaffold protein, cut clustering and raised pausing across genes. The work supports a role for TAF1 in releasing paused machines into active copying.
pmc-13439275:
Chang Seok Bang and Eun Jeong Gong weigh two routes for feeding tubes that reach the small bowel, in a 2026 commentary. Some patients cannot be fed into the stomach, due to a still stomach, a blockage, or high risk of food entering the lungs. Parkinson's patients on gel medicine also need steady delivery into the jejunum. Two scope-based routes exist: a tube threaded through a stomach opening, or a tube placed straight through the jejunal wall.

The through-stomach route is simpler to place, yet its thin extension slips or clogs often and sends patients back for repeat scopes. The direct route is harder to perform but holds up far longer once placed. The writers argue that the kinder choice is the one that lasts, sparing frail patients repeated procedures. Skill at the centre should shape which route is offered.
pmc-13440675:
Calderón-Garcidueñas and colleagues document brain-disease proteins in young Mexico City residents exposed to heavy air pollution. Their 2026 forensic autopsy study examined 189 brains, average age 26, mostly from the metropolitan area where fine particle pollution is high, plus ten low-pollution controls. Using targeted staining, they measured Alzheimer-type change, the Parkinson protein alpha-synuclein, and TDP-43, a third disease-linked protein.

Overlaps were common even in children. Among 37 children averaging 13 years, about a quarter showed Alzheimer-type change alone, and most of the rest carried two or three protein pathologies combined. Adults aged 18 to 40 showed similar stacking, with half carrying Alzheimer change plus alpha-synuclein. The authors propose routine measurement of these abnormal proteins in young urban autopsies to size the problem and guide prevention and pollution control.
pmc-13441375:
Perrykkad and colleagues tracked sense of coherence in 680 Australian women. Sense of coherence is a person's feeling that life makes sense and can be handled. The women were tracked four times across pregnancy and the postpartum year. Earlier work tied higher coherence to less pregnancy distress and better births. But how the trait moves through the period around birth was unknown.

A growth mixture model split the women into four paths. A high group held steady at 67 percent of women, and a low group sat at 21 percent. A rising group made up 8 percent, and a falling group 3 percent. An early-pregnancy depression label pointed most to landing in the low and rising paths. Childhood trauma history pointed to the low and falling paths. Trauma survivors were most likely to end the postpartum year with drained coping reserves. The authors urge support around birth to protect those reserves.
pmc-13441775:
Tim Salomonsson and colleagues test a specialised MRI method for predicting a gene switch that governs brain tumour drug response, reporting in 2026. Methylation of the MGMT promoter shapes how high-grade gliomas answer chemotherapy, yet measuring it needs tissue. Chemical exchange saturation transfer imaging reads protein-related signals without a biopsy. Forty-four patients with grade four gliomas or glioblastoma had such scans before surgery, with tumours outlined by hand and by two machine learning segmenters.

Unmethylated tumours showed higher signal peaks in dead tumour core across every outlining method. Machine-drawn outlines added further separations in living tumour rim. Patterns held within the glioblastoma-only group as well. The authors read the consistency across segmenters as encouraging for automated pipelines. Fluid-suppressed versions of the signals are presented as candidate non-invasive markers of methylation status, pending larger validation.
pmc-13442875:
Zahra Ghoreyshi and colleagues build a physics-led model that predicts what a T cell will target in a 2026 paper. T cells read short bits shown on cell surfaces, and guessing their targets from receptor codes alone is error-prone. Their frame joins receptor text with shape data for receptor-target pairs, drawn from past work and from computer builds.

Tests used stem cell transplant samples and a set of HLA-A*02 shown bits from flu, a herpes virus, and a melanoma mark. Forecasts for fresh receptors from donors and patients hit the mark, and gains grew when like receptors were grouped first. Shape-led learning stayed strong even with thin training sets. The authors offer the frame for cell therapy design, shot work, and immune watch in clinic samples.
pmc-13443175:
Nurzhan Abishev and colleagues report surgery for weak-bone spine breaks in two patients in a 2026 paper. Bone loss makes spine screws grip poorly, so firm fixation is a known hard step. Both patients had pathologic breaks that pressed the spinal canal.

Care used cemented hollow screws plus a cage that fuses the spine from the front path. Pain scores fell from 7.3 points before surgery to a mark of 1.2 points right after, and to 0.5 points by two years. A function index fell from 69 percent to 20 percent across the same span. Curve angle eased from 38.0 degrees to a value of 29.0 degrees after surgery. No bone loss ringed the screws at checks. The authors share the tweak as a workable path for frail spines.
pmc-13443675:
Ecem Kara tested how five heavy metals affect seed sprouting and early growth in two onion types, Gence and Karbeyazı, grown in lab dishes. The 2026 study used controlled doses to screen which metals harm young plants most.

Seeds grew on a standard plant medium with copper, cadmium, lead, nickel, or cobalt at four dose levels. Kara tracked sprouting rates, root and shoot length, and plant weight at each dose. Higher doses mostly cut sprouting, root growth, and weight gain. Copper and cadmium pulled sprouting rates down by more than twenty points. Nickel behaved oddly, lifting final sprouting at low doses while weakening early vigour. Gence kept higher final sprouting, while Karbeyazı held on to root traits better, so final sprouting alone misses much of the harm.
pmc-13444075:
Samuel Benedict and colleagues show mycobacteria firing a wall-cutting toxin at rival kin in a 2026 study. These germs were thought to shun toxin duels, since their thick waxy walls look like full armor. Their type VII secretion system, a needle-like exporter, ships an enzyme that cleaves the arabinogalactan layer of rival walls.

Structure and chemistry work maps how the cutter grips and snips its target layer. A shield protein family guards the shooter from its own toxin. Genes for like toxins dot the wider mycobacterial order, which hints at widespread duels. The authors reframe these germs as active rivals, not lone dwellers. Wall layers once read as pure defense now double as the duel's weak point.
pmc-13445675:
Zhaoyan Meng and colleagues examine a 2026 two-study investigation of whether being ignored for a phone, called phubbing, drives people to watch for digital cues during face-to-face talk. A survey of 845 people tested the link, and an experiment with 220 people staged phubbing during conversation and recorded phone checking during a wait.

Being phubbed linked to online vigilance in the survey, and the experiment showed phubbing raised vigilance mainly among people with moderate to high intolerance of uncertainty. High-uncertainty participants checked digital information more often after being phubbed. The work ties a common relational slight to later screen attention, with uncertainty as the amplifier.
pmc-13445775:
Khonakdar and colleagues scoped the evidence on AI for checking suspected acute coronary syndrome before hospital arrival. In the field, care teams carry limited tests and doubt runs high. Using scoping review rules, they searched four databases to May 2026. They mapped diagnosis, prediction, and triage uses.

19 studies covering 319,709 patients met the bar for the final evidence map. Electrocardiogram-based deep learning and multimodal models performed best. Discrimination values ran from about 0.81 at the low end to 0.99 at the high end, with sensitivity of 73 to 94 percent and specificity spanning 56 to 99 percent across studies. Risk prediction models were more variable, ranging roughly from 0.71 at the bottom to 0.95 at the top for discrimination. New uses covered flagging cardiogenic shock and the need for revascularization. The authors call for future multi-site checks before routine rollout.
pmc-13447275:
Jaiteg Singh and fellow editors introduce a 2026 collection on machine learning for cognitive ageing and behaviour change. Ageing affects memory, attention and self-control unevenly across people, and dementia now burdens families and health systems worldwide. Standard tests and clinic visits often miss that variety, while learning algorithms can sift imaging, body signals and digital records at scale.

Contributions gathered here span early warning signs of mild impairment, personalised support and risk prediction in older groups. One line of work uses skin features around the eye as a non-invasive marker of biological ageing, analysed with learning models. Other papers tackle behaviour patterns and health outcomes from mixed data sources. The editors stress that models must stay interpretable, fair and valid beyond their training data to earn clinical trust.
pmc-13447575:
Rui-Feng Zhang and colleagues study antibody-making plasma cells inside bowel cancer in 2026 work on immunotherapy response. Checkpoint drugs free the immune system to attack cancer, yet many bowel cancer patients never respond. Most research focuses on T cells, while B-lineage plasma cells inside tumours have gained attention as possible helpers or blockers depending on their state.

One plasma cell group, marked by a specific antibody type, gathered in tumours of patients who responded to checkpoint treatment. Those cells ran programmes for showing tumour material to other immune cells and for a central inflammatory switch. Activity of that switch in B cells boosted T cell killing power and restrained tumour growth in the authors' tests. The subset is offered as both a response marker and a lever for improving therapy.
pmc-13448175:
Yuheng Zhu and colleagues report a 2026 mechanism by which the OAS1-FASN axis drives pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma through lipid stress and the unfolded protein response. OAS1 runs high in pancreatic tumors and tracks poor prognosis, and the team traced its binding to fatty acid synthase and downstream stress signaling.

OAS1 preserved FASN protein levels, fueling lipid synthesis and droplet buildup that triggered adaptive ER stress through the PERK-ATF4 axis. The coordinated lipid overload and pro-survival stress response promoted proliferation and metastasis. OAS1 emerges as both a biomarker and a metabolic target in this aggressive cancer.
pmc-13448275:
Gecici and colleagues at the University of Pittsburgh Medical Center studied which clinical and genetic features predict survival after surgery for cancer spread to the brain. Their 2026 conference report covers 228 patients whose tumors were removed, most often cancers that began in the lung, breast, urinary tract, gut, or skin. Survival after such surgery varies widely, and genetic predictors remain poorly understood.

Gecici profiled tumor genes in about three fifths of the patients and ranked predictors using forest models and survival analysis. TP53 gene changes were most common, followed by KRAS changes and losses near CDKN2A and CDKN2B. Patients in good physical condition before surgery lived far longer than frail patients, with median survival more than three times as long. Extra KRAS copies and poor condition predicted worse survival, while systemic drug treatment after surgery strongly predicted longer life, supporting combined genetic and clinical risk scoring.
pmc-13448475:
Zhang and colleagues built in 2026 a nano-delivery system to rescue immune therapy for tumors choked by lactate, the acid waste that builds up in cancer tissue and suppresses immunity. Response rates to PD-L1 blocking drugs sit low, at one to three in ten patients. Their micelles, carrier spheres made with hyaluronic acid, haul a lactate-eating enzyme plus copper-doped carbon dots into tumors displaying the CD44 docking protein.

Zhang shows the cargo releases in the acidic tumor setting. The enzyme clears lactate and produces peroxide that feeds copper-driven reactions, triggering cuproptosis, a copper-linked form of cell death. In dishes, the system matured dendritic cells and flipped suppressive macrophages toward an attacking type. In mice, adding the carriers to laser treatment and the immune drug shrank treated and distant tumors while staying safe. MSFRTransMorph extends TransMorph with multi-scale feature tuning, guided by brainstem marking during training without tumour labels.

Better overlap came with more local warping folds, trading shape evenness for sharpness. Balancing matching fit against warping realism is the next design goal for tuned beam care.
pmc-13471575:
Baptiste Thibault and colleagues studied ionised hypocalcaemia in 2026 before continuous renal replacement therapy with regional citrate anticoagulation. Citrate anticoagulation is first-line therapy, yet no international guidance governs pre-treatment ionised calcium measurement, and consequences of pre-existing low calcium were unmapped. A retrospective single-centre study covered 200 patients treated from June 2021 to April 2023.

Only 117 patients, 59%, had ionised calcium measured before therapy; among them 60% were normal, 19% had corrected hypocalcaemia, and 21% had uncorrected ionised hypocalcaemia. Mean calcium normalised within 12 hours of therapy start, and half reached target range within 72 hours. Pre-treatment measurement is thus inconsistent, but early therapy largely restores calcium even without prior correction.
pmc-13471875:
Aiswarya Puzhakkara Chennas and colleagues use genetics in 2026 to ask whether blood pressure drugs change the risk of gum disease and tooth decay. Direct trials would be slow and confounded, so the team used inherited variants near each drug target gene as stand ins for lifelong drug action. Twelve antihypertensive classes were instrumented this way, drawing on huge blood pressure genome studies.

One signal survived correction for many tests: genetic mimicry of diazoxide, acting through a potassium channel gene, raised the odds of chronic gum disease slightly per unit of lowered pressure. The link held after removing variants tied to diabetes, a possible side path. No other drug class showed an association with gum disease, and none with tooth decay. Checks for shared causal variants accompanied the main analysis.
pmc-13471975:
Gordon Jewett, Reed Ferber, Colin B Josephson, Lawrence Korngut, and Joon Lee compare in 2026 step counts from a consumer smartwatch against a research grade accelerometer in people with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. Objective function measures that scale beyond the clinic are scarce in this disease. Forty participants wore a Fitbit on one wrist long term and a research device on the other during clinic aligned windows, yielding thousands of monitoring days.

On five hundred three days when both devices had solid wear, their counts correlated strongly. The smartwatch still read lower on average, by close to six hundred steps a day, with wide agreement limits for individuals. Among those with six months of overlap, both devices charted similar decline over time. The authors call long term smartwatch monitoring feasible, if imperfect, for tracking this population.
pmc-13473075:
Massalha and co-authors built a bedside tool estimating whether a woman carrying a growth-restricted baby can deliver vaginally, sparing an unneeded caesarean. Their 2026 model came from 477 single-baby pregnancies with late-onset fetal growth restriction managed at one large center from 2017 to 2024, all attempting labor with no prior caesarean.

Most succeeded: 378 women, or 79.2% of the cohort, delivered vaginally despite intrapartum caesarean rates of 20 to 40% typical for this condition. Four factors lowered the odds on their own, led by first-time motherhood at an odds ratio of 0.22 against women who had given birth before, plus higher pre-pregnancy body mass index, an abnormal cerebroplacental ratio, and pre-existing diabetes. Decision-curve analysis showed the model helps once predicted chances pass a 55% threshold.
pmc-13473375:
Yin and colleagues report a 2026 study of awake prone positioning, lying face down while breathing on one's own, in severe lung inflammation caused by cancer immunotherapy drugs.  The team reviewed 120 matched patients with severe disease and breathing failure at one center, comparing those who spent at least ten hours prone with those who did not.

After one week, the prone group held clearly better blood oxygen levels than the control group. Far fewer prone patients needed a breathing tube: about eighteen percent against forty-five percent. Their intensive care stays ran about four days shorter, and fewer had died by day twenty-eight, about eighteen percent against thirty-five percent.
