Prone positioning is free and low-tech, though only a randomized trial can confirm the benefit.
pmc-13473575:
Anthony Lavertu and two colleagues introduced in 2026 a benchmark for models that predict antimicrobial peptide activity. Antimicrobial peptides offer an alternative to standard antibiotics, but progress has been hard to measure because datasets and test rules differ from study to study. That gap lets models look better than they are. The new benchmark, called QMAP, predicts two properties: potency against microbes (minimum inhibitory concentration), and toxicity to red blood cells (HC50).

QMAP enforces strict homology limits between training and test sets, so performance reflects genuine learning on new peptide families rather than memory of near-duplicates. Re-testing existing potency models under these rules suggested limited progress in six years, weak performance for highly potent peptides, and poor prediction of haemolytic activity. The team released a Python package with a fast Rust engine to ease adoption. For drug discovery, the message is sobering: standardised testing must come first.
pmc-13474575:
Anneliese Ceisel and a large team clarify how a cell-killing switch works in 2026 for building disease models on demand. The switch pairs an enzyme with a drug that turns it toxic, letting researchers kill chosen cells at a chosen time. Past reports disagreed on which death path the switch triggers. The team tested it in zebrafish eye cells and in human stem-cell-grown retina tissue.

One death path, called parthanatos, showed up in every setting tested. A second path, apoptosis, appeared in some settings but not others. A new enzyme variant worked well in the human tissue model. Since parthanatos also acts in real nerve diseases, the switch suits models of those diseases.
pmc-13474775:
Hatice Sağlam and Hakan Arslan tested in 2026 whether anxiety before root canal treatment predicts pain afterwards in sore lower molar teeth. They asked 132 patients to rate dental anxiety before treatment, then to record daily pain for seven days on a visual scale.

Pain differed between anxiety groups over the first three days, with the clearest gap between moderate and high anxiety groups. Sex mattered only on day 3, while painkiller use also differed across groups. After adjusting for confounders, anxiety still tracked postoperative pain. The authors suggest screening anxiety and easing it could reduce pain after treatment.
pmc-13474875:
Dan Fang and eight colleagues investigated in 2026 whether a pain receptor in the brain's fear centre links orthodontic tooth movement to pain and anxiety in mice. They applied forces of 0, 10, 30, and 50 centinewtons plus a blank group to 25 mice, tracking face rubbing, touch sensitivity, and anxiety behaviours.

The strongest force produced the most face rubbing and lowest touch thresholds on day one, and the 30 and 50 groups showed more anxiety by day 28. TRPV1 levels in the central amygdala rose with force, peaking on days 1 and 28 in the 30 group. The findings give early evidence that this receptor helps drive both orthodontic pain and its emotional fallout.
pmc-13474975:
Zainab Hanjra and co-authors compare a stress gene family across seven plant genomes in 2026. The family, called WRKY, helps plants answer drought, salt, and attack. Counts ran from fifty-one genes in African rice to one hundred twenty-six in Asian rice. Family trees split the genes into three broad groups.

One group made up about seventy percent of cereal genes but only a quarter in the model weed. Extra copies arose mainly by side-by-side duplication in cereals. Selection kept most copies on a tight leash across history. Knowing which copies expanded helps breeders target stress toughness.
pmc-13476875:
Wusiman Maihemuti and co-authors train lab-grown heart tissue in 2026 with pulses of water pressure to speed its maturation. Stem-cell heart tissue stays immature, which limits repair use. Tissue built from heart and vessel cells plus matrix got one hour of pressure daily for three days after two weeks of growth. Single-cell reading and function tests judged maturity.

Pressure-trained tissue showed aligned muscle cells, richer energy parts, and stronger contraction and calcium flow. Vessel cells proved required, since tissue without them failed to mature. Pressure plus flow also grew vessel networks inside the tissue. Grafts of trained tissue lifted heart pump scores in rats after heart attack.
pmc-13477975:
Luca Loiodice and four colleagues built in 2026 a fast graph-network tool to judge which pores threaten fatigue life in 3D-printed nickel alloy parts. Full crystal plasticity simulation captures grain-level fatigue but takes months, so they trained surrogate models on such data to predict grain stresses and damage energy.

The models predicted grain-average and grain-maximum stress and accumulated plastic strain energy, a damage marker tied to crack starts, though accuracy fell for extreme plastic cases. Predicted peak damage energy flagged whether fatigue hotspots sat beside pores. The tool enables rapid screening of fatigue-critical pores in printed components.
pmc-13478375:
Aumueller and colleagues in Germany tested in 2026 a robot workflow for planting tiny radio seeds in the prostate under MRI watch. Seed therapy is a set cure for low risk prostate cancer, but seed spots must be exact to spare the gut and bladder. Their robot arm was first built for MRI led needle biopsies. The team rewrote its steps for seed work and ran the full chain on a life like pelvis dummy.

The robot's aim was sharp: seeds sat less than a hair's width off the guide path on most runs. The full gap from plan to dropped seed was a few millimeters, with the drop step itself the chief source of drift. Dose cover of the target fell from full to a still strong level after two needles. Seed spotting by MRI alone lagged CT checks, a gap the team wants to close.
pmc-13479475:
Yoshioka, Fujita, and Ochiya mapped in 2026 what blocks tiny cell bubbles, called extracellular vesicles, from wide clinic use. The bubbles ferry signals in blood and show rich promise for tests and cures. Yet few goods have cleared review, and rogue clinics sell unproven bubble shots. The authors sort the blocks into six knots: what the goods are, how pure, how strong, how checks match, how they are made, and how safe.

World rules from the field's main society, worn as the MISEV guide, set shared terms and lab habits. Gaps stay where loose guide words must turn into hard specs for a review file. Japan serves as the case study, with talks among its drug agency, its field society, and firms. The authors close with a staged road map, split by near, mid, and far goals, to bring safe bubble goods to market.
pmc-13479575:
Yuqi Cao and colleagues present a 2026 computer vision study on outlining lesions in photographs of oral potentially malignant disorders, mouth changes that can precede cancer. Training segmentation models needs expert-drawn outlines, which are scarce where specialists are few. The team built a self-supervised pre-training method that learns image features from unlabeled photos first.

Their internal set held 3,417 photographs, with two outside hospital datasets reserved for validation. Patient-level splits prevented the same person's images from leaking across training and testing. The model, a multiscale attention design paired with self-generated masks and teacher-student consistency rules, reached about 84 percent on the Dice overlap score. The authors aim to carry specialist-level outlining into clinics that lack specialists.
pmc-13480075:
Palo set out in 2026 a clear path for spotting bone marrow necrosis, a rare state where the soft core of bone dies while the hard shell stays whole. It shows in well under one in fifty marrow samples, and its look under the lens can fool staff, since dead marrow blurs into other ills. Palo ties the harm to lost blood flow in the marrow's fine vessels, and sorts causes into groups.

Blood cancers, above all fast leukemias and lymphomas, top the cause list, with spread from solid tumors next. Sickle cell disease, severe infections, some drugs, and clot prone states fill out the table. Palo urges a step by step workup: read the smear with care, hunt for hidden cancer, and weigh the whole clinic picture. Early cause finding matters, since the outlook rides on the root ill, not the dead marrow itself.
pmc-13480475:
Patel and co-workers at a United States lab tested in 2026 how man made versions of the hormone progesterone act on immune cells, set beside the natural form. Such drugs are used in birth control and menopause care, across four design waves. The team dosed blood cells from healthy women with each drug at body like levels. They then read signal proteins and gene shifts, and tracked which cell types made them.

A split pattern stood out. Only the natural hormone raised IL-10, a calming signal. Nearly all the man made forms pushed IL-6, a heat raising signal, far above plain broth levels. Cell sorting pinned most of that IL-6 on monocytes, a front line white cell. The natural hormone also curbed one helper T cell path and fed another. The man made forms did not copy that steer at all.
pmc-13481675:
Shenkman and colleagues tracked daily loneliness and well-being in 2026 among middle-aged and older adults of differing sexual orientation. Loneliness is tied to poorer well-being in later life, but how the link moves day to day. Whether it differs for lesbian, gay, and bisexual elders who carry both age and minority stigma, was unclear. One hundred fifty-one community-dwelling adults aged 50 to 79 reported loneliness, happiness, and mood daily for two weeks.

Older sexual minority respondents reported lower happiness and more negative mood than heterosexual peers. Across all participants, lonelier days brought lower happiness and positive mood and higher negative mood. That daily swing was stronger for sexual minority elders on happiness and negative mood, though not on positive mood. The authors say daily loneliness may hit minority elders harder, which matters for designing support that reaches them.
pmc-13482175:
Abrahamson and colleagues in the United States checked in 2026 what a new brain scan tracer truly sticks to after death. The tracer, called SMBT-1, was built to flag reactive astrocytes, star shaped support cells that flare in Alzheimer's disease. Scans in living people had linked its signal to amyloid, the sticky protein of the disease. The team ran binding tests, enzyme assays, and stains on brain samples from Alzheimer's cases, kin tau diseases, and healthy controls.

Tracer binding rose and fell with the target enzyme, MAO-B, and with a classic amyloid tracer. Levels ran highest in Alzheimer's brains. Under the lens, the tracer sat on MAO-B rich astrocytes that hugged amyloid plaques and vessels. It matched tau deposits far less well. In tau only diseases, values fell between the healthy and Alzheimer's ranges. The authors name SMBT-1 a sound marker of these reactive cells.
pmc-13483575:
Roben Ohev Shalom reports a 2026 case of heart valve infection caused by a drug-resistant gut bacterium on the tricuspid valve. The patient was a 75-year-old man who fainted one week after hospital care for bloodstream infection with ESBL-producing E. coli, a strain that resists many antibiotics. Heart tracings now showed worsening conduction delay with episodes of high-degree block.

A standard chest ultrasound missed the problem, while an ultrasound passed through the esophagus revealed a growth on the tricuspid valve. Because a wire-based pacemaker would risk spreading active infection, surgeons placed pacing leads on the heart surface as a bridge. Six weeks of ertapenem cleared the growth, and a permanent dual-chamber device followed. The case stresses early deep imaging and pacing choices during active infection.
pmc-13486875:
Meiqi Wang and others test whether dietary myo-inositol protects grass carp from intestinal swelling in intensive farming. In 2026, the feeding trial assigns 450 adult carp to six dietary levels for eight weeks, then induces gut swelling with dextran sulfate sodium. Enteritis already affects a large share of farmed fish and threatens productivity.

Fish on the basal diet without added inositol showed stunted gut development, worse structural damage, fewer mucus-producing goblet cells, and higher enteritis rates. Deficiency disrupted early endosome formation and blocked internalization of a death dock called TNFR1, keeping an swelling pathway switched on and triggering cell death. Adequate inositol therefore supports gut barrier health through a defined cellular mechanism.
pmc-13487175:
Obai and team compared urine samples from car mechanics and non-mechanics in Iraq's Al-Najaf region to gauge workplace exposure to metals and radon. Mechanics breathe fumes and handle parts daily, and urine reveals what the body has absorbed. Their 2026 study tested twenty mechanics and five comparison volunteers for chromium, cadmium, and lead by atomic absorption, plus radon using a plastic track detector that counts radiation marks.

Mechanics carried higher average levels of every substance measured than the comparison group in the samples collected. Cadmium showed the starkest gap, averaging roughly forty times the comparison group's mean value in this small sample. Radon in mechanics' urine averaged about six times the comparison level, with wide variation between individuals. Lead stayed within allowable limits despite the elevation. Obai flags inhalation and skin contact on the job as the likely routes.
pmc-13488075:
Federico Biscetti and colleagues test a blood fat marker after leg artery repair in people with diabetes in a 2026 prospective study. Patients had type 2 diabetes plus chronic limb-threatening ischemia, where poor flow endangers the leg, and all had a procedure to reopen leg arteries. The marker, apolipoprotein B100, counts harmful cholesterol particles more directly than standard cholesterol measures. Follow-up lasted twelve months with regular visits.

Heart and limb events were common, affecting about half of the 167 patients in combined counts. Higher marker levels at the start predicted both kinds of events, even after accounting for other risks, and adding the measure sharpened risk models notably. The authors suggest using it to tailor follow-up and treatment intensity.
pmc-13488175:
Debebe Birhanu and co-authors test a plant compound against bacteria and fungi in a 2026 laboratory study from Ethiopia. The plant Impatiens rothii, found only in Ethiopia, is used in folk medicine for infections, and its tuber was extracted with methanol. Chemical separation yielded a plant sterol called spinasterol, whose identity was confirmed by standard instruments. Testing covered twenty-six bacterial and four fungal strains, plus computer docking against two microbial enzymes.

Extract and pure compound both killed a broad range of germs, with the strongest effects against two common gut bacteria at low doses in the reported tests. Fungal effects were weaker. Docking suggested plausible binding to both target enzymes. The authors call spinasterol a starting scaffold that needs strengthening and direct enzyme tests.
pmc-13488575:
Jonika B. Hash and colleagues study childhood adversity and new mothers' mental health in a 2026 analysis of an under-resourced United States sample. Two hundred forty-four Spanish- and English-speaking mothers, referred during pregnancy for mental health concerns through a community service, reported childhood experiences and symptoms six to twelve weeks after birth. The survey covered the classic ten adversity types plus five added types meant to capture harms missed in disadvantaged and minority groups.

Every classic adversity type was reported more often than in the landmark reference sample from a large health plan population. Mothers who arrived in the United States as adults reported fewer adversities than those born in the country. Adversity scores related to depression, anxiety, and post-traumatic stress symptoms after birth in the reported analyses.
pmc-13490375:
Lizal and team investigated why inhaling furosemide, a common diuretic, so inconsistently relieves breathlessness despite promising logic. They propose a dyspnoea paradox: the gasping breaths of air-hungry patients create an aerodynamic barrier that filters the medicine out before it lands. Their 2026 study ran a vibrating mesh nebulizer under simulated breathless breathing, tested deposition in a realistic airway replica, and modeled airflow computationally.

Standard pharmacy tests rated the aerosol excellent, with particle sizes in the ideal range and over eighty percent fine particles. In the realistic airway, though, most drug slammed into the upper airways, driven by a fast jet through the voice box. Both bench and computer results agreed on the barrier. Lizal warns that standard tests give false reassurance for breathless patients and argues trials should model real gasping.
pmc-13493875:
Nayak and co-authors built a single score for judging how well crops withstand drought on rain-fed farms, where no irrigation softens a dry year. Their Composite Crop Resilience Index, described in 2026, blends three parts: exposure to bad rainfall, sensitivity measured by how sharply yields answer rainfall swings, and stability of yields over time. They computed it for rice, maize, and millets across Indian districts using rainfall and harvest records from 1998 to 2023.

Rice came out most fragile, with drought-year yield losses frequently running into the tens of percent and the highest sensitivity to rainfall. Millets consistently lost less in dry years, answered rainfall more calmly, and held steadier yields, earning the top resilience scores. Rechecking the index under different weightings left the rankings intact. Crop choice mattered more than which district a farm sat in, so the authors promote millet-based diversification for drought-prone regions.
pmc-13493975:
Jiaqi Cao and five colleagues hunt in 2026 for the mitochondrial genes behind painful diabetic nerve damage, a burning complication with few good treatments. Single-cell gene readings from two datasets were intersected with mitochondria related gene lists, and three names survived both screens: Hmgcs2, Nudt5, and Cpt1c. Rat models of the condition confirmed the trio genuinely shifts in the nerve relay station, the dorsal root ganglion.

Direction of change depended on cell type: support cells called fibroblasts turned two genes down and one up, while immune macrophages flipped the pattern almost exactly opposite. Each cell type's metabolism told a matching story in pathway analysis. Computer docking even found two common diuretic drugs that grip one of the proteins stably, hinting at repurposing candidates for a condition short on options.
pmc-13495175:
Andrés Ramírez and a large team test, in a 2026 study from Ecuador, a short questionnaire on childhood abuse and whether it measures the same way across sexual orientations. Abuse in childhood scars mental and social health for life, so sound screening tools matter. Their short form asks about physical, emotional, and sexual abuse and about feeling afraid, trapped, or abused.

The study enrolled 520 adults, split evenly between homosexual and heterosexual groups. The form showed strong internal consistency and clean validity scores, and a two-factor shape fit the answers near perfectly. Scores meant the same thing in both groups, a check called measurement invariance. A network view of the items found one item at the center of the web, and tighter item webs in lesbian respondents than in gay respondents. The authors offer the form as a sound, fair tool for prevention and care planning.
pmc-13495475:
Jie Shang and nine co-authors drained a long blood clot from the spines of two men with a stiff spine disease, in a report published in 2026. The disease makes the spine brittle, so fractures often pair with long clots that crush the spinal cord. The standard fix cuts many back bones, which can wreck the rear brace of the spine. Their method cuts a small window, then threads a soft tube along the clot.

Suction and rinse steps alternate until the flow runs free and the cord sac sits loose. Scans showed full clearing in both men. One walked on his own by six months, with near full scores. The other, who arrived with no cord function, regained deep feeling and partial movement. The authors call the method sound and kind to the spine.
pmc-13496375:
Saibal Das and co-authors gather in 2026 the widest level of evidence on helping older adults manage complex drug regimens safely. Many older patients take numerous medicines for several conditions, which raises the chance of errors and harm. Their umbrella review, meaning a review of prior systematic reviews, asks which approaches improve prescribing and daily use.

Searching five databases up to 2024, the team included 71 reviews covering well over a million participants in total, and rated their quality with a standard tool. Pharmacist-led reviews and planned stopping of unneeded drugs most clearly improved how suitable medicines were. Team-based care and computer decision support also helped adherence and prescribing, while gains in quality of life and survival were mixed across studies.
pmc-13498875:
Atzori and colleagues ran the first numerical simulation of inhaled air through a twenty-three-generation lung model, in a 2026 fluid dynamics study. Airflow in the lung connects to flow upstream, but models simplify the deepest passages into calm, breathing-rate-only motion. Their airway tree branched twenty-three times, with no turbulence model or regime assumptions, at a flow matching peak inhaler use.

Atzori showed the flow changing along the generations. A turbulent-like regime near the top gives way to unsteady laminar flow, then to viscosity-driven Stokes flow in the smallest airways. Yet the deepest flow pulsed. Its fluctuations were fast and large compared with the mean flow, contradicting the picture that only the breathing frequency matters near the air sacs. The team traced those pulses to flow splitting at the upper branchings, and argues many lung models rest on assumptions needing revision.
pmc-13499475:
Dhiren R Rajagopal, Dipti Anand, and Melissa D Babcock report in 2026 a shingles case with inflamed small blood vessels in the skin after a steroid injection into the knee. Shingles comes from reactivation of the chickenpox virus resting in nerve tissue, and steroid shots into joints are a less clear trigger than steroids taken by mouth. Their patient was a 70-year-old man with knee arthritis and no immune suppression, malignancy, or chronic steroid use.

Five days after the injection, a painful eruption appeared on the same leg, starting as grouped blisters along one nerve band and progressing to bloody, crusted sores. A skin biopsy confirmed tissue death in the surface layer with inflammation around vessels in deeper skin layers. Cases joining shingles, vessel inflammation, and a joint injection in a person with normal immunity were described as previously unreported, prompting discussion of how local steroids may wake the virus.
pmc-13499775:
Ann Childress, Hirah Malik, and Jim Potenziano pool studies of driving risk in untreated ADHD in a review from two thousand twenty-six. Attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder is common, and its untreated form may endanger drivers. The team compared its crash risk with better-known hazards.

Four studies put crash odds ninety-three percent higher for untreated ADHD drivers than for the general driving public. By contrast, cannabis use raised odds eighty-five percent, sleepiness one hundred sixty-two percent, and sedative drugs fifty-three percent. Only alcohol and speed analyses stood apart from that set. The authors argue untreated ADHD deserves the same public attention as those famous risks. Treating the disorder, they note, improves driving.
pmc-13500675:
Haiquan Zhang and colleagues test in 2026 a combined brain stimulation and exercise therapy for stroke survivors who cannot swallow safely. Swallowing training helps, yet purely peripheral practice has limits. The team added magnetic pulse stimulation over both sides of the cerebellum, the brain's coordination hub, paired with throat elevation exercises guided by real-time biofeedback. Forty-five recovery-phase patients were randomised to usual care, sham stimulation plus training, or active stimulation plus training, with 42 finishing four weeks.

All groups improved on standard swallowing scores in the reported results. Both training groups outperformed usual care, and the active stimulation group beat the sham group on both swallowing safety and function measures. Brain imaging with light-based sensors showed the active group boosting activation in right frontal and premotor areas and strengthening connections within and between hemispheres, a plausible route for the added benefit.
pmc-13500875:
Hosam Elhalis, writing alone, argues that a neglected yeast genus could improve coffee in a 2026 review. Coffee fermentation shapes bean quality and flavor. Most starter cultures rely on one standard yeast. Wild yeasts beyond it offer richer chemistry and genetic range. Species of Pichia, a yeast genus proven in wine and beer, are barely tried in coffee.

The review collects what is known about Pichia species and their traits. Several species ferment strongly even under flooded, washed-coffee conditions. Distinct members bring gifts: heavy ester output for aroma, enzymes that break down pectin, and tolerance of harsh conditions. Together they can steady the microbial mix and deepen flavor. The author calls Pichia an underexploited resource for washed coffee. Knowledge from wine and beer, he argues, can be transferred to guide coffee trials.
pmc-13500975:
Akash Panda leads a five-author team reporting a 2026 case of primary distal ileal volvulus, a rare twisting of the small intestine. A healthy 52-year-old woman arrived after three days of worsening abdominal pain, inability to pass stool, and swelling. Examination found tenderness in the right lower abdomen with a cystic swelling, and imaging showed dilated small-bowel loops. A contrast CT scan showed a transition point low in the distal ileum, pointing to volvulus.

Emergency surgery found a 360-degree anticlockwise twist spanning about 20 centimetres of the terminal ileum, with irreversible ischemic damage. Surgeons removed the gangrenous segment plus part of the caecum and brought the ends out as a double-barrel ileocolostomy. Apart from a minor wound infection the recovery was smooth, and the stoma was reversed two months later. Tissue examination confirmed ischemic death of the bowel wall, with no cancer or tuberculosis.
pmc-13501575:
Gaia Leuzzi and others explore how young adults experience health apps and wearables, with public involvement in the research. In 2026, the qualitative study runs focus groups with sixteen people aged eighteen to twenty-six who tracked at least one health variable, analyzing transcripts with reflexive thematic analysis. Five themes emerged from their accounts.

People valued having health information in one place, catchy personalized graphics, a path from tracking to healthier habits, and achievements plus social connection. They also worried about data rightness and about giving too much weight to tracked numbers, mainly for sensitive users. Designers gain guidance to balance empowerment traits with safeguards against over-tracking.
pmc-13501675:
Haley J. Fortin leads a four-author team reporting a 2026 mouse genetics study of how distant DNA variants reshape the three-dimensional folding of the genome. Comparing embryonic stem cells from two mouse strains, C57BL/6J and DBA/2J, the team used HiChIP to map contacts between regulatory elements. They found 4,962 interactions that differed between the strains, and 71 percent of them overlapped known accessibility trait loci, showing the differences are mostly inherited rather than noise.

Loci controlled from afar, in trans, carried a signature: their weaker contacts were enriched for H3K9me3-marked heterochromatin, the genome's tightly packed silent form. Hybrid cells showed dominant repressive effects matching that picture. To prove cause, the team bred congenic strains swapping one trans-acting region between backgrounds. The swapped locus coordinated accessibility, both chromatin marks, and contacts at hundreds of elements, with 73 to 94 percent of directional predictions confirmed.
pmc-13503775:
Valerie Y. H. van Weperen leads a team that tested whether pain-sensing nerves in the spine drive nerve damage after a heart attack, in a 2026 study in male pigs. After an attack, the vagus nerve weakens and stress signals surge, which raises the risk of deadly heart rhythms.

The team used a potent plant toxin, placed near the upper spine, to kill pain-sensing nerve cells before causing an attack. Treated pigs kept more vagus tone and steadier reflex control weeks later. Their spinal cords showed less swelling and immune cell activity, and rhythm tests were more stable. In a second group, the same step after an attack quickly restored vagus function and cut risky rhythms.
pmc-13504275:
Frederiksen and colleagues tested whether narasin, an ionophore feed additive used in standard broiler chicken production, promotes vancomycin-resistant gut bacteria of a species that also infects people. Their 2026 controlled animal study used three lab-built strains of Enterococcus faecium with different resistance traits. Chickens were fed diets with selected ionophores, additives that shuttle ions across membranes, with bacterial groups tracked on special plates and by genome sequencing.

Frederiksen showed narasin in feed selected for vancomycin-resistant E. faecium in the birds, and that the NarAB trait, a pair of genes giving narasin resistance, was needed for that co-selection to happen. Resistant species were also part of the birds' gut flora, and bacteria resistant to both drugs appeared only in narasin-fed birds, showing it grows resistant groups. The authors warn vancomycin and narasin resistance may be more common in broiler flocks than assumed, a concern for human health.
pmc-13504975:
Mahdis Sharifikia leads a team tracking stress and iron-linked markers after heart attack treatment, in a 2026 pilot study. Reopening a blocked heart artery saves muscle, but the rush of blood back can itself harm tissue. Oxidative stress and an iron-driven cell harm path are suspects in that second injury.

Twenty-five patients had blood drawn before the artery procedure and four times in the two days after. Defense enzymes peaked early, within six to twelve hours, while fat damage products also crested at six hours. Iron dipped briefly and its storage protein rose. Higher defense activity went with less heart enzyme leakage, a sign of smaller injury, while damage products and iron went the other way. The authors call for larger studies.
pmc-13507075:
Alireza Seif and colleagues show, in 2026 work, that entangled quantum memory still helps learn noise in quantum devices even when the memory itself is noisy. Learning a full quantum process normally needs a fast-growing number of measurements. Linking test qubits to memory qubits can cut that cost sharply for a common error model, called a Pauli channel.

The team added error cleanup for the memory and tested the method on a superconducting processor. Checks ran with up to 64 qubits, while full learning used up to 16 qubits in parallel gate layers. Measured extra cost per qubit stayed below the floor for methods without entanglement. Real devices can keep the learning edge.
pmc-13507275:
Payam Shafigh and colleagues analyzed cement paste color in two thousand twenty-six. Low-carbon cement is spreading through construction. Slag from steel furnaces replaces much ordinary cement. Engineering properties are well studied already. Color properties remain poorly documented, though. The team tested grey and white cement pastes. Slag replacement reached high volume levels.

A standard formula measured color differences precisely. Water-cured white paste showed the most uniform color. Slag lightened grey paste but darkened white paste. Heavy slag mixes differed most from plain controls. Adding red pigment shrank those differences notably. Architects gain data for visible concrete finishes. Appearance matters in exposed sustainable concrete.
pmc-13507475:
Iwona Swiderska and three co-authors compare two ways of imaging the electric potential across cell membranes, in work published in 2026. Both ways use second harmonic light, a signal made when light hits a surface. One uses water itself as the probe, with no added dye. The other uses a dye that responds to voltage and sits in the membrane. The team tested both on free-standing lipid films while applying a known voltage.

The two signals did not report the same thing. Water gave a clean reading of the voltage across the whole membrane. The dye instead reflected the surface on its own side, mixed with changes in dye density and tilt. Combining both could pair the accuracy of water with the much faster timing of the dye.
pmc-13507575:
Zachary Eidman and seven co-authors describe a way to reroute signals from cytokines, the small proteins cells use to signal each other, in 2026 work. Their system builds on synthetic Notch receptors, lab-made sensors that switch on chosen genes when triggered. The team found these receptors could respond to free-floating multi-part cytokines in solution, a mode not reported before. That response reached up to 24-fold between off and on states.

To sense single-part cytokines too, the group built nMATRIX, pairing engineered cells with matched materials. It detected two inflammatory signals, IL-1β and IL-6, with a range above 68-fold. The platform then turned those danger signals into calming outputs that changed nearby immune cell behavior. Readers see a flexible design for treatments that sense a problem and respond on their own.
pmc-13508275:
Jing Yin leads a twelve-author team tracing how fat builds up inside immune cells of the brain after a stroke, in 2026 mouse work. Brain immune cells called microglia normally clear fat droplets through a cleanup process named lipophagy. After a blocked blood vessel stroke, that cleanup stalled and fat droplets piled up for at least three weeks. Re-reading cell-level gene data pointed to a subgroup of microglia high in a regulator called IRF7.

Mice bred to lack IRF7 only in microglia recovered cleanup and shed the fat overload. They also showed stronger nerve connections and better movement recovery after stroke. The same gains appeared in an aged mouse stroke model and in cell tests. The team traced the harm through a target gene, and blocking it eased the cleanup failure too. The work names a drug target for aiding stroke recovery.
pmc-13508375:
Ela Lazeron-Savu and seven co-authors set out the design of a study testing a blended care program for fatigue after brain injury, in a 2026 protocol. Fatigue is common after stroke or head injury and disrupts daily life, yet proven treatments are scarce. Their program, Tied by Tiredness, mixes phone-based momentary check-ins with personal feedback sessions over six weeks. A pilot found the approach workable. The new study spans several centers and plans to enroll 45 adults seeking help for fatigue.

Patients choose their own path: the new program or usual care with weekly occupational therapy. Fatigue and wider outcomes like mood, thinking complaints, participation, and quality of life are tracked before care, after care, and at three and six months. A cost study from a social viewpoint runs alongside. The design aims to show both whether patients improve and what the program costs society.
pmc-13509975:
Vitória Nedel Rech and three colleagues test a blood pressure system peptide against asthma in rats, in a study from two thousand twenty-six. Alamandine, part of the renin-angiotensin system, calms inflammation in other parts of the body. Its role in allergic airway disease was unexplored in past work. The team set out to test what it can do there.

Twenty rats were sensitized and challenged with ovalbumin to mimic asthma. Some got alamandine preventively, for thirty-three days in all. Others got it therapeutically, for twenty-one days of the run. Ventilation mechanics were gauged under a methacholine challenge in each case. Lung inflammation was gauged by eosinophil counts in the tissue. Receptor expression was assayed in the lab as well. Airway hyperresponsiveness, the twitchiness that marks asthma attacks, was the outcome of interest. The study sets a cardiovascular peptide in place as a candidate respiratory therapy.
pmc-13510575:
María Merino-País and six co-authors review animal studies on whether exercise changes gut microbes in Alzheimer disease models, and what that might mean for the brain, in 2026 work. Gut imbalance has been tied to this disease, and exercise is known to help thinking in models of it. The team searched three major databases through July 2025 for controlled animal trials that measured gut microbes after exercise programs.

Eight studies covering 126 animals entered the review. Only two could be pooled in a combined analysis. Exercise lowered the share of one large bacterial group by a small yet clear amount. No clear effects appeared for other groups at phylum or genus level. Results varied between studies, and the pooled base was thin. The authors say exercise seems to reshape gut microbes in selective ways, and that far more work is needed to trace how those shifts reach the brain.
pmc-13511075:
Mira Kheil and ten co-authors review outcomes when chemotherapy comes before surgery for advanced cancer of the womb lining, in 2026 work. Many such patients arrive with disease that cannot be removed safely at once, so drugs are given first to shrink the cancer. The team studied records of 42 patients who received that sequence and then had interval surgery to remove leftover tumor.

Most patients saw their tumors shrink after chemotherapy, and more than eight in ten had no visible tumor left after surgery. No single patient trait or molecular feature predicted survival once other factors were counted. Tumor shrinkage and full removal each hinted at links to longer time without the cancer returning. The authors add their results to growing support for drug-first care in chosen patients and call for larger studies to pin down who benefits most.
pmc-13511175:
Wenteng Li, Tong Li, and Jingwei Mao review how low oxygen drives liver scarring through a star-shaped liver cell, in 2026 work. Scarring builds when injury persists and these stellate cells switch on, laying down excess tissue matrix. Low oxygen steadies a set of sensor proteins that switch on growth and stiffening genes, while vessel lining cells in the liver change form early in the process.

Once active, stellate cells worsen vessel changes and deepen oxygen shortage, and their signals feed back to strengthen the same sensors. That loop keeps scarring moving toward cirrhosis and raises death risk from chronic liver disease. The review maps current treatments, then weighs drug targets along the oxygen pathway by how likely they are to reach patients. The authors aim to guide the search for anti-scarring drugs that break the loop.
pmc-13511475:
Hafize Nalan Güneş and six co-authors compare high pressure inside the skull of unknown cause in patients with and without swelling of the optic disc, in 2026 work. The swollen-disc sign, called papilledema, is a classic marker, yet a growing share of patients lack it. Records from a tertiary neurology center were sorted by exam, spinal fluid pressure, and brain imaging findings.

Nearly a third of patients fell into the group without disc swelling. That group showed more migraine-like features, including light and sound sensitivity plus nausea and vomiting, in early exploratory comparisons. One imaging sign, flattening at the back of the eyeball, also differed between groups. The authors caution that the sorting rules themselves shape such gaps. They argue that missing disc swelling should not by itself rule out real pressure disease when other evidence lines up.
pmc-13512075:
Li and colleagues catalog the 14-3-3 gene family in peanut, a group of regulatory genes that help plants respond to stress, in 2026 genomic research. These genes, also called general regulatory factors, act as molecular adaptors inside cells. The team searched the genomes of cultivated peanut and its two wild ancestors, Arachis duranensis and Arachis ipaensis. They then compared gene structures, shared motifs, chromosome positions, and evolutionary relationships across the three species.

Cultivated peanut carried 22 of these genes, against 10 in Arachis duranensis and 12 in Arachis ipaensis in the final counts. Large stretches of the cultivated genome matched the ancestors closely, and the authors identify segmental duplication, where blocks of DNA are copied, as the main engine expanding the family. Switch-like DNA elements in the gene promoters suggest many family members switch on under drought, salt, or other stresses. Li presents the catalog as groundwork for breeding tougher peanut varieties.
pmc-13512375:
Zhuomiaoyu Chen, Fumei Cao, and Zhao Li build a genetic case that a protein regulator called PPP1R1B raises risk of cancer inside the liver bile ducts, in 2026 work. Several public datasets were joined, spanning genetic association data, single-cell readings, bulk tumor readings, and two patient cohorts. A Mendelian randomization test, which uses inherited variants as a natural experiment, tied higher gene activity to higher cancer risk.

Single-cell maps showed the gene concentrated in malignant cells. Bulk data and stained tissue slides confirmed higher levels in tumors than in normal tissue. Patients with high levels lived shorter lives in the survival checks. Sensitivity tests backed the main genetic result. The authors offer the gene as a risk-linked candidate marker for this hard-to-treat cancer and as a template for similar hunts in other rare tumors.
pmc-13512875:
Petrova and colleagues wrote a 2026 review on monkeys and apes as models of epigenetic aging. Epigenetic marks are chemical tags on DNA that shift as bodies age. Close primate kin share these systems with humans and live long enough to track. The review gathers what is known across primate species and tissues.

Human-built aging clocks predict primate ages well in the gathered studies. Many age-linked tag patterns are shared across the primate family tree. Most marks, though, hold in only one tissue or species at a time. Rank, sex, stress, and early hardship all bend aging paths in primates. The authors urge wider species coverage, including the great apes. Only a narrow set of species, mostly macaques, dominates current data.
pmc-13515575:
Toru Ichiseki argues, in a 2026 opinion article, that rotator cuff research should widen its choice of lab cells. Rotator cuff tears are common tendon injuries, and their biology spans inflammation, oxygen shortage, cell ageing, and scar-like matrix change. Most lab work uses cells taken from patients' own torn tendons.

Shop-bought tendon cells from healthy tissue offer the opposite profile: easy supply, standard quality, and large batches, at the cost of the wrong home address. No proven marker yet separates rotator cuff cells from other tendon cells anyway. Ichiseki proposes a ladder: screen ideas in commercial cells, check the winners in true rotator cuff cells, then confirm in tissue, animal, or patient studies. The aim is not replacement but a wider doorway into the field, so more labs can test ideas before precious samples are spent.
pmc-13515675:
Karthik Chandrasekharan and five colleagues review, in a 2026 article, inflammation as a treatable driver of atherosclerotic heart disease. Even with strong cholesterol, pressure, and sugar control, many patients keep a leftover risk that tracks inflammation in the artery wall. Stenting a narrowed artery adds its own inflammatory flare, which can worsen outcomes. Signals such as C-reactive protein and the interleukins IL-1 and IL-6 mark this hidden risk.

Trials of anti-inflammatory drugs have mostly disappointed so far. Colchicine stands alone with large-trial proof strong enough for guideline backing. Other candidates lack that level of evidence. Open questions include whether colchicine should be given around the time of stenting and which immune signals it truly changes. Chandrasekharan's team frames the hunt for further proven therapies as the field's next step.
pmc-13516275:
Belgin Sever, Hasan DeMirci, and Halilibrahim Ciftci introduce a journal special issue on structure-based drug design in a 2026 editorial. Drug hunting has shifted from trial-and-error toward rational design powered by high-resolution structures, simulations, and artificial intelligence. The collected papers span cancer, infections, brain disease, drug resistance, and metabolic disorders, all sharing computational and structural methods.

A leading theme is structure-guided chemistry against kinases, the signalling enzymes central to many cancers. Highlighted studies build new compound families against the epidermal growth factor receptor, mixing modelling, synthesis, and biological testing to refine leads. Other themes follow the same pattern across the issue's disease areas. The editors argue that combining computation with experiments gives mechanistic insight and speeds the road from molecule to medicine. Readers get a guided map of the issue and of where rational design is heading.
pmc-13517275:
Ekramy Elmorsy and a large team report a rat study, published in 2026. It tests whether limonene protects kidneys against the pesticide chlorfenapyr. Limonene is a citrus compound. Rats were dosed for thirty days in six groups. Plain limonene was compared with a nano-liposomal version. These are tiny fat bubbles that carry the compound. Both were set against the pesticide's damage.

The pesticide caused wide harm in the kidneys. Dysfunction, tissue damage, and inflammation appeared. Antioxidant pathways were suppressed. Energy failure hit kidney cells. Plain limonene softened all of these changes. The nano-liposomal version improved matters still further. Kidney function, tissue structure, chemical balance, and cell survival all improved. The authors present this as a candidate strategy against pesticide kidney injury.
pmc-13517675:
Ligue-Sabio and six co-authors reviewed models of African swine fever in twenty twenty-six. The viral disease strikes domestic and wild pigs and has spread again across borders. Models help officials understand spread and plan control, but the literature is scattered.

The team screened studies through twenty twenty-four and kept one hundred fifty-one papers. Step-by-step mechanistic models and statistical models dominated, while machine learning grew in recent years. Each type had its own typical job, from judging control plans to mapping risk areas. Most work came from Europe and Asia. The authors found checks of model quality were often missing or uneven. They call for better coverage of regions and spread routes, plus more consistent testing of models.
pmc-13518475:
JiangLi Zhao and colleagues offer a two thousand twenty-six pan-cancer analysis of a gene called reticulocalbin-1 and the tumour immune surroundings. The gene lives in the cell's protein-folding factory and was tied to spread and drug response in some cancers. Its wider meaning was unclear.

Public multi-layer datasets charted the gene across many cancer types. Immune cell mixes and survival models were computed per cancer. Focused lab work in glioma tested the gene's role directly. Responses to four standard glioma drugs were also probed. The study positions the gene as a possible forecast marker and treatment clue.
pmc-13519775:
Kun Wang and colleagues modeled how the flu drug oseltamivir should be dosed in infants under two years old. Published in 2026, the study reused drug-level and virus data from an earlier trial run by a national allergy and infectious diseases study group. A population drug model was joined to a viral dynamics model, then run across many doses to find exposures giving 95 percent of maximum viral suppression.

The analysis used hundreds of blood samples from 78 infants, with a median age of eight months, plus virus measures from 62 babies over twelve days. Modeled target exposures were set for both total drug exposure and trough concentration. The authors argue that such modeling can stand in where direct dose-response data are missing, including for preventive once-daily dosing, which fell short for infants already carrying virus. Readers get a dosing compass for a group rarely studied directly.
pmc-13520175:
Marine Massy leads a thirteen-author investigation in 2026 into why multiple sclerosis sometimes flares after patients stop the drug fingolimod, and whether women face higher risk. Reactivation hits roughly a tenth of patients who stop this drug class. The team combined a literature review, two adverse-event registries, a mouse model, and human brain biopsies.

Across eight studies covering 2,579 patients, female sex associated with reactivation, echoed strongly in both registries. Female mice also fared worse after withdrawal, with a 2.5-fold severity rise and more S1PR1 receptors on T cells. Biopsies from reactivating patients showed the same receptor elevation in active lesions. Massy and colleagues nominate the receptor as a mechanistic lead.
pmc-13520275:
Xiaojing Ren leads a six-author multi-omics study in 2026 hunting for signals that predict which liver cancer patients respond to chemoembolization, a standard artery-blocking treatment whose benefit varies widely. Stool chemistry was profiled in 30 patients before treatment and four days after, then compared at pathway level with tumor gene data from a separate public cohort.

Treatment shifted stool fats called lysophosphatidylcholines upward, marking acute tissue injury. Responder tumors, meanwhile, ran hotter on bile acid production and tryptophan metabolism, while non-responders favored cell division programs. Ren and colleagues read the overlap as a gut-liver axis signature and propose stool lysophosphatidylcholine as a non-invasive early readout of treatment effect rather than a direct tumor kill marker.
pmc-13520375:
Kristyna Maskova and colleagues show in 2026 that different faults in the BBS1 gene break a transport machine inside hair-like cell structures in distinct ways. Bardet-Biedl syndrome affects eyes, weight, fingers, kidneys and learning, while BBS1 helps build the machine that moves cargo through those structures.

One common variant blocked early assembly, another blocked both maturation and travel toward the structure, and a third left assembly intact while weakening one cargo link. Faulty export of a signalling receptor followed in that last case. Sorting variants by failure step may help explain why illness severity differs between families.
pmc-13522275:
Yaozhuang Zhou and colleagues construct in 2026 a four-gene diagnostic model for nasopharyngeal carcinoma, a cancer hidden deep behind the nose where late detection worsens outcomes. Single-cell data from tumour and control tissue resolved seven cell populations and their signalling exchanges.

Candidate genes from cell markers, bulk differences and network modules were fed to four selection algorithms, which agreed on four core genes tied to tissue structure and immune signalling. Model accuracy stayed high in both validation sets, with a web tool provided for exploration. Immune cell links, prognosis checks and compound docking extend the analysis toward treatment hypotheses.
pmc-13522475:
Ashenafi Syoum and collaborators assess meat hygiene in Hawassa city, Ethiopia, in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Questionnaires and direct observation covered forty slaughterhouse workers and one hundred fifty beef shop workers between late 2022 and mid 2023. Checks focused on handwashing, protective gear, cleaning of knives, meat display, and cooling.

Serious gaps appeared in both settings, including missing handwashing sinks, uncovered meat on display, and little use of protective clothing. Fewer than half of slaughterhouse workers and about one fifth of shop workers showed good handling practice. Food safety training was linked to better practice in both groups, and higher education helped among shop workers. The authors recommend broad training, continuing education, and regular monitoring.
pmc-13523275:
Jing Xu and colleagues test a simple blood index as a predictor of heart events in people with both diabetes and fatty liver disease in a 2026 two-cohort study. The triglyceride-glucose index combines blood fat and sugar values as a stand-in for insulin resistance. More than one thousand hospital patients were followed for a median of over four years, with a large United States survey cohort used for support.

Higher index values were linked to greater risk of death and of major cardiovascular events, with the event link stronger in patients under sixty. Kidney function explained about a tenth of the effect, and a body shape index explained a smaller share of the death link. Adding the index to standard risk models improved prediction accuracy, supporting its use in this high-risk group.
pmc-13523475:
Wanyang Li and colleagues report the 2026 development and validation of a scale measuring body-related distress in Chinese adults with obesity. Body dissatisfaction can weigh heavily on this group, yet existing tools were not built for Chinese cultural context or for obesity specifically. The new patient-reported scale targets adults with a body mass index of 28 or higher.

An item pool grew from semi-structured interviews, guided by a symptom experience model and international standards for patient-reported measures. Cognitive interviews and a panel of ten experts refined the wording, leaving 25 statements. Factor analysis in 415 participants produced constructs explaining about seven tenths of the variance, with good model fit. Reliability estimates for the constructs were high. The authors offer the scale for clinical and research use in China.
pmc-13524875:
Fan and colleagues published a 2026 study of stomach acid suppressing drugs in people on peritoneal dialysis, a home treatment that cleans the blood through the belly lining. Its feared complication is peritonitis, infection of that lining. Whether acid suppressants raise that risk has long been debated.

Using Hong Kong health records from 2006 to 2019, Fan emulated a trial design that compares new users with non-users fairly. Starting a proton pump inhibitor, the stronger drug class, came with about half again the risk of peritonitis and of death overall. The weaker blocker class also raised both risks, though by less. Head to head, the stronger drugs carried higher death rates than the weaker ones, so the authors urge caution.
pmc-13527275:
Lippe and Hoerr introduce a modeling method for chemical exchange saturation transfer imaging, in this 2026 MRI methods paper. The technique detects dilute molecules like glucose and glutamate. It reads their proton-swapping with water. Standard analysis breaks down when exchange runs fast, exactly the regime of several interesting metabolites, so they built a compact model named AB-MT+n.

The model describes the measured spectrum with a five-parameter base covering direct water saturation, the tissue's semisolid background, and fast exchange, extendable with extra components for slower pools. In phantom experiments, older Lorentzian fitting quantified the glutamate pool reliably. It explained above 95 percent of variance. Fast-exchanging glucose defeated those methods, at under 45 percent in the same tests. A simple asymmetry parameter in their framework kept linearity with glucose above 80 percent, and reduced model versions handled mouse brain glucose imaging in living animals.
pmc-13527975:
Noel Mark Makwinya and Thabita Lameck Lupeja study what female students in Tanzania know about sexual health. They surveyed 255 students at Sokoine University of Agriculture. The survey asked what students knew about preventing pregnancy. It also asked about risky sexual behavior. The team looked at personal, family, and housing factors together.

Most students scored low to moderate on knowledge. About sixty-four percent reported moderate to high risky behavior. Students raised in towns scored higher on both counts. Talks with parents were the best predictor of both knowledge and behavior. Yet knowledge alone did not predict behavior. The authors say schools should help parents talk with their daughters. They also urge care in how student housing is assigned.
pmc-13528075:
Xiaoyan Li, Bangzhu Mo, and Chunbao Xie set pregnancy-specific ranges for blood clotting tests in a 2026 study. Standard ranges come from non-pregnant adults and can mislead in pregnancy. The team studied 2,657 healthy pregnant women at a Sichuan hospital in 2024. A control group of 198 non-pregnant women joined. Five clotting measures were tracked by trimester.

Three timing tests shortened as pregnancy advanced. Fibrinogen and D-dimer rose steadily across trimesters. Age under or over thirty made no real difference. The team built percentile ranges for each trimester using guideline methods. A small fresh sample checked that the ranges held. The authors say trimester-matched ranges should sharpen judgments about bleeding and clot risk. Labs elsewhere can adapt the approach to their own populations.
pmc-13528175:
Xinqi Huang and five colleagues review clear aligner treatment for adults whose front teeth fail to meet in a 2026 paper. The bite fault is called anterior open bite. Four databases were searched for clinical studies. Ten studies with 421 treated adults qualified. Most were look-back designs, and nine carried serious bias risk.

Pooling five finished cohorts showed bite overlap growing by about three millimeters. A wider check of seven studies gave a similar gain. Changes centered on the front teeth rather than the jaw angle. Back teeth and jaw plane moved little and unevenly. Certainty was rated very low overall. The authors say aligners may help picked adult cases. They cannot promise true skeletal correction. Future trials should be prospective and measure each bite part directly.
pmc-13529575:
Emily Clark, Danielle Gunn-Moore, and Conor O'Halloran published this veterinary case report in 2026. It describes two UK cats infected with Mycobacterium caprae, a tuberculosis relative more often linked to livestock. Both cats arrived with chronic coughing, tiredness, and weight loss. Chest imaging showed widespread lung changes in the first cat, a young Savannah. The second cat, a British shorthair, had two hollow masses in one lung.

Washings from the airways contained acid-fast bacteria in both cases. Lab tests confirmed the species, by culture in one cat and by DNA test in the other. Each cat received three antibiotics daily for nine to eleven months. Both recovered fully, and their chest images improved and then stayed stable before treatment stopped. At checks ten and twelve months after treatment ended, both cats remained well. The report shows this rare infection can be cured in pet cats with long combination therapy.
pmc-13530175:
Xiaohan Zhang proposes a 2026 scheduling method for solar power in local distribution grids that keeps forecasts at every level in agreement. Solar output swings make day-ahead planning tricky, and forecasts for single sites often clash with totals for the whole network. A reliability score judges which site forecasts deserve trust.

A forecasting model reads frequency patterns alongside raw output to feed that trust score. The system then either builds totals upward from trusted sites or splits totals downward through a constrained neural network. Tests on a standard 33-bus network showed a workable balance between grid safety and scheduling speed.
pmc-13530575:
Katanbaf and colleagues present in 2026, as conference poster 98, a large database comparison of two operations for one-sided knee arthritis. The operations are high tibial osteotomy, which realigns the leg, and partial knee replacement. Surgeons customarily reserve the realignment for patients under sixty.

Querying a national all-payer database of more than 170 million records covering 2010 to 2023, the team matched the groups into 4,706 pairs split by age at sixty. Conversion to a full knee replacement, the failure endpoint, was consistently less likely after realignment. In patients sixty or younger, the odds of conversion after the osteotomy were a fraction of those after partial replacement at ninety days, one year, and two years alike. Older osteotomy patients also converted less at one and two years, while partial replacement rates looked the same across ages.
pmc-13531075:
Keisuke Miyamoto and co-authors recount a 2026 valve delivery that failed through the neck artery and was rescued by a companion balloon. The 93-year-old man had severe valve narrowing, narrow leg arteries, and a heavily diseased descending aorta, steering the team to the carotid route. A steep aortic angle and bulky calcium blocked valve crossing.

Inflating a balloon beside the delivery path shifted the forces enough for the valve to advance right after deflation. Final imaging confirmed success. The lesson warns that even a short, direct route cannot guarantee crossing when angle and calcium conspire.
pmc-13531875:
Yawen Li and co-authors review in 2026 strategies to widen a precision cell therapy for solid tumors that engineers a patient's T cells with a chosen receptor. Such receptor therapy can reach targets that antibody-guided rivals miss, yet solid tumors blunt its impact through harsh surroundings and tricky production.

The review catalogs current limits, recent fixes, and trial results in solid tumor patients. Stronger receptors, broader target menus, combination regimens, and smoother manufacturing form the upgrade path. The authors expect those advances to extend benefit beyond the narrow groups reached so far.
pmc-13531975:
Zhongyan Cao and colleagues tested whether expressing breast milk before birth helps breastfeeding after birth. Published in 2026, the systematic review searched eleven databases through January 2026, pooling eleven randomized trials with 1,571 women, eight of them in meta-analysis. Antenatal expression aims to promote breastfeeding, but its safety and benefit were unsettled.

Women who expressed milk before birth faced far lower odds of delayed copious milk secretion beyond seventy-two hours, with about one case prevented per eight women treated. They were also far more likely to breastfeed exclusively in the first day and at one to four weeks. Maternal and infant safety outcomes did not differ from standard care. The authors back antenatal expression as effective and safe, with trial quality caveats noted.
pmc-13532175:
Daniel A Green weighs in a 2026 commentary the tradeoffs between targeted and broad testing for bird flu H5N1 in people. Current guidance tests mainly those with known animal exposure. Two cases found through universal subtyping of flu-positive samples at a California center had no known exposure, so targeted rules would have missed both.

One case was confirmed and matched cattle-linked virus strains, while the other stayed probable after repeated detection. Green draws on past pandemic lessons to argue surveillance must adapt as transmission routes shift, balancing early warning against laboratory resources and false alarms.
pmc-13534775:
Skye Stephens and colleagues evaluate in 2026 the feasibility of Talking for Change, a Canadian therapy programme that aims to prevent child sexual exploitation before offending. Little research exists on such programmes where reporting duties are mandatory. Referrals reached 162 people and grew each year, with 40 clients studied in depth.

Clients showed risk factors tied to paraphilic interests and self-regulation, plus high rates of other mental health problems and prior illegal material use. Interviews praised group support for acceptance and accountability, while noting a one-size approach as a weakness. Prevention work appears workable in this legal setting.
pmc-13536275:
Jean-Leonard Stor and colleagues sample in 2026 spiders across 234 forest patches in Germany to test whether making forests more varied helps spider diversity. Modern forestry has evened out forest structure, and effects at landscape scale were unknown. One district per site was opened with gaps, thinning, and deadwood, while a matched district stayed uniform.

Based on 18,540 spiders from 206 species, varied districts held lower local and total diversity across measures, despite higher turnover between patches. Spiders were more abundant in varied patches, yet strong habitat filtering cut diversity, so turnover could not offset local losses.
pmc-13536575:
Erhan Bozkurt and colleagues ask in 2026 which fluid strategy shortens hospital stay in mild acute pancreatitis. Fluids are the core early treatment, yet the best fluid type and rate remain unsettled. Records covered 204 patients at one centre from 2018 to 2024, grouped by fluid type and infusion rate.

Two common fluids gave similar stays, both shorter than the other options tested. Fluid type and rate interacted: moderate to brisk rates with the two leading fluids gave the shortest stays. Fluid choice, rate, severity score, age, and blood pressure all predicted stay length in the model.
pmc-13536875:
Azzam Zrineh and colleagues survey epilepsy knowledge among child doctors in the West Bank, Palestine, in a 2026 study. General child doctors often serve as the first contact for children with epilepsy where specialists are few. A total of 246 residents, general doctors, and subspecialists answered a validated questionnaire from late 2025 to early 2026 covering causes, long-term care, related conditions, quality of life, and first aid.

Overall answers were correct at a moderate rate, strongest for first aid and long-term care and weakest for quality of life. Gaps included social difficulties, aggression, hyperactivity as related features, and sudden death risk in epilepsy. Professional role shaped several scores, while age and school location did not. The authors call for focused continuing teaching on life impact and related conditions.
pmc-13537075:
Sébile Tchaicha and eleven colleagues survey genetic testing practice at expert epilepsy centers across Europe, in a paper dated twenty twenty-six. Gene tests now play a growing role in finding the cause of rare epilepsies, yet access and methods vary by country. The team sent a survey to fifty centers in a European expert network across twenty-seven countries. Forty-six centers replied.

Most centers could test genes, often in their own labs. Whole-exome reading was on hand at eighty-five percent, while full genome reading was less common. Standard tests took one to six months in most places. The authors flag wide gaps in speed, teamwork, and counseling, and call for shared standards across Europe.
pmc-13538275:
Xavier Duralde, Caroline Heramb, and Jennifer Blanda grade a scope-based biceps fix with a standard suture anchor. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-six. The fix moves a sore biceps tendon to a new grip above the chest muscle, for patients whose plain care has failed. They review one surgeon's past cases with two years of watch at least.

Most patients keep a normal arm shape. Shoulder scores leap, and pain scores halve, with most past the mark of a gain that counts. A few small ills show, and a few need a redo for a failed fix or held pain. The team calls the method safe and strong, with fewer traps than the open cut.
pmc-13538475:
Xufeng Tao and colleagues trace a new RNA-tagging pathway in acute pancreas inflammation in a 2026 study. Levels of an editing enzyme, METTL1, and its chemical marks on RNA ran high in patient blood, mouse pancreas tissue, and lab models of injured pancreas and immune cells. Combined mapping pinpointed a target gene whose message lasts longer under the marks. Cell and animal tests then followed the chain from mark to tissue harm.

Stabilized target message switched on a major inflammatory signal, pushing immune cells toward an aggressive state and injuring pancreas cells. Silencing the enzyme in the pancreas eased disease in mice. A dead-enzyme version proved that tagging activity itself drives the harm. The authors propose blocking the pathway as a treatment route for pancreas inflammation.
pmc-13539675:
Silva and co-authors dissect an enzyme that the leishmaniasis parasite cannot live without, hoping to turn it into a drug target. Leishmania and its kin cannot build purines, the letters of DNA, from scratch and must recycle them; adenylosuccinate lyase performs one essential recycling step toward AMP. Their 2026 work measured the Leishmania major enzyme's kinetics, solved its crystal structure, and traced how distant parts of the protein communicate through its structure.

The team also showed, in the related parasite Trypanosoma brucei, that losing this enzyme cripples normal growth, evidence the target is essential rather than a bystander. Computer docking and dynamics simulations nominated a drug, the antifungal itraconazole, specifically a phenylpiperazine relative of it, as a selective fit for the enzyme's substrate pocket. The authors present the structure, the communication map, and the candidate compound as a package to seed selective anti-leishmanial drug design.
pmc-13539875:
Xianlong Wu and four colleagues present a 2026 case report of a newborn boy with a rare condition in which a malformed twin grows inside its sibling's body. The mass sat in the baby's abdomen and was attached to an undescended testis, a pairing the authors call exceptionally uncommon.

Jaundice and a lump led to scans that showed fat, soft tissue, and striped calcified parts, leaving doctors unsure whether the growth was this condition or a teratoma tumor. Surgery removed the mass, and examination found an organised spine plus brain, gut, liver, bone, and skin tissue. That organised structure settled the diagnosis under the classic Willis criterion.
pmc-13540075:
Sema Dalkılıç surveys, in a 2026 nationwide study, how well health management students in Türkiye rate their own modern workplace skills. Future health managers need critical thinking, digital literacy, leadership, and problem solving to run complex, technology-heavy services.

An online questionnaire reached 565 undergraduates, scored on a five-part scale. Overall ratings sat above average, strongest for career awareness and for information and technology literacy. Entrepreneurship and innovation scored lowest, with critical thinking close behind. Older students and those further into their degrees rated themselves higher, while women led on career awareness. Grades mattered most for technology and critical thinking scores, the analysis found.
pmc-13540675:
Okely and colleagues measured in 2026 the burden of childhood obesity across twenty-two Pacific Island Countries and Territories. Rates there rank among the highest in the world. As the first paper in a three-part series, it gathered prevalence data for children aged two to about twelve. Twenty-nine studies, covering more than 33,000 children in all, were included.

Prevalence varied hugely, from about three percent in the Marshall Islands to over half of children in Wallis and Futuna and American Samoa. Polynesian and Micronesian countries showed the highest rates, often several times the global average. Obesity generally rose with age and was often higher in boys than girls. Pacific Islander children faced the greatest risk among ethnic groups. The authors call the pattern a region-wide epidemic needing stronger surveillance and culturally grounded prevention.
pmc-13540875:
Li Gao leads a 2026 study of HIV strains in Yunnan, China. The team found two newly recognised recombinant forms of HIV-1. Recombinants arise when two virus strains mix inside one person. Tracking them shows how the epidemic keeps changing. The patients were heterosexual and not yet on treatment.

Genes from 636 patients were analysed for diversity and resistance. Drug resistance appeared in about six percent of cases. One signature mutation led the list. Full genomes revealed two second-generation recombinants. Their names are CRF190_0708 and CRF191_0708. Their ancestors date to about 1999 and about 2010. Over five years, viral rebound was more common in the first group.
pmc-13541575:
Kunaraj Perumalu and three colleagues describe, in a 2026 case, ablating a troublesome extra heartbeat buried deep inside the heart muscle wall, a location catheters struggle to reach. The origin was the posterior superior process of the left ventricle, an anatomically awkward corner.

Their patient, a 22-year-old woman with stimulant use disorder and methamphetamine-linked heart muscle disease, suffered disabling palpitations with extra beats making up nearly half of all heartbeats. Ultrasound imaging from inside the heart, fused with three-dimensional electrical mapping, guided precise burns and watched lesion depth in real time. No recurrence appeared during follow-up. The authors credit the imaging for safe contact and for spotting anatomical barriers.
pmc-13541775:
Chijioke Chukwudi and a team including Asishana Osho review heart bypass outcomes in dialysis patients who also have an arm fistula for dialysis access. Their study was published in twenty twenty-six. Surgeons worry that using the chest artery on the same side as the fistula could let blood steal away from the heart graft.

The team reviewed one hundred and twenty-two dialysis patients who had bypass surgery at two centers between twenty fifteen and twenty twenty-three. Sixty-six had the chest artery graft on the fistula side; fifty-six had it on the other side or as a free graft. The main measure joined death, heart attack, and stroke. Side measures covered problems around surgery, ischemia during dialysis, and three-year survival. The study tests whether the same-side worry is borne out in real outcomes.
pmc-13541875:
Rahat Khan and a team of co-authors measure chromium pollution in river mud near a relocated tannery in Bangladesh. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-six. Moving a dirty industry can just move its contamination, and the buried footprint is rarely mapped.

Sixty mud samples from eighteen sites on the Dhaleshwari River were tested for fifteen elements. Chromium at the outfall hit about two hundred sixty times the average crust level. Levels fell with distance, and half the samples passed a known harm threshold for wildlife. Layers near the surface in close cores were enriched, matching episodic dumping. Statistical unmixing blamed only a modest share of overall variation on human input, but that share was chromium-heavy. The risk screening flags the outfall zone.
pmc-13541975:
Lisa Gensthaler and nine colleagues review, in a 2026 Vienna case series, an anti-reflux metal stent used to keep a cancer-narrowed or leaking gullet open. Standard expanding stents ease swallowing yet bring chest pain, reflux, and slipping out of place.

Twenty patients treated between 2016 and 2021 were analysed, most of them men with advanced oesophageal cancer. Placement succeeded in every case, and reflux, swallowing difficulty, and regurgitation resolved in all patients afterwards. Three stents slipped and were managed endoscopically. Average working life was about eighty-eight days, with thirty-day safety high and no stent-related deaths. The authors call the early results promising for selected patients.
pmc-13542075:
Yan Li and colleagues built a scan-plus-clinic model that flags rapid decline on liver cancer immune therapy. Published in 2026, the multi-clinic look-back study covered 665 patients with advanced liver cancer on PD-1 triple therapy. Hyperprogressive disease, a swift surge after PD-1 drugs, can kill and shut the door on later treatments, yet pre-treatment warnings were lacking.

The HOPE model fused two-phase CT scans with clinic factors and scored 0.801 inside its home data and 0.687 on outside data, beating clinic-only and scan-only rivals. Knock-out checks backed the fusion, and heat maps showed where the model looked. Subgroup and outcome checks further backed its risk sorting. The authors pitch HOPE as a clear pre-treatment aid for closer watch and risk-tuned care of high-risk patients.
pmc-13542175:
Maha Khan and four colleagues fabricate, in a 2026 study, a flexible enzyme electrode printed on a silver-coated transparency sheet, aimed at cheap biofuel cells that harvest electricity from glucose. The design grows a conducting polymer, polyindole, directly on the sheet while trapping the enzyme glucose oxidase and a helper molecule inside.

The polymer network ferried electrons from the enzyme's buried active site to the surface, and the helper, vitamin K3, shuttled charge in a body-friendly way. In a strong glucose solution the electrode delivered a healthy current density and stayed electrically stable. The authors promote the disposable sheet platform for wearable bioelectronics, where light weight and low cost matter.
pmc-13542275:
Baoxia Su published a 2026 physics paper seeking one scheme for both electromagnetism and gravity in the classical domain. The work starts from a long-standing puzzle: equal electric charges push apart, while equal masses pull together. Su builds a flat spacetime geometry suited to special relativity, defines new product and curl moves within it, and rests the rest on three stated postulates: relativity, energy conservation, and charge.

From those postulates come four widened Maxwell equations plus matching force laws, derived with no free parameters. The equations recover how electricity and magnetism act, and gravitational attraction beside them, at once with a mirror twin the author presents as settling the repulsion puzzle. The treatment stays strictly classical, setting aside spin and radiation effects, and applies to gravity only under stated quasi-charge terms. A thought test is offered to check the fit with relativity.
pmc-13542375:
Kleoniki Athanasiadou and colleagues published a 2026 review guiding clinicians through two fresh guideline updates on thyroid disorders in pregnancy. One came from a British obstetrics college in 2025, the other from the American Thyroid Association in 2026. Thyroid hormone from the mother matters greatly early on, because the fetal gland only begins making its own hormone partway through pregnancy. Older guidance pushed intervention at milder levels of dysfunction.

Both new guidelines step back from fixed trimester cut-offs for thyroid stimulating hormone and favour laboratory-specific ranges, with a diagnostic threshold of 4.0 milliunits per litre where local ranges are missing. Diagnosis and treatment targets are now kept distinct. Women already taking levothyroxine are advised to raise their dose by roughly a fifth to a third once pregnant, returning to the earlier dose after delivery. The review walks through testing, dosing, and follow-up in this gentler, more individualised framework.
pmc-13542575:
