Engie Salama and thirteen co-authors published a survey study in twenty twenty-six on a quiet problem in drug development: exposure-response confounding for large molecule medicines. Sicker patients may clear a drug differently, making dose effects look real when they are not. The IQ Consortium asked industry specialists how they handle it.

One hundred twenty-five clinical pharmacologists, pharmacometricians, and statisticians from twenty-three companies answered. Nearly nine in ten recognized the problem, though many were unsure how common it is outside oncology. Dose-ranging study designs won broad support as the best defense. Advanced causal statistics were used by under half, and confidence in them was mixed.
pmc-13543375:
Xinxin Li and colleagues published a 2026 study putting forward CKAP2, a protein tied to the cell's internal skeleton, as a diagnostic marker for bladder cancer. Bladder cancer recurs often and lacks specific early markers. The team combined gene-expression mining, machine learning selection, and a Mendelian randomisation analysis, which uses genetic patterns to probe cause. They then validated a CKAP2-based model on 127 real tissue samples, including fifty matched tumour and normal pairs.

CKAP2 ran much higher in tumours than in healthy tissue, and the genetic analysis supported a possible causal link to cancer risk. The diagnostic model separated cancer from non-cancer with an area under the curve of 0.931, and its predicted risks matched observed outcomes closely. Single-cell data placed the protein mainly in cancer cells themselves. A marker this strong could support earlier detection, though the authors frame it as a candidate needing wider testing.
pmc-13545075:
Magdalena Oleksy-Sobczak and colleagues published a 2026 evaluation of six biomass combustion ashes as soil improvers in a circular economy. The ashes came from wood chips and forest residues to maize cobs, plum pits, beet pulp, and distillery residue. Chemistry and leaching tests came first, then a pot trial with beet plants testing doses and blends. The ashes were rich in calcium, potassium, magnesium, and phosphorus, confirming fertilising value.

Two ashes broke European arsenic limits, one by up to five and a half times, and the distillery ash surrendered its arsenic to water in leaching. In pots, ash corrected soil acidity and boosted fresh plant weight by up to fifty-nine percent, best when nutrient-rich and calcium-rich ashes were combined. Heavy blends, however, pushed lead and cadmium into roots. Feedstock screening and dose discipline, the authors conclude, decide whether ash is a resource or a contaminant.
pmc-13545475:
Alice Knapton and nine colleagues traced how a pancreas hormone, amylin, damages the liver and heart in type 2 diabetes. In insulin resistance the pancreas oversecretes amylin, which clumps into amyloid. Deposits appear in failing hearts and in the brain vessels of Alzheimer's patients. The team used rats engineered to make human amylin in their pancreas. Their liver and heart tissues were compared with several control rat strains at fourteen to sixteen months.

The amylin-producing rats accumulated more hypoxia signaling proteins in their livers. Mitochondrial changes accompanied the signal in both organs. Control strains separated the effects of amylin from plain high blood sugar. The findings extend amylin's harm beyond the pancreas and kidneys. The twenty twenty-six study reframes a diabetes hormone as a systemic, vessel-damaging agent.
pmc-13547175:
Ghozzi Khemissa and colleagues reported in 2026 the first molecular evidence of the parasite Toxoplasma gondii in marine fish from Tunisia. The parasite spreads widely through the environment and can infect people, raising questions about seafood as a route of exposure. The team collected 559 fish from 32 species along the Tunisian coast and tested pooled tissue samples with a sensitive DNA method.

Sixteen of 100 pooled samples tested positive, covering 13 species from both wild and farmed fish. Gills carried the parasite most often, and meat-eating fish showed the highest detection rates. Fish themselves do not seem to host the parasite's full life cycle, so the authors treat them as passive carriers and as warning signs of coastal contamination.
pmc-13547375:
Amar M Singh and a large team reported in 2026 a way to grow drug-carrying vesicles from human neural stem cells. The vesicles are loaded with a cancer drug that can cross into the brain. The blood-brain barrier blocks most medicines, and vesicles from neural stem cells home toward brain tissue, yet producing enough was the bottleneck. Their answer is a floating cluster culture that manufactures vesicles at scale, plus a new alkaline soaking method that packs the drug doxorubicin inside efficiently.

Loaded vesicles killed glioma cells in dishes and crossed the barrier better than free drug in animals. The authors present the system both as a candidate treatment for glioblastoma and as a general delivery vehicle for brain diseases.
pmc-13548475:
Yuan-Ming Yeh and colleagues used long-read sequencing in 2026 to fix the gene map of Trichomonas vaginalis, the parasite behind the world's commonest non-viral sexually transmitted infection. Its huge genome carries tens of thousands of predicted genes, yet the introns, the segments spliced out of gene messages, were barely validated, and short-read studies can misplace splice points. The team combined three sequencing approaches and confirmed candidates with targeted tests.

Starting from 31 historically listed introns, they validated 17 more, lifting the confirmed set to 48, and corrected five earlier records, including two false introns. The long reads also mapped where transcripts end and how their tails are built. The authors offer the cleaned annotation and workflow as a resource for parasite biology and diagnostics.
pmc-13548575:
Christopher J. Miller and colleagues report a 2026 trial of coaching support for team-based mental health care in United States veterans' clinics. Collaborative chronic care models organize outpatient mental health work around teams, yet clinics struggle to adopt them. Eight medical centers received hands-on implementation facilitation in waves between 2022 and 2024, while eight matched centers relied on central technical assistance alone.

Staff surveys suggested small gains in role clarity and team focus after facilitation, though neither reached statistical significance. Mental health hospitalization rates for the more than twenty thousand patients at participating sites matched those at comparison sites. Team scores at the start already resembled end scores from an earlier trial, hinting that central assistance alone may have lifted team function. The authors conclude intensive facilitation added little beyond the lighter support.
pmc-13548675:
Urban and colleagues published in twenty twenty-six an imaging study of early breast cancer found by biopsy. Ductal carcinoma in situ stays inside the milk ducts, but surgery sometimes reveals invasive cancer too. That upgrade changes treatment plans. The team studied ninety patients with biopsy-proven disease who had detailed MRI scans before surgery. They compared scan features between patients with and without invasive cancer at final testing.

Over a third of patients were upgraded after surgery. Invasive cases more often showed combined mass and non-mass patterns. They also had larger lesions, spread across sites, and faster contrast uptake. Three features predicted upgrade on their own in the final model. One of them, a bright signal on a certain scan type, had not been reported before. The model could help sort patients by risk.
pmc-13550375:
Jiujie He and colleagues chart the literature on artificial intelligence in ovarian cancer with bibliometric tools, in a 2026 analysis covering 2006 to 2025. Ovarian cancer kills largely because it is found late, and AI promises earlier detection and sharper treatment choices, yet nobody had mapped the field whole. Pulling 786 papers from a major database, the team visualized output trends, leading countries, institutions, journals, and keyword movement.

Publication grew exponentially, sprinting after 2019. China, the United States, and the United Kingdom led the output. Hot topics clustered around AI-assisted diagnosis, prognosis models, imaging-based radiomics, and biomarker hunting. Keywords drifted from simple classification toward high-grade serous cancer, multimodal learning that fuses data types, and explainable AI. The authors urge explainable systems, richer data fusion, and closer clinician and engineer teamwork to carry models into clinics.
pmc-13550475:
Ziyu Zheng, Xinfeng Ye, and Sathiamoorthy Manoharan propose a cleaner way to read emotion from video, where face, voice, and words arrive together but noisy, in a 2026 machine learning paper. Most fusion methods obsess over combining the streams and ignore the junk inside them. Their framework fuses the streams progressively. It then squeezes the result through an information bottleneck that strips task-irrelevant noise. A dedicated recovery module finally patches back any useful signal the squeeze discarded.

On two standard benchmark collections of opinion videos, the method set new marks for correlation with human emotion ratings and for two-way sentiment accuracy. Gains over the strongest previous systems were modest but consistent across both datasets. The authors argue that deliberate denoising, balanced against information loss, is the missing half of multimodal sentiment analysis.
pmc-13550875:
Wang and co-authors build a machine learning model for vision outlook after diabetic eye surgery. The study held 609 patients with proliferative diabetic retinopathy. All had vitrectomy at Shanxi Eye Hospital from 2022 to 2025. Data split into training and validation sets at eight to two. Screening tools picked the strongest risk factors first.

Kidney failure raised poor outlook odds near sevenfold. Iris vessel growth raised odds over sevenfold as well. Silicone oil use nearly tripled the odds. Higher indirect bilirubin slightly cut the odds. LightGBM beat rival models for long-term vision calls.
pmc-13550975:
Moseley and nine co-authors weigh breast test marks and their sway on care and cost in this twenty twenty-six paper. Small marks left at a test spot let teams find that spot in scans and cuts. They grew from plain wire bits to rich multi-stuff tools in past years.

Inside, marks now guide cut plans, ray aim, and cross-ward care in one chain. Long watch shows them safe, with few harms in scores of case runs. They also save cash by sharp cuts and fewer re-cuts of the same spot. Drift, skin rash to parts, and dim sight on sound scans still snag use. New forms with no wire and glow tricks aim to fix those snags.
pmc-13551575:
Johnson and colleagues present a 2026 pilot study of a scan measure that may spot breast cancer left behind after surgery or chemotherapy. The measure, signal enhancement ratio, comes from contrast MRI and reflects how a spot takes up and releases dye. Fourteen women at one Indian center were studied; leftover cancer was confirmed in four and ruled out in ten.

Leftover tumors showed far higher median enhancement ratios than clear cases. Judging by shape features alone caught every cancer but wrongly flagged half of clear cases. Adding a ratio cutoff of ninety raised correct clear calls to nine in ten, with no cancers missed. A cheap calculation on scans patients already receive could cut needless repeat surgery, though fourteen patients is too few to set policy.
pmc-13551775:
Rebekah Eleazer, with ten colleagues, published a 2026 study of cancer-like change without gene mutations. Most cancer models blame driver mutations in DNA. The team exposed human airway cells to low-dose arsenic over a long period. They tracked a protein called SATB2, which folds DNA to control genes. Tests covered cell chemistry, gene activity, and cell behavior.

SATB2 made a circular RNA that itself builds a small peptide. Adding SATB2 or that RNA reshaped access to genes. Gene programs like those driven by the cancer gene KRAS switched on. Cells took on change linked to cancer, with no arsenic and no added mutations. Both RNAs also persisted in human lung tumors. The team reads this as a non-gene route to cancer programs.
pmc-13552575:
Gunnar Hägglund and Ann Alriksson-Schmidt report a 2026 Swedish registry study of stiff muscles in children with cerebral palsy. Their data cover 3,216 children aged one to fifteen, recorded during 2023 and 2024. Tone was scored in the calf, hamstring, and groin muscles with a standard scale. The team linked tone to age, sex, type of palsy, and level of movement skill.

Stiffness proved most common in the calf, where it touched more than four in five children. Rates were lower in the hamstrings and lower still in the groin muscles. Patterns shifted with age, and children with worse movement had more stiffness. Those with palsy on both sides, or with jerky movements, showed the highest levels, a point planners of treatment should weigh.
pmc-13554275:
Dinesh Kumar Prabhakar leads a seven-author team designing a two-port terahertz antenna that hides from radar while sending in circles in a 2026 study. Terahertz waves promise very fast links, yet military uses also demand low visibility. A stair-shaped feed excites a silicon cylinder to produce circular waves. Mirrored feeds between the two ports cut crosstalk sharply.

A patterned surface layered around the build lowered its radar echo by a wide margin. The antenna works across a broad terahertz band, with clean circular behaviour through the middle stretch. Echo reduction held across that working band. Broadside radiation and strong port isolation suit radar and fast-link uses. The authors back the design for future terahertz systems needing stealth and variety.
pmc-13554875:
Alvin M Ho leads a ten-author team reporting three cases of an ultrasound probe buckling inside the food pipe in a 2026 paper. The probe, passed through the mouth to image the heart from behind, can fold back on itself in rare cases. Pulling a folded probe risks tearing the food pipe, a life-threatening injury. Each case in the series was spotted promptly and checked with bedside imaging.

Patients were moved to a procedure suite, where the probe was advanced into the stomach under X-ray guidance. Freed from the tight passage, the probe straightened and slid out without difficulty. No patient suffered the feared tear. The authors lay out a step-by-step response and warn that suspicion must stay high, above all with slim, flexible probes.
pmc-13555875:
Fengjiao Wang leads a seven-author team reporting a family whose inherited protein S shortage caused a brain vein clot in a 2026 study. Protein S normally brakes blood clotting, and lacking it raises clot risk sharply. The patient showed low protein S activity and antigen levels, matched by her father, two sisters, and two nephews. Brain vein imaging confirmed an extensive clot in the head's drainage sinuses.

Gene sequencing found the same single-letter variant in the PROS1 gene across affected relatives. The variant sits in a conserved stretch and likely weakens the protein, though its class stays uncertain. Her blood also generated thrombin, the clotting enzyme, at a heightened rate. The authors urge full cause screening and family counselling in unexplained clots.
pmc-13555975:
Sayed Shoaib Ghafari leads an eight-author team comparing tooth decay in Iranian and Afghan teens in Tehran in a 2026 study. Their survey covered 761 students aged thirteen to fifteen from eighteen schools, picked by staged random sampling. Questionnaires captured family background and brushing habits, while dentists scored decayed, missing, and filled teeth plus plaque. Afghan students made up nearly half the group.

Decay touched about seventy-two percent of students in both nationalities alike. Plaque presence raised decay odds in both groups. Among Afghan students, better-educated mothers and smaller families tied to less decay. Among Iranian boys, decay ran lower, while reported flossing oddly tied to more decay. The authors urge school programmes on plaque control tailored to each community.
pmc-13556075:
Carla Vargas-del Río and nine colleagues pinned down in 2026 which part of a Salmonella Dublin weapon does its antibacterial work. This cattle-associated bacterium carries a type VI secretion system, a molecular syringe that injects rival bacteria, on a genomic island called SPI-19. Earlier work had shown that one injected protein, SED_RS06335, kills competitors, and the new study tested its tail segment, an enzyme-like domain named M91.

Competition experiments and tests in a foreign host showed that the M91 segment alone carries the killing activity. A three-dimensional model of the domain closely resembled a known bacterial toxin enzyme from the botulism bacterium. The finding explains how this Salmonella strain clears rivals while colonising its host. It also adds a characterised piece to the catalogue of bacterial secretion weapons that researchers compare across species.
pmc-13557875:
Feng Su and four colleagues examined in 2026 whether surgery still has a place for lung cancer patients whose tumours were first judged inoperable. These patients carried EGFR mutations and began treatment with targeted kinase inhibitor pills, which usually work for a time before resistance sets in. The single-centre review covered 26 people who went on to radical salvage surgery after that drug treatment.

Nearly every operation removed all visible tumour with clean margins, mostly through minimally invasive routes, though two cases converted to open surgery. Operations ran a median of about two and a half hours with little blood loss. Complications struck four patients, and people who had taken the pills for more than six months stayed in hospital longer afterwards. The authors judge salvage surgery feasible for carefully chosen patients.
pmc-13558375:
Mark R. Baniqued and three colleagues surveyed in 2026 the research on diet and nutrition therapy for inflammatory bowel disease, where food sits close to both cause and treatment debates. The review walks through a long menu of named diets, from low fibre and Crohn's exclusion plans to Mediterranean, low FODMAP, and gluten-free patterns, and weighs what each can claim. Feeding support through gut or vein, and a shelf of supplements, receive the same scrutiny.

Tube feeding can induce remission in some settings, and nutritional support matters around surgery and when patients are malnourished. Among supplements, the review finds possible benefit in probiotics, vitamin D, omega-3 fats, and certain plant compounds, with evidence quality varying. Practical barriers get attention too, including food avoidance, insecurity, and cultural practice. The authors recommend deciding with a full gastroenterology team rather than by diet fashion.
pmc-13558575:
Jakub R. Bieliński and three colleagues surveyed Polish parents in 2026 about what they would actually do if a child were choking. Choking is a leading childhood emergency, and parental knowledge is rarely measured with realistic questions. Their online pilot survey, run over the winter of 2024 to 2025, used open-ended scenarios rather than tick boxes and gathered 156 parents.

Median scores were low: parents earned about a third of the available points for rescue manoeuvres, though they handled the cardiac arrest questions better. Confidence ran ahead of knowledge, since parents who felt sure scored only modestly better. In the final model, earlier hands-on training was the one clear predictor of doing well. The authors caution that the sample is small, yet they argue for skills-based courses aimed squarely at parents.
pmc-13558675:
Masoud Saberi and four colleagues compared in 2026 five ways of cooling and lubricating the milling of GTD-450, a tough iron-nickel alloy used in turbines and landing gear. The alloy's heat strength and poor heat conduction chew tools and roughen surfaces, and no earlier work had tried nanoparticle-enriched sprays on it. Strategies ranged from dry cutting and water immersion to minimal mist lubrication, plain or loaded with aluminium oxide or zinc oxide particles, across varied feeds, speeds, and depths.

Tool flank wear and surface roughness were the scorecards, and analysis of variance ranked which factors governed each. Lubrication strategy and its particle additives sat at the centre of the comparison, interacting with the cutting settings. The study's stated first is the nanoparticle mist on this alloy. Full statistical rankings guide machinists toward settings that stretch tool life while holding surface quality, a direct cost lever in turbine part production.
pmc-13558775:
Harvey Rutland and six colleagues automated in 2026 the feeding of a hybrid reactor that pairs anaerobic digestion with a microbial electrolysis cell. Such systems make fuel gas from waste, yet operators usually watch the gauges and decide feeds by hand, risking overload. Their design reads the reactor's electric current as a stand-in for how hungrily the microbes are consuming feed. A finite state machine converts current patterns into feeding decisions in real time. That machine is a rigid rule structure with defined states.

Lab reactors ran continuously for four months on molasses feedstock under this control. Feed volume and timing adjusted themselves as microbial activity rose and fell, and the scheme worked across reactors set to different retention times. The authors present the state machine as a predictable, structured alternative to human judgement calls, while noting that scale-up and wider feedstocks remain to be investigated.
pmc-13559075:
Wei Jing and four co-authors test how growth stage shapes harm in lab-grown heart cells hit by immune cell waste. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-six. Heart muscle swell in kids is driven in part by germ-eater cells, but young versus grown heart cells may not bear that hit the same way. The team grew heart cells from stem cells and bathed them in fluid from fired-up immune cells.

Young cells, at day seven, lost life and leaked harm marks far more than day twenty-one cells. A stress protein rose with the hit, and when it was curbed, leak fell and cell power held up in part. The team notes the lab set is a rough stand-in for the real ill.
pmc-13559575:
Tagging proteins with a small partner called UFM1 can go wrong in ways that feed cancer, and a 2026 narrative review by Lu Fang and Fan Yang pulls the evidence together. The authors searched the medical literature for work linking this tagging system to tumors.

The review lists the proteins the system marks, then explains how faults in it, from gene variants to changed activity, help tumors start, grow, and resist treatment. It covers solid tumors in most depth and ends with the overlap between this system and the better known ubiquitin system. The authors see the tagging machinery as a possible source of new drug targets.
pmc-13559675:
Chaolin Pan and four colleagues pool phase 3 trial evidence on adding PD-1 or PD-L1 immune inhibitors to chemotherapy for advanced squamous non-small cell lung cancer. Their 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis searched six databases to May 2026 and kept only randomized phase 3 trials in stage IIIB to IV disease. Bias and evidence certainty were graded with standard tools.

Fourteen trials with 4,481 patients qualified. The combined treatment improved overall survival and progression-free survival over chemotherapy alone, with hazard ratios of 0.73 and 0.54 in the pooled estimates. Responses lasted longer and occurred more often with the combination. Benefit looked strongest in patients whose tumors expressed PD-L1 at 50 percent or more. Immune-related side effects, including severe ones and events forcing treatment stops, rose with the added drugs. The authors support the combination while urging careful monitoring for immune toxicity.
pmc-13559975:
Sarah B Windle and colleagues systematically review quasi-experimental studies on how cannabis policy changes affect substance use. Their 2026 review gathered 176 reports published between 1993 and 2024, most from the United States and most using difference-in-differences designs. Medical and recreational legalization were examined for effects on cannabis itself, plus alcohol, tobacco, and opioids.

Legalization may raise cannabis initiation across age groups, with clearer increases among young adults and adults than among youth. Cannabis-related health care visits rose among adults in the studies reviewed. Alcohol findings split by policy type: use may fall after medical legalization yet rise among young adults after recreational laws. Tobacco use seemed to decline across groups, and opioid outcomes mostly held steady or improved, though mortality evidence was patchier. Decriminalization studies were few. The authors rate the findings as suggestive rather than settled.
pmc-13560275:
Dongmei Zhong and colleagues build and validate a tool for judging how implementable a clinical practice guideline is, meaning how readily its design invites real-world use. Their 2026 study drew its test material from guidelines recorded in the STAR repository during 2022. Sixty seasoned raters scored the guidelines, with the data split between exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses.

Sixteen items survived, grouped into four parts: sound methods, clear advice, fit to practice, and ease of acting on it. The confirmatory analysis supported that structure in the held-back half. Internal consistency, split-half, test-retest, and inter-rater reliability all came out strong in the full sample. The authors present the tool for use during guideline writing as well as after release. Their aim is cheaper, broader improvement in how evidence reaches practice.
pmc-13560375:
Jin-Ye Liu and colleagues map the bacteria living on and inside bryophytes, the mosses and their kin, in two subtropical Chinese nature reserves. Their 2026 study reads bacteria from ten bryophyte species across three zones: the soil around them, the leaf surface, and the plant's insides. Host kind, zone, and sampling site were tested as shaping forces.

Richness, structure, and likely roles shifted with all three forces at once. Raw makeup and assembly, though, were ruled mainly by zone. Surface and inner groups leaned more on chance than soil groups and formed tighter, shorter-pathed networks. Inner bacteria varied in makeup between sites yet matched in function, favoring chemical pathways for terpenoids and foreign-compound breakdown. The authors frame bryophytes as a test of whether rules learned from flowering plants hold for older lineages.
pmc-13563775:
Mingming Dong and two colleagues weigh two hip operations for elderly patients with nerve or muscle disorders who shatter the top of the thigh bone. Such patients dislocate replacement hips at high rates because their muscles cannot guard the joint. One option replaces half the joint the standard way. The other uses total replacement with a constrained liner that mechanically locks the ball in place. The 2026 review covered unstable, multi-fragment fractures treated at one institution between 2011 and 2016.

The locked operation took longer and bled more: about 110 minutes and 276 millilitres against 91 minutes and 205. Its transfusion rate also ran higher. In exchange, dislocation odds fell steeply, to roughly a tenth. The costs were more stray bone growth around the joint and a hint of more loosening. Long-term hip function ended level. The authors judge the overall bargain limited, reserving the lock for those whose dislocation risk dominates.
pmc-13563975:
Minjeong Kim and co-authors study, in a 2026 video review, how eye surgery fellows learn scleral encircling, an operation that places a band around the eye to support a detached retina. Videos of fifty-five operations by six fellows at one academic center from 2018 to 2024 were timed step by step across a two-year training span.

Total operating time averaged about 132 minutes and fell for five of six fellows, mostly within their first five cases. One step, examining the eye with an indirect viewing tool, varied most between fellows and never sped up for anyone. Trainers learn which step needs targeted teaching rather than simple repetition.
pmc-13564075:
Madhavi Annamanedi, Jessica M. Povroznik, Samantha Arevalo-Marcano, and Cory M. Robinson test, in a 2026 mouse study, blocking an immune signal called IL-27 as a way to prevent or treat sepsis in newborns. Newborn pups were infected with a coated strain of E. coli, a model of the blood infection that kills many fragile infants.

Antibody given before infection improved bacterial clearance and weight gain. Given two hours after infection together with a low dose of the antibiotic gentamicin, it cleared bacteria better than the antibiotic alone, steadied blood sugar, lowered harmful inflammation, and improved survival. The pairing could matter where antibiotic resistance limits standard care for newborn sepsis.
pmc-13564475:
Gu Yu studies medical students' willingness to join in academic assessment in a paper from two thousand twenty-six, written alone. The work sits under a national push to reform medical education in China. Current systems lean hard on measurable scores and may miss learning processes and creative skills.

Yu surveyed two hundred forty-eight students in their second to fourth years at one medical college. Two theories guided the study, one on planned behavior and one on self-belief. Social norms, confidence, and assessment literacy all raised willingness to take part. Literacy also carried part of the effect of the other two factors. Yu offers steps to build student skill and give students more chances to join assessment.
pmc-13565875:
Wang, Shao, Xu, and Wang report repair of a single atrium in a postpartum woman. Single atrium is a rare heart defect fixed in infancy. The patient was 33 and came in at 30 weeks pregnant. Breathlessness grew worse as pregnancy advanced. Scans showed one shared atrium with a common valve.

A cesarean was done days later on team advice. Symptoms stayed, so heart surgery followed six months after. The chest was left open due to swelling and instability. It closed on day four, and she left on day 27. At six months she had top-grade heart function.
pmc-13566475:
Monika Klírová and co-authors review, in a 2026 article, repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation for obsessive-compulsive disorder, in which magnetic pulses through the skull nudge brain circuits tied to obsessions and compulsions. Studies vary widely in target and protocol, which has blocked uniform guidelines.

Smaller trials and pooled analyses suggest moderate benefit for several targets, and faster schedules may shorten time to response. Combining stimulation with therapy or medication also looks promising, though large definitive trials are still missing. Clinicians get a clear summary of a useful add-on treatment and the personalization research now trying to predict who will respond.
pmc-13566675:
Tatjana Ábel and Éva Csobod Csajbókné present a review from twenty twenty-six on fatty liver disease tied to metabolic flaws. The old view blamed plain fat storage in the liver. The new view casts the disease as a rewiring of how the liver handles fats. Too much food, insulin resistance, and sick fat tissue tip the scales of fat in, fat made, fat burnt, and fat shipped out.

The fats that pile up are not inert. Some act as stress signals that wreck insulin paths, strain the cell's power and fold shops, and spark cell death and scar growth. Maps of fat kinds may sort patients more well than total fat. The review weighs drugs aimed at these paths and their caps.
pmc-13568575:
Alja Zottel and co-authors wrote a study from 2026 on small RNA molecules that may tune an immune brake shared by two hard cancers. Drugs that release this brake, the PD-1 and PD-L1 pair, changed cancer care, yet they help few brain tumor patients and only some bowel cancer patients. Tiny RNAs that dial genes down after they are read could explain part of that uneven response. The team hunted for ones that act the same in both cancers.

Five tiny RNAs passed their tests, all shifted the same way in both tumors. Two were raised in both and tracked with better survival. Two others tracked with better outcomes as well. The fifth fell in both yet tracked with worse survival. Several moved opposite to the brake genes, as a dial should.
pmc-13570575:
Dongyang Sun, Mengyi Yang, Jiangyun Zhu, Changyang Zhong, Xiaoyu Yin, Jianghao Zhou, and Cong Wu measure bone thinning in older adults in eastern China in work dated two thousand twenty-six. Osteoporosis grows as China's population ages, yet fresh community data were scarce. The study enrolled more than two thousand five hundred adults aged sixty-five and up in Hangzhou.

Bone density was read at the spine, hip neck, and full hip with a dual-energy X-ray scan. About a third of the group met the bar for osteoporosis. Rates in women ran near half, far above men's, and rates climbed with age from the sixties into the eighties. Surveys on habits and health fed a model of lone risk factors.
pmc-13570675:
Ekta Rani, Saloni Saloni, and Sonam Juneja present seven cases of a rare inflammatory disease of the fallopian tube and ovary that mimics cancer. Their case series appeared in 2026. The condition destroys tissue slowly and is not itself a tumor. Its scans and symptoms often look like advanced ovarian cancer or stubborn pelvic infection. Only tissue examination settles the question. The patients, aged 24 to 68, came to a rural tertiary center.

Most had belly pain, fever, a felt mass, or odd bleeding. Scans mostly showed complex masses that suggested malignancy. Surgery ranged from removing a cyst to removing the womb and both ovaries. Under the microscope, the tissue was replaced by fat-laden scavenger cells mixed with other immune cells. The authors urge doctors to keep this mimic in mind before radical surgery.
pmc-13570875:
Yuyin Zhou and colleagues run, in a 2026 multicentre non-randomized trial across six designated hospitals in Zhejiang Province, China, an early-warning program for heart disease risk in people living with HIV. Participants told their personal five- and ten-year risk received a short, tailored behavior session in person or online, while controls got routine education only, with checks at three and six months.

As HIV becomes a manageable chronic condition, traditional risks such as smoking, inactivity, and diet drive most heart risk, outweighing virus-related factors. The design tests whether simply knowing a personal risk number, backed by brief coaching, changes behavior and measured risk. Results would guide clinics caring for an aging HIV population.
pmc-13570975:
Federico Miozzo reviews, in a 2026 article, a family of cell adhesion molecules called nonclustered protocadherins as strong genetic candidates in autism. These molecules sit on neuron surfaces and help cells recognize each other. They guide how circuits wire up during growth, while also carrying signals triggered by neural activity.

Evidence from human genetics and rodent models ties them to neuron production, migration, and synapse maturation. Activity-driven signaling acts as the hub that refines connections and balances excitation against inhibition. Autism affects nearly two percent of people worldwide and is strongly heritable. Learning how these surface codes work could clarify how diverse gene changes converge on one condition and where treatments might intervene.
pmc-13572475:
Lei Sun, with three colleagues, reports a 2026 study of fill walls that hold up a coal mine entry as the seam beside it is dug out. In thick seams under hard roofs, these walls can tilt or fail when pressure sheds unevenly. The team built a new test rig that presses and shears samples at once, with fast strength build-up and varied tilt angles.

Peak strength fell as the shear share rose, and failure shifted from crushing toward sliding. A formula linked wall width to roof sag. The high-strength fill then went into a real mine face, with a design to stop tilting. Measured roof sag came in 59.4 percent below the forecast value, and the wall showed no clear damage. The results give design data for mines in like conditions.
pmc-13572875:
Jordan Karubian and colleagues argue that field stations in the tropics, not just pledges, will decide whether 2030 climate and nature targets are met. With deadlines for the Paris Agreement and global goals only years away, pledges still outrun progress. This 2026 essay looks at field stations as the places where global plans meet local ground, above all in the tropics, where wildlife and carbon stakes run highest.

Strong stations work with local people, support jobs at the edge of wild areas, and weave Indigenous and old knowledge into science. The authors sum up those gains and urge funding to expand stations' power for fair, fact-based conservation. Their message is blunt: fund the links now, or watch another round of targets slip.
pmc-13573375:
Ebru Temizsoy, with four colleagues, reports a 2026 trial of a gentler airway suction method for preterm babies on breathing support. Babies born early often need non-invasive ventilation, which spares the lungs a tube. Clearing the nose and throat by suction, though, can cause pain, stress, and dips in heart rate and oxygen.

The randomised trial compares a less invasive suction protocol with the standard deep method in preterm infants on that support. Pain scores and body stability signs, such as heart rate and oxygen levels, form the core outcomes. The gentler protocol trims how deep and how long the suction tube goes. If it proves kinder at no cost to airway clearing, neonatal units could adopt it as routine. The design speaks to a daily tension in intensive care: keeping airways open without hurting fragile patients.
pmc-13573475:
Mohammed Sadeq AlKhalaf, with two colleagues, reports a 2026 case of sudden kidney injury after chemical hair straightening. Such products often hold formaldehyde kin, chemicals that can enter through the scalp or shift under heat. The injury they cause is little known outside kidney circles, so a clear case carries weight.

The patient was a healthy 39-year-old woman who fell ill with vomiting, diarrhoea, and back pain after a straightening session. Her creatinine, a kidney marker, stood far above normal, and urine showed white cells. A biopsy found allergic-type swelling in the kidney tissue, tubule injury, and oxalate crystals, the breakdown path of formaldehyde. Steroid treatment brought a slow, full recovery with no dialysis needed. The authors urge tighter product checks before market entry.
pmc-13573575:
Gerard de Vries and nine co-authors weighed the national migrant tuberculosis screening in the Netherlands from twenty nineteen to twenty twenty-three, in twenty twenty-six. Migrants from high-burden lands face raised risk, so screening covers active disease and silent infection. Records for one hundred forty-nine thousand two hundred fourteen migrants were linked across national systems.

Active disease was found in sixty-nine immigrants and one hundred seventy asylum seekers. Rates were seventy-nine and two hundred seventy-six per hundred thousand screened. Most lung cases had no cough. Treatment completion ran high in both groups. Silent infection rose with age, from under one percent in children to near thirteen percent in adults. Most who started preventive treatment finished it. The authors say it finds disease early and backs targeted screening.
pmc-13574775:
Caixia Lan, with four colleagues, reports a 2026 study of mineral growth inside lab-made protein fibres for bone and tooth repair. Bone scaffolds work best when they copy the mineral-rich mesh of real tissue. The team spun elastin-like protein into nanofibres, then bathed them so bone mineral could grow the way nature lays it down.

Two protein versions were spun, one carrying a saliva-protein snippet known to draw mineral, one without. A liquid-precursor bath seeded calcium phosphate that later hardened inside the fibres. X-ray and microscope checks confirmed the mineral was hydroxyapatite, the same crystal as in bone, packed within the fibres. Mineral made the fibres stiffer and harder. Bone-forming starter cells grew well on them and matured toward bone. The authors pitch the mats for jaw, gum, and dentin repair.
pmc-13574875:
Julia Camps-Herrero, with thirteen colleagues, presents a 2026 European consensus on scans before breast cancer surgery. Practice swings widely across Europe, from plain mammograms to full MRI for nearly all. Four European societies in breast care joined to set one shared path.

A panel of thirteen experts voted on statements covering every staging method, from standard mammography and ultrasound to contrast mammography and MRI. Full agreement landed on about two thirds of items, a majority on most of the rest, with a small share left open. MRI reads tumour extent best, yet access and habit vary by country and hospital. From the votes the panel built a hands-on toolbox for picking the right scans per case. The aim is even, well-grounded staging for every patient, wherever she is treated.
pmc-13575175:
Louis-Maël Guéguen leads a 2026 paper introducing META-DIFF, a tool that finds DNA fragments differing between groups in metagenomic samples. Standard studies label microbes or genes first, which limits them to known entries and splits type from function. Assembly-based fixes still leave much data unused.

META-DIFF works from short DNA snippets called k-mers, needing no prior labels. It rebuilds longer sequences from the snippets that differ and picks the set that best separates the groups. Benchmark tests showed steady, careful performance, favouring precision over recall when changes were small or data thin. Applied to a colorectal cancer dataset, it reproduced known findings and added new ones. The authors present it as a way to use every read, including unknown DNA.
pmc-13575275:
Yeonsoon Jung and three colleagues report a 2026 case where a kidney that had silently stopped working was hidden inside a polycystic kidney diagnosis. A woman aged 55 who had autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease came to discuss tolvaptan, a drug that slows cyst growth. Scans showed large cystic kidneys, and her kidney function was lower than expected for her age.

She started the drug, yet a follow-up MRI a year later told a different story. The left kidney was swollen with trapped urine from a blocked junction, a problem the earlier CT scan had missed among the cysts. A tracer scan showed that kidney had no remaining function. With no guidance for using the drug in people with one working kidney, treatment stopped. Her function then fell steadily over three years.
pmc-13575775:
A team of clinicians tracks seizure drug use in pregnancy at an Irish hospital in a paper from 2026. Women with epilepsy often need these drugs, but some carry risks for the baby. The team used health records from a large Dublin maternity hospital. They covered pregnancies from 2018 to 2023, a span with more than nine thousand births each year.

Nearly all women with epilepsy in the sample used a seizure drug in pregnancy. Two drugs with safer profiles made up most of the use. A quarter of pregnancies involved more than one such drug. Use patterns were mostly stable over time. The authors call for more data on newer drugs and birth outcomes.
pmc-13576175:
William D Duncan, Christopher J Mungall, and Robert P Guralnick present a practical bridge between data tables and formal ontologies in a 2026 paper. Most life science data live in flat tables, while ontologies, the shared vocabularies that let computers reason, are layered. Turning tables into rich semantic data is usually laborious.

Their recipe pairs LinkML, a language for defining and checking table schemas, with a trick called punning that lets one term serve as both class and property. A mammal trait dataset from a ranges digitisation project shows the method at work. Gains include keeping schema, ontology, and documentation in step and lowering modelling effort, while staying friendly to normal database work. Full logical reasoning is weaker than with heavyweight translations, a trade-off the authors accept for discovery-focused uses.
pmc-13576775:
Stefanie Föller, Attila Teleki, and Ralf Takors test whether blue light can raise antibody output from factory cell cultures, in a 2026 bioprocess study. The cells are CHO cells, the hamster-derived workhorse of drug manufacturing, engineered to make an IgG1 antibody. The team ran batch, fed-batch, and continuous perfusion cultures in controlled 3 litre reactors.

Blue light raised output per cell by about 30 to 37 percent in batch and fed-batch runs. In perfusion it added up to 13 percent overall, with far larger gains in some phases. Lactate output rose while glucose use barely changed. Amino acid pools inside cells shrank, hinting at faster protein building. Energy charge dipped slightly yet stayed in a healthy range. Cell redox state grew more reduced, against the team's stress hypothesis. The authors pitch tuned light as a gentle process booster.
pmc-13577175:
Seven doctors report on a three-part treatment for advanced liver cancer in a paper from 2026. Some patients also have an abnormal link between an artery and a vein inside the liver. That link makes the usual vessel-blocking treatment fail, and outlook is poor. The team tried chemo pumped into the liver artery, plus two drugs given to the whole body.

They reviewed fifty-one patients treated at one hospital as a first therapy. Half the group lived about fifteen months, and most tumors shrank. The abnormal link closed in most patients, and closure linked to longer life. Side effects were manageable, with no deaths from treatment. The authors see the mix as a workable option.
pmc-13578275:
Juan J Novoa and a large team of co-authors describe a 2026 gene edit meant to make lab grown human stem cells safer to transplant. Cells from a donor carry ID tags called HLA that can trigger rejection. The usual fix deletes a gene and strips all tags away, yet that total loss can draw attack from a second immune cell type.

The team instead slipped in a virus gene, US2, at a safe spot in the cell DNA. The gene removed one tag type from the cell surface while leaving a low level of the rest. In dish tests, T cells no longer fired against the edited cells, and the second cell type stayed calm. One precise edit may thus beat a blunt deletion.
pmc-13579175:
Bradley Diggines and colleagues build a robot run microfluidic line that brews and screens lipid nanoparticles at high speed, in a 2026 study. Fat based particles carry drugs and gene cargo, yet their recipe space is huge: fat choice, ratios, size, and shape all interact. Hand brewing explores that space far too slowly, so the team put mixing on a chip with precise fluid metering.

Particles form in a steady flow and a robot collects them into standard lab plates. The line turns out more than two hundred distinct recipes an hour, orders of magnitude faster than bench work. Runs mapped how composition shapes particle traits, checked known trends in gene delivery, and found odd shaped recipes with top performance. The authors see the platform feeding data driven and AI guided searches.
pmc-13580075:
CongBing Yan and co-authors review qualitative studies on what helps or hinders clinical nurses in building innovation and research skills. Such capacity drives better patient outcomes and stronger health systems, yet the evidence sits scattered across cultures and settings. The review follows a standard institute method for synthesizing qualitative work. The team searches ten databases from their start through mid-2026 and screens reference lists as well.

Twenty-eight studies qualify, with samples from 6 to 120 nurses. Quality is rated with a standard checklist, and findings are merged by meta-aggregation. The synthesis yields four grouped findings, the first covering how nurses navigate organizational culture and structural support, and another covering the dual nature of professional knowledge. The authors turn the results into suggestions for nursing practice, education, and health policy.
pmc-13580275:
Kaidan Yang and colleagues hand energy from a light catcher to plant based starter molecules to cure resins with visible light, in a 2026 study. Starters that wake only under ultraviolet light miss the safer, deeper reach of LEDs and sunlight. Their starters were built from plant sourced aldehydes, and a high energy catcher dye was paired with them.

Laser and spin probes showed the catcher passes its energy package directly to the starter, a contact handoff that skips the electron route. The woken starter snaps a nitrogen oxygen bond and sheds carbon dioxide, freeing radicals that start curing. The pair cured faster, deeper, and more fully than either part alone, matched industry benchmarks, stayed stable in storage, and proved gentle to cells.
pmc-13580875:
Ceshae Harding and colleagues check how often new mothers see a primary care doctor after a complicated pregnancy. Their 2026 study uses a national survey. The pregnancies involved high blood pressure or diabetes, which raise lifelong heart risk. The year after birth is prime time to tame that risk. Records came from a federal spending survey spanning 2016 to 2022. It covered 696 postpartum people across public and private coverage.

Only about a third had any primary care visit in that year. Well over half saw a pregnancy specialist instead. Mothers with complicated pregnancies matched the rest on primary care, a flat result the authors call a missed chance. Their one clear gap ran the wrong way: slightly more emergency room visits. The team urges better hand offs into ongoing primary care.
pmc-13581875:
Jinping Wan and co-authors describe patients whose nerve disease and kidney disease share an antibody. Autoimmune nodopathies attack the nodes of nerve fibers; in some patients the same antibody, anti-CNTN1, appears alongside kidney damage. From sixty-nine nodopathy patients, eleven carried this antibody. Compared with the rest, they had more hypertension, more protein in the urine, and far more kidney disease. Women in this group were especially prone to the kidney pairing.

Kidney biopsies in four patients showed mostly membranous nephropathy, a filter disease, plus one case of lupus nephritis. The protein stained positive in kidney tissue only in the antibody patients with the filter disease. Onset ages ranged widely and the course was chronic. The authors see an immune link between the nerve and kidney conditions. Finding the antibody should prompt kidney checks, and they call for work on the shared mechanism.
pmc-13581975:
Yixin Zhu, Barry Bradford, and Neil Mabbott review, in a 2026 paper, the search for treatments for prion diseases, a family of rare, always fatal brain disorders. The diseases spread when a normal brain protein folds into a harmful shape that copies itself. No approved drug yet slows them, thanks to fast course, late diagnosis, and the odd target.

Older work leaned on repurposed small drugs with weak logic. Newer work aims at the root: cutting the normal protein's output with gene-silencing tools, or blocking it with immune therapies. Brain immune cell damage is another rising target. Human trial proof is still thin or absent, the authors stress, so claims should stay modest.
pmc-13582275:
Eloise Pedersen and Craig B Stanford ask whom chimpanzees copy when rank and reward point in opposite directions, in a 2026 study at a Ugandan sanctuary. Thirty five chimps watched two female demonstrators trade tokens for food. One setup paired a low ranking model with the prized pineapple and a high ranking model with plain carrot. The second setup swapped the pairings.

In the first setup the chimps split their copying evenly, pulled both ways. In the second, where rank and prize aligned, the high payoff act spread more. Rank alone thus did not rule; a prized act traveled best from a high ranking model, and a low payoff act from a liked model could hold it back. The authors suggest such tangles help explain why chimp culture stays simpler than human culture.
pmc-13584375:
Gaole Song and colleagues run a pilot survey on double stigma in Trinidad and Tobago for this 2026 report. Their group was cancer survivors who also live with HIV, two illnesses that both draw harsh judgment in the Caribbean. Surveys were handed out in person and scored with standard scales for HIV stigma and cancer stigma, so the two could be compared item by item.

HIV stigma came out higher on most counts. Nearly all who answered said telling someone about their HIV felt risky, while only a small share felt the same about cancer. Most also believed the public looks down on HIV far more than on cancer. Cancer, though, drew the darker beliefs about health outcomes, with over half saying a person with cancer can never be normal again. The authors call for stigma work that treats both illnesses together.
pmc-13585475:
Sankarshan Chaudhuri, Supratim Dutta, and Ramesh Krishnamurthy wrote a study from 2026 on how sloth bears in central India keep breeding and non-breeding animals apart. A population's future rests on breeding, yet the habits of this shy, solitary carnivore are poorly known. Keeping cubs away from lone adults can cut the risk of cub killing and ease competition for food. The team tested for such separation with camera traps in a tiger reserve.

Surveys over four years fed models of where each group spends time and when it moves. Mothers with cubs favored hotter, rugged ground. Lone adults preferred mixed forest and cooler spots. In summer, richer forage softened the split but did not erase it. The two groups also split their hours, active at different times in every season. The authors read the pattern as cub protection, bought at a real energy cost to mothers.
pmc-13585975:
Kent Lloyd describes a new testing center at UC Davis in this 2026 paper. Biomedical research is shifting toward human-based test systems that can replace animal work. The hard question is no longer just how to build such models. It is how to tell when a model is valid and predictable for a given use.

The NAMs Testing Center answers that need with independent evaluation. It joins comparative biology, engineering, clinical insight, and computing in one team. Candidate methods are tested against defined research purposes rather than praised in general. Lloyd presents the center as one working model of the testing infrastructure the field now needs. The goal is trustworthy evidence for when new approach methods can stand in for older ones.
pmc-13586875:
Yuxin Zhao and Haitian Fan review the flu drug baloxavir in a 2026 study of changes that can arise in the virus during treatment. Certain changes in a viral protein, known as PA I38T/M substitutions, may weaken the drug, and the pair set out to measure how often they appear and what they do to recovery.

Pooling five clinical trials, the authors found the changes in about one in ten patients, with the highest rates in children. Recovery took longer when the changes appeared, and the gap was far larger in children, who also shed live virus for much longer. The review calls for age-based checks for drug resistance and study of combined drug plans.
pmc-13587075:
Atale and co-authors map how a statin reshapes breast cancer spread in mouse liver. Spread breast cancer still lacks a cure. Prior hints said statins may slow spread growth. The team used spatial gene mapping on liver deposits. Tissue came from control mice and atorvastatin-treated mice.

Eight cell clusters sat in the tumor-adjacent fields they sampled. The drug thinned two fibroblast groups that aid tumor spread. It also cut a macrophage group tied to spread. Gene shifts matched a less friendly soil for tumor growth. Stains confirmed the cell type calls in both mouse groups.
pmc-13587275:
Meilin Ye, Zengzhen Lin, Yanling Yi, and Lei Jia test how self-esteem shapes what people remember of social feedback. People constantly receive praise and put-downs, and can be told to forget some of it, a setup called directed forgetting. Their 2026 study ran two experiments comparing people with high and low self-esteem, using feedback that varied in warmth and strength.

In the first experiment, self-esteem colored which feedback stuck through a self-protective memory filter, yet it did not change directed forgetting. The second added a round where people judged each other, and there self-esteem did steer forgetting, but by the strength of the feedback rather than its warmth. People with high self-esteem forgot neutral and strong feedback of both kinds. Those with low self-esteem showed no clear directed forgetting at all, a gap the authors flag for social support work.
pmc-13587575:
Barbora Procházková and Kateřina Zábrodská present a 2026 interview study on stress among art students in Czech universities. Student mental health is a global worry, and art students may be especially exposed. Thirty students across visual, audiovisual, and performing arts described the pressures of their training. The analysis sorted stressors into three levels: institutional, organizational, and interpersonal.

Institutions demanded total commitment and sold a meritocratic myth of success. Programs imposed crushing time loads, subjective grading, and emotionally brutal final critiques. Between people came blurred teacher boundaries, generational friction, and peer rivalry. Across all three, exhaustion and self-sacrifice were treated as the normal price of becoming an artist, a hidden curriculum of endurance. The authors argue the stress is manufactured by the culture of training itself. Fixes must target that culture, not just counsel the students.
pmc-13588275:
Yu Xin and a large team study kidney injury during sepsis in a 2026 mouse study. Sepsis can damage the kidneys fast and raises death risk in critically ill patients. The team built a detailed atlas of kidney chemistry and proteins over space and time in mice, hunting for treatment targets.

Amino acid handling stood out, though adding one amino acid did not help. An enzyme called ARG2 rose sharply in kidney tubules and immune cells. Blocking the enzyme with a drug, or switching it off in tubules, eased injury and improved kidney function. Lab work in cells and organoids supported the effect, which worked in part by cutting fat buildup in the kidney.
pmc-13589575:
Dayong Shen and nine co-authors test whether blood markers of inflammation and metabolism forecast results after clot-removal treatment for stroke. Their multicenter cohort study was published in twenty twenty-six. Outcomes after the procedure vary widely despite better technique.

Seven hundred and forty patients with large-vessel strokes at three centers were followed. Over half had a poor outcome at ninety days. Marker levels on admission were tied to outcome types separately: poor function, early decline, and bleeding in the brain. Models adjusted for known clinical and scan factors and were checked internally. Marker profiles added signal beyond the usual predictors, and different markers mapped to different harms.
pmc-13589675:
Ellen McCreedy leads a 2026 pilot study from Bluestone, a group that serves people living in assisted living homes. When one of those clients arrived at an emergency room, an electronic alert told the care team at once. A case manager then phoned the emergency staff with fresh facts about the client and faxed a short form. The aim was to help staff decide who truly needed a hospital stay.

Over eight months the team logged 1,989 emergency visits by 1,376 clients, most of them older women. Staff reached a provider by phone in 43 percent of visits. Case managers said their calls likely kept 94 people out of hospital. The authors note that this gain rests on self reports, so a formal trial is still needed.
pmc-13590075:
Zha and co-authors build a label-free microscope that reads the wrinkled structure of gut tissue grown from organoids. Wrinkles in epithelial sheets encode how tissues form and sense force. Standard study needs dyes and slicing, which distort the picture. Their ultraviolet photoacoustic scope uses the natural absorption of DNA at 266 nm. Nuclei and wrinkle shapes appear with no labels at all. Measures include wrinkle spacing, a wrinkle index, and nucleus stretching under strain.

Chemical stress tests showed the scope catching damage patterns too. The tissue came from human intestinal organoids grown into sheets. Multi-scale readouts link shape to mechanics in one pass. The tool suits drug screens on living tissue models.
pmc-13591175:
Paul Winston reports, in 2026, a single case that tests a listed ban on a cold based nerve treatment. Cryoneurolysis freezes a nerve to ease stiff, tight muscles, and it can free movement for months. Cold urticaria, a hive reaction to cold that can turn severe, normally rules the treatment out. His patient was a 10 year old girl with cerebral palsy whose toe walking had returned after surgery.

Winston used careful skin warming to keep her skin above the point that triggers hives, while guiding the cold probe to nerve branches. She carried an epinephrine pen as a backup, yet no reaction occurred. Her muscle tone and walking improved clearly. The case suggests the ban may bend when heat guard steps are planned with care.
pmc-13591275:
Zhenyi Luo, Aleta Sprague, Michael McCormack, and Jody Heymann offer a two thousand twenty-six study of how state paid sick leave laws reach immigrant workers. Noncitizens cluster in public-facing jobs yet often lack employer sick pay. State laws expanded fast, with eligibility rules varying quietly.

Eligibility rules from fifteen states and the capital district were linked to national labour data. Coverage ran lower for noncitizens than citizens overall. Gaps were significant in six jurisdictions and widest in Connecticut. Simulations fingered exclusions for independent contractors and small-firm staff as the main drivers of inequality.
pmc-13591675:
Klaus Christian Haggenmüller leads a team following student health across the undergraduate years at a Munich technical university. Their group held 128 sport and health science students, mostly women, tested about two and a half years apart. Checks covered peak oxygen use on a treadmill test, body makeup, blood pressure, and heart rate. Students also reported training hours, smoking, drinking, and diet style.

Peak oxygen use rose and resting heart rate fell in simple paired checks. Once sex, age, program, and training hours were factored in, though, time alone no longer explained the fitness gain. Weekly training volume stood out as the steady link to higher fitness. Weight and body fat stayed much the same, while muscle mass edged up.
pmc-13591875:
Andrew Papworth and Guerry Windell explore, in 2026, health care access for the Rama people, an Indigenous group of about 2,000 on Nicaragua's Caribbean coast. Most work on cultural safety in care comes from rich nations, so this study shifts the lens. Interviews with 49 Rama and non Rama participants ran in two rounds, in 2016 and again in 2024.

Care was free on paper, yet shortages of supplies and staff pushed many Rama families toward costly private care. Distant hospitals, language gaps, and felt bias further discouraged visits. Use of traditional medicine fell across the study years. Papworth and Windell suggest training more Rama health workers and posting outside staff for longer stays.
pmc-13592575:
Guillaume P Fernandez and three colleagues test whether a speaker's wider social circle shapes how much they echo a conversation partner's word choices. Accommodation theory says speakers align their language to signal closeness, yet most studies stop at the pair. Their group held 21 young adults who recorded about three talks each, giving 71 discussions, alongside maps of each speaker's personal network. Intensifier use measured the echo.

Speakers echoed partners more when the partner sat at the center of a tight, uniform cluster inside the speaker's network, the models show. A partner on the fringe drew less alignment. Fernandez and the team argue that dyads are embedded: network position quietly steers how language bends between two people.
pmc-13593475:
Min Li and co-authors described a new wound spray in a 2026 study on burns in people with diabetes. Such burns heal slowly because of stress inside cell power parts, long swelling, germs, and weak regrowth of skin. The spray holds honokiol, a plant compound that fights cell stress and swelling but does not stay on a wound for long.

The team built a gel from a changed sea-based sugar that sticks to skin and lets the drug out slowly. They made two gels with distinct firmness and tested their traits, drug release, germ killing, and safety with cells. The work also probes a cell protein whose loss may slow repair, and it aims to restore that signal.
pmc-13594175:
Romy Vos and co-authors built a knowledge graph, a structured network of facts a computer can reason over, devoted to kidney injury caused by medicines. Their 2026 project gathered what is known about drugs that harm the kidneys from several trusted sources and rewrote it in standard international vocabularies so systems can share it.

The team tested the graph with expert questions drawn from realistic tasks. Two uses stand out. The graph can feed decision support tools that warn about kidney side effects and harmful drug combinations, especially for people with chronic kidney disease. It can also help researchers pick the right variables and confounders for machine learning studies. Reviewers found the graph genuinely applicable, though not yet ready for the clinic. The authors expect it to support question-answering systems and cleaner causal analyses of drug-related kidney harm.
pmc-13594375:
Yuhong Tang, Dezhao Liu, Beibei Luo, and Feng Huang review the contact zones between two cell compartments in heart disease, in a 2026 paper. These zones link the endoplasmic reticulum with mitochondria. They manage calcium flow, fat handling, and stress signals. They also steer cell survival and death. When the coupling goes wrong, heart and vessel disease follows. Too much or too little contact can both cause harm.

The review maps the main protein bridges at these zones. It then walks through disease settings one by one. Clogged arteries, lung pressure disease, and heart attack injury all appear. Diabetes-linked and enlarged heart failure forms are covered too. Preserved contact supports energy supply and stress coping. Broken contact drives calcium overload, toxic byproducts, and cell death. The authors weigh drugs that might restore the balance. They stress that context decides whether a fix helps or hurts.
pmc-13595575:
Wani, Yoon, and Kim warn that thymus free mice can underrate chemo drugs that work through the immune system in twenty twenty-six. These mice lack mature T cells, the adaptive arm of immunity. Many modern chemo drugs kill partly by waking T cells to attack the tumor. In mice without them, that boost goes unseen.

Suppressor cells then run unchecked, which further dulls measured effects. The authors still value the mice for direct tumor response and first graft tests. They urge pairing them with immune intact or humanized mice. That pairing would capture the full benefit of host dependent drugs, they argue.
pmc-13597475:
Arian Taheri Amin and co-authors pooled forty-five studies of genicular artery embolization, a catheter procedure that blocks the small knee arteries feeding inflamed joint lining, as a pain treatment for knee osteoarthritis. Their 2026 meta-analysis covered 2,205 patients, most from studies without control groups, and graded the certainty behind each result.

Pain scores dropped by roughly thirty-seven points on a hundred-point scale within a month. They held that gain at a year. Standard function and pain indices also improved beyond the thresholds patients can feel. Whether the blocking particles dissolved or stayed permanent made no clear difference. Side effects were mostly minor and passing, led by temporary skin discoloration in about one in nine patients and bruising in a few percent. The authors are candid that certainty rates only very low to low, so controlled trials remain essential.
pmc-13597975:
Lucca D'Arco Correa and colleagues read all past work on egg-sac fluid chemistry in varied female fertility ills for IVF care. Egg-sac fluid feeds and talks to the egg, so its small-molecule mix may flag egg worth and birth odds. The team used strict review rules, combed Embase, MEDLINE, and Cochrane, and kept works by set rules.

Sugar, lactate, fats such as diacylglycerols, triacylglycerols, fatty acids, sphingomyelins, and oleic acid, plus amino acids such as lysine, valine, glutamate, histidine, and glutamine, kept showing up changed. Fluid chemistry could thus hone IVF lab work, aid egg choice, and lift birth odds, though no one marker earns a lone vote yet.
pmc-13598375:
Emad Dawoud leads a thirteen-author retrospective study of how the targeted drug palbociclib is actually used for advanced hormone-sensitive breast cancer across the Arabian Gulf, where real-world data were scarce. Records from seven sites covered 258 patients who began the drug with hormone therapy between 2015 and 2019.

Most patients started at the full dose, split between first-line use and later lines, paired either with aromatase inhibitors or with fulvestrant. Median time before the disease progressed reached about twenty-six and a half months overall. It reached forty months when the drug was used first. The authors note these figures align with trial results and real-world reports elsewhere. Later-line use still bought meaningful control. The authors present TREASURE as the region's baseline picture of this treatment class in routine practice.
pmc-13599775:
Beller and colleagues chart in 2026 how depressive symptoms have changed across Europe since 2006, and for whom. Depression is a central public mental health concern, and averages can hide diverging fortunes between social groups.

Using four waves of the European Social Survey covering fifteen countries and 106,814 people, the team scored symptoms on an eight-item depression scale. They modeled trends by age, gender, education, income, occupation, health limitation, and region. Symptoms fell substantially among older adults and slightly among the middle-aged, with the strongest gains in Eastern Europe. Among younger adults the trend was flat overall and rising in Northern Europe, including among the better educated and better paid. People living with health limitations kept an extremely high symptom level throughout, especially the young, which leads the authors to urge targeted interventions.
pmc-13602375:
Lara Feulner and ten co-authors present a 2026 study charting gene activity in the mouse heart around birth, cell by cell. The heart remodels fast in the days before and after birth, and this change is vital for survival. The gene programs behind it, for many cell types, were still missing.

The team read the full gene output of nearly fifty thousand single cells from fetal and newborn mouse hearts. Tracking tools ordered the cells along a time path. One long non coding gene faded over time in most cell types but held steady in the lining of the heart's inner wall and valves. The team then built a human stem cell model to chase that lead.
pmc-13602475:
Eric Nyarko and colleagues model HIV treatment adherence at Pantang Hospital in Accra, Ghana, in a 2026 study. Antiretroviral therapy only works when people take it steadily, and missed doses remain a major barrier in sub-Saharan Africa. Between July and October 2025, the team surveyed 151 randomly sampled patients receiving HIV care at the hospital, asking about daily habits around their medication. They then trained six machine learning models to rank what predicts poor adherence.

Participants had a median age of 42, and three quarters were women. Slips were common: 66.9 percent forgot doses, 64.2 percent admitted carelessness, and 85.4 percent stopped when they felt worse. An Elastic Net model performed best overall. The strongest warning signs were skipping medication over the past weekend and missing doses six to ten times in the past week. These concrete habits, the authors argue, give clinics practical targets for adherence support, which should also cut community transmission risk.
pmc-13603575:
Toishimanov and a large team study how age and foaling count shape the bodies and milk of Kushum mares in twenty twenty-six. Mare milk is prized for its food value, but data on this local breed were thin. Forty-one healthy mares were grouped by age and by how many foals they had borne. Body and udder measures were taken in June, and milk was drawn five times a day.

Some body and udder traits split clearly by both age and foaling count. Daily milk yield, though, did not split by either factor. Milk makeup did shift: sugar, salts, and acidity traits varied by group. Fat and protein held steady. Small udder groups limit the claims, the authors note.
pmc-13603775:
Bingao Zhang and Shengyong Xu built a computer model that predicts how eye nerve cells respond to ultrasound at different pitches, in this 2026 paper. Retina cells fire more or less depending on the sound frequency used, but no single model had been tested against published results on one shared scale. The authors set out to build and test such a model.

Their model links a stand-in measure of tissue stress to a simulated group of retinal ganglion cells. One shared rule then maps simulated spikes onto the published response scale for three frequencies. Tested by leaving one frequency out at a time, the model matched held-out data well. A high-threshold blocking part improved the fit where strong sound makes responses fall off.
pmc-13604575:
Sebastian Dzierzęcki and colleagues ask whether brain surgery still works after radiation has failed for facial pain. Trigeminal neuralgia brings stabbing facial pain; Gamma Knife radiosurgery controls it in most patients, but pain returns for many. Microvascular decompression, surgery that lifts a blood vessel off the trigeminal nerve, is the fallback. Whether radiation leftovers, thickened membranes, adhesions, and nerve shrinkage, make that surgery riskier or weaker was unresolved.

In a two-center review, 35 patients who had surgery after radiosurgery were compared with 60 who had surgery first. Good long-term pain control came to 88.6 percent in the irradiated group and 91.7 percent in the rest, well within chance. Radiation-related tissue changes appeared in every irradiated patient and made dissection harder, yet complications were no more frequent, and no one died or suffered major neurological harm. The authors conclude prior radiosurgery is no bar to later decompression in well-chosen patients.
pmc-13604675:
Lei Nie, Yingying Liang, Yiran Lin, and Wei Guo build an injectable gel for covering wounds. Their paper, from twenty twenty-six, blends two changed natural polymers. One comes from hyaluronic acid and the other from shell-derived chitosan. Magnesium ions link into the mix and add function. Fast blood clotting and calm tissue stress are the design goals.

The gels set fast under body-like conditions and can be pushed through a needle. They also heal their own cuts and stick to wet tissue. In mice with tail wounds, blood loss fell by about four-fifths. Clotting time dropped to a third. The gel also mopped up harmful oxygen radicals well.
pmc-13608375:
Benali and four co-authors doped a multiferroic material in this study from twenty twenty-six. The base compound, bismuth ferrite, holds both magnetic and electric order. Swapping a fifth of the bismuth for barium was done with a sol-gel recipe. Diffraction showed the crystals took a tetragonal shape.

The swap raised the leftover and saturation magnetization along with the field needed to flip it. The material also kept a high dielectric constant with low energy loss. Those traits suit capacitors and memory devices, the authors argue. The structural distortion from the barium is credited for the gains. The paper links shape change to property change in a candidate device material.
pmc-13609575:
Deniz Baklacı and four co-authors weigh signs that a mouth cancer has spread to neck nodes in secret. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-six. The cancer is squamous cell carcinoma of the mouth. In patients whose neck feels clear, hidden spread still shows in a share of cases after surgery. That risk guides whether the neck is cut at all.

They review past surgical cases and test depth of growth, vessel and nerve invasion, and tumour grade. A depth cut point from their own data sorts risk well. Vessel invasion and grade also track with node spread. But few node cases and the late reach of some signs limit use, so more proof is called for.
pmc-13610375:
Yiming Zhong and co-authors test a cell-born peptide as a shield against liver harm in severe Klebsiella infection, in a study from two thousand twenty-six. Blood levels of the peptide, Humanin, were first compared in twenty patients and twenty healthy peers. Mice then got the peptide for five days before a vein challenge with the germ.

Patient blood held more of the peptide than healthy blood. Treated mice showed less liver harm, lower harm enzymes, and calmer swelling genes. A master swelling path was dialed down in liver and in immune cells. The higher dose worked better and lengthened survival. Targets of the peptide stay unknown, the authors note. Readers get a guarded lead.
pmc-13610575:
Zhihao Lu leads a large team on a gene that controls fruit acid and color. Their study from twenty twenty-six deals with purple wampee fruit. Citric acid and anthocyanins set fruit taste and color.

One wampee type builds both acid and color dyes at once. Tests proved one gene boosts acid build up in fruit. The known color switch gene has lost that power in wampee. A kin gene was found that boosts both traits at once. It was raised in citrus and hushed in wampee to prove this. The gene is strong in fruit pulp most of all.
pmc-13611975:
Faisal Alousi and Abdel Alli wrote this 2026 review on ion channels in SARS-CoV-2 infection. Ion channels are tiny gates that let charged atoms cross cell walls. The review pulls together work on how these gates act in the life of the virus and in the host response. It gives special weight to viral proteins called viroporins.

Viroporins sit in cell membranes and help the virus copy itself, build new copies, and slip past host defenses. The authors trace how these proteins aid viral survival and how they stir the immune response. They also weigh the case for drugs aimed at such channels. Readers get a broad map of one less known side of COVID-19.
pmc-13615075:
Mamoru Hashimoto leads a large team asking in 2026 whether the timing of skin rash during a two-drug treatment for advanced bladder cancer predicts how well patients do. The pairing of enfortumab vedotin with pembrolizumab has improved survival, yet skin trouble is a common side effect. The team split 210 treated patients into three groups: no rash, rash within the first month, and rash at one month or later.
